0.title: The Son of God on the Move: The Gospel According to Mark
0.overview:
The message. Mark tells who Jesus is and what he came to do, and he tells it at a run. His first sentence is the title of the whole book: “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1). Before a parable is told, demons have been cast out, a fever has broken, a leper has been made clean, and four fishermen have left their nets to follow a man they have known for minutes. Again and again the question is asked, “Who then is this?” (4:41), and the answer comes in two halves: he is the Son of God with authority over everything, and he is the Son of Man who “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45). To follow him is to take the same road.

Background: the writer. The Gospel names no author, but the early church agreed that it was written by John Mark. His mother’s house in Jerusalem was a meeting place for the first believers (Acts 12:12). He set out with Paul and Barnabas and turned back (Acts 13:13), and was the cause of their parting (Acts 15:37–39). Yet he was later restored to Paul’s confidence, “he is very useful to me for ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11), and was with Peter in Rome, who calls him “Mark, my son” (1 Peter 5:13). He knew failure and restoration, and his Gospel does not hide the disciples’ failures.

Peter’s witness. Early in the second century Papias, a bishop in Asia Minor, passed on what he had been told: that Mark, Peter’s interpreter, wrote down accurately, though not in strict order, what Peter remembered of the Lord’s words and deeds. Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria say the same, and the book bears it out with the concrete details of someone who was there: the cushion in the stern of the boat (4:38), the “green grass” at the feeding of the five thousand (6:39), the look of anger on Jesus’ face (3:5). Peter is named first and last among the disciples (1:16; 16:7), and his own denial is told without softening (14:66–72).

The first readers. Mark wrote chiefly for Gentile believers, probably in Rome. He explains Jewish customs such as the washings of the Pharisees (7:3–4), translates Aramaic phrases (3:17; 5:41; 7:34; 15:22, 34), and uses Latin words Roman readers knew: legion, denarius, praetorium, and centurion. The church in Rome knew suffering. In AD 64, after the great fire, Nero blamed the Christians and had many of them put to death, and by tradition Peter and Paul died there soon after. To believers who might stand before governors and be betrayed by their own families (13:9–13), Mark showed a Lord who walked that road first and calls his followers to take up their cross (8:34).

When was it written? Most scholars think Mark was the first Gospel, and that Matthew and Luke drew on it; this commentary agrees, though many in the early church put Matthew first. Many date Mark about AD 65–70, around the Jewish war and the fall of Jerusalem; others place it in the late 50s or early 60s, while Peter was still alive. This commentary holds that it was written probably in Rome in the 60s, from Peter’s preaching, and nothing in its reading depends on the exact year. Mark 13 is real prophecy of the temple’s fall whenever it was written down.

Why shorter, and without a birth story? Mark gives mostly what Jesus did rather than long teaching, and about a third of the book to his last week. He begins where the apostles’ preaching began, with John the Baptist (compare Acts 10:37–38), and leaves the birth to Matthew and Luke. Shorter is not lesser: Mark often tells a story in sharper detail than the others.

How the Gospel makes its case. The first half (1:1–8:26) shows Jesus’ authority, mostly in Galilee. He comes announcing, “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel” (1:15). He teaches “as one who had authority, and not as the scribes” (1:22), and shows it over demons, disease, sin (2:10), the Sabbath, the sea and death. Mark’s favourite word, euthys (“immediately”), comes some forty times: when the King arrives, things happen. Yet opposition grows (2:1–3:6), his family think him out of his mind (3:21), and even the disciples do not understand (6:52; 8:17–21). Then comes the hinge at Caesarea Philippi: “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answers, “You are the Christ” (8:29). At once Jesus begins to teach that “the Son of Man must suffer many things” (8:31). Then 8:27–10:52 is the road to Jerusalem, with three predictions of the cross (8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34), three failures of the disciples to grasp it and three lessons in what following means, framed by two healings of blind men (8:22–26; 10:46–52). Chapters 11–16 are the last week: the King enters the city, judges the barren temple and its leaders (chapters 11–12), foretells the temple’s fall and his own return (chapter 13), and goes to his death (chapters 14–15). Jesus kept commanding silence about who he was, because “Christ” could not be understood until the cross showed what it meant. There a Gentile centurion becomes the first human being in the book to call him the Son of God: “Truly this man was the Son of God!” (15:39). The women find the tomb empty and hear, “He has risen; he is not here” (16:6). This commentary holds that 16:9–20 was most likely added early, probably in the second century; whether Mark meant to end at 16:8, with the women silent and afraid, is less certain.

Where it leads: to Christ. Mark tells the story of Jesus’ suffering and death with a long introduction, and the introduction is glorious. Everything before 10:45 shows who he is; everything after shows what his service cost. The Son on whom the Father’s voice rests at the baptism (1:11) and on the mountain (9:7) is the Servant who gives his life as “a ransom for many”, taking up Isaiah 53, and who in the garden accepts the cup of God’s wrath: “not what I will, but what you will” (14:36). His cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (15:34), is the forsakenness of the one who bore sin for others, and when he breathes his last the temple curtain is torn in two (15:38): the way to God is open. At the empty tomb the risen Lord goes ahead of his scattered disciples, Peter included, to Galilee (16:7).

For us. Mark presses on every reader the question Jesus put to his disciples: “But who do you say that I am?” (8:29). He will not let us have a Christ of power without a cross, or a discipleship of comfort: “whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel’s will save it” (8:35). Yet his Gospel is also full of hope for failures. The disciples misunderstand, quarrel and run away, and Peter denies him three times, yet the message from the tomb is “tell his disciples and Peter” (16:7). The Lord who calls us to follow does not abandon those who stumble on the way.

1.title: The Kingdom Breaks In
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. <sup>2</sup>As it is written in Isaiah the prophet, “Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way, <sup>3</sup>the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight”— <sup>4</sup>John appeared, baptizing in the wilderness and proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. <sup>5</sup>And all the country of Judea and all Jerusalem were going out to him and were being baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. <sup>6</sup>Now John was clothed with camel’s hair and wore a leather belt around his waist and ate locusts and wild honey. <sup>7</sup>And he preached, saying, “After me comes he who is mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. <sup>8</sup>I have baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.” <sup>9</sup>In those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. <sup>10</sup>And when he came up out of the water, immediately he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. <sup>11</sup>And a voice came from heaven, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.” <sup>12</sup>The Spirit immediately drove him out into the wilderness. <sup>13</sup>And he was in the wilderness forty days, being tempted by Satan. And he was with the wild animals, and the angels were ministering to him. <sup>14</sup>Now after John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the gospel of God, <sup>15</sup>and saying, “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.” <sup>16</sup>Passing alongside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew the brother of Simon casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. <sup>17</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men.” <sup>18</sup>And immediately they left their nets and followed him. <sup>19</sup>And going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who were in their boat mending the nets. <sup>20</sup>And immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him. <sup>21</sup>And they went into Capernaum, and immediately on the Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching. <sup>22</sup>And they were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes. <sup>23</sup>And immediately there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit. And he cried out, <sup>24</sup>“What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.” <sup>25</sup>But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!” <sup>26</sup>And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him. <sup>27</sup>And they were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves, saying, “What is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.” <sup>28</sup>And at once his fame spread everywhere throughout all the surrounding region of Galilee. <sup>29</sup>And immediately he left the synagogue and entered the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John. <sup>30</sup>Now Simon’s mother-in-law lay ill with a fever, and immediately they told him about her. <sup>31</sup>And he came and took her by the hand and lifted her up, and the fever left her, and she began to serve them. <sup>32</sup>That evening at sundown they brought to him all who were sick or oppressed by demons. <sup>33</sup>And the whole city was gathered together at the door. <sup>34</sup>And he healed many who were sick with various diseases, and cast out many demons. And he would not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him. <sup>35</sup>And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed. <sup>36</sup>And Simon and those who were with him searched for him, <sup>37</sup>and they found him and said to him, “Everyone is looking for you.” <sup>38</sup>And he said to them, “Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out.” <sup>39</sup>And he went throughout all Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and casting out demons. <sup>40</sup>And a leper came to him, imploring him, and kneeling said to him, “If you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>41</sup>Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him and said to him, “I will; be clean.” <sup>42</sup>And immediately the leprosy left him, and he was made clean. <sup>43</sup>And Jesus sternly charged him and sent him away at once, <sup>44</sup>and said to him, “See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>45</sup>But he went out and began to talk freely about it, and to spread the news, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town, but was out in desolate places, and people were coming to him from every quarter.
1.overview:
Where we are. The chapter is Mark’s prologue, which tells the reader who Jesus is (vv. 1–13), and the start of the Galilean ministry, which shows what he does when he arrives (vv. 14–45). Mark is not writing a full biography; he lets the deeds speak.

The message. The God of Israel has come to his people in Jesus, the Messiah and the Son of God, and his kingdom has come with him. He has God’s authority over everything that ruins human life, demons, disease and uncleanness, and he uses it for those who cannot help themselves: he comes near the unclean, touches them, and by the end of the chapter has taken the outcast’s place outside the towns. The only fitting answer is the one he asks for: repent and believe.

Why it was said. Mark’s first readers, Gentile believers probably in Rome, had staked their lives on a crucified Galilean while the empire announced the “good news” of Caesar (see the introduction). They needed to know that Jesus was no novelty but the coming of the God the prophets had promised, who had met the enemy and stood firm before they had to.

How the chapter makes its case. The prophets and John announce the Lord’s arrival (vv. 1–8). At the Jordan the Father names his beloved Son, and at once the Son is tested in the wilderness and stands (vv. 9–13). He proclaims that the time is fulfilled, and his word calls four fishermen from their nets (vv. 14–20). One Sabbath in Capernaum shows the kingdom at work in synagogue, house and crowded doorway (vv. 21–34). Before dawn he prays and leaves the crowd to preach elsewhere (vv. 35–39), and he touches a leper and makes him clean (vv. 40–45). Mark’s word “immediately” drives it all: when the King comes, things happen.

Where it leads. The heavens torn at the baptism point to the curtain torn at his death (15:38), and the Father’s words join the royal Son, the beloved son who is offered and the Servant who suffers. The chapter ends with an exchange: the cleansed leper walks into the towns, and the one who cleansed him must stay outside. It is a first picture of the cross, where the Clean One took the place of the unclean outside the gate.

For us. Mark asks every reader at once who this is, and what we will do with his call. The voice that said “Follow me” has not weakened, and the hand that touched the leper still answers anyone who wonders whether he is wanted: “I will; be clean.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Prologue: The Son Announced, Baptized, and Tested
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before Jesus says a word in public, Mark tells us who he is: the Lord the prophets promised, the Son the Father loves, and the one who has met the enemy and stood firm. Scripture announces the coming of the Lord himself (vv. 1–3), and John, dressed as Elijah, prepares the way and points beyond himself to the stronger one who will baptise with the Spirit (vv. 4–8). At the Jordan the sinless Son stands with sinners, the heavens are torn, the Spirit descends and the Father speaks (vv. 9–11). At once the Spirit drives him into the wilderness, where Satan tests him (vv. 12–13). Mark gives the temptation no dialogue and does not explain the victory: the reader will see its evidence as demons flee before him.
verseByVerse.theology:
At the baptism (vv. 9–11) the Son is baptised, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father speaks: the three persons of the one God revealed together. In the Father’s words the King and the suffering Servant meet in one person (see vv. 10–11).

Why was the sinless Jesus baptised with a baptism of repentance? To stand where sinners stand (see the note on v. 9).
verseByVerse.examples: John wore the dress of Elijah, a visible claim (see vv. 6–8). He preached in the desert, not in Jerusalem, and the city of priests and scribes largely missed the moment. God’s preparing voice does not always come from where we expect it.

verseByVerse.quote: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark’s first sentence names the subject of his whole book: Jesus is the promised Messiah and the Son of God, and the news about him is good news. Everything that follows is the evidence.

Of the gospel. Gospel means good news (euangelion), in the first century not chiefly a religious word. A herald ran back from a won battle with good news of victory, and an inscription from Priene in 9 BC calls the birthday of Caesar Augustus the beginning of the good news for the world. Mark gives Caesar’s word to a crucified Galilean. In Isaiah the good news is that God reigns and comes himself to save his people (Isaiah 40:9; 52:7): the decisive battle has been joined and won, and the one who won it is Jesus of Nazareth. The emperors’ gospels are inscriptions in museums; this King’s good news has outlived every empire that tried to silence it, because it is not the news of a man who seized a throne but of the Son of God who came down from one.

Of Jesus Christ. Jesus means the LORD saves. Christ is the Greek for Messiah, the Anointed One, the King God promised to send: not a surname but a title, and to say it in Rome was to name a king other than Caesar.

The Son of God. The title frames the whole Gospel. It stands here at the start; the Father says it at the baptism (1:11) and on the mountain of transfiguration (9:7); and at the cross, when the body hangs dead and there is nobody left to impress, a Roman centurion says it aloud: “Truly this man was the Son of God!” (15:39). The great question of this Gospel is who Jesus is, and Mark gives the reader the answer in the first sentence. The disciples will take eight chapters to see half of it.

Who was Mark, and can his account be trusted if he was not one of the Twelve? He was very probably John Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10), who left Paul and Barnabas halfway through their first journey (Acts 13:13), so badly that Paul refused to take him again (Acts 15:37–39), and whom Paul later called “very useful to me for ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11). So probably the earliest Gospel was written by a man who had failed and been restored, which is a gospel in itself. His account rests on Peter, an eyewitness from the first day at the lake to the empty tomb (see the introduction), and details like the cushion in the boat and the hired servants are just what Peter’s memory would supply. Vividness alone cannot prove an eyewitness, but it fits what the early church reported.

Uncertain wording. Verse 1 has no verb, and Mark does not say what “the beginning” covers. It may head only the opening section, John’s ministry, where the apostles’ preaching of Jesus began (Acts 10:37). More likely it titles the whole book, as “In the beginning, God created” titles Genesis, announcing something new and as large as creation; then it may also hint that the story of Jesus’ life is only the beginning of the gospel, which runs on through the church to the ends of the earth, and has reached you.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts omit “the Son of God”, including the original hand of the great fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus. Most, including Codex Vaticanus and very early and diverse witnesses and translations, include it. The likeliest explanation is mechanical rather than theological. Ancient copies wrote the sacred names as abbreviations, two letters with a stroke above, and in this phrase four such contractions fall one after another, a row of nearly identical short forms: exactly where a copyist’s eye slips and a phrase drops out. This commentary’s view: probably original; it fits the shape of the whole Gospel. And nothing depends on it. Strike it out and Mark still spends sixteen chapters proving it from every direction. The title does not rest on a disputed line in the first sentence; it rests on the book.
verseByVerse.note: “Gospel” means good news. “Christ” is the Greek form of the Hebrew “Messiah”: the anointed one, the promised king. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit “the Son of God.”

parallels.desc: John’s opening: the Word who was God

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written in Isaiah the prophet, "Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way, the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight"—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark begins with the prophets because the coming of Jesus is God keeping his promise to come himself: a messenger prepares the way, and then the Lord arrives. The messenger is John; the Lord whose way he prepares is Jesus.

As it is written. Mark combines three Old Testament texts: Exodus 23:20, where God sends an angel before Israel on the road; Malachi 3:1, “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me”; and Isaiah 40:3, a voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the LORD. He names Isaiah, the best-known prophet and the source of the main theme, as Jewish writers sometimes did when combining texts.

My messenger. In Malachi, God is speaking about himself: the messenger goes ahead of the LORD, and “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple”. In Mark the words are spoken to Jesus: “before me” has become “your way”. The way of the LORD is the way of Jesus.

The voice. In Isaiah 40 this voice announces comfort to God’s people in exile: their warfare is ended, their iniquity is pardoned, and God himself is coming to lead them home through the desert in a new exodus. Mark begins his Gospel inside that comfort.

Prepare the way. Before a king visited a province, roads were straightened, valleys filled and hills levelled; John prepares hearts by calling them to repent. And “LORD” in Isaiah, in small capitals in your Bible, is the divine name itself. Without argument or apology Mark applies two passages about clearing a road for God to the arrival of a Galilean carpenter: two sentences in, he has identified Jesus with the God of Israel. The God of the burning bush did not send a deputy. He came himself, by the road Isaiah promised, on the feet of a man from Nazareth. So when this man forgives sins and the scribes ask who can forgive sins but God alone (2:7), or stills the sea and the disciples ask who this is (4:41), they are asking the right question, and Mark has already answered it.

In everyday life. A road is prepared by taking out what is in the way: the hill of pride, the hollow of discouragement, the crooked place where you have learned to go round a sin instead of dealing with it. Name one such thing to Christ today. Isaiah’s call came wrapped in comfort, and he does not wait for the road to be perfect before he walks it.

Why does Mark start with old prophecies instead of with Jesus himself? Because the good news is not a new idea that turned up in the first century but the keeping of a promise, and Mark’s Gentile readers needed to know that Jesus was no religious novelty. It also tells you how to read your Old Testament: not as a different religion that the New Testament replaced, but as the road on which the Lord was always coming.

Textual note. Later scribes, puzzled that words partly from Malachi are credited to Isaiah, changed “Isaiah the prophet” to “the prophets” in some manuscripts, and the KJV and NKJV follow them; the earliest manuscripts read “Isaiah”, as most modern Bibles do.
verseByVerse.note: Mark names Isaiah, the better-known prophet, though the first line comes from Malachi.

verseByVerse.quote: John appeared, baptizing in the wilderness and proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. And all the country of Judea and all Jerusalem were going out to him and were being baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John calls the nation out into the wilderness to confess its sins and be washed, making it ready for the forgiveness God was about to bring.

In the wilderness. After a long age in which Israel had felt that prophecy was silent, a prophet, John the Baptist, stands up, and in a chosen place: the wilderness, where Israel was born as a nation and where the prophets said the restoration would begin (Isaiah 40:3; Hosea 2:14). To go out there was to go back to the beginning, past the temple and the whole apparatus of religion in Jerusalem, and start again.

A baptism of repentance. Baptism means washing, immersion. Ritual washing was ordinary in Judaism, but something you did to yourself, repeatedly. Later Jewish sources describe a once-for-all washing for Gentile converts (how early it began is disputed); if John knew it, he was giving the washing meant for outsiders to Abraham’s descendants, telling them their ancestry would not save them. Repentance (metanoia) is a change of mind and heart, turning from sin to God, and the baptism expressed it.

For the forgiveness of sins. John’s baptism pointed to the forgiveness God would give through the one coming after him (v. 8); he told the people to believe in that one, that is, Jesus (Acts 19:4).

Confessing their sins. “All” exaggerates naturally, but the movement was huge. People do not confess their sins in a river because a preacher is eloquent, but because he has said aloud what they already suspected about themselves. They do it at the Jordan, where Israel had crossed into the promised land (Joshua 3), as if Israel had to cross in again. Most were the ordinary population of a religious country, and what John got them to admit was that religion had not dealt with their sin: still one of the hardest admissions a churchgoer makes, and there is no way to the rest of this book that goes round it.

The one who came down into the same river. John could wash bodies and name sins; he could not carry them away. Within a few verses the one who would carry them walks down into the same water (see the note on v. 9). He bears Joshua’s name, the LORD saves, and he goes down into the Jordan ahead of his people to lead them into a rest Joshua never gave (Hebrews 4:8–10).

What it does not mean. Not that water baptism itself forgives sins. Forgiveness comes from God to those who repent and believe; baptism is the outward sign, and no rite takes away sin by itself (Hebrews 10:4).

How is John’s baptism different from Christian baptism, and what does that mean for me? John’s baptism looked forward to a Saviour who had not yet died and risen; Christian baptism looks back to one who has, and is into his name. What carries across is the order: repenting and confessing, then baptism. If you have repented and trusted Christ and have never been baptised as a believer, speak to your church about it. It is the ordinary first step of obedience, not a reward for advanced Christians.

Where Christians differ: who should be baptised? Many faithful brothers and sisters baptise the infants of believers, seeing baptism as the covenant sign for Christian families as circumcision was for Israel’s, and we honour them as fellow servants of the same Christ. This commentary’s view: baptism is for those who personally repent and believe, as the 1689 London Baptist Confession holds, which is the order seen at the Jordan.
verseByVerse.note: The Jordan runs south from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea. John’s baptism was a public washing that marked a turning from sin; confession came with it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now John was clothed with camel's hair and wore a leather belt around his waist and ate locusts and wild honey. And he preached, saying, "After me comes he who is mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. I have baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John comes dressed as Elijah, the promised forerunner, and points away from himself to one far greater, who will do what only God can do: pour out the Holy Spirit.

Camel’s hair. Not simply practical desert clothing. Elijah wore “a garment of hair, with a belt of leather about his waist” (2 Kings 1:8), and Malachi closes by promising that Elijah would come before “the great and awesome day of the LORD” (Malachi 4:5). John is dressed like Elijah, deliberately, in public, and Jesus later confirms it: “Elijah has come” (9:11–13).

Locusts and wild honey. The food of the desert; locusts were clean food under the law (Leviticus 11:22). Not penance, but a life stripped to what God supplies, outside the religious system he was sent to confront.

Not worthy to untie. Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s task, so lowly that a saying recorded in later rabbinic writings allowed a disciple to do every service for his teacher except this one. The greatest of the prophets (Matthew 11:11) places himself below even that. That is genuine preparation: pointing away from yourself so insistently that when the one you announce arrives, people recognise him.

The stronger one. “Mightier” is the ordinary Greek word for strong (ischyros), and Jesus picks it up when he is accused of casting out demons by Satan: no one can plunder a strong man’s house unless he first binds the strong man (3:27). John announces the stronger one, who walks into the enemy’s house and takes back what was stolen.

With the Holy Spirit. Jesus would do what only God can: pour out the Holy Spirit, as the prophets promised for the last days (Joel 2:28; Ezekiel 36:26–27). This happened at Pentecost (Acts 1:5; 2:33). To be baptised with the Spirit is to be brought into new life by him, cleansed and indwelt: he comes to live in you not as a visitor but as a resident, your body becomes his temple (1 Corinthians 6:19), and he does not leave (John 14:16–17).

If John was Elijah, why did he deny it? When the priests asked, “Are you Elijah?” he said, “I am not” (John 1:21). He denied being Elijah returned in person, which is what they meant; he came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17). Scripture knows nothing of reincarnation: “it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Hebrews 9:27). John was a new man, born to Zechariah and Elizabeth, sent in Elijah’s role, and the costume told the truth before he opened his mouth.

How do I know I have the Spirit if I have never had a dramatic experience? By what he does, not by how it felt. The Spirit makes you call God Father with real trust (Romans 8:15–16). He makes Jesus precious to you and Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3). He makes you hate and fight the sin you once loved, and slowly produces love, joy, patience and kindness (Galatians 5:22–23). If you have turned from sin and are trusting Christ, you have the Spirit, whether or not you can name the day (Romans 8:9). Ask him to fill you afresh, and keep in step with him.

Where Christians differ: is baptism with the Spirit a second experience after conversion, for some believers only, as some Pentecostal traditions teach? Many who use that language love Christ deeply and have known real seasons of fresh blessing; the difference is over what to call them, and later fillings with the Spirit are real and to be sought. This commentary’s view: Spirit baptism happens at conversion, for Paul says all believers were baptised in one Spirit into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13); believers are then filled with the Spirit again and again (Ephesians 5:18).
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job.

parallels.desc: Elijah’s dress: hair and a leather belt

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus comes from an obscure village and joins sinners in the water of repentance, not because he has any sin to confess, but to stand where they stand.

In those days. One sentence is Mark’s entire account of the first thirty years of the Lord’s life. No genealogy, no manger, no shepherds: Jesus is simply there, a grown man of about thirty (Luke 3:23), walking into a river.

From Nazareth of Galilee. Both words were a problem. Galilee was looked down on by Jerusalem, and its accent gave Peter away in a courtyard (14:70). Nazareth was a village of perhaps a few hundred people, never mentioned in the Old Testament: “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” (John 1:46). If John was near Jericho, it was a walk of three or four days, taken to join a queue of people confessing their sins. The Lord whose way was prepared comes from nowhere important.

Baptised by John. A surprise. John’s baptism was for repentance and confession of sins, and Jesus had none to confess (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15). Matthew records why he was baptised: to fulfil all righteousness (Matthew 3:15). He identified himself with sinners, standing in the water with them, as he would later take their place on the cross (10:45). He obeyed every command of God on our behalf, so that his perfect obedience could be counted to people who have none. What he finishes at Golgotha he starts here, waist-deep in the Jordan.

In everyday life. If you have ever thought that the important things happen elsewhere, among people with better names and better postcodes, remember where the Son of God grew up. And if your sin puts you at the back of the queue, remember who chose to stand in it.

Why do the Gospels differ so much in what they include? Each writer selected from far more than he could record (John 21:25) and arranged it for his purpose and his readers. Matthew opens with the genealogy from Abraham, Luke gives the birth, John begins before creation; Mark, writing for persecuted believers who needed to know who Jesus is and what following him costs, goes straight to the action. The four do not compete: they are four witnesses to one Lord, and together give a fuller portrait than any one alone.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth was a small village in the hill country of Galilee, never mentioned in the Old Testament.

parallels.desc: “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came up out of the water, immediately he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. And a voice came from heaven, "You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus comes up out of the water, heaven is torn open, the Spirit comes down to anoint him, and the Father declares him his beloved Son. In those words the King and the suffering Servant meet in one person.

Immediately. Mark’s favourite word, here for the first time. It beats through this chapter like footsteps and gives his Gospel its urgency.

Torn open. Matthew and Luke say opened; Mark says ripped. Isaiah had prayed, “Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down” (Isaiah 64:1), and now God has done it. Mark uses the word only once more, when the temple curtain is torn in two at Jesus’ death (15:38): the two tearings frame the whole Gospel. And what came through the torn heaven was not thunder but love: the eternal Father looked on his eternal Son, standing in the river with sinners, and said, my beloved, my delight.

Like a dove. The Spirit anoints Jesus, marking him out and equipping him for his work as Messiah, as the prophets promised (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1). The dove may recall the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), signalling a new creation, or the dove that came back to Noah with peace after the flood (Genesis 8:8–12).

My beloved Son. Mark gives the words as spoken to the Son himself (Matthew has “this is my beloved Son”), an intimate word before the battle begins. They join three Scriptures. “You are my Son” comes from Psalm 2:7, the coronation psalm. “Beloved” recalls Genesis 22:2, your son, your only son, whom you love, spoken of Isaac, who was to be offered. “With you I am well pleased” echoes Isaiah 42:1, the Servant who will bear the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12). Israel had not expected these figures to meet in one person; the Father lays all three on Jesus.

The Trinity. The Father speaks from the torn heaven, the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends upon him: the three persons of the one God, revealed together, in the open, at the start.

Before he has done anything. The Father affirms before the Son serves, before a single miracle or sermon. That becomes the pattern of the Christian life, because those who are in Christ are accepted in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6): we serve from the security of the Father’s voice, not in search of it. On your best day and your worst he regards you as he regards his Son, because you are joined to his Son by faith and clothed with him (Galatians 3:26–27).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus became the Son of God at his baptism, as the early heresy called adoptionism taught. Mark’s first verse already calls him the Son of God; the baptism reveals and anoints who he already is.

Does God still speak from heaven like this? Not with new words to be added to Scripture. The voice at the Jordan was part of God’s once-for-all revelation of his Son, written down so that we could hear it, and God now speaks to us by his Son through the Scriptures, which are complete and sufficient (Hebrews 1:1–2; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). When Christians say God spoke to them, they usually mean that he pressed a truth or a prompting on their heart; such impressions are to be tested by Scripture and never carry its authority. That is no smaller gift: open your Bible to this verse and you hear the same Father say the same thing about the same Son.

parallels.desc: the servant in whom God delights

verseByVerse.note: “Torn open” (schizō) is the word Mark uses again when the temple curtain is torn at Jesus’ death (15:38).

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit immediately drove him out into the wilderness. And he was in the wilderness forty days, being tempted by Satan. And he was with the wild animals, and the angels were ministering to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straight from the Father’s voice, the Spirit sends Jesus into the wilderness to be tested by Satan, and he stands where Adam and Israel fell.

Drove him out. A strong word, the one Mark uses again and again for casting out demons. The Spirit who descended at the baptism thrusts Jesus into the desert, from the Father’s voice straight into the face of the enemy: the test was God’s purpose, not an accident.

Forty days. The number is never decorative in Scripture. Moses was forty days on the mountain (Exodus 34:28), and Elijah walked forty days to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8). Above all, Israel, called God’s son (Exodus 4:22), was forty years in the wilderness, tested with hunger, and grumbled and turned to idols (Deuteronomy 8:2). Jesus, the true Son, is tested in the desert and stays faithful; Matthew and Luke show him answering Satan each time from Deuteronomy, the book of those wilderness years (Matthew 4:4; Deuteronomy 8:3). He is the faithful Israel God always looked for, and his obedience is counted to those joined to him by faith.

Being tempted by Satan. Satan means adversary: a real, personal enemy who tempted the first Adam and succeeded (Genesis 3). Now he tempts Jesus, whom Paul calls the last Adam, the head of a new humanity (1 Corinthians 15:45).

With the wild animals. Only Mark mentions this. Some hear menace and loneliness; others hear Eden and the peaceable kingdom where the wolf shall dwell with the lamb (Isaiah 11:6–9). It may hold both. And Mark’s first readers in Rome, whose fellow believers Nero had dressed in the skins of animals to be torn to death by dogs, as Tacitus records, would take comfort that Jesus too had been among wild beasts and was kept.

The angels were ministering. Serving him, perhaps with food, as an angel fed the exhausted Elijah in the desert (1 Kings 19:5–8). Satan, the wild animals, and heaven feeding him in the middle of it: a fair picture of the Christian life, with real opposition, real exposure and real provision in the same wilderness.

Two men tested. Adam was tested in a garden, full and safe and in company, and he fell. The Son of God was tested in a desert, hungry and alone, and he did not. Every demon that flees in this Gospel, every disease that lifts, the tomb that empties, rests on the fact that the enemy came at him with everything and could not move him. He did it for us, in our flesh: the first battle of the war he finished at the cross. And because he met the enemy on the enemy’s ground before he preached, when demons cry out at him the reader knows why they are afraid (1:24; 3:27).

Being tempted is not sinning. We have a high priest who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). So the arrival of a foul thought is not evidence that you are a fraud, only that you are being tempted, as the sinless Son of God was. What matters is what you do next, and the one who did not give way is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18).

If the Spirit led Jesus into temptation, why do we pray, lead us not into temptation? Because God and Satan had different purposes in the same wilderness: Satan meant a trap; God meant a test, to prove his Son and begin his victory. God tempts no one to sin (James 1:13), but he does lead his people through testing for their good (James 1:2–4). Jesus went in our place into the full strength of the enemy’s attack, so we pray humbly, as he taught us, not to be brought into it, and to be delivered from evil. And when testing comes, we are not alone in it: he has been there, and won, and God provides the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13).
verseByVerse.note: Matthew and Luke record the three temptations; Mark gives only the fact.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — The Kingdom Announced and the First Disciples Called
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom of God has come near in Jesus, and it calls for an answer now. John’s arrest marks the handover from the forerunner to the one he announced (v. 14). Jesus gives the gospel in four phrases: the time is fulfilled, the kingdom is at hand, repent, believe (v. 15). It is an announcement that requires an answer, not an offer to think about. Then two pairs of brothers show what the answer looks like: at his word they leave their nets, their boat and their father to follow him (vv. 16–20). Mark does not explain it; he shows what happens when people meet someone with this authority.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 15 is the thesis of Mark’s Gospel. Each of its four phrases is unfolded in the note on that verse. The kingdom is not a programme or an idea but a Person.
verseByVerse.examples: Simon, Andrew, James and John left their nets, and Zebedee was left in the boat with the hired servants (see vv. 19–20). The call of Jesus still comes before every other claim.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the gospel of God, and saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When John is silenced, Jesus begins: he goes into Galilee announcing God’s own good news.

After John was arrested. Literally “handed over”. Herod Antipas imprisoned John for condemning his marriage to his brother’s wife, as Mark tells in chapter 6 (6:17–18). The same word is later used of Jesus being handed over to death (9:31; 10:33; 15:1): the forerunner’s fate foreshadows the Messiah’s.

Into Galilee. The northern region around the lake, with a mixed population of Jews and Gentiles, far from every institution with the authority to certify him. He will get to Jerusalem, and it will kill him; but first he goes where ordinary people live.

The gospel of God. In verse 1 it was “the gospel of Jesus Christ”; now it is “the gospel of God”: God’s own announcement of what God is doing, not a proposal for consideration. Proclaiming is a herald’s word: you either believe the report or you do not.

In everyday life. They silenced John, and God opened the mouth of his Son. If you are discouraged at how small your church or your witness looks, remember that the preaching tour that changed the world was conducted among farms and fishing boats.
verseByVerse.note: Galilee was the northern region of the land, around the lake. John was imprisoned by its ruler, Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s appointed time has come and his reign has drawn near in Jesus, so the only right response is to turn from sin and trust the good news.

The time is fulfilled. The appointed time, the decisive moment, not the ticking of the clock. The long wait of the Old Testament is over: “when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son” (Galatians 4:4).

The kingdom of God. God’s reign: God acting as King to save his people and judge evil, as the prophets promised (Isaiah 52:7; Daniel 2:44; 7:13–14). It is not a place, nor merely a future heaven. “At hand” means it has come near, within reach, arriving in Jesus himself, as his healings and exorcisms show (3:23–27). So it is both present and still to come: where Jesus is, the kingdom has come near, yet it waits for its completion when he returns in glory (13:26).

Repent. Turn around: a change of mind so thorough that it changes direction, away from sin and self-rule toward God; not an emotion, nor self-improvement. You can feel dreadful about your sin for years and never repent, because remorse looks at yourself while repentance turns to God. In practice it is concrete: naming the particular thing, agreeing with God about it, and turning, usually by a decision this week that costs something. Luther opened the Reformation by saying that the whole life of a believer is repentance.

Believe in the gospel. Rely on the good news; stake your life on it: the news that the King has come and has done what was needed. Believing that a chair will hold you and sitting down in it are two different things, and only the second is faith. Repentance and faith are two sides of one turning, and they do not earn the kingdom; they receive it.

How do I know whether I have really repented and believed? Look at direction rather than intensity: is Christ my hope, and am I fighting my sin rather than making peace with it? And if you find you cannot turn, ask. Scripture speaks of repentance as something God grants (Acts 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25), so the very thing commanded here can be requested from the one commanding it. That is why this is good news and not a hurdle. The King does not stand at a distance demanding that you climb; he has come near, and the command to turn is itself the outstretched hand.

Is it arrogant of Jesus to call everyone to repent? Only if he were saying that some people are better than others, and he is saying the opposite. The call goes to everyone in the same terms, the religious leader and the tax collector, the respectable and the disgraced, because before a holy God all need the same mercy (Romans 3:22–24). Arrogance looks down on others; repentance is the one posture in which nobody can look down on anybody. And the King who calls came near and went to the cross to make the turning possible: a call to come home is an invitation, not an insult.

Is the kingdom of God the same as the church? Not quite. The kingdom is God’s reign, wider than the church: Christ already reigns over all things for his church (Ephesians 1:22), and one day his rule will fill a new heaven and a new earth. The church is the people gathered under that reign, where the kingdom shows its face now, in forgiven sinners worshipping their King, so belonging to a local church is not optional for a citizen of the kingdom.
verseByVerse.note: “The kingdom of God” means God’s reign, his rule as King. “At hand” means it has come near.

verseByVerse.quote: Passing alongside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew the brother of Simon casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And Jesus said to them, "Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men." And immediately they left their nets and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls two fishermen with two words, and they leave their nets at once: this is what repenting and believing looks like on an ordinary working morning.

Casting a net. The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake about thirteen miles long, ringed with fishing towns. The circular casting net, weighted round the rim and thrown by hand, takes years to learn: a skill, an income and an identity. Since Mark’s Gospel probably comes from Peter’s preaching, this is Peter telling of the morning his life changed, with his brother Andrew beside him.

Follow me. Literally “come behind me”. Students usually chose their rabbi, it seems; Jesus chooses his disciples, and calls them not to a set of teachings but to himself. He walked along a beach and spoke two words, and working men walked out of their lives into his. That is the voice that called the worlds into being, and it has not weakened.

Fishers of men. Men means people. He does not tell them to abandon what they are but what they are for: every instinct the lake taught them, patience, early starts, working all night for nothing, will be needed, aimed now at people. And “I will make you become” is a promise that takes time. The disciples in Mark are often confused, fearful and faithless, yet they are the ones he is making. The calling comes before the competence.

Repent and believe, with a name attached. Verses 16–20 show what repenting and believing (v. 15) looked like for four particular men. Not every Christian must leave his job, but every disciple must put Jesus before everything.

Had they met Jesus before? Very probably. John’s Gospel records an earlier meeting at the Jordan: Andrew heard the Baptist say of Jesus, “Behold, the Lamb of God”, spent a day with him, and told his brother, “We have found the Messiah” (John 1:35–42). That makes Mark’s point firmer. He records not the moment they first believed but the moment they were called into service, when following came to mean leaving everything: the harder step, and the one he wants you to see.

I am not a preacher, so what does fishing for people look like for me? Mostly ordinary faithfulness where you already are. Pray by name for a few people who do not know Christ. Be the kind of neighbour and colleague whose life raises questions, and answer them gently (1 Peter 3:15). Invite people to your home and to church. Tell your own story of what Christ has done, simply. Fishermen work in teams, and so do Christians: you may never draw the net in, but the one who cast it, mended it or rowed the boat is part of the catch.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake about 13 miles long. A casting net was a round net thrown by hand into shallow water.

parallels.desc: Luke’s account of the call by the lake
Andrew and Simon first meet Jesus

verseByVerse.quote: And going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who were in their boat mending the nets. And immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two more brothers leave their boat, their family business and their father to follow Jesus. His call comes before every other claim.

Mending the nets. The second pair are called off the unglamorous half of fishing, the half that never ends. James and John, with Peter, became Jesus’ inner circle (5:37; 9:2; 14:33). He nicknamed them Sons of Thunder (3:17), and John became the disciple who wrote of love.

They left their father. Only Mark mentions the hired servants. Zebedee ran a business with employees, and the brothers left a prosperous family firm and their father in mid-work. The detail also shows the business did not depend on them alone: a real cost, and not a cruelty.

The Son who left his Father’s house. The one calling them knows that cost from the other side. The eternal Son came out from the Father into a world that did not receive him (John 1:11; 16:28), and his own family would soon try to take him home, convinced he was out of his mind (3:21). He never asks a disciple to leave what he did not leave first, and he calls them into a family of his own: whoever does the will of God is his brother and sister and mother (3:35). No one has left anything for him and been the poorer: he gives back a hundredfold, and in the age to come eternal life (10:29–30).

What if following Jesus divides me from my family? Jesus warned it would sometimes happen (Matthew 10:34–37). Following him first does not mean despising your family. Keep honouring your parents, loving them and serving them in practical ways; these sons did not leave their father helpless. But when their wishes and Christ’s commands collide, Christ comes first. Do it gently, without self-righteousness, and keep praying. Many families hurt by a believer’s choice have later been won by the same believer’s patient love.
verseByVerse.note: James and John left “hired servants” with their father, so Zebedee ran a working fishing business.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–45 — Authority in Capernaum and Beyond
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus has the authority of God over everything that ruins human life, and he uses it to come near to people. One Sabbath in Capernaum shows it: in the synagogue he teaches on his own authority and silences a demon with a sentence (vv. 21–28); in a home he lifts a woman from a fever (vv. 29–31); at the door after dark he heals the sick of a whole town (vv. 32–34). Before dawn we see the prayer behind it all, and he leaves the crowd to preach in the next towns, because that is why he came (vv. 35–39). Finally he touches a leper, makes him clean and takes the outcast’s place outside the towns (vv. 40–45).
verseByVerse.theology: In the synagogue (vv. 21–28) the unclean spirit names Jesus accurately as “the Holy One of God”, and Jesus silences it (on why, see the note on vv. 32–34). Throughout Mark, Jesus will not let the wrong voices tell the right story.
verseByVerse.examples: The leper (vv. 40–45) prays the most honest prayer in the chapter. Jesus answers it by touching him: I will; be clean (see vv. 40–42). The answer stands for anyone who comes to God unsure whether he really wants them.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went into Capernaum, and immediately on the Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching. And they were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the synagogue at Capernaum Jesus teaches on his own authority, not by quoting other teachers, and his hearers are struck by it. Verses 21–34 give one Sabbath from morning to night, a sample of the kingdom he has just announced, and Mark puts the teaching first.

Capernaum. A fishing town on the north-west shore, on the trade road, with a customs post and a Roman centurion (Luke 7:1–5), and the base of the Galilean ministry (2:1). Archaeologists have found a later synagogue perhaps on the foundations of the one Jesus knew, and a house venerated from early times as Peter’s.

The synagogue. The synagogue was the local meeting place for prayer and the reading and teaching of Scripture, the most public platform a town had, and visiting teachers could be invited to speak (Luke 4:16; Acts 13:15).

As one who had authority. Astonished means struck, knocked out of their composure, not by a better speaker but by the basis on which he spoke. The scribes, as far as later Jewish writings show, taught by quoting earlier teachers, tracing a ruling back through a chain of rabbis; their authority was borrowed. Jesus quotes no rabbi. He speaks as a man reporting what is the case, and a room trained to expect footnotes is struck. They had come to hear the Scriptures explained, and got the Author reading his own book aloud. Mark does not even record what he taught; the focus is on who he is.

In everyday life. Take one thing Jesus says plainly, about worry, money, forgiveness or anger, that you have treated as advice, and treat it as a command from the one who has the right to give it, and who by his Spirit gives the strength to keep it.

Should my pastor teach with authority like this? Only in a borrowed and lesser way. Jesus’ authority was his own. A faithful preacher’s authority is exactly as great as his faithfulness to Scripture: when he says what the text says, receive it as God’s word (1 Thessalonians 2:13); beyond it, he speaks only as a man. So test what you hear by the Bible (Acts 17:11), and when it is true, do not treat it as one opinion among many. The scribes’ failure was not that they quoted others but that they never brought people face to face with God’s own voice.
verseByVerse.note: Capernaum was a fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake, and became Jesus’ base in Galilee. Scribes were the trained teachers of the law of Moses.

parallels.desc: the same astonishment after the Sermon on the Mount

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit. And he cried out, "What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus walks into the synagogue, an unclean spirit hidden in the congregation cries out in panic, because it knows exactly who he is.

An unclean spirit. A demon: a fallen angel, morally impure, which defiles and torments the person it controls. And it is not among the tombs, but in the synagogue, on the Sabbath, during the service. Whatever was in this man may have sat quietly through the readings week after week, until Jesus walked in. The presence of Christ does not create the problem; it brings it to the surface. Things that have lived comfortably alongside religion for years become unbearable the moment he is actually in the room.

What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? A Hebrew idiom: what is there between us? Leave us alone. And “us”: the demon speaks for the whole kingdom of evil spirits.

Have you come to destroy us? Not defiance but panic. The Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8), and this spirit knows exactly who has walked in and how the story ends.

The Holy One of God. The demon recognises what the people do not. Holy means utterly pure and set apart (Isaiah 6:3–5), and an unclean spirit cannot be at ease in his presence. Demons in Mark recognise Jesus before the disciples do (3:11; 5:7), yet knowing who he is does not make them his followers; they believe and shudder (James 2:19). Some suggest that naming him was an attempt to gain power over him, as ancient magic held that knowing a name gave control. If so, it failed in the next breath.

What is an unclean spirit? Scripture treats demons as real personal beings, fallen and malevolent, not a first-century label for illness that we have outgrown. And the Gospel writers keep the categories apart: a few verses on, the people bring all who were sick or oppressed by demons, and Jesus healed many who were sick and cast out many demons (vv. 32, 34): two groups, two verbs, side by side. Luke, a doctor, keeps the same distinction. (On whether it happens now, see the note on vv. 25–26.)
verseByVerse.note: An “unclean spirit” is a demon. “The Holy One of God” is a title for the one set apart by God: the demon names who Jesus is.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus rebuked him, saying, "Be silent, and come out of him!" And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With one sentence Jesus silences the demon and orders it out, and it has to obey.

Be silent. Literally “be muzzled”. Why, when it was telling the truth? Because Jesus would not accept testimony from demons, nor be proclaimed Messiah before the cross had shown what kind of Messiah he is (see the note on vv. 32–34).

Come out of him! Ancient exorcists named a superior spirit and used formulas, rings or roots; their power was borrowed, and it might not work (compare Acts 19:13–16). Jesus uses no name but his own, no formula and no delay: he tells it to be quiet and get out, and it does. All the power of hell, in a synagogue on a Sabbath morning, lasted one sentence against him.

Convulsing him. A last violent display, but it had to obey, and Luke adds that it did the man no harm (Luke 4:35).

Does it still happen? Two ditches. Yes, and there are two ditches. One is to deny the whole category, a modern reflex rather than a biblical conclusion. The other, in our churches the more damaging, is to see a demon behind everything. Treating depression, epilepsy, trauma or a chemical illness as a spirit to be cast out has done lasting harm to people who needed a doctor and got an exorcism. When the apostles write about the Christian’s daily struggle, they speak overwhelmingly of sin, the flesh and the world, and the weapons they prescribe are ordinary: Scripture, prayer, truth, the armour of God, the company of the church (Ephesians 6:10–18). If you are unwell in body, see a doctor; if you are struggling in mind or spirit, talk to your pastor and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up. Any treatment the doctor recommends is not a failure of faith but an ordinary mercy God provides.

In everyday life. Whatever has a grip on you must obey his word. Bring it to him by name in prayer, and tell one trusted believer about it. Shame keeps things in the dark; Christ’s word brings them out.

Could what happened to this man happen to a Christian? No. You cannot be owned by what has already been beaten; a believer has already been spoken for. “He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4), and a person indwelt by the Spirit, bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20), is not available for occupation: harassed sometimes, tempted certainly, but not possessed. Some Christians believe a believer can be troubled by evil spirits more deeply than this, but the New Testament never describes a believer as possessed. If a passage like this frightens you at night, resist the devil by the ordinary means and he will flee from you (James 4:7). And if you have dabbled in the occult, renounce it plainly before God, get rid of anything connected with it (Acts 19:18–19), tell a pastor, and rest in Christ’s finished victory.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus uses no ritual, no formula and no appeal to another power: a command alone.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves, saying, "What is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him." And at once his fame spread everywhere throughout all the surrounding region of Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people see that Jesus’ word has power even over evil spirits, but they ask “What is this?” when the real question is who he is.

A new teaching with authority! New (kainē) means new in kind. They rightly connect the astonishing teaching of verse 22 with the expulsion of verse 26, for in this Gospel the word and the power are never separate: what he says happens, whether he says it to a room or to a spirit. But they ask “what is this?”, not “who is this?”, the question the whole Gospel is driving at (4:41; 8:29).

Even the unclean spirits. The evidence that the kingdom of God has arrived: the strong man is being bound (3:27). They have watched a man command a demon out of a neighbour with a sentence, and their category for it is “a new teaching”, a very good lesson. It is not wrong; it is nowhere near big enough. It was the voice of the Creator in a village synagogue, the word that said “let there be light” now saying “come out”, and being obeyed.

His fame spread. The news is out of the building before the Sabbath is over, and soon it has the whole district. That fame is what Jesus will spend the rest of the chapter, and much of the Gospel, trying to manage: silencing demons and the healed, withdrawing to desolate places (see the note on vv. 32–34). He is not building a following. He is going to a cross, and a crowd that wants a miracle worker will not follow him there.

Is it wrong to be amazed by Jesus without fully understanding him? No, it is often where faith begins. But amazement is a doorway, not a room to live in; these crowds were amazed and many later drifted away. The amazement that saves moves from “what is this?” to “who is this?”, then to “you are the Christ”, and finally to the trust that follows him to the cross. If you are amazed by Jesus but not yet sure who he is, keep reading Mark. Its whole purpose is to take you from wonder to faith.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately he left the synagogue and entered the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John. Now Simon's mother-in-law lay ill with a fever, and immediately they told him about her. And he came and took her by the hand and lifted her up, and the fever left her, and she began to serve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the synagogue Jesus goes into Peter’s home, takes a sick woman by the hand and lifts her up, and she rises to serve. His power is for ordinary households, not only for public occasions.

Simon’s mother-in-law. Peter was married, and this is very likely Peter describing his own front room. In the ancient world fevers killed, and they told Jesus about her at once: bringing the need to him is the beginning of every answer to prayer.

Lifted her up. The word used for resurrection (16:6): a small sign of the greater raising to come.

She began to serve. No time of recovery needed. The word is the one Mark used of the angels ministering to Jesus in the wilderness (1:13), and the one Jesus will use of himself: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (10:45).

The kingdom’s first stop. After the synagogue, a sickroom off somebody’s kitchen: that is the kind of King he is: Lord of angels, and not too great to take a feverish woman by the hand.

Is it demeaning that the healed woman goes straight to the kitchen? Not in Mark’s eyes: serving Jesus a meal puts her in very high company. Hospitality is honoured throughout Scripture (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2), and the women who served Jesus were the faithful witnesses at the cross and the tomb (15:40–41). Every Christian, man or woman, is healed in order to serve, and no service done for Christ is small.

Where Christians differ: must those who lead the church be unmarried? The Roman Catholic Church names Peter the first pope and, in the Latin tradition, requires its priests to be unmarried, a discipline it acknowledges was not the apostles’ own rule. This commentary’s view: years into the work Peter was still travelling with a believing wife (1 Corinthians 9:5). This is no argument against celibacy freely chosen, which Paul commended and lived (1 Corinthians 7:7–8); but a rule that forbids marriage to those who hold Peter’s office cannot appeal to Peter, and Scripture expects that a pastor may well be the husband of one wife (1 Timothy 3:2).

parallels.desc: Peter was married, and his wife travelled with him

verseByVerse.quote: That evening at sundown they brought to him all who were sick or oppressed by demons. And the whole city was gathered together at the door. And he healed many who were sick with various diseases, and cast out many demons. And he would not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as the Sabbath ends, the whole town brings its sick and oppressed to Jesus, and he heals many and silences the demons who know him.

That evening at sundown. The Sabbath ended at sunset, and only then could people carry the sick without breaking the Sabbath rules about carrying burdens. The door they crowded round was Peter’s, and the scene has the feel of a householder’s memory.

Healed many. “Many” means a great number, and in Hebrew idiom can mean all of a large company; Matthew writes that he “healed all who were sick” (Matthew 8:16). Picture the little house at dusk, the whole town pressing round the door, and one man moving among them, touching, speaking, healing, until the last of them went home. He never turned anyone away for being too much trouble.

Why does Jesus keep telling people to be quiet about him? Scholars call this silencing, which runs right through Mark, the messianic secret. Jesus is not hiding; the crowds see everything he does. He refuses to let the word “Messiah” be shouted before it can be rightly understood. In Galilee it meant a conquering king who would drive out Rome, and to be hailed too early would light a political fire. He will not be crowned before he is crucified, so he controls the timing, so that when the title is finally confessed it will be defined by his death and not by the crowd’s dreams. With demons there is a further reason: praise from liars is no honour to the Holy One. The secret is not concealment but protection: the right truth, at the right time, on the right lips.

Does he heal everybody, and if not, why not me? The honest thing first: that night in Capernaum was not normal and was never claimed to be. Such miracles clustered around Jesus and his apostles to authenticate the message while it was being given (Hebrews 2:3–4); that abundance is nowhere promised now, and anyone who guarantees it promises what Scripture does not. Yet God has not retired. He remains free to heal, and still does, and the church is told plainly to pray for the sick and expect him to act (James 5:14–15). So we ask, honestly and often, and leave the outcome where it belongs.

The signpost is not the country. The deeper thing is where the comfort lies. Every person healed in this chapter died later. Each healing was not the destination but a signpost, a piece of the new creation pushed early into the old, so that we would know what the King is going to do with the whole of it. What is guaranteed to the believer is not healing now but resurrection then, and a body that will never need healing again (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Revelation 21:4). If you are not healed, it is not that your faith was too small or he unwilling. The signpost is not the country, and you are still on the road to it.

Where Christians differ: do gifts of healing continue? Many brothers and sisters expect them still, and we honour them. This commentary’s view: the apostles’ sign-gifts ceased with them, because their purpose of confirming the apostolic message was fulfilled. All agree that God hears prayer for the sick.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown. Only then could people carry the sick through the town without breaking the Sabbath rules.

verseByVerse.quote: And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed. And Simon and those who were with him searched for him, and they found him and said to him, "Everyone is looking for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the busiest day yet, Jesus slips away before dawn to pray alone, and his disciples come to pull him back to the crowd.

Very early. This verse shows what lay beneath the exhausting evening. The authority was his own, as the eternal Son, yet he exercised it as a man living in unbroken dependence on his Father (John 5:19). The Son who shared the Father’s glory before the world was slipped out of a sleeping house in the dark to be with him.

A desolate place. The word for wilderness. Mark shows Jesus praying at three key moments, each at night: here, after feeding the five thousand (6:46), and in Gethsemane (14:32–39). Early, before anyone could reach him; alone, out of range; and first, before the day’s demands arrived rather than after they were met.

Searched for him. The word means hunted him down. “Everyone is looking for you”: the disciples see popularity, crowds, success, and in effect tell him he is missing his moment.

The tyranny of being wanted. “Everyone is looking for you” is the sentence many of us live for. Pascal noticed, long before notifications, that we pursue company and busyness largely so that we never have to be alone with ourselves; even a king, he said, left with nothing to do but think about himself, would be miserable. Our age has made being in demand a proof that we matter. Jesus is wanted by a whole town and walks away to the next (v. 38), not because he does not care, but because he does not need the crowd to tell him who he is. He had heard who he was at the river, before he had done anything at all: “You are my beloved Son” (v. 11). Someone who has heard that voice can be needed without being ruled by it, and can go where love sends rather than where applause calls. In Christ that same verdict is spoken over everyone who trusts him (see the note on Galatians 1:10).

In everyday life. Name the time and the place you will be alone with God, and guard them. If you have failed at this for years, do not start with guilt. He has prayed for you far more faithfully than you have ever prayed for yourself. Start tomorrow, small.

Do I have to pray at five in the morning? No. Many have read this verse, set an alarm for five, managed it for nine days, and concluded they are second-rate Christians. Mark is recording what Jesus did, not legislating an hour, and the Lord himself kept no fixed slot: he prayed through a whole night before choosing the Twelve (Luke 6:12), and in the evening after feeding the crowd (6:46). What is constant is not the clock but the withdrawal: he was getting somewhere he could not be reached. In a life with no margin, prayer is never found. It has to be taken.

What should I actually do when I get alone with God? Keep it simple. Read a passage slowly, perhaps a chapter of a Gospel or a psalm, and ask what it shows you of God and of yourself. Then pray from it: praise him for what you have seen, confess what it exposed, thank him for his mercies, and bring your requests and other people’s by name, with the Lord’s Prayer as your pattern (Matthew 6:9–13). Ten honest minutes most days is better than an hour you never reach; if your mind wanders, bring it back without fuss. You are not performing; you are a child talking to your Father.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out." And he went throughout all Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and casting out demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus leaves a town that wants him to preach in the next towns, because proclaiming the kingdom is what he came to do. The healings serve the message, not the other way round.

The next towns. A whole town wants him, and a genuinely good thing is on offer: more healing, more obvious fruit. He says no, because he had settled in prayer, in the dark, what the day was for. He loved those crowds, yet would not let their approval choose his road. Everyone was looking for him, and he went looking for everyone else: the next village, the far country, the lost sheep.

Throughout all Galilee. Weeks of work in a sentence. Preaching and casting out demons go together: the word of the kingdom does not only inform; it changes the places it enters. The order is set for the whole Gospel, which is why chapter 2 opens with Jesus preaching to a packed house before anyone is healed (2:2).

In everyday life. If you do not decide before the demands arrive, the demands will decide, and you will spend your life on whatever shouts loudest, which is usually good, and usually not what you were sent to do. The voice hardest to refuse is often not an enemy’s but a friend’s, telling you that everyone is looking for you.

How do I know what my main calling is? Start with what Scripture makes plain for every Christian: love God and your neighbour, belong to and serve a church, make Christ known. Then add what your place in life gives you: a spouse, children, a job, parents to honour. Your gifts, the church’s counsel and the needs in front of you fill in the rest. Most people do not need a new calling so much as the courage to say no to good things that crowd out the ones already given.

Uncertain wording. “That is why I came out” may mean that he came out from Capernaum that morning, or, more deeply, that he came from the Father into the world (John 16:28). Mark’s words allow either. Luke has “I was sent for this purpose” (Luke 4:43), which points to his mission from God; either way, preaching is what he was sent to do.

verseByVerse.quote: And a leper came to him, imploring him, and kneeling said to him, "If you will, you can make me clean." Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him and said to him, "I will; be clean." And immediately the leprosy left him, and he was made clean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is not only able but willing to make the unclean clean, and he shows it by touching a man no one else would touch.

A leper. Leprosy in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases (Leviticus 13–14). A leper was ritually unclean; he had to live outside the town, wear torn clothes, cover his lip and call out “Unclean, unclean” (Leviticus 13:45–46). Cut off from worship, family and all human touch, he was thought as hard to cure as the dead to raise (2 Kings 5:7). This man breaks every expectation, comes close, and kneels.

If you will. A small masterpiece of faith: he does not doubt the power; he leans his whole weight on it. He is uncertain only about the heart.

Moved with pity. Deep, gut-level compassion (splanchnistheis). On the reading “moved with anger”, see the textual note below.

He touched him. Perhaps no one had touched this man for years. Jesus could have healed with a word; the touch is deliberate. When Jesus touches a leper, the uncleanness does not pass to him; his cleanness passes to the leper. That is the direction grace always moves.

I will. The direct answer to the man’s question: not “I might”, or “in the right circumstances”. And he was not only healed but clean: restored to God’s people and to worship.

The Holy One was not stained. The Holy One rested his hand on a ruined body and was not stained by it, as at the cross he would bear the moral uncleanness of his people and remain the Clean One. Every outcast who has knelt and wondered whether he is wanted has the same answer, spoken once on a Galilean road and sealed at the cross: “I will; be clean.”

What it does not mean. Not that we should pray “if you will” about forgiveness, which God has promised to all who come to him (1 John 1:9); we may pray it about healing or circumstances, which he has not promised. What Jesus settles here is his willingness to receive and cleanse the person who wonders whether he is wanted, not a promise that every disease will be removed on request (see the note on vv. 32–34).

In everyday life. Who in your world is treated as untouchable: the lonely, the ill, the disgraced, the person everyone avoids? A hand on the shoulder, a meal or a visit may be the first human touch they have had in a long time.

What if what makes me feel unclean is something I did, not something that happened to me? Then this story is for you even more. The leper’s disease was a picture of sin: it spread, defiled, and cut people off from God and one another. The cleansing Jesus gives reaches the guilty conscience as well as the wounded body: the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7), including the thing you are most ashamed of. Come as the leper came, kneeling and honest. You do not need to clean yourself up first; that is what he came to do.

Textual note. One ancient Greek manuscript and several early Latin translations read “moved with anger” (orgistheis). The two words look nothing alike in Greek, so a slip of the eye is unlikely; a scribe softening a startling anger to a gentle pity is the easier change to explain, which is why some scholars think the harder reading may be original.
