This commentary’s view: the evidence is divided; pity is better supported, though anger may be the harder and therefore original reading. Either way, Jesus is moved deeply. Most English Bibles read pity or compassion; the NIV follows the other reading and says Jesus was indignant.

If Mark wrote anger, at what? Not at the man; Jesus touches him in the same breath. At the thing that has him: the disfiguring, isolating cruelty of the disease, the whole ruin the enemy has worked in God’s good world. It is the same holy indignation with which he would groan in spirit at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:33, 38). Love for the sufferer is fury at what is destroying him, and both bend the same hand toward the untouchable to make him clean.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases. A leper had to live apart from others, so touching one was unheard of.

parallels.desc: the leper must live alone, crying “Unclean”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus sternly charged him and sent him away at once, and said to him, "See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, for a proof to them." But he went out and began to talk freely about it, and to spread the news, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town, but was out in desolate places, and people were coming to him from every quarter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sends the cleansed man to be restored through the priest, but the man spreads the news, and the one who made him clean must now stay outside the towns.

Sternly charged. Snorting with indignation, the verb John uses of Jesus at the grave of Lazarus. If Mark wrote anger in verse 41, the two fierce words belong together in a scene otherwise pure tenderness.

Say nothing. As at verse 34 (also 3:12; 5:43; 8:30), and here the practical reason shows: crowds that made his preaching in the towns impossible (v. 45).

Show yourself to the priest. The law of Moses required a priest to examine and declare a leper clean, with offerings of birds, lambs, flour and oil (Leviticus 14:1–32). Jesus wants the man fully restored, not only in his skin but in his place among God’s people.

For a proof to them. Evidence the priests could not deny. A king of Israel had once cried that only God, who kills and makes alive, could cure a leper (2 Kings 5:7), and now a cleansed leper would be standing in front of them with his offering.

He began to talk freely. He disobeyed, out of joy, and it is understandable: he had been made to shout his own contamination at anyone who came near, and a man had put a hand on him. But even happy disobedience had consequences.

Out in desolate places. The man who had been shut out of the towns is now free to walk into any of them, and the one who freed him has taken his place outside. This exchange is a small picture of where the whole Gospel is heading: he took the leper’s place, as he would take ours when he suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12). The clean man goes in; the one who made him clean goes out. And even there people kept coming to him from every quarter; he could not be hidden.

So should I keep quiet about what Jesus has done for me? No. This command was for a moment before the cross, when talk of a miracle worker would hinder his mission; after the resurrection it is the opposite: go and tell (16:7; Matthew 28:19–20). Even in Mark, the healed man of Gerasa, in Gentile territory, is told to go home and tell how much the Lord has done for him (5:19). The lesson is not silence but obedience: to tell what he has done in the way and at the time he commands, which now means gladly, plainly and often.
verseByVerse.note: The cleansing involved the priest’s inspection, two birds, and offerings on the eighth day.

1.theology:
Before his ministry begins, Jesus is identified from three directions: by the Father (my beloved Son), by Scripture (as it is written), and by his own announcement that the kingdom of God is at hand. So when the demons recognise him and the crowds are astonished, the reader already knows why.

Jesus silences the demons and tells the healed not to speak. This is not evasion but timing (see the note on vv. 32–34), and fittingly the great confession comes from a Roman soldier at the foot of the cross (15:39).
1.examples: The disciples here are responsive but unformed. They leave their nets and follow, and they come looking for him to report the crowds, but they do not yet understand whom they are following. Discipleship often begins like that: answering Jesus before you have the words to explain him. The understanding comes later, often painfully.

keyVerse.quote: The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.
keyVerse.note: This is Jesus’ whole message in one sentence and the thesis of Mark’s Gospel. It says what time it is (the waiting is over), what has arrived (God’s reign, come near in Jesus himself) and the only fitting answer (turn and trust). Every scene after it shows the kingdom arriving, and every call shows what repenting and believing look like.

1.reflection:
Mark’s first verses apply promises about the coming of the LORD himself to Jesus (vv. 1–3). How does it change the way you hear his commands and invitations in this chapter to know that in him God has come in person?

The Father says “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased” before Jesus has preached or healed anyone (v. 11). In Christ, believers too are accepted before they serve. Where do you still work or serve in order to be accepted, and what would change if you served from that acceptance instead?

Four fishermen left their nets, their boat and their father at Jesus’ call (vv. 16–20), and Jesus himself turned down a whole town that wanted him in order to do what he was sent to do (vv. 35–39). What good things in your life most easily crowd out following him, and how could you guard time alone with the Father as he did?

Jesus touched a leper whom no one else would touch (vv. 40–42). Who are the people treated as untouchable around you, and how might we, as a group, come near them? And what does his touch say to someone who wonders whether Christ really wants them?

2.title: Who Has Authority to Forgive?
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And when he returned to Capernaum after some days, it was reported that he was at home. <sup>2</sup>And many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even at the door. And he was preaching the word to them. <sup>3</sup>And they came, bringing to him a paralytic carried by four men. <sup>4</sup>And when they could not get near him because of the crowd, they removed the roof above him, and when they had made an opening, they let down the bed on which the paralytic lay. <sup>5</sup>And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” <sup>6</sup>Now some of the scribes were sitting there, questioning in their hearts, <sup>7</sup>“Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?” <sup>8</sup>And immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they thus questioned within themselves, said to them, “Why do you question these things in your hearts? <sup>9</sup>Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise, take up your bed and walk’? <sup>10</sup>But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic— <sup>11</sup>“I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home.” <sup>12</sup>And he rose and immediately picked up his bed and went out before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, “We never saw anything like this!” <sup>13</sup>He went out again beside the sea, and all the crowd was coming to him, and he was teaching them. <sup>14</sup>And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him. <sup>15</sup>And as he reclined at table in his house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many who followed him. <sup>16</sup>And the scribes of the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, “Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>17</sup>And when Jesus heard it, he said to them, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” <sup>18</sup>Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him, “Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?” <sup>19</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. <sup>20</sup>The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in that day. <sup>21</sup>No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the patch tears away from it, the new from the old, and a worse tear is made. <sup>22</sup>And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins—and the wine is destroyed, and so are the skins. But new wine is for fresh wineskins.” <sup>23</sup>One Sabbath he was going through the grainfields, and as they made their way, his disciples began to pluck heads of grain. <sup>24</sup>And the Pharisees were saying to him, “Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?” <sup>25</sup>And he said to them, “Have you never read what David did, when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: <sup>26</sup>how he entered the house of God, in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him?” <sup>27</sup>And he said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. <sup>28</sup>So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”
2.overview:
Where we are. After the welcome of chapter 1, chapter 2 opens a run of five conflict stories (2:1–3:6) that ends with the Pharisees plotting to destroy him.

The message. Jesus does what only God can do, and he does it for sinners. He forgives sins on his own authority, calls the most despised man in town to follow him, names himself the bridegroom of God’s people and claims to be lord of the Sabbath. Each claim is larger than the last, and each is used in mercy: a paralysed man forgiven, tax collectors welcomed, hungry friends fed. The old religious forms cannot contain what he brings.

Why it was said. Mark’s readers in Rome were following a man their neighbours knew as a condemned criminal (see the introduction). Here they see why the leaders turned against him: not for any wrong, but because he claimed what belongs to God. And the welcome that had reached Gentiles like them was there from the start, at a tax collector’s table.

How the chapter makes its case. Jesus forgives a paralysed man and proves the unseen pardon by a healing everyone can see, while the scribes silently call it blasphemy (vv. 1–12). He calls Levi and eats with sinners, because a doctor comes for the sick (vv. 13–17). Asked about fasting, he calls his presence a wedding and warns that his new wine cannot go into old wineskins (vv. 18–22). Accused of letting his disciples break the Sabbath, he points to David’s hungry men and claims to be the Sabbath’s lord (vv. 23–28). All the while the opposition hardens, from silent questioning (v. 6) to complaint (v. 16) to open challenge (v. 24).

Where it leads. The key sentence is spoken over the paralysed man: “Son, your sins are forgiven.” Only God can say it, and this man does. Yet the cross already falls across the chapter. The verdict of blasphemy will be repeated at his trial (14:64), the bridegroom will be taken away (v. 20), and the pardon given so freely in Capernaum will be paid for outside Jerusalem, where the Physician takes the disease into himself and the Lord of the Sabbath wins rest for his people.

For us. Mark asks again who this is, and the chapter will not let us settle for a good teacher: either he blasphemes or he is God. And it tells us whom he wants: not those who think themselves well, but the sick who know it. Our sin is not what keeps us from him; it is what he came for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Paralytic and the Authority to Forgive
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus has authority on earth to forgive sins, and he proves it. The house in Capernaum fills to the door while he preaches the word (vv. 1–2), and four men dig through the roof to lower their paralysed friend (vv. 3–4). Jesus goes first to the man’s deepest need and forgives his sins, and the scribes silently charge him with blasphemy, rightly reasoning that only God forgives (vv. 5–7). He reads their hearts and stakes the unseen pardon on a healing everyone can see (vv. 8–11), and the man walks out before them all carrying his bed (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the first place in Mark where Jesus does what belongs to God alone. Mark lets the scribes’ logic stand (see vv. 6–7), and the pardon is given on earth, to a man who had brought no sacrifice (see vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: four men digging through a roof because the door was blocked by admirers (see vv. 1–2, which ends with a warning to those already inside). Now: the friend or parent who keeps carrying a name to God for years while the door seems shut; Jesus saw their faith (v. 5).

verseByVerse.quote: And when he returned to Capernaum after some days, it was reported that he was at home. And many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even at the door. And he was preaching the word to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowds pack the house in Capernaum, and Jesus gives them what matters most: the word of God. The miracles drew them; the message was the main work.

The connection. Mark 2:1–3:6 is a series of five conflict stories: over forgiving sins (2:1–12), eating with sinners (2:13–17), fasting (2:18–22) and the Sabbath (2:23–28; 3:1–6). The opposition grows from silent questioning (2:6) to complaint (2:16), to open challenge, to a plot to destroy him (3:6).

After some days. After his preaching tour of Galilee (1:39). The healed leper had spread the news so widely that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town (1:45); he had been driven into the countryside by his own success.

At home. Probably Peter’s house (1:29). Capernaum was a fishing village of perhaps fifteen hundred people, with single-storey houses of black basalt round a courtyard, roofed with beams, branches and packed mud; a family room might be eighteen feet square. The Son of God, in this Gospel, has no headquarters. He has a friend’s spare room, packed to the door and beyond.

Preaching the word. The crowd has come because of a demon silenced, a fever broken, a leper touched, and what Jesus is doing is talking. The word is the message of the kingdom (1:15); the miracles were never the main work but the proof that the message was true. The voice filling Peter’s front room is the voice that said “let there be light”, and within the hour it will forgive a man’s sins and stand him on his feet. When Jesus preaches, the word does what it says.

In everyday life. If you are a regular in the crowded room, notice whether anyone is being kept outside because those already inside are comfortable where they are.

Is my faith fake if I first came to Jesus because I wanted help with a problem? No. Many came to him first for healing, and he received them; the four friends who came to this very house came for legs, and he gave them more. If you came for help and stayed for Christ himself, that is the ordinary story of countless believers. The danger is only in never moving past the problem: wanting Jesus as a means to something else rather than as the one worth having even if the problem stays.
verseByVerse.note: “At home” probably means Peter’s house in Capernaum (1:29).

verseByVerse.quote: And they came, bringing to him a paralytic carried by four men. And when they could not get near him because of the crowd, they removed the roof above him, and when they had made an opening, they let down the bed on which the paralytic lay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four friends refuse to let a crowd keep their paralysed friend from Jesus, and dig through the roof to reach him. Their faith is bold and costly, and it is aimed at the one person who can help.

Carried by four men. Only Mark mentions that there were four, one at each corner of the mat. The man could not come on his own. They are never named; their whole recorded contribution to the kingdom of God is that they would not accept a blocked door.

They removed the roof. Houses had flat roofs, reached by an outside staircase: beams, branches and reed matting under a thick layer of mud and straw. Literally they unroofed the roof and dug it out: mud, straw and matting came down on a packed room, and then a man on ropes. Luke speaks of tiles (Luke 5:19), picturing it for Greek city readers; Mark gives you the dirt. If this is Peter’s house, a man who had just left his nets to follow Jesus watched his own ceiling come down into his front room, and Mark records not one word of complaint. A man outside needed to get in; the roof was only a roof.

The one beneath the hole. Nobody digs through a roof for a lecture. They were sure that Jesus could heal their friend, and that he would. There is one door in the world that is never finally blocked, because the one behind it has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). Friends can carry a man to the edge. Only Christ can deal with what is lying on the mat.

What does carrying someone to Jesus look like today? Mostly ordinary things done stubbornly: praying for someone by name, for years if necessary; inviting them to church, driving them there and sitting with them; reading a Gospel with them; meeting a practical need, the childcare, the lift, the meal, so that a barrier comes down. Sometimes it means removing obstacles Christians themselves have put up, like jargon or unfriendliness. You cannot make anyone believe, but you can get them to the place where Jesus speaks.
verseByVerse.note: Houses had flat roofs of beams covered with branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stair. An opening could be dug through and repaired.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, "Son, your sins are forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sees the friends’ faith and meets the man’s deepest need first: he forgives his sins. The legs everyone is looking at can wait a moment; the guilt no one can see cannot.

When Jesus saw their faith. Faith in Scripture is not a private feeling; it climbs stairs and digs through roofs. “Their faith”: the four friends, and perhaps the man himself, though Mark tells us nothing of what he believed. Jesus looked up through the dust and saw faith, and he loved it. He is glad to be interrupted by people desperate to bring him someone they love.

Son, your sins are forgiven. “Son” is literally child, the warm word a father uses. Lowered, filthy from the ceiling, into a room of strangers and religious professionals, the man hears first a family word. “Are forgiven” is present tense: it is happening now, on Jesus’ word. God cancels the debt and will not hold it against him again: “as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12).

Why this, and not the legs? Jesus saw the ruined man, not only the ruined body. A paralytic who walked home that afternoon and died unforgiven forty years later would still be lost; a paralytic forgiven and never healed, carried on that mat to the end of his life, would be eternally safe. Jesus will heal the legs to prove that he has dealt with the soul, but he leaves nobody in doubt about which was the emergency.

Sin and sickness. Was the paralysis caused by a particular sin? Not necessarily. Sometimes suffering is tied to a specific sin (John 5:14); often it is not: of the man born blind Jesus says “it was not that this man sinned, or his parents” (John 9:1–3). But all sickness belongs to a world broken by sin, and Jesus deals with the root first.

Can my faith do for someone else what these four did for their friend? Yes and no. Yes: your faith can carry a person to the place where Jesus is, and that is what intercession does. You can bring them again and again under the preached word and into the company of his people, and refuse to accept that the case is closed. No: the man did not stay a spectator of his own healing. No one was forgiven in his place or repented for him; each must finally meet Christ himself. Your part is the roof and the ropes; the rising is God’s to give and theirs to receive. Many a believer today was once only a name on somebody’s stubborn, seemingly unanswered prayer list. Do not stop digging.

How can I know that my sins are forgiven? As this man did: by Jesus’ word. He did not feel forgiven first; he was told, and the healing confirmed it. Your confirmation is greater than his legs: the cross and the empty tomb. God promises that everyone who believes in Christ is forgiven and has peace with him (Acts 10:43; Romans 5:1), and that if we confess our sins he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9). Feelings come and go. Rest your assurance on what he has said and what Christ has done, not on how you feel this morning.
verseByVerse.note: “Son” is a warm address, like “my child.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now some of the scribes were sitting there, questioning in their hearts, "Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribes rightly see that only God can forgive sins, and wrongly conclude that Jesus is a blasphemer. In their silent verdict the charge that will one day condemn him is already formed.

Some of the scribes. Experts in the law, seated while others stood: men who had come to assess rather than to listen, and who question silently.

He is blaspheming! Blasphemy means speaking against God or claiming for oneself what belongs to God alone, and it was punishable by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). Fix the word in your mind, because it is a death sentence. At the night trial the high priest tears his garments and says, “You have heard his blasphemy”, and they all condemn him as deserving death (14:63–64). The verdict that kills Jesus is reached, silently, in a crowded front room in Capernaum, twelve chapters before it is carried out. Everything in between is the trial.

Who can forgive sins but God alone? They were right: all sin is finally against God (Psalm 51:4), and only the one offended can wipe the account; no priest, prophet or rabbi ever forgave a man in his own name.

No third option. Run their logic honestly. Only God forgives sins; this man has just forgiven sins. Either Jesus is blaspheming, or he is God. What has never been available is the comfortable middle position that he was a fine moral teacher who would be appalled at what his followers made of him. This is how Jesus claimed to be God: not with a slogan but by doing what only God does, forgiving sins, reading hearts (v. 8), and claiming lordship of the Sabbath (v. 28). His enemies understood the claim and called it blasphemy.

In everyday life. The scribes’ theology was correct, and they used it to condemn the one who forgives. It is possible to hold every doctrine correctly and still reject the Person the doctrines are about. Before you enjoy their mistake, ask whether your settled convictions about how God works have room in them for God turning up and working.
verseByVerse.note: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him alone.

parallels.desc: the same charge at his trial

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they thus questioned within themselves, said to them, "Why do you question these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Rise, take up your bed and walk'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus reads the scribes’ unspoken thoughts and turns their objection into a public test. Anyone can say that sins are forgiven; only one with God’s authority can make a paralysed man walk.

Perceiving in his spirit. Jesus answers an objection that was never spoken. Only God knows the heart: “you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind” (1 Kings 8:39; Jeremiah 17:10). So within moments he does two things that belong to God alone, forgiving sin and reading the heart, and the men best equipped to notice are the ones being read.

Which is easier. Easier to say: the exact wording decides the argument. “Your sins are forgiven” is the easy sentence, because nothing visible changes when you say it; a charlatan could say it in every village in Galilee for a decade and never be caught. “Rise, take up your bed and walk” is checkable in about four seconds in front of a packed room, and if the man does not move you are finished. To actually do either requires the power of God.

The reverse of a fraud. So Jesus does the opposite of what a fraud does: he hangs the invisible claim on a visible, immediate, public test, and tells the room in advance. The apostles do the same with the resurrection. Paul does not tell the Corinthians to rest on an experience; he says that if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Corinthians 15:14, 17), and he lists the surviving eyewitnesses. Christianity has always staked itself on things that happened in public.

Can a modern person really believe a healing like this? The honest answer turns on who Jesus is. If he is only a man, a paralysed man standing up at a word is impossible. If he is the God who made that man’s legs and holds every nerve in being (Colossians 1:16–17), it is no harder for him than speaking was at creation. Mark asks you not to believe in miracles in general but to look at this person, his words, his claims, his death and his empty tomb, and decide who he is; though, as Jesus warned, a heart set against him may not be persuaded even by a miracle (Luke 16:31). And notice what your own faith rests on: not a mood that no fact could confirm or disprove, but public, historical facts, a man who died under Pontius Pilate and rose bodily on the third day, seen by many witnesses. Feelings are good gifts, but they are the weather; the facts are the ground.

verseByVerse.quote: But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins"—he said to the paralytic— "I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, the Son of Man of Daniel’s vision, proves his authority to forgive sins on earth by commanding the paralysed man to rise and go home. The argument is for the scribes; the command is for the man on the floor.

But that you may know. The visible healing will prove the invisible forgiveness. Mid-sentence Mark notes that Jesus turns: “he said to the paralytic”.

The Son of Man. This is the first time in Mark that Jesus names himself, and it is his favourite name for himself. In ordinary Aramaic the phrase could mean simply a human being, but Jesus is reaching back to Daniel 7, where the prophet sees one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, presented before God, and given dominion and glory and a kingdom, so that all peoples and nations should serve him, an everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13–14). In the Old Testament the one who rides the clouds is God, yet Daniel’s figure is truly human: Jesus says that he is that figure, and he uses the authority of that everlasting kingdom on a Galilean afternoon to forgive a paralysed man and send him home. Before Mark is finished, this name will carry both his throne and his cross: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45).

On earth. Two small words move the place where forgiveness is found: not in heaven after you die, nor ninety miles south in Jerusalem through a priest and a lamb and a curtain and a fee, but here, in a crowded front room, from the mouth of a man you could touch, to somebody who had brought no sacrifice and could not have carried one if he had.

Go home. Three commands, all impossible for a paralysed man, and carrying his own mat would show the healing was complete. The third is the tender one. He is not sent to the temple or to a rabbi, but home, where whoever had learned to step around a mat on the floor is about to look up and see him in the doorway on his own legs, carrying the thing that carried him. Jesus does not merely repair you and leave you standing in the road. He sends you home.

In everyday life. If there is something you keep confessing because you do not believe it has really been forgiven, take this verse as the receipt, and go home today as someone forgiven.

Should I confess my sins to a pastor or priest to be forgiven? You need no one but Christ between you and God. “There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5), and you may go to him directly, at any time, and be forgiven. Scripture also tells believers to confess their sins to one another and pray for one another (James 5:16). A trusted, mature Christian cannot absolve you, but can pray for you, hold you to account and remind you of the gospel. That is a mercy, not a requirement for forgiveness.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man receives everlasting dominion

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and immediately picked up his bed and went out before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, "We never saw anything like this!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man walks out healed before them all, the public proof that his sins are forgiven, and the crowd glorifies God. Yet their amazement stops at the miracle and does not reach what it was for.

Before them all. “Immediately”: no convalescence, and the test is settled publicly, in front of the very scribes who had silently convicted him. The crowd that had blocked the man’s way in now parted to let him walk out, and the mat that had been the sign of his helplessness went home over his shoulder as evidence.

Never anything like this. Something new had come, and they glorified God. But no one in that room is recorded asking, “If he can do that to a man’s legs with a word, what has he just done to a man’s guilt, and could he do it for me?” They had been handed the proof, in the terms Jesus himself set, and their astonishment stopped at the miracle and never reached the thing the miracle was for.

Pardoned and whole. God’s forgiveness and God’s power stood in one room in one man, and a paralysed sinner walked out pardoned and whole. Nobody had seen anything like it, because nothing like him had ever walked the earth. Glory to God, who in Jesus forgives all our iniquity and heals all our diseases, redeems our life from the pit and crowns us with steadfast love and mercy (Psalm 103:3–4). The man had his legs for the rest of his earthly life. The pardon he walked out with, he has still.

Is it wrong to pray about my circumstances rather than my soul? No. The four friends came for the legs, and Jesus did not scold them; God invites us to bring him everything, including health, money, work and family (Philippians 4:6). The danger is when the whole list is legs: when we want him for what he might fix and never come to him for what he came to forgive. Ask for both, and put them in his order.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — Levi, Sinners, and New Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus has come for sinners, and what he brings is a wedding, not a patch. He calls Levi the tax collector from his booth with two words (vv. 13–14), and at Levi’s table, crowded with people the religious had written off, he answers the scribes’ complaint: a doctor comes for the sick (vv. 15–17). Asked why his disciples do not fast, he calls himself the bridegroom, whose presence is joy, and gives the first hint that he will be taken away (vv. 18–20). Two household pictures, cloth and wineskins, make one point: his new life cannot be sewn onto the old religion (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The two small parables of vv. 21–22 are the hinge of the chapter. In both, the old thing is asked to hold what it was never made to hold, and the last clause is the promise: new wine is for fresh wineskins. Both points are unfolded in the note on vv. 21–22.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Levi cannot yet explain a doctrine, so he cooks, and gets the only people he knows into a room with Jesus. Now: the newest Christian usually knows many people outside the church. Levi’s method needs no course: buy the food, make the call, be in the room (on going as a follower of Christ, see vv. 15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: He went out again beside the sea, and all the crowd was coming to him, and he was teaching them. And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, "Follow me." And he rose and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls Levi, a despised tax collector, to follow him, and Levi leaves his booth at once. The authority that has just forgiven a paralysed man now reaches the man the whole town had written off.

Beside the sea. Jesus teaches along the shore and passes a customs post. Mark puts the call straight after the healing, and the order makes the point: Jesus has just shown his authority to forgive (2:10), and now he uses it on the most obviously sinful man in town.

Levi the son of Alphaeus. Levi is called Matthew in the first Gospel (Matthew 9:9; 10:3), probably his birth name and his later one. The first Gospel, which the early church held to be Matthew’s own, adds “the tax collector” to his name in the list of apostles, which nobody else does. A forgiven man is not embarrassed by his past. His booth was probably on the trade road near Capernaum, taking customs at the border between the territories of Herod Antipas and Philip: a licence to print money. The man who once kept the accounts of the ruling powers now keeps, in the first book of the New Testament, the record of the King.

Tax collectors. The collector bid for the contract, paid the authorities up front, and lived on whatever he could extract above that figure. Tax collectors were despised for serving the ruling powers, for cheating, and for contact with Gentiles that made them ritually unclean. They were classed with sinners and prostitutes (Matthew 21:31). And there was worse. The road back for a thief ran through restitution: you repaid what you took and added a fifth (Leviticus 6:5; Numbers 5:7). A tax collector who had defrauded hundreds of people over years could hardly trace them all, and to his own religion his repentance looked impossible. That is the man Jesus stops for.

Follow me. The same call as to the fishermen (1:17), with no interview, no probation, and no requirement that he first put anything right. That is the grace of God in Christ: it does not wait for us to make ourselves acceptable; it calls us, and the call makes us new.

He rose and followed. Peter’s nets were still there to go back to (John 21:3). Levi stood up from a booth that somebody else would be sitting in by the afternoon; there was no going back, and everyone in Capernaum knew it. Money, the thing he had sold his good name for, could not come with him. When Christ becomes the treasure, the old treasure loses its grip, not because it is torn away but because something better has come in (Matthew 13:44).

The debt he could not pay. The one who stopped at the booth had come to settle an account no tax collector could ever settle. The debt Levi owed to God, larger than everything he had taken from his neighbours, would be met by the man now calling him, who came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45). God has cancelled the record of debt that stood against us, setting it aside by nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). Levi made out other men’s bills for a living. Christ came to pay his.

In everyday life. Who have you written off: a relative, a colleague, yourself? Bring each of them to God this week. The man Jesus chose to be an apostle was the one man in town whose religion had already given up on him.

If I become a Christian, must I leave a job that is morally compromised? It depends on what makes it compromised. Collecting taxes was not itself sinful: John the Baptist told tax collectors to collect no more than they were authorised to (Luke 3:12–13), and Paul tells Christians to pay taxes (Romans 13:6–7). What had to stop was the fraud; when Zacchaeus met Jesus he gave half his goods to the poor and repaid fourfold anyone he had cheated (Luke 19:8). If your work requires you to lie or cheat, you must stop, even if it costs you the job. If the work is lawful but your practice has been crooked, change the practice, put right what you can, and serve Christ there. Ask a wise pastor to help you think it through.
verseByVerse.note: Tax collectors gathered tolls for the ruling authorities and were widely despised as collaborators and cheats.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he reclined at table in his house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many who followed him. And the scribes of the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, "Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sits at table with tax collectors and sinners, and the scribes are scandalised, because a shared table meant acceptance. That is exactly what Jesus meant it to say.

At table in his house. Levi’s first act as a disciple is to give a party: Luke tells us he made Jesus a great feast in his house (Luke 5:29). Guests reclined round a low table, as at a banquet.

Tax collectors and sinners. Levi invited the only people he knew. “Sinners” was almost a technical term for people known for immoral lives, or whose way of life put them outside the purity rules: everyone the religious establishment had written off. And they were already drawn to him. Timothy Keller often pointed out, in The Prodigal God, that the people drawn to Jesus were the irreligious and the morally loose, while the devout were offended by him; and that if our churches do not draw the kind of people Jesus drew, we may not be preaching the message he preached.

Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners? The question comes from the scribes of the Pharisees, a name that probably means the separated ones: a movement devoted to strict keeping of the law and its traditions, including purity rules about food and table company. In that world a shared table meant acceptance and friendship, peace between the people at it. To eat with a man you regarded as unclean was to say in the most public way available that there was no barrier between you. Jesus did it, and everybody in Capernaum could read what that said. The scribes take their complaint to his new followers, who are easier to unsettle.

This man receives sinners. That is how Luke words the same complaint on another occasion (Luke 15:2). It is meant as an accusation, and it is the gospel. Isaiah had promised that on God’s mountain the LORD would make for all peoples a feast of rich food and well-aged wine, and swallow up death for ever (Isaiah 25:6–8). The peace Jesus offered over Levi’s food was real, because he would make it real: he came to reconcile enemies to God by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). The Pharisees saw the company he kept. They did not see that the true host at this table was the LORD, beginning the feast Isaiah promised.

How do I keep real friendships with people far from God without condemning them or signing off on everything? Jesus answers by being at the table rather than drawing a line around it. But he is not there blending in, nor as a fellow patient: he ends the evening by calling the guests sick people who need a doctor (v. 17). So go, eat, listen, laugh and love; and go as yourself, a follower of Christ, unashamed of him. Most of us fail in one of two directions. The Pharisees would not go in at all and called it holiness. Others go in, sit down, say nothing about Christ for fifteen years, and call it grace. Jesus went in, and went in as himself.

How far can I join in? In everything good: the food, the friendship, the conversation, the celebration. Not in what is sinful: drunkenness, crude talk, gossip, cruelty. Jesus was accused of being a drunkard (Matthew 11:19), but the accusation was false. If time with certain friends regularly draws you into sin, change the setting: invite them home, meet over coffee, or take a Christian friend with you. “Bad company ruins good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33), but holy company can be the best thing that ever happened to a sinner.

Uncertain wording. Mark says only “in his house”, which on its own could mean Jesus’ house or Levi’s; Luke makes clear it was Levi’s (Luke 5:29). The next phrase is also compressed, literally for there were many, and they were following him. It most likely means that many tax collectors and sinners had begun to follow Jesus, though it could mean simply that great crowds were following him.
verseByVerse.note: At a formal meal guests lay on couches around a low table, leaning on one elbow, hence “reclined.” “Sinners” here means people known for ignoring the law.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus heard it, he said to them, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus came as a doctor for the sick: he calls those who know they are sinners, not those who think they are well. His holiness does not shrink from sinners; it heals them.

No need of a physician. Jesus is not agreeing that the Pharisees are spiritually healthy. He is taking them at their word: very well, if you are well, you will not want a doctor, and you will not get one. The man who will not admit he is ill dies of something treatable.

I came. He states it of his whole mission. On the lips of the one who says he came from the Father into the world (John 16:28), the words mean more than that he arrived to do a job: he was somewhere before, and had business here.

Not to call the righteous, but sinners. The righteous are those who think they are, like the Pharisees, and so see no need of him; in truth no one is righteous (Romans 3:10). Luke adds: “to repentance” (Luke 5:32). And here is what makes it good news rather than merely fair-minded: the only thing that qualifies you for Christ is the very thing you thought ruled you out.

It cuts two ways. If you fear you are too far gone, read the sentence again: he did not come for the respectable and take the odd sinner as an exception. You are not the awkward case; you are the stated purpose of the visit. But if your quiet position is that you are basically all right, decent, churchgoing, never did anybody much harm, then this verse is not a comfort and is not meant to be. There are the sick who know it and the sick who do not, and only one group ever sends for the doctor. The Pharisees went home from Levi’s house with their reputations intact and their sins intact.

The Physician died of it. Doctors keep their distance; this one came into the ward, took the disease into his own body, and died of it, so that the patients would live. By his wounds we are healed. At Levi’s table he was beginning that work, and he has never lost a patient who came to him.

If Jesus came for sinners, why should I try to be good? Because the doctor does not come to the sick to leave them sick. He calls sinners to repentance, and those he heals begin to get well. You do not try to be good to qualify for him; you try because he has taken you on as his patient and the medicine is working: his Spirit now lives in you (Romans 8:11). You will not be fully well this side of glory (1 John 1:8), and you need not be: the Physician was the one healthy man, his perfect obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), and your halting obedience is accepted for his sake. Sin is the disease, not the freedom. Anyone who wants Christ’s forgiveness but not his healing has not understood what kind of doctor he is.

parallels.desc: “to seek and to save the lost”

verseByVerse.quote: Now John's disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him, "Why do John's disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?" And Jesus said to them, "Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in that day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ disciples do not fast because the bridegroom is with them, and Jesus is that bridegroom. His presence is a wedding, not a funeral; but he will be taken away, and then they will fast.

John’s disciples and the Pharisees. An odd alliance, united in bewilderment, because everybody serious fasts. The law required only the fast of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29), but the Pharisees fasted twice a week; the man in Jesus’ parable says so with some pride (Luke 18:12). John was by now in prison (1:14), but his disciples kept up the disciplined life he had taught them, fasting often and offering prayers (Luke 5:33). By any measure of the day, a teacher whose followers did not fast was not a serious teacher; it was a fair question.

Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? Jesus does not defend his disciples; he changes the question, with a picture every listener had stood inside. A Jewish wedding lasted up to a week, a time of feasting and joy. The wedding guests are literally the sons of the bridechamber, the groom’s closest friends, who ran the celebration; later rabbinic writings record that they were excused from certain religious duties for the week, because you cannot mourn and rejoice at once. Fasting then would be like refusing the food in the corner of a wedding feast, with the bridegroom in the room.

Who is the bridegroom? In the Old Testament that role belongs to one Person, and there is no second candidate. “Your Maker is your husband, the LORD of hosts is his name” (Isaiah 54:5). “As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5). “I will betroth you to me forever” (Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus takes God’s own title without a word of explanation, in an answer about diet: the second enormous claim of the chapter, and this time nobody seems to have noticed. And it tells you what he thinks his presence is: not an inspection but a wedding, the happiest week in a village’s life, food and wine and noise and a groom who cannot stop smiling. If your religion feels nothing like that, it is worth asking whether you have understood who is in the room.

When the bridegroom is taken away. Then the light goes out of the sentence. Bridegrooms are not removed from their own weddings. “Taken away” may suggest violent removal: this is Jesus’ first hint in Mark of his death, dropped into a cheerful answer about fasting, before any opponent has laid a finger on him.

Then they will fast. After his departure his disciples did fast (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). Jesus did not abolish fasting; he said its time was coming. And when he taught about it he said not “if you fast” but “when you fast” (Matthew 6:16–17), which is not the language of an optional extra for specialists.

What fasting is for. Not to get God’s attention or pay something off, but to make the body say what the heart means: you go hungry for a few hours so that a real, insistent ache reminds you, every twenty minutes, of a deeper hunger you have been feeding with everything except God. And Jesus gives the reason: we fast because the Bridegroom has been taken away and we want him back. It is not gloom. It is longing for someone who has promised to return.

How do I start fasting, and who should not? Start absurdly small. Miss one meal this week, tell nobody (Matthew 6:17–18), and spend the time with the Bible open, praying about one specific thing. Drink water. If you are pregnant or nursing, diabetic, on medication that must be taken with food, elderly and frail, or have ever struggled with an eating disorder, do not fast from food without medical advice; fast instead from something else, a screen, a habit, a pleasure, for the same purpose. Fasting is never a measure of your standing with God, and no one should be pressured into it.
verseByVerse.note: A wedding lasted days and was no time for fasting.

parallels.desc: the one yearly fast the law commanded
a Pharisee who fasted twice a week

verseByVerse.quote: No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the patch tears away from it, the new from the old, and a worse tear is made. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins—and the wine is destroyed, and so are the skins. But new wine is for fresh wineskins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new life Jesus brings cannot be sewn onto the old religion or poured into its old forms; it needs something new to hold it. Two household pictures, cloth and wine, make one point.

Unshrunk cloth. New cloth off the loom is unshrunk. Sew a piece of it onto a garment washed a hundred times, and it looks like a decent repair until it gets wet; then the patch pulls tight, rips away and takes the old fabric with it. Mark’s summary is bleak and exact: “a worse tear is made”, and the repair did it.

New wine. Wine was carried in whole goatskins. New wine is still fermenting; it gives off gas and swells hard against its container, so it went into a new skin with stretch left in it. An old, stiff skin simply bursts.

Different in kind. Neither picture attacks the old thing; it is asked to hold what it was never built to hold. The life Jesus brings cannot simply be patched onto the Pharisees’ religion, with its traditions, fasts and purity rules. It is different in kind, and the joy and freedom of the kingdom need new forms.

Patchwork religion. Most of us instinctively approach religion as patchwork. We take the life we have, with the self firmly in charge, and sew something on: church on Sunday, a habit of prayer, a tidied-up vocabulary, a few things given up. So half-Christianity keeps tearing under strain, and people conclude that faith does not work, when what has failed is the repair job. Patchwork is now also the respectable way to be spiritual. In the 1980s the sociologist Robert Bellah and his colleagues, in Habits of the Heart, interviewed a young nurse who called her religion “Sheilaism”: “Just my own little voice.” Many today build the same way: a little mindfulness, a favourite verse, an idea or two from the East. But a god assembled from my own preferences can never tell me anything I do not already think. He cannot surprise me, contradict me or forgive me, because he is only my own voice played back. The Pharisees sewed their patches onto the law; the modern seeker sews them onto the self; both keep the old garment and stay in charge of the sewing.

Fresh wineskins. Jesus offers neither a patch nor a style. He offers himself, new wine that fits no container we design, and the gospel is in the last clause: he gives the skin. “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26). Whoever is joined to Christ is a new creation, the old gone and the new come (2 Corinthians 5:17). This does not erase your personality; God gives new desires at the root, so that you begin to want him, to hate the sin you once enjoyed and to love his people, and a heart like that can hold the life Christ pours in without tearing (Philippians 2:13). Making the vessel is his work, which is exactly why you can ask him for it. Only a God who is not my own creation can love me as I am and still make me new.

The wine he would pour. The new wine is the life of the kingdom, and Mark will show what it cost. At the last supper Jesus took the cup, called it his blood of the covenant, poured out for many, and said he would not drink of the fruit of the vine again until he drinks it new in the kingdom of God (14:24–25). The wine that bursts old skins was pressed out of him. It can never be stitched onto anyone’s religion as an improvement: it is a covenant made in his blood.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is worthless; Jesus fulfils it (Matthew 5:17). The old garments and wineskins are the human traditions of the religious system, not God’s word. Nor is Jesus contrasting old-fashioned with modern, hymns with new songs, or liturgy with informality. A brand-new church can be as much a patch on the old self as an ancient one, and many old forms rooted in Scripture are excellent wineskins for the new wine. Ask of any practice not whether it is old or new but whether it serves the free grace of Christ or competes with it.
verseByVerse.note: Wineskins were goatskins. New wine is still fermenting and expanding; an old skin has lost its stretch and splits.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Sabbath is God’s gift to people, and Jesus is its Lord. The disciples pluck grain as they walk, which the law allowed, and the Pharisees count it as Sabbath work (vv. 23–24). Jesus answers with the story of David, the anointed but rejected king, given the holy bread for his hungry men (vv. 25–26). Then two sentences reset everything: the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath, and the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology: To be lord of the Sabbath is a very large claim. The day goes back to creation and to Sinai, and the rest it pointed to is found in a Person (see vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: hungry men eating grain on a walk, and experts who had gone out into a field on a Sabbath to watch for an infringement. Now: the same instinct wherever keeping a form matters more than the person it was meant to serve: the church that notices a visitor’s clothes before his face, the family where the standard is enforced and the child is not enjoyed.

verseByVerse.quote: One Sabbath he was going through the grainfields, and as they made their way, his disciples began to pluck heads of grain. And the Pharisees were saying to him, "Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees accuse Jesus’ hungry disciples of breaking the Sabbath for doing what the law itself allowed. Their rules had made them sharp-eyed about the deed and blind to the men.

Through the grainfields. The Sabbath was the seventh day, Saturday, when God commanded rest from work, remembering creation and the exodus (Exodus 20:8–11; Deuteronomy 5:12–15); it was the sign of the covenant with Israel (Exodus 31:13). The disciples are walking a path through standing grain; fields were unfenced and paths ran between them.

Pluck heads of grain. Luke adds that they rubbed them in their hands (Luke 6:1), loosening the husk so that the chaff could be blown away and the grain eaten. It is what a hungry man does on a walk, and the law of Moses expressly allowed it: travellers could pick grain by hand from a neighbour’s field, though not put a sickle to it (Deuteronomy 23:25). This is not a story about stealing; the issue was the day. And the Lord of the harvest walked through his own fields with his hungry friends, and let them eat.

Why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath? The Pharisees’ traditions listed thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work, and the disciples had touched three of them in a single mouthful: pulling the head off was reaping, rubbing it was threshing, blowing away the husk was winnowing. The list was written down later, in the Mishnah (about AD 200), but it gathers rulings already taught in Jesus’ day. The earlier disputes in this chapter ended in an answer; the two Sabbath scenes end in a plot (3:6), because the Sabbath was the most visible mark of Israel’s faithfulness, and a teacher who claimed to be its Lord was touching the centre.

How did the Pharisees see it? They were there: on a Sabbath, out along a path through the fields, close enough to watch whether any of these men would put a hand out. Their first word, “look”, is almost a shout; they had been waiting for this. That energy is alive in every generation, dressed as faithfulness. It is possible to be scrupulously careful about a rule and hard as flint about a person; to notice at a glance everything out of place in somebody’s life, and never once notice that he is hungry. Their own Scriptures had told them what to look for: “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6).

The charge is brought to the Master. The Pharisees accuse the disciples, but they bring the accusation to Jesus, and he takes it up as his own. This teacher never leaves his people to face their accusers alone. He stands between them and the charge, a small scene of something far larger: Christ Jesus, who died and was raised, is at the right hand of God interceding for us, and no charge against God’s elect can stand (Romans 8:33–34).

In everyday life. The next time you are sharply critical of another Christian, how he brings up his children, what he does with his Sundays, ask whether you are standing at the edge of the field with a clear view of the rule and none at all of the man.

Is it wrong to have rules in a church or a family? No. Rules can be wise and loving, like a church’s rule that its children’s workers be checked. The trouble comes when human rules are treated as God’s law, used to judge other believers, or kept in a way that crushes the people they were meant to serve. Ask of any rule: does Scripture command this, or did we decide it? If we decided it, hold it humbly and do not bind other consciences with it (Colossians 2:20–23). That includes the Lord’s Day itself (see “Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today” in the note on vv. 27–28). And never let a rule stop you from seeing the person in front of you.
verseByVerse.note: The objection was that plucking counted as harvesting, which was work.

parallels.desc: picking grain by hand was allowed

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Have you never read what David did, when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God, in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers from Scripture: when David and his hungry men ate the holy bread, Scripture did not condemn them, because God’s ceremonial rules were never meant to leave the needy unfed.

What David did. The story is 1 Samuel 21:1–6. David is already anointed king and not yet on the throne. He is running from Saul with a few men, in need and hungry, and at the tabernacle at Nob he is given the holy bread by the priest.

The bread of the Presence. Twelve loaves placed fresh before the LORD each Sabbath, the old ones afterwards eaten by priests only, as a most holy portion (Leviticus 24:5–9).

The argument. David ate the holy bread and gave it to those who were with him, breaking a ceremonial law, and neither God nor the narrator rebukes him. Human need takes priority over ceremonial rules. But the choice of this story makes a second, sharper point. Jesus picks the anointed king, rejected, unrecognised, on the road with his men, being fed from the holy table. If David’s men could eat the holy bread because of who was with them, how much more the disciples of David’s greater Son. He is the true bread of the Presence, the bread of God come down from heaven, and he does not keep the holy things from his hungry people.

Does this mean I may break any rule when I am in need? No. Jesus is speaking about ceremonial rules, like the bread of the Presence, and about the Pharisees’ additions to the Sabbath law. He never suggests that need excuses breaking God’s moral law: hunger does not justify stealing, and loneliness does not justify adultery. God’s moral commands, to love him and our neighbour, are themselves the shape of mercy. But his laws were given for our good, and a reading of them that leaves a hungry man unfed has misunderstood the God who gave them.

Uncertain wording. “In the time of Abiathar the high priest.” A reader with a reference Bible will notice that 1 Samuel 21 names the priest as Ahimelech, Abiathar’s father. Abiathar was there (he escaped the massacre that followed, 1 Samuel 22:20) and later became the more famous high priest under David. There are good answers. The phrase may mean in the days of Abiathar, who was a priest then and became the better-known high priest, as we might say in the days of King David about events before he was king. Or it may mean at the passage about Abiathar: with no chapter numbers, a teacher located a text by its best-known figure, as Jesus does with “the passage about the bush” (12:26); then Jesus is giving a reference, not a date. Or the names were sometimes interchanged (2 Samuel 8:17 and 1 Chronicles 18:16 have Ahimelech son of Abiathar). None is certain, but each is reasonable. This commentary’s view: no error; the phrase identifies the period or passage by its most famous priest. Nothing in the argument depends on it: Jesus is not resting his case on which priest was on duty, and the Pharisees, who knew that chapter far better than we do, are not recorded raising the objection.
verseByVerse.note: On the name Abiathar (1 Samuel 21 names the priest Ahimelech), see the commentary.

parallels.desc: the bread of the Presence, eaten by priests

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made the Sabbath as a gift for people, not a burden to carry, and Jesus, the Son of Man, is its Lord. He has the right to say what the day means, and what it pointed to is the rest he gives.

Made for man. Only Mark records this saying. Its roots go back before Israel: God rested on the seventh day, blessed it and made it holy (Genesis 2:2–3), centuries before Sinai, though the command to keep it was first given to Israel (Exodus 16:23–30; Nehemiah 9:14). It was a kindness: rest for weary people, a day to delight in God (Isaiah 58:13–14; Exodus 23:12). In Deuteronomy it comes with the memory of Egypt, where slaves had no such day (Deuteronomy 5:15). The Pharisees had taken a day designed to lift a burden off a man’s back and turned it into a burden to carry, as if people existed to serve the rules. The gift had become an examination.

Lord even of the Sabbath. The Sabbath was the LORD’s day (Exodus 20:10). Jesus claims authority over it: the right to say what it means and how it should be kept, a claim only God could make. If the day was made for man, then the Son of Man, the one Daniel saw given dominion over all peoples, is its lord. He is telling a group of experts, in a cornfield, that the day belongs to him.

The Sabbath and Christ. The Sabbath always pointed past itself, to the rest Jesus gives (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). For more than a thousand years a nation rehearsed every seventh evening something it did not yet have. Then the rest itself walked through the standing grain with a handful of hungry men, and was told off for it by the people guarding the rehearsal. After his resurrection on the first day of the week, Christians gathered on that day, the Lord’s Day (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10). That is what it means to say the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ: not that rest no longer matters, but that what the day pictured has arrived in a person.

The Sabbath that will never end. He still says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). He is Lord of the Sabbath because he made it, and he gave its rest at the cost of a Friday on which he had no rest at all; he lay in the tomb through the Sabbath and rose on the first day of a new week. Because he finished his work, whoever trusts him may cease from working to earn God’s favour (Hebrews 4:10), and the rest he won is the one Sabbath that will never end.

What it means to rest in Christ. Many of us are never truly off duty, even on holiday, because underneath the busyness runs a project: proving that we are worth something, to others, to ourselves, to God. The rest Christ gives is not first a day off but a verdict: the case for your worth before God has been settled by his life, death and resurrection, and you cannot add to it or take from it. It shows when you can fail and not be destroyed, go to bed with the work unfinished, let someone else take the credit. When the old drivenness rises, name it to him, and remind yourself that the work that matters most is already finished.

What neither side disputes. The day is a gift and not a scoring system. Do you stop? Not slow down; stop. Most of us now miss the gift of rest not by putting a hand to grain, but by never taking a hand off anything. Stopping is frightening because things carry on without you, and you find out you were not holding the world up: the humiliation in it, and precisely the rest in it. “It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2). A day of rest is a weekly, physical confession that you are not God.

What if my job requires me to work on Sundays? Then you are in good company: doctors, nurses, carers, police, firefighters and many others do necessary and merciful work that cannot stop, and Jesus himself defended doing good on the Sabbath (3:4). On this commentary’s view (see the box below) you are not sinning by doing it; and even those who hold the stricter Westminster and 1689 view count works of necessity and mercy as right on the Lord’s Day (Westminster 21.8; 1689 22.8). Do your work as service to Christ. Then guard what you can: gather with God’s people whenever possible, perhaps at another service, and take a real day of rest elsewhere in your week. If you have a choice and Sunday work keeps you from church week after week, ask whether you could rearrange things. The aim is not a rule kept but a heart that gathers with God’s people, worships and rests.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Christians who love the Bible have not landed in the same place on this. Some keep Saturday as the Sabbath. Many Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, holding that the fourth commandment, rooted in creation and written into the Ten, still binds one day in seven, now observed on the day of the resurrection (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8); this view is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, so that no day is binding as a Sabbath, pointing to Paul: one person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike (Romans 14:5–6), and let no one pass judgment on you with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath (Colossians 2:16–17); Sunday is then the Lord’s Day for gathering. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest. The Lord’s Day is a gift: Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom, not as a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). Believers who keep a stricter Sabbath should be honoured, not judged.

2.theology:
The scribes and Pharisees are not cardboard villains. They are serious people defending serious convictions, and on forgiveness they are exactly right. Their error is that they have not recognised the one the law was pointing to, and they try to fit him into their old forms, like new wine into old skins.

So the chapter shows four reasons Jesus could not simply be absorbed into the religion of his day: he forgives sins directly, not through the temple; he welcomes the excluded to his table; he calls his presence a wedding, not a fast; and he claims lordship over the Sabbath itself. Not because he is lawless, but because he is the law’s Lord.
2.examples:
The Pharisees’ unease at Jesus eating with sinners deserves a fair hearing: their concern for purity was a serious attempt to guard the holiness God commanded, under pagan occupation. But they assumed that eating with a sinner meant approving of his sin. Jesus was among sinners as a physician among the sick (see v. 17).

Then: Pharisees keeping their distance to stay clean, while the one truly clean man in Capernaum reclined at a tax collector’s table. Now: the two opposite failures named in the note on vv. 15–16.

keyVerse.quote: But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins
keyVerse.note: This is the claim the whole chapter turns on. Jesus does what the scribes rightly say only God can do, and stakes it on a healing everyone can see; the doctor of sinners, the bridegroom and the lord of the Sabbath are the same authority, always used in mercy. It is also the first time in Mark that Jesus calls himself the Son of Man, the name that will carry both his throne and his cross.

2.reflection:
The four friends would not let a crowd or a roof keep their friend from Jesus (vv. 3–5). Who is on your heart, and what might it look like to carry them to him in the coming weeks, in prayer and in practical help?

Jesus dealt with the man’s sins before his legs (v. 5). What do you most often ask God for, and what would it mean to put his priorities first in your prayers, while still bringing him everything else?

The scribes were right that only God can forgive sins, yet used that truth to condemn Jesus (vv. 6–7), and the Pharisees were careful about the Sabbath and blind to hungry men (vv. 23–24). Where might our own correct convictions keep us from seeing Christ, or from seeing the people in front of us?

Jesus came not for the righteous but for sinners, like a doctor for the sick, and he calls his presence a wedding (vv. 17, 19). How does it change the way you see yourself, and the people you find hardest to welcome, that sin is what he came for? Whom might we invite to our table?

3.title: By Whose Power?
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Again he entered the synagogue, and a man was there with a withered hand. <sup>2</sup>And they watched Jesus, to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him. <sup>3</sup>And he said to the man with the withered hand, “Come here.” <sup>4</sup>And he said to them, “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?” But they were silent. <sup>5</sup>And he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored. <sup>6</sup>The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him. <sup>7</sup>Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great crowd followed, from Galilee and Judea <sup>8</sup>and Jerusalem and Idumea and from beyond the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon. When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him. <sup>9</sup>And he told his disciples to have a boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they crush him, <sup>10</sup>for he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him. <sup>11</sup>And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out, “You are the Son of God.” <sup>12</sup>And he strictly ordered them not to make him known. <sup>13</sup>And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. <sup>14</sup>And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach <sup>15</sup>and have authority to cast out demons. <sup>16</sup>He appointed the twelve: Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter); <sup>17</sup>James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder); <sup>18</sup>Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Zealot, <sup>19</sup>and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. <sup>20</sup>Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. <sup>21</sup>And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, “He is out of his mind.” <sup>22</sup>And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem were saying, “He is possessed by Beelzebul,” and “by the prince of demons he casts out the demons.” <sup>23</sup>And he called them to him and said to them in parables, “How can Satan cast out Satan? <sup>24</sup>If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. <sup>25</sup>And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. <sup>26</sup>And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end. <sup>27</sup>But no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house. <sup>28</sup>“Truly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, <sup>29</sup>but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin”— <sup>30</sup>for they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.” <sup>31</sup>And his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent to him and called him. <sup>32</sup>And a crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, “Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you.” <sup>33</sup>And he answered them, “Who are my mother and my brothers?” <sup>34</sup>And looking about at those who sat around him, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! <sup>35</sup>For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother.”
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 ends the five conflict stories begun in 2:1 and opens a new stage: rejected by Israel’s leaders, Jesus begins to gather a new people around himself.

The message. Jesus is not a teacher to be admired from a safe distance; he is the stronger one who has come into Satan’s house to set his captives free, and everyone must decide where they stand with him. Opposition hardens on every side, from the leaders, his family and Jerusalem’s scribes, yet he chooses twelve to be with him, offers forgiveness for every sin but one, and names as his family all who do the will of God.

Why it was said. Mark’s first readers knew what it was to be called mad or dangerous for following Jesus, and to be handed over by their own families (13:12–13; see the introduction). Here they saw their Lord walk that road first, and learned where their true home was.

How the chapter makes its case. In a watched synagogue the Lord of the Sabbath restores a withered hand, and the Pharisees walk out to plot his death with Herod’s supporters, parties who agreed on nothing else (vv. 1–6). The whole land, Jew and Gentile, crowds to him at the lake, and demons who know him are silenced (vv. 7–12). On the mountain he appoints twelve, Israel beginning again, first to be with him and then to be sent out (vv. 13–19). Then Mark sets the scribes’ verdict, evil, inside his family’s verdict, mad (vv. 20–35). Jesus answers with the strong man bound and plundered and a warning about blasphemy against the Spirit, and the chapter ends with his relatives outside and a crowd of strangers inside at his feet.

Where it leads. The stronger man would bind the strong man by letting himself be bound: in the garden, before the council, and on the cross, where he disarmed the powers of darkness (Colossians 2:15). The hand stretched out and restored points to his own hands stretched out on the wood. The one who suffered outside the gate brings outsiders in, and he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

For us. The chapter puts to every reader the question of its last scene: inside with him, or outside sending messages in? Nearness and correct beliefs do not settle it; the demons knew his name. Come and sit at his feet, and you will find yourself in a family.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Withered Hand and the Widening Response
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath who does good, and his goodness divides people: the leaders who should have rejoiced plot his death, while the whole land comes to him. In a watched synagogue he restores a man’s withered hand and asks the question his critics cannot answer: is the Sabbath for doing good or harm? (vv. 1–5). Their silence becomes a plot, as Pharisees and Herodians, who agreed on nothing else, unite against him (v. 6). He withdraws to the lake, where crowds from every region, Jew and Gentile, press to touch him (vv. 7–10), and he silences the demons who know exactly who he is (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Why does Jesus silence the demons when what they say about him is true? Partly timing, and partly because right belief about Christ is not the same as belonging to him (both are treated fully at vv. 11–12). This chapter will end by saying who does belong.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man with a withered hand told to stand up in the middle of a watched synagogue, before anything had been healed.

Now: obedience that makes a person visible before the outcome is known: the first time you say at work that you are a Christian; an apology with no guarantee it will be received. (On being exposed first and healed second, see vv. 3–4.)

And the watchers saw a crippled man made whole and were not moved at all. It is possible to sit in a room where God is plainly at work and be occupied only with whether it is being done properly.

verseByVerse.quote: Again he entered the synagogue, and a man was there with a withered hand. And they watched Jesus, to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ enemies watched him not to learn from him but to catch him, using a disabled man as bait. To them the withered hand was a test case, not a lost livelihood.

Again he entered the synagogue. The fifth of five conflict stories (2:1–3:6), and the second about the Sabbath. A Galilean synagogue was small: stone benches round the walls, the congregation facing inward, everybody able to see everybody.

A withered hand. Dried up, the muscle wasted. Luke, the doctor, notices it was his right hand (Luke 6:6), in a world of manual labour the difference between a tradesman and a beggar. An early Jewish-Christian gospel, quoted by Jerome, has him say: “I was a mason, earning my living with my hands; I beg you, Jesus, give me back my health, that I need not beg my bread in shame.” The scribal rule, later written down in the Mishnah (Yoma 8:6), allowed healing on the Sabbath only when life was in danger. This could wait a day, which is precisely why the case suited the Pharisees.
