They watched Jesus. Kept him under observation, the way you watch a man you have already decided about. They did not doubt he could heal; they wanted to see whether he would break their rules, so that they could bring a charge.

Religion detached from love. The most religious men present looked at a man with a wrecked livelihood and saw a test case. Religion that comes away from love rarely collapses into open wickedness; these men would have been horrified to be called wicked. It happens by degrees, until a suffering man in your own congregation is mainly an issue to be handled. A man with a withered hand, and men with withered hearts: only one of them knew he needed healing.

The rest the day was waiting for. The Sabbath was a weekly picture of God’s rest: burdens lifted, the creation enjoyed with its Maker. On that day the Lord of the Sabbath (2:28) gives a man who cannot work the use of his hand. The rest the Sabbath pictured is found in Christ’s finished work (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17).

Why did Jesus heal on the Sabbath when he could have waited a day? Because waiting would have conceded that their rules were God’s, and that doing good to a suffering man was work God forbade. Every day of waiting was another day of shame and begging. Mercy delayed for the sake of a human tradition is not holiness.
verseByVerse.note: A “withered” hand is shrunken or paralysed. Healing a condition that was not life-threatening could wait a day, which is why they watched.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the man with the withered hand, "Come here." And he said to them, "Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?" But they were silent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus brings the man into the open and changes the question from what counts as work to what the Sabbath is for: doing good and saving life. His critics cannot answer without condemning themselves, so they say nothing.

“Come here”. Literally “rise into the middle”. If the healing is to be treated as a crime, he will commit it where everyone can see, and put his own life at risk for the man. That is how he has always loved: openly, at cost, in full view of his enemies. And spare a thought for the man, who has not asked for any of this. He has probably kept the hand out of sight for years, and now he is exposed first and healed second.

Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill? They were braced for an argument about what counts as work. Jesus asks instead what the Sabbath is for, and leaves no third option: to have the power to do good and withhold it is itself a choice, and it does harm (James 4:17). And the second half cuts close. Before the day is out these men will be planning a death (v. 6). On the Sabbath he restores a hand they begin to plot a murder, and of the two it is the plot that breaks the Sabbath.

But they were silent. The question has only one honest answer, and it costs them the case. Most of us have used that silence: not denying what has been said, and not acting on it either. A man who says nothing has not stayed neutral; he has decided, and avoided the cost of saying so.

In everyday life. Think of the last time a clear word from Scripture met you and you answered it with silence. Silence before God is not a hiding place, and you need none: the voice that searches you is the voice that heals. Answer him.

Was healing on the Sabbath forbidden in the law? No. Moses forbade work on the Sabbath but nowhere forbade healing. The ban came from the scribal rules built around the law. Jesus was not breaking Moses; he was breaking the fence the teachers had built around Moses.

Where Christians differ: is the Lord’s Day the Christian Sabbath? Many godly brothers, following the Westminster Confession (21.7–8) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (22.7–8), hold it to be so, and they are to be honoured. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, the Lord of the Sabbath (2:28). The Lord’s Day is a gift that believers gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy rather than as a law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience over it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). And the question Jesus asks still stands over every day of the week.

verseByVerse.quote: And he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, "Stretch out your hand." He stretched it out, and his hand was restored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus looks at hard hearts with anger and grief in the same glance, and then his word gives the man power to do what he could not do. His anger is the anger of love, and his command carries the strength to obey it.

With anger. He looked round the room, face by face. This is the only place in the Gospels where “anger” is used of Jesus; Matthew and Luke leave it out, and Mark keeps it. It was righteous anger, at religion that used a suffering man instead of loving him, and God is angry at such things (Psalm 7:11). An endlessly mild Jesus who is never provoked is not the Jesus of the Gospels: he made a whip and cleared the temple courts (John 2:15) and called men whitewashed tombs to their faces (Matthew 23:27), and he never sinned once. It is possible to be angry and holy at once: “Be angry and do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26).

Grieved at their hardness of heart. “Hardness” comes from a word for a callus, skin thickened until it can no longer feel. They were not merely mistaken; their hearts were closed. Righteous anger is never without sorrow for the sinner.

“Stretch out your hand”. A command he could not obey in his own strength; if he could have stretched out that hand, he would have done it long ago. Jesus’ word gave the power to obey, and the hand was restored at once. He did not touch the man or lift a finger: there was nothing to accuse him of except the healing itself.

His own hands, stretched out. One hand withered and useless, held out at his command and made new. And his own hands, sound and strong, a workman’s hands, stretched out one Friday on a piece of wood and ruined, so that the ruined might be restored. His anger at sin and his grief over sinners met at the cross, and there he made us whole.

The order of obedience. The stretching is where the healing happens, and that is the order of the Christian life. Faith is not a feeling of confidence you wait for before you move; it is moving on his word while you still feel as incapable as you did a minute ago. Many believers are quietly stuck on the thought, “I would obey if I had more faith.” You will find you had the faith in the doing of it. Make the phone call; open the Bible when nothing in you wants to. The strength arrives in the stretching, never before it, and it is the strength of the Spirit Christ has put in you (Philippians 2:13).

How can I tell righteous anger from sinful anger? Mark answers in the same sentence, with the word “grieved”. Sinful anger enjoys itself. It wants the other person diminished; it rehearses the argument in the shower; it would be quietly disappointed if they repented, because then there would be nothing to be right about. Righteous anger grieves. It wants the wrong put right and the wrongdoer restored, and would be delighted to be made unnecessary. Try that test on the last thing you were angry about: did you want the person changed, or beaten? You will know in about four seconds.
verseByVerse.note: Mark alone records Jesus’ anger and grief here; Matthew and Luke do not mention them.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faced with an undeniable act of mercy, the guardians of orthodoxy join their political enemies to plan Jesus’ death. It is the first plot against his life in Mark, and from here the road runs to the cross.

The Pharisees went out. After a miracle done to a man they had probably seen in that synagogue for years, they walk out. Nobody congratulates the man.

Counsel with the Herodians. “Immediately”: no pause for reflection. The Herodians supported the rule of Herod Antipas and cooperated with Rome: worldly, political, comfortable. The Pharisees were strict separatists who regarded collaboration with Rome as filthy compromise. On religion, politics, money and nationhood they agreed on nothing, yet they unite against Jesus within minutes, as they will again (12:13). Nothing makes allies like a shared hatred of the light.

How to destroy him. Not discredit him: destroy. The plot comes as early as chapter 3 of sixteen, and it is made on the Sabbath. From here Jesus walks, eyes open, toward a verdict already reached, and heals somebody in nearly every chapter on the way.

Against the LORD and against his Anointed. Psalm 2 had foreseen this alliance: “the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed” (Psalm 2:2). The church in Acts saw it fulfilled when Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered against God’s holy servant Jesus to do what his hand and plan had predestined (Acts 4:25–28). This meeting in Galilee is its first small beginning, and the psalm already says how it ends: “He who sits in the heavens laughs” (Psalm 2:4), and the Son they plot against is the King set on Zion.

He did not stop healing. They planned his death on a Sabbath, and he went on healing. Months later, on another Sabbath, he lay in a borrowed tomb, resting from a finished work, while his enemies posted a guard. Then came the first day of the week, and the stone was rolled back. The one they met to destroy has destroyed death itself, and every counsel taken against him has ended at an empty grave and a throne.

Correct theology is not a preservative. This is what a hardened heart looks like from the inside: convinced it is defending God while it plans a murder. These were the orthodox party. They believed in the resurrection, the authority of Scripture, the coming Messiah and the moral law, and they left a service in which God had visibly acted and went straight into a meeting about how to kill him. The safeguard was never the doctrine on its own, but whether it was still attached to love for God and pity for people, and in these men it had come away.

How do I guard my heart against this kind of hardness? Hardness grows by small refusals: hearing God’s word and not doing it, seeing a need and looking away, being corrected and defending yourself. So the remedy is small obediences, made promptly. When Scripture convicts you, act on it the same day; when you are shown to be wrong, say so. Keep company with believers who will tell you the truth, and “exhort one another every day … that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13). Pray over what you believe: truth that is not prayed and loved soon becomes a weapon. And if you fear your heart has already hardened, take comfort: the men in this verse felt no such fear. A heart that grieves over its own coldness is one God is already softening (Ezekiel 36:26).
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians were supporters of the Herod family’s rule, unlikely allies for the Pharisees.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great crowd followed, from Galilee and Judea and Jerusalem and Idumea and from beyond the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon. When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejected by the leaders, Jesus is sought by the whole land and beyond it, Jews and Gentiles alike: a first sign that God’s promise to bless the nations is being kept. The leaders walk out, the land walks in, and Jesus begins to form a new people around himself (vv. 13–19).

Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea. Away from the synagogue and the plot. He does not escalate. He goes down to a shoreline that could hold thousands, and what was meant to stop him only widens his work.

A great crowd followed. Mark rarely names places, and here he lists six. Galilee is home. Judea and Jerusalem are the religious heartland, several days’ walk south. Idumea is ancient Edom, forcibly converted and thought barely Jewish: Herod’s own people. Beyond the Jordan is the east bank, with Gentiles mixed among the Jews. Tyre and Sidon are Phoenician port cities to the north-west, not in Israel at all.

All that he was doing. Many came for healing, not teaching: a crowd assembled by reports of power, and much of it will not last. The day comes when he says something hard, and “many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him” (John 6:66).

The shape of the list. It runs outward from the centre in every direction and takes in Jew, half-Jew and Gentile: a small picture of the church that is coming, and the first sign of an older promise being kept. To Abraham: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). To the Servant: “I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). By Acts the list will reach Rome. The crowd on that shore was the first trickle of a river that will not stop until a multitude no one can number stands before his throne (Revelation 7:9).

Is a large crowd a sign of God’s blessing? Not by itself. Crowds gathered around Jesus, and crowds also shouted for his crucifixion. Some on that shoreline came for what he could give, some for who he was; the beach looked the same either way, but only those who came for him kept following when it became costly. A large church may be blessed or merely popular; a small one may be faithful or merely stuck. The measure Jesus uses is not attendance but whether people do the will of God (v. 35). Pray for crowds, but pray more for disciples.
verseByVerse.note: Idumea (old Edom) lay south of Judea; Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities on the coast to the north. The crowd came from every direction.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told his disciples to have a boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they crush him, for he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pressed by desperate crowds, Jesus takes a sensible precaution and goes on healing all who come, whatever their motives. He lived within human limits, and he did not turn away people who came to him for mixed reasons.

A boat ready. A small fishing boat kept just offshore: a platform to teach from (4:1) and a way out.

Lest they crush him. The verb you would use of a mob pressing a man against a wall: desperate, sick people, every one trying to get a hand on him. And Jesus, who could have stilled them with a sentence, quietly asks his friends to get a boat. He did not let himself be trampled to prove something about faith, nor stay available every hour people wanted him: he withdrew (v. 7), slept in boats (4:38), and rose before dawn to pray alone (1:35).

All who had diseases. The word is the ordinary word for whips: illnesses that had flogged people for years. They believed that touching him would heal them (5:27–29; 6:56), and he healed them. They had no theology and no understanding of who he was, and he did not lecture them about their motives first.

In everyday life. Remember this mercy when you come to him with mixed motives, wanting relief far more than you want him. He has never yet turned away a person for coming to him badly. Come as the crowd came, and let him sort out your motives once you are near enough for him to reach.

Isn’t it selfish to set limits when people need me? No. Limits are not a character flaw; they are how you were made, and the Lord himself lived within them. The needs around you are endless and your strength is not, and pretending otherwise is not devotion but a slow way of becoming useless to everybody. If you are the person everyone comes to, in a family, a church or a job, take the boat: rest, sleep, say no to some things, let others help, so that you can serve for the long haul. And remember that you are not the Saviour. He is, and his strength has no limit.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out, "You are the Son of God." And he strictly ordered them not to make him known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The demons know exactly who Jesus is and cower before him, but he will not let them be his heralds. Right belief about him is not the same as belonging to him, and he will not be proclaimed before the cross shows what kind of Son of God he is.

They fell down before him. Not in worship but in terror. In that whole crowd the only voices that say exactly who he is belong to the demons: the truth the Father spoke at the Jordan (1:11; compare 1:24, 34), more than the disciples have yet said. And it does them no good at all.

Not to make him known. Jesus would not accept testimony from demons. The truth about the Son of God is not to be carried on the tongue of the father of lies; that commission belongs to a fisherman, a tax collector, a Zealot, and to you. Nor would he have his identity broadcast before people understood that the Son of God must suffer (8:29–31). He will not be crowned before he is crucified. At the cross a Roman officer says the words (15:39), and nobody can mistake what kind of King he is.

Every knee. Their bowing is an unwilling foretaste of the day when “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Philippians 2:10), these included. The only question any creature decides is whether it bows now in love or later in ruin. And the Lord before whom demons cower calls sinners to come near and bow in love, and lifts them up as brothers and sisters.

A creed can be word-perfect and worthless. Even the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). These spirits confess his identity aloud and remain exactly what they are. The difference between their confession and a Christian’s is not accuracy. One says “you are the Son of God” and means “keep away from me”; the other says the same words and means “have me”. Mark will end this chapter by showing which you are: not by what you can recite, but by whether you do the will of God (v. 35).

If every knee will bow, will everyone be saved in the end? No. Every knee will bow, but not every knee in love; the demons here bow and remain his enemies. Philippians 2 describes the acknowledgement of Christ’s lordship on the last day, willing or unwilling, and Jesus is clear that those who reject him “will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46). Today you may bow willingly and be received as a child. One day you will bow regardless. Bow now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–35 — The Twelve, the Accusation, and the True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus gathers a new family around himself, and by the end every person in the story is either inside with him or outside. On the mountain he chooses twelve, Israel beginning again, to be with him and to be sent out; the list ends with Judas (vv. 13–19). His family says he is out of his mind, and scribes from Jerusalem say he is possessed (vv. 20–22). He answers that Satan is not fighting himself: a stronger man has bound him and is carrying off his goods, and to call the Spirit’s work the devil’s is the one sin never forgiven (vv. 23–30). Then his mother and brothers stand outside, and he names those sitting around him his family: whoever does the will of God (vv. 31–35).
verseByVerse.theology: The picture of the strong man in verse 27 is the key to the chapter. Jesus grants that there is a real kingdom of darkness; he denies that he serves it. He has come to rob it, and he bound the strong man by being bound himself (both are unfolded in the note on v. 27).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men appointed to be with him, and only then sent out. They spent a long season watching him before they were sent to preach (6:7–13).

Now: it is possible to be very busy for God and seldom with him: to run a rota, lead a group and defend the faith online, and go months without an unhurried hour in his company. (See vv. 13–15, which ends with comfort for the person who can no longer do much.)

verseByVerse.quote: And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach and have authority to cast out demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus chooses twelve men, Israel beginning again around himself, and calls them first to be with him and then to be sent out with his message and his authority. The order matters: company with him comes before work for him.

Up on the mountain. Mountains are places of revelation and covenant in Scripture: at Sinai Moses went up and came down with a nation ordered around twelve tribes. Luke adds that Jesus spent the whole night in prayer before he chose (Luke 6:12).

Those whom he desired. Not those who volunteered or qualified, but those he wanted: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). If you belong to Christ, that is the reason: he wanted you. Nothing lies behind it but his own free love, and since it never rested on anything in you, nothing in you can undo it.

And they came to him. His wanting produces their coming. The call is not an offer left on the table but a summons that creates the answer, as the same voice once said “let there be light”, and there was light.

And he appointed twelve. Literally “he made twelve”. Nobody in Israel could miss the number: twelve sons of Jacob, twelve tribes. Ten of those tribes had been scattered for seven hundred years, and the prophets had promised they would be gathered again. Jesus preaches no sermon about restoring Israel; he appoints twelve men, and the claim is made without a word of argument. The Lord of the new Israel chose his people before they could choose him, and called them first of all to himself.

So that they might be with him. The first purpose of the Twelve is not to be useful but to be in his company: some three years mostly watching him pray, handle a hostile room, touch a leper. Almost none of it will feel like ministry. All of it is the training.

Sent out to preach. The second purpose is mission: they are apostles, “sent ones”, envoys carrying their sender’s authority, even over demons (6:7, 13). And the order never reverses: those he sends must first be with him. When a church or a Christian swaps them round, the work hollows out from the inside. That is the diagnosis for a common kind of Christian tiredness: not too much work, but too much work done on too little time with Christ, and the cure is to go back and be with him.

How do I be with him now? The Twelve walked beside him on the road; we cannot. But he promised, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20), and he keeps that promise by his Spirit through ordinary means. Listen to him. Read a Gospel slowly, and let him speak before you speak. Talk with him. Pray through the day in short sentences: on the bus, at the sink, before the meeting. Eat with him. Come to his table and to his people; much of the Twelve’s training happened over meals. Watch him. Before a hard conversation, ask how he handled a hostile room, and do that. Stay when it feels like nothing. Most of their time with him felt ordinary. You are not earning his company: he “called to him those whom he desired”, and he wanted you there first.

In everyday life. There is a mercy here for anyone who can no longer do much: the elderly, the ill, the housebound, the one whose usefulness has been taken away. The first calling on every disciple is one no illness can revoke. You are called to be with him, and you can do that from a bed.

Does “those whom he desired” mean that God chooses who will be saved? The verse is about choosing the Twelve for their office, but it shows the pattern of all God’s saving work, and that is a comfort, not a threat. God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world, not for anything foreseen in them but in love, according to the purpose of his will (Ephesians 1:4–5), and those he calls he effectually draws (John 6:44): the call does not merely invite, it brings. Their coming is no less real for that, and the door is never closed to anyone who wants to come (John 6:37).

Is it unfair that he chooses? Remember what is being chosen out of: rebels who deserve nothing. Grace is by definition owed to no one, and the wonder is not that God passes some by but that he sets his love on any of us at all (Romans 9:15–16).

Where Christians differ: why does God choose? Many faithful Christians understand election as God choosing those he foresaw would believe. This commentary’s view: the Reformed reading rests on texts like these, which ground the choice in his will and love alone.

Where Christians differ: do Christians have this authority today? Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, often sincere brothers and sisters, believe they do and practise deliverance ministry. This commentary’s view: with many Reformed Christians, it holds that this authority was given to the Twelve among the signs that marked the apostles (2 Corinthians 12:12), and that such sign-gifts belonged to the apostles’ founding work (Ephesians 2:20). The letters never tell believers to cast out demons; they tell them to resist the devil (James 4:7), put on God’s armour (Ephesians 6:10–18), and pray. The devil still works, but Christ has bound the strong man (3:27), and the believer facing evil fights with the word, prayer and the fellowship of the church. Continuationist brothers read the evidence differently, and both agree that God still delivers the oppressed in answer to prayer, and that the victory is Christ’s alone.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, lack “whom he also named apostles” here, though several early ones have it; it is certainly in Luke 6:13.
verseByVerse.note: “Apostle” means one who is sent.

parallels.desc: the Twelve and the twelve tribes

verseByVerse.quote: He appointed the twelve: Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter); James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder); Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Zealot,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus takes his twelve as they are, rash, obscure and bitterly divided by politics, and names some of them for what his grace will make them. What they became was his gift before it was their achievement.

Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter). Peter means rock, and Simon was anything but: impulsive, loud, and a few years from swearing in a courtyard that he had never met the man. Jesus named him for what grace would make him. In the Old Testament the great covenant renamings are God’s own work: Abram became Abraham and Jacob became Israel, each new name a promise God would keep (Genesis 17:5; 32:28). Now Jesus does the same by his own right, as the one who “calls into existence the things that do not exist” (Romans 4:17). Peter would become a rock only by being joined to the true foundation, the stone the builders rejected (1 Peter 2:4–8).

Sons of Thunder. Only Mark records this nickname, affectionate and honest. These are the brothers who wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54) and asked privately for the two best seats in the kingdom (10:35–40). Jesus knew their temperament the day he chose them, gave it a name, and appointed them anyway. And John, the son of thunder, became the apostle of love (1 John 4:7–21).

Andrew. Peter’s brother, who spends his New Testament career bringing people to Jesus and then disappearing: his brother, a boy with some bread and fish, some Greeks (John 1:40–42; 6:8–9; 12:22). If your service is small and nobody attaches your name to it, Andrew is your man.

The middle of the list. Bartholomew is probably Nathanael (John 1:45). Matthew is Levi, the tax collector of 2:14, the collaborator his own people would have written off. Thaddaeus is probably the Judas son of James of Luke 6:16. We have not one line from James the son of Alphaeus. They are known to history as names in a list, and their names are written on the foundations of the city of God (Revelation 21:14). If it troubles you that your life will leave no trace anyone can point to, look hard at the middle of this list.

Simon the Zealot. Literally “the Cananaean”, from the Aramaic for zealous. He may have belonged to the Zealots, who wanted to overthrow Rome by force, and to whom a Jew collecting taxes for the occupiers deserved a knife. Jesus put a former tax collector and a man whose very name spoke of zeal against Rome in the same group, sharing meals for three years. Nothing in the politics of the day could have reconciled them; nothing did, except the man in the middle.

Can my temperament really change? Yes, though usually slowly and never by willpower alone. The Spirit does not turn you into someone else; he makes you more truly yourself, with the sin burned out of your strengths. Peter stayed bold, and his boldness became courage for Christ; John stayed intense, and his intensity became love. Bring your temper, anxiety, coldness or need to control honestly to Christ: confess its sinful expressions, ask for the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), and stay close to him and his people. Look back in ten years, not ten days.

Uncertain wording. “Boanerges” is a Greek spelling of an Aramaic nickname, which Mark translates: “Sons of Thunder”. The first part clearly means “sons”; how the second comes to mean thunder is not clear, and scholars propose different Aramaic words behind it. The meaning is certain, because Mark gives it; only the original word is not.
verseByVerse.note: Peter means “rock.” Thaddaeus is probably the “Judas the son of James” of Luke’s lists.

verseByVerse.quote: and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list ends with the man who would betray Jesus, chosen with the rest and close to him for years without ever belonging to him. Mark tells the end of the story at the start, and Jesus was not caught out.

And Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. Judas is always last in the lists, and every list attaches the betrayal. Yet he was appointed with the rest, present at every private explanation of every parable, and sent out to preach with authority over demons (6:7, 13), with no hint that his mission failed or that the others suspected him. When Jesus said at the last supper that one of them would betray him, each asked whether it was himself (14:19). Being close to Jesus, even serving in his name, is not the same as belonging to him.

Judas for money, the Father for love. Behind Judas stood the Father, who “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32), and the Son himself, “who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). Judas handed him over for money, the Father for love, the Son out of love for his Father and for us. The darkest deed of the night served the brightest purpose of eternity: he was “delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25).

What it does not mean. Not that Judas was forced. God’s plan included the betrayal (Acts 2:23), yet Judas acted freely and was responsible: “the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed!” (14:21). God planned it, and Judas chose it.

Did Jesus know? Yes: “Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him” (John 6:64; compare 6:70). There is a strange comfort here for anyone betrayed by someone close. Your Lord chose his betrayer with his eyes open, kept him at his table, washed his feet, and called him friend in the garden. He was not caught out, and nothing that has been done to you has caught him out either.

Can I fall away like Judas? This question keeps sensitive people awake, so let it be answered plainly. Judas was never a believer who lost his salvation; he was near Christ without ever being in Christ, and John tells us how it went wrong: “he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it” (John 12:6). The rot was private, ordinary and financial, and it ran for years under a spotless public record. A true believer cannot be snatched out of the Father’s hand (John 10:28–29). Do not use that as a reason to skip examining yourself; use it as the reason you can bear to.

Peter and Judas. The test is not whether you have ever sinned badly; Peter denied him with oaths that same week and was restored on a beach. The test is what you do afterwards. Judas felt remorse, threw the money into the temple and went out to a rope. Peter wept, and came back. Remorse looks at itself and despairs; repentance turns to Christ and lives. If you fear you are a Judas, that fear is not the mark of a Judas. Go to Christ with the thing you are afraid of: the one move Judas never made, though it was always open to him. And if despair like his ever pulls at you, do not carry it alone: tell someone you trust today, and if you are in danger, get help at once.

Uncertain wording. The meaning of “Iscariot” is not known for certain. It is often taken as “man of Kerioth”, a town in southern Judea, which would make Judas the only one of the Twelve not from Galilee; other explanations have been offered, but none is sure.
verseByVerse.note: “Iscariot” is often taken to mean “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea, but that is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, "He is out of his mind."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ own family, hearing that he cannot even stop to eat, set out to take him home, convinced he has lost his mind. They probably meant well, but Mark sets their verdict around the scribes’ accusation (vv. 22–30), and the two are uncomfortably close.

They could not even eat. Home is probably Peter’s house in Capernaum (2:1). The Son of God missed meals because of the volume of human need at the door.

To seize him. Word travels some twenty-five miles to Nazareth, and his family, his mother and brothers among them (v. 31), set out. The verb is strong and physical, the word used later of the mob in the garden (14:46). They mean to take him home before he embarrasses the family further or gets himself killed.

“He is out of his mind”. He is neglecting food, provoking the authorities and claiming divine authority. They were protecting him, and the family’s name, from the pressure every family knows: what will people say? Reputation is a quiet idol, and Jesus would not bow to it, even for his mother. His brothers did not believe in him until after the resurrection (John 7:5; Acts 1:14). The people who had watched him grow up called him mad, and he went on loving them.

A stranger to his mother’s sons. Psalm 69, which the New Testament keeps quoting about Christ (John 2:17; 15:25; Romans 15:3), describes this afternoon: “I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother’s sons. For zeal for your house has consumed me” (Psalm 69:8–9). What his family called madness was zeal: love for his Father’s will so complete that meals and reputation counted for nothing beside it. Measured by the world, a man who will go to a cross for his enemies is out of his mind. Measured by heaven, it is the sanest love there has ever been.

Mary among them. The first name in verse 31 is his mother: Mary, who had heard the angel and treasured the shepherds’ words (Luke 1:26–38; 2:19), now on the road to take him home. She was not a woman of finished faith standing serenely above ordinary disciples; she had to grow, sometimes painfully. The Mary who stands outside here stands at the foot of the cross when nearly all the Twelve have run (John 19:25), and prays with the believers after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). If your own coming to Christ has been uneven, with long stretches when you did not understand him at all, you are in the company of his mother.

Should I neglect food and rest for ministry, as Jesus did here? Not as a rule. This was a season of extraordinary demand; the same Gospel shows Jesus telling his disciples to come away and rest a while, because they had no leisure even to eat (6:31). Sometimes love means missing a meal or a night’s sleep for someone in crisis. But a life that never eats, rests or stops is not more spiritual; it is usually less wise. Jesus’ family were wrong about his sanity, but your family may be right about your exhaustion. Listen to them.

Uncertain wording. “His family” is literally “those beside him”, which can mean friends or associates as well as relatives; here it most likely means his family, since his mother and brothers arrive in verse 31. And “they were saying” could refer to the family, or to people in general, whose talk the family had heard. Most take it of the family, which fits their attempt to seize him.
verseByVerse.note: “His family” means his relatives.

parallels.desc: even his brothers did not believe

verseByVerse.quote: And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem were saying, "He is possessed by Beelzebul," and "by the prince of demons he casts out the demons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The official verdict from Jerusalem is that Jesus’ power comes from the devil himself. The scribes cannot deny what he does, so they slander the power by which he does it.

The scribes from Jerusalem. The second verdict comes with authority: an official delegation of scribes from the religious capital, some ninety miles away, sent to assess the healer as priests and Levites had once been sent to question John the Baptist (John 1:19).

What they cannot do. The people best placed to expose a fraud admit that the demons were driven out and dispute only the power behind it. That is strong evidence that these things happened: no church would invent such a charge against its own Lord, and centuries later the Talmud still remembers Jesus as a sorcerer (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 43a).

He is possessed by Beelzebul. By Jesus’ day Beelzebul was a title for the prince of demons, Satan himself (v. 23). They accuse Jesus not only of being in league with the devil but of having Satan living in him.

The Anointed called unclean. At the Jordan the Spirit came down on Jesus (1:10–11), the Servant on whom God had promised to put his Spirit (Isaiah 42:1), and every demon driven out in this Gospel has been driven out by that Spirit. In Matthew Jesus draws the conclusion the scribes will not: “if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28). The men who came to judge him called the Spirit-filled Messiah the devil’s house. Yet he is master of a house, and it is God’s: Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son, and we are his house (Hebrews 3:6). The one they named Beelzebul (Matthew 10:25) is building a temple for the Holy Spirit out of sinners, living stones taken from the very house he was accused of serving.

Three verdicts. His family says he is mad; the theologians say he is evil. Between them they cover the ground people have covered ever since: he is deluded, or dangerous, or what he says he is, and the third verdict is costly, because if it is true he must be obeyed. Some suggest a fourth, that his followers later inflated a simple teacher, but even the earliest accounts, like this one, show him claiming an authority no mere teacher claims. A gentle teacher everyone can admire was never on offer. Even the crowds who called him a prophet (6:15; 8:28) knew that a prophet speaks with God’s authority and demands an answer. People loved him or wanted him dead.

Why didn’t the miracles convince them, and would miracles convince people today? These scribes had the best religious education in the world and the Scriptures largely by memory. They walked ninety miles, watched the power of God set people free before their eyes, and wrote it up as demonic. The problem was never the evidence. When a heart has decided, it will build a theology to house the decision, and the better educated it is, the better the theology. As Abraham says in Jesus’ parable, “If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead” (Luke 16:31). Evidence matters, and Christianity rests on it, but only the Spirit opens closed hearts. So when you share the faith, give reasons, and pray.

Uncertain wording. Where the name Beelzebul comes from is not certain. Behind it stands Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2), whose name means “lord of the flies”, perhaps an Israelite mockery of a grander title. Beelzebul itself may mean “lord of the dwelling”, which would sharpen Jesus’ picture of the strong man’s house (v. 27), or “Baal the prince”. Whatever its origin, by Jesus’ day it named Satan, as verse 23 shows.
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan (v. 23).

verseByVerse.quote: And he called them to him and said to them in parables, "How can Satan cast out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus shows that the scribes’ charge is absurd: Satan does not wreck his own work, and if he did, his kingdom would already be falling. He answers the gravest accusation in the Gospel with reasoning, not outrage.

He called them to him. They have said he is possessed by the devil, and he invites them closer; the Lord of glory could have crushed them with a word. “Parables” here means picture-sayings, comparisons.

How can Satan cast out Satan? Why would Satan free the very people he has enslaved? Civil war destroys nations, as Israel had learned when it split after Solomon, and division destroys families. If the devil were expelling his own troops, the scribes would be announcing the end of the kingdom of darkness, exactly what they came to deny. Either the exorcisms are not from Satan, or Satan is finished.

Coming to an end. In fact Satan is coming to an end, not because he is divided, but because someone stronger has come (v. 27).

How Jesus argues. He grants what is true: he does not deny the devil, but shows that their theory will not carry the weight they put on it. That is how a Christian should handle an argument: take seriously what is right in it, and press the part that fails. There is a place for argument in defending the faith, and the Lord uses it. Yet the argument changed nobody we hear of. Argument can clear away an obstacle, but it has never on its own changed a heart. That is the Spirit’s work, the very Person these men are about to be warned against resisting.

Does a house divided mean churches must never divide? Unity is precious, and most church splits come from pride, not principle; believers are to be “eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit” (Ephesians 4:3). So work hard for peace, forgive quickly, and do not leave over preferences. But Jesus’ point is about Satan’s kingdom, not a rule that Christians must stay together whatever is taught. Where the gospel itself is denied, faithfulness may require separation (Galatians 1:8–9; 2 John 10–11). Even then, go with grief and humility, never with contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: But no one can enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is not Satan’s servant but his conqueror: the stronger one who has entered the strong man’s house to tie him up and set his captives free. With one picture he turns the accusation inside out.

A strong man’s house. The strong man is Satan, and the goods are people: every possessed man in Galilee, every reader of this page before Christ came for them.

First binds the strong man. To rob a strong man you must first overpower him and tie him up. John the Baptist had called Jesus the mightier one (1:7), and Isaiah had promised that the captives of the mighty would be taken, for God himself would contend with the contender (Isaiah 49:24–25). The scribes say Jesus works for the owner, but a servant does not tie up his master and carry off his goods. Jesus is in the house as the raider, and the owner is on the floor with his hands tied: binding first, plundering afterwards.

Then he may plunder. Every exorcism, every healing, every sinner forgiven is Jesus plundering Satan’s house. The New Testament keeps the picture when it describes what happened to you: God “delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son” (Colossians 1:13), with a word used of moving whole populations from one land to another.

When was the strong man bound? The binding began in the wilderness (1:12–13) and was completed at the cross. And here is the strangest and best turn in the faith: the stronger man let himself be bound first. In a garden soldiers tied Jesus, and he did not resist. They led him bound to a high priest and to a governor, and fastened him to a cross with his arms open and immovable, the posture of a man who can plunder nothing. And that was the binding of Satan. God “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15); through death Christ destroyed “the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). The strongest man who ever lived walked into the house, let the owner tie him up, and died, and that is how Satan came to be the one tied up.

In everyday life. If you are in Christ, you are not a volunteer who signed up. You are rescued property. Somebody broke in and carried you out over his shoulder, and the price of the raid was his life. Live today like someone who has been carried out.

What it does not mean. Not that Satan is now inactive. He still “prowls around like a roaring lion” (1 Peter 5:8). But he cannot stop the gospel or hold those whom Christ frees.

If Satan is bound, why is there still so much evil? Because a bound enemy can still do damage within the length of his chain. Satan is defeated but not yet destroyed; that comes at Christ’s return (Revelation 20:10). He cannot stop the gospel spreading among the nations, keep one of God’s elect in his house, or separate a believer from Christ, but he still tempts, accuses and deceives, and the world still groans under sin. We live between the binding and the end, the decisive battle won and the war not yet over, so we resist him firm in the faith: “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20).

Where Christians differ: Satan bound and the thousand years. Revelation 20:1–3 pictures Satan bound so that he cannot deceive the nations, and brothers who expect a future thousand-year reign on earth read it as still to come. This commentary’s view: the thousand years are the present gospel age, between Christ’s two comings, partly because Jesus speaks of Satan as bound already. Both rejoice that the decisive victory is already won.

parallels.desc: the prey taken from the mighty

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin"— for they were saying, "He has an unclean spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus promises forgiveness for every sin and blasphemy, with one exception: the hardened refusal that calls the Spirit’s work in him the work of the devil. That sin is never forgiven because it shuts the only door through which forgiveness comes.

Truly, I say to you. The word behind “truly” is “amen”, the formula Jesus uses to put his own authority behind a statement.

All sins will be forgiven. He begins with the widest promise in the Gospel: all sins, and every blasphemy, the things said in rage, the years spent mocking him, the words you would not repeat to anyone. Blasphemy, speech that insults or slanders God, is forgiven too when repented of; Paul was a blasphemer and was forgiven (1 Timothy 1:13). Do not hurry past this on the way to the exception. It is one of the most sweeping sentences about mercy Jesus ever spoke, and he spoke it to men who had just called the Holy Spirit a devil.

An eternal sin. One whose guilt is never lifted, in this age or in the age to come (Matthew 12:32). Mark ties it to what was said in that room: “He has an unclean spirit.” The scribes saw the Holy Spirit’s work in Jesus clearly and deliberately called it Satan’s. This is blasphemy against the Spirit: not a careless word, doubt or confusion, but a settled, wilful rejection of the Spirit’s clear testimony to Christ, looking straight at the light and naming it darkness. It is unforgivable not because God’s grace is too small, but because it refuses the only way to be forgiven. The Spirit convicts of sin and leads to Christ (John 16:8–11); whoever calls his work satanic has shut the door on the only way back, and has no wish to be forgiven.

The one sinned against most. How can a holy God promise forgiveness for “whatever blasphemies they utter”? Because the man speaking was on his way to bear those sins himself. Mark uses the same word at the cross: “those who passed by derided him”, literally blasphemed him, “wagging their heads” (15:29). From the middle of the blasphemy he prayed, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34; the prayer is missing from some early manuscripts of Luke, though many scholars judge it authentic). He gave his life as a ransom for many (10:45), and that ransom covers every word ever flung at him. The promise of “all sins” rests on the blood of the one who was sinned against most.

Have I committed it? Let the answer be given straight, because you may be living inside this question. If you are afraid you have committed the unforgivable sin, you have not. That is not a comforting fiction. Fear of this sin means you want to be forgiven, care what God thinks of you, and are horrified at being cut off from him, and none of that comes from a hardened heart. Hardened hearts do not lie awake worrying about their standing with God; the scribes went home untroubled. Your distress is evidence of a conscience still alive under the Spirit’s hand, and the Spirit does not trouble a man he has abandoned. The hardness that commits this sin does not tremble. It calculates.

Then come. Can you say honestly that if he would have you, you would come? Then come. “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37), and that sentence has no clause excepting people afraid they have gone too far. Your fear is not your danger. If the fear keeps returning however often it is answered, tell your pastor or a biblical counsellor; such fears are common and can be helped, and a medical check-up is wise as well.

verseByVerse.quote: And his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent to him and called him. And a crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, "Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ mother and brothers stand outside and send for him, while a crowd of strangers sits around him inside. Where people stand carries the lesson of the whole chapter: being near Jesus is not the same as belonging to him.

Standing outside. The family who set out to seize him (v. 21) arrive. Mark says “outside” twice (vv. 31, 32), and the word carries the scene. They do not come in. They send for him, as you do when you expect to be obeyed: family authority, requiring the eldest son to come out so that they can take him home.

A crowd was sitting around him. Inside, they sit listening, the posture of disciples (Luke 10:39). You can be his mother and be outside, while strangers sit at his feet.

He went outside for those outside. At the end of the Gospel the places are reversed. He is led out of the city, as the sin offering was carried outside the camp: “Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). He went out to the place of rejection so that people standing outside could be brought in: “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). That is how his own mother and brothers came in, and it is the only way anyone does. If someone you love is still outside, take heart: nobody in that street was beyond the reach of the man in that house.

In the room, or at the door? This is the most searching thing in the passage for religious people, and it is not really about Mary. It is about anyone whose connection to Christ is nearness rather than surrender: raised in it, married into it, employed by it, on the rota, known by name to everyone in the congregation, and still, in practice, outside, sending messages in, wanting Christ to come out and fit into a life organised without him. So ask, without panic but without dodging it: am I in the room, or at the door? Not whether you have been around this a long time; the family had been around him for thirty years. The question is whether you have sat down before him as someone who wants what he says more than a Christ you can manage.

Where Christians differ: who were his brothers? Jesus’ brothers were James, Joses, Judas and Simon (6:3). Two other views arose in the early church, both to protect the belief that Mary remained a virgin all her life, a belief many Christians through history, some Reformers among them, have sincerely held: that they were Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage, or that they were cousins. This commentary’s view: they were most naturally Mary’s later children, Jesus’ younger brothers. Matthew names them and adds sisters (Matthew 13:55–56); John says not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5); Acts sets them beside Mary but apart from the apostles (Acts 1:14). Scripture never calls them step-brothers or cousins, and Matthew says Joseph “knew her not until she had given birth to a son” (Matthew 1:25), which most naturally implies that afterwards they lived as husband and wife. None of this lessens Mary’s honour as the mother of our Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, "Who are my mother and my brothers?" And looking about at those who sat around him, he said, "Here are my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus names everyone who does the will of God as his brother, sister and mother: a new family gathered around him and open to anyone. This is not the demotion of his natural family but the announcement of a second one.

Who are my mother and my brothers? A startling question in a culture where family was everything, asked in order to be answered, and the answer is astonishing news for ordinary people.

Looking about. Only Mark mentions the look. Earlier he looked around at hard men with anger (v. 5); here he looks around at a floor full of nobodies, face by face, and says, “Here are my mother and my brothers!” He said it while his mother stood in the street, but not at her expense.

Whoever does the will of God. “Whoever”: no pedigree or record required. Membership in Jesus’ family is not by birth but by doing God’s will: hearing his word, repenting, believing and obeying (1:15). Not admiring it, or believing the correct things about it; the demons on the beach had the doctrine right and were no relation of his. Lest anyone turn this into a place earned by performance, John records the Lord’s own definition of the work God requires: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent” (John 6:29). None of us does God’s will perfectly (James 3:2); the one Son who did it without fault did it in our place, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), which is why our faltering obedience is welcome in the family.

My brother and sister and mother. He reaches for the closest words the language has, and he says “sister”, when a rabbi’s disciples were all men. The church is a family.

Not ashamed to call them brothers. To the believer with a family gone quiet, the empty chair at Christmas, the brother who does not call, and to the one with no family left at all, the Lord Jesus Christ looks round a room and says that these are his. He is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). He said it on the afternoon he was called mad by his family and demonic by the theologians, on his way to a cross where he would make a family out of people who had none.

In everyday life. Who in your church family sits alone this week: the widow, the student far from home, the believer whose relatives have cut them off? Invite one of them to a meal. The mismatched congregation you sit among on Sunday is not a social arrangement you could improve by finding people more like yourself. It is your family, given to you by Christ, and he named them before you did.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus rejected his mother or family. He provided for his mother from the cross (John 19:26–27), and he said that setting aside duty to parents for a religious excuse makes void the word of God (7:11–13). His brothers later came to faith. But blood ties are not the deepest ties. Nor does this passage support praying to Mary as one who pleads for us with her Son: Jesus pointed away from family to faith.

Does this mean I should put church above my family? Not in the sense of neglecting them. Anyone who does not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8), and your husband or wife, children and parents are people God has given you to love first and most practically. What this passage sets is the order of loyalties: Christ above all, and his family a real family, not a club. Where your natural family opposes Christ, you follow him while still loving them. And where you have no natural family, or have lost them, the church is meant to be home.

3.theology:
Two of the most-asked questions in Mark come in this chapter.

Was Jesus’s anger sinful? No, and verse 5 shows how to tell, because it puts the anger and the grief in one breath: he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart. (See the note on v. 5.)

What is the unforgivable sin? Mark answers it himself in verse 30: for they were saying, He has an unclean spirit. What that means, and why the person terrified of having committed it has not, is set out in the note on vv. 28–30.
3.examples:
The chapter sets two alliances side by side.

Then: Pharisees and Herodians, who despised each other, agreeing on how to destroy him (v. 6). So Pilate and Herod became friends over him (Luke 23:12).

And then: Matthew the tax collector and Simon the Zealot on the same list of twelve (see vv. 16–18).

Now: a congregation can be held together by what it is against, and it will feel like unity without being unity. Or it can be people with little in common except Christ. If your church contains people you would never otherwise have chosen, that is the evidence of his work.

keyVerse.quote: But no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house.
keyVerse.note: This one picture answers the question the whole chapter asks: by whose power does Jesus act? He is not Satan’s servant but his conqueror, come into the enemy’s house to carry off his captives, and every healing and exorcism is plunder taken. He would bind the strong man in the strangest way of all, by letting himself be bound and crucified.

3.reflection:
The Pharisees watched a man with a withered hand and saw only a test case (vv. 1–6). Where are we most tempted to let rules, habits or reputation matter more than the person in front of us, and how does Jesus’ question in verse 4 expose it?

Jesus called the Twelve first “so that they might be with him”, and only then to be sent out (v. 14). What does being with him look like in your ordinary week, and what most often crowds it out?

Jesus pictures himself as the stronger man who binds the strong man and plunders his house (v. 27), and he did it by being bound himself. How does it change the way you think about your own conversion, and about your fears of evil, to know you are rescued property?

His family stood outside while a crowd of strangers sat at his feet (vv. 31–35). How is it possible to be near Jesus for years without belonging to him? And who in our church family could we treat more truly as brother, sister or mother this week?

4.title: Seed, Soil, and the Sleeping Lord
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Again he began to teach beside the sea. And a very large crowd gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, and the whole crowd was beside the sea on the land. <sup>2</sup>And he was teaching them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them: <sup>3</sup>“Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow. <sup>4</sup>And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it. <sup>5</sup>Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. <sup>6</sup>And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away. <sup>7</sup>Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no grain. <sup>8</sup>And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.” <sup>9</sup>And he said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>10</sup>And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. <sup>11</sup>And he said to them, “To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, <sup>12</sup>so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven.” <sup>13</sup>And he said to them, “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? <sup>14</sup>The sower sows the word. <sup>15</sup>And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them. <sup>16</sup>And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. <sup>17</sup>And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away. <sup>18</sup>And others are the ones sown among thorns. They are those who hear the word, <sup>19</sup>but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. <sup>20</sup>But those that were sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.” <sup>21</sup>And he said to them, “Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? <sup>22</sup>For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest; nor is anything secret except to come to light. <sup>23</sup>If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>24</sup>And he said to them, “Pay attention to what you hear: with the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. <sup>25</sup>For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.” <sup>26</sup>And he said, “The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. <sup>27</sup>He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. <sup>28</sup>The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. <sup>29</sup>But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.” <sup>30</sup>And he said, “With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? <sup>31</sup>It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth, <sup>32</sup>yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.” <sup>33</sup>With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. <sup>34</sup>He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything. <sup>35</sup>On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, “Let us go across to the other side.” <sup>36</sup>And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. And other boats were with him. <sup>37</sup>And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. <sup>38</sup>But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. And they woke him and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” <sup>39</sup>And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. <sup>40</sup>He said to them, “Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?” <sup>41</sup>And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
4.overview:
Where we are. After chapter 3, where the scribes call Jesus possessed and his own family think him out of his mind (3:21–35), comes Mark’s longest block of teaching, ending with the first of four mighty works that run through chapter 5.

The message. The kingdom of God has truly come in Jesus, but it comes like seed. It is sown by a word, received or lost according to how people hear, small and hidden for now, and certain of a harvest beyond hope. So listen to him, and do not judge his kingdom by its size, for the one who sows this word is the Lord of the wind and the sea.

Why it was said. If Jesus is the King, why does his kingdom look so small: a preacher in a borrowed boat and twelve ordinary men? Mark’s readers in Rome, a small church that knew suffering (see the introduction), faced the same question, and had watched some receive the word with joy and fall away when it cost them (vv. 16–17).

How the chapter makes its case. The sower (vv. 1–9) shows the word falling on four kinds of ground: three losses, and one harvest of thirty, sixty and a hundredfold. Jesus explains why he speaks in parables (vv. 10–12) and interprets the soils (vv. 13–20). The lamp and the measure (vv. 21–25) say that what is hidden now is hidden in order to be shown, and that how we listen decides what we receive. The seed growing while the farmer sleeps answers the fear that nothing is happening (vv. 26–29); the mustard seed, the fear that it is all too small (vv. 30–32). After a summary (vv. 33–34), Jesus takes his disciples across the lake into a storm (vv. 35–41).

Where it leads. The chapter about hearing the word ends with the word spoken to a storm: “Peace! Be still!” Only the LORD rules the raging of the sea (Psalm 89:9), so the disciples’ question, “Who then is this?”, has its answer in Mark’s first verse. And the harvest of the parables will come from his own death, the grain of wheat that falls into the earth and dies, and so bears much fruit (John 12:24).

For us. Ask what kind of ground your heart is, and bring it to the one who makes hard ground good. Keep sowing, sleep while God gives the growth, and when the water comes over the side, remember who is in the boat.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Sower and the Purpose of Parables
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How people hear the word decides what it does in them, and the harvest is certain despite every loss. Jesus teaches the crowd from a boat (vv. 1–2) and tells of seed falling on a path, on rocky ground, among thorns and on good soil: three losses and one astonishing harvest (vv. 3–9). Alone with those who stayed to ask, he explains that the parables give understanding to those who come and confirm the refusal of those who will not, as Isaiah foretold (vv. 10–12), and then interprets the four soils (vv. 13–20). A lamp is lit to be seen, and what is hidden now will be shown; so take care how you hear, for the measure you bring is the measure you receive (vv. 21–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 11–12 are the hardest words in the chapter. Matthew says Jesus speaks in parables because people do not see (Matthew 13:13); Mark says so that they may not see, lest they should turn and be forgiven.

They are opened up, in three steps, in the note on vv. 10–12.

So the same parable is judgment and mercy at once: it hardens the scornful and keeps the truth within reach of anyone who will come and ask.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a farmer scattering seed by hand over ground he has not sorted, some of it landing where it has no chance.

Now: every preacher, parent and friend who keeps sowing without being able to see the soil. Their task was the sowing (see vv. 3–4), and the harvest is not in doubt (see vv. 8–9).

verseByVerse.quote: Again he began to teach beside the sea. And a very large crowd gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, and the whole crowd was beside the sea on the land. And he was teaching them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sits down in a boat to teach the great crowd, and he teaches them in parables. The pictures he takes from ordinary life will show who truly hears him and who does not.

He got into a boat. The boat kept ready in 3:9. Jesus has it pushed out a few yards and sits down in it, the posture of a teacher. Near Capernaum the shore rises from the water in natural curves, where a man in a boat could be heard by thousands without shouting.

As the psalm foretold. Matthew saw a psalm fulfilled here: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world” (Matthew 13:35, from Psalm 78:2). Asaph told Israel’s history in riddles; the Son of David tells the secrets of God’s kingdom, and he can utter what was hidden since the foundation of the world because he was there when it was laid (John 1:1–3).

Many things in parables. Much of the Lord’s time went on teaching. A parable is a story or picture from ordinary life, farming, lamps, measures, seeds, placed beside a spiritual truth to light it up. The Creator used his own creation as his pulpit, and he spoke so that farmers and fishermen could understand. Yet a parable is neither a children’s illustration nor a code: it usually makes one main point, and it makes you work.

Why stories? A plain statement, such as “people respond differently to the word of God”, is easy to nod at and easier to forget. Hand a man a picture of a field with four kinds of ground, and he finds himself walking round the edge wondering which patch he is standing on; once inside the story, it has him. A story slips past the defences that an argument runs straight into. Nathan did not begin by telling David that he was the man; he told him about a poor man’s one little ewe lamb, and let David pass sentence on himself first (2 Samuel 12:1–7). So read this chapter expecting to be handled the same way: Jesus is about to walk you out into a field and ask where you are standing.

How should I read a parable? Start with the setting: who Jesus is speaking to and what question is in the air. Look for the main point, often in the surprise or the ending, such as the enormous harvest. Where Jesus explains a parable, let his explanation govern yours. Do not press every detail for a hidden meaning; a story needs scenery. Ask the question a parable is designed to make you ask: “where am I in this?” Then bring Jesus what you do not understand, as the disciples did (v. 10).
verseByVerse.note: Teaching from a boat let the whole crowd on the shore see and hear him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sower scatters God’s word freely, and some of it never gets in at all: it lies on hard ground until it is snatched away. Jesus begins with “Listen!” and ends with “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (v. 9), because the great issue of the chapter is how we listen.

The sowing. A Galilean farmer carried the seed in a bag at his hip and threw it in a wide arc as he walked, often before ploughing, so it fell everywhere: on paths, on limestone a few inches down, on last year’s thorn roots. He is not careless; he cannot see what lies under the surface.

Along the path. The path is not bad soil by nature. Nobody decided to make it hard; the same feet went over it, day after day, until it set like a floor and nothing could get in.

The birds came and devoured it. At once. Jesus will say who the birds are: Satan comes and takes the word away (v. 15). So sitting through a sermon and remembering none of it by lunchtime is not always a neutral lapse of concentration; something can be at work in it. And the path is the soil nobody worries about being, which is its danger. It feels nothing. The word lies there and is carried off, and the man goes home to his lunch undisturbed and slightly bored.

A sower went out. The first sower in this parable is the man telling it: “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man” (Matthew 13:37). “That is why I came out”, he said (1:38). He came from the Father to sow the word in a world of paths, rocks and thorns, and flung it wide, to Pharisees and fishermen, to Judas and to Peter. He does not ration his mercy to the promising. Every faithful preacher since is only scattering from his bag.

The first comfort. Here is the first comfort in the chapter, for anyone who has taught, preached, raised children in the faith, or spoken of Christ to a friend and watched nothing happen. You are not asked to survey the soil first; you cannot see into another human being. Sow. The results were never the part assigned to you.

I forget sermons by lunchtime. What can I do? Help the seed go in before the birds arrive. Pray beforehand that God would open your heart. Read the passage first if you know it. Listen with a pen and write down one sentence to remember. Talk about the sermon over lunch, and come back to the passage during the week. Above all, act on one thing it said. Truth that is obeyed is not easily stolen.
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some seed springs up fast and withers just as fast, because nothing has gone down beneath the surface. Quick early growth is no proof of life; roots are.

Rocky ground. Not soil full of stones but a thin skin of earth over limestone bedrock, common in Galilee. It looks exactly like the rest, and, cruelly, it performs best at first.

Immediately it sprang up. It came up fast because the soil was shallow: it warmed quickly, and since the seed could not go down, everything went up. The fastest, greenest growth in the field is the growth that is going to die. Anyone long in church life has watched it: the radiant new convert at everything, and gone in three years, and nobody can say quite when they stopped coming.

It withered away. The sun that made it sprout killed it, while in the good soil it ripened the harvest; the difference is underground. The same bereavement or diagnosis will strengthen one believer and break another, and the difference was decided long before the heat arrived.

A root out of dry ground. The deepest roots in Scripture belong to Christ. The Servant “grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground” (Isaiah 53:2), and never withered, because his life was drawn from his Father. Lasting faith is rooted not in our depth of character but in him: Paul prays that believers be “rooted and grounded in love”, and tells them to walk in Christ, “rooted and built up in him” (Ephesians 3:17; Colossians 2:6–7). Shallow faith rests on an experience of Jesus; rooted faith rests on Jesus.

Roots are grown in private. The question is not how green you look this month but what is happening in the dark. Roots go down in the unglamorous stretches: the half-hour with a Bible on a wet Tuesday when nothing in you wants it, prayers that feel like talking to the ceiling, Sundays you attend when you would rather not, doctrine learned before you need it. None of it shows. That is the point of it.

What it does not mean. If a loss has shaken you badly, that is not the same as withering. A believer can be “struck down, but not destroyed” (2 Corinthians 4:9), and the very fact that you still reach for him in the dark is a root holding.

How can I tell whether my faith has roots, or whether I am rocky ground? Look below the feelings. Rooted faith keeps going when they go: you still pray when prayer is dry, still trust when God seems silent, still belong to his people when church disappoints, and you have come through some heat clinging to Christ rather than resenting him. If you are unsure, do not torment yourself with introspection. Go to Christ, ask him to root you, and start digging: Scripture, prayer, church, obedience, day after ordinary day.
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no grain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some seed survives but is crowded out by other growth, until it bears nothing at all. The danger here is not wickedness but ordinary things allowed to take all the room.

Among thorns. The thorns are invisible at the sowing: last season’s roots, burned off at the surface.

Choked. Then the rains come, wheat and thorns come up together, and the thorns grow faster. Choking is silent but total. Nobody digs up the wheat; it is crowded, shaded and starved by things that are also alive and also using the ground.

It yielded no grain. Only Mark adds this. The plant is still there, green and standing; it simply never produces anything.

The thorns are not scandalous sins. Jesus explains them later in the chapter (vv. 18–19): not adultery, theft or blasphemy, but worry, money and the wanting of ordinary things. So this soil cannot be diagnosed by examining your conduct. None of it is wicked; all of it uses up the room the word needs. The sign is not a sin committed but a fruit you cannot find: the prayer that has quietly stopped, the Bible opened only on Sunday, the conversation about Christ you have not had in a year, not because you decided against it, but because there has been no room.

Thorns and the crown. Thorns entered the Bible with the curse: “cursed is the ground because of you”; “thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you” (Genesis 3:17–18). Every heart crowded by care is that curse at work inside. On the morning of his death soldiers twisted a crown of thorns and put it on Jesus’ head (15:17).
