The King wore the curse of the ground as his crown, so that ground choked by the fall could be made good. The cure for a choked life is not first a better schedule but a Saviour who has already borne the curse that makes the thorns grow.

Is it wrong to plan, work hard and provide for my family? No. Scripture commands it (1 Thessalonians 4:11; 1 Timothy 5:8; Proverbs 6:6–8). The problem is not that these things exist but that they take first place. The test is whether your work and plans are done before God, with prayer, and leave room for worship, his word, his people and generosity. “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33). Thorns grow where good things are allowed to grow unweeded.

verseByVerse.quote: And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold." And he said, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some seed falls on good soil, and despite every loss the harvest is far beyond anything a farmer could hope for. God’s word will not fail, so hear it with more than your ears.

Good soil. After three failures, the harvest. The good soil does nothing to make itself good; it receives what falls on it and lets it go down. Mark alone says the grain was “growing up and increasing”: this growth takes its time. Fast is not the same as fruitful, and slow is not the same as dead.

A hundredfold. A normal harvest was perhaps seven to tenfold, out of which next year’s seed had to come. Thirty was excellent; a hundred was astonishing, the blessing Isaac received in the year God prospered him (Genesis 26:12). Three of the four kinds of ground are a loss, and the harvest is still extravagant.

Ears to hear. A call to hear with understanding and respond, the refrain that sounds again over the seven churches (Revelation 2–3). Everyone on that beach had ears; a person can hear the sound and miss the meaning. Spiritual hearing is a gift, and whoever wants it has only to ask the one in the boat.

The grain that dies. A harvest like this comes from the Sower’s own death. In the week he died, Jesus said of himself, “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). The hundredfold of the gospel age, the church gathered from every nation, is the fruit of one grain buried in a garden tomb and raised on the third day, the firstfruits of all who will rise (1 Corinthians 15:20).

The accounts at the end. In Galilee that year it looked as though this was going badly: the scribes called him possessed, his family thought him out of his mind, and the crowds wanted healings. Jesus tells them what the accounts will say at the end: the harvest far outweighs the losses. Hold on to that when your own field shows mostly loss: children not walking with God, years of teaching that seemed to change nobody, a church smaller than it was. The losses are real, but they are not the end of the story. God “will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness” (2 Corinthians 9:10).

What is the fruit, exactly? Not only converts, though bringing others to Christ is part of it. The fruit is a life changed by the word: the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), good works (Colossians 1:10), repentance that shows in what you do (Matthew 3:8), praise (Hebrews 13:15) and generosity (Philippians 4:17). It grows slowly and is often seen more clearly by others; ask someone who knows you well whether they see more of Christ in you than five years ago.

In everyday life. Bring to mind one person you have been sowing into for a long time with little to show for it, and pray for them, trusting the harvest to the one who promised it.
verseByVerse.note: A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. And he said to them, "To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who come to Jesus and ask are given the secret of the kingdom; for those who refuse him, the parables become a judgment, as Isaiah foretold. The same stories that open the truth to the seeking leave it closed to the hard.

They asked him. The crowd goes home, and a smaller group, those around him with the Twelve, stays behind and asks. They are not insiders because they understood (v. 13 shows they did not), but because they stayed and asked.

The secret of the kingdom. “Secret” in the New Testament is not a puzzle for clever people but a truth once hidden and now revealed by God. The secret is that the kingdom has come in Jesus, but in a hidden, unexpected way: like seed, not like a conquering army; in a carpenter from Nazareth who is going to a cross. And it “has been given”: understanding is God’s gift (Matthew 16:17). So is the faith that receives it.

Those outside. Those who have rejected Jesus. Mark used the same word of his family, standing outside the house (3:31–32).

See but not perceive. The hardest sentence in the chapter, and it must not be smoothed over: it sounds as though Jesus speaks in stories so that people will not repent. Three things open it up. First, these words quote Isaiah 6:9–10. God sent Isaiah to a people who had refused the truth for generations, and Jesus’ parables work the same way on those who have rejected him: a judgment on hearts already closed, the passage the New Testament reaches for again and again to explain unbelief (Matthew 13:14–15; John 12:40; Acts 28:26–27). Second, it is Scripture being fulfilled (see “Uncertain wording” below), the pattern Paul describes when God gives people over to what they have already chosen (Romans 1:24, 26, 28): the darkness they preferred, finally granted.

Lest they should turn. “Turn” is repentance, a change of mind that turns the whole person from sin to God (1 Thessalonians 1:9). And third, decisively, the door is never bolted against anyone who knocks. The proof is sitting in the room: the only thing separating the Twelve from the crowd walking home is that they asked. “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find” (Matthew 7:7).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus wanted to keep willing people from being saved. Those who wanted to understand asked, and he explained (v. 34); the hardening falls on those who refuse, and the parables are also meant to reveal, as a lamp is meant to be seen (v. 21). God is sovereign in revealing and hiding (Matthew 11:25–26), and people are responsible for refusing.

Am I one of those outside if I do not understand much of the Bible? No. The disciples did not understand either, and were still slow years later. Being inside is not about how much you understand but whether you have come to Jesus and keep coming. If you love him and bring him your questions, the secret has been given to you. Understanding grows over a lifetime: keep reading, keep asking, and be patient with yourself.

Uncertain wording. The small words “so that” and “lest” are hard to pin down. The Greek hina usually expresses purpose and mēpote normally means “lest”, so the plain sense is that the parables were meant to have this effect on those outside. Some take “so that” to describe the result rather than the aim; others take it as shorthand for “so that the Scripture might be fulfilled”, as Matthew puts it: “in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled” (Matthew 13:14). A few suggest that “lest” could mean “unless perhaps”. What is clear is that Jesus is applying Isaiah’s sentence of judgment on hearts that had refused God’s word, while the door stays open to all who come and ask.
verseByVerse.note: A “secret” (mystery) in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? The sower sows the word. And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seed is God’s word, and in some who hear it, Satan snatches it away before it can take hold. Jesus begins to explain the parable, and it is the key to all the others.

Do you not understand this parable? There is a sigh in “How then will you understand all the parables?”, and Mark is not embarrassed to record it. But it is said in the middle of explaining: he asks, and then tells them. That is mercy for slow disciples, which is all of us: the men who were with him some three years were consistently baffled, and the Lord kept teaching them. Understand how the word is received, and you can understand everything else.

The sower sows the word. The seed is the word, not a mood but sentences that can be spoken and heard; the sower is Jesus, and all who preach his word after him. “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17); we are born again “through the living and abiding word of God” (1 Peter 1:23). So an unremarkable sermon in a half-empty building on a wet Sunday is not a low-grade activity. It is the sowing.

Satan immediately comes. Jesus names the birds. Satan is a personal being, and he takes the word by distraction, mockery, doubt or forgetfulness: “the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:4). “Immediately”: in the car park, on the walk home. The word did not fail to be good; it was removed before it could get in.

If Satan takes the word away, are people who reject the gospel still responsible? Yes. Satan blinds, but he blinds people who prefer the dark (John 3:19). The path was hardened by traffic it allowed; the hearer is a willing participant in his own forgetting, and Scripture never lets us blame the devil for our unbelief, any more than Eve could (Genesis 3:13). Yet God can break up hard ground, and invites everyone to ask. Responsibility and the need for grace stand together.

In everyday life. If you have started to find God’s word dull, take that to God tonight, in exactly those words. He has never refused a man who asked him to break up his own hard ground: “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). The path cannot plough itself. It does not have to.

parallels.desc: the god of this world has blinded the minds

verseByVerse.quote: And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some receive the word gladly but have no root, and when following Christ begins to cost them, they fall away. Joy at the start is good, but it is not the same as life that lasts.

Receive it with joy. It looks like conversion, and there is nothing wrong with the joy, which needs saying, because this soil frightens sensitive people. Real conversion is glad (Matthew 13:44). The problem is not that they were happy but that happiness was all there was.

No root in themselves. Not “no root in the church”, but “no root in themselves”: something was never made their own. Their faith lived on its surroundings, the music, the friendships, the feeling in the room, a preacher they admired, and never went down into private ground. And they “endure for a while”, which is why it takes time to tell: for a season this soil looks like good soil, at first even better. It might be two years.

On account of the word. The heat is the cost of the faith itself: friendships that cool once you are known as a Christian, the promotion that goes elsewhere, and in much of the world far worse, as Mark’s first readers knew (see the introduction). This soil discovers Christianity is expensive, having assumed it was free.

They fall away. “Fall away” means stumble, be tripped up, the root of Paul’s word for the cross as a stumbling block (1 Corinthians 1:23). Mark uses “immediately” at every stage of this soil: it springs up, receives and falls away immediately (vv. 5, 16–17).

You will all fall away. Jesus uses the same verb on the night he is arrested: “You will all fall away” (14:27), and every one of them fled (14:50). So what separates the Twelve from the rocky ground? Not the strength of their roots that night, but the grip of their Shepherd. In the same breath he promised, “after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee” (14:28), and to Peter he said, “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32). They stumbled and were brought back, because their faith was rooted in a Saviour who intercedes. Every true believer has that root.

How do I help a new believer put down roots? Do not dampen their joy; build under it. Read a Gospel with them a chapter at a time and show them how to pray from it. Bring them into a church where people will know them, not just greet them. Teach them the basics of the faith. Warn them honestly that following Christ will cost something, so the heat does not surprise them. And keep in touch when they go quiet. Roots grow best in company.

Where Christians differ: were these true believers who lost their salvation? Arminian Christians (who hold that God’s grace can be resisted and true faith finally lost), brothers who take the Bible’s warnings seriously, read the rocky soil as real faith, received with joy and then lost (compare Hebrews 6:4–6). This commentary’s view: Jesus says they have “no root in themselves”; something was missing from the start. The joy was real, but it was not the life of a new heart: “they went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). The fruitless soils describe profession without possession. A true believer may stumble and struggle, but the word that has truly taken root goes on to bear fruit, because God who began a good work will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

verseByVerse.quote: And others are the ones sown among thorns. They are those who hear the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some hear the word and let worry, the lie of wealth and the wanting of other things crowd it out, until it bears no fruit. This is the particular danger of churchgoers in a comfortable country, and Jesus names its three weeds.

The cares of the world. Not open sin, but ordinary anxieties (the word Peter uses in “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you”, 1 Peter 5:7). The mortgage, the scan result, the parents growing frail: most come with real duties. They strangle the word because worry takes the room that hearing God requires.

The deceitfulness of riches. Not riches, but the lie they tell, that a little more will make you safe and you do not need God (10:23–25; 1 Timothy 6:9–10). It is told to the man with little as loudly as to the man with much, so this weed grows in every income bracket.

The desires for other things. Only Mark has this phrase: the extension, the holiday, the hobby you think about while other people are talking. None of it is wrong, which is why it is hard to see from inside. Good things become thorns when they take first place.

It proves unfruitful. These things “enter in”, one reasonable thing at a time, until the word is crowded to the edge. The faith is never renounced; the plant survives, but bears nothing, sometimes for years in church.

The surpassing worth. Thorns are crowded out not by willpower but by a greater love, God’s love “poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5:5). Paul counted everything as loss “because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8). The remedy is not a life emptied of ordinary goods, but a heart in which Christ has become the treasure worth selling all for (Matthew 13:44), so that money, plans and worries are put back beneath him. A choked heart does not need less to love. It needs to see how much more there is to love in him.

How do I weed the thorns? By small, regular weeding, done in the light of how much you are loved. Name them. Notice what took up most of your thinking this week; thorns grow best unnoticed. Hand over the cares. Turn each worry into a specific request and leave it with him. Give first. Decide what you will give before what you will spend; nothing loosens the grip of riches like an open hand. Guard the ground. Keep a fixed time for his word before the other voices arrive. Ask what you are really wanting. Behind most “desires for other things” lies a longing for security or significance that Christ has already given you. You are not weeding to win his favour, but making room for a Saviour who already loves you.

Is it wrong to be wealthy? Not in itself: Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly. But wealth is unusually dangerous because it deceives (10:23–25). Paul tells the rich not to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches but on God, and to be generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–18). So hold money with an open hand: give generously, live below your means, and ask whether your security is in your savings or your Saviour. The test is not how much you have but how easily you could give it away.

Where Christians differ: is this hearer a Christian at all? Some teach that he is a carnal Christian, saved but fruitless and unrewarded (compare 1 Corinthians 3:15). This commentary’s view: in the parable only the good soil yields a harvest, and Jesus says elsewhere that every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down (Matthew 7:19). A life that bears nothing at the harvest shows a faith that never truly lived. A believer may have seasons of little fruit and be pruned (John 15:2), but the word truly received does not stay barren for good.

verseByVerse.quote: But those that were sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good soil hears the word, welcomes it and bears fruit, and every yield, thirty, sixty or a hundred, is a harvest God calls his own. What marks it out is not hearing, which all four soils do, but welcoming.

Hear and accept. Three verbs, in an order that cannot be rearranged: hear, accept, bear fruit. Hearing is where everyone starts and where three of the four stop. “Accept” (paradechontai) means welcome, the way you receive a guest rather than a leaflet; Luke says they “hold it fast” (Luke 8:15). It is not merely agreeing that the sermon was true, but letting the word in with authority, to contradict you and change what you do on Monday.

And bear fruit. Fruit is not the price of acceptance but its result, though we keep turning the order round. No plant produces grain by straining; it receives light and water, and the fruit comes out of that. “Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me” (John 15:4). That answers the exhausting effort of many sincere Christians to squeeze fruit out of themselves. You are asked not to manufacture fruit but to receive, and keep receiving.

All three are good soil. The kindness is in the last clause: the yields differ, and all three are good soil. The thirtyfold Christian is not second-class; the Lord of the harvest rejoices over thirty, sixty or a hundred, and calls it all his.

Where does good soil come from? Every heart is hard by nature, and God makes it good: he gives a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26), he opens hearts, as he opened Lydia’s (Acts 16:14), and he gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). Our part is to receive the word humbly (James 1:21). The Sower knew exactly what was under the surface of your life when he threw his seed there, and he is the one who breaks up the ground.

What if I see very little fruit in my life? First, do not measure yourself by others. Some believers are given health, gifts and opportunity, and their lives are visibly fruitful. Others are ill, poor, obscure or worn down, and what they produce is thirty: a marriage held together, a few people prayed for by name for decades, a faith kept where nobody applauded. Both are gathered into the same barn. Second, fruit is often invisible to the tree; ask a mature friend what they see. Third, if there really is nothing, go back to the root: are you abiding in Christ, in his word, in prayer, among his people? Fruit comes from there, not from trying harder.

parallels.desc: whoever abides in me bears much fruit

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest; nor is anything secret except to come to light. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The truth Jesus brings is hidden for a time only so that it may finally be seen by all. A lamp is lit to give light, and the kingdom veiled now will one day blaze into the open.

Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket? After hard words about seeing and not perceiving (vv. 11–12), Jesus asks a question a child could answer. A household lamp was a small clay bowl of olive oil with a wick; the basket (modios) was a grain measure, and the bed a low couch. The question is faintly comic on purpose: no one lights a lamp to hide it. The Greek says literally, “Does the lamp come?”, and some see Jesus himself as the lamp come into the world.

Hidden to be made manifest. If the parables conceal, is God in the business of hiding things? No. The kingdom is hidden now (vv. 10–12), but the purpose of the hiding is the showing.

Nothing secret except to come to light. The secret will be proclaimed after the resurrection (9:9). Jesus silences demons and hushes the healed, then dies in public in the busiest week of the year, and a Roman centurion says aloud what nobody was allowed to say (15:39). The secret was protected until it could be understood, the way you shield a flame with your hand while carrying it; then he was lifted up in the sight of all, and the light broke out over the nations. One day every hidden thing will be revealed, and the brightest thing revealed will be the glory of the Lamb.

The dark parts of your own story. Here is comfort for the parts of your life that make no sense yet. The verse does not promise an explanation next Tuesday; it promises that nothing in the hands of God is hidden for the sake of being hidden. “Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

Will my secret sins be exposed on the day of judgment if I am a Christian? The New Testament does say that “nothing is covered up that will not be revealed” (Luke 12:2), and that “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10). But for those in Christ it is not condemnation (Romans 8:1). Your sins were brought into the light at the cross, judged there, and removed as far as the east is from the west (Psalm 103:12); whatever is shown that day will be shown as forgiven, to magnify his grace. So you need not dread exposure. Bring your secrets into the light now, to God and, where wise, to a trusted friend (1 John 1:7).
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick; the “basket” was a grain measure.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Pay attention to what you hear: with the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Listen with care, because what you do with what you hear decides how much more God gives you. Whoever takes in the word and acts on it receives more; whoever neglects it loses even what he has.

Pay attention to what you hear. Literally “see what you hear” (Luke 8:18 has “take care then how you hear”). Listening is something you do, well or badly.

The measure you use. A merchant’s picture: bring a thimble and you carry home a thimbleful, however generous he is. The attention and response you give to God’s word determine how much understanding you receive. Then Jesus goes beyond the picture: “still more will be added”. God gives more than you brought room for.

To the one who has. It sounds like the rich getting richer, but this is how understanding works. Everything you take in and act on enlarges the vessel you bring next time, as a man who learns a little of a language starts hearing words where he heard only noise. And “even what he has” is lost: a truth heard and never obeyed hardens, and is easier to ignore next time. That is how the hard path of the parable is made.

Listen to him. On the mountain the Father said: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him” (9:7). God has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and therefore “we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away from it” (Hebrews 2:1). To give the eternal Son only a little of our attention is not caution. It is a small view of a great Saviour.

Does this mean God gives more to clever people? No. The measure is not intelligence but obedience. A child who believes and obeys a simple truth receives more than a scholar who studies Scripture and does nothing with it. Some of the wisest people in any church have little formal education; they have spent decades doing what God says. Anyone can bring a heart that hears and obeys.

In everyday life. Recall the last thing God said to you that you knew you were meant to do: the conversation, the person to forgive, the money to give. Did you do it? If yes, expect more. If no, he has not stopped speaking, but the next thing he says will be fainter, for obedience is the only container that ever gets bigger. None of us brings a full measure (James 3:2), but Christ obeyed perfectly in your place, his obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), and so your small, real obedience, worked in you by his Spirit (Philippians 2:13), is accepted for his sake. And if your feelings have gone flat through grief, illness or depression, do not read this as your case: numbness is not disobedience, and he does not break a bruised reed (Isaiah 42:3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–41 — The Growing Seed, the Mustard Seed, and the Storm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom grows by God’s power, not ours, and its King rules even the sea. Seed sprouts while the farmer sleeps, he knows not how, until the harvest comes (vv. 26–29), and the smallest seed becomes the largest garden plant, with birds nesting in its shade (vv. 30–32). Mark sums up: parables for the crowd, as they were able to hear, and everything explained to his own (vv. 33–34). Then at evening Jesus takes them across the lake, at his own word, into a storm. He sleeps; they accuse him of not caring; he speaks, and the wind and the sea obey, leaving them asking, “Who then is this?” (vv. 35–41).
verseByVerse.theology:
The stilling of the storm shows who is in the boat. In the Old Testament it is God who rules the sea (see v. 39).

Jesus was asleep because he was exhausted, and he silenced the sea with a word. Fully man in his tiredness, fully God in his voice.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: experienced fishermen bailing with their hands, sure they were about to die, while their Lord slept beside them.

Now: believers in a storm still ask do you not care? (On such prayers, see vv. 37–38.)

He stilled the storm first and asked about their faith afterwards, and their great fear after the calm was the beginning of knowing who he is (see vv. 40–41).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom grows by God’s power, not ours: the seed sprouts and ripens while the farmer sleeps, until the harvest comes. Only Mark records this parable, and it is the most restful thing in the chapter.

In the flow. Three seed parables, three worries: why so few bear fruit (the sower), why nothing seems to be happening (this one), and whether it is all too small to matter (vv. 30–32). The kingdom is not failing. It is growing in the ground.

He sleeps and rises night and day. The farmer sows, and then, the surprise of the story, does nothing. He goes to bed; he gets up. There is no anxious digging up of seed to see how it is doing. Beneath much of our anxiety about others’ growth is a wish to be in control, and the parable gently takes it out of our hands: the growth belongs to God, and so does the timing. “He gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2).

He knows not how. His ignorance does not slow the crop by a day. To twelve men just appointed to a mission and unqualified for it, Jesus says: you scatter, and then you sleep. The power was never in the sower.

The earth produces by itself. “By itself” (automatē, from which we get automatic) means without visible cause: not without God, but without the farmer. “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6).

First the blade. The tenderest line for anyone worried about slowness: a blade is not a failed ear but exactly what a healthy plant looks like in April. God is not disappointed with a young Christian for not being an old one, and he is not finished with an old one either.

The harvest has come. The words echo Joel: “Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe” (Joel 3:13), a text about the final judgment of the nations. The harvest pictures the end of the age (Matthew 13:39). The long, quiet middle of history, where the kingdom looks small and slow, is not drift but growing season: the life of the kingdom is his life, hidden in the soil of the world, rising in its seasons, unstoppable.

One like a son of man, with a sickle. John saw “one like a son of man” with “a sharp sickle in his hand” (Revelation 14:14). Jesus says the same in Mark: the Son of Man will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds (13:26–27). The sleeping sower cannot make the seed grow, but the reaper at the end is the Lord himself: the one who sowed the word in Galilee will gather the grain on the day his Father has set (13:32).

What it does not mean. Not passivity: the farmer sows and reaps. But we cannot force growth, in our children, our church or ourselves.

Why can’t we leave anything alone? Modern life is a machine for control. We track our sleep, our steps and our children’s progress. The German sociologist Hartmut Rosa argues that the driving project of modernity is to make the world controllable, and notices the irony: the more of it we master, the more the world seems to fall silent, because what makes life worth living, love, trust, real joy, cannot be produced to order. Religious people try to manage God by performance, secular people try to manage life by technique, and both lie awake. The farmer is not lazy. He is free. He does his part and goes to bed, because the growth belongs to someone else. That is the shape of the gospel: we are not saved by managing the outcome but by trusting the one who has already secured it, and who goes on working while we sleep.

How should I pray for a child or friend who shows no sign of growth? Keep sowing and praying, and then actually go to bed. Pray that God would open their heart, as he opened Lydia’s (Acts 16:14). Live out the faith in front of them with warmth rather than pressure, and keep the door open. Do not dig up the seed every week; nagging rarely helps. Many a believer looks back on years when others saw nothing while the seed was at work underground. The harvest comes when the grain is ripe, not when we are ready.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records this parable of the seed growing by itself.

parallels.desc: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe
the farmer waits for the precious fruit

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth, yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom begins as small as the smallest seed and grows into a great plant where the nations find shelter. Never judge it by how it looks in the palm of your hand.

With what can we compare the kingdom of God? Jesus thinks aloud, as a teacher does when he wants the class leaning in, and reaches for an answer deliberately, almost comically, small.

A grain of mustard seed. The black mustard seed was the proverbial picture of tininess; you could lose it in the creases of your palm. Yet the plant could grow three metres high in one season, “larger than all the garden plants”, and nothing in the seed announces it.

Nests in its shade. In the Old Testament a great tree with birds in its branches pictures a great kingdom sheltering the nations (Ezekiel 31:6; Daniel 4:12). In Ezekiel 17:22–23 God takes a tender sprig from the top of the cedar, the royal line of David, and plants it on the mountain height of Israel, and under it every kind of bird will nest. The birds are the nations.

This kingdom has a boat. Consider who is listening: a dozen men on a beach in an occupied province, following a village carpenter whose family thinks he is out of his mind and whose leaders call him demonic. Rome has legions and roads and an emperor. This kingdom has a boat. And Jesus says: the kingdom of God is that speck in your hand. Yet it has grown into a worldwide kingdom, not by strategy or numbers but by the life God put in the seed. Small is not weak, and slow is not failing.

A shoot from the stump of Jesse. That sprig is the King, the Branch, a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5), and Isaiah adds that the nations will inquire of him and his resting place will be glorious (Isaiah 11:10). The kingdom is small at first because the King came small: a tender shoot from a felled royal house, laid in a manger. The tree that shelters the nations grows from him, and to rest in its shade is to rest in Christ. Planted in the ground like a seed on a Friday, he rose on the Sunday as the firstfruits of a harvest without end.

In everyday life. If the kingdom you can see is discouragingly small, an ageing congregation, the one believer in a family, remember that you are not looking at the tree. You are looking at the seed, and you were never given the ability to tell the difference by looking.

Was Jesus wrong that mustard is the smallest of all seeds? No. He was not lecturing on botany but using the everyday proverb of his hearers about the seeds a Galilean farmer actually sowed, of which mustard was the smallest, just as we say “the sun rises” without being wrong about astronomy. Speaking in the ordinary language of one’s hearers is not error; it is how all clear speech works.

Where Christians differ: will the world become Christian before Christ returns? Postmillennialists (who expect the gospel to bring a long golden age before his coming) read the parables of growth that way, a hope many godly Reformed believers have held. This commentary’s view: amillennial (Christ reigns now, through the whole age between his two comings, with no separate earthly millennium still to come). The parables of growth stand alongside those of mixed fields and continuing evil (Matthew 13:24–30): the kingdom grows powerfully through the whole gospel age, but not into a Christian world before his return, and comes to its fullness when Christ returns.
verseByVerse.note: Mustard seed was proverbially tiny; the plant can grow taller than a man.

verseByVerse.quote: With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus taught the crowds in parables at the pace they could take, and explained everything to those who came to him. Mark steps back for two verses to tell us how the Lord taught.

As they were able to hear it. One of the kindest clauses in the Gospel: he measured his words to what they could bear (compare John 16:12). The Son of God, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, stooped to the measure of fishermen. Parables were both a mercy, making truth memorable, and a test, concealing it from the unwilling.

He explained everything. The difference between the two audiences is not intelligence but willingness to come: the crowd got the story, the ones who stayed got the meaning (v. 10), and the door was never locked.

Two lessons. If you are impatient with your own understanding, he is not withholding out of displeasure, but giving at the rate you can receive. And if the Lord matched what he said to his hearers, so should we. Some zealous Christians unload every hard truth at once onto a new believer or someone just bereaved, and call it faithfulness. Say what they can take in now. There will be other days for the rest.

How do I ask Jesus to explain Scripture today? By his Spirit through his word, so use the ordinary means. Pray before you read, asking him to open your eyes (Psalm 119:18). Read slowly, with the surrounding chapters, since Scripture interprets Scripture. Bring your questions to faithful preaching, mature Christians, a good commentary or a small group. And obey what you do understand, because understanding grows through obedience (John 7:17). He gives no new revelation, but light on what he has said.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, "Let us go across to the other side." And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. And other boats were with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is Jesus who sends his disciples out onto the lake that evening, and his word is a promise that they will reach the other side. The storm that follows meets them in the middle of obeying him.

In the flow. The teaching ends and the deeds begin: four mighty works, over the sea, a legion of demons, a long illness and death itself (4:35–5:43), each answering “who then is this?” a little more fully.

When evening had come. After a long day of teaching, as it was getting dark.

Let us go across to the other side. To the eastern shore, largely Gentile territory (5:1). Going out onto that lake was his idea, and his word was a promise that they would arrive.

Just as he was. He was already in the boat (v. 1), with no going ashore and no meal, which explains his sleep (v. 38).

Other boats. Only Mark mentions this, and it is easy to skip. There were other people out on that water in the dark, with no one aboard who could still a wave. Mark says nothing more, and the silence is its own comfort: when the calm came, it came over the whole lake, for some who never knew who had done it. Much of what God does in answer to the church’s praying spills far past the church, and is never traced back.

Does a storm in my life mean I have disobeyed God? Not necessarily. When trouble comes we search backwards for the wrong turn: what did I miss, where did I disobey? Sometimes there is one, and it should be repented of. But this boat is in this storm because Jesus put it there; they sailed into it by obeying him. Job did not suffer because he had drifted; the book opens by insisting he was blameless. Paul was in the will of God on the ship that broke up under him (Acts 27). Your storm may not mean anything has gone wrong at all. It may be part of the cost of going where he sends you.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. And they woke him and said to him, "Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A storm is about to sink the boat while Jesus sleeps, and his terrified disciples wake him and accuse him of not caring. In one scene Mark shows us both the true humanity of Jesus and what fear does to us.

A great windstorm. A furious squall that hits without warning. The Sea of Galilee lies about 700 feet below sea level in a bowl of hills, and cold air rushing down onto the warm lake can take it from glass to breaking waves in minutes.

The boat was already filling. Waves are coming in over the side. At least four of these men are fishermen who have worked this lake since boyhood. When men like that conclude they are about to drown, they are almost certainly right.

Asleep on the cushion. Only Mark mentions the cushion, the kind of detail an eyewitness remembers. And the sleep is a window onto who Jesus is: the Son of God got properly tired. He was hungry (11:12), thirsty (John 19:28), and wept at a graveside (John 11:35). And his sleep showed complete trust in his Father: “In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (Psalm 4:8). He can sleep in a storm on a lake he made.

Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing? Only Mark records the question in these words, and he did not tidy it up. It is not a request but an accusation: not “save us”, but “do you not care?” That is what fear does. It goes past the danger and attacks the character of God: the one in charge has gone quiet and might not be bothered. In storms we often feel the same. But he did care. He was with them in the boat.

Is it wrong to complain to God like that? Scripture is full of honest complaint, and preserves this sentence rather than hiding it. “Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord?” (Psalm 44:23). “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1). God would rather have that cried out to him from four feet away than have you drown politely at the other end of the boat. What is wrong is accusing him and walking away. These men got one thing right amid everything else: when they were sure they were dying, they went to him. So pour out your heart, and then, as the psalmists did, remind yourself of his steadfast love.

Uncertain wording. “The cushion” translates a word (proskephalaion) that means a headrest or pillow, and Mark writes as if it were a familiar part of the boat. What exactly it was is not known: perhaps a leather cushion for the helmsman or an oarsman, perhaps a sandbag kept in the stern as ballast. Either way, Jesus lay down in the stern, the most sheltered place in the boat, and slept.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common. The cushion was probably the helmsman’s seat or a sandbag in the stern.

parallels.desc: the sleeping prophet in the storm
awake! why are you sleeping, O Lord?

verseByVerse.quote: And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, "Peace! Be still!" And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus speaks to the wind and the sea as their Lord, and they obey him at once. He does what the Old Testament says only God can do.

He rebuked the wind. He does not take the helm or pray for deliverance; he speaks to the weather. “Rebuked” is the word used for silencing a demon (1:25), as for a hostile thing that has no business being there, and “Be still!” is literally “Be muzzled!”, the very word spoken to that demon.

Only God rules the sea. To Israel the sea was chaos, the old enemy, which only God rules. “You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them” (Psalm 89:9; compare 65:7). “Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed” (Job 38:11). And this is a carpenter, standing in a fishing boat, wet through, speaking to a storm in the dark.

A great calm. Normally the swell outlives the storm. Here the calm is instant: a great storm (v. 37), a great calm, and one sentence between them. Every other help you have ever had works with the situation, manages it, gets you through it. He speaks to it.

The storm nobody rebuked. Once more in Mark the world goes dark and then quiet. On a hill outside Jerusalem the sky turns black at noon for three hours, a man cries out that God has forsaken him, and he dies (15:33–37). That day nobody rebuked the storm. He went into it and let it break over him with nothing held back, and it was not muzzled, and it did not stop until it had finished with him. The voice that could have silenced anything said nothing at all, so that when the storms come for us they come as hard weather and never as God’s wrath against us.

If Jesus rules the wind and the sea, why does he allow storms and disasters? Scripture gives no full explanation, but enough to trust him. Natural disasters belong to a creation subjected to futility because of human sin, groaning to be set free (Romans 8:20–22). God rules them still, and works through all things for the good of those who love him (Romans 8:28). Sometimes disasters warn a careless world to repent (Luke 13:4–5). And the one who stilled one storm on one lake will one day remove every storm from a renewed creation, where there is no more sea (Revelation 21:1). Until then, we bring our fears to the one who rules the waves.

parallels.desc: you rule the raging of the sea
he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?" And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, "Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus rebukes his disciples for fearing as if he were not with them, and the calm leaves them more afraid than the storm did, asking who he can be. The danger is over; now they are face to face with the one who ended it.

Why are you so afraid? It sounds hard, but two things take the sting out of it without taking away the point. First, he stilled the storm and then asked the question. He did not require better praying before he would act; he dealt with the water first, and only afterwards with what was wrong inside the boat. Remember that when you are ashamed of how badly you prayed in a crisis. Second, the word (deiloi) means timid, cowardly: not that they felt fear but that they feared as if he were not there. They had every reason to fear the lake and none to fear with him aboard. The rebuke is not, “you felt something”. It is, “you forgot who was aboard”.

Have you still no faith? “Still” is the sad word: after a leper cleansed, a paralytic walking, demons obeying him. Faith here means trusting Jesus to keep his word: he had said they would go to the other side (v. 35). We know the gap between what we believe on a Sunday and what we can hold on to at three in the morning, when the water comes over the side.

They were filled with great fear. Literally “they feared a great fear”. The lake is like glass, and the disciples are more frightened than during the storm: no longer of drowning, but of the man standing in the boat with them, dripping wet, an arm’s length away. This is not a failure of faith but the beginning of understanding. It is the fear of God, as the sailors in Jonah’s storm feared the LORD exceedingly when the sea grew calm (Jonah 1:16), and as Isaiah, seeing the Lord, said, “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isaiah 6:5). The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: not the cringing dread of a slave, but the awe of a creature who has seen how great and holy God is, which draws him near in worship rather than driving him away: “But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared” (Psalm 130:4).

Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? The question of the whole Gospel. They ask it of each other, in the dark, on flat water, and do not answer it; Mark leaves it hanging, because the whole Gospel is the answer, complete only at the cross and the empty tomb. But their own Scriptures had already answered it. Of the LORD, Psalm 107:29 says, “He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed.” Jesus has done what only God does; there is one name in the Old Testament that fits. The answer to their question is in Mark’s first verse: the Son of God.

That is who was in the boat. The man asleep on the cushion is the one who said to the ocean, “Thus far shall you come, and no farther”, before there was a man alive to see it. The Lord of the wind and the sea lay tired out in the stern, in a body he took so that he could sleep, and thirst, and bleed, and die, for the men bailing water round his feet. “Who then is this?” He is the Son of God, and he is ours.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus always removes life’s storms when we ask. Sometimes he calms the storm; sometimes he calms us in it. The story is first about who he is.

Is fear always a lack of faith? No. Fear is a natural response to real danger, and Jesus himself was greatly distressed in Gethsemane (14:33). Scripture tells us what to do with fear: “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you” (Psalm 56:3). The disciples’ problem was not that they felt afraid in a sinking boat, but that fear made them doubt his care and forget his power. So do not add guilt to fear. Take it to Christ, tell him plainly, and remind yourself who is in the boat.

Hasn’t science ruled this out? Many thoughtful people feel that it has: we know how storms work, and a man speaking to the weather sounds like the world before meteorology. But notice who is telling it: fishermen who knew exactly how storms on this lake behave, which is why they were terrified. A miracle only registers with people who know the regularities well. C. S. Lewis, in Miracles, offered a picture. Put six pennies in a drawer on Monday and six more on Tuesday, and the laws say you will find twelve on Wednesday, unless a thief has been at the drawer. The laws were not broken; something entered from outside. Science can tell us how nature runs when nothing interferes, but not whether there is anyone who might. So the real question is the one the disciples asked: who then is this? If the God who made the sea had come aboard, a calm lake is the least surprising thing in the story, and the order the sceptic relies on is his gift in the first place.

parallels.desc: who stills the roaring of the seas

4.theology:
Why parables? Verses 11–12 quote Isaiah 6:9–10 (see the note on vv. 10–12).

Who is in the boat? In the Old Testament only God rules the sea, so the disciples’ closing question has one answer (see vv. 40–41). And Mark shows that he is both man and God within a few feet (see vv. 37–38 and v. 39).
4.examples:
The four soils are four possibilities in any congregation on any Sunday.

The path was made hard by traffic, not by a decision (see vv. 3–4).

The rocky ground grows fastest because the soil is shallow, and the same sun that ripens the good grain withers it (see vv. 5–6).

The thorns are not scandalous sins but cares, riches and the desires for other things (see v. 7 and vv. 18–19).

The good soil yields thirty, sixty or a hundred, and all three are good soil (see v. 20).

keyVerse.quote: And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
keyVerse.note: The chapter about hearing the word ends with the word spoken to a storm, and with the question the whole Gospel exists to answer. The disciples know their Scriptures: only the LORD stills the sea, so the man in the stern is more than a teacher. Their fear is the right kind, the awe that begins true knowledge of who Jesus is.

4.reflection:
Jesus describes four kinds of ground: the hard path, the rocky ground, the thorns and the good soil (vv. 3–20). Which of the dangers he names do you find most at work in your own hearing of God’s word at the moment, and what would help the word go deeper?

The farmer sows and then sleeps, and the seed grows “he knows not how” (vv. 26–29). Where are you anxious about growth you cannot control, in a child, a friend, your church or yourself? What would it look like to keep sowing and leave the growth to God?

The kingdom looked tiny in Galilee, like a mustard seed in the palm (vv. 30–32). Where are you tempted to judge God’s work by its size or speed, and how does this parable change the way you see it?

In the storm the disciples asked, “Do you not care that we are perishing?”, and afterwards, “Who then is this?” (vv. 38, 41). What storms are you facing, and how does knowing who is in the boat with you change the way you bring your fears to him?

5.title: Legion, Daughter, and the Hand That Takes Hold
5.text: <sup>1</sup>They came to the other side of the sea, to the country of the Gerasenes. <sup>2</sup>And when Jesus had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit. <sup>3</sup>He lived among the tombs. And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain, <sup>4</sup>for he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. No one had the strength to subdue him. <sup>5</sup>Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones. <sup>6</sup>And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him. <sup>7</sup>And crying out with a loud voice, he said, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.” <sup>8</sup>For he was saying to him, “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!” <sup>9</sup>And Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He replied, “My name is Legion, for we are many.” <sup>10</sup>And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country. <sup>11</sup>Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, <sup>12</sup>and they begged him, saying, “Send us to the pigs; let us enter them.” <sup>13</sup>So he gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs; and the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea. <sup>14</sup>The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. And people came to see what it was that had happened. <sup>15</sup>And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. <sup>16</sup>And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. <sup>17</sup>And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region. <sup>18</sup>As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed with demons begged him that he might be with him. <sup>19</sup>And he did not permit him but said to him, “Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.” <sup>20</sup>And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled. <sup>21</sup>And when Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered about him, and he was beside the sea. <sup>22</sup>Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, and seeing him, he fell at his feet <sup>23</sup>and implored him earnestly, saying, “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.” <sup>24</sup>And he went with him. And a great crowd followed him and thronged about him. <sup>25</sup>And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, <sup>26</sup>and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse. <sup>27</sup>She had heard the reports about Jesus and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. <sup>28</sup>For she said, “If I touch even his garments, I will be made well.” <sup>29</sup>And immediately the flow of blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease. <sup>30</sup>And Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him, immediately turned about in the crowd and said, “Who touched my garments?” <sup>31</sup>And his disciples said to him, “You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, ‘Who touched me?’” <sup>32</sup>And he looked around to see who had done it. <sup>33</sup>But the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth. <sup>34</sup>And he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.” <sup>35</sup>While he was still speaking, there came from the ruler’s house some who said, “Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?” <sup>36</sup>But overhearing what they said, Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue, “Do not fear, only believe.” <sup>37</sup>And he allowed no one to follow him except Peter and James and John the brother of James. <sup>38</sup>They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly. <sup>39</sup>And when he had entered, he said to them, “Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping.” <sup>40</sup>And they laughed at him. But he put them all outside and took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him and went in where the child was. <sup>41</sup>Taking her by the hand he said to her, “Talitha cumi,” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, arise.” <sup>42</sup>And immediately the girl got up and began walking (for she was twelve years of age), and they were immediately overcome with amazement. <sup>43</sup>And he strictly charged them that no one should know this, and told them to give her something to eat.
5.overview:
Where we are. Mark 5 completes a run of four mighty works that begins with the storm on the lake. The storm ended with the disciples asking, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (4:41), and this chapter answers: a legion of demons, a chronic disease and death itself, obey him too.

The message. No power that holds a human being is too strong for Jesus, and no one is too unclean for him to touch. Here are three impossible cases: a man no one could restrain, a woman no one could cure, a child already dead. In each, the unclean does not defile him; his holiness and life flow out to it. And the faith that receives this may be very small, so long as it reaches him.

Why it was said. Mark’s first readers, living among idols under threat of persecution (see the introduction), needed to know that their Lord rules the spiritual powers, incurable suffering and the grave, and that his mercy crosses into Gentile country.

How the chapter makes its case. Graves, a discharge of blood and pigs all made a person unclean under the law, and all are here. Among tombs and pigs Jesus frees a man held by a legion of demons; the town begs him to leave, and the freed man is sent home to tell of the Lord’s mercy (vv. 1–20). Then Mark wraps one story inside another (vv. 21–43): on the way to a synagogue ruler’s dying daughter, an untouchable woman is healed by touching Jesus’ cloak; the delay seems to cost the girl her life, but Jesus takes the dead child by the hand. The two stories are tied by twelve years, the length of the woman’s suffering and of the girl’s life, and by one word: Jesus calls the woman Daughter.

Where it leads. This is the gospel in miniature: the clean one touching the unclean, and making them clean. Jesus would himself die outside the city, where the unclean were sent, so that his blood might cleanse and his life overcome death; and his word to the girl, “arise”, is the word spoken of him at the empty tomb (16:6).

For us. Bring him the case everyone else has closed, and reach out, however frightened your faith. When his delays cost you dearly, hear him say, “Do not fear, only believe.” And ask which response is yours: the town that begged him to leave, or the man who begged to be with him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is stronger than every power that enslaves, and he crosses a storm to free one man the world had given up on. The man is past all human help, living among the tombs and cutting himself with stones (vv. 1–5). The powers in him are beaten before Jesus says a word: they bow, try to bind him by oath, and must give their name, Legion (vv. 6–10). Sent into the pigs, they show what they do to everything they enter, and everyone can see the man is free (vv. 11–13). Then come the two responses to Jesus: a town that fears his power and begs him to leave (vv. 14–17), and a freed man who begs to be with him and is sent home to tell of the Lord’s mercy (vv. 18–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
Under the law, contact with a grave (Numbers 19:11–16), a discharge of blood (Leviticus 15:25–27) or a pig (Leviticus 11:7) made a person unclean. This man lives among tombs, near pigs, in Gentile country, and Jesus walks straight in.

Jesus is not setting the law aside here but fulfilling its purpose (see the note on vv. 27–29).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a town given back a neighbour, clothed and in his right mind, alongside a hillside of lost livestock, and it asks the Healer to go.

Now: the same choice is made by ordinary people who have counted what Christ might disturb (a business practice, a relationship, a habit, a plan) and would rather keep things as they are. (See vv. 16–17, on why they wanted him gone and what he left behind.)

verseByVerse.quote: They came to the other side of the sea, to the country of the Gerasenes. And when Jesus had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus crosses a storm into Gentile, unclean country to meet one man everyone else had abandoned, a man held by an unclean spirit and living in a graveyard.

The other side. They land where Jesus said they would (4:35). The stormy night that nearly drowned a boatload of men was the journey to this one man, whose own town had given up on him.

To the country of the Gerasenes. Gentile territory on the eastern shore: the region of the Decapolis, ten Greek cities, pagan country with pig farms on the hillsides. It is the first time in this Gospel that Jesus sets foot outside Jewish land, and he goes there to fight. (On the name, see the textual note below.)

Out of the tombs. The boat grounds and the man is coming down at them out of the rocks, where tombs were often caves cut in the hillside. A man is living in a graveyard, the town knows it, and nobody has come to bring him home.

Unclean three times over. Under the law a grave defiled anyone who touched it for seven days (Numbers 19:16). This man is demon-possessed, living among the dead, in a Gentile land near pigs: shut out of the town and of worship, counted with the dead rather than the living.

One man or two? Matthew says two (Matthew 8:28); Mark and Luke follow the one who spoke and was sent home to tell his story, and neither says there was only one.

The Holy One walks into the graveyard. Under the law uncleanness was catching; with Jesus, cleanness is. Holy means set apart for God and utterly pure, a purity so bright that a man in Israel who handled the ark carelessly died on the spot (2 Samuel 6:6–7). Holiness like that ought to consume the unclean; in Jesus, the Holy One of God (1:24), it comes to make them clean. And this beach previews everything he came to do. He would be counted among the transgressors, led out of the city to die where the unclean were sent (Hebrews 13:12), and laid in a tomb cut in the rock like the caves on this hillside. He went into our graveyard not to be held by it but to empty it from the inside. The man coming down out of the tombs is running towards the one who will walk out of a tomb himself.

In everyday life. Think of the person you know who is furthest from God. Pray for him by name this week, and be ready to cross some small storm of your own (an awkward conversation, an inconvenient visit) on his account.

Does demon possession happen today? The New Testament treats it as real and never says the devil’s work ended with the apostles; missionaries among open idolatry have often met things they could describe no other way. But Scripture distinguishes the possessed from the sick (1:32–34), and most suffering of mind and body has ordinary causes and needs ordinary care. Avoid both errors: demons behind every illness, and no devil at all. What drives out evil is not a technique, a ritual or a gifted specialist, but Christ himself, sought in prayer and trusted through his word (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7).

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? No. A believer is indwelt and sealed by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19; Ephesians 1:13); he can be tempted and attacked, but the one in him is greater than the one in the world (1 John 4:4).

Textual note: Gerasenes, Gadarenes or Gergesenes? Manuscripts vary between Gerasenes, Gadarenes (as in Matthew 8:28; the KJV reads Gadarenes here too) and Gergesenes, and a reader with a map will notice a puzzle. Gerasa was a large city about thirty miles southeast, far too far for a herd to run into the sea; Gadara was about six miles off, still not on the shore; Gergesa (perhaps modern Kursi) was on the shore itself, where steep slopes come down to the water. The likeliest answer is that the names refer to regions: the districts of the well-known cities Gerasa and Gadara reached down to that shore, and each writer named the region by the city his readers would recognise, as one might say a village lies in greater London. The place was probably near Kursi. This is likely rather than certain, but the shoreline fits the story.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Gergesenes, some Gadarenes. The region lay on the east side of the lake, Gentile country. Tombs were unclean places.

verseByVerse.quote: He lived among the tombs. And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain, for he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. No one had the strength to subdue him. Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every human attempt to help this man had failed, and the power that held him was destroying him. Three verses of description come before a word is spoken, and every clause shows he was past help.

No one could bind him anymore. “Anymore” tells the history: the town had tried force, repeatedly, and had stopped. He wrenched the chains apart with a strength no ordinary illness gives (compare Acts 19:16), and no one could subdue him, a word used of taming an animal. They had failed at that too, and written him off; night and day they heard him screaming on the hills.

Cutting himself with stones. This should be handled gently, because a great many people know exactly what it describes. It shows the power in him. The demons have taken his home, his town, his clothing and his mind, and now they turn his own hands against his own body. That is the enemy’s settled programme wherever he is given room: not pleasure, not power, but ruin, worked where possible through the victim’s own hands. “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy” (John 10:10).

The stronger man has come. Jesus has already said that “no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man” (3:27). The strong man is Satan; here is his house, a graveyard, and here are his goods, a human being. The town tried to bind the man and could not; Jesus binds the power that owns him, with a word. It is a foretaste of the greater binding: at the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15), so that the devil’s captives, chained far more deeply than this man, could walk free.

The direction the story runs. If you hurt yourself, or love someone who does, take from this passage the direction the story runs. The man nobody could hold or help is soon sitting quietly, dressed, talking, in his right mind, with the marks of the stones still on his arms. And the one who put him back together did not flinch at meeting him at his worst. He came to that beach on purpose.

What it does not mean. Not that people who harm themselves or suffer mental illness are possessed. The Gospels distinguish illness from possession (1:32–34), and pain, shame and illness explain most of what human beings do to themselves. Those who self-harm need compassion, safety and care, medical and spiritual; going to a doctor is an ordinary mercy from God and not a failure of faith. But this man’s torment was demonic, and only Jesus could free him.

In everyday life. If you or someone you love is self-harming, please tell someone and seek help today: a doctor, or an emergency line if you are in danger, and also your pastor and a trusted friend, who can help you find a biblical counsellor to walk with you. That is not weakness; it is taking hold of the help God has put within reach.

How can I tell whether a struggle is spiritual or medical? Usually you do not need to choose, because every human trouble is both: we are bodies and souls together, in a fallen world with a real enemy. So do both. Talk to your pastor and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will ask you to have a medical check-up so that any bodily cause is found and treated; if the doctor recommends treatment, medication included, accept it with thanks, as you would for a broken leg. And bring the whole thing to Christ in prayer, Scripture and the fellowship of his people, asking your pastor and elders to pray with you (James 5:14). Be wary of quick spiritual diagnoses from people who do not know you well, and of anyone who says faith means refusing treatment. The man in the tombs was beyond every remedy; most of us are not, and God normally heals through means.

parallels.desc: who sit in tombs, who eat pig’s flesh

verseByVerse.quote: And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him. And crying out with a loud voice, he said, "What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The power that held the man falls down before Jesus, knows exactly who he is, and can only plead.

He ran and fell down. Who did the running? A man who has wanted help for years, and a power that can do nothing in the presence of the Son of God but bow. Both arrive at the same feet. The powers that chain men cannot hold their ground before him, and they know his name better than his friends do.

What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? The question means, leave me alone; what is there between us (1:24)? Yet once again in Mark the clearest statement of who Jesus is comes from a demon (1:24; 3:11). “Most High God” was a title often used by or to Gentiles for the supreme God: Melchizedek uses it (Genesis 14:18–22), so does Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 3:26), and so does the spirit in the slave girl at Philippi (Acts 16:17). On the pagan side of the lake the demon uses the local title.

I adjure you by God. To adjure is to put under oath, the standard technique of an exorcist: he named a higher power and bound the spirit by it. So the demon tries to drive away the one who has come to drive it out, calling on God to bind the Son of God. It does not work for a moment.

Do not torment me. Matthew records the fear underneath: “Have you come here to torment us before the time?” (Matthew 8:29). Demons know judgment awaits them, and all they can argue about is when. The kingdom of darkness in this Gospel is not confidently opposing Christ. It is already defeated, and pleading for a delay.

In everyday life. If the powers of evil frighten you, look at who is on the ground and who is standing. The demons in Mark shout, beg, bargain and go; he never has to raise his voice. So when fear comes at night, or temptation presses, do not argue with it on its own terms. Go straight to Christ, speak his name in prayer, and stand on what he has already done.

If demons believe the truth about Jesus, what makes my faith different? Saving faith is not only knowing who Jesus is; it is trusting him and coming to him to be saved. The demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19): they know he is the Son of God, hate it, and want him to go away. A Christian knows the same truth and wants him to come nearer. The test is not whether you can say the right words about Christ, but whether you rest on him and want to be with him. If you find in yourself even a weak longing for him, and grief that it is not stronger, that is not the faith of demons. It is the work of his Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: “Most High God” is a title often used by or to Gentiles.

parallels.desc: even the demons believe — and shudder

verseByVerse.quote: For he was saying to him, "Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!" And Jesus asked him, "What is your name?" He replied, "My name is Legion, for we are many." And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus commands the spirit by his own authority and makes it name itself: an army, reduced to begging.

Come out of the man. Jesus had already commanded it; the screaming and bargaining of v. 7 are what a thing does on its way out. No ritual, no formula, no higher name: the authority is his own.

What is your name? The only time in the Gospels that Jesus asks a demon its name, and he plainly does not need the information, nor is he gaining power over it, as the magicians of the day believed naming did. Two things are being done. One is for the man. Everything that has happened to him has happened in the dark, unnamed, for years; now what has been destroying him is forced to say out loud, before witnesses, what it is, before it is thrown out. The other is for the record: Mark’s readers learn the scale of what they are watching, a figure only the enemy could supply.

Legion. The word would have chilled anyone in that district. A Roman legion had up to about six thousand soldiers, and legions had marched up their road. A legion arrives, occupies and stays. The name suggests a vast number of demons, organised like an army, and it describes exactly what they had done to this man: moved in, taken possession, held territory. It also tells you why nothing had worked. The town had been trying to chain one man, when an army was holding him.

Two occupations. The man was occupied, as the land was occupied by Roman legions (the tenth legion later carried a boar among its emblems, which gives the pigs a sharp edge). One occupation everybody could see; the other nobody could do anything about. Jesus evicts the second with a sentence. He will deal with the first in his own way and at his own cost, when Rome nails him to a cross outside Jerusalem and finds that it cannot hold him either.

Not out of the country. Mark’s word is “begged”: the strongest power in the district has been reduced to asking. Luke tells us what they most feared: “they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss” (Luke 8:31), the prison of evil spirits.

Should Christians name demons, or bind spirits over places? No. This scene is not a method to copy. Jesus asked the name for the man’s sake and ours, not because naming gives power, and the demon’s own attempt at a formula failed. Nowhere does the New Testament tell believers to interrogate spirits, map territorial demons, or command the devil by special words. The apostles cast out demons in Jesus’ name (Acts 16:18), but every Christian’s instructions are plainer: be sober and watchful, resist the devil, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), and take up the armour of God, which is truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word of God and prayer (Ephesians 6:10–18). Our weapon is not a technique but the Lord himself.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him, saying, "Send us to the pigs; let us enter them." So he gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs; and the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The demons can go nowhere without Jesus’ permission, and when they enter the pigs, their destructiveness is shown in the open and the man’s freedom made plain.

A great herd of pigs. Pigs were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:7), and no Jewish district would have two thousand of them on a hillside. This was Gentile country, and a valuable business: the pigs are somebody’s livelihood.

Send us to the pigs. The Legion can only plead; it cannot go anywhere without Jesus’ permission. Nothing in this world lies outside his control.

Down the steep bank. Two thousand animals over a cliff, and a reader who cares about somebody’s ruined business may fairly ask what this was for. First, the demons drove the herd, not Jesus. He granted their request and let their intention show in the open: everything they enter goes straight over the edge. The pigs are the man’s story acted out in a few seconds on a hillside, and everyone could see that the demons had gone.

The arithmetic of heaven. Second, one human being matters more to Jesus than two thousand pigs. He had said so in a synagogue argument: “Of how much more value is a man than a sheep!” (Matthew 12:12). God’s care for animals is real: the righteous man “has regard for the life of his beast” (Proverbs 12:10). But set the two against each other and there is no contest. This Lord counts one person worth more than any property.

The real price of his freedom. Yet the pigs were not what this man’s freedom cost. The true price was paid on another hill. The Son of Man came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45). “You were ransomed,” says Peter, not with silver or gold “but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). The town counted the cost at two thousand pigs. Heaven counts it as the life of the Son of God.

Why would Jesus grant a request from demons at all? Because their going into the pigs served his purposes, not theirs: it proved the man was free, exposed what the demons are, and put the town’s heart to the test. God permits evil powers to act only within limits he sets, and turns their harm to good (Job 1:12; 2:6; Genesis 50:20). The demons got what they asked for and lost everything: they wanted a home and ended in the sea. That is the pattern of every concession evil wins from God. It is never a defeat for him; it is always a rope by which evil hangs itself.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law; a herd of two thousand shows this was Gentile country.
