verseByVerse.quote: The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. And people came to see what it was that had happened. And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man everyone had given up on is found whole, sitting, clothed and sane, and the people who see him are afraid.

The herdsmen fled. Soon the whole district knows, and people come to see “the one who had had the legion”: even now that is his name in this town. Mark gives three small details.

Sitting there. This man has probably not sat still in years. Luke adds where: “sitting at the feet of Jesus” (Luke 8:35), the posture of a disciple.

Clothed and in his right mind. He had been naked (Luke 8:27); now his dignity is restored along with his mind. “In his right mind” is a single word, sound-minded: he can hear his own thoughts for the first time in years.

And they were afraid. Not glad for him, but afraid of the power that had done it, as the disciples were in the boat (4:41): the fear of a power you can neither explain nor control. Awe in the presence of God is right; what this town does with it in the next two verses is another matter.

The one who would be stripped. Mark’s readers knew how this Gospel ends. The man who gave this naked man back his dignity would himself be stripped, and soldiers would divide his garments, casting lots (15:24). He would hang uncovered under the shame that the tombs had put on this man and that our sin has put on us all. That is how clothing is given in the kingdom of God. The Lord God covered Adam and Eve with skins after the fall (Genesis 3:21), and Christ gives his people the robe of his own righteousness (Isaiah 61:10) because he went out naked to Golgotha in their place. So God sees in a believer not the stained record of what we have done but Christ’s perfect obedience, counted as ours (2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9): we are accepted not because we have cleaned ourselves up but because we are dressed in him.

A case everybody else had closed. No process, no gradual rehabilitation: he came down out of the rocks screaming, and he is sitting on the ground in a borrowed coat, listening. The town could only chain him; Christ loved him, and his love was stronger than all their iron. Say it to anyone praying for someone long beyond reach, the addict, the one not in his right mind, the family member nobody knows how to help. This town had concluded that nothing could be done. They were right that they could do nothing, and wrong that nothing could be done. The one who could do it arrived by boat.

Is the change always this sudden? The freeing was instant, and so is the new birth: God gives a new heart, and a person passes from death to life (John 5:24; Ephesians 2:4–5). But what follows is usually slow. This man had to learn to live in a town, rebuild trust, and face people who remembered him; the sitting, the clothing and the right mind were the beginning of a life, not the end of it. So ask boldly for the decisive work only Christ can do, and then be patient with the long recovery afterwards, in others and in yourself. Christians are being transformed by the renewal of the mind (Romans 12:2), and that is a lifetime’s work.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Weighing a freed man against a drowned herd, the town chooses the herd and asks Jesus to leave. No one disputes what he has done; they simply do not want him near.

What had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. The witnesses report both, and the town has to weigh one against the other. Their neighbour is sitting in front of them in his right mind. The demons begged not to be sent away; the townspeople beg Jesus to go away, and their unanimous request is that the man who did it should get back in his boat.

Why did they want him gone? They preferred their pigs and their comfort to the one who sets people free. They had just watched a hillside of assets go into the water, and they had understood what many who admire Jesus never grasp: he is not safe, and no one can set a limit on what he may cost. A man who can do that to a herd of pigs might do it to anything. They preferred a misery whose cost they knew to a mercy whose cost they could not control. So they chose the graveyard they knew, and the terrible thing is how ordinary that choice is.

And Jesus left. He does not force himself on those who do not want him; he makes no argument and no second attempt. “Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone” (Hosea 4:17) is a real sentence in the Bible. The most frightening answer God can give is to leave people alone, as they asked.

The first of many who sent him away. “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11): Nazareth next (6:1–6), and at the last Jerusalem, which will lead him out of the gate to be crucified. Yet that rejection is the very road of salvation: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (12:10). He let himself be sent away so that those who sent him away could be brought near.

Not the end of the account. He leaves the district the one thing it cannot chain or drive away: a man with a story. And when Jesus returns to that side of the lake, the crowds come out to meet him (7:31–37; 8:1–10). He is the God who is shut out and still knocks (Revelation 3:20), whose mercy outlasts the refusals of whole towns.

In everyday life. Is there any part of your life where you would rather Jesus stayed away, because his presence might cost you something: the relationship, the way you make your money, the evening habit? Name it to him today, and ask him to stay.

If I have pushed Jesus away before, has he left me for good? Not if you want him now. The danger in this passage is a settled preference for life without him, not a single moment of fear or refusal. The Gerasenes sent him away, and by chapter 7 that same region is bringing him their sick. Peter denied him three times and was restored on a beach (John 21:15–19). Your trouble over it is itself a sign that he has not left you to yourself. Whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). So do not wait to feel worthy: ask him back today, and he will come.

verseByVerse.quote: As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed with demons begged him that he might be with him. And he did not permit him but said to him, "Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you." And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The freed man begs to stay with Jesus, but Jesus sends him home as his witness instead, and the Gentile cities hear what the Lord has done.

That he might be with him. The last begging in this scene, and the best. It is the phrase used of the appointing of the Twelve, “so that they might be with him” (3:14): the man is asking to be a disciple in the strictest sense.

And he did not permit him. He permitted the demons, not the man: the only time in Mark that Jesus refuses a request to follow him, not because he did not want him, but because he had another calling for him.

Go home to your friends. Instead of a place in the boat, a whole district to reach; instead of nearness to Jesus, a task from him. And he is sent home, to the town that chained him, to neighbours who had heard him screaming on the hills for years, to the family that gave up: often the hardest mission field on earth, because they remember what he was. That is exactly why they cannot argue with his story.

How much Jesus had done for him. Jesus told him to tell what “the Lord” had done; he told what “Jesus” had done. A believer of a few hours, he had already grasped that the man on the beach and the Lord God of Israel were one and the same. What Jesus did, God did, and the mercy of God has a human face. On his first day he saw what the disciples had not yet grasped after months.

And everyone marveled. Ten cities, and one man telling the only story he had. The district that begged Jesus to leave got him back, because the man they could not chain would not stop talking. The first person in Mark to preach Jesus to Gentiles is a man who that morning was naked among the tombs: a foretaste of the day when “the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations” (13:10).

What it means to have mercy. We tend to hear “mercy” as a judge letting someone off lightly. In the Bible it is warmer and stronger: God’s heart going out to someone in misery who has no claim on him, and acting to help. Grace gives what we do not deserve; mercy stoops to what we cannot mend. This man brought Jesus nothing; his only words were a plea to be left alone (v. 7). And it was costly mercy: the Lord who crossed a storm to reach him would be counted unclean, led out of the city and killed, so that every believer can say, “he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy” (Titus 3:5). As Timothy Keller put it in The Meaning of Marriage, “We are more sinful and flawed in ourselves than we ever dared believe, yet at the very same time we are more loved and accepted in Jesus Christ than we ever dared hope.” This man learned both halves in a single morning. So when you tell your own story, do not start with how far you came. Start with how far he came. See also Mercy in the Theological Dictionary.

When the best prayer is refused. If you have prayed the best prayer you know and been refused, you are in good company. Paul asked three times to have the thorn removed and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Jesus himself asked in a garden that the cup might pass, and it did not (14:36). A no from Christ does not mean you asked badly or that he has stopped caring. Sometimes he is sending you to serve somewhere else.

Why is this man told to tell, when others are told to be silent? Elsewhere Jesus commands silence (1:44; 5:43). But in Gentile territory there was no crowd waiting for a Jewish Messiah to lead a revolt against Rome, and Jesus would not be staying, so the danger that made silence wise in Galilee did not apply. And the man is to tell what the Lord has done for him, not to proclaim a title.

What if I am not equipped, or my story is not dramatic? This man had no training and no years with Jesus, only what had happened to him, and he had been out of his mind that morning. And the heart of his message was not the drama but the mercy. Every Christian has the same two things to say: what the Lord has done for me, and how he has had mercy on me. If you grew up in a Christian home and cannot remember not believing, that is mercy too, God keeping you from what this man went through. Speak simply of what Christ has forgiven and how he has held you, pointing to him, not yourself. You are not asked to impress anyone, only to be honest about the Lord.
verseByVerse.note: The Decapolis was a league of about ten Greek cities, mostly east of the Jordan.

parallels.desc: Jesus later returns to the Decapolis

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–43 — Jairus’s Daughter and the Woman with the Bleeding
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is Lord over disease and death, and the smallest faith that reaches him finds him enough. Mark wraps one story inside another. A synagogue ruler falls at Jesus’ feet for his dying daughter (vv. 21–24). On the way a woman unclean for twelve years touches his cloak from behind and is healed, and Jesus stops to call her out of hiding and name her Daughter (vv. 25–34). The delay seems to cost the girl her life, but Jesus says, “Do not fear, only believe” (vv. 35–36). In a house of mourners who laugh at him, he takes the dead child by the hand and raises her with a word, then tells them to give her something to eat (vv. 37–43).
verseByVerse.theology:
Mark sets one story inside the other, and they explain each other: twelve years, two daughters, a touch each way, and made well, the word for saved (see vv. 21–24).

And the delay matters: what it cost Jairus and what it was for are treated at vv. 35–36.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a woman who had tried everything, coming from behind in a crowd, hoping to be healed without being seen.

Now: everyone who comes to Christ after the money, the specialists and the years have run out, and finds that he should have been the first resort.

Jesus drew her out, not to shame her, but because he wanted more for her than a cure (see vv. 33–34).

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered about him, and he was beside the sea. Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, and seeing him, he fell at his feet and implored him earnestly, saying, "My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live." And he went with him. And a great crowd followed him and thronged about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A synagogue leader with everything to lose falls at Jesus’ feet for his dying daughter, and Jesus goes with him at once.

Back across. Back to the Jewish western shore, where the crowd is waiting on the beach. Then a man comes through it who should not be there.

Jairus by name. Mark rarely names people; perhaps Jairus was known in the church afterwards. A ruler of the synagogue was the senior layman who appointed the readers and kept the building. Leaders of his kind have already plotted to destroy Jesus (3:6), and everything in his position points away from this beach.

He fell at his feet. In front of everyone: a dignitary on his face in the sand before a preacher his colleagues have written off. A dying child burns away every other worry, and there is mercy hidden in it: the grief destroying him has brought him to the only place where help was.

My little daughter. The Greek is a diminutive. She is twelve (v. 42): in that world nearly a woman, and still his little girl.

Lay your hands on her. He has a method in mind: Jesus must come and touch her. Most of us pray the same way. Jesus does not correct him; he simply intends to do more than Jairus asked (Ephesians 3:20).

So that she may be made well and live. “Made well” is the verb usually translated saved. Without knowing it, Jairus has named the two gifts Jesus came to give, salvation and life, and Jesus can give both because of who he is. “In him was life” (John 1:4); he is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25), and death has no claim on him. But he would give that life to others only by going down into death himself. The man walking with Jairus towards a house where a child is dying is walking, in the end, towards a cross, where he will die so that daughters and sons beyond counting may be saved and live.

And he went with him. At once, setting no conditions: the Lord of glory can be stopped by a frightened father and turned towards a sickroom. But the crowd thronging him is an obstacle: a man with a dying child is moving at the pace of a mob, and it is about to stop altogether.

The structure. Jairus’s story (vv. 21–24, 35–43) frames the woman’s (vv. 25–34), and each interprets the other: two daughters, twelve years, uncleanness, faith, and Jesus’ power over disease and death.

In everyday life. Bring your children to Jesus by name, whatever their age and state. And ask whether pride or reputation is keeping you from going to Christ, or from asking his people to pray with you, over something you cannot fix. Jairus lost his dignity on that beach and found the Lord of life.

Does “made well” mean healed or saved from sin? Both, in the way Mark tells it. The same Greek word covers rescue from illness, from danger, and from sin and judgment, and Mark uses it on purpose. Jairus means: heal her. But in this Gospel every healing is a sign of the larger salvation Jesus brings, the whole person made right with God and one day the body raised. So when we pray for healing we ask for a small piece of what Christ will finally give in full. He may give it now; he will certainly give it at the resurrection (Romans 8:23).
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services and cared for its building.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark breaks into the journey to introduce a woman whose twelve years of bleeding had cost her health, money, worship and every human touch, and had only grown worse.

Twelve years. Her condition was probably bleeding from the womb that never stopped. The twelve years match the girl’s age (v. 42): about the time Jairus’s family received a child, this woman’s life began to fall apart.

Her situation. Under the law a woman with a discharge of blood was unclean for as long as it lasted, and anyone or anything she touched became unclean (Leviticus 15:25–27). For twelve years she had been shut out of the temple courts and normal social contact, probably unable to marry or stay married. No embrace, no worship, no place at anyone’s table: whatever the bleeding did to her body, the loneliness did something worse.

Under many physicians. Only Mark adds this frank detail, and his word is strong: she suffered under them. Ancient remedies were often unpleasant and useless; the Talmud lists some, including carrying the ash of an ostrich egg in a linen rag. Luke, a doctor, softens it: no one could heal her (Luke 8:43). And she had spent everything, penniless in the way that leaves a person feeling foolish, having paid for it all herself, one hopeful appointment at a time.

Rather grew worse. This sentence will find some readers where they live. If you have a chronic illness, or a chronic anything, a marriage every attempt has made colder, a child who has moved further away with each intervention, a sin you have fought with every weapon you own and are visibly losing to, this verse is in your Bible on purpose. Mark does not hurry past it to the good part.

A flow of blood that cleanses. Her own flow of blood had made her unclean for twelve years. What would make her clean before God for ever was another flow of blood: the blood of the man whose cloak she was about to touch. The law could declare her unclean; it could not cure her. But the prophet had promised a fountain opened for the house of David to cleanse from sin and uncleanness (Zechariah 13:1), and at Calvary it was opened. “The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7). In Scripture blood stands for a life given up in death (Leviticus 17:11): Christ bore the guilt of his people’s sin in their place, so that God no longer holds it against those who trust him (1 Peter 2:24).

In everyday life. Look around your church for the person whose trouble has made them lonely. A hand on the shoulder or a meal at your table may be the first in years.

Was God saying her body was sinful? No. Ritual uncleanness was not sin. Childbirth, a skin disease, touching a dead relative while burying him: all made a person unclean, and none was wrong. The laws of cleanness taught Israel that life and holiness belong together, and that death and all that leaks life away are out of place before God; they pointed forward to the one who would make the unclean clean. Those ceremonial laws were fulfilled in Christ and no longer bind Christians (Hebrews 9:9–14; Westminster Confession 19.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.3). No woman today is less welcome before God because of her body.

Is it wrong to keep seeking medical help? No. Mark is not mocking doctors, and Luke, who was one, tells the same story. Medicine is a good gift of God, and Paul travelled with the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14). Doctors are not useless but limited, and the last word on any case belongs to Christ. So keep the appointments, take the treatment, and bring the whole thing to him, the remedies that work and the ones that do not. Trust him above the means, and do not despise the means.
verseByVerse.note: A woman with a flow of blood was ritually unclean and made others unclean by touch; twelve years meant twelve years of exclusion.

parallels.desc: a woman with a discharge of blood

verseByVerse.quote: She had heard the reports about Jesus and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. For she said, "If I touch even his garments, I will be made well." And immediately the flow of blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With nothing but what she has heard of Jesus, the woman reaches out and touches his cloak, and is healed at once. Her uncleanness does not pass to him; his power passes to her.

She had heard the reports about Jesus. That is all she has. Faith at its beginning is often no more than this: something heard about Christ, taken seriously enough to move on. “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17).

Came up behind him in the crowd. Probably ashamed: to approach openly would mean explaining what was wrong with her, and admitting she had no business in that crowd. The real risk was not embarrassment. Every person she pushed past was defiled by her under Leviticus 15, and if she were recognised there would be an uproar. Think what it took for an untouchable woman to walk into a crowd.

Touched his garment. Matthew and Luke say the fringe, the tassel at the corner of the cloak that every Jewish man wore under Numbers 15:38–39 to remind him of the commandments of the LORD. It was the furthest, lowest edge of him. Yet the tassel that reminded Israel of the law was worn by the one man who had kept every commandment it stood for, and even its edge was enough.

If I touch even his garments, I will be made well. “Made well” is again saved. Her faith was real, perhaps mixed with superstition, as though the power were in the cloth. But it was directed towards Jesus, and he does not correct her theology; he never refuses someone for coming with a poor grasp of how it works. What saved her was not the accuracy of her understanding but that she put out her hand.

Immediately the flow of blood dried up. Instantly, after twelve years. “Disease” is the word for a whip (as in 3:10): she had been flogged by her own body for twelve years, and she felt it stop.

The contagion went backwards. Every law of uncleanness in Israel ran one way: the unclean contaminates the clean, never the reverse. Touch a corpse and you are defiled; the corpse is not raised (Haggai 2:11–13). By every rule she knew, this woman should have made Jesus unclean. Instead she was made clean. Jesus is not breaking the law here. He is what the law was preparing for: Israel had been taught that sin spreads and holiness does not, so that when a man came whose holiness was catching, they would know what they were looking at.

Should Christians use prayer cloths, relics or holy objects? No. The power was not in the cloak, and Jesus says so in a moment: her faith, resting on him, made her well. God did once work unusual miracles through cloths taken from Paul (Acts 19:11–12), but those were signs confirming the apostles’ message in a unique moment, not a pattern for us. Scripture never tells us to seek healing through objects, and the medieval trade in relics shows where that road leads. We have something better than his cloak: direct access to Christ himself, at the Father’s right hand, through prayer in his name (Hebrews 4:16).

parallels.desc: touching the fringe of his garment

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him, immediately turned about in the crowd and said, "Who touched my garments?" And his disciples said to him, "You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, 'Who touched me?'" And he looked around to see who had done it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stops, with a dying girl waiting, to find the one person whose touch was faith, because he will not let her slip away unseen.

Power had gone out from him. Not a charge that leaked out of him: a power that simply drained away would not go looking for anybody. He looks for a person, and will say “your faith has made you well”, not “my cloak has”: it was personal from both ends. And something did go out of him: healing costs him something, and at the end of this Gospel saving his people will cost him his life.

Who touched my garments? … You see the crowd pressing around you. The scene stops dead: a man with a dying child stands waiting while Jesus asks an apparently unanswerable question. You can hear the exasperation; Peter thinks the question absurd (Luke 8:45), and Mark has never minded making the Twelve look foolish. Fair enough, but they have missed the distinction the whole Gospel turns on. The crowd was pressing against him; one woman took hold of him. Many touched him by accident; one touched him in faith, and Jesus knows the difference. Contact is not faith. There were hundreds of hands on Jesus that afternoon and exactly one of them got anything.

He looked around to see who had done it. He will not let her stay hidden. It is a kindness, though it will not have felt like one: rather than let her go home cured and unknown, he will keep a dying child waiting. He has something for her that she did not think to ask for, and it is worth the delay.

Did Jesus not know who had touched him? His question was not for his own information but to draw her out, as God asked Adam, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9), knowing where he was and wanting him to come out. Even so, Mark does not hide that in his earthly life the Son accepted real human limits: the day of his return, he says, is known only to the Father (13:32). He is fully God and truly man, and he wanted her face to face.

How do I reach out to him, rather than just being in the crowd? By coming to Christ yourself, with your own need. Speak to him directly: tell him you are a sinner, that you have nothing to bring, that you trust him alone to forgive and make you clean, and ask him to receive you. Then keep reaching: in his word, in prayer, at the Lord’s Table. The crowd brushes against Jesus. Faith takes hold of him and will not let go.

verseByVerse.quote: But the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth. And he said to her, "Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman tells the whole truth, and Jesus gives her far more than a cure: he calls her daughter, says her faith has saved her, and sends her away in peace.

In fear and trembling … the whole truth. She comes forward afraid of being condemned before everybody for touching him in her uncleanness, and tells twelve years of shame before the crowd, not a summary. That is confession, and why we avoid it: not a general admission that we are sinners, but the whole truth, in particular words, to the one entitled to hear it. She was already healed; he draws her out because he wants more for her than a cure taken from behind and carried off in secret.

Daughter. That one word is why he stopped the procession. She is the only woman in the Gospels whom Jesus calls daughter. She has been nobody’s anything for twelve years: untouchable, unwelcome in worship, a name people lowered their voices about, and his first word gives her a place in a family. And Jairus is standing a few feet away with his own daughter dying at home. The most respected man in the town and the least respected have come to the same feet with the same empty hands. His standing cannot buy his daughter’s life, her shame cannot keep her from his welcome: both depend entirely on his grace.

Your faith has made you well. “Made you well” is saved you (sesōken): healed and saved. The power lay not in her touch or his cloak but in her faith in him, and her faith was small, frightened, muddled and reaching from behind. That is all it has ever taken. Faith saves not because it is impressive but because of who it takes hold of. His public word also restored her: everyone heard that she was clean.

Go in peace. Behind the words stands the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, the whole person put right with God. She came for a healed body and is sent away with a new life. Peace with God means the war is over: God is for her, not against her. Paul calls the root of it being justified, God declaring a sinner right in his sight, not because of anything in her but because of Christ, received by faith (Romans 5:1).

Be healed of your disease. A word of permanence: she might have spent her life waiting for it to start again, and he tells her it is over. A few hours earlier he had asked his disciples, “Have you still no faith?” (4:40); now the faith he commends belongs to an unclean woman reaching from behind. And into the silence at the end of his sentence the messengers arrive from Jairus’s house, where Jairus, who has just heard faith praised, must keep believing with no human hope left at all.

Does this mean that enough faith guarantees healing? No. Faith is the hand that reaches; Christ heals, and as he wills. Paul prayed three times for his thorn to be taken away and was told, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9), and he left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). Timothy had frequent ailments and was told to take a little wine (1 Timothy 5:23), not to believe harder. A believer who is not healed has not necessarily failed to believe. Faith trusts Christ whether he heals now or raises us whole at the last.

Do I need to confess my sins publicly like this? Not usually. Confession is first to God, who already knows and wants to hear it from us (1 John 1:9). Confess to the person you have wronged, and seek their forgiveness (Matthew 5:23–24). James tells us to confess our sins to one another and pray for one another (James 5:16), normally a trusted brother or sister, a pastor or an elder, especially with a sin you cannot break alone. Public confession before the church is for public sins that have harmed the church. The point here is not the size of the audience but the honesty: the whole truth told to Christ, who receives it with the word “Daughter”.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, there came from the ruler's house some who said, "Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?" But overhearing what they said, Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue, "Do not fear, only believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When word comes that the girl is dead and Jesus need not be troubled further, he tells Jairus to stop fearing and keep believing. Death has not changed who Jesus is.

While he was still speaking. Mark’s timing is merciless: the word of the woman’s peace is barely spoken when the men arrive. While Jesus stopped for her, Jairus’s daughter died.

Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further? In two kindly meant sentences they say all the world believes about death: once it comes, nothing more can be done. The fact is true. But the conclusion rests on what they think Jesus is, a teacher: a fine thing to bring to a sickbed and no use at a graveside. Their view of him is too small, and the advice sounds entirely reasonable. It is still given, kindly: the marriage is over; he is seventy-eight and hardened; stop praying. It always rests on a true fact and too small a view of Christ.

The cost of the delay. From where Jairus stands, the interruption killed his daughter: a stranger’s twelve-year complaint, which could have waited an hour. It is one of the hardest things about the way God works. His delays are real, they cost real people real things, and they are not accidents. Yet see what this one gave: Jairus has just watched a hopeless twelve-year case healed and heard her called daughter, the lesson he would need, ten minutes before he needed it. Sometimes God’s delays are how he teaches us what we will need next.

Do not fear, only believe. Both commands, in the Greek, speak of something ongoing: stop being afraid, keep on believing. Nothing has changed about who Jesus is. Jairus had believed he could heal; now he must believe he can raise the dead. And “only” is the tender word: not feel confident, not understand why the woman came first, just this one thing.

More than a Teacher. The messengers had the right fact and the wrong Christ. The one they called Teacher is the one the prophet saw coming to swallow up death for ever (Isaiah 25:8), and this is how he will do it. He shared our flesh and blood “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death”, and “deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:14–15). That is why his first word to Jairus is “Do not fear”. He is the only man who has ever had the right to say it at a deathbed.

How do I keep believing when the news is bad? Jairus did very little, and it was enough. He listened to Jesus over the messengers. Their report was true but not the last word; when bad news comes, go to what Christ has said before you decide what the news means. He kept walking with him. He did not go home to the mourners; faith often looks like simply not leaving. He had just seen what Jesus can do. Rehearse what Christ has done, in Scripture and in your life. He did not need to understand. Faith does not have to explain; it has to hold on, and it may pray, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (9:24). Jesus says “only believe” because he is about to do the work himself: your faith does not raise the dead; he does.

What does “only believe” mean when Jesus did not raise the one I lost? It means trusting him with what he has not yet done. Jesus raised only a handful of people, and each died again. Those signs were not a promise that every Christian’s child will be restored this side of the grave, but a pledge of what he will do for all his people at the last day (John 11:25–26). If you have buried someone who trusted Christ, “only believe” means: he is not dead to Jesus, and Jesus will wake him. If you are unsure of the person’s faith, it means trusting the Judge of all the earth to do right (Genesis 18:25), and resting on his character. Fear says it is over. Faith says he has the last word.

Matthew says the girl had already died. In Matthew Jairus says at the start that his daughter has just died (Matthew 9:18). Matthew, telling it briefly, gives the outcome from the start; Mark and Luke tell it in sequence. Both are true accounts, at different lengths.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “overhearing” (parakousas) can mean either overhearing or ignoring, and it is not certain which Mark intends. Both fit, and he may mean both: Jesus heard the message and refused to let it stand. Either way, the news does not get the last word; he does.

verseByVerse.quote: And he allowed no one to follow him except Peter and James and John the brother of James. They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus takes three chosen witnesses into a house where death has been declared and the mourning has begun, and he sees the grief.

Peter and James and John. The first time in Mark that these three are taken aside from the others, as they will be to see his glory (9:2) and his agony (14:33). First they watch him in a dead child’s bedroom, and if the early tradition is right, Peter told the story to Mark years later.

Weeping and wailing loudly. Mourning was loud, immediate and public. A later Jewish rule required even the poorest husband to provide two flute players and one wailing woman when his wife died; a man of Jairus’s standing would have had a houseful. Matthew mentions the flute players (Matthew 9:23), and burial was usually the same day. Nothing was false about the sorrow. But nobody sends for mourners while there is a pulse: their presence settles what Jesus means by sleep. She was dead.

Jesus saw a commotion. He did not push through it or shout over it; he looked at it. The Lord of life does not stand far off from death. He will stand at another graveside and weep (John 11:35), knowing perfectly well that he is about to empty the tomb. The knowledge that he can undo death has never made him indifferent to it. He is not embarrassed by grief and does not hurry anyone through it.

In everyday life. Jesus does not avoid places of grief, and so his people walk into them. If someone you know is newly bereaved, do not wait until you know the right thing to say; go, sit, bring food, and let your presence say that they are not alone. And if you are the one grieving, do not hide your tears from him. He sees.

Is loud grief a lack of faith? No. Jesus wept, and so did Paul’s friends at Ephesus (Acts 20:37–38); devout men made great lamentation over Stephen (Acts 8:2). Paul tells believers not to “grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13): not a command to stop grieving, but to grieve with hope. Tears at a graveside are love, and death is an enemy worth weeping over (1 Corinthians 15:26). What Jesus rebukes in that house is not the tears but the certainty that death has the final word.
verseByVerse.note: Peter, James and John were the inner three, with Jesus again at the transfiguration and in Gethsemane. Hired mourners were customary at a death.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered, he said to them, "Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping." And they laughed at him. But he put them all outside and took the child's father and mother and those who were with him and went in where the child was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls the dead girl sleeping, not because she had not died, but because in his presence death is something you wake from. The mourners laugh, and he puts them out.

The child is not dead but sleeping. For two hundred years some have seized on this sentence to claim she was never really dead, a coma, a faint, a lucky misdiagnosis, so that this is no resurrection at all. The reading does not survive a careful look. Everyone present was certain: the messengers reported her death as fact, the house was full of professional mourners, and they laughed at Jesus precisely because they knew a corpse when they saw one. Luke, a physician, states plainly what happened when Jesus spoke: “her spirit returned” (Luke 8:55).

So what does sleeping mean? Not a second opinion on her pulse, but his settled way of speaking about the death of those he intends to raise. Of Lazarus, four days in the tomb, he said, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep”, and when the disciples took it literally he told them plainly, “Lazarus has died” (John 11:11–14). The New Testament calls believers’ death sleep because they will be raised, with Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14; 1 Corinthians 15:20). So in calling it sleep Jesus claims not less than a raising from the dead but far more. To him death was as temporary as a night’s sleep, and waking this child would cost him no more than a parent leaning over a bed in the morning. He does not deny that she died. He announces that death, in his presence, has become something you get up from.

And they laughed at him. Wailing a moment ago, jeering now. The world usually treats the resurrection so: it does not argue, it laughs, and feels clever for laughing (Acts 17:32). The one person in that room who knew what he was talking about was the one being mocked. The laughter of unbelief has echoed for two thousand years, and it has never once kept him from walking into the room.

But he put them all outside. Firmly, all of them. “Put outside” is the word Mark uses for casting out demons: Jesus removes unbelief from the room.

The child’s father and mother. Five go in with him: Peter, James, John, and the parents, who are not left in the corridor. The mother appears here for the only time in the story, unnamed, having probably been in that house all afternoon.

Is death simply natural? That is the modern consolation: death is part of life, the circle closes. There is something brave in it, but we do not live as if we believed it. The historian Philippe Ariès argued that the modern West, after centuries of dying at home among family, made death hidden and almost shameful, moved to the hospital ward and out of polite conversation. We call death natural and cannot bear to look at it; and no one in Jairus’s house would have called it natural for a girl of twelve. Jesus is more radical than both the despair in that house and the calm acceptance of our age. He will not call death natural: at Lazarus’s tomb he is deeply moved and weeps (John 11:33–35), and Scripture names it “the last enemy to be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 15:26). Nor will he call it final. He calls it sleep, because he wakes the sleepers. Only someone who has beaten death can let us grieve it fully and hope beyond it at the same time.

Does sleep mean the dead are unconscious until the resurrection? No. The word describes how death looks from this side and how temporary it is, not what the soul experiences: it is the body that lies down and will be raised. Believers who die go at once to be with Christ, conscious and blessed. Jesus told the dying thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). To depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). The souls of the righteous, made perfect in holiness, are received at once into heaven (Westminster Confession 32.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). There is no soul sleep and no purgatory. The Christian dead are awake in the presence of Christ, waiting for the morning of their bodies.

verseByVerse.quote: Taking her by the hand he said to her, "Talitha cumi," which means, "Little girl, I say to you, arise." And immediately the girl got up and began walking (for she was twelve years of age), and they were immediately overcome with amazement.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus takes the dead child by the hand, speaks two words, and she gets up and walks. Death lets go of her at his touch.

Taking her by the hand. Before a word is spoken, he takes hold of a dead child, though touching a dead body made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11–13). It is the third time in the chapter that Jesus goes straight to where uncleanness lives, and each time the opposite of defilement happens. The tombs did not defile him; the man came out of them. The bleeding did not contaminate him; it dried up. And death does not make him unclean: he takes hold of it, and it lets go. There is also the plain tenderness of it. He could have spoken from the doorway. He takes her hand, because that is what you do for a twelve-year-old, and because her mother and father are watching.

Talitha cumi. Mark keeps the Aramaic Jesus spoke, perhaps because Peter never forgot it. Not a magic formula: the words a parent might use to wake a child. Talitha means little girl (it may come from a root used of a young lamb, though in use it simply meant a young girl): little one, get up.

I say to you, arise. No prayer, no invocation. The authority in “I say to you” is the authority that told a storm to be quiet. “Arise” (egeire) is the resurrection word the angel will use of Jesus himself: “He has risen” (16:6).

Immediately the girl got up and began walking. Not weak and slowly recovering: she walked about the room in front of her mother. Then the detail that ties the chapter together, “for she was twelve years of age”: twelve years of a girl’s life, twelve years of a woman’s suffering, both touched on the same afternoon by the same hands. And they were “overcome with amazement”, literally amazed with a great amazement. There is no adequate reaction to this, and they did not manage one.

The cost of the word. Here raising the dead cost him two words in a child’s ear. Raising all his people will cost far more: the hand that took this girl’s hand will be pierced by a nail, so that everyone who sleeps in him can be told, one morning, to get up.

In everyday life. Read 1 Corinthians 15 this week, slowly, as the long answer to this short scene. If you fear death, yours or another’s, picture this room: the hand that takes hold, the gentle word, the girl walking. That is death for those who belong to Christ. And if you have buried a child of your own, this room is not set before you as a reproach that yours was not raised now. It is a glimpse of the Lord into whose hands you may commit your child, the Judge of all the earth who will do right (Genesis 18:25), and who took this girl so tenderly by the hand.

Can a thinking person really believe a dead girl got up? Everyone in that room knew dead girls do not get up; that is why they laughed. The question is whether Jesus is who he says he is. If God gave life in the first place, giving it back is no strain for him. And notice the marks of an eyewitness rather than a legend: a named synagogue ruler people could ask about, Aramaic words kept in a Greek book, the embarrassing laughter, the order to give her something to eat. These do not prove the event, but they show Mark telling a report, not a fable. In the end it all hangs on Jesus’ own resurrection, which Paul says was seen by more than five hundred people, most of them still alive when he wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3–8).

Was this the same as the resurrection Jesus will give us? Not quite. The girl was brought back to ordinary mortal life, and years later she died again. Jesus was raised never to die again, in a body glorified and immortal (Romans 6:9), the firstfruits of that harvest (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). What happened in this room was a sign and a promise. The same voice, with the same authority, will one day speak to all who sleep in him, and they will rise not to die again but to live for ever, with bodies like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).
verseByVerse.note: “Talitha cumi” is Aramaic, the everyday language Jesus spoke; Mark keeps his very words.

verseByVerse.quote: And he strictly charged them that no one should know this, and told them to give her something to eat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus forbids publicity and tells them to feed the girl: the Lord of life is no showman, and he cares about her ordinary needs.

That no one should know this. An emphatic command, and impossible for long: the girl will be seen in the village tomorrow. This is what is often called the messianic secret, Jesus’ habit of hushing the news of who he is (1:44). He did not want to be known chiefly as a wonder-worker, or to stir political hopes, before his identity could be understood through the cross. In Galilee then, for many, Messiah meant a king who would drive out Rome. He will not be hailed as King until he has been lifted up on a cross. Nor is this a performance: parents get their daughter back in a quiet room with four others present. He is not using this family; he is helping them.

Give her something to eat. It proves she was truly alive, not a ghost (compare Luke 24:41–43). And it is practical care: her parents are past speech, and the Lord of life says, in effect, she will be hungry. The one who raises the dead also thinks about lunch.

Mighty enough, humble enough. In him the greatest power and the smallest household kindness belong together. After his own resurrection the risen Christ, having conquered death, lit a charcoal fire on a beach and cooked breakfast for seven tired disciples (John 21:9). The chapter began with a man nobody could chain and ends with a girl being handed a plate. This is our Lord: mighty enough to command the abyss, humble enough to send for bread. Nothing is too great for his power or too small for his love, and he who conquered death for one little girl has conquered it for ever, for all who are his.

Why was this kept quiet, when we are told to tell everyone? Because the time was different. After his death and resurrection the full truth could be told: who he is and why he came. So Jesus himself sends his disciples to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19). We are not under the secret but under the command to tell, and to tell it as Mark does, with the cross at the centre.

In the flow. The storm ended with the disciples asking, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (4:41). Chapter 5 is Mark’s answer: demons, disease and death obey him too. Yet the next scene is his home town of Nazareth, where people who know his family take offence at him and he marvels at their unbelief (6:1–6). Power alone does not create faith.

5.theology:
Legion. An army was holding the man the town had tried to chain, and Jesus evicts it with a word (see vv. 8–10).

Why the pigs? The demons drove the herd, not Jesus. One man restored is worth more than the herd (see vv. 11–13).

Not dead but sleeping. The girl had not fainted. Sleep is Jesus’ way of speaking about the death of those he will raise, and he is claiming more, not less (see vv. 39–40).
5.examples:
Then: the freed man begs that he might be with him, the phrase used of the Twelve (3:14), and Jesus says no.

Now: anyone whose best prayer has been refused. (See vv. 18–20.) This man was sent home with one commission: tell them how much the Lord has done for you.

keyVerse.quote: But overhearing what they said, Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue, “Do not fear, only believe.”
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this command, spoken at the moment every human hope has ended. It rests not on the strength of Jairus’s faith but on who Jesus is: the Lord whom demons, disease and death all obey. It is what the frightened town lacked and the trembling woman had, and it is his word to every believer at a graveside.

5.reflection:
The town begged Jesus to leave, and the freed man begged to be with him (vv. 17–18). What made the difference? Is there any part of your life where you would rather Jesus kept his distance because of what he might cost you?

The woman’s faith was frightened, muddled and reaching from behind, yet Jesus said it had made her well and called her “Daughter” (v. 34). What does this teach about the faith that saves, and about how Jesus treats people who come to him ashamed?

Jesus’ stop for the woman seemed to cost Jairus his daughter (vv. 35–36). Where have you felt God’s delays, and how does “Do not fear, only believe” speak to them?

In each scene Jesus touches what should have made him unclean, and his cleanness and life pass to them instead. How does that point to the cross, and how should it shape the way a church welcomes people others avoid?

6.title: Refused at Home, Broken Bread, and a Prophet’s Head
6.text: <sup>1</sup>He went away from there and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him. <sup>2</sup>And on the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished, saying, “Where did this man get these things? What is the wisdom given to him? How are such mighty works done by his hands? <sup>3</sup>Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?” And they took offense at him. <sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own household.” <sup>5</sup>And he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. <sup>6</sup>And he marveled because of their unbelief. And he went about among the villages teaching. <sup>7</sup>And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits. <sup>8</sup>He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts— <sup>9</sup>but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics. <sup>10</sup>And he said to them, “Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there. <sup>11</sup>And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them.” <sup>12</sup>So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. <sup>13</sup>And they cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them. <sup>14</sup>King Herod heard of it, for Jesus’ name had become known. Some said, “John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him.” <sup>15</sup>But others said, “He is Elijah.” And others said, “He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old.” <sup>16</sup>But when Herod heard of it, he said, “John, whom I beheaded, has been raised.” <sup>17</sup>For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, because he had married her. <sup>18</sup>For John had been saying to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” <sup>19</sup>And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death. But she could not, <sup>20</sup>for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly. <sup>21</sup>But an opportunity came when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. <sup>22</sup>For when Herodias’s daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. And the king said to the girl, “Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.” <sup>23</sup>And he vowed to her, “Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.” <sup>24</sup>And she went out and said to her mother, “For what should I ask?” And she said, “The head of John the Baptist.” <sup>25</sup>And she came in immediately with haste to the king and asked, saying, “I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter.” <sup>26</sup>And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her. <sup>27</sup>And immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John’s head. He went and beheaded him in the prison <sup>28</sup>and brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. <sup>29</sup>When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb. <sup>30</sup>The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught. <sup>31</sup>And he said to them, “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.” For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. <sup>32</sup>And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves. <sup>33</sup>Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. <sup>34</sup>When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things. <sup>35</sup>And when it grew late, his disciples came to him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late. <sup>36</sup>Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat.” <sup>37</sup>But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.” And they said to him, “Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?” <sup>38</sup>And he said to them, “How many loaves do you have? Go and see.” And when they had found out, they said, “Five, and two fish.” <sup>39</sup>Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. <sup>40</sup>So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties. <sup>41</sup>And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. <sup>42</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. <sup>43</sup>And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. <sup>44</sup>And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men. <sup>45</sup>Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd. <sup>46</sup>And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray. <sup>47</sup>And when evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land. <sup>48</sup>And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them, <sup>49</sup>but when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost, and cried out, <sup>50</sup>for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” <sup>51</sup>And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded, <sup>52</sup>for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened. <sup>53</sup>When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. <sup>54</sup>And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him <sup>55</sup>and ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. <sup>56</sup>And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
6.overview:
Where we are. Jesus has just shown his authority over storm, demons, disease and death (4:35–5:43). Now the disciples’ question, “Who then is this?” (4:41), is answered wrongly by a village and a king, and slowly by the Twelve, on the way to Peter’s confession (8:29).

The message. Jesus is the Shepherd God promised, and more: God himself come to feed and rescue his people. He has compassion on the helpless and gives out of his own fullness. What keeps people from him is not knowing too little but thinking they already know him: the town that thought it knew him stayed as it was, while those who knew only that they needed him were made well. And carrying his message may cost everything, as it cost John.

Why it was said. Mark’s first readers, very probably a small church in Rome that had seen believers die under Nero (see the introduction), needed to know that rejection, even by family, was what their Lord met first, and that a witness killed with no rescue has not been abandoned.

How the chapter makes its case. At Nazareth the questions asked about Jesus are exactly the right ones, and the conclusion drawn is one of the worst in the book (vv. 1–6). He answers by multiplying his voice through the Twelve (vv. 7–13), and Mark tells how John died before he lets them come back (vv. 14–29): anyone reading to find out what following costs has just been told. Herod, the false shepherd-king, feasts the powerful and kills the prophet. The second half answers the first. Jesus meets a crowd that ruins his disciples’ rest with compassion, because he sees sheep without a shepherd (vv. 30–34); five loaves in his hands feed a wilderness crowd with twelve baskets over (vv. 35–44); he comes to his struggling disciples on the sea, saying, “it is I” (vv. 45–52); and at Gennesaret all who touch his garment are made well (vv. 53–56).

Where it leads. John’s death foreshadows his Lord’s, but the tomb that received Jesus could not keep him. At the feeding Jesus takes, blesses, breaks and gives, as at the Last Supper: the King who refuses a crown from a fed crowd will be broken himself to feed the world. And on the water he does what Scripture says God alone does, and speaks God’s own name to frightened men.

For us. Do not let familiarity make him ordinary. Bring him what little you have, rest when he calls you away, and when you are rowing against the wind where he sent you, remember that he sees you from the mountain, and comes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Rejection, Mission, and the Death of John
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is rejected by those who know him best, yet his word goes out further, and those who carry it must be ready to pay as John paid. At Nazareth the village asks the right questions about his wisdom and mighty works and takes offence at the answer, and he marvels at their unbelief (vv. 1–6). His reply is to multiply his voice: the Twelve go out in pairs, carrying almost nothing but his authority over unclean spirits (vv. 7–13). While they are away, Mark tells how John the Baptist died: a ruler who liked hearing a preacher and would not be changed by him, a nursed grudge, a dance, a rash oath and a head on a platter (vv. 14–29).
verseByVerse.theology:
Could he not, or would he not? Verse 5 should not be softened: Mark wrote he could do no mighty work there, where Matthew writes did not do many (Matt. 13:58). But the words that follow settle the sense: his power had not failed (this is treated fully at vv. 4–6).

And he marvelled. Only two things in the Gospels are said to have astonished Jesus, and one was the unbelief of the village that had raised him (see the note on vv. 4–6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Herod feared John, knew he was a righteous man, and heard him gladly.

Now: the honest question is not whether you enjoy good preaching. Herod did. It is whether it is changing anything (see “A divided heart” at vv. 19–20).

verseByVerse.quote: He went away from there and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him. And on the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished, saying, "Where did this man get these things? What is the wisdom given to him? How are such mighty works done by his hands?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus comes home to Nazareth and teaches in its synagogue, and the village is astonished, but it asks its questions only to dismiss the answer. Every question they ask is the right one; their conclusion is one of the saddest in this Gospel.

His hometown. Nazareth, the small village in the Galilean hills where he grew up (1:9), a place of a few hundred people where he had lived for some thirty years. Joseph has vanished from the record; Mark names only Mary. Jesus knew the very seats they were sitting in.

And his disciples followed him. He comes home as a rabbi with a following, which is what a village finds hardest to swallow, and the disciples see how his own town receives him before he sends them out.

He began to teach in the synagogue. As a visiting teacher, invited to read and explain Scripture in the synagogue. Luke records a visit, probably an earlier one, when he read from Isaiah 61 and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:16–30). Mark gives only the reaction.

Astonished. The same verb was used of the crowd in Capernaum (1:22), where it led people towards faith. Here it turns into offence. Astonishment is not faith.

Where did this man get these things? This first question has an answer they would not accept: from God. As far as they knew he had had no rabbinic training (compare John 7:15), and nobody in Nazareth had taught him this.

What is the wisdom given to him? They can hear that it is wisdom; they are not pretending it was a poor sermon. And the word “given” admits that his wisdom came from somewhere beyond himself. They have half the answer in their own question and do not follow it.

How are such mighty works done by his hands? News from Capernaum has reached them, and they do not dispute it. Their objection is not that the reports are false.

The Branch from Nazareth. The answer had been written centuries before. Isaiah saw a shoot coming up from the stump of Jesse, and on him the Spirit of the LORD would rest, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and might (Isaiah 11:1–2). He does not merely have wisdom; he is the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Nazareth asked where the wisdom came from while the Wisdom of God stood in front of them. That is the humility of our God: he comes near enough to be overlooked.

Near is not the same as in. A person can grant that Jesus’ teaching is extraordinary and his influence hard to explain, and still stop there for good, because the next step would rearrange his life. Nazareth was near the kingdom, and near is not the same as in.

Is it enough to admire Jesus as a great teacher? No, and in the end it is not even possible. A man who claimed to forgive sins (2:5–10), to be Lord of the Sabbath (2:28), and to be the one the prophets foretold, was either telling the truth or was not good at all. Admiration that stops short of worship is not a compliment; it is a refusal to answer his question. “Where did this man get these things?” has only one honest answer: from the Father, because he is the Son. To admire him without bowing to him is to stand in the doorway of the synagogue and never go in.
verseByVerse.note: His hometown is Nazareth.

verseByVerse.quote: Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?" And they took offense at him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The village takes offence at Jesus because it knows him: the carpenter, Mary’s son, whose brothers and sisters live among them. They cannot believe that God’s wisdom and power could come through someone so ordinary and so near.

Is not this the carpenter? Here the astonishment curdles. This is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus himself is called a carpenter. The Greek tektōn means a builder or craftsman in hard materials: wood, and in that stony country very often stone as well. He made ploughs, yokes, doors, roof beams and houses.

They had his furniture. For perhaps eighteen years the eternal Son of God worked in a village workshop, and the people in front of him very likely had his work in their houses. The Word through whom all things were made took up a carpenter’s tools and made doors for Nazareth. To the townspeople this settled it: you cannot easily worship a man who fixed your door.

The son of Mary. A phrase with a barb in it. A man was normally called his father’s son, even if the father was dead; to call him his mother’s son was a slight, and there may be a whisper behind it. A village can count the months between a wedding and a birth, and rumours about Jesus’ origins seem to surface elsewhere too (compare John 8:41).

And brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? “And are not his sisters here with us?” They name four brothers and gesture at the sisters, apparently sitting in the room. James later led the church in Jerusalem and wrote the letter of James; Judas (Jude) wrote the letter of Jude. The most natural reading is that they were Mary and Joseph’s children born after Jesus. Matthew says Joseph “knew her not until she had given birth to a son” (Matthew 1:25), and Luke calls Jesus her “firstborn” (Luke 2:7), a word that suggests other children followed.

They took offense at him. “Took offence” (eskandalizonto) is the root of our word scandal: they stumbled over him, and what they tripped over was that they knew him. They could not imagine the incarnation: God the Son becoming man, and without ceasing to be God, truly man, with a real body, a real trade and a real family (John 1:14).

The brothers who came to believe. During his ministry these brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5). Here they are among the offended; three chapters back they came to take him home as a madman (3:21, 31). Afterwards they are in the upper room, praying with the believers (Acts 1:14). James becomes a pillar of the Jerusalem church and writes the letter that opens, “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ”. Something happened between Nazareth and Acts 1, and Paul names it in one line: “Then he appeared to James” (1 Corinthians 15:7).

The vaccine of a little Christianity. Familiarity does not produce faith. Anyone raised in a Christian home can grow so used to the most extraordinary Person who ever lived that he no longer astonishes them, and whole cultures do the same. Many in the West feel they already know Christianity from school assemblies, weddings and half-remembered Bible stories, and have moved on. Søren Kierkegaard saw this in nineteenth-century Denmark, where everyone was a Christian by birth, and argued that a nation full of churches had made it almost impossible to become one, because everybody assumed they already were. It works like a vaccine: a small, weakened dose gives immunity to the real thing. G. K. Chesterton put it sharply: “The Christian ideal has not been tried and found wanting. It has been found difficult; and left untried.” Nazareth had the carpenter and missed the Christ. The remedy is not to know less but to look again: the familiar Jesus of the village was the Word made flesh, still stranger, and far better, than anything we have filed him under.

Were those years in the workshop wasted? No. For most of his life the Son of God did ordinary work for ordinary customers, and that was not a delay before his real work but part of his obedience: keeping the law perfectly in a carpenter’s shop, honouring his parents, giving fair measure, doing good work for people who would later despise him, all of it part of the righteousness credited to those who trust him. So your ordinary work matters to God: “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord” (Colossians 3:23). A plumber, a nurse, a mother at home, a clerk at a desk can serve Christ in the work itself, because Christ himself did.

Does it matter whether Mary had other children? A little. Nothing in the gospel hangs on it: Christ was born of a virgin, and that is the article of faith. But the belief in Mary’s perpetual virginity grew alongside the view that married love is less holy, and that Mary should be honoured as more than a believing servant of God. Scripture calls her blessed (Luke 1:48), but never makes her an object of prayer or a mediator; the honour of standing between God and sinners belongs only to the son she bore, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Reading the brothers plainly keeps Mary where she placed herself: among those who need a Saviour (Luke 1:47).

Where Christians differ: Jesus’ brothers. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary remained a virgin all her life, and takes the brothers to be cousins (so Jerome). Orthodox tradition takes them to be Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage. Some Reformers, Luther among them, kept the older belief, so this is no line between the godly and the ungodly. This commentary’s view: the natural reading of the Gospels is that they were Mary’s younger children, Jesus’ half-brothers and half-sisters, born in the ordinary way. Nothing in Scripture requires otherwise. Mary’s honour is not a lifelong virginity. It is that she bore and raised the Son of God, believed God’s word (Luke 1:38, 45), and then mothered his brothers.

Textual note. Matthew’s version has “the carpenter’s son” (Matthew 13:55), and a few manuscripts of Mark read that way too, though most Bibles follow the better-supported reading, “the carpenter”.
verseByVerse.note: “Carpenter” is a general word for a builder or craftsman in wood or stone.

parallels.desc: even his brothers did not believe

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "A prophet is not without honor, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own household." And he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. And he marveled because of their unbelief. And he went about among the villages teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejected at home, Jesus names it as the old lot of God’s prophets, and the settled unbelief of his own town shuts it off from the mighty works he did elsewhere. He marvels at their unbelief, and moves on to the next villages.

A prophet is not without honor. Probably a proverb already. Only Mark adds “among his relatives”, and the sentence narrows as it goes: the town, the wider family, the house he grew up in. His own brothers are in the room (3:21; John 7:5).

He could do no mighty work there. A startling sentence, not to be smoothed away. Matthew says “he did not do many mighty works there” (Matthew 13:58); Mark says could not. The words that follow settle what it means.

Except that he laid his hands on a few. This was not a failure of power: sick people in that village got up well. He could not because it would not have been right. Miracles were signs meant to lead to faith; in a place that had already decided what he was, mighty works would have been mere spectacle, and Jesus does not perform (8:11–12; Luke 23:8–9). And people did not bring their sick to someone they despised.

He marveled. Only twice are we told that Jesus marvelled: at a Roman officer with no Bible and no synagogue behind him, who asked him only to say the word (Luke 7:9), and here, at the village that had raised him on the Scriptures. The people with none of the advantages astonished him by their faith. The people with all of them astonished him by their unbelief.

He went about among the villages. Rejection at home did not stop him for a day.

The title he wears for ever. He carried the dishonour of Nazareth all the way to Golgotha, where the sign over his head named him “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews” (John 19:19). The town that would not honour him gave him the title he wears for ever, and he wears it as a crown.

What it does not mean. Not that faith is a power that controls whether God can act, as though belief were the coin you put in a machine. Faith receives what God gives; unbelief does not disable God, but makes his help unwelcome, and he does not force it on a town that has made up its mind.

Can my unbelief stop God from working in my life? It cannot defeat his purposes, but it can keep you from receiving what he offers. Weak faith does not limit him; he healed the son of the father who said, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (9:24). What closes the door is settled refusal, which has decided in advance what Jesus can and cannot be. So bring small faith to him as it is and ask him to increase it; and where you have stopped expecting anything of him, confess it and begin to pray again.

How do I love a family that rejects my faith? Remember first that he was not spared this: his family thought him out of his mind, and he had to rise from the dead to convince his own brothers. Then love them patiently and warmly, neither preaching at every meal nor hiding what you believe. Honour your parents (Ephesians 6:2), keep showing up, serve them, and let your life speak before your words do (1 Peter 3:1–2); when they ask, answer gently. Do not take their scorn as a judgment on Christ or on you; he met it first. And pray for each of them steadily, because their faith will not depend on your arguments but on the risen Lord showing himself to them, as he did to James.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits. He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts— but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejected by his own town, Jesus multiplies his voice: he sends the Twelve out in pairs with his own authority, carrying almost nothing, so that they must depend on God. Between their going out and their return (v. 30), Mark tells how Herod killed John, so that the mission and its cost stand side by side.

He began to send them out. To send out (apostellō) gives us apostle, a sent one. These men have not grasped who he is (4:41), and before this chapter is out they will fail to understand the loaves. He sends them anyway, with real authority. If you are waiting to feel qualified before you speak of Christ to anyone, nobody in this group was.

Two by two. For support, safety and credible witness, since a charge stood on the evidence of two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). The early church followed the pattern (Paul and Barnabas, Peter and John). Each of the Twelve probably went with a colleague he had not chosen, and someone had to walk the roads with Simon the Zealot, someone with Matthew the tax collector.

Authority over the unclean spirits. It is his own authority, lent to them: his victory over Satan, the strong man of 3:27, not a skill built up or a technique learned by watching. That is why they will fail in chapter 9, when they try without depending on God in prayer (9:28–29).

Nothing for their journey except a staff. Matthew and Luke say not even a staff (Matthew 10:10; Luke 9:3). With Matthew the verbs help: his is acquire, Mark’s is take along, so Mark may mean take the staff you have, Matthew do not get another. Luke uses Mark’s verb, so there the answer lies elsewhere, perhaps a walking staff in one and a club for defence in the other. No suggestion settles it beyond doubt, and believers can hold the Gospels true while admitting this small question is not fully resolved. One plain instruction stands behind all three: travel light.

No bread, no bag, no money in their belts. Coins were carried in folds of the belt. The bag was a traveller’s pack, or possibly a beggar’s bag for collecting gifts, the mark of the wandering religious tricksters of the day.

Not two tunics. A second tunic was the ordinary traveller’s blanket. Not hardship for its own sake: Jesus makes them dependent on purpose, on God’s provision through those who welcome them. They will eat only if somebody feeds them, so they cannot keep their distance from the people they are sent to.

The Sent One sends. Behind the sending of the Twelve stands a greater sending. Jesus is himself “the apostle and high priest of our confession” (Hebrews 3:1), and everything the Twelve carry is his: “As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you” (John 20:21). The mission does not finally depend on how well they understand him. It depends on his hold on them.

What it does not mean. Not a permanent rule for all missionaries, but the instruction for one short mission in Galilee. Later Jesus reminded them of it, “When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything?”, and then told them that things were now different: “let the one who has a moneybag take it” (Luke 22:35–36). The principles remain: urgency, simplicity and dependence on God.

Does this mean Christian workers should not be paid? No. Those who preach should live from those who receive the message, as Jesus said when he sent out the seventy-two: the labourer deserves his wages (Luke 10:7). Paul argues the same: “the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14), and elders who labour in preaching are worthy of double honour (1 Timothy 5:17–18). So churches should support their pastors and missionaries generously, and those workers should live simply, avoid the appearance of greed, and trust God rather than their reserves.
verseByVerse.note: Coins were carried in the belt; the “bag” was a traveller’s pack for supplies.
