verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there. And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The messengers are to stay where they are first welcomed, and where a town will not hear them, to leave it to God with a solemn sign, neither bitter nor guilty.

Stay there. A visiting teacher with a following would attract offers, and the temptation was to move up from the first house that took you in to a wealthier host. Stay behind the first door that opens. That protects the poor family that risked something to receive you (see hospitality), and it protects the message: a preacher working his way towards the best address in town has said something about himself that drowns out what he says about Christ. Every church has its own version of this: being warmer to people the more influential they are.

If any place will not receive you. Rejection was expected, as at Nazareth, and he gives them a way to leave.

Shake off the dust. Jewish teachers counted the soil of Gentile lands as unclean, and strict Jews coming home from abroad are said to have shaken its dust off their feet rather than carry it into the holy land. For the apostles to do this to a Jewish town was startling: by rejecting God’s message, the town had made itself like pagan territory. Paul and Barnabas did it at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51).

As a testimony against them. A solemn warning, done in sorrow, not anger, leaving them to God’s judgment: the responsibility now rests with you. Scripture asks how we shall escape if we neglect such a great salvation (Hebrews 2:3).

Whoever receives you receives me. The dust carries such weight because of who sent them: “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me” (Matthew 10:40). A door opened to two tired fishermen was a door opened to the Son of God. It still is when the gospel is told at a kitchen table: the King himself is asking to come in.

The mercy in the instruction. They are told in advance what to do when it does not work: say your piece, and if they will not have it, go, neither bitter nor guilty, and do not carry the weight of that town away with you. If you have spoken of Christ to someone for years and got nowhere, that is not necessarily a verdict on your competence; where the message was brought faithfully and refused, the refusal belonged to the hearer.

When should I stop talking to someone about Christ? Rarely, and never stop praying for him. The dust-shaking was given to the apostles on a particular mission, for towns that had heard and rejected the message; it is no licence to write off a friend. But when someone has clearly heard the gospel and asked you to stop, respect that: do not nag, argue at every meeting, or turn every conversation into a sermon. Keep the friendship, keep loving, answer if asked (1 Peter 3:15), and keep praying, because God can open a heart long after you have run out of words (Acts 16:14).
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. And they cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Twelve preach repentance as John and Jesus did, and the authority he gave them proves real: demons are cast out, and the sick are anointed with oil and healed.

That people should repent. The message of John and Jesus (1:4, 15). Repentance is not the same as being sorry: remorse looks at yourself and feels bad; repentance turns round and goes the other way. It is a direction, not a mood.

They cast out many demons. The seventy-two, sent out later, came back astonished at the same thing (Luke 10:17).

Anointed with oil. Olive oil was used as medicine (Luke 10:34; Isaiah 1:6), and as a sign of God’s blessing and presence. This is the only place in the Gospels where anointing with oil accompanies healing, and James tells the church to do the same: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord” (James 5:14–15).

So what is the oil for? Not medicine here, for these are miracles, and not magic, for nothing in the New Testament puts power in the oil. It is a sign laid on the body of a sick person, saying that God is being asked to act here, on this man, now; in the Old Testament oil marked out kings, priests and the tabernacle furniture as set apart for God. And see where James puts the power: “And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up.” The Lord will. Not the oil, and not the elders.

The oil and the Anointed One. Messiah and Christ both mean the Anointed One, and Jesus read it of himself: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Luke 4:18). Peter later summed up the whole ministry: “God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:38). The apostles anointed the sick because the Anointed had sent them; the oil on a fevered forehead was a small sign of the Christ.

What it does not mean. Not the sacrament of extreme unction, or last rites, which the medieval church developed for preparing the dying for death. This anointing was for healing. Reformed churches do not treat it as a sacrament, though some practise it in prayer for the sick (James 5).

Should we expect healings like these today? These were signs given through the Twelve as they were sent out, part of the apostolic witness that confirmed their message (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians, Pentecostal and charismatic believers among them, expect gifts of healing to continue today; this commentary holds that such sign-gifts belonged to the apostles’ founding work (the view called cessationism), while gladly agreeing that God still heals in answer to prayer. What continues is what James describes: the elders praying over the sick, with oil as a sign of setting them before the Lord. God hears such prayers and sometimes heals, often through ordinary means and sometimes beyond them. But no one is promised recovery every time, and when healing does not come, the prayer has not failed. The final healing waits for the resurrection.

Should I ask my elders to pray over me when I am ill? Yes, if you are seriously ill. The New Testament does not tell you to suffer privately and hope somebody remembers you in a service, but to send for the elders and ask them to pray over you. It is a concrete thing you are entitled to ask for, and many churches have quietly let it drop. James joins it to confession and forgiveness (James 5:15–16), so it is also a time to make sure all is well between you and the Lord, and then to rest in his will.
verseByVerse.note: Olive oil was used as medicine and as a sign of God’s blessing.

parallels.desc: anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord

verseByVerse.quote: King Herod heard of it, for Jesus' name had become known. Some said, "John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him." But others said, "He is Elijah." And others said, "He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old." But when Herod heard of it, he said, "John, whom I beheaded, has been raised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ fame reaches Herod, and while the people guess that he is John raised from the dead, or Elijah, or a prophet of old, Herod’s guilty conscience settles on the man he killed.

King Herod heard of it. Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruler of Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. His official title was tetrarch, a minor ruler (Matthew 14:1), but people called him king, and Mark uses the title the locals used. When he later asked Rome for the title, he was exiled instead.

For Jesus’ name had become known. Six pairs of preachers have covered the district, and the noise has reached the palace.

Like one of the prophets of old. Elijah was the prophet expected before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). The crowd reaches for the greatest kind of person it already knows. Ask today and you hear the same kind of answer: a great teacher, a moral genius, a revolutionary. All respectful, all far too small, and often for the same reason: none of them asks anything of us. He is not one of the prophets come back; he is the one all the prophets were pointing to.

In the flow. Herod’s verdict is one more answer to Mark’s driving question: who is this? The demons know (1:24), the disciples ask it (4:41), Nazareth thinks it knows (6:3), and here the crowds and the king guess wrong, until Peter answers it with this same list in front of him (8:27–29).

John, whom I beheaded. Chilling, because of one word: “I”. He could have said, “John, who was beheaded”, and blamed his wife, the oath or the guests; but the sentence comes out in the first person.

What guilt does. A guilty conscience keeps an accurate record. Ignored guilt does not fade; it goes underground and comes out in dreams, irrational fears, the inability to enjoy anything. Herod kept a prophet in his cellar who pointed to the Lamb of God, and preferred listening to obeying. Now he has a ghost.

The resurrection Herod did not expect. Herod’s guilty guess named the wrong man, but something like it was going to happen. A prophet would be put to death by a ruler who knew he was innocent, and raised: not John, but the one John had pointed to, rising not as a ghost to haunt his killers but as the Lord who forgives them. Herod would meet him face to face in Jerusalem, and ask him for a trick (Luke 23:8–11).

What do I do with a guilty conscience? Bring it to Christ, specifically and honestly. Name the sin to God without excuses: not “it happened”, but “I did it”. Believe that the blood of Christ purifies the conscience from dead works (Hebrews 9:14), and that “if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us” (1 John 1:9). If your sin has injured another person, go to them and repair what can be repaired, as Zacchaeus did (Luke 19:8). And if the guilt keeps returning after you have confessed and been forgiven, that is no longer conscience but accusation: answer it with the cross, where the debt was fully paid (Romans 8:1, 33–34).
verseByVerse.note: “King” Herod is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea; his official title was tetrarch.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because he had married her. For John had been saying to Herod, "It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark goes back to explain how John came to be in Herod’s prison: he had kept telling the ruler that his marriage to his brother’s wife broke God’s law. One plain sentence, said to a ruler’s face, cost the prophet his freedom and then his life.

Bound him in prison. According to the historian Josephus, John was held at Machaerus, a grim hilltop fortress east of the Dead Sea: the man who had baptised thousands in the open air of the Jordan, shut in a cell in a desert castle.

His brother Philip’s wife. The tangle is the point (see the Herod family). Herodias, granddaughter of Herod the Great, was the niece of both her husbands. She had been married to Antipas’ half-brother (called Philip in the Gospels); Antipas fell in love with her, and both divorced their spouses to marry each other. Antipas put away his first wife, the daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, which would eventually cost him a war.

It is not lawful. “Had been saying”: repeatedly, to the ruler’s face. The law forbade marrying a brother’s wife while the brother lived (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). John confronted the ruler with God’s law, like Elijah before Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kings 21).

How John spoke. A model of something the church constantly gets wrong. It is short: no treatise on marriage. It is specific: not a general denunciation of immorality in high places, which costs nothing and changes nobody, but this man and this marriage. It is said to Herod, not about him to a crowd who already agreed. And it is about his sin, not his politics. It is safe to denounce sins in general; the moment a name is attached, it becomes expensive. Yet this is no licence for the sharp tongue: John had a word for the crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers too (Luke 3:10–14), tailored to each.

The friend of the Bridegroom. It is fitting that John should die defending a marriage. He called himself “the friend of the bridegroom” (John 3:29), and the Bridegroom was Jesus. From the beginning marriage was a picture of the covenant love of God for his people, and in the end of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Herod’s marriage was a lie about that love; John’s rebuke guarded the picture. And the Bridegroom himself would keep his covenant by laying down his life for a bride who had been unfaithful, to make her clean (Ephesians 5:25–27).

Was Herod’s marriage wrong only because of the law about a brother’s wife? No; it was wrong twice over. Each abandoned a living spouse without any ground God allows, and then they married within a forbidden degree of kinship. Scripture permits divorce only for adultery or for wilful desertion that cannot be remedied (Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15; Westminster Confession 24.5–6), and Jesus calls remarriage after any other divorce adultery (10:11–12). Persistent, serious abuse can itself amount to desertion, as the elders judge each case, and anyone abused should seek safety at once. John named the most public offence, but the whole arrangement was built on two broken covenants, and rank exempts no one from God’s law about marriage.

Should Christians speak out against the sins of leaders today? Yes, with John’s wisdom. Pray for rulers first (1 Timothy 2:1–2) and honour them (1 Peter 2:17). Speak about what God’s word plainly says, not your political preferences dressed up as prophecy, and to the person where you can, not merely about him. Speak with grace, seasoned with salt (Colossians 4:6), and be ready to pay for it. And deal first with your own sins: John’s courage before Herod grew out of a life that had already bowed to God.
verseByVerse.note: Herodias had been married to Antipas’s half-brother; the law forbade marrying a brother’s wife while he lived.

verseByVerse.quote: And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death. But she could not, for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herodias nursed a murderous grudge against John, but Herod both feared him and liked to hear him, and so kept him alive without ever doing what he said.

Herodias had a grudge. Literally held it in: a nursed, settled hatred, not a flash of temper but a campaign, waiting for its chance. Bitterness kept and fed becomes murderous (Ephesians 4:31).

What the truth does to some people. John’s sentence was aimed at Herod, but Herodias could not live with it, because it named her position exactly. When a sin is named, some repent, some argue, and some set out to destroy the one who named it, as if the sin would disappear with him. It never does.

Herod feared John. Only Mark tells us of Herod’s inner conflict, and it is searching, because Herod is not a monster. He feared John with awe, the respect a morally careless man cannot help feeling before a serious one, and against his own wife he used his authority to keep John alive. Matthew says that Herod wanted to put him to death but feared the people (Matthew 14:5). Both are true: a man can want a voice silenced and still be drawn to it.

He heard him gladly. Picture the ruler of Galilee going down into his own prison to listen to the man he has chained there, upset by what he hears, and returning to be upset again.

A divided heart. One of the most dangerous conditions in this Gospel, because it looks so like the real thing: interest, respect, emotion, protection of the preacher, real disturbance of conscience, and no repentance. Herodias stayed. He is the thorny ground of chapter 4 given a name and a palace (4:18–19). A man who will not repent must eventually silence the voice that keeps asking him to; Herod did not want John dead, but it took only a party, a dance and an audience to finish what had been decided long before.

The Holy and Righteous One. Herod could bear neither to obey John nor to lose him; yet John was only a lamp (John 5:35). The truly Holy and Righteous One was walking the roads of Galilee, and Herod would one day dress him in splendid clothing to mock him (Luke 23:11). What Herod needed was not a better preacher in the dungeon but a new heart, and by his Spirit Christ gives one that actually wants what God wants (Ezekiel 36:26–27), so that his word is no longer a voice you visit in the cellar and leave there, but the voice you live by.

Am I a Herod? If you fear so because you still fight a sin you hate, see the difference. Herod did not want to give up Herodias and never tried. A believer who hates the sin he still falls into, and keeps bringing it to Christ, is not divided like that; the fight itself is the Spirit’s work in him (Galatians 5:17).

Is it wrong to enjoy sermons? Not at all. Delight in God’s word is a mark of grace (Psalm 119:103), and it is right to be moved by faithful preaching. The danger is not enjoying it but stopping there. “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves” (James 1:22). A simple test: after a sermon that moves you, ask what one thing it calls you to do, believe or stop, and tell someone. Enjoyment that leads to obedience is the Spirit at work. Enjoyment that replaces obedience is Herod in the dungeon, nodding.

verseByVerse.quote: But an opportunity came when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. For when Herodias's daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. And the king said to the girl, "Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you." And he vowed to her, "Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herodias’s chance comes at Herod’s birthday feast, where, pleased by her daughter’s dance before his guests, he swears a vast and empty promise.

An opportunity came. Literally a good day, a well-timed day. Herodias has been waiting for one.

On his birthday. Every man in the region whose opinion Herod cares about is in one hall, on the most public night of his year.

Herodias’s daughter. Josephus tells us she was called Salome; Mark calls her “the girl”, probably a teenager. For a princess to dance before drunken men was shameful, and the performance was very possibly arranged by her mother: if so, that is the measure of the grudge.

Up to half of my kingdom. It is for show: Herod is performing for the room (oaths, plural, v. 26). It is empty: he ruled at Rome’s pleasure and had no kingdom to give. And it is borrowed: it echoes the Persian king’s words to Esther (Esther 5:3, 6; 7:2), where a brave woman used the offer to save a nation. Here the same words fetch a prophet’s head.

A man who cannot say a small true sentence. Herod could never say “I was wrong”, yet he cannot stop himself making a large empty promise. A man who inflates his words to impress a room will one day find himself standing behind a promise he never meant, before people he cannot bear to disappoint.

Two kings, two feasts. Mark sets this banquet deliberately beside the meal that follows. In the palace, a king gives a feast for the powerful, and the last course is a prophet’s head on a platter. In the wilderness, the true King spreads a meal for the shepherdless poor, and the leftovers fill twelve baskets. At Christ’s table the King himself is the one who dies, and his people feed on his life: “Take; this is my body” (14:22). Every Lord’s Supper is the answer to Herod’s birthday.

Should Christians take oaths at all? Yes, when solemn and lawful, but never casually. Jesus forbade the everyday swearing that props up words not otherwise trusted (Matthew 5:33–37). Yet God swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13–17), Paul calls God as his witness (2 Corinthians 1:23), and Reformed and Baptist confessions alike teach that a lawful oath in court or on a solemn occasion is an act of worship (Westminster Confession 22.1–3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 23.1–3). What is forbidden is the rash oath, the oath to do evil, and the oath as performance. Let your ordinary word be so reliable that you rarely need more.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus names Herodias’s daughter Salome.

parallels.desc: up to half of my kingdom

verseByVerse.quote: And she went out and said to her mother, "For what should I ask?" And she said, "The head of John the Baptist." And she came in immediately with haste to the king and asked, saying, "I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter." And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prompted by her mother, the girl asks for John’s head, and Herod, though deeply grieved, will not break his oath in front of his guests.

She went out and said to her mother. Given an open cheque before the whole court, the girl has to leave the room and ask her mother what she wants. She is the instrument of her mother’s hatred.

The head of John the Baptist. No hesitation: the answer had been ready for months. Offered half a kingdom, she asks nothing for herself or the girl. A nursed grudge eats every other appetite.

Immediately with haste. Before Herod could sober up and change his mind. And she improves on her mother’s answer: at once, and on a platter, a serving dish, as if it were another course at the feast. Mark does not comment.

Exceedingly sorry. Deeply grieved: the word is strong, and Herod’s distress is entirely real.

Because of his oaths and his guests. That is the whole reason a man is beheaded tonight. Herod is careful to keep an oath and ready to murder a prophet, and would have told you, quite sincerely, that a man must stand behind what he has sworn.

Two men exceedingly sorrowful. Mark uses this word only once more, of Jesus in Gethsemane: “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (14:34). Herod, sorrowful, does evil to keep his word to a girl and his face before his guests, and another man dies. Jesus, sorrowful to death, does the Father’s will and keeps his word to his people, and he is the one who dies. Herod would not lose face to save a righteous man; the Righteous One lost everything to save the unrighteous. The sorrow is the same word; the love beneath it is the whole difference between this world and the gospel.

The fear of man. One of the most ordinary motives for the worst things people do. The snare Proverbs describes was laid for Herod by a room full of faces, and only trust in the LORD could have kept him out of it (Proverbs 29:25). Christ is the King who was never once trapped by the opinion of a room, and he frees his people from the fear of man by giving them a better fear, the fear of the Lord.

Was Herod bound to keep his oath? No. An oath to do evil binds no one; it should be repented of, not carried out (Westminster Confession 22.4, 22.7). The law made provision for someone who had sworn rashly (Leviticus 5:4–6), and Jephthah’s vow stands in Scripture as a warning, not an example. Herod’s real bond was not to God but to the faces around his table. Not conscience: he knew John was righteous and holy. Not law: no law said a prisoner should die to settle a dinner-party promise. He could not bear to look foolish in front of people whose opinion he had spent his life courting.

What if I have already made a promise I should not have? If keeping it would mean sinning, do not keep it: confess the rash promise to God and to the person, apologise, and bear the embarrassment. If it is merely costly, a godly person keeps his word even when it hurts (Psalm 15:4), unless the other person releases him. The cross covers rash words too, and it is far better to look foolish before people than to do wrong before God.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John's head. He went and beheaded him in the prison and brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is beheaded in the prison, with no rescue and no last word recorded, and his disciples come and bury him. Mark tells it plainly, and it points ahead to another death.

An executioner. Immediately: as long as it takes to walk down to the cells and back. Mark uses a Latin word (spekoulatōr) for a soldier of the guard, perhaps because he was writing in Rome.

Beheaded him in the prison. A door opening in the dark and a soldier with an order: that is all we are told. This is the man Jesus called the greatest born of women (Matthew 11:11), who baptised the Son of God, saw the heavens torn open and the Spirit descend, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). He died alone in a dungeon, killed at a drunken party to satisfy a vengeful woman and a weak man’s pride.

There is no rescue. Jesus was alive and a few days’ walk away, healing strangers, and John, who had been shut in that fortress long enough to send messengers asking, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” (Matthew 11:3), was not delivered. The answer he got back was not “I am coming to get you”, but a message about the blind seeing, and a blessing on whoever did not lose faith in him (Matthew 11:6). John died with the question answered and the door still locked.

Took his body. The one clean act in the whole squalid story, by men with no power and everything to lose. They could not save him or avenge him. They could carry him, and they did, and laid him in a tomb.

Why Mark tells this story. It is almost the only story in Mark not directly about Jesus, and every detail foreshadows his death: Pilate will know Jesus is innocent and yield to pressure, and Jesus will be laid in a tomb by friends who came and took the body (15:15, 45–46). The difference is what came next. Herod’s dungeon kept John. The tomb outside Jerusalem could not keep the one John had pointed to, and because it could not, John’s story does not end in that cell: he too will rise. For Mark’s first readers, very probably believers in Rome who had watched fellow Christians die under Nero, this was not distant history.

The morning belongs to Christ. Herod silenced the voice, and could not touch the Word. The voice in the wilderness fell quiet in a cellar, while the one it announced was speaking in every village of Galilee. The head on Herod’s platter was a trophy of a night; the Lamb John named reigns for ever, and John lives before his throne with every martyr since (Revelation 6:9–11). The world has the last word only until the morning, and the morning belongs to Christ.

Faithfulness is not a contract with providence. If you serve God faithfully and your circumstances are getting worse, that is in your Bible on purpose; it is not a sign that something has gone wrong. Some by faith stopped the mouths of lions and escaped the edge of the sword, and others, by the same faith, were sawn in two and killed with the sword (Hebrews 11:33–37). Hebrews puts them in one list and calls it all faith. A faithful witness can be killed with no rescue, and that is no sign that Christ has abandoned him.

Why did God let John die like that? God was not absent, John’s work was complete, and death was not the end: nothing, not even the sword, can separate his servants from his love (Romans 8:35–39).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–56 — The Feeding, the Walking, and the Healings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is the Shepherd God promised, who feeds his flock in the wilderness and comes to his people across the sea as only God can. The apostles return and he calls them away to rest, but the crowd is waiting, and he meets a wrecked day off with compassion, teaching first (vv. 30–34). In a desolate place five loaves and two fish in his hands feed five thousand men, with twelve baskets over (vv. 35–44). That night, after praying alone, he sees his disciples straining at the oars and comes to them on the water: “Take heart; it is I” (vv. 45–52). At Gennesaret whole villages carry their sick to him, and all who touch even the fringe of his garment are made well (vv. 53–56).
verseByVerse.theology:
He meant to pass by them (v. 48) is not what it sounds like. Passing by is the Old Testament’s own vocabulary for God making himself visible (see the note on v. 48).

Then, when they scream, he speaks: Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid. The middle phrase is egō eimi, I am: an ordinary way to say it is me, and, spoken on that water, also God’s own name from the burning bush (see the note on vv. 49–50).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve exhausted men doing sums in front of a hungry crowd, and hearing you give them something to eat.

Now: the parent who has run out of wisdom, the pastor of a small church looking at a large town. Jesus asks the practical question: How many loaves do you have? Go and see. Not how many you need, but how many you have (see the note on vv. 38–40). And the men who had nothing to give carried back the surplus, one basket each.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught. And he said to them, "Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while." For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the apostles return full of what God has done through them, Jesus’ first concern is their rest: he calls them away with him to a quiet place.

The apostles returned. Almost the only time Mark calls them apostles, sent ones, as they return from being sent (compare 3:14). It had worked. They come back straight after the story of John’s death, and its shadow falls across this scene: the world kills God’s messengers, and the Lord gathers his own to himself. The quiet place they sail to will become the wilderness where he feeds five thousand.

Rest a while. Only Mark records this tender invitation. Not a strategy session on building momentum, but rest. “He knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14). He notices when we have not eaten, and calls us away before we break.

No leisure even to eat. Not a hard week, but a pattern (3:20). When meals are eaten standing, sleep is the thing always cut and days off quietly become nothing, something has gone wrong that no fruitfulness justifies, and Jesus treated it as a reason to stop.

They went away in the boat. The desolate place (erēmos) is the wilderness, where God fed Israel (Exodus 16), and what follows will recall that. The rest he planned will in a moment be taken by the crowds, as planned rest sometimes is.

Come away with me. The rest is by yourselves, with him. The one inviting them is the Lord of the Sabbath (2:28), who said, Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). Their deepest weariness is not in their feet but in their souls, and he is the only rest for that: rest from earning and proving, the rest of those whose work is finished because his is (Hebrews 4:9–10). You serve because God has accepted you, not in order to be accepted.

Christians are peculiarly bad at this. Some serve God as if tiredness were a badge and rest a shameful concession; that is not in this Gospel. With a district newly stirred up, the Lord of the harvest took twelve effective men away for a rest. Often what drives overwork is not love for people but a quiet idol: the need to be needed, or the hope of proving by exhaustion that we are worth something. If the Lord can do without you for a day, you were never the one holding things up.

Is it selfish to rest when there is so much need? No. Jesus sent his apostles to rest while crowds were still coming, and God built rest into creation and into his law (Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 20:8–11). The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and the Lord’s Day is his gift: Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy rather than as a law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). Many godly Reformed brothers keep it as the Christian Sabbath, and they are to be honoured. All agree that a weekly rhythm of worship and rest is God’s gift, and that you are not the Saviour of the world; the need will always be greater than your strength. Rest is an act of trust that God keeps the world running while you sleep (Psalm 127:2).

How do I rest with him? The rest he gives is first rest for the soul: your standing with God was settled at the cross and does not rise or fall with this week’s output. Then make it concrete. Keep a weekly day. Put the Lord’s Day in the diary for worship and rest before anything else can claim it. Guard your sleep. Going to bed is a small daily confession that you are not God. Get alone with him. A psalm read slowly and your load handed to him by name do more than a frantic hour. Say no to something. Ask which demand you keep meeting because you need to be needed, and let it go. Receive his gifts. A walk, a meal with friends, a good book: enjoy them with thanks. And when the crowd breaks in, as it did here, you can still rest inside: “Return, O my soul, to your rest; for the LORD has dealt bountifully with you” (Psalm 116:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd ruins the day of rest, and Jesus meets it not with irritation but with compassion: he sees sheep with no shepherd, and feeds them first with his teaching.

Got there ahead of them. The plan fails at once: twelve exhausted men, promised a quiet day, see the shore covered with people. Anyone who has needed a day off knows what rises in the chest. Jesus too is tired.

He had compassion. Gut-level compassion (splanchnizomai), from the word for the inward organs.

Like sheep without a shepherd. An Old Testament phrase that carries a great deal (see shepherds). Moses prayed “that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd” (Numbers 27:17). Behind it stands Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel’s shepherds, who fed themselves and not the flock, and promises to shepherd his people himself through a new David: “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep” (Ezekiel 34:15).

The false shepherd and the true. Mark has just shown what kind of shepherd Galilee had (see “Two kings, two feasts” at vv. 21–23). Jesus is the true Shepherd those promises were waiting for, and he will now feed his flock in the wilderness.

He began to teach them. What the compassion produces first is not loaves but teaching (2:2), because the deepest thing wrong with sheep that have no shepherd is that nobody has been feeding them (Deuteronomy 8:3). He will get to their stomachs before the day is out.

How do I find compassion when I am exhausted? Not by trying to feel it, but by drawing on his compassion rather than your reserves. Ask him to show you what he sees: not interruptions, but sheep without a shepherd. Remember how he has had compassion on you when you came at inconvenient times. And be honest about your limits; his compassion did not stop him sending the crowds away that evening and going to pray. Compassion is not saying yes to every demand. It is meeting people with his heart, and trusting him with what you cannot do.

parallels.desc: not as sheep without a shepherd

verseByVerse.quote: And when it grew late, his disciples came to him and said, "This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late. Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat." But he answered them, "You give them something to eat." And they said to him, "Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples sensibly propose sending the hungry crowd away; Jesus hands the need back to them, far beyond their means, and they answer with arithmetic.

Send them away. The disciples are right about the facts: a desolate place, the hour late. Their answer is the standard shape of religious problem-solving: the need is real, the resources are insufficient, therefore reduce the need. It never occurs to them that the man beside them might be a factor in the sum.

You give them something to eat. The pronoun is emphatic. He hands twelve tired men a task plainly beyond them, to show them their inadequacy and his sufficiency. It is one of his settled habits, the command that cannot be obeyed from your own resources (3:5; Matthew 28:19), and it is always an invitation to depend on him. He gives commands bigger than our resources because his resources are bigger than his commands, and he is never caught by surprise at nightfall in a desolate place: he knew all along what he was going to do (John 6:6).

Two hundred denarii worth of bread. A denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer, so this was some seven or eight months’ wages: far more than they had, and not to be spent in a village at dusk anyway. They have done the sum on the spot, and their answer is probably half sarcastic: not quite rude and not quite faith, a man showing his working to prove the thing cannot be done.

Can God spread a table in the wilderness? Israel once asked that very question in unbelief, though God had just split the rock and given them water (Psalm 78:15–16): “Can God spread a table in the wilderness?” (Psalm 78:19). The disciples ask it again with a calculation, while the answer stands beside them. This is not a prophet who will ask God for bread; it is the God who fed Israel for forty years, come in the flesh to a desolate place to do it again. Every human sum about the wilderness leaves him out, and every time he is the whole of the answer. He would one day give a bread no money could buy, his own flesh for the life of the world (John 6:51).

A spreadsheet beside the Son of God. These men have seen a paralytic walk, a girl raised from the dead and a storm muzzled, and their considered response to a catering problem is a spreadsheet. Before we blame them, be honest: we pray about the things we already half expect to manage and quietly do arithmetic about the rest. Their sum was correct, and completely beside the point, because they had left Jesus out of it.

Is it wrong to plan and count costs? No. Jesus told his hearers to count the cost (Luke 14:28), and planning is good stewardship. The disciples’ fault was that they counted without him. Plan and budget, then bring the plan and the shortfall to him in prayer, expecting him to act according to his will. The question is not whether you do arithmetic, but whether Christ is in the sum.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer; two hundred denarii was most of a year’s wages.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "How many loaves do you have? Go and see." And when they had found out, they said, "Five, and two fish." Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks what they have, and has the crowd sit down in ordered groups on the green grass, as a shepherd settles his flock to be fed.

How many loaves do you have? Go and see. He does not answer the objection. Not how much do you need, which has paralysed them, but how many have you got? Go and count. When a need is obviously beyond you, stop calculating the gap, find out exactly what is in your hands, however little, and bring it to him. The gap is his business; counting what you have is yours.

Five, and two fish. John says they came from a boy in the crowd, and that they were barley loaves, the bread of the poor (John 6:9). The fish would have been small and salted, the relish you ate with bread rather than a meal. Christ has never once been hindered by the smallness of what was brought to him; he has often been hindered by its being kept back.

On the green grass. Only Mark mentions that the grass was green, a detail that fits the early church’s report that Peter’s memories stand behind this Gospel; the hills are green for a few weeks in spring, near Passover (John 6:4). And it puts a psalm into the scene: “He makes me lie down in green pastures” (Psalm 23:2). The Shepherd is making his shepherdless sheep lie down in green pasture, and will feed them.

By hundreds and by fifties. Literally, in garden beds: from the hillside the crowd would have looked like a garden laid out in plots. Hundreds and fifties recalls how Moses organised Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 18:21, 25). Jesus is forming a new Israel in the wilderness and feeding it like a new Moses, and he is greater than Moses, who never made a loaf in his life.

What if what I have really is too little? Bring it anyway. The miracle began with a boy’s lunch, and Jesus chose to work through it rather than without it. Your time, your small gift of money, your stumbling words to a friend, your weak prayers: none of them is impressive, and none of them is the point. He is the point. “God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27). The only gift he cannot use is the one we keep.
verseByVerse.note: The groups of hundreds and fifties recall the way Moses organised Israel in the wilderness.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. And they all ate and were satisfied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gives thanks over the little there is, breaks it and gives it through his disciples, and thousands eat until they are full.

He looked up to heaven. Like the head of a Jewish household at a meal, blessing not the food but God for it, probably in words like the familiar Jewish grace: “Blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth.” He thanks his Father over food that is obviously not enough, before a single extra crumb exists. Gratitude before the provision arrives is one of the plainest marks of faith.

Broke the loaves and gave them. He took, he blessed, he broke, he gave: the same four verbs as the Last Supper (14:22), and the sequence by which the Emmaus disciples will recognise him (Luke 24:30–31). This is not the Lord’s Supper, but Mark lays the two scenes on top of each other on purpose. The man who feeds a hillside with broken bread is going to be broken himself, and the church has been fed from that ever since.

The bread went out through their hands. Somewhere between the Lord’s hands and the hundredth row there kept on being more, and the carriers were the men who had proved by arithmetic that it could not be done. That is how he still works: he gives his provision to his church to carry, and the carriers discover that there is enough only as they hand it out.

They all ate and were satisfied. A plain, earthy word for being fed until you want no more, with fish as well as bread. In the wilderness God gave Israel manna, and they were satisfied (Exodus 16:12; Psalm 78:24–29). Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty loaves (2 Kings 4:42–44). Jesus feeds thousands with five. He is greater than Moses and Elisha, and John records his explanation: “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35).

What it does not mean. Not that people simply shared hidden lunches. The Gospels describe a miracle of creation. If it were a lesson in sharing, nobody would have tried to make him king that night (John 6:14–15), and nobody would have needed twelve baskets for the leftovers.

Should we give thanks before every meal? A good and biblical habit, though no rule requires a set form. Jesus gave thanks here, at the Last Supper and at Emmaus; Paul gave thanks for bread before a shipload of pagans in a storm (Acts 27:35), and says that everything God created is made holy by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:4–5). A few honest words before a meal keep gratitude from going stale and teach children where their daily bread comes from.

Can a thoughtful person today believe this really happened? Yes, and the question is really about Jesus, not bread. If God made the world out of nothing, bread from five loaves is no strain on him; the miracle is impossible only if there is no God, which is the very thing in question. So the issue is whether Jesus is who he claimed to be, and the strongest evidence is his resurrection, reported by people who had seen him alive and would die rather than deny it (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). The feeding is told in all four Gospels, with details that fit eyewitness memory: the green grass, the barley loaves, the count of baskets. Details alone cannot prove a miracle, and some say the church invented such stories later; but the Gospels were written while many who had been on that hillside were still alive, and the weight finally rests on the witnesses to the risen Christ. Faith here is not believing against the evidence. It is trusting the one the evidence points to.

verseByVerse.quote: And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twelve baskets of leftovers are gathered, more than there was at the start, after some five thousand men have eaten.

Broken pieces. John tells us the gathering up was commanded: “Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost” (John 6:12). The one who has just created bread will not have scraps trodden into the grass. Abundance in the kingdom of God never licenses waste.

Twelve baskets. One for each disciple, or a sign for the twelve tribes, and perhaps both. Each man who went out among the rows with an impossible task comes back carrying a full wicker basket (kophinos). More food at the end than at the start: that is how the arithmetic of God’s kingdom comes out, and why two hundred denarii was the wrong question. “God is able to make all grace abound to you” (2 Corinthians 9:8).

Five thousand men. The word means adult males; Matthew adds, “besides women and children” (Matthew 14:21). Perhaps fifteen to twenty thousand people altogether, probably more than any town in Galilee except Tiberias and Sepphoris.

What the crowd did not understand. John records that they tried to make him king by force that night (John 6:15). They had eaten from his hands and concluded that such a man should be running the country: nearly right, and entirely wrong. He had not come to be a king who keeps a nation fed, but to be the bread, and when he said so the next day, many of them left (John 6:66).

More fragments than there were loaves. With Christ there are always more fragments than there were loaves, and not a crumb of what he gives is lost. He is the King who would not be crowned by a full crowd because he had come to be broken for an empty world. As he gathered the fragments from the grass, so he will lose nothing of all that the Father has given him, but raise it up on the last day (John 6:39).

Does this mean God will always give me plenty? No. God promises to supply every need of his people (Philippians 4:19), not wealth or comfort, and Paul learned contentment in hunger as well as plenty (Philippians 4:11–13). Many faithful Christians are poor, and some go hungry for Christ’s sake. This miracle promises that the Lord knows our needs, cares about our bodies, is never short of resources, and will give us all we need to do his will and reach his kingdom. The abundance he guarantees without limit is grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd. And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray. And when evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sends his disciples away by boat, dismisses the crowd that wants to make him king, and goes up the mountain alone to pray.

He made his disciples get into the boat. He compelled them (ēnankasen); plainly they did not want to go. John tells us why: the crowd wanted to take Jesus by force to make him king (John 6:14–15). Five thousand fed men in an occupied country is a rebellion looking for a leader, and one of the Twelve was a Zealot, from a movement that fought Rome. So he sent the disciples ahead to Bethsaida (John 1:44) before they were swept up in it.

While he dismissed the crowd. He refused the crown they offered, freely, by the shout of a crowd, without a cross. That shortcut to glory had been laid before him already, by the devil in the wilderness (1:13; Matthew 4:8–9). He walked away from a crown that would have cost him nothing, because he had come to wear one that would cost him everything.

On the mountain to pray. He has had no rest, has taught for hours, fed thousands and defused a political crisis, and he spends the first free hour praying on a hill in the dark. This is the second of three times Mark shows Jesus praying alone at night (1:35; 14:32–39), each at a moment of temptation or decision: success, the offer of glory and the approach of death, all met the same way. We tend to pray hardest at the third kind of moment and hardly at all at the first two, treating prosperity as a season that needs no prayer, though it is the season in which many are most easily lost (Deuteronomy 8:10–14).

Alone on the land. They cannot see him, and night has come down between them. That is what a hard stretch feels like from inside the boat. But a man alone on a mountain at night, praying, is not absent from the boat. He is keeping watch over it.

Why did Jesus refuse to be made king? Because he was already King, and the crown they offered was the wrong one. They wanted a ruler who would drive out Rome and keep the bread coming. He had come to deal with a deeper enemy, sin and death, and that could only be done by the cross. He would be crowned, but with thorns first, and then at the Father’s right hand (Philippians 2:8–11). His kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36); it comes by word and Spirit, not by force.

Should Christians then avoid politics? No. Christians may serve as rulers, judges and officials, as Joseph and Daniel did, and should seek justice and the good of their city (Jeremiah 29:7). What this passage warns against is confusing Christ’s kingdom with any political cause, or trying to bring in his rule by force, popularity or votes. No party is the kingdom of God. Serve where you are placed, pray for those in authority, and fix your deepest hope on the King who refused a crowd’s crown and will return in glory.

verseByVerse.quote: And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the mountain Jesus sees his disciples straining at the oars against the wind, and in the last watch of the night he comes to them, walking on the sea.

He saw. Perhaps the most comforting word in the chapter. He is up a mountain in the middle of the night, and they are three or four miles out on the lake (John 6:19). Whatever kind of seeing this was, he watched them the whole time, while every fact available to them said they were alone. He sees every boat in the dark, and none of his people rows unwatched.

Making headway painfully. Tormented, tortured (basanizomenous). Not a storm that threatens to sink them, as in chapter 4, but something worse in its own way: hours of grinding, unrewarded effort. They row and the shore does not get closer.

For the wind was against them. They are out there because he sent them: obedience put them in the wind. That is the shape of much Christian experience: you are where he put you, pulling hard, nothing is moving, and he seems to be somewhere else. The verse tells you what you cannot know from inside the boat: he went up the mountain to pray, and from that mountain he saw them. Both are still true: “he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25), and the Father always hears the Son (John 11:42).

The fourth watch. Between about 3 and 6 a.m. (see watches of the night), after perhaps nine hours of rowing. He came in the last watch, when men have stopped talking and are simply pulling. He is never early, as we would arrange it, and he has never yet been late.

Walking on the sea. In the Old Testament, only God walks on the sea. Job says that God “alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea” (Job 9:8); the psalmist says, “Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters” (Psalm 77:19).

He meant to pass by them. In the Old Testament, God passing by is how he reveals his glory: he passed by Moses in the cleft of the rock and proclaimed his name (Exodus 33:19–22; 34:6), and passed by Elijah at Horeb (1 Kings 19:11). And Job, describing the God who trampled the waves, says three verses later, “Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not” (Job 9:11). He was not passing them by, but passing before them, so that they could see who had been watching from the mountain.

If Jesus sees me struggling, why does he wait so long? Because his timing serves purposes we cannot see from the boat. That night they learned what they could not have learned at the first hour: that he watches, that he comes, and that he is the Lord of the sea. Delay is not neglect (2 Peter 3:9), and meanwhile he is interceding. Keep rowing where he has put you, keep praying, and expect him, not on your schedule, but certainly on his.

Uncertain wording. “He meant to pass by them” is found only in Mark. The words say that he wished or intended to pass by, but not why. Some take it that he meant to walk on past to draw them to call out to him, or to reach the shore ahead of them. The Old Testament use of “pass by” for God showing his glory, in passages this scene echoes, makes the meaning given above the most likely.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth watch was about 3 to 6 a.m. “Pass by” recalls God “passing by” Moses and Elijah to show his glory.

parallels.desc: I will make my goodness pass before you

verseByVerse.quote: but when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost, and cried out, for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said, "Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terrified, the disciples take him for a ghost, and at once he speaks to them. He calms their terror not by first changing the weather but by telling them who he is.

They thought it was a ghost. Of course they did. Mark’s word is phantasma: an apparition, perhaps an evil sea spirit, in the dark before dawn. Their instinct was human: the one thing that could save them looked, in the dark, like the thing most likely to kill them. God has a way of coming to his people in the shape of what they most dread: Joseph’s brothers did not recognise their salvation in the man who had them arrested. What bears down on you out of the dark may be the Lord at work, though you may not know it at the time.

They all saw him. Not one man’s imagination: four were fishermen who had spent their lives on that water at night. And their terror is more fitting than they know. When the holy God draws near, sinful people tremble, as Isaiah did in the temple and Peter did in another boat (Isaiah 6:5; Luke 5:8). What they took for a ghost was the Holy One himself, and that is why his first word to them is mercy.

Immediately he spoke. Before anything about their circumstances changes, he tells them who he is. That is the order in which he deals with frightened people.

It is I. Literally “I am” (egō eimi). It can simply mean “it is me”, as you identify yourself in the dark. But it is also God’s name, revealed to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14), and God’s words in Isaiah: “I am he. Before me no god was formed” (Isaiah 43:10), and “I, I am he who comforts you” (Isaiah 51:12). And they are spoken by a man standing on a sea that the Scriptures say God alone tramples.

Do not be afraid. God’s words when he reveals himself (Genesis 15:1; Isaiah 41:10). The command rests on the middle phrase: the reason not to fear is not the weather but a Person, and the name he uses is the name from the bush. He does not say the wind will drop; he tells them who is with them, and treats that as sufficient. It is. That is the whole of Christian comfort in three phrases, and every one of them was spoken from the middle of the water they were afraid of.

Is Jesus really claiming to be God here? Yes, in the way Mark loves, by deeds and echoes rather than a lecture: walking on the sea, passing by, and “I am”. Any one might be a coincidence; all three in one scene are a revelation. The same Jesus will say “I am” before the high priest and be condemned for blasphemy (14:62–64). The disciples would not grasp it fully until after the resurrection, but Mark wants his readers to grasp it now: the man in the boat is the LORD.

What do I do with fear that will not go away? Follow the order of his words: he does not first remove the storm, but tells you who he is. So when fear grips you, do not only ask him to change your circumstances; remind yourself who is with you: the Lord who made the sea, walked on it, died and rose and holds your life. Speak his promises aloud (Isaiah 41:10; Hebrews 13:5–6), and bring the fear to him in prayer as it is (Philippians 4:6–7). If anxiety is constant and crippling, seek help as well: talk to your pastor and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up; that is not unbelief. And expect that faith may coexist with trembling for a while. Courage is not the absence of fear but trust in the One who is greater.
verseByVerse.note: “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

verseByVerse.quote: And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded, for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He climbs into the boat and the wind stops, and the disciples are astounded, because, as Mark frankly says, they had not understood the loaves: their hearts were hardened.

The wind ceased. After a night of terror the ending is almost domestic: a man climbs over the side and sits down with them. He does not even rebuke the wind this time; it simply stops, because he is aboard. (Mark does not record Peter walking on the water; Matthew does, Matthew 14:28–31.)

Utterly astounded. Beyond measure astonished, as when the little girl got up (5:42). And then Mark says something about his own leaders that a church inventing flattering stories would hardly have written.

They did not understand about the loaves. Only Mark adds this: the walking on water astonished them because they had not understood the loaves. That afternoon they had carried food out of his hands to thousands and drawn no conclusion from it about who he was. A new trouble knocks us flat for the same reason: we drew nothing from the last deliverance.

Their hearts were hardened. Mark used the same root of the Pharisees who watched a withered hand restored and walked out to plan a murder (3:5). Now he uses it of the apostles (compare 8:17), and it does not announce itself. It is not disbelief; the Twelve believed a great deal. It is slowly becoming unable to be moved: the same truths arrive and produce nothing, and a man can carry the bread and never taste it. If Peter is Mark’s source, Peter told this story against himself.

He gets into the boat. The hardening was real, and it was not final. He kept them, was denied by them, and after the resurrection fed them breakfast on a beach. He does not give up on hard-hearted disciples, and he does not wait for us to understand before he comes aboard.

What it does not mean. Not that the disciples were unbelievers like the Pharisees. But even true followers need God to open their eyes again and again (8:22–26). And if you fear this describes you because your feelings have gone flat, remember that grief, exhaustion and depression can numb a believer whose heart is still turned towards Christ; that is weakness to be carried, not hardness to be feared.

In the flow. Mark will press the point again in another boat (8:17–21), and then Peter at last confesses, “You are the Christ” (8:29). The slow eyes of the Twelve, and the patience of the One who opens them, run through the whole Gospel.

How can I stop forgetting what God has done? By deliberately remembering. Israel was told to set up stones, keep feasts and tell their children (Joshua 4:6–7; Deuteronomy 6:12). Keep a record of answered prayers and deliverances, and read it back when trouble comes. Speak of God’s past mercies at home and in church. Come to the Lord’s Supper as a feast of remembrance (1 Corinthians 11:24–25). And ask the Spirit to soften your heart, because remembering is not merely a technique; it is grace. “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2).

verseByVerse.quote: When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him and ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Gennesaret whole villages carry their sick to Jesus, and everyone who touches even the fringe of his garment is made well.

Gennesaret. A fertile plain on the north-west shore, between Capernaum and Magdala. He had sent them towards Bethsaida; the night’s headwind is the likeliest reason they land somewhere else.

On their beds. Carried on mats, as the paralysed man had been (2:3). He keeps moving, so the beds are carried after him all day by relays of neighbours and relatives.

In the marketplaces. The sick are laid out in rows in everybody’s way. These people have stopped caring how it looks, a desperation that has burned through embarrassment, and Christ has never once despised it.

Even the fringe of his garment. The tassel on the corner of a Jewish man’s garment, commanded as a reminder of the commandments of the LORD (Numbers 15:38–40). A woman with twelve years of bleeding had reached from behind to touch his garments (5:27–34), and now a whole region is doing what she did: somebody tells what happened to them, and a district comes.

As many as touched it. The word for made well can also mean saved. Not one was turned away, and no one’s theology was corrected first. Their understanding was thin and probably half superstitious, as hers had been; he does not lecture them about the tassel, but heals them. His power is undiminished by our ignorance, his mercy undeterred by our superstitions, and his welcome as wide as the marketplaces of Galilee.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ clothes had magical power. The power was his own, received by faith.

The contrast. The chapter began in a hometown that rejected him and saw few miracles; it ends with crowds who sought him and were healed. Nazareth had every advantage and would not stretch out a hand; Gennesaret had almost no understanding and grabbed the hem of his coat. What separated them was never how much they knew. One town thought it already knew him. The other only knew it needed him. That is good news for the irreligious, who fear they know too little to come to him, and a warning to the religious, who are sure they know enough not to need to.

In the flow. In the very next scene Pharisees from Jerusalem complain that his disciples eat with unwashed hands (7:1–5). Here the sick touch him and are made whole; there religious men worry about the dirt on other people’s hands. What matters is not how clean you are when you come, but whom you touch.

Why does Jesus not heal everyone like this today? These mass healings were signs of who he is and of what his kingdom will finally bring, given as the King arrived, not a promise that every illness will be removed in this life. Christ still heals, in answer to prayer and through medicine, as he wills. But the full fulfilment of this scene is still ahead: on the last day every one of his people will be raised with a body no disease can touch, and there will be no more mourning, nor crying, nor pain (Revelation 21:4). Gennesaret was a preview. The resurrection is the whole picture.

In everyday life. Who is the sick or burdened person you could carry to him this week, in prayer, by a visit, by bringing them to church? Be one of the neighbours who carry the beds; no one who comes to him is turned away.
verseByVerse.note: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the north-west shore of the lake. The fringe was the tassel the law required on a garment.

6.theology:
The loaves and the sea are one lesson. The feeding shows the Shepherd of Psalm 23 and a greater Moses; the walking on the sea shows the God who alone tramples the waves (Job 9:8) and speaks his own name in the dark. The disciples were astonished at the sea because they did not understand about the loaves (v. 52).

And their hearts were hardened is said of the apostles, in the word used of the men who watched a hand restored and left to plan a murder (3:5). What that hardening is, and why it was not final, is treated at vv. 51–52.
6.examples:
Then: a king who kept his oath and killed a prophet, because of his oaths and his guests (on what drove him, see the note on vv. 24–26).

Now: Peter is eight chapters from exactly this, in a courtyard, in front of a servant girl (on the fear of man behind it, see vv. 24–26). The fear of man lays a snare (Prov. 29:25). The way out is to fear God more than people: someone who already has God’s approval in Christ can afford to lose face rather than do wrong.

keyVerse.quote: When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things.
keyVerse.note: Set straight after Herod’s birthday feast, this verse shows what kind of King Jesus is. Israel’s rulers had fed themselves and left the flock to scatter, and God had promised, “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep” (Ezekiel 34:15); here that promise stands on the shore, tired and interrupted, and moved to the depths by what he sees. Everything that follows, the teaching, the loaves and the crossing in the night, flows from this compassion.

6.reflection:
The people of Nazareth asked the right questions about Jesus and still took offence, because they thought they knew him (vv. 2–3). How might long familiarity, from a Christian home, church or culture, have made him ordinary to you? What would help you look at him again?

Herod feared John, protected him and heard him gladly, but would not give up Herodias (vv. 18–20). Where is it easiest to enjoy God’s word without letting it change us? What one step of obedience is it asking of you now?

The disciples did the sums correctly and left Jesus out of them (vv. 35–44). Where are you facing a need beyond your resources, and what would it look like to bring him what you have, however little?

The disciples rowed against the wind where Jesus had sent them, while he watched from the mountain and came in the last watch saying, “Take heart; it is I” (vv. 45–52). How does knowing who he is change the way you face a long, hard stretch?

7.title: What Really Defiles a Man
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem, <sup>2</sup>they saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed. <sup>3</sup>(For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands properly, holding to the tradition of the elders, <sup>4</sup>and when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. And there are many other traditions that they observe, such as the washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches.) <sup>5</sup>And the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?” <sup>6</sup>And he said to them, “Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; <sup>7</sup>in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’ <sup>8</sup>You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men.” <sup>9</sup>And he said to them, “You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition! <sup>10</sup>For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother’; and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.’ <sup>11</sup>But you say, ‘If a man tells his father or his mother, “Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban”’ (that is, given to God)— <sup>12</sup>then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, <sup>13</sup>thus making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do.” <sup>14</sup>And he called the people to him again and said to them, “Hear me, all of you, and understand: <sup>15</sup>There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him.” <sup>17</sup>And when he had entered the house and left the people, his disciples asked him about the parable. <sup>18</sup>And he said to them, “Then are you also without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, <sup>19</sup>since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled?” (Thus he declared all foods clean.) <sup>20</sup>And he said, “What comes out of a person is what defiles him. <sup>21</sup>For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, <sup>22</sup>coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. <sup>23</sup>All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person.” <sup>24</sup>And from there he arose and went away to the region of Tyre and Sidon. And he entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not be hidden. <sup>25</sup>But immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard of him and came and fell down at his feet. <sup>26</sup>Now the woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth. And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter. <sup>27</sup>And he said to her, “Let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” <sup>28</sup>But she answered him, “Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” <sup>29</sup>And he said to her, “For this statement you may go your way; the demon has left your daughter.” <sup>30</sup>And she went home and found the child lying in bed and the demon gone. <sup>31</sup>Then he returned from the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the region of the Decapolis. <sup>32</sup>And they brought to him a man who was deaf and had a speech impediment, and they begged him to lay his hand on him. <sup>33</sup>And taking him aside from the crowd privately, he put his fingers into his ears, and after spitting touched his tongue. <sup>34</sup>And looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened.” <sup>35</sup>And his ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly. <sup>36</sup>And Jesus charged them to tell no one. But the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it. <sup>37</sup>And they were astonished beyond measure, saying, “He has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.”
7.overview:
Where we are. Mark 7 stands between the two great feedings (6:30–44; 8:1–9), late in Jesus’ work around Galilee. The disciples still do not understand (6:52), and the experts from Jerusalem, who have already put his power down to Beelzebul (3:22), come back to investigate.

The message. What makes a person unfit for God is not what goes into him but what comes out of his heart, and no washing can reach it. Religion that works from the outside in can be kept perfectly by hearts far from God, and can even cancel what God commands. Jesus says so, and then, having taken down the wall such rules had built between clean and unclean, Jew and Gentile, he walks through the gap with his mercy.

Why it was said. Mark’s readers were mostly Gentile believers, probably in Rome (see the introduction), where the church had already been divided over food and holy days (Romans 14:1–6). Must they keep the Jewish purity and food laws to belong to God’s people? Mark gives them Jesus’ answer.

How the chapter makes its case. A delegation travels some ninety miles to raise the matter of unwashed hands (vv. 1–5). Jesus answers with Isaiah, lips near and hearts far, and proves the charge with Corban, a vow that put a man’s money beyond his parents’ reach in God’s name (vv. 6–13). Then he tells the crowd that nothing going into a person can defile him, and Mark adds, “Thus he declared all foods clean” (vv. 14–19). The real defilement comes out of the heart, twelve sins no ritual can touch (vv. 20–23). The food laws had kept Jew and Gentile at separate tables, so that boundary goes too, and Jesus crosses it: a Phoenician mother takes his own hard saying about the children’s bread and finds hope in it (vv. 24–30), and a deaf man in the Decapolis, brought by friends, is given his hearing with one Aramaic word (vv. 31–37).

Where it leads. The experts go home unmoved; the outsiders receive the bread. The crowd’s verdict, “He has done all things well”, is bigger than they know: it echoes God’s verdict over his finished creation, and their wonder that the deaf hear is Isaiah’s sign that God himself has come to save. The heart he diagnoses he came to make new, by being counted unclean himself at the cross, so that sinners of every nation may sit at his table.

For us. Ask where your religion works from the outside in, and where a good custom has taken the place of God’s word or excused you from loving those God gave you. Then come as the Syrophoenician woman came, claiming nothing and trusting his generosity, and carry to him those who cannot come themselves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Tradition, the Word of God, and the Human Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God looks at the heart, not the hands, and no human tradition may stand in the place of his word. Inspectors from Jerusalem fault the disciples for eating without the elders’ ritual washing (vv. 1–5). Jesus answers that their worship is lips without heart and that their rules have displaced God’s commandments, and proves it with Corban, a vow that let a man neglect his parents in God’s name (vv. 6–13). Then he goes further, to the food laws God himself gave: nothing that goes into a person can defile him, and Mark adds that he declared all foods clean (vv. 14–19). In private he shows where defilement really comes from: the human heart, which no washing can reach (vv. 20–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Why does your Bible skip verse 16? The numbers run 15, then 17, and nothing has been lost or hidden (see the textual note at the end of the note on vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Corban, a rule invented to honour God, turned into a device for robbing your parents, with a straight face and in God’s name.

Now: the same thing still happens, and almost never with conscious dishonesty (see “Corban in modern clothes” at vv. 11–13). Jesus attacks not tradition as such but tradition set level with Scripture and then used against it. And the test case he chooses is one anyone can measure: not prayer or fasting, but whether the old people in your family are being looked after (see “Obedience you can measure” at vv. 9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem, they saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A delegation of experts from Jerusalem comes to inspect Jesus, and the fault they find is that his disciples eat without the ritual washing of hands.

The Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem. They collect around him, the way a committee collects. This is the second delegation from Jerusalem in Mark; the first decided that Jesus cast out demons by Beelzebul (3:22). These men have come some ninety miles as inspectors, not learners. The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to strict keeping of the law, who applied to ordinary daily life the purity rules the Old Testament gave to priests. The scribes were the professional experts in the law, many of them Pharisees.

Hands that were defiled. The crowds are being fed, healed and taught (6:30–56); the inspectors stand before a man who has raised a dead girl and fed a district on five loaves, and they have taken notes on his catering. The word (koinais) literally means common: not set apart as holy, and therefore ritually unclean. Mark explains it, “that is, unwashed”, for Gentile readers.

An honourable intention. To be fair to them, they meant well. The law required priests to wash before handling holy things (Exodus 30:19–21). Wanting the whole nation to be what God had called it, “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6), the Pharisees extended the priestly rule to every Jew and every meal: every table was to be treated like an altar. A good idea had hardened into an obligation with the force of a commandment, and men were being judged by it.

The hands that make clean. Jesus touched a leper, and instead of the leper’s uncleanness passing to him, his cleanness passed to the leper (1:41–42); a bleeding woman touched his garment and was healed (5:27–29). With Jesus the contagion is reversed, and holiness is what spreads. The inspectors are checking the disciples’ hands while standing beside the only man in Israel of whom Psalm 24:4 is wholly true, “clean hands and a pure heart”.

How it happens. Nobody sets out to replace Scripture. A wise practice is adopted for good reasons. In a generation it is the way we do things; in three, a man who does not do it is regarded as unsound, and nobody can say which verse required it. The Pharisees did not steal the Bible. They buried it under good ideas.
