What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was careless about hygiene. The washing had nothing to do with germs; it was a religious rite that the law of Moses did not command for ordinary people.

Were the Pharisees simply bad people? No, and that is what makes them a warning rather than a cartoon. Many were sincere and disciplined; they prayed, fasted, tithed and knew their Bibles thoroughly. Paul was one, blameless by their standard (Philippians 3:5–6). Their danger was not indifference to God, but trust in their own carefulness and judging others by rules God had not given. That temptation waits for every earnest believer, and the more serious you are, the more you need to watch for it.
verseByVerse.note: The washing in question was a ritual of purity, not hygiene.

parallels.desc: the Pharisee astonished that Jesus did not wash

verseByVerse.quote: (For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands properly, holding to the tradition of the elders, and when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. And there are many other traditions that they observe, such as the washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches.) And the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, "Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark explains the washing rules for readers who did not know them, and the Pharisees’ question shows where their trust really lay: not in what God had commanded, but in “the tradition of the elders”.

For the Pharisees and all the Jews. A generalisation: the practice was widely respected, even if not all kept it strictly. Mark explains it for Gentile readers (see the introduction), fitting for a chapter that ends with Jesus helping a Gentile woman and a Gentile deaf man.

Holding to the tradition of the elders. The key phrase. The tradition (paradosis, what is handed down) was the body of oral rules the rabbis had built around the written law as a fence, so that no one would come near breaking the law itself. It was later written down in the Mishnah (about AD 200), with a whole tractate on hand-washing. The Pharisees held these rules as binding as the written law, and the rabbis after them taught that they went back to Moses on Sinai (Mishnah Avot 1:1). Jesus flatly denies it: he calls it “the tradition of men” (v. 8).

From the marketplace … cups and pots and copper vessels. In the market you might brush against a Gentile or touch something unclean, so you washed, or even immersed yourself (the Greek is literally baptise themselves), before eating. Vessels could become unclean (Leviticus 11:32–35), and the tradition multiplied the rules. Mark’s list is faintly comic: there were rules for all of it, down to the furniture.

Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders? To walk is the Jewish way of speaking of how you live (the rabbis called their rules halakah, from the word for walking). The question is an accusation against the teacher who is responsible for his disciples. And the wording gives them away: they do not ask why the disciples break the law of God, but why they do not keep the tradition of the elders, and they are sure that settles the matter.

The tradition worth holding. The same word stands at the heart of the New Testament. Paul delivered what he had first received (1 Corinthians 15:3), and what he hands on is not a rule about water but a Person: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, was buried, and was raised on the third day. The elders’ tradition fenced people away from the edge of the law; the apostles’ tradition announces the one who kept the whole law from the heart, and who brings sinners near to God.

Where the authority has moved. Men who think like this can no longer feel the difference between what God said and what their tradition says God meant. Ask it of your own convictions: when challenged, do you reach first for the text, or for the settled instinct of the people who formed you? The second is not always wrong, but a man who cannot tell which one he is using has already made the Pharisees’ mistake.

How do I tell a command of God from a human tradition? Ask three questions. Where does Scripture actually say this, read in context? Is it a command for all Christians, or wisdom for a particular situation? And would I think less of a faithful Christian who did it differently? The length of a service, styles of dress, how often you have a quiet time, or which translation you read may be wise or unwise, but they are not commands. Keep your good habits gladly, but do not bind other people’s consciences with them: God alone is Lord of the conscience (Westminster Confession 20.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 21.2).

Uncertain wording. “Properly” translates a single Greek word, pygmē, which literally means “with a fist”, and nobody now knows exactly what gesture it described. Suggestions include washing up to the wrist, rubbing a fist in the cupped palm of the other hand, or pouring water over hands held in a loose fist. Clearly it named a careful, prescribed rite, the sense the ESV gives.

Textual note. Some manuscripts lack “and dining couches”, and scholars differ over whether it was added later; the meaning is unaffected.
verseByVerse.note: Mark explains Jewish customs for readers who did not know them, likely Gentile Christians, perhaps in Rome. The “tradition of the elders” was the body of oral rules built around the law.

parallels.desc: zealous for the traditions of my fathers

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, 'This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.' You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not defend his disciples’ hands; he exposes their accusers’ hearts. With Isaiah he charges them with worship that is all lips and no love, and with putting human rules in the place of God’s commandment.

Well did Isaiah prophesy of you. Jesus goes to the root, the authority of their tradition, and opens with the prophet they revered. Isaiah 29:13, spoken about Jerusalem in the eighth century BC, describes a kind of religion that reached its worst in the generation that met the Messiah.

You hypocrites. The only time Mark uses the word. A hypokritēs was an actor on a stage, wearing a mask. It need not mean deliberate pretence, which is why we cannot shrug the charge off: it means a gap between what a person shows and what he is, in which the show has taken over.

Lips near and heart far. Isaiah first spoke these words to men who were scrupulously religious, and that is what makes them so searching. The heart, in the Bible, is the centre of the person: thought, will and love (1 Samuel 16:7). The lips are close to God, the heart far from him, and the right words are exactly what make the far-off heart so hard to detect.

In vain do they worship me. Pointlessly: worship offered to the right God that achieves nothing. That should sober anyone who assumes that attendance is the same as acceptance.

Teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. The second fault: their authority is wrong. The fault is not having human customs, which every church must, but teaching them as though they came from God, and so binding consciences where God has not bound them.

You leave the commandment of God. “Leave” means let go; “hold” means grip tightly: a man with both hands full who has to drop one thing to grip another. Every one of them would have said he was defending the commandment, so Jesus proves the charge with one plain example (vv. 9–13).

The wonder Isaiah promised next. The Lord who exposes the distance between our words and our love is the one who closes it. He gave his Son, whose lips and heart were never once apart, who honoured the Father perfectly in secret and in public, so that our hollow worship could be covered by his true worship. And Isaiah 29 goes straight on: “I will again do wonderful things with this people” (Isaiah 29:14), and “in that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book” (29:18). Before this chapter ends Jesus opens a deaf man’s ears (7:35): the one who diagnoses the far-off heart is himself the wonder Isaiah promised.

How would you know? Two tests. What happens to your religion when nobody is watching? Prayer only in company, a Bible opened only where somebody might see, generosity that is known about: none of these is wrong, and all of them can be kept up by a heart that has quietly gone somewhere else. Subtract the audience and see what is left standing. And when did you last enjoy God: not a service or a sermon, but him? A far-off heart can keep every observance long after it has stopped finding pleasure in the Person they are about, and stopped noticing that it stopped. If the honest answer frightens you, take heart: a heart that is truly far off rarely stops to ask, and grief, dryness or depression can take away the feeling of joy without taking away the love. The way back is the same in every case: come to him as you are, and hope in God (Psalm 42:5).

But are creeds and confessions not tradition too? Yes, and good ones are a gift: the Apostles’ and Nicene Creeds, and confessions like the Westminster and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, summarise what the church has learned from Scripture. The difference is their claim. They do not claim to be a second source of revelation but to be faithful to the first, and they invite testing by it; they themselves say that councils may err and are a help in faith, not its rule (Westminster 31.4). Learn from them humbly, and let Scripture have the last word.

Does this mean religion itself is the problem? No, though Jesus’ words are often borrowed to say so. He did not walk out of the synagogue or scorn the temple; he condemned worship that had lost its heart and rules that had replaced God’s word. The irreligious have their own traditions of men, the unwritten rules of a profession, a social circle or a political tribe, kept carefully and used to judge outsiders. The far-off heart can hide behind a hymnbook or behind a scornful laugh at hymnbooks, and both need what Isaiah promised next: God himself coming to give hearing to the deaf and a new heart to the hollow.

Where Christians differ: Scripture and tradition. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Scripture and sacred tradition together form one deposit of revelation, both to be received with equal reverence, interpreted by the teaching office of the church. Protestants hold sola Scriptura: Scripture alone is the final authority, and every tradition, however old and useful, must be tested by it; they value tradition (the creeds, the councils, the wisdom of the church) as a servant, not a master. This commentary’s view: this passage is one of the clearest grounds for the Reformation principle. Jesus judges a revered, ancient tradition, believed to come from Moses, by the written word of God, and condemns it where it contradicts that word.

parallels.desc: this people draw near with their mouth

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition! For Moses said, 'Honor your father and your mother'; and, 'Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus proves the charge from the fifth commandment: their tradition did not merely add to God’s law but cancelled it, and the command it set aside was one nobody could dispute, to honour your father and mother.

A fine way of rejecting. “Fine” (kalōs, beautifully) is sarcastic: how skilfully you do it! “Rejecting” means setting aside, declaring void. The tradition had become the goal and God’s law the obstacle, and setting the law aside was not an accident; it was how the tradition worked.

For Moses said. Jesus treats Moses’ words as God’s commandment (v. 8) and God’s word (v. 13). What Moses wrote, God said.

Honor your father and your mother. The fifth commandment, the first with a promise (Exodus 20:12; Ephesians 6:2), taken in its plain sense, which we have sentimentalised. It is not chiefly about the manners of small children. There were no pensions; children were their parents’ security. To honour your father meant to feed him when he could no longer work.

Whoever reviles father or mother. Exodus 21:17. To revile is to curse, to treat with contempt, and the death penalty showed how seriously God took it. Yet their own school taught a legal device that let a man walk away from his father and mother and feel devout while doing it.

The son of Mary. The God who wrote the fifth commandment on stone kept it as a man, all his life. In Nazareth he was submissive to his parents (Luke 2:51); even on the cross he made sure his mother had a home (John 19:26–27); and behind that stands an eternal obedience, for he honoured his Father in everything (John 8:49). He kept perfectly the very commandment the Corban scholars had found a way not to keep.

Obedience you can measure. Jesus’ chosen example of real obedience to God is not a spiritual exercise. It is a middle-aged man paying his mother’s bills, and that is the kind of test the New Testament keeps applying to a person’s religion (James 1:27): “If anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8).

What if my parents were cruel, or are not Christians? You are still to honour them, but honour is not the same as obedience in everything, and it never means accepting abuse. Honour means treating them with respect as the parents God gave you, speaking of them without contempt, praying for them, and caring for their real needs when they are old, as far as you are able. It does not mean doing wrong at their request (Acts 5:29), keeping silent about abuse, or putting yourself or your children in danger. Abuse is never to be tolerated, and if a parent has harmed you, wise distance and the help of your church and, where needed, the authorities are right. Even then, you can refuse bitterness and leave judgment to God, and still see that they do not go without food or care.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “to keep your tradition” instead of “to establish”; the meaning is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: But you say, 'If a man tells his father or his mother, "Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban"' (that is, given to God)— then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, thus making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Corban rule let a man declare his money “given to God” and so put it beyond his parents’ reach, and the scribes held him to it: one rule about vows was used to cancel God’s command about parents.

Corban. “But you say”: God said one thing; you say another. Qorban is Hebrew for an offering, something brought near to God (Leviticus 2:1), and Mark glosses it for his readers. A man could declare his property or money Corban, dedicated to the temple as though laid on the altar. He might keep using it himself; but it could no longer be used for anyone else, including his parents.

Whatever you would have gained from me … you no longer permit him. A man owes his ageing parents a real, calculable sum and cannot simply refuse without disgrace. So he says the word, and his hands are tied, and it looks like devotion: the money is holy, and a vow may not be broken. Even if he regretted it, the scribes held him to it (Numbers 30:2). They used one law, about vows, to cancel another, about parents, choosing the interpretation that cancelled the greater command; in effect the system forbade a man to repent and put things right (later rabbis, to their credit, allowed such vows to be released). So an old man goes hungry, and his son is regarded as devout.

Thus making void the word of God. A legal word: annulling a document, as you might annul a will. “And many such things you do”: Corban is not the disease, only its clearest symptom.

The offering brought near. One offering was more wholly given to God than any temple gift, and it shut no one out: Christ “through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God” (Hebrews 9:14), and by it those who were far off have been brought near (Ephesians 2:13). At the cross devotion to the Father and provision for sinners were one act. So no gift to God can excuse withholding love from people.

What it does not mean. Not that vows and giving to God do not matter. But God does not want gifts taken from the mouths of your parents.

Corban in modern clothes. The same thing still happens, and it is almost never consciously dishonest. It is the man at church four nights a week whose mother has not had a visit since March; the money given to a fund while a brother in the same congregation cannot pay his heating bill. Ask it in one sentence: is anything I do for God costing somebody else something God told me to give them? That is Corban, whatever it is called. The way back is open to the forgiven: stop, and give what is owed.

How do I balance caring for parents with my other duties? Scripture gives an order without making it a formula. Your first earthly duty is to your spouse and children (Genesis 2:24; 1 Timothy 5:8), and care for parents should not destroy a marriage. But within that, parents are not optional. Share the load openly with your siblings, involve your parents in decisions where they are able, use other help, including professional care, without guilt where it is needed, and ask your church for practical support, as the early church cared for widows together (Acts 6:1–3). The aim is not that you do everything yourself, but that your parents are honoured and not neglected.
verseByVerse.note: Property declared Corban, dedicated to God, could no longer be used to support one’s parents.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the people to him again and said to them, "Hear me, all of you, and understand: There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing a person eats can make him unclean before God; what defiles him comes out of him. Jesus now goes beyond the elders’ rules, which God never gave, to the food laws God did give, and he says it to everyone.

He called the people to him again. Jesus turns from the scholars to the ordinary people: what the experts will not like he says to everybody. “Hear me, all of you, and understand”: not only listen but think, because what follows is compressed and easy to misunderstand.

Nothing outside a person. Hear it as a Jew in that crowd would have. The food laws (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14) and the hand-washings rested on the idea that what you eat or touch can make you unclean before God. It ran through every meal and every dealing with a Gentile neighbour; men had died in the Maccabean persecution rather than eat pork. And Jesus says: uncleanness that separates you from God is not a matter of what goes into your stomach.

The things that come out of a person. Real defilement is moral, not ceremonial. Either the saying is an outrage against God’s own law, or the one the food laws were pointing to has arrived. There is no third option.

The picture fulfilled. The food laws had always been a picture, drummed into a nation meal after meal for fifteen centuries, so that they would know in their bones that holiness matters. A picture is not abolished when the thing it pictured arrives; it is fulfilled and put away. Jesus cites no precedent; he says, “Hear me.” Only the Lord who gave Leviticus 11 has the right to retire it, and he does it not by relaxing holiness but by moving it to where it always belonged, the heart, where no washing can reach but his blood can. And the laws that kept Jew and Gentile at separate tables end as he sets out for Tyre, having come to break down the dividing wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14–15).

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament food laws were wrong or foolish. God gave them, for a time, as a picture of holiness and to mark Israel off from the nations.

Does this mean it does not matter what I take in, what I watch, read or drink? No. Jesus is speaking about the food laws, not about everything that enters through the eyes and ears. Sin comes from the heart, but what we feed the heart matters: “Keep your heart with all vigilance” (Proverbs 4:23). The lustful look is adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:28), and drunkenness is still sin (Ephesians 5:18). No food can make you unclean before God, but your choices about what you look at and consume are not morally neutral.

Has something been taken out of my Bible? No. We now have older and better copies than were available four hundred years ago, and where they show that a sentence crept in later, honest translators tell you in the margin instead of quietly leaving it in. Nothing Jesus taught is lost: the same words stand in 4:9 and 4:23. A faith that hid its own manuscripts would have something to hide. This one prints the workings at the bottom of the page.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verse 16: “If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.” It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added from 4:9 and 4:23, perhaps first written in a margin. The KJV and NKJV print it; the ESV puts it in a footnote. Verse numbers were added only in the sixteenth century, so translators left the number empty rather than renumber the New Testament, which is why the verses jump from 15 to 17.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 16: “If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.”

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered the house and left the people, his disciples asked him about the parable. And he said to them, "Then are you also without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled?" (Thus he declared all foods clean.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
In private Jesus explains the riddle: food goes into the stomach, not the heart, so it cannot make anyone unclean before God. Mark draws out what that means: the food laws are at an end.

He had entered the house. The pattern of Mark 4: public teaching in riddles, private explanation to the disciples (4:10, 34). “Parable” here means a riddle, a saying that needs unlocking, and the men who get the explanation are the ones who stayed and asked; Matthew tells us Peter asked (Matthew 15:15).

Then are you also without understanding? “Also”: like the crowd, like the Pharisees. There is a weariness in it; these are the men who have watched everything. The rebuke runs through Mark’s middle section, as the disciples keep failing to understand (6:52; 8:17–21). But he answers, in the same breath, as in chapter 4 (4:13). He does not withhold teaching from slow disciples; he sighs, and teaches them.

Since it enters not his heart but his stomach. The logic is simple, almost crude, and deliberately so. Food goes to the stomach, not to the heart, the moral and spiritual centre, and then, literally, out into the latrine. It cannot reach the place where a person is clean or unclean before God. Jesus separates ceremonial uncleanness, a person’s fitness to join in Israel’s worship, from moral defilement, the sin in the man himself. The Pharisees had treated the first as the second, and ended up, as Corban showed, ceremonially spotless and robbing their parents.

Thus he declared all foods clean. One of the most far-reaching asides in the Bible: Mark’s own comment, given by God’s Spirit, on what the saying meant. With one sentence the Lord of the Sabbath became the Lord of the kitchen. For Mark’s Gentile readers, among whom believers had already been divided over food and holy days (Romans 14:1–6), the aside settled it: they sat at the Lord’s table as full members of his people without first becoming Jews.

Holiness found in a Person. The food laws taught that God is holy and his people must be distinct (Leviticus 20:24–26); Hebrews calls them “regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation” (Hebrews 9:10), and that time arrived in the man explaining himself in this house. He is “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26), yet he eats with sinners to make them his. Israel was kept distinct by what it would not eat; his people are made distinct by whom they belong to. Holiness has not been lowered but located in Christ, and shared with everyone joined to him by faith: his perfect standing is counted as theirs (1 Corinthians 1:30), and his Spirit begins to make them like him from the inside.

Peter learned it slowly. Peter was in that house. Years later, on a rooftop in Joppa, he still said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean”, and had to be told three times, “What God has made clean, do not call common” (Acts 10:9–16). Even after that Paul had to rebuke him at Antioch for pulling back from Gentile tables (Galatians 2:11–14), before the church settled it (Acts 15; Romans 14:14; Colossians 2:16–17). So the aside in verse 19 is the note of a man who finally understood what he had been told to his face long before.

The comfort in a slow learner. You can be taught a truth clearly, by Christ himself, and go for years before it lands. That is not a sign that you were never taught; it is what learning looks like in creatures like us. Peter needed a vision, a Gentile household, a council and a public rebuke, and he got there. And if Peter is Mark’s source, he is the one who tells us that he had been told all along.

So are Christians free to eat any food? Yes. The food laws of Moses no longer bind anyone in Christ (Acts 10:15), for “everything created by God is good” (1 Timothy 4:4). Love may still limit that freedom. A Christian should not insist on his rights in a way that wounds a weaker believer (Romans 14:13–21; 1 Corinthians 8:13), and those who keep kosher out of conscience or for the sake of witness to Jewish friends are free to do so. What no one may do is make food a condition of standing with God.

Then which Old Testament laws still apply? Reformed Christians have long distinguished three kinds of law. The ceremonial laws (sacrifices, food laws, purity rites) were shadows of Christ, fulfilled and set aside (Hebrews 10:1). The civil laws governed Israel as a nation and expired with that state, though their general justice still teaches us. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, reflects God’s own character and still binds everyone, not as a way to be saved but as the shape of a grateful life (Westminster Confession 19.3–5; 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.5). Not every verse fits neatly into one box, but the principle is sound: ask how a law points to Christ, and how Christ applies it to his people.

Textual note. In the Greek the words can be joined to the sentence in two ways, and older translations (like the King James) took them as describing the latrine: “purging all meats”. Most modern scholars, following the ancient interpreters Origen and Chrysostom, take it as Mark’s comment on Jesus’ words, as the ESV does.
verseByVerse.note: The food laws of Leviticus 11 had marked Israel off from the nations; Mark draws out that Jesus set them aside.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "What comes out of a person is what defiles him. For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything that truly defiles comes from the human heart: every sin on Jesus’ list grows from inside us, where no washing can reach.

Out of the heart of man. Notice where sin comes from before you read the list, because that is the main teaching. Its source is not finally outside us, in our food, upbringing or company, though all these can tempt and shape us. It is the heart: what you love, choose, decide and are (Jeremiah 17:9). That does not mean every person is as wicked as he could be, but that sin has reached every part of us: we do not catch it from outside like a cold; it grows from inside like a root (Psalm 51:5).

Evil thoughts. First, because they are the root of the rest: reasonings, schemes, the plans of the mind. Every evil act begins as an evil thought.

The list. Twelve vices follow. The first six are plural in Greek and describe acts; the last six are singular and describe dispositions. Sexual immorality: any sexual activity outside marriage. Theft, murder, adultery: three of the Ten Commandments, named flatly. Coveting: the restless desire to have more, which drives a great deal of the rest. Wickedness: deliberate malice. Deceit: trickery, like bait on a hook. Sensuality: indulgence that no longer feels any shame. Envy: literally an evil eye, the grudging look at another’s good. Slander (blasphēmia): abusive speech against God or people. Pride: setting yourself above others and above God. Foolishness: not lack of intelligence but the moral folly of living as if there were no God (Psalm 14:1).

A mixed list. Murder sits beside envy, adultery next to pride, theft beside foolishness. We would have graded them. Jesus does not, because he is not ranking behaviours by their social damage but naming what comes out of one source.

They defile a person. Not hands, cups or food. To be defiled is to be made unfit to stand before the holy God. When Isaiah saw the Lord, he did not say that his hands were unclean; he said, “I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). In the presence of real holiness a man discovers that the problem is himself.

Follow your heart? Our culture says the opposite. Much modern talk about human trouble is almost entirely external: people go wrong because of what was done to them, because of systems, pressures and pasts. Some of that is true; the Bible is fierce about oppression and tender about wounds. But the modern remedy follows the modern diagnosis: change the environment, trust yourself, follow your heart. Jesus says the heart is where it comes from. That is either the most pessimistic sentence in the chapter or the most hopeful, depending on what comes next. A diagnosis is where the cure begins, and this diagnosis is the reason the gospel exists.

The only remedy that reaches. Not a better system, and not a stricter one, but the one God promised: “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26). That is what the man in front of them had come to do, by being treated as defiled himself, made sin for us who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21).

He let the list be charged to him. Out of one human heart has come nothing on this list: in him there was no evil thought, no envy, no pride. Yet he was condemned at last for blasphemy (14:64), the very word in the list, so that sinners whose hearts produce every item of it might be reckoned clean, and what comes out of them can finally be something other than this list. The Lord who sees to the bottom of us is the Lord who went to the bottom for us.

The uncomfortable look. Envy is nearer than murder: the small drop in your stomach when a colleague does well. So is slander, which needs only a true thing said to lower someone. If those are in you, no washing of hands will touch them; but his remedy does.

Do Christians not simply pick and choose, dropping the food laws but keeping the sexual ones? The distinction is Jesus’ own, made in this very passage. In one breath he declares all foods clean (v. 19); in the next he names sexual immorality and adultery among the things that truly defile (vv. 21–22). The food laws were a picture of holiness for one nation for a time, fulfilled in him. Sexual faithfulness reflects the character of God and the meaning of marriage from creation (Genesis 2:24; Mark 10:6–9), so it does not expire. Christians are not choosing by taste; they are following the Lord who gave both laws and explained which kind each was.

If I am a Christian, why do I still find these things in my heart? Because the new heart God gives is real, but the old sin is not yet gone. Sin no longer reigns (Romans 6:14), but it still remains and fights (Galatians 5:17; Westminster Confession 13.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 13.2). The difference is that a Christian now hates these things, confesses them, fights them by the Spirit, and is slowly changed. Finding envy or pride in yourself is not proof that you were never born again; being untroubled by it would be more worrying. Bring each one to Christ as you notice it: his blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7).

Does this mean what was done to me does not matter? No. Scripture takes seriously the harm others do, and God is the defender of the wronged (Psalm 10:14, 17–18). Abuse, neglect and trauma shape people deeply, and they need care, justice and time. But our own sins come from our own hearts, and that is good news: if my sin came only from outside, I would be helpless until my circumstances changed. Because it comes from my heart, Christ can deal with it directly, forgiving it and changing me, whatever my circumstances. You can be both a person who was wronged and a sinner who needs grace, and Christ is enough for both.

parallels.desc: the heart is deceitful above all things

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–37 — Two Healings Beyond Israel’s Borders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having taken down the wall between clean and unclean, Jesus walks through it, and his mercy reaches people outside every boundary Israel had. In pagan Tyre a Gentile mother hears his hard saying about the children’s bread, agrees with it, and finds in it room for her daughter, who is freed by his word at a distance (vv. 24–30). In the Decapolis a deaf man carried by friends is taken aside, spoken to by touch, and opened with one word (vv. 31–36). The astonished crowd says more than it knows: he has done all things well, and the deaf hear, as Isaiah promised when God came to save (v. 37).
verseByVerse.theology:
Was Jesus being cruel to the Syrophoenician woman? No: the word first, the house dogs under the table and the outcome settle it without softening the difficulty (this is treated fully at v. 27, under “Why speak like this?”).

And the deaf man’s healing is the new creation beginning. He has done all things well echoes Genesis 1:31, and he even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak is Isaiah’s sign of the day God comes to save (Isa. 35:5–6; both are treated at v. 37).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man who could not hear, brought by friends who could.

Now: every person carried to Christ by somebody else. And see how he handles him: aside from the crowd, in touch, the only language the man has, and with a groan (all treated at vv. 33–34).

verseByVerse.quote: And from there he arose and went away to the region of Tyre and Sidon. And he entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not be hidden. But immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard of him and came and fell down at his feet. Now the woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth. And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having taken down the barrier between clean and unclean, Jesus walks across it into pagan Tyre, and a Gentile mother, an outsider in every way, falls at his feet and begs him to free her daughter.

The region of Tyre and Sidon. Tyre was a great Phoenician port about 40 miles (65 km) northwest of Capernaum, in modern Lebanon: Gentile and pagan, the country of Jezebel’s father (1 Kings 16:31), a city the prophets denounced (Ezekiel 26–28). Yet Jesus had said that if his mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented (Matthew 11:21).

He did not want anyone to know, yet he could not be hidden. He was seeking rest with his disciples, away from the crowds and the territory of Herod. But his reputation has crossed the border ahead of him, and underneath it is simply not possible for this Person to be concealed, not in a house in Tyre, not in a tomb in Jerusalem.

Little daughter. A tender word, the same as Jairus used (5:23). She has probably already tried everything Tyre had to offer.

Fell down at his feet. The posture of a suppliant who has no claim. She is a woman, approaching a male Jewish teacher, uninvited, in a private house, on behalf of a child who is not present.

A Syrophoenician by birth. Literally a Greek: Greek in language and culture, from Phoenicia in the Roman province of Syria. Matthew calls her a Canaanite (Matthew 15:22), the ancient name of the peoples Israel was commanded to drive out. A woman, a Gentile, from a pagan city, with a demon-possessed child: she is an outsider in every way there was.

She begged him. She kept on asking, while the disciples wanted her sent away (Matthew 15:23), and into that scene comes perhaps the hardest sentence Jesus speaks to anyone in this Gospel.

One greater than Elijah on this coast. Jesus had once pointed his hometown to this very region: Elijah was sent to none of Israel’s widows but to a widow of Zarephath in the land of Sidon (Luke 4:25–26), and gave her son back alive (1 Kings 17:8–24). Now another Gentile mother comes for her child. Elijah stretched himself on the boy three times and cried to the Lord; Jesus will free this daughter with a sentence spoken in another house. The prophet carried the Lord’s word. This is the Lord, and his mercy reaches past every border his people drew, to the very nations they were once told to drive out. The outsider on the floor is nearer to his heart than the inspectors from Jerusalem.

Was Jesus sent only to Israel? In his earthly ministry, first to Israel: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24). Before the cross Christ came first as a servant to the circumcised (Romans 15:8); the nations would be reached after his death and resurrection (Matthew 28:19). But the promise to Abraham was always that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3), and the word “first” in verse 27 shows that the Gentiles were to come in their turn. This woman is an early firstfruit of that harvest, and so are we.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre was a Gentile port city on the coast north-west of Galilee. “Syrophoenician” means a Phoenician from the Roman province of Syria; Matthew calls her a Canaanite.

parallels.desc: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath, near Sidon

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, "Let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells her that the blessing of his ministry must go first to Israel, God’s children, and it is a hard saying; yet the word “first”, and dogs that are inside the house, leave a door open.

Let the children be fed first. The children are Israel, God’s covenant people: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22). The bread is the blessing of the Messiah’s ministry, “to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16). Only Mark records the word “first”, and a man who says “first” has a second course in mind. She is not being told there is no place for her, but about the order.

Throw it to the dogs. The saying makes readers wince, and must not be explained away: “dogs” was a known Jewish insult for Gentiles, as unclean as street dogs. But see the picture he draws: a family at a meal, children being fed, and dogs under the table, inside the house, not the scavengers that ran in packs outside the town. The outsider is already in the room. His severity is never without mercy: he held back the bread for a moment only so that she might discover how much was on the table.

The bread on the table. Mark has filled these chapters with bread: five loaves (6:41), bread eaten with unwashed hands (7:2), seven loaves in Gentile country (8:6), a boat with one loaf (8:14). The bread on Jesus’ table is finally himself: “This is my body” (14:22). Israel’s teachers had just turned away from it over hand-washing; it would be broken on a cross and carried to the nations, in exactly the order Jesus states to this woman.

Why speak like this? Several reasons come together. First, it states a fact about God’s plan: his covenant was with Israel, so Israel was to be served first. Second, it tests her faith, as God tested Abraham and Jacob, to draw it into the open. Jesus already knew what he would do; he tests faith to bring it out, not to break it, as with Jairus, kept standing in the street while his daughter died. Third, the saying was a picture with a door in it. His tone and look we cannot see, but the house dogs and the word “first” left room for her, and everything she needs is in his own sentence. And watch what he does: he grants her request at once, at a distance, and Matthew records his verdict: “O woman, great is your faith!” (Matthew 15:28). That is the loudest commentary available on the tone of verse 27, and it is not the commentary of a man who has just insulted somebody.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus despised Gentiles, or was racist, or that he learned from her to widen his mission, as some modern readers suggest. He had already healed Gentiles (5:1–20) and declared all foods clean (v. 19). He is in control of this conversation from beginning to end.

Does God still test us like this? Yes, though not usually with words spoken aloud. Our prayers sometimes meet silence, delay, or what looks like a refusal, and the testing of our faith produces steadfastness (James 1:2–4). God does not test us to discover what is in us; he already knows. He tests us to bring it out, to strengthen it, and to show us his faithfulness. When God seems hard, do not conclude that he is against you. Look again at what he has said, as she did, and you will often find a door in it.

Uncertain wording. Jesus uses kynaria, a diminutive of the ordinary word for dog. Diminutives can soften (“little dogs”, pets), but by this time they often made little or no difference to the meaning, so how much gentleness the word itself carries is uncertain. The setting he gives it is not: dogs under the family’s table, fed in the house.
verseByVerse.note: “Dogs” was a common Jewish insult for Gentiles; here the picture is of household dogs under the table. “First” implies the Gentiles’ turn will come.

parallels.desc: to the Jew first and also to the Greek

verseByVerse.quote: But she answered him, "Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She accepts his words and finds hope inside them: she claims no place at the table, only the crumbs that fall to the dogs beneath it, because she believes there is more than enough where he is.

Yes, Lord. She does not protest the word “dogs”. She agrees with his description of her: yes, the children come first. She has stopped arguing about her standing, which is the argument she could never win, and she is about to argue about his generosity, which is an argument nobody has ever lost. “Lord” (kyrie) can mean simply sir, but she is the only person in Mark who addresses Jesus as Lord.

Even the dogs under the table. Brilliant faith. She takes his own picture: he put the animal under the table, and dogs in a house are fed too, without depriving a single child. There is always overflow where he is. Mark’s readers have just counted twelve baskets of it (6:43).

The one who answered him back. It may be the only place in the Gospels where somebody answers Jesus back and he commends the answer. She has argued with Jesus from Jesus: not from her rights or her need, but from his own words and character. That is what makes her faith great (Matthew 15:28): humble, claiming nothing; persistent at an apparent refusal; and confident that there is so much grace in him that even what falls from the table is enough.

Why a crumb is enough. A crumb is enough only because of whose table it falls from. In Jesus the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9), and the least he gives is given by all that he is. The experts resisted his word and the disciples failed to understand it (v. 18); this woman, with no Scriptures, sees that where he is there is no shortage.

How to pray like her. She did not take offence and walk away, nor plead louder to wear him down. She took hold of the very word that sounded like a refusal and pressed further in, resting on his goodness, not her persistence. If you are praying into silence, do not read the delay as the final verdict. Plead his own word back to him: “you said”, “you promised”, “you are the God who”.

Within his purpose, not against it. This is not a technique for bending God to your will. The Lord himself, praying in Gethsemane with perfect faith, added, “Yet not what I will, but what you will” (14:36), and the cup did not pass. Her persistence was answered because it pressed within his purpose, not against it. So pray like her, and trust like him, that the Father’s no, when it comes, is as wise and as loving as his yes.

Is it presumptuous to argue with God in prayer? Not when you argue from his own word and character, humbly. Scripture is full of such prayers: Abraham pleading for Sodom, Moses reminding God of his promises, the psalmists asking how long; and God invites it: “Put me in remembrance; let us argue together” (Isaiah 43:26). What is presumptuous is demanding what God has not promised, or arguing from our own deserving. She said, “Yes, Lord”, first: agree with God about yourself, then plead his mercy, and you stand where every saint has stood.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, "For this statement you may go your way; the demon has left your daughter." And she went home and found the child lying in bed and the demon gone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers her word with his own: the demon has already gone, at a distance, and she goes home on nothing but what he said, and finds her daughter free.

For this statement. Literally, because of this word: what moved him was her sentence, the one she made out of his own. The only two people Jesus commends for great faith are this woman and a Gentile centurion (Matthew 8:10), neither of them raised on the Scriptures.

The demon has left your daughter. Past tense: it is already done, at a distance. Mark’s exorcisms are usually close-range and noisy; here there is a sentence in one house and a quiet room in another, as with the centurion’s servant (Matthew 8:5–13).

She went home. The last act of her faith, and easy to miss. She has been given a sentence and nothing else, and she walks back, quite possibly a long way, on nothing but what he said. That is what faith always finally looks like: going home on the word.

Lying in bed. Literally thrown down, which may suggest she had been exhausted by the final convulsion, as with the boy in 9:26. Mark’s detail is beautifully understated: her mother comes in and finds her at peace.

He sent out his word. Psalm 107:20 says of the Lord, “He sent out his word and healed them.” In Tyre the Lord of that verse stands in a house and speaks, and it is how he still works. Every Gentile who has believed since has been reached as this girl was healed: at a distance from his body, by his word alone. From the Father’s right hand his word runs faster than any messenger and further than any road, and wherever it goes, the darkness leaves. A few verses on, still in Gentile country, he will feed four thousand (8:1–9). She asked for a crumb; the nations would soon be given the whole loaf.

In everyday life. The people we are most desperate about are usually not in the room: a son who will not answer his phone, a parent whose mind is going. His word can reach them. Pray, and then go on with your day the way she walked home, on the strength of what he has said.

Does my faith help someone who does not believe? Yes, in this sense: God hears his people’s prayers for others and acts in answer. This girl was freed because her mother believed and asked; Paul prayed for Israel’s salvation (Romans 10:1), and the church prayed for Peter in prison (Acts 12:5). But no one can believe on another’s behalf for salvation; each must come to Christ himself (John 3:36). So pray for your unbelieving children and friends with confidence, because God is pleased to use prayer to open hearts, and leave the result with him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he returned from the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the region of the Decapolis. And they brought to him a man who was deaf and had a speech impediment, and they begged him to lay his hand on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus takes a long road through Gentile country, and in the Decapolis people bring him a deaf man who can hardly speak, begging him to lay his hand on him. The man does not come; he is brought.

Through Sidon. A long detour: Sidon is about 25 miles (40 km) north of Tyre, the wrong direction entirely for the Sea of Galilee. Then round to the Decapolis, east of the lake: perhaps 120 miles (200 km) on foot, almost every mile of it Gentile ground.

In the region of the Decapolis. The Ten Cities, a league of Greek cities mainly east of the Jordan, where the townspeople had begged him to leave and he left one restored madman with a story and no training (5:1–20). Now people come bringing him their sick. One man told one district what had happened to him, and the ground was ready.

Deaf and had a speech impediment. The word for his speech (mogilalon) appears only here in the New Testament and once in the Greek Old Testament, in Isaiah 35:6: then shall the tongue of the mute sing for joy. Mark has chosen a word that points to Isaiah’s prophecy of what happens when God himself comes to save.

They begged him to lay his hand on him. Like the four men who lowered their friend through the roof (2:3–5): a person who could not get to Jesus, and someone who would not let that be the end of it. If you are praying for someone who cannot or will not pray, this is the man in the Bible for you. Nobody recorded the names of those who brought him, and, humanly speaking, without them he would have lived and died deaf.

Other sheep not of this fold. Why does the Son of God spend weeks on foot in pagan country? Because he is the shepherd who goes after his sheep where they are: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also” (John 10:16). On this long road a Gentile’s ears are opened before the mission to the Gentiles has begun. Israel’s Messiah is already behaving as the Saviour of the world (John 4:42).

How do I bring someone to Jesus who cannot or will not come? Pray for him, first and persistently, because only God can open ears (Acts 16:14). Then do what these friends did: go where he is, find a way to communicate he can understand, and bring him into contact with Christ, through a kind word, a Gospel to read, an invitation to hear the word preached, or your own life of love. Do not wait for him to ask. Many come to Christ because someone carried them. Your name may never be recorded, but your carrying is seen.

Uncertain wording. It is not certain whether mogilalon means that the man could not speak at all or that he spoke only with great difficulty. In Isaiah 35:6 the word stands for the mute, and the crowd says Jesus makes “the mute speak” (v. 37); but “his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly” (v. 35) suggests he had been making sounds no one could understand, perhaps because he could not hear himself. The ESV’s “speech impediment” takes that likelier sense.

Textual note. The KJV, following later manuscripts, reads “from the coasts of Tyre and Sidon”, which removes the detour; the earliest manuscripts have “through Sidon”, as most modern Bibles do.
verseByVerse.note: Going from Tyre through Sidon to the Decapolis is a long loop through Gentile territory.

parallels.desc: the healed man proclaims in the Decapolis

verseByVerse.quote: And taking him aside from the crowd privately, he put his fingers into his ears, and after spitting touched his tongue. And looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, "Ephphatha," that is, "Be opened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus takes the deaf man aside, tells him by touch what he is about to do, looks up to the Father with a groan, and with one word, “Be opened”, gives him his hearing.

Taking him aside. Think what a jostling crowd is like for a man who cannot hear: faces turned towards him, mouths moving, people pointing, and not one word he can follow. Jesus deals with him alone, face to face: a rebuke to every way of helping people that turns the person into a show.

His fingers into his ears. One of the most elaborate healings in Mark, and modern readers find it odd. It is not odd once you ask how you tell a deaf man what you are about to do. You cannot say it, so he says it in the only language available: signs. Fingers into the ears: this is what I am dealing with. Saliva on the tongue: this too. It is a conversation without words, and it makes clear that the healing comes from Jesus. He could have healed him with a word, as he had just healed a girl miles away; instead the Word who made the ear puts his fingers into a deaf man’s ears, and takes the trouble to be understood by one man, in the man’s own language.

Looking up to heaven. Towards the Father, in prayer (6:41; John 11:41), and the man could see it: help comes from God.

He sighed. A deep groan: not strain but grief at the ruin sin and suffering have brought on the world. Paul uses the same word for creation and believers groaning as they wait for the redemption of our bodies (Romans 8:22–23). Here is the Creator, in a body, groaning over the wreckage. He does not treat the physical ruin of the world as a small matter to be tolerated until souls are saved. It draws a groan out of him, over a man whose name nobody bothered to write down.

Ephphatha, that is, Be opened. Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, preserved as talitha cumi was (5:41): both times a word spoken to somebody helpless, in a private place, and remembered exactly. Not only the ears but the whole man, closed in silence, is opened. One word, to a man who could not hear it, and heard it.

Does God care about disability? Deeply. Jesus treated the man not as a case but as a person, and groaned over his condition. Disability belongs to a world marred by the fall, but it is not usually the result of a person’s own particular sin (John 9:1–3), and disabled people are not less in God’s image or less welcome in his church (Luke 14:13, 21). God may heal now, and he certainly will at the resurrection, when every body of his people will be made whole. Meanwhile churches should make room for disabled believers, communicate in ways they can receive, and learn from their faith, as Jesus took the trouble to speak this man’s language.

Why did Jesus heal this man and not every deaf person? Because his healings were signs, not a programme to end all suffering before its time. Each showed who he is and what he will finally do: Isaiah 35 promises a whole creation made new, and this man is its first instalment. Jesus once left Capernaum while the whole town was still looking for him, because he had come above all to preach (1:35–38) and to give his life as a ransom (10:45). The full healing waits for his return, when the dead are raised. So the man in the Decapolis is not the exception to God’s plan but the preview of it.
verseByVerse.note: Saliva was widely believed to have healing power. “Ephphatha” is Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke.

parallels.desc: spitting on the blind man’s eyes

verseByVerse.quote: And his ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly. And Jesus charged them to tell no one. But the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At once the man hears and speaks plainly, and though Jesus orders silence, the news spreads all the more.

His ears were opened. The word is the one Jesus used. Imagine the first second of it: a man who has lived inside silence, and suddenly there is wind, and voices, and his own breathing.

His tongue was released. Literally, the bond of his tongue was loosed. Ancient people sometimes spoke of a demon binding the tongue, though Mark does not say this man was possessed.

He spoke plainly. Correctly, at once. In human terms that is the strangest part: you learn to speak by hearing, and this man had no learning at all, which tells you that what happened here was not a repair. It was a creation. And the tongue he loosed that day was the first of countless tongues he has loosed since, to sing the praise of the God who opens the ears of the deaf.

Tell no one. The messianic secret again, as scholars call his repeated orders to keep quiet about him (1:44; 5:43). A reputation as a healer is a fragment of the truth that people can believe enthusiastically while understanding nothing; who he truly is could only be understood in the light of the cross.

The more zealously they proclaimed it. “Proclaimed” is the word for preaching. Their disobedience was understandable but still disobedience, as with the cleansed leper (1:45). The irony is that in Mark, people told to keep silent proclaim, while the disciples sent out to proclaim (3:14; 13:10) were slow to understand. These people had little knowledge and no instruction to speak, and they could not stop talking: nobody has to be persuaded to talk about something that has just happened to them.

How can I get back the wonder of a new believer? Not by manufacturing excitement, but by looking again at what Christ has done for you; wonder fades when grace becomes familiar. Remember what you were without him (Ephesians 2:1–5), read the Gospels slowly enough to be surprised, hear new Christians’ stories, and ask God to restore the joy of your salvation (Psalm 51:12). The more clearly you see your own deafness and the voice that opened your ears, the less you will need to be pushed to speak of him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were astonished beyond measure, saying, "He has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The astonished crowd sums up what they have seen in words fuller than they know: the Creator is at work again, and the day Isaiah promised, when God comes and the deaf hear, has begun.

Astonished beyond measure. A double strengthening in the Greek, used only here in the New Testament: Mark has run out of ordinary words. And both halves of the crowd’s sentence are echoes of Scripture they did not realise they were making.

He has done all things well. Many readers have heard an echo of Genesis 1:31: “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.” The crowd means something modest, but they have said something very like the sentence pronounced over the finished creation: the one who made ears has repaired a pair of them. This is no rescue bolted on to a ruined world, but the Creator returning to his own marred work and beginning, one man at a time, to make it good again.

He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak. Mark’s point is Isaiah 35:4–6: “Behold, your God will come… He will come and save you. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped.” The rare word in verse 32 pointed here. In Jesus, God has come. And these Gentiles of the Decapolis, who had no part in the promises and could probably not have quoted Isaiah, are the ones who see it.

The wider meaning. This healing stands next to the disciples’ spiritual deafness: “Having ears do you not hear?” (8:18). The man pictures what the disciples need, and what every person needs. We cannot open our own ears to God’s word; only Christ can say to us, “Be opened.”

“Be opened” over every grave. The chapter began with men measuring the cleanness of cups; it ends with the Creator groaning over one broken body and saying, “Be opened.” He has done all things well: at creation, at the cross, in the opening of every deaf heart. One day he will say “Be opened” over every grave that has ever been dug, and the redeemed will rise with ears to hear and tongues to sing, and once again the verdict of heaven over his finished work will be: “very good”.

How can I say he has done all things well when my life is going badly? Because the sentence is about him, not about your circumstances this week. It does not mean that everything that happens is pleasant, but that everything he does is right, wise and good, even when we cannot yet see how (Romans 8:28; Genesis 50:20). The deaf man had lived years in silence; the crowd’s cry came at the end of a long wait. Say it by faith now, and you will say it by sight later, as many Christians have written it over the hardest chapters of their lives, looking back. The cross itself looked like the worst thing ever done, and it was the best.

parallels.desc: the ears of the deaf unstopped, the tongue of the mute sings

7.theology:
The Lawgiver retires his own picture. The food laws were God’s gift, a lesson in holiness drummed in at every meal. Only the Lord who gave Leviticus 11 could retire it (see the note on vv. 14–15), and holiness is not lowered but located in him (see “Holiness found in a Person” at vv. 17–19).

And the real defilement is inside. Evil thoughts, envy, pride and the rest come out of the heart of man (v. 21), so no washing can reach them; on the only remedy that does, see vv. 20–23.
7.examples:
Then: Peter was in that house and heard the explanation of v. 19 with his own ears, and still took years to act on it (see “Peter learned it slowly” at vv. 17–19).

Now: Christ is patient with slow learners: Peter got there (see “The comfort in a slow learner” at vv. 17–19).

keyVerse.quote: There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this saying. It exposes the washing rules of the first half, and it opens the door to the Gentiles of the second half, for if no food defiles, the tables that kept Jew and Gentile apart are gone. And it turns every reader’s eyes inward, to a heart no ritual can clean, which only Christ can make new.

7.reflection:
The Pharisees’ hand-washing began as a good idea and hardened into a rule by which others were judged (vv. 1–8). What good habits or customs among Christians you know are in danger of going the same way, and how can you tell a command of God from a human tradition?

Corban let a man neglect his parents and still feel devout (vv. 9–13). Is anything you do “for God” costing someone else what God has told you to give them, whether time, care or money?

Jesus says that evil comes “from within, out of the heart of man” (v. 21). How does that differ from the way people around you usually explain wrongdoing, and why is it, in the end, good news?

The Syrophoenician woman agreed with Jesus about herself and then pleaded his generosity (vv. 27–28), and the deaf man was carried to Jesus by friends (v. 32). What do these two scenes teach you about how to pray, and about bringing others to him?

8.title: Who Do You Say That I Am?
8.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days, when again a great crowd had gathered, and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples to him and said to them, <sup>2</sup>“I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. <sup>3</sup>And if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the way. And some of them have come from far away.” <sup>4</sup>And his disciples answered him, “How can one feed these people with bread here in this desolate place?” <sup>5</sup>And he asked them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven.” <sup>6</sup>And he directed the crowd to sit down on the ground. And he took the seven loaves, and having given thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd. <sup>7</sup>And they had a few small fish. And having blessed them, he said that these also should be set before them. <sup>8</sup>And they ate and were satisfied. And they took up the broken pieces left over, seven baskets full. <sup>9</sup>And there were about four thousand people. And he sent them away. <sup>10</sup>And immediately he got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha. <sup>11</sup>The Pharisees came and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven to test him. <sup>12</sup>And he sighed deeply in his spirit and said, “Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation.” <sup>13</sup>And he left them, got into the boat again, and went to the other side. <sup>14</sup>Now they had forgotten to bring bread, and they had only one loaf with them in the boat. <sup>15</sup>And he cautioned them, saying, “Watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.” <sup>16</sup>And they began discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread. <sup>17</sup>And Jesus, aware of this, said to them, “Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened? <sup>18</sup>Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? And do you not remember? <sup>19</sup>When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?” They said to him, “Twelve.” <sup>20</sup>“And the seven for the four thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?” And they said to him, “Seven.” <sup>21</sup>And he said to them, “Do you not yet understand?” <sup>22</sup>And they came to Bethsaida. And some people brought to him a blind man and begged him to touch him. <sup>23</sup>And he took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village, and when he had spit on his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked him, “Do you see anything?” <sup>24</sup>And he looked up and said, “I see people, but they look like trees, walking.” <sup>25</sup>Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; and he opened his eyes, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. <sup>26</sup>And he sent him to his home, saying, “Do not even enter the village.” <sup>27</sup>And Jesus went on with his disciples to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. And on the way he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that I am?” <sup>28</sup>And they told him, “John the Baptist; and others say, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets.” <sup>29</sup>And he asked them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered him, “You are the Christ.” <sup>30</sup>And he strictly charged them to tell no one about him. <sup>31</sup>And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes and be killed, and after three days rise again. <sup>32</sup>And he said this plainly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. <sup>33</sup>But turning and seeing his disciples, he rebuked Peter and said, “Get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.” <sup>34</sup>And calling the crowd to him with his disciples, he said to them, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. <sup>35</sup>For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel’s will save it. <sup>36</sup>For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul? <sup>37</sup>For what can a man give in return for his soul? <sup>38</sup>For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.”
8.overview:
Where we are. Mark 8 is the hinge of the Gospel. The first half has kept asking, “Who then is this?” (4:41); here Peter answers, and from v. 31 Jesus turns towards Jerusalem and the cross (see the introduction).

The message. Jesus is the Christ, and the Christ must go to a cross; whoever follows him walks the same road. To see that he is the Christ is not enough without seeing what kind of Christ he is, so the chapter is about sight: people with every piece of evidence and none of the sight, and a Lord who keeps touching blind eyes until they see clearly.

Why it was said. Mark’s first readers in Rome were losing reputation, property and life for a crucified Lord (see the introduction). They needed to know that the cross had not overtaken Jesus by accident but was the “must” of God’s plan, and that what they lost for him was not failure but following.

How the chapter makes its case. Jesus feeds four thousand, probably mostly Gentiles (vv. 1–10); the Pharisees, with all the evidence they could want, demand a sign from heaven (vv. 11–13); in the boat the disciples worry over one loaf: “Do you not yet understand?” (vv. 14–21). So Mark places next a blind man healed in two stages, who first sees people “like trees, walking” (vv. 22–26), a picture of the men in the boat. At Caesarea Philippi, in a city named for Caesar, Peter sees: “You are the Christ” (vv. 27–30). But when Jesus says plainly that the Son of Man must suffer, be killed and rise, Peter takes him aside to correct him and is called Satan (vv. 31–33): he sees, but blurred. Then everyone is told the terms: deny yourself, take up your cross, follow me (vv. 34–38).

Where it leads. Every part of the chapter leans towards the cross. The hands that break bread with thanks will do so again on the night he is betrayed; the only sign he will give is his own death and resurrection; the ransom no one can pay for his soul (v. 37) he will pay himself (10:45). And the Son of Man who will come in his Father’s glory with the holy angels is first the one rejected and killed, who walks ahead on the road he calls us to take.

For us. The question at the centre of the chapter is put to every reader: “But who do you say that I am?” Do not settle for a Christ without a cross, or for a following that costs nothing. And if your sight is still blurred, come back for the second touch: he does not leave a man until he sees.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Four Thousand Fed, a Sign Refused, and the Leaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus has fed his people, Jew and Gentile alike, with more than enough, yet even those closest to him do not see who he is. Out of compassion he feeds four thousand in the wilderness from seven loaves, with seven baskets left over (vv. 1–10). The Pharisees, with all that evidence, demand a sign from heaven, and he refuses and leaves them (vv. 11–13). In the boat the disciples worry over one loaf, so he warns them against the leaven of unbelief and worldliness and makes them recite the baskets: “Do you not yet understand?” (vv. 14–21). Hard hearts are not found only among his enemies.
verseByVerse.theology:
Are the two feedings one story told twice? Mark closes that off himself: in vv. 19–20 Jesus makes the disciples recite both, with the figures, as two events they were present at (see the box “Where Christians differ: one feeding or two?” at the end of the note on vv. 1–3).

The settings differ too: Jews on the green grass of Galilee with twelve baskets over; Gentiles in the Decapolis with seven, some from far away (on that phrase, see vv. 1–3; on the numbers, vv. 8–10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men in a boat, worrying about having one loaf between them, having twice watched thousands fed out of nothing.

Now: we have evidence of God’s provision, the job that came, the diagnosis that was not what we feared, and the next shortage finds us doing arithmetic as though none of it had happened. Jesus locates the failure in memory: And do you not remember? (On the remedy, see “Make yourself recite it” at vv. 19–21.)

verseByVerse.quote: In those days, when again a great crowd had gathered, and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples to him and said to them, "I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the way. And some of them have come from far away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sees the hunger of a crowd, probably mostly Gentiles, before anyone asks, and he will not send them away empty. His compassion reaches their bodies as well as their souls.

Again a great crowd. Mark’s signal that we have been somewhere like this before (6:30–44). Jesus is still in the Decapolis, on the largely Gentile side of the lake (7:31), where the man freed from Legion and the healed deaf man had spread the news (5:20; 7:36); this crowd is probably the fruit of what they told. Having declared all foods clean (7:19) and given the crumbs to a Gentile woman (7:28), he now feeds a Gentile crowd, and not with crumbs.

I have compassion on the crowd. He speaks first, before anybody asks. The word (splanchnizomai) means moved in the inner parts. At the first feeding he had compassion because they were “like sheep without a shepherd” (6:34); here it is for their hunger. Three days sleeping rough in a desolate place is long enough for any food they brought to run out, and in the middle of teaching thousands he has kept track of what they have had to eat.

They will faint on the way. At the first feeding the disciples raised the problem (6:35); here Jesus does, and he is thinking of the walk home: people going light-headed on a hot road with miles still to go, the children, and the old.

From far away. Pastoral care for those with the longest road; but underneath, the phrase echoes the language used of the Gentiles, those who were far off (Isaiah 60:4; Acts 2:39; Ephesians 2:13): Jesus is thinking of their tired legs, and Mark is hinting who they are. He is the Lord who counts the days his people have waited, knows the length of every road, and brings near those who were far off.

Does Jesus care about my body, or only my soul? Both, and this verse proves it. After three days feeding their souls with his word, he would not send them home hungry. God made us bodies and souls together, and he will raise our bodies at the last (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). So you may pray about food, rent, health and sleep without embarrassment; your Father knows you need these things (Matthew 6:32). And Christians should care for the bodily needs of others too, not instead of the gospel but alongside it, as Jesus did (James 2:15–16).

Where Christians differ: one feeding or two? Some critical scholars argue that the feedings of the five thousand and the four thousand are two versions of one event. This commentary’s view: there were two. Mark and Matthew record both, and Jesus himself refers to both separately, with different numbers and different baskets (vv. 19–20); the place, crowd, loaves, baskets and timing all differ. A teacher followed by crowds into empty country could easily meet the same need twice, and scholars who see one event retold are reading the evidence differently, not dishonestly.
verseByVerse.note: This crowd, in the Decapolis, was probably largely Gentile.

verseByVerse.quote: And his disciples answered him, "How can one feed these people with bread here in this desolate place?" And he asked them, "How many loaves do you have?" They said, "Seven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples, who have already watched Jesus feed five thousand, leave him out of the sum, and he begins, as before, with what they have.

How can one feed these people with bread here in this desolate place? An astonishing question from men who had seen him do exactly this, perhaps only weeks before, and gathered twelve baskets of leftovers; “they did not understand about the loaves” (6:52), and Jesus will press the point in vv. 17–21. Yet do not rush to enjoy their failure. The question is impersonal, and that is its trouble: they survey the situation, report that the resources are inadequate, and are entirely right, and the Person standing beside them does not appear in the calculation at all.

Desolate place. A wilderness, like the one where God fed his people with manna, and the disciples’ question is a very old one. When Israel wanted meat, Moses said to the LORD, “Where am I to get meat to give to all this people?” (Numbers 11:13), and God answered, “Is the LORD’s hand shortened?” (Numbers 11:23). Now the LORD whose hand is not shortened stands in a wilderness asking how many loaves they have: the wilderness question answered by the God of the wilderness, in a human voice (John 6:32–35).

How many loaves do you have? The same question as before (6:38), and the same method. He does not argue with their arithmetic or lecture them about faith; he asks what is actually in their hands, and multiplies what is offered. That is the practical antidote to being overwhelmed. Faced with something too big, the mind lists everything that is missing and freezes. He turns it round: never mind the gap, what have you got? Count it. Bring it.

Seven. More than the five loaves of the first feeding, for fewer people, and nobody says, Lord, last time you did this with five. They give the number and wait, not resisting him, simply expecting nothing.

Is it a lack of faith to feel overwhelmed? Not in itself. Feeling the size of a need honestly is not unbelief; Moses felt it, and so did Paul (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). The fault comes when we leave Christ out of the sum, as though the problem and our resources were all there is. So tell God plainly, as the psalmists do, and then do the two things Jesus asks here: look at what you actually have, and bring it to him. Faith is not the absence of the feeling but the decision to count him in.

parallels.desc: Moses asks how so many can be fed

verseByVerse.quote: And he directed the crowd to sit down on the ground. And he took the seven loaves, and having given thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd. And they had a few small fish. And having blessed them, he said that these also should be set before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gives thanks over too little and feeds the crowd through the very disciples who said it could not be done.

On the ground. No green grass this time (6:39), and no seating in ranks of hundreds and fifties, the arrangement that recalled Israel in the wilderness. These are Gentiles, and Mark does not impose the pattern on them.

Having given thanks, he broke them and gave them. Gave thanks (eucharistēsas), from which comes Eucharist. At the first feeding Mark used blessed (6:41), the Jewish form; here gave thanks, the word Paul uses for the Lord’s Supper (1 Corinthians 11:24). The sequence is the same as before (6:41) and at the Last Supper (14:22): took, gave thanks, broke, gave.

To his disciples to set before the people. Twice in one verse Mark names the disciples as the servers: the men who said it could not be done find out that it can, by carrying it. He does not wait for his servants to believe before he uses them, and their doubts do not shrink the bread.
