Much of the church’s best work is done like that: by tired, half-persuaded people handed something by Christ and told to pass it on, who learn what he can do only while they are doing it.

A few small fish. Probably dried or salted, handled in a separate sentence, as if remembered halfway through. And he gives the fish a blessing of their own: the scraps are not beneath his notice.

The Son gives thanks over too little. He looked at seven loaves in a desolate place and thanked his Father, and on the night he was betrayed he took the cup that meant his own blood poured out, and gave thanks over that too (14:23). His thanksgiving did not wait for plenty; it made plenty.

What then happens at the Lord’s Supper? The bread and wine do not change into Christ’s body and blood, and Christ is not sacrificed again (Hebrews 10:10–14). But the Supper is far more than a bare reminder. Believers who receive it in faith feed on Christ spiritually, nourished by all the benefits of his death, as truly as the crowd was fed on that hillside (1 Corinthians 10:16; 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7): the Holy Spirit takes what the bread and cup picture, his body given and his blood shed for you, and makes it real to your heart, so that you go away more sure that he is yours and more bound to him in love. So come to the Table as hungry people come to a meal, not because you are worthy but because you need him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they ate and were satisfied. And they took up the broken pieces left over, seven baskets full. And there were about four thousand people. And he sent them away. And immediately he got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone ate their fill and far more was left over: Jesus gave the nations more than enough. Then he crosses back to the Jewish shore, where a very different welcome waits.

They ate and were satisfied. Everyone, fully: the same emphatic words as in chapter 6 (6:42). The psalms use the word of God’s own provision: “he satisfies the longing soul” (Psalm 107:9).

Seven baskets full. The basket here (spyris) differs from the one at the feeding of the five thousand (kophinos, a small wicker basket a Jew might carry). The spyris could be large: Paul was lowered from the wall of Damascus in one (Acts 9:25). Fewer baskets this time, but perhaps more bread.

Twelve and seven. The numbers may well carry meaning. Twelve is the number of the tribes: he fed Israel, and there was a basket for every tribe. Seven is the Bible’s number for fullness and completion: he has fed the nations, and there was more than enough. The table he spread in the Decapolis is a foretaste of the feast at the end of the age, when “people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God” (Luke 13:29).

About four thousand. Matthew adds, “besides women and children” (Matthew 15:38). Unlike the first feeding, there is no attempt to make him king (John 6:15), probably because most of these are Gentiles, without the Jewish political hopes of a Messiah.

The district of Dalmanutha. Probably on the western, Jewish side, for the Pharisees meet him there (v. 11). Having fed the Gentiles, he comes home to a delegation asking him to prove himself.

Satisfied for good. The four thousand were hungry again by the next evening. “Whoever comes to me shall not hunger,” Jesus said (John 6:35), and he meant a hunger seven loaves cannot touch. Those who feed on him by faith are never sent away empty, because the bread is no longer only something he hands out. It is what he is.

Should we look for hidden meanings in the Bible’s numbers? Cautiously. Some numbers clearly carry meaning in Scripture, such as forty for testing. But the Bible never asks us to build doctrines on number codes, and readers who do so usually end up reading their own ideas into the text. Take a number’s meaning where Scripture itself makes it plain, hold suggested meanings lightly, and keep your eyes on the main point, which here is unmistakable: Jesus gave more than enough, to Israel and to the nations.

Uncertain wording. Dalmanutha is mentioned nowhere else in ancient literature, and no one knows where it was. Matthew’s parallel has Magadan (Matthew 15:39), also unknown, though often linked with Magdala on the western shore. The meaning does not depend on the spot.
verseByVerse.note: The word for these baskets differs from the one used at the feeding of the five thousand and could mean a large hamper. Dalmanutha’s location is unknown; Matthew says Magadan.

parallels.desc: Paul let down in such a basket

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees came and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven to test him. And he sighed deeply in his spirit and said, "Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation." And he left them, got into the boat again, and went to the other side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees demand proof on their own terms, and Jesus refuses: their trouble is not a lack of evidence but an unwilling heart.

A sign from heaven. Gentiles have just been fed by a miracle, and on the Jewish shore the religious leaders demand a sign: a spectacular proof directly from God, beyond any possibility of doubt, like fire from the sky on Carmel. Healings and exorcisms could be explained away as Satan’s work (3:22); they wanted something undeniable, on their terms.

To test him. The word used of Satan testing him in the wilderness (1:13): an examination set by men who have already decided that he has failed, while somewhere behind him four thousand people are walking home fed.

He sighed deeply. A stronger word than the sigh of 7:34, a groan from the depths, found nowhere else in the New Testament. He groaned over ears that could not hear; he groans over men who will not see, and the second is deeper.

Why does this generation seek a sign? “This generation” carries Old Testament echoes: the wilderness generation that saw God’s works for forty years and still tested him (Psalm 95:8–10; Deuteronomy 32:5, 20). The Pharisees are repeating Israel’s ancient sin.

No sign will be given. A Hebrew oath form: literally, “if a sign shall be given”, with the unspoken ending, “may God punish me”. Mark records the flat refusal of any proof on request; Matthew adds the exception, the sign of Jonah, meaning the resurrection, “three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:39–40; 16:4). The two accounts fit together.

He left them. A solemn act of judgment. He does not argue or stay to win. It is the third time he has walked away from people who did not want him (5:17; 6:6). He never forces himself on anybody, and there are few more sobering facts about him than that.

The sign they could not see. They ask for a sign from heaven from the one who has come from heaven. They will ask once more, beneath the cross: “Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe” (15:32), and he will refuse them for the same reason. The sign God was giving was never a man escaping a cross, but a man staying on it, and rising three days later: God’s sign from heaven, written not in the sky but in an empty tomb.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus gave no evidence; his whole ministry was full of signs. What he refuses is a miracle produced on demand as a condition of belief. Signs confirm faith; they do not compel the unwilling (Luke 16:31). When somebody did rise from the dead, the men who had the report first paid soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matthew 28:12–15).

When the problem is not the evidence. Not every doubter is like them, and honest questions deserve honest answers (1 Peter 3:15). But the sceptic’s question is worth turning round: not only “What evidence would convince me?” but also “What would it cost me if it were true?” A man who suspects it would cost him his independence will tend to find the evidence never quite enough, and only God can change that, by giving him a heart that wants Christ to be true.

Is it wrong to ask God for a sign? Not when a believer asks for help or wisdom (James 1:5). But we are not to demand proof before we will believe what God has already said; his written word, with the sign of the risen Christ, is how he guides us now.

verseByVerse.quote: Now they had forgotten to bring bread, and they had only one loaf with them in the boat. And he cautioned them, saying, "Watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod." And they began discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus warns his disciples against two quiet corruptions, the unbelief of the Pharisees and the worldliness of Herod, and they think he is talking about lunch.

They had forgotten to bring bread. After the seven basketfuls! Only Mark records the one loaf: thirteen men, one loaf, and one Person in the boat who has twice fed a multitude from a few loaves. Mark does not spell it out, but the conversation that follows expects us to think of the one loaf they really had, the bread of life (John 6:35).

Watch out; beware. Two words of warning together; the tense means keep on watching.

The leaven of the Pharisees. Leaven was a piece of old, souring dough kept back and worked into the new lump, and “a little leaven leavens the whole lump” (1 Corinthians 5:6): a small quantity changes the whole mass, silently, from inside. Luke says the leaven of the Pharisees is hypocrisy (Luke 12:1); Matthew, their teaching (Matthew 16:12). Here it is their unbelief dressed up as carefulness: a mind that keeps asking for one more proof because it has no intention of yielding to any.

The leaven of Herod. Mark has given sixteen verses to Herod so that we know what this means: he heard John gladly, and killed him “because of his oaths and his guests” (6:14–29). His leaven is the habit of bending to power: religion kept as a hobby, and conscience overruled whenever it clashes with what the people around you expect. The Pharisees and the Herodians had already plotted together (3:6): different leavens, the same hardness towards Jesus.

Two ways to be lost. Set side by side, the two cover most of the ways a person is lost. One is too clever to believe; the other believes well enough and will not pay. And Jesus warns his own disciples about both, so neither is a danger only to outsiders.

Discussing with one another. They think he is scolding them for forgetting lunch, and have turned the deepest warning of the chapter into a domestic grievance. Anyone can sit under a sermon that names the thing quietly killing him and spend the drive home discussing the length of the service. The mind reaches for the smaller subject because it is the more comfortable one.

How do I watch out for leaven in my own life? Look for the small, quiet influences: the cynicism of the commentators you follow, the habit of asking for one more reason before you obey, the instinct to keep faith a private interest that never costs you at work or with friends. Ask a trusted Christian friend where they see these in you. Feed on Scripture daily, for a heart full of God’s word has less room for the old dough (Colossians 3:16). And when a warning lands in a sermon, do not change the subject; stay with it and ask what it means for you.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) works invisibly through a whole lump; it pictures a corrupting influence. Herod stands for worldly power and its politics.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, aware of this, said to them, "Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened? Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? And do you not remember?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks his own disciples whether their hearts have grown hard to all they have seen, and calls them to look and remember. He puts it as questions, not a verdict.

Aware of this. He is not told (compare 2:8), and this time it is his own men. Then come five questions, among the sharpest rebukes he gives the disciples in Mark. The first holds the absurdity up: you are in a boat, with me, discussing a shortage of bread.

Do you not yet perceive or understand? The painful word is “yet”. It has been eight chapters: a leper, a paralytic, a storm, a legion, a dead girl raised, five thousand fed, a man walking on water, four thousand fed. Yet.

Are your hearts hardened? This sentence should stop any Christian reading comfortably. Mark has used the word of the men who watched a withered hand restored and went out to plot a murder (3:5), and of the disciples after the walking on the water (6:52); now Jesus says it to their faces. It pictures skin or stone grown hard, like a callus that can no longer feel. It is not disbelief: these men had left everything and had recently been casting out demons in his name (6:12–13). It is the loss of the capacity to be affected, and a hardened heart can carry the bread and never taste it. A person can hold the correct doctrine, attend the right church and do genuine work in Christ’s name while steadily losing the ability to be moved by him. And he puts it as a question rather than a verdict, which is the mercy in it: the loss is hard to detect from inside, so he asks them to check.

Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? The language of Jeremiah 5:21 and Ezekiel 12:2, about rebellious Israel, and of Isaiah 6:9–10, which Jesus applied to outsiders (4:12). It lands like a slap: the men given the secret of the kingdom (4:11) are described in the words used of those outside, because they are in danger of becoming like them. And the words point to the healings on either side, the deaf man (7:31–37) and the blind man (8:22–26). The disciples need the same miracle in their hearts.

And do you not remember? Memory is essential to faith. Israel was always told to remember what God had done (Deuteronomy 8:2–3), and failed, and forgetting God’s past works breeds anxiety in the present. This question has an answer, and he will not supply it; he is about to make them say it themselves.

The one heart that was never hard. Hungry in the desert, Jesus answered the tempter from the very chapter about the manna: “Man shall not live by bread alone” (Matthew 4:4; Deuteronomy 8:3). He is the servant whose ear the Lord God opened morning by morning, and who was not rebellious (Isaiah 50:4–5). And he is not only their example but their cure: the eyes and ears and heart they lack are found in the one asking the questions, and he has come to share them.

How do I know if my heart is hardening? Watch for the loss of feeling rather than the loss of belief: Scripture that once moved you now passes without effect; you can hear about sin, including your own, without grief; prayer has become a formality; sermons irritate you more than they search you; God’s past kindness to you no longer produces thanks. If you recognise these, do not despair, because the fact that you are concerned is itself a sign of life.

When it is not hardness. Be careful with that list: grief, depression, exhaustion and illness can produce several of these signs in a believer whose heart is not hard at all. A widow who cannot feel her prayers, or a depressed believer for whom Scripture has gone grey, is not hardened but suffering, and the Lord who will not break a bruised reed (Isaiah 42:3) carries her; hardness does not care, while sorrow grieves that it cannot feel. If that is you, speak to a pastor and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up (treatment, if needed, is no failure of faith), and keep coming to Christ even when you feel nothing. Where the cause is a heart cooling towards him, confess it, return to the means of grace (the word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of his people), and ask God for what Ezekiel promised: a heart of flesh for the heart of stone (Ezekiel 36:26). “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:7–8).

verseByVerse.quote: When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?" They said to him, "Twelve." "And the seven for the four thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?" And they said to him, "Seven." And he said to them, "Do you not yet understand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus makes the disciples recite the facts of the two feedings, so that they will reason from the baskets to the one who filled them.

How many baskets? He does not preach at them; he makes them recite facts they already know. “Twelve,” they say, straight away, perhaps because each of them had carried one. “Seven,” again instantly. Their memory of the facts is perfect. And Jesus carefully uses the two different words for basket, kophinous for the twelve and spyridōn for the seven. He remembers every basket and every crumb, and he remembers us.

What should they have understood? At the least, that bread was no problem with Jesus in the boat; he could supply from one loaf, or none. But more: the feedings revealed who he is. He is the one who feeds his people in the wilderness, as God did with manna, the shepherd of Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34, the giver of the messianic banquet (Isaiah 25:6). Listen to how he puts it: “When I broke the five loaves.” The subject of both feedings is “I”. The point was never the bread but the one who broke it, and he is in the boat.

Do you not yet understand? The last word of the scene, a question left hanging; Mark records no answer, so that the reader too must give one. It is the question of the whole first half of Mark: who is this? The answer will come at Caesarea Philippi (v. 29), after the healing of the blind man.

He did not put them out of the boat. He takes them on to Bethsaida, where the very next thing Mark records is a blind man given his sight in two stages. That story stands there on purpose: the Lord who asks the hard question is also the one who opens the eyes.

They remembered everything and understood nothing. They could produce the figures on demand. What they had never done was reason from the figures to the Person: he did that, so he can do this. Christians of many years know the disease: we are not short of information about the provision that came or the year we could not have got through and did, and the next difficulty still finds us doing sums in a boat.

Make yourself recite it. The remedy is what he does here. Write down what God has actually done for you, and keep the list where you will see it when the next thing comes. Israel piled twelve stones out of the Jordan so that the fathers would have to tell the story (Joshua 4:6–7), and “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2) is a man giving orders to his own memory.

Why does Jesus ask questions instead of simply telling them? Because understanding drawn out of us goes deeper than understanding handed to us. Jesus does this throughout the Gospels: “Who do you say that I am?”, “What do you want me to do for you?”, “Do you love me?” Questions make us look at what we already know and draw the conclusion ourselves, and they show us where our hearts are. When you read Scripture, notice the questions God asks and answer them honestly. They are not rhetorical. He is still asking.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–38 — Two-Stage Sight and the Great Confession
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus opens blind eyes, sometimes in stages, and the first thing opened eyes must learn is the cross. A blind man sees, first dimly and then clearly (vv. 22–26), a picture of the disciples. At Caesarea Philippi Peter sees that Jesus is the Christ (vv. 27–30), but when Jesus teaches plainly that the Son of Man must suffer, be killed and rise, Peter tries to stop him and is rebuked as thinking Satan’s thoughts (vv. 31–33). Then Jesus calls everyone to the same road: deny yourself, take up your cross and follow, because the life kept for yourself is lost, the life lost for him is saved, and he is coming in his Father’s glory (vv. 34–38).
verseByVerse.theology:
Why two touches? Not because the first failed: I see people, but they look like trees, walking is where the Twelve now stand (this is treated fully at vv. 24–26).

Why “after three days”? Mark writes after three days (v. 31; 9:31; 10:34) where Matthew and Luke have on the third day. It is the Jewish way of counting (see the note on vv. 31–32).

Why “Get behind me, Satan”? Not because Peter was demonic, and not a verdict on his soul: his objection was the wilderness temptation returning through the mouth of a friend (see the note on v. 33).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a crowd in Galilee hearing take up his cross, in a country where crucifixion was within living memory. Nobody heard a metaphor.

Now: we have worn the phrase smooth: a cross has become any difficulty. What it meant, why he called the crowd, and the three words deny, take up and follow, are treated at v. 34.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Bethsaida. And some people brought to him a blind man and begged him to touch him. And he took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village, and when he had spit on his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked him, "Do you see anything?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus takes a blind man by the hand, leads him out of the village and begins to heal him, in a story Mark has placed with great care.

The placing of the story. Only Mark records this healing, and he has put it at the hinge of his Gospel. A matching healing of blind Bartimaeus closes the next section (10:46–52), and between the two blind men Jesus teaches about the cross.

Bethsaida. A fishing town at the north end of the lake, where the Jordan flows in, home of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44). Jesus had pronounced woe on it for its unbelief (Matthew 11:21).

A blind man. Again the man is brought by others, like the paralytic through the roof and the deaf man in the Decapolis.

He took the blind man by the hand. One of the tenderest sentences in Mark. The Lord of glory takes a blind man’s hand and walks him out of town: a man in the dark, holding on, led by somebody he has never met. That is how Christ treats people who cannot see. He does not shout instructions from a distance; he takes the hand, and he has never once let go of a hand he has taken.

When he had spit on his eyes. Again, touch that the man could feel, telling him what Jesus was doing (compare 7:33). He is not squeamish. This is a very physical Saviour.

Do you see anything? The only time in the Gospels that Jesus asks about the progress of a healing, which has always puzzled readers. But he is not finding out whether it has worked: this is the man who had just fed four thousand and stilled a storm with a word. He is doing something deliberate, and it prepares for what follows.

Does Jesus still lead people by the hand? Yes, now by his word and Spirit. He promised: “I will lead the blind in a way that they do not know, in paths that they have not known I will guide them” (Isaiah 42:16). The Good Shepherd goes before his sheep (John 10:4), and the Spirit guides his people into the truth (John 16:13). Often we see only the next step, but that is no sign he has let go. Hold on to him through Scripture, prayer and the counsel of his people, and trust that the hand holding yours knows where it is going.
verseByVerse.note: Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the lake, home of Peter, Andrew and Philip.

parallels.desc: Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter

verseByVerse.quote: And he looked up and said, "I see people, but they look like trees, walking." Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; and he opened his eyes, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. And he sent him to his home, saying, "Do not even enter the village."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man sees, but only dimly, until a second touch makes his sight complete: a picture of disciples who are beginning to see Jesus, but not yet clearly.

I see people, but they look like trees, walking. A sentence that reads like the man’s own words remembered. He can tell they are people because they are moving; standing still they would be a wood. He is genuinely seeing, and genuinely not seeing properly: he could not have crossed a street.

He saw everything clearly. The only healing in the Gospels done in two stages. Three descriptions of complete healing are piled up where one would do, so that nobody should wonder whether the work was finished.

Do not even enter the village. Go home, not back to the crowds. Given the town’s unbelief (Matthew 11:21), the instruction reads like mercy: a man with new eyes is not to be turned into a spectacle for people who will not be changed by him anyway.

Why two stages? Not because Jesus’ power was weak, or because the man’s faith was lacking; the text says nothing of his faith. Jesus chooses to do it this way, and the healing is a parable in action. Look where Mark has put it. Six verses ago Jesus asked the Twelve, “Having eyes do you not see?” Five verses later Peter will say, “You are the Christ”, and three verses after that he will try to correct Jesus about the cross. That is a man seeing people like trees walking: Peter sees that Jesus is the Christ (v. 29), but blurred, a Christ without a cross (v. 32). The disciples need a second touch, and full sight will come only after the cross and resurrection, and the gift of the Spirit.

The Lord of the second touch. Jesus did not open the man’s eyes halfway and walk off satisfied. He laid his hands on him again, and did not stop until he saw everything clearly. The same hand that gave the first touch gave the second, and the King we now glimpse in outline we shall behold in his beauty (Isaiah 33:17): the first face we see clearly will be his.

Do not despise dim sight, and do not settle for it. Many honest believers are no longer blind but not yet seeing clearly: prayers that feel like talking to a ceiling, promises believed and not felt. Partial sight is real sight. But keep coming for the second touch, in the word, at the Table, on your knees, and know that the clearing of your sight is finally his work: the hand that starts the work carries it through (Philippians 1:6).

Does conversion happen in stages then? The new birth itself is a single act of God: a person is either dead in sin or made alive in Christ, with no halfway (John 3:3–8; Ephesians 2:4–5). But understanding of what has happened often grows slowly, and some cannot name the day it began; and sanctification is a lifelong process of seeing more clearly and growing more like Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18). So do not demand of yourself or others a dramatic moment, and do not mistake slow growth for no life. The question is not how sharp your sight is, but whether you are looking at Jesus.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add to v. 26 words like “or tell anyone in the village” (so the KJV: “Neither go into the town, nor tell it to any in the town”). The shorter reading is very probably original, and the sense is the same.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records this two-stage healing; it sits just before the disciples see who Jesus is, but only in part.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went on with his disciples to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. And on the way he asked his disciples, "Who do people say that I am?" And they told him, "John the Baptist; and others say, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the road, in a pagan city, Jesus asks what people are saying about him, and every answer is a compliment that is far too small.

The turning point. Here the Gospel pivots (see the introduction): from who Jesus is to what kind of Messiah he is, and where he is going.

The villages of Caesarea Philippi. About 25 miles (40 km) north of the Sea of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon: a Gentile city named for Caesar, with a cave shrine to the god Pan cut into the cliff and a white marble temple to Augustus as a god. Among pagan gods and a divine emperor, Jesus asks who he is.

On the way. “The way” becomes a key word in this section (8:27; 9:33–34; 10:17, 32, 46, 52). Jesus is on the way to Jerusalem and the cross, and disciples are those who follow him on it.

Who do people say that I am? Jesus is not seeking information; he is preparing them to state what they believe. He starts with the safe question, the one anybody can answer because it requires nothing of the person answering: report the opinions.

John the Baptist. The same opinions reported to Herod (6:14–15): months of ministry, and the public verdict is where it was. John, Elijah, a prophet: every answer is a compliment, the highest rank people could think of, and every one is far too small. You can admire a prophet from a distance. You cannot admire the Son of God; you either fall down or walk away.

The messengers and the message. Each answer names a man who pointed beyond himself. John said, “After me comes he who is mightier than I” (1:7); Elijah will soon stand beside Jesus on a mountain while the Father says, “This is my beloved Son; listen to him” (9:7). God spoke long ago by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). The crowd puts him in the line of the messengers, when he is the message.

Gentle enough to ask fishermen. Every god in that cliff was dead stone. The one asking is the living God in human flesh, too great for every box the world has built, and gentle enough to ask fishermen their opinion. Caesar’s temple is a ruin now, and at the name of Jesus every knee will bow (Philippians 2:10).

What do I say to someone who calls Jesus a good teacher? Agree, and then gently show what he taught about himself. He forgave sins against others as though he were the one offended (2:5–7), and claimed to be Lord of the Sabbath (2:28), to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45), and to return in his Father’s glory to judge (8:38). A merely good teacher would not say such things: either he was who he said, or he was badly mistaken or worse. Then invite your friend to read a Gospel and meet him for himself. Arguments help, but it is Christ himself, speaking in his word, who opens eyes.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea Philippi was a Gentile city at the foot of Mount Hermon, north of the Sea of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: And he asked them, "But who do you say that I am?" Peter answered him, "You are the Christ." And he strictly charged them to tell no one about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter confesses that Jesus is the Christ, God’s promised King, and Jesus silences them, because they do not yet know what kind of Christ he is.

But who do you say that I am? Everything turns on the “but”, and the weight falls on “you”, emphatic and plural: but you, all of you, what about you? This is the question the whole Gospel has been walking towards. You can spend years discussing what people say about Jesus, what the church teaches, what your parents believed, all at a comfortable distance. Then the question is put to you directly, and nobody can answer it on your behalf: not a godly mother, not a good church, not a tradition you still respect. If you have never answered it in your own words, you have not yet been asked anything by Christianity. You have only been informed.

You are the Christ. Peter, as usual, speaks for the Twelve. “Christ” translates the Hebrew Messiah, the Anointed One: not a surname but a title carrying the whole weight of Israel’s hope. The Messiah was the promised King, the son of David, who would bring in God’s kingdom (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 9:6–7). Mark’s first line called Jesus Christ (1:1); now, for the first time, a human being says it, and Jesus does not correct it.

What Mark leaves out. Matthew records the fuller confession and Jesus’ blessing on Peter, with the promise about the rock and the keys (Matthew 16:16–19). Mark has none of it. Writing probably from Peter’s own preaching, he records the bare confession and moves straight to Peter’s failure, as if Peter himself told it that way. This Gospel gives Peter’s finest hour in four words and his worst moment in full.

Tell no one about him. The right answer, and immediately silenced, with the word used for silencing demons (1:25; 3:12). In most minds the title meant a military deliverer who would drive out the Romans. Peter has said the true word with a false picture behind it, as his rebuke of Jesus will soon show. Only after the cross and the resurrection could the title be preached rightly (9:9). Jesus will accept it openly before the high priest, on the night it condemns him (14:61–62), when there is no possibility of misunderstanding what kind of king he is.

What if I am not sure what I say about Jesus? Then take the question seriously, and do not settle for borrowed answers. Read one of the Gospels (Mark is short), asking at each page who this man is; ask God honestly to show you; bring your doubts into the open with a Christian you trust. Peter reached his answer not by debate but by following Jesus and watching him, and it was the Father who revealed it to him (Matthew 16:17). So ask the Father. And if you find that you believe he is the Christ, say so, to him first and then to others: faith confessed grows stronger (Romans 10:9–10).

Where Christians differ: the rock in Matthew 16. Mark does not record the saying about the rock, but it belongs to this scene, so briefly: Roman Catholic teaching takes the rock to be Peter and his successors, the popes; others take it as Peter’s confession, or Christ himself. This commentary’s view: the most natural reading is that Peter, as the first to confess Christ, is the rock in the sense that the apostles are the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20). But a foundation is laid once, and nothing in the text speaks of successors, so it gives no ground for a papacy. Christ alone is the head of the church (Colossians 1:18).
verseByVerse.note: “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah, the promised king. Popular hopes for a political Messiah may explain the command to silence.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes and be killed, and after three days rise again. And he said this plainly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus now teaches plainly that, by God’s will, the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed and rise again, and Peter tries to stop him.

He began to teach them. Something starts here that had not been said before, and from now on it is his main subject: three times in this section he foretells his suffering and death (8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34).

The Son of Man. Jesus’ favourite title for himself. It comes from Daniel 7:13–14: one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven, to whom the Ancient of Days gives everlasting dominion over all peoples. A title of glory, less politically loaded than Messiah, and here he does what his hearers did not expect: he joins the glorious figure of Daniel to suffering and rejection. The Son of Man suffers before he reigns.

Must suffer many things. “Must” (dei) speaks of God’s purpose, not of a man resigned to his fate. What is coming is not a tragic accident but God’s plan, written in Scripture (Isaiah 53; Psalm 22): “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23).

Rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes. The three groups that made up the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem. The leaders of God’s people will reject God’s Messiah, the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22, quoted in 12:10). “And be killed”: flat, with no euphemism, and unthinkable for a Messiah in Jewish expectation.

After three days rise again. The resurrection is part of the prediction from the start, in the same sentence as the death, the first time he speaks plainly of either. The disciples seem not to have heard it (9:10).

He said this plainly. Openly, no longer in riddles; only Mark records it. Up to now demons were silenced and healed men told to say nothing. The moment they get the title right, the first plain thing he says is that he is going to be killed. That shows what the silence was guarding against: not people knowing that he was the Christ, but people getting wrong what kind of Christ he was.

Peter took him aside. A private word, kindly meant, and then the verb: “rebuke”, the word used of Jesus silencing demons and the wind. To Peter a suffering Messiah was a contradiction: “Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you” (Matthew 16:22). And he does it out of love; everything decent in him wants to stop it. It is the most affectionate sentence in the chapter, and it gets one of the hardest answers in the book.

Why must he die? Because of sin. The Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45), dying in the place of sinners and bearing the punishment their sins deserved, as the Servant of Isaiah 53 was pierced for our transgressions, with the LORD laying on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:5–6). He who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). This is God’s way, foretold in Scripture, to save the guilty without denying his justice: the Judge himself takes the sentence, and there was no other way for sinners to be forgiven and God to remain just (Romans 3:25–26). Paul’s word there is propitiation: a sacrifice that bears the full weight of God’s holy anger against sin, which is not a flash of irritation like ours but his unchanging resistance to all that destroys what he made. At the cross it fell on his Son instead of on us. And the “must” of the cross is followed by the “must” of the empty tomb, and both are for us.

Is it cruel of the Father to lay this must on his Son? Only if the Son were an unwilling victim and the Father a third party punishing him. But Jesus has embraced the “must”: he came to give his life (10:45), and no one takes it from him; he lays it down of his own accord (John 10:18). The Father and the Son are one God, and the cross is not God punishing someone else but God himself, in the person of the Son, bearing the cost of his own justice and mercy. The Father who gave his Son loved the world (John 3:16), and the Son who went loved the Father and us. At Calvary the whole Trinity is on the same side, ours.

Does “after three days” contradict “on the third day”? No. Mark writes “after three days” here and twice more (9:31; 10:34), where Matthew and Luke say “on the third day” (Matthew 16:21). In Jewish counting any part of a day counted as a whole day, so Friday, Saturday and Sunday are three days. Scripture itself settles it: the chief priests tell Pilate that Jesus said, “After three days I will rise”, and in the same breath ask for a guard “until the third day” (Matthew 27:63–64), men with every motive to be exact. Two idioms, one promise.

verseByVerse.quote: But turning and seeing his disciples, he rebuked Peter and said, "Get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus rebukes Peter for speaking Satan’s temptation, a Christ without a cross, and calls him back to his place behind him. Peter is thinking man’s thoughts, not God’s.

Turning and seeing his disciples. Only Mark records this. Jesus turns towards the others and only then speaks, because every man there is thinking Peter’s thought. Then he rebuked Peter, the third use of the word in the scene: Peter rebuked Jesus; Jesus rebukes Peter.

Get behind me. Literally, go behind me: the same words as Jesus’ first call, “Follow me” (literally “come behind me”, 1:17). He is not saying “get away from me”; he is telling Peter where to stand. Peter had stepped in front of Jesus to give directions; he must go back behind and follow.

Satan! Perhaps the hardest sentence any disciple ever heard, spoken to the man who moments earlier had given the best answer in the Gospel. Peter was doing what Satan did in the wilderness: tempting Jesus to reach the kingdom by a shorter road, without the cross (Matthew 4:8–10). Peter was not possessed, but Satan was using his love and his ignorance.

The things of man. Setting your mind means having an outlook (Philippians 2:5; Romans 8:5), a way of thinking, not a crime. Peter was not being wicked; he was thinking like a man: a good plan does not end in a grave, and if you love somebody you get them out of danger. All of that is decent, and all of it is the things of man, and when it is set against the declared purpose of God it becomes, whatever the intention, the devil’s argument. This is the great clash of the Gospel (1 Corinthians 1:18–25).

He would not save himself. Jesus has heard this temptation before, and he will hear it again at the end, from passers-by at the foot of the cross: “save yourself, and come down from the cross!” (15:30). The temptation was real for him, which is why the answer is so sharp. He set his face like a flint (Isaiah 50:7), and would not save himself, so that he could save us.

Opposition from those who love you. The most dangerous opposition to the will of God in your life may come from people who love you, taking you aside for a quiet word, and from the reasonable voice in your own head that says: Surely not this. Peter’s motives were good. Peter was wrong. And the two facts sat together in one man.

What it does not mean. Not that Peter was rejected. Jesus still loved him, kept him, took him up the mountain in the very next chapter, and later restored him on a beach (John 21:15–19). But even a sincere believer can speak for Satan when he puts human comfort above God’s purposes.

How do I tell whether advice is from God or only from man? Test it by the cross and by Scripture. Advice that always steers you away from cost, sacrifice and obedience, and towards comfort, safety and reputation, should be examined carefully, however kindly it is meant. Ask: does this fit what God has plainly said? Does it ask me to step in front of Christ or to follow him? Would it have kept Jesus from the cross? Godly counsel can certainly warn against foolish risks; wisdom is not recklessness. But when the clear will of God is costly, beware of the friend, and the inner voice, that says, Surely not this. And when you give advice, check whose thoughts you are thinking.

verseByVerse.quote: And calling the crowd to him with his disciples, he said to them, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who wants to follow Jesus must give up the right to run his own life, accept the cost of loyalty to him, and keep walking behind him.

Calling the crowd. He could have said this to the Twelve alone. Instead he states the terms out loud to the general public, and that settles a question for good: cross-bearing is not an advanced course for the heroic few but the shape of every disciple’s life, stated openly to anyone thinking of following him.

If anyone would come after me. Jesus sets out the terms honestly before anyone chooses. To come after somebody is to walk behind him, exactly where Peter has just been told to get back to. Then come three things, in an order that cannot be rearranged.

Let him deny himself. Not denying yourself things, like giving up chocolate for Lent, but saying no to self as the centre and master of your life. The same word is used of Peter denying Jesus (14:30, 72): to deny yourself is to say about yourself what Peter said about Christ, “I do not know this man”; the self no longer gets the deciding vote. It is not self-improvement, and it is not self-hatred; the Bible never asks you to despise a creature God made and Christ died for.

Take up his cross. We have worn this phrase smooth. Nobody in that crowd could hear it as a gentle metaphor: within living memory, when revolt broke out after Herod the Great died, the governor Varus had crucified two thousand Jews. A condemned man carried the crossbeam to the place of execution, a walk in one direction only, and Mark’s first readers heard it more sharply still, for Tacitus records that under Nero some Christians were fastened to crosses. To take up the cross is to accept rejection, shame and death, if need be, for Jesus’ sake: not ordinary troubles like an illness (though he helps his people bear those), but the costly path of loyalty to him in a world that rejects him, and “daily”, as Luke adds (Luke 9:23). Paul took the call as his own: “I have been crucified with Christ” (Galatians 2:20). Joined to Christ by faith, his old self was put to death with him (Romans 6:6), and he now lives by faith in the Son of God who loved him.

Follow me. To Jerusalem, and keep on following. The third command turns the first two from grim heroism into something else. You are not asked to carry a cross into the dark by yourself, but to walk behind someone who is going first, and who asks nothing he has not already accepted (John 19:17). The difference between Christian self-denial and religious severity is in those words: not a discipline but a Person, walking ahead, whose back you can see.

Our Lord went first. The beam he carried out of the city should have been ours. Simon of Cyrene carried the wood part of the way (15:21); our guilt he carried alone, to the end of the road. So our crosses are light: they carry no atonement, only love. And the one who calls, “Follow me”, has already walked through death and out the other side, so that every step behind him leads to life.

What it does not mean. Not that we save ourselves by self-denial, or earn salvation by suffering. Jesus alone bears the cross that atones for sin (10:45); the disciple’s cross pays for no sin, but is the shape of a life that belongs to the one who was crucified. Nor is it a call to seek suffering for its own sake. And our self-denial is never complete (1 John 1:8); his was, and his perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so our faltering following is accepted for his sake.

What does taking up my cross look like on an ordinary day? Usually something quieter than martyrdom, but the same shape: obeying Christ when it costs you. Telling the truth at work when a lie would be easier, refusing the sexual relationship he forbids, giving money you would rather keep, forgiving someone who has not apologised, being known as a Christian in a room where that will lower you; and in many parts of the world, literally risking prison or death. Name the place in your week where loyalty to Jesus costs you something; if you cannot, ask whether you are following him or only admiring him. And if you are already carrying more than you can name, a long illness, a lonely obedience, a grief, he walks ahead of you and bears you up as you go.

Does self-denial mean I can never enjoy anything? No. God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and the Christian life is full of joy: food, friendship, marriage, beauty and rest received with thanks. Self-denial is not rejecting God’s gifts but dethroning self as the one who decides. A person who has denied himself can enjoy a good meal more, not less, because he receives it as a gift rather than demanding it as a right. And Jesus promises that those who lose for his sake receive a hundredfold, now and in the age to come (10:29–30).
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it. For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul? For what can a man give in return for his soul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Following Jesus is the only way to keep your life: hold on to it for yourself and you lose it, and nothing in the world can buy it back.

Whoever would save his life. He does not say, “because I say so”; he gives a “for”, four in a row (vv. 35–38), each showing that following him is truly in our own interest. “Life” (psychē) means the self, the whole person, life now and life eternal; the same word is translated “soul” a sentence later, and the play on the one word is the whole point. Hold on to your life, protecting it from the cost of following Jesus, and you lose it, eternally.

For my sake and the gospel’s. Only Mark adds “and the gospel’s”. To be loyal to Jesus is to be loyal to the message about him, and Mark’s readers might lose their lives for preaching it. Whoever loses his life for him finds that it was safe in his hands all along.

For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul? The language of a business deal, and Jesus gives the other side its best possible case: not a good career or a comfortable house, but the whole world, all its wealth, pleasure and power, with nothing left over for anyone else. Suppose you won completely. “Forfeit” (zēmiōthēnai) means suffer the loss of, be fined: the world gained, the soul paid for it. Even on those terms the deal fails, because the self you handed over is the one who would have enjoyed it.

For what can a man give in return for his soul? The last question is about redemption, the price that buys a life back, and it echoes Psalm 49:7–8: “no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly and can never suffice”. Nothing in the world is large enough. Only one ransom can, and Jesus will give it: he came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45). The price no man could pay was paid, not by the world, which was never worth it, but by him.

The smaller prices. Nobody is actually offered the whole world. What people trade their souls for is usually smaller: a promotion, a relationship that could not survive their being a Christian, the good opinion of a particular set of people. If the whole world is a bad price, what is the price you are quietly considering?

Something you can see for yourself. A life lived for itself gets steadily smaller. The people who have genuinely spent themselves, on their children, on the sick, on the work of God in some obscure place, are often the ones with the most life in them. Jesus is telling you where the arithmetic actually comes out.

Is this salvation by self-sacrifice? No. Losing one’s life for Christ is not the price of salvation; it is the shape of the life that faith produces. We are saved by grace through faith, and created for good works (Ephesians 2:8–10). But the faith that saves is the faith that follows Christ, and following him costs everything (Luke 14:26–33).

What if I am afraid I would not stand firm if I were persecuted? Most Christians have felt that fear, and it is not a sign that you lack faith. Peter boasted he would never fall, and fell; later, strengthened by the Spirit, he stood before the council and, the early church tells us, died for Christ (Acts 4:13, 19–20; John 21:18–19). Grace for martyrdom is given when it is needed, not in advance. God will not let you be tested beyond what you can bear (1 Corinthians 10:13), and the one who keeps you is Christ, not your courage (John 10:28–29). So do not try to feel brave about tomorrow. Be faithful in today’s small costs, and trust him for the large ones.

parallels.desc: the ransom of a life is costly

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is ashamed of Jesus now will find Jesus ashamed of him when he comes in his Father’s glory as Judge.

Ashamed of me and of my words. He does not say, “whoever denies me”, though Peter will do that within months. He says “ashamed”, which is not usually one decision or one moment but a settled attitude, as steady as the temperature of a room. To follow a crucified man was shameful in the Roman world (1 Corinthians 1:23), and the pressure was usually not a sword but a sneer. “And of my words”: a man can be content to be associated with Jesus in general and embarrassed by particular things he said.

In this adulterous and sinful generation. “Adulterous” is not primarily about sexual sin. It is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God, like a wife who leaves her husband for other lovers (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3; Ezekiel 16). Before this kind of audience the disciple is tempted to be ashamed: among such people, keeping quiet about him feels like good manners.

Of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed. Measure for measure: shame now, shame then. Jesus will not acknowledge at the judgment those who would not acknowledge him now (Matthew 10:32–33), and to be disowned by him then is the ultimate loss. Do not soften it; but it is not a threat over one failure of nerve (see below). He is describing a life in which he was quietly kept out of sight because the cost of being known with him was judged too high.

In the glory of his Father. The Son of Man of Daniel 7 again, now in full glory. The one about to be rejected and killed will return as judge of all. The glory is his Father’s, so he is the Son; the angels are his servants. And the speaker is a Galilean carpenter who has just said that his nation’s leaders will have him executed.

What “glory” means. Glory is a church word we sing without weighing. Timothy Keller often pointed out that the Old Testament word for it, kabod, carries the idea of weight: the glory of something is its weightiness, what it truly is when all its worth is on show. God’s glory is his infinite worth made visible, the beauty of his holiness and love. And it has already been seen, in the most unlikely place: “we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Three of these men will soon see it blaze on a mountain (9:2–3), yet its clearest display is the road he has just described (v. 31): “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (John 12:23), he said in the week he died. We are ashamed before whatever feels heaviest, and a colleague’s raised eyebrow is heavy only when Christ feels light. When the sneer comes, put the two on the scales, and remember which of them will come with the holy angels. See also Glory in the Theological Dictionary.

A question of timing. There is a case for being embarrassed by him now: a provincial nobody with a crucifixion in front of him. But a day is coming when the Son of Man arrives in his Father’s glory and every one of the people you were afraid of is looking at him, and nobody will be ashamed of him then. The only question is whether, on that day, the one thing you want is to hear him say your name in front of the holy angels. He bore our shame on the cross, despising it for the joy set before him (Hebrews 12:2), and to be owned by him in front of heaven is worth every sneer on earth.

How it operates. Very few Christians in a comfortable country face a moment of open denial. What we face is a thousand small pressures towards silence, each with a respectable name: the sentence you do not say when the conversation turns, the phrase “I am not one of those Christians” offered to buy a little distance, the belief not mentioned to the colleague after four years. None of it feels like betrayal. All of it is what this verse is about.

Embarrassed is not the same as refuted. Why does belief feel awkward in some rooms and not in others? The sociologist Peter Berger argued that what any of us finds believable leans heavily on the people around us, supports he called plausibility structures. A conviction feels reasonable when the people we respect share it, and faintly ridiculous when they do not, whatever the arguments. Nobody at the dinner table has disproved the resurrection; it is simply not said there, and the silence does the work of an argument. The blush in the staff room tells you about the room, not about the truth. That is also why Jesus never meant his followers to stand alone: he gathers them into a church, where his words are said aloud week after week and what the world finds strange becomes real again. And beneath the church stands Christ himself, who was content to be “numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12) so that people like us could be numbered with him.

I have been ashamed of Christ. Is there any hope for me? Yes, the same hope Peter had. He denied Jesus three times with curses, and the risen Lord sought him out, asked him three times if he loved him, and gave him work to do (John 21:15–17). The warning is against a settled life of shame, not against the believer who has failed and grieves over it. Confess it to the Lord plainly, receive his forgiveness (1 John 1:9), and then take the next opportunity, however small, to own him: a sentence at work, a grace at a meal, an honest answer to a question. He is not ashamed to call his people brothers (Hebrews 2:11), even those who once were ashamed of him.

Must I talk about Jesus in every conversation? No. Not being ashamed of Christ does not mean forcing him into every sentence or being tactless. There is a time to keep silence and a time to speak (Ecclesiastes 3:7), and speech should be gracious and wise (Colossians 4:5–6). It means not hiding that you belong to him, not denying him when asked, not pretending to agree with what dishonours him, and being willing to speak when the moment comes, even if it costs you. Live openly as his, and you will find that opportunities come more often than you expected.
verseByVerse.note: “Adulterous” is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God.

8.theology: Why no sign? Not because evidence is illegitimate; he had given a great deal and would give more. What he refuses is a miracle produced on demand as the price of belief (see the note on vv. 11–13).
8.examples:
Then: whoever is ashamed of me and of my words (v. 38): not “whoever denies me” but “ashamed”, a settled attitude.

Now: what we face is seldom open denial but a thousand small pressures towards silence, and the way back is Peter’s (both are treated in the note on v. 38).

keyVerse.quote: And he asked them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered him, “You are the Christ.”
keyVerse.note: The whole first half of Mark has been asking who Jesus is, and here, at the turning point of the Gospel, the question is put to the disciples and answered. Everything after it shows what kind of Christ he is, the Son of Man who must suffer, die and rise (v. 31), and what it means to follow him (v. 34). It is a question no one can answer on another’s behalf.

8.reflection:
The disciples had seen Jesus feed five thousand, yet asked, “How can one feed these people?” (v. 4), and later worried over one loaf (v. 16). Why do past mercies so easily fail to shape our response to the next difficulty? What could you do to remember what God has done for you?

Jesus warns against the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod (v. 15): unbelief that always wants one more proof, and a faith that bends to power and approval. Which of the two is the greater danger for you, and how does it work quietly?

Peter rightly said “You are the Christ” and then tried to talk Jesus out of the cross (vv. 29–33). Where are we tempted to want Jesus without the cross, for him or for ourselves? How can we tell loving advice from “the things of man”?

Jesus calls everyone to deny himself, take up his cross and follow him (v. 34), and warns against being ashamed of him (v. 38). Where does following him cost you something in an ordinary week, and how does knowing that he went first, and bore the cross that saves, change the way you carry yours?

9.title: Glory on the Mountain, Failure in the Valley
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And he said to them, “Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power.” <sup>2</sup>And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James and John, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them, <sup>3</sup>and his clothes became radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them. <sup>4</sup>And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus. <sup>5</sup>And Peter said to Jesus, “Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah.” <sup>6</sup>For he did not know what to say, for they were terrified. <sup>7</sup>And a cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came out of the cloud, “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.” <sup>8</sup>And suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only. <sup>9</sup>And as they were coming down the mountain, he charged them to tell no one what they had seen, until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. <sup>10</sup>So they kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead might mean. <sup>11</sup>And they asked him, “Why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come?” <sup>12</sup>And he said to them, “Elijah does come first to restore all things. And how is it written of the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be treated with contempt? <sup>13</sup>But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him.” <sup>14</sup>And when they came to the disciples, they saw a great crowd around them, and scribes arguing with them. <sup>15</sup>And immediately all the crowd, when they saw him, were greatly amazed and ran up to him and greeted him. <sup>16</sup>And he asked them, “What are you arguing about with them?” <sup>17</sup>And someone from the crowd answered him, “Teacher, I brought my son to you, for he has a spirit that makes him mute. <sup>18</sup>And whenever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid. So I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able.” <sup>19</sup>And he answered them, “O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him to me.” <sup>20</sup>And they brought the boy to him. And when the spirit saw him, immediately it convulsed the boy, and he fell on the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth. <sup>21</sup>And Jesus asked his father, “How long has this been happening to him?” And he said, “From childhood. <sup>22</sup>And it has often cast him into fire and into water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.” <sup>23</sup>And Jesus said to him, “‘If you can’! All things are possible for one who believes.” <sup>24</sup>Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, “I believe; help my unbelief!” <sup>25</sup>And when Jesus saw that a crowd came running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it, “You mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him and never enter him again.” <sup>26</sup>And after crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out, and the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said, “He is dead.” <sup>27</sup>But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose. <sup>28</sup>And when he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately, “Why could we not cast it out?” <sup>29</sup>And he said to them, “This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer.” <sup>30</sup>They went on from there and passed through Galilee. And he did not want anyone to know, <sup>31</sup>for he was teaching his disciples, saying to them, “The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise.” <sup>32</sup>But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him. <sup>33</sup>And they came to Capernaum. And when he was in the house he asked them, “What were you discussing on the way?” <sup>34</sup>But they kept silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. <sup>35</sup>And he sat down and called the twelve. And he said to them, “If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all.” <sup>36</sup>And he took a child and put him in the midst of them, and taking him in his arms, he said to them, <sup>37</sup>“Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me, receives not me but him who sent me.” <sup>38</sup>John said to him, “Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us.” <sup>39</sup>But Jesus said, “Do not stop him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. <sup>40</sup>For the one who is not against us is for us. <sup>41</sup>For truly, I say to you, whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ will by no means lose his reward. <sup>42</sup>“Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him if a great millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea. <sup>43</sup>And if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire. <sup>45</sup>And if your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than with two feet to be thrown into hell. <sup>47</sup>And if your eye causes you to sin, tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than with two eyes to be thrown into hell, <sup>48</sup>‘where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.’ <sup>49</sup>For everyone will be salted with fire. <sup>50</sup>Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”
9.overview:
Where we are. Mark 9 runs straight on from Peter’s confession and the first plain word about the cross (8:27–38). On the road to Jerusalem, it holds the second of Jesus’ three predictions of his death (v. 31; see the introduction).

The message. The Messiah who must suffer is the beloved Son of God in glory, so listen to him, above all when he speaks of the cross. The road to his glory runs through suffering; so his people’s greatness is a servant’s greatness, and their power is dependence on him. Mark sets his brightest and bleakest scenes back to back, mountain and valley, and the join is the point.

Why it was said. Mark’s first readers in Rome were sharing the contempt the world had shown their Lord (see the introduction). They needed to know that he is the Son the Father delights in, that wavering faith is not turned away, and that rivalry denies the Master who made himself last.

How the chapter makes its case. Jesus promises that some will see the kingdom come with power (v. 1), and six days later three see his glory and hear the Father’s only command in this Gospel: “listen to him” (vv. 2–8). Coming down, he ties the glory to his rising and to the suffering Scripture foretold, which John, the promised Elijah, has met (vv. 9–13). The nine have failed; a father prays, “I believe; help my unbelief!”, and Jesus frees his son, then teaches that such work depends on prayer (vv. 14–29). On the road he foretells his death again, and the disciples argue about who is greatest (vv. 30–34). So he teaches greatness: serve all, welcome a child, do not stop an ally (vv. 35–41); never trip up a little one, deal ruthlessly with your own sin, and be at peace (vv. 42–50).

Where it leads. The Son who shone is the Son of Man handed over to men. He who raised a boy who looked dead is going to Jerusalem to rise himself, and he who warns of the unquenchable fire is the sacrifice who went into it for his people. The glory three men saw for a few minutes he will wear for ever, and his people will share it.

For us. Listen to him where his words are hard. Bring him your faith as it is, doubts and all. And measure greatness by how you treat those who can do nothing for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — The Transfiguration and the Failure in the Valley
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Son whose glory three disciples saw on the mountain comes down into a valley of unbelief and suffering, and there he is just as mighty. Jesus promises that some will see the kingdom in power (v. 1), and three of them do: his glory unveiled, Moses and Elijah attending, and the Father’s command, “listen to him” (vv. 2–8). Coming down, he links that glory to his rising and to the suffering written of him, which John, the promised Elijah, has already met (vv. 9–13). Below, the nine have failed; a father’s honest, mixed faith is heard, and Jesus frees and raises his son (vv. 14–27). In private he names what was lacking: prayer, dependence on God (vv. 28–29).
verseByVerse.theology:
What happened on the mountain? Nothing was added to Jesus; for a moment his glory was no longer veiled (see “Borrowed light and native light” at vv. 2–3).

Why Moses and Elijah? Between them they stand for the Law and the Prophets, come not to be admired alongside Jesus but to attend on him (see the note on v. 4, and “Jesus only” at vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: three men who had seen the glory of God walked down into a shouting crowd and nine colleagues who had just failed in public.

Now: the Sunday that lifted you is followed by a Monday, and what waits at the bottom of the hill is often the same marriage, the same diagnosis, the same failure. The mountain was given so that three men could go into the valley knowing who walked beside them. The hands that lift the boy off the ground are the hands that shone on the mountain.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus promises that some of the men standing with him will see God’s kingdom come in power before they die. Mark answers at once: six days later three of them see it on the mountain (v. 2).

The setting. This verse belongs with the end of chapter 8: Peter’s confession, the first plain word about the cross, Peter called Satan, and the call to take up a cross. Into that heavy week Jesus makes a promise.

Truly, I say to you. Others said amen (amēn) at the end, to agree with what had been said. Jesus says it at the beginning, because what follows needs no one’s agreement to be true.

Will not taste death. Not all; some. To taste death is a Hebrew idiom for dying: death as a bitter cup every person must drink.

After it has come with power. The tense means they will see it as already having come, established, not a rumour; and with power, not hidden like a seed in the ground (4:30–32) but openly shown.

What is the kingdom of God? God’s royal reign, arriving in the person of his King: not first a place on a map but a rule over people, so that where Jesus is obeyed as Lord, the kingdom has come. It came in hiddenness when Jesus began to preach (1:15) and with power at his resurrection and the giving of the Spirit; it grows as the gospel goes out, and it will come in fullness when he returns. You enter it now by repentance and faith, and wait for it to be revealed in glory.

Why make this promise at that moment? They had just been told he would be rejected and killed, Peter had been rebuked in front of them all, and they had been told to take up a cross. Jesus gave three frightened men a sight of the end of the story to carry them through the middle of it, and one of them was still writing about it as an old man facing his own death (2 Peter 1:14–18).

Did Jesus promise something that failed? Everyone standing there has long since died, so it can look that way. But Mark answers in the next sentence, with one of his rare exact intervals: “after six days”. Some standing there would see it, and six days later three of them did.

Where Christians differ: what did they see? Some take it as a promise of the second coming, and conclude Jesus was mistaken about its timing. Others see the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, or Pentecost. This commentary’s view: Mark places the transfiguration immediately after (v. 2), where three of those standing there, Peter, James and John, saw the kingdom in power, Jesus in his glory. That is the first and clearest fulfilment, and Peter himself understood it so: he called himself an eyewitness of Christ’s majesty on the holy mountain, and offered it as evidence of the power and coming of the Lord Jesus (2 Peter 1:16–18). But the transfiguration was a foretaste of something larger. The kingdom came with power in the resurrection, by which Jesus was declared Son of God in power (Romans 1:4), at the ascension, at Pentecost, and in the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, all within the lifetime of some standing there. Jesus was not mistaken.

verseByVerse.quote: And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James and John, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them, and his clothes became radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six days after speaking of his cross, Jesus takes three disciples up a mountain and lets them see the glory his ordinary humanity has veiled all along. Nothing is added to him; for a few minutes the veil is drawn back.

And after six days. Mark rarely dates anything, and he dates this. A Jewish reader would hear Sinai: when Moses went up the mountain, the cloud covered it six days, and on the seventh day God called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud (Exodus 24:16). Mark tells you what kind of scene this is before it starts: the whole passage is full of Sinai.

Peter and James and John. The inner circle again: the three who saw the little girl raised (5:37), and who will be taken further into the garden at Gethsemane (14:33). The men chosen to see him in glory are the men chosen to see him in agony. Neither sight is complete without the other.

A high mountain. Mark does not name it. Tradition says Tabor, but Tabor is low and probably had a fortress on its summit; Mount Hermon, about 9,200 feet (2,800 m) and near Caesarea Philippi, fits better. Either way the point is the isolation, and mountains in Scripture are places of revelation.

He was transfigured. Changed in form (metemorphōthē, from which comes “metamorphosis”); Matthew says “his face shone like the sun” (Matthew 17:2). This is not a light turned on him from outside: the ordinary appearance he had worn since Bethlehem was lifted, and the disciples saw the glory he had with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5), the glory he would wear after his resurrection. John, who was there, would write: “we have seen his glory” (John 1:14).

Radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them. Glistening, like polished metal; white is the colour of divine glory (Daniel 7:9). Then a homely detail, very probably Peter’s own: the fuller, who whitened cloth, was the best whitener anyone knew, and Mark says, not like that. A fisherman reaches for the only comparison he has and admits it will not do.

Borrowed light and native light. Set it beside Moses, because Mark expects you to. When Moses came down Sinai his face shone, and he put a veil over it (Exodus 34:29–35). But that light was borrowed: he had stood near a glory and carried some of it away, and it faded, which Paul says is why he covered it (2 Corinthians 3:7–13). Here the veil is Jesus’ own human body, and the glory is inside it, shining from within. They had watched him sleep in a boat and seen him tired, and all the time this was what was underneath.

Was Jesus less divine when he was not shining? No. He was fully God and fully man the whole time. When the Son took our nature he did not lay aside his deity; he veiled its glory. He “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), not by subtracting anything from what he was but by adding what he was not. The transfiguration did not make him more divine for a few minutes; it let three men see what had been true all along. So the ordinary-looking Jesus of the rest of the Gospel can be trusted and worshipped: the one who wept and hungered is the one who shone. He hid it so that he could reach us, and he will not hide it for ever.

What does this mean for me? Paul uses the same verb for Christians: “be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12:2); we are “beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18). What broke out of him on the mountain is being worked into us, slowly, as we look at him in his word, and at his appearing it will be finished: “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). The change in you is real even when it is slow, and it has a destination.

Why did Jesus take only three? Not because he loved the others less, or because the three were better men: Peter would deny him, and James and John would ask for the best seats. They were to be witnesses, and the law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). If you are not given the experiences others seem to have, the remedy is not envy. Their testimony was given for you too; Peter wrote it down so that you would have it (2 Peter 1:15–16).
verseByVerse.note: The mountain is unnamed; tradition says Tabor, but Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi, is also suggested. A fuller bleached and whitened cloth.

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses and Elijah, the Law and the Prophets in person, appear in glory and talk with Jesus. The whole Old Testament comes to attend on him.

Elijah with Moses. Moses the giver of the Law and Elijah the greatest of the prophets represent the whole Old Testament. The Law and the Prophets bear witness to Jesus (Luke 24:27; Romans 3:21), and here they do it in person.

Why these two? Both met God on Sinai, also called Horeb (Exodus 24; 1 Kings 19:8); both had unusual ends, one buried by God himself, the other taken up alive; and both had a place in Israel’s hope for the end: the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15), and Elijah before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:4–5, where the two are named together in the closing verses of the prophets). And there is more. Moses asked to see God’s glory and was hidden in a cleft of the rock while it passed by (Exodus 33:18–23). Elijah stood at the mouth of a cave on the same mountain while the LORD passed by (1 Kings 19:8–13). The two men in all Scripture who had asked to see the glory of God and been given a glimpse of it now stand on another mountain, looking straight at it, and it has a face and a name and is going to Jerusalem to die.

And they were talking with Jesus. Luke says they spoke of “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31), and the word is exodos. Moses led the first exodus, out of slavery in Egypt; here he discusses the greater one, out of slavery to sin and death, with the man who will lead it, through a cross instead of a sea, and by his own blood instead of a lamb’s. Six days ago Peter tried to talk Jesus out of the cross. Now the Law and the Prophets appear in glory and talk about nothing else.
