What this says about death. Moses died on Nebo and God buried him (Deuteronomy 34:5–6); Elijah went up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). Both are here, alive, recognisable and busy. Whatever happens to God’s people when they leave this world, it is neither extinction nor an unconscious sleep: they are alive to God (12:26–27).

Will I know my loved ones in heaven? This scene gives real grounds for hope that you will. Moses and Elijah were themselves, and the disciples knew them without being introduced. Death does not dissolve the person God made: the believer who dies is with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), awaiting the resurrection of the body. Scripture does not answer every question about that life, but it never suggests that we become strangers to one another. Above all we will know him, and in knowing him we will not lose those who are his.
verseByVerse.note: Moses and Elijah stand for the Law and the Prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to Jesus, "Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah." For he did not know what to say, for they were terrified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terrified and not knowing what to say, Peter offers to build three shelters, treating Jesus as one of three great men and trying to make the glory stay. It is a warm, reverent mistake, and the voice from the cloud is about to correct it.

Rabbi, it is good that we are here. There is nothing to criticise in the gladness. But “Rabbi”, teacher, falls far short of what he has just seen.

Let us make three tents. Booths, shelters of branches; the word also means tabernacles, like the tent in the wilderness where God’s glory dwelt among Israel (Exodus 40:34). Peter very likely had the Feast of Booths in mind, when Israel lived in leafy shelters for a week to remember the wilderness, and which the prophets made a picture of the age to come (Zechariah 14:16–19). So he thinks: the age of God dwelling with men is beginning; let us set up and stay.

One for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah. Three things are wrong with it. He wants to stay: six days ago he objected to the cross, and on a mountain full of light his instinct is to make the moment permanent, anything but the road down. He wants to build: faced with the unveiled glory of God, he gets busy, when the moment called him to stand still and behold. And he makes it three: equal accommodation, equal honour. It is the kindest possible mistake, and still a mistake.

They were terrified. Early tradition says that Mark wrote down what Peter preached (see the introduction); if so, this is Peter, years later, admitting that he had no idea what to say, so he said something. When Isaiah saw the Lord he cried, “Woe is me!” (Isaiah 6:5): a sinful man before perfect holiness sees at once what he is. The fear was the right reaction to the holy God, and only the Son’s presence made it survivable.

The true tabernacle. Peter wanted to build the Lord a shelter, and the Lord was about to build Peter one: not of branches but of his own body, broken and raised, the true tabernacle in which God dwells with men for ever (John 1:14; 2:19–21). And the Son of God bore with a frightened fisherman’s talk in the very hour of his glory, and did not withdraw.

Jesus in a row of great men. People still make Peter’s warm mistake: Jesus placed respectfully in a line of great teachers, honoured among the founders of the world’s religions. He fits nowhere in such a row. He is not the best of the prophets; he is the one the prophets came to see.

Filling the silence. Before something too large, real glory or real grief, the impulse is to fill the space. Job’s friends did well for seven days while they said nothing, and went wrong the moment they opened their mouths. At a graveside or a hospital bed the pressure to produce a sentence is enormous and almost always better resisted: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10).

Is it wrong to want to stay on the mountain? Not to love it. The longing to remain in God’s presence is holy, and it will be satisfied when God dwells with his people for ever (Revelation 21:3). Peter’s mistake was timing: he wanted the glory without the cross, the end before the road. So treasure the moments of nearness God gives you, in worship, in Scripture, at the Lord’s Table, but do not try to live in them. They are given to strengthen you for the valley, not to excuse you from it.
verseByVerse.note: The tents may recall the Feast of Booths.

verseByVerse.quote: And a cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came out of the cloud, "This is my beloved Son; listen to him." And suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself answers Peter: Jesus is not one of three but his beloved Son, and the one thing to do is listen to him. When the cloud lifts, only Jesus remains.

And a cloud overshadowed them. Not weather. The cloud went before Israel out of Egypt, settled on Sinai, and filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter (Exodus 13:21; 24:15–18; 40:34–35): the visible sign that God himself has come down. “Overshadowed” is the word used of the cloud settling on the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35), and the word the angel used to Mary (Luke 1:35). So Peter, who wanted to build three shelters, is enveloped in the real one. God does not need his branches.

And a voice came out of the cloud. The Father speaks, as at the baptism (1:11), the only other time in Mark that God speaks from heaven. At the Jordan he spoke to Jesus: “You are my beloved Son.” Here he says, “This is my beloved Son”: the same testimony turned outward, to three men standing there.

This is my beloved Son. This answers Peter’s mistake. Jesus is not one of three equals: Moses was faithful in God’s house as a servant, Christ over it as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6). “Beloved” may also carry the sense of only, as with Isaac, the son Abraham loved and was told to offer on a mountain (Genesis 22:2). And notice the timing: the Father’s public endorsement comes six days after the Son announced that he would be rejected and killed, just where the plan looks like failure, as if to say: this is the one I love, and the road he has described is the road I sent him down. The eternal delight of God in his Son broke through the cloud in words, and the words were for us.

Listen to him. The only command the Father speaks from heaven in the whole Gospel of Mark. Not build for him, as Peter proposed; not feel something, as the moment invited. Listen. Moses, standing there, would have recognised the echo: God would raise up a prophet like him, and “it is to him you shall listen” (Deuteronomy 18:15). The promise has arrived.

Listen to him about what? About what they had refused to accept: that he must suffer and die (8:31), and that they must take up their cross (8:34). Peter had rebuked him; the Father says: do not correct him; hear him. Not your instincts about what the Christian life ought to look like, not the version of Jesus you find manageable, but him, including the parts you would rather he had not said.

Jesus only. This is the phrase the whole scene exists for. The Law and the Prophets have done their work and stepped back. Everything Israel had been given over more than a thousand years pointed at this man, and when he is fully in view the pointers are not needed. What is left is what was there before the vision began and will be there after every vision any Christian ever has: an ordinary-looking man from Nazareth who is the Son of God, and no one else. And he is enough.

How do I listen to Jesus today? Through his word: he speaks now by the Spirit through the Scriptures, and listening means reading and hearing them meaning to obey. Come to hear, not only to read. Ask him to speak, and expect that he will. Stay where it pinches. The words you are most tempted to skip, like the ones about the cross that Peter could not bear, are often the ones meant for you this week. Do one thing. Take one sentence away and obey it before the day is out, because in the Bible listening includes doing (James 1:22). Listen with his people. Sit under the preaching on the Lord’s Day as someone hearing Christ, not rating a speaker. And when you find you have not been listening, remember who is speaking: the beloved Son who says, “Come to me” (Matthew 11:28), the Shepherd whose sheep hear his voice because he laid down his life for them (John 10:11, 27).
verseByVerse.note: The cloud recalls the cloud of God’s presence at Sinai and over the tabernacle.

parallels.desc: it is to him you shall listen

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were coming down the mountain, he charged them to tell no one what they had seen, until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. So they kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead might mean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus forbids the three to tell what they saw until he has risen, because his glory cannot be rightly understood until the cross and the empty tomb explain it. They obey, but cannot yet fit a rising from the dead into their picture of the Messiah.

As they were coming down the mountain. The shelters were never built, and within a paragraph the three are back in a shouting crowd. Nobody lives on the mountain.

Tell no one … until. Not even the other nine. But for the first time in Mark the silence has an end date, the resurrection, which shows what the secret was always for: not permanent concealment but timing. Tell people of his glory without his cross, and they will expect exactly the conquering Messiah Peter had in mind six days ago. After the resurrection the glory can be told, because then it will be understood.

So they kept the matter to themselves. For once in this Gospel, people told to keep quiet about him actually do; the healed leper and the crowds in the Decapolis had spread the news at once (1:45; 7:36). But they were puzzled.

What this rising from the dead might mean. They have just seen the Son of God shining, and they walk down the hill arguing about what he means by rising from the dead. Jews who believed in resurrection, as the Pharisees did, expected it at the end of the age, for all the righteous together (Daniel 12:2; John 11:24). What they could not fit together was a Messiah who dies and then, alone, in the middle of history, gets up, nor a Messiah who must die at all.

A story nobody expected. This counts against the idea that the disciples made the resurrection up. People do not easily invent a story they were plainly not expecting, had no framework for, and did not understand when it was explained to them in advance; and a church inventing stories later would hardly make its own leaders look so slow. Mark records their bafflement without embarrassment, most naturally because it is what happened.

What if I have read something many times and still do not understand it? You are in good company, and it is not necessarily unbelief. These three heard the words plainly and could not take them in. Sometimes a truth is bigger than the categories you have, and it will not fit until something makes room for it: for them an empty tomb; for you perhaps years of reading, a trial, or a sermon that suddenly joins two passages. Keep reading, keep asking, and read with the cross and resurrection in view, because they are the key that opens the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, "Why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come?" And he said to them, "Elijah does come first to restore all things. And how is it written of the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be treated with contempt? But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promised Elijah has already come in John the Baptist and been killed, and Scripture says the Son of Man must suffer as well. The disciples’ puzzle about the order of events opens onto the hard truth they keep missing.

Why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come? They have just seen Elijah, so the question follows. The scribes taught it from the closing words of the prophets: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes” (Malachi 4:5). So if Elijah has only now appeared, to three men in private, where was the forerunner who should have come first? The scribes very likely pressed exactly that objection: he cannot be the Christ, because Elijah has not come.

To restore all things. Jesus agrees: the scribes are right about the order, and Elijah’s work is restoration, turning the hearts of fathers to their children and of children to their fathers (Malachi 4:6).

And how is it written of the Son of Man? Then he turns the more important question back on them: what have you done with what is written about the Son of Man? “Treated with contempt” (exoudenēthē) means regarded as nothing, and he assumes they know where it is written: “He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows” (Isaiah 53:3); “All who see me mock me” (Psalm 22:7); “The stone that the builders rejected” (Psalm 118:22); they will look on him whom they have pierced (Zechariah 12:10). Israel had read and sung these for centuries, yet built a Messiah out of the conquering passages and quietly stepped over the suffering ones. Both are true: Elijah would come and restore, and the Messiah would still be rejected.

Elijah has come. The forerunner had been and gone, and they missed him, because he did not look like Elijah returned in fire but like a man in camel’s hair by a river, dressed like Elijah himself (1:6; 2 Kings 1:8). Matthew says the disciples understood that he meant John the Baptist (Matthew 17:13), and the angel had said before John was born that he would go before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17).

Whatever they pleased. Herod beheaded him, and his head was carried into a banquet on a platter because a girl danced well (6:17–29). As Jezebel had sought to kill the first Elijah (1 Kings 19:2), so Herodias destroyed the second. “As it is written of him” points not to a single prophecy of John’s death but to the pattern of Elijah’s life in Scripture: a prophet persecuted by a wicked king and queen.

The herald and the King. The point is not the order of end-time events. God’s plan often looks like failure, and what happened to the herald will happen to the King: they did to John whatever they pleased, and they will do the same to the Son of Man. He walks down the mountain with the glory barely faded from him, and he did not walk into his death by accident. He read it in his own Scriptures and went toward it with open eyes, because those Scriptures said it would bring many sons to glory (Hebrews 2:10). The Christ the scribes could not imagine, crowned with thorns, is the only Christ who could save us.

The verses we skip. The temptation is ours too: to assemble a picture of God from the verses we like and treat the rest as background noise, the promises without the warnings, the comfort without the cost, the Jesus who accepts without the Jesus who commands.

Was John the Baptist Elijah come back? Not in person. Asked directly, John said he was not Elijah (John 1:21), and he was right: he was not the Tishbite returned from heaven, and Scripture gives no support to the idea of souls returning in new bodies. But he came in Elijah’s spirit and power and did Elijah’s work. So both statements are true: John was not Elijah, and Elijah has come.
verseByVerse.note: Elijah, in Jesus’ words, is John the Baptist.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the disciples, they saw a great crowd around them, and scribes arguing with them. And immediately all the crowd, when they saw him, were greatly amazed and ran up to him and greeted him. And he asked them, "What are you arguing about with them?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus comes down from glory into a crowd, an argument and his disciples’ public failure, and at once he steps into the middle of it. His glory does not take him away from the misery of the world; it sends him into it.

From the mountain to the valley. Mark cuts straight from the light on the mountainside to the noise at the bottom. Raphael’s last painting puts the transfigured Christ in the upper half of the canvas and this scene in the lower, the convulsing boy and the pointing hands, because the two belong in one frame.

Scribes arguing with them. A great crowd: this is public. The scribes have found the disciples in a failure and are pressing it in front of everybody, probably to discredit their master. Nine men had promised something and not delivered, with a sick child on the ground and their critics in full voice.

Greatly amazed. A strong word, used for the women’s alarm at the empty tomb (16:5–6), and Mark does not say why. Perhaps something of the glory lingered on him, as on Moses’ face when he came down (Exodus 34:29–30), though here people ran toward him rather than away; perhaps it was the shock of his arrival in the middle of a public humiliation. Either way, the argument stops and everybody runs.

What are you arguing about with them? With one question he takes possession of the scene. He does not upbraid the nine in front of the crowd; by asking, he moves himself into the middle of the argument, and the scribes are now arguing with him. He steps between his failed disciples and the men attacking them, and that is the first act of the rescue. Whatever he has to say to the nine he will say privately, in a house (v. 28).

The come-down. It does not mean the mountain was false. The three had truly seen the glory of God, and it did not exempt them from a shouting match. The retreat ends and Monday arrives: that is the shape of the Christian life, and Mark has arranged his Gospel to prepare you for it.

In everyday life. If you lead or correct others, treat them as he treated the nine: defended in public, dealt with in private.

verseByVerse.quote: And someone from the crowd answered him, "Teacher, I brought my son to you, for he has a spirit that makes him mute. And whenever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid. So I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A desperate father explains that he brought his tormented son for Jesus, and the disciples could not help. The scene now hangs on whether the Master can do what his servants could not.

Teacher, I brought my son to you. “Teacher”: the smallest title in the chapter. “I brought my son”: he has done the one thing open to him; Luke adds that the boy was his only child (Luke 9:38). And “to you”: he came looking for Jesus, Jesus was up a mountain, and he got the disciples instead.

A spirit that makes him mute. The boy cannot speak, and verse 25 adds that he cannot hear. He has never told his father what it is like.

It throws him down. A father’s detail; he has watched this many times. The symptoms resemble epilepsy, and Matthew uses the ordinary word for a person with seizures (Matthew 17:15). But Mark is clear that the cause here was a demon, which Jesus casts out (v. 25). Not all illness is demonic, and the Gospels list the sick and the demonised separately (1:32–34); but this case was.

They were not able. Said quietly, without accusation, and everything that follows turns on it. Jesus had given them authority over unclean spirits (6:7), and they had cast out many demons (6:13); now they could not. He will give the reason in verses 19 and 29: unbelief, and prayerlessness.

To you, and not to them. Their authority had always been his, lent and never owned, and what the servants could not do, the Master will do with one sentence. The church can fail a sufferer; Christ never has, and the father’s “to you” was aimed at the right person all along.

What if I am caring for someone who cannot be fixed? Then this man is in your Bible on purpose. For years he has watched his child thrown to the ground and lifted him off floors, and Jesus is about to give him a great deal of time. Your long, unseen labour is known to the Lord, and he is not impatient with your weariness or your questions. Bring the one you care for to him, again and again. And if the church has let you down, do not let that become your final word about Christ.

In everyday life. Find someone carrying a long burden, a sick child, a disabled spouse, an ageing parent, and do one concrete thing for them this week: a meal, an hour so they can sleep, a message that says you are praying.

Should seizures or mental illness be treated as possession? No, and it must not be made to follow from this passage. That inference has done immense harm to suffering people, and the Bible does not license it. Scripture distinguishes ordinary illness from demonic affliction; this is a specific case in which the two were bound together, and Jesus knew it because he knows all things. We do not. If your child has epilepsy, this passage is not a diagnosis. Take them to a doctor, which is an ordinary mercy of God, and pray for them, which is another. Medicine and prayer are not rivals, and using medicine is no failure of faith.

Is belief in demons just ancient superstition? The Gospels do not blame everything on demons; they keep illness and possession apart. But Jesus spoke of Satan and evil spirits as real persons, and calmly, as a master speaks of servants who must obey. If he is who the voice from the cloud said he is, his view of the unseen world is better informed than ours. And the modern world has not made evil smaller, only harder to name.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, "O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus grieves over a whole generation’s unbelief, as God grieved over Israel in the wilderness, and in the same breath calls for the boy. His sorrow at unbelief does not stop the rescue.

O faithless generation. One of the sharpest things Jesus says in the Gospel, and a hasty reading makes it impatience with a suffering father, which it is not. Mark says “he answered them”, plural: a generation, taking in the nine who failed, the scribes who argued and the crowd who came to watch, not the father, the one person there doing the right thing. The words echo God’s complaint against Israel in the wilderness: a crooked generation, “children in whom is no faithfulness” (Deuteronomy 32:5, 20).

How long am I to bear with you? Not irritation at inconvenience but God’s own language: “How long will this people despise me? And how long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs” (Numbers 14:11). It is the grief of a God who has done everything and been believed by almost nobody, spoken by one who has come from the Father and is going back. “Bear with” (anexomai) means put up with, endure, and it shows the real cost to Jesus of living among sinners, even his own disciples. There is a shadow of the cross in it too: he will not be with them much longer, and he is measuring the time left against how slowly they learn. He bore with them in Galilee, and at the cross he bore far more than their slowness: he bore their sin.

A second Sinai. Moses came down from the mountain of glory to find Israel worshipping a calf (Exodus 32); Jesus comes down to find a faithless generation. But where Moses broke the tablets, Jesus calls for the boy: “Bring him to me.” The rebuke ends and the rescue begins in the same breath.

Does Jesus get tired of me? He feels the weight of unbelief, as this verse shows, and you should not make his patience cheap. But look at what his weariness does: it does not withdraw; it calls the boy over. His patience is not a fuse that will one day run out on a believer who keeps coming. It is the patience of the God who passed before Moses as “merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love” (Exodus 34:6). If you have hesitated to bring something to him because you were ashamed of the state of your faith, this verse holds a hard word about unbelief and an immediate invitation, in the same voice. The rebuke is real. It is not a refusal.

parallels.desc: a perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought the boy to him. And when the spirit saw him, immediately it convulsed the boy, and he fell on the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth. And Jesus asked his father, "How long has this been happening to him?" And he said, "From childhood. And it has often cast him into fire and into water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In front of Jesus the spirit throws the boy into his worst fit, yet Jesus stops to ask the father about his son, and hears a hope worn down to “if you can”. The Lord attends to the person as well as the problem.

And when the spirit saw him. The demon recognises Jesus and rages, as demons have since chapter 1 (1:24; 3:11). There is a hard mercy in the timing, though it will not have felt like one to the father: the worst seizure the boy has, he has in front of Jesus, in the one place where something can be done about it.

How long has this been happening to him? A boy is convulsing at his feet; Jesus has driven out a legion of demons and silenced a storm with a word; and he turns to the father and asks about the case history. Whatever he already knew, the question is for the father. Nobody has asked this man anything. He has carried this alone for years and has just been let down in front of a crowd, and the Son of God stops the scene and lets him talk. Faced with a crisis, we go straight to the problem; he goes to the person.

From childhood. A hard case, long established. The father may never have heard his son’s voice; the boy has hardly known a normal day.

Into fire and into water, to destroy him. Every hearth and every well has been a threat for years. And he knows what he is dealing with: not bad luck, but an intention. That is Satan’s purpose for every human being: “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy” (John 10:10).

But if you can do anything. He did not arrive with that clause. The doubt got in through the crack the nine’s failure made, and it still works that way. People’s confidence in the Lord is regularly damaged by his people: the church that let them down, the Christian who wronged them, the leader who fell. They come to Christ afterwards with an “if you can” that was not there before.

Have compassion on us. Not “on him” but “on us”: it is the whole family’s affliction. He asks for compassion, the word used of Jesus’ own heart for the crowds (6:34).

In everyday life. When you are with someone in trouble, copy the Lord’s question: ask how long it has been, and listen to the answer before you offer anything else.

Why does God allow a child to suffer for years? Scripture does not give us the whole answer, and we should not pretend it does. But this passage gives what we most need. It names the evil for what it is: not God’s delight but an enemy’s work, aimed at destruction. It shows the suffering seen, in detail, by Jesus. And it shows him overthrowing it. God permits evil for a time for purposes he has not fully explained, but he is not its author as the destroyer is, and he has not left it unanswered. His final answer is a cross where he took the worst of it upon himself, and a resurrection that promises its end.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "'If you can'! All things are possible for one who believes." Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, "I believe; help my unbelief!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turns the father’s doubt about his power into a call to trust, and the father answers with the most honest prayer in the Gospels: “I believe; help my unbelief!” Weak, mixed faith brought to Christ is not turned away.

“If you can”! Jesus hands the man’s own words back, abruptly but not in mockery. The “if” is in the wrong place: the father has attached it to Jesus’ ability, and the question is not whether Jesus can but whether the father will trust him.

All things are possible for one who believes. This sentence has been made to say something cruel that it does not say. It is not a formula: believe hard enough and you will get what you want. That teaching has crushed many suffering people, told that a diagnosis stands because their faith fell short. Faith is not a force that makes things happen. It is trust in God, for whom all things are possible (10:27; 14:36): empty hands held out to someone who has everything.

I believe; help my unbelief! Only Mark records it, and the father cries it out: a shout, not a carefully worded statement. “I believe”: he will not deny the faith that brought him here. “Help my unbelief”: he will not pretend it is more than it is. He does not ask for stronger faith so that he can then qualify; he asks Christ to help the very thing that disqualifies him. And Jesus accepts it, and does the very thing the doubt said he could not do. We can affirm every article of the creed and lie awake unable to feel a word of it, and the temptation is to sort ourselves out before we come, as though faith were the entry fee. This man brought both halves and laid them at Christ’s feet. Our salvation never rested on the strength of our grip, but on the strength of the hands that hold us.

All things are possible for you. In Gethsemane Jesus himself will pray, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you” (14:36). There is the one man whose faith had no unbelief in it at all, and the cup was not taken from him. He trusted the Father perfectly and was handed over, so that people whose faith is half doubt might be heard for his sake. The father in the valley could bring his ragged prayer because the Son would bring a perfect one, and drink the cup anyway, in his place.

If my prayer is not answered, was my faith too weak? Not necessarily, and usually not. Paul prayed three times for his thorn to be removed and was told no, because God’s grace was sufficient and his power made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Faith does not dictate outcomes to God; it trusts him with them. Sometimes he heals; sometimes he gives grace to bear what he does not remove; always he hears. Never let anyone tell you that a sickness persists because you did not believe hard enough.

Is doubt a sin? Unbelief that refuses God’s word is sin, and Jesus has just grieved over it (v. 19). The struggling faith of a believer who wants to trust and finds it hard is weakness, and the remedy for weakness is to bring it to Christ, as this man did. Fight doubts not by staring at your faith but by looking at the one you trust: his word, his promises, his cross and empty tomb. Feed faith with Scripture, pray this prayer, stay among God’s people, and do not make major decisions to walk away in a dark hour.

Why do we doubt our faith but never our doubts? Our culture casts the doubter as the honest one and the believer as afraid of questions. But a doubt is never an empty space. To doubt that God raised Jesus, you must be fairly sure of something else: that the dead stay dead, that nothing exists beyond nature, that the witnesses were mistaken. Every doubt is a belief in disguise, and those beliefs deserve the same hard questions. Timothy Keller often pointed out that sceptics should learn to doubt their doubts, and that believers should face theirs honestly instead of burying them; both come out with something sturdier. This father takes his doubt to Jesus rather than away from him. What saves is not the size of your certainty but the one you bring it to.

Textual note. In verse 23 some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “If thou canst believe”, which puts the “if” on the father’s faith; the earliest have Jesus simply handing the father’s words back to him, as most modern Bibles do. Either way Jesus’ power was never in question. In verse 24 some later manuscripts, again followed by the KJV, add “with tears” after “cried out”; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles leave it out.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records the father’s cry.

parallels.desc: without faith it is impossible to please him

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus saw that a crowd came running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it, "You mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him and never enter him again." And after crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out, and the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said, "He is dead." But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By his own word Jesus drives the spirit out for good, then takes the boy who looks dead by the hand and raises him. The deliverance is complete, and it is permanent.

You mute and deaf spirit, I command you. He names it precisely: the thing has shut the child in, both ways. The “I” is emphatic. He calls on no one, uses no set form of words and appeals to no higher name; the master commands in his own authority.

Never enter him again. Nowhere else in the Gospels does Jesus add this. The fear in that household, after years, is that it will keep happening. So Jesus closes the door and tells the father it is closed, as he told the woman with the bleeding, “be healed of your disease” (5:34): a word of permanence for someone who would otherwise wake every morning waiting for it to come back.

It came out. The last thing it does is hurt him as much as it can. The powers of darkness in this Gospel are malicious to the final second, and they always obey.

Like a corpse. The crowd concludes that the healer has killed him. The father has just prayed the truest prayer of his life, and his son lies on the ground looking dead. The moment before deliverance can look exactly like the disaster you feared: Israel was never more trapped than with the sea in front and the chariots behind.

Lifted him up, and he arose. He took him by the hand, as with the dead girl in Jairus’ house (5:41–42). “Lifted him up” and “arose” are the two words used for Jesus’ own resurrection (16:6; 8:31), in the chapter where he spoke of rising and nobody understood (vv. 9–10). Before a crowd that has pronounced the boy dead, the Son of Man takes a child’s hand and raises him: a small, dusty rehearsal of what he is walking to Jerusalem to do. He does not merely drive out the enemy; he lifts us up, and one day he will take every sleeping believer by the hand and say, “Arise.”

Can Christians be possessed? Christ’s victory here is a reason for confidence, not fear. A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit and belongs to Christ; Scripture never describes a Christian as possessed, and “he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4). Believers are tempted and attacked, and we resist the devil by faith, prayer and the word (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7). Where real spiritual oppression is suspected, the remedy is the ordinary means: the gospel, repentance, prayer by the elders, and patient care, without theatre and without neglecting medical help.

Where Christians differ: should we be casting out demons today as the apostles did? Many faithful believers, Pentecostal and charismatic brothers among them, hold that the extraordinary sign gifts continue. This commentary’s view: the sign gifts that marked the apostles’ ministry served to confirm their message (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12), and with many Reformed Christians this commentary holds that once that message was complete in Scripture those gifts ceased. We hold this without doubting their love for Christ.

parallels.desc: he took her by the hand

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately, "Why could we not cast it out?" And he said to them, "This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples failed because they had drifted from dependence on God, and such work is done only through prayer. Jesus is not prescribing a step they forgot on the day; he is diagnosing a life.

Why could we not cast it out? The conversation happens indoors, in private; he never humiliated them in the valley. Their question is fair: they had done this before (6:13), and they know something has gone wrong that they cannot account for.

Anything but prayer. “This kind” suggests that some demons were stronger than others. But the answer is not a technique, a better formula or more authority; they had all the authority they needed. It is prayer.

Prayer as the posture of a life. Jesus himself does not pray in this passage: he speaks a sentence, and it is done. His praying was done very early in the morning in a desolate place (1:35), and he has just come down from a mountain of communion with the Father, while the disciples had been arguing with scribes. So prayer here means settled, daily, unspectacular dependence on God, the only way such authority ever works. Faithlessness (v. 19) and prayerlessness are the same thing from two sides: prayer is faith expressing its dependence on God, and a prayerless believer has quietly concluded that he can manage.

The drift from dependence. These men had come back from their mission delighted. Somewhere between that success and this valley, the authority had quietly become a possession, something they carried about rather than a gift held moment by moment from the hand that gave it. They did not stop believing; they stopped depending, and the two are almost impossible to tell apart from the inside until the day the thing does not work. Every generation of the church faces the same drift: serving on skill and experience, without the closeness to God that gives the work any power.

The Son who never drifted. Set beside the nine the one man who never treated his power as a possession. The eternal Son chose to live as a man in moment-by-moment dependence: “the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). And his praying did not end with his earthly life. He lives at the Father’s right hand to intercede for his people (Hebrews 7:25), so that what the disciples lacked in the valley, their Lord supplies from the throne.

How do I build a life of dependent prayer? Start small and real. Set a fixed time each day, even ten minutes, with your Bible open, and pray back what you read. Pray before the things you think you can do, not only the things you know you cannot: the meeting, the lesson, the hard conversation. Keep a short list of people and situations, and pray through it. Pray with others, in your church’s prayer meeting and with your household. And when you find you have gone days without real prayer, do not wait to feel spiritual again. Confess it and begin again today.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add “and fasting”. The words are missing from the two earliest and most reliable manuscripts, and were probably added later as the church came to practise fasting more. The ESV puts them in a footnote. Fasting is good, and Jesus expected his disciples to fast (Matthew 6:16–18), but it is not the secret here. Jesus’ point is dependence on God in prayer.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “and fasting.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–50 — The Second Prediction and the Argument on the Road
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the kingdom of a crucified King, greatness is service, and the danger to fear is sin, beginning with your own. Jesus tells the Twelve a second time that he will be handed over, killed and raised; they do not understand and dare not ask (vv. 30–32). Instead they argue about rank, so he makes the first last and servant of all, and puts a child among them: to welcome the least in his name is to welcome him and the Father (vv. 33–37). Do not stop an ally because he is not of your group; even a cup of water given to his people is remembered (vv. 38–41). Never trip up a little one, cut off whatever trips you up, keep your salt, and be at peace (vv. 42–50).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two sayings that seem to collide. The one who is not against us is for us (v. 40) sits beside whoever is not with me is against me (Matt. 12:30; Luke 11:23). They answer different questions (see the note on vv. 38–40).

The verses your Bible skips. A King James Bible has the refrain of v. 48 three times, at verses 44, 46 and 48 (see the textual note at the end of the note on vv. 43–48).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men argued about which of them was the greatest, on the road after being told their Master would be handed over and killed.

Now: the same argument runs with better manners (see “The silent argument in church” at vv. 33–35). Jesus does not abolish the wish to be first; he turns it round: last of all and servant of all. And the test is the child in his arms (vv. 36–37).

verseByVerse.quote: They went on from there and passed through Galilee. And he did not want anyone to know, for he was teaching his disciples, saying to them, "The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise." But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells the Twelve a second time that he will be handed over, killed and raised, and they neither understand nor dare to ask. His priority now is to prepare them for the cross.

Through Galilee. Quietly, through his own home region. The public Galilean ministry is over; from here the Gospel narrows to fewer crowds, more instruction, and the road to Jerusalem.

Delivered into the hands of men. This second foretelling (the first was 8:31) has a new word, the darkest in the sentence. “Delivered” means handed over: the word is used of Judas (14:10), of the priests handing Jesus to Pilate (15:1), of Pilate handing him over to be crucified (15:15), and of God giving up his Son for us all (Romans 8:32). Here it does not say who is doing it, and behind all of them stands the Father’s purpose. There is a play on words too: the Son of Man is handed over to men, humanity in general, and so the reader as well.

After three days he will rise. In none of his plain predictions of his death does he leave out the rising.

Love going all the way down. He knew every hand that would pass him along: the friend’s, the priest’s, the governor’s, the soldier’s. And he walked toward them, because behind every one of those hands stood the Father who did not spare his own Son. Every handing over was love going all the way down.

Afraid to ask him. Not understanding is forgivable and by now familiar. Being afraid to ask is not ignorance but a choice: perhaps because the last time Peter raised it he was called Satan (8:33), perhaps because they suspected they would not like the answer.

The questions we do not ask. There are questions Christians decline to ask God because we half know the answer, and it would require something: the passage you skip, the part of your life you have agreed with yourself not to discuss with him. That is not doubt, which at least engages; it is avoidance. The disciples do not ask about the cross, and fill the rest of the walk with an argument about rank. The unasked question leaves a space, and something always moves into it.

If God handed him over, are the betrayers less guilty? No. Peter preached that Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, and in the same sentence that his hearers crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). God ordains what happens without being the author of sin, and human beings act freely and are fully responsible for their wickedness (Westminster Confession 3.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.1). God planned the cross, yet the greed in Judas’ heart was Judas’ own, and God did not put it there (James 1:13); Judas was not a puppet, but chose for silver. And God in his wisdom used the worst thing ever done to accomplish the best. That is why the cross is both the guilt of the world and the gift of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Capernaum. And when he was in the house he asked them, "What were you discussing on the way?" But they kept silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. And he sat down and called the twelve. And he said to them, "If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Jesus walks toward the cross, his disciples argue about rank, and he teaches that the first place belongs to the one who makes himself last of all and servant of all.

And they came to Capernaum. Probably Peter’s house (1:29). Whatever Jesus heard on the road, he says nothing until the door is shut, the same restraint he showed with the nine.

What were you discussing on the way? He very likely knew already (Luke 9:47), but he does not accuse; he asks. And “on the way” is loaded in Mark: it is the road to the cross, and on it they had been arguing about greatness.

But they kept silent. The silence is a confession: you do not go quiet about a conversation you are comfortable with. Some talk cannot be repeated in front of him, and that it cannot is itself the verdict on it.

Who was the greatest. Perhaps the choosing of three for the mountain had stirred jealousy. The argument kept coming back (10:35–45; Luke 22:24): pride is among the most persistent of sins, even in disciples.

He sat down. The posture of a teacher giving formal instruction: what follows is a lesson for the men who will lead his church.

Last of all and servant of all. “If anyone would be first”: the wanting is allowed to stand. He tells them where the front of the queue actually is, and “all”, used twice, makes it impossible to soften. “Last of all”: bottom. “Servant of all”: diakonos, the table-waiter, from which comes our word deacon. Not servant of the deserving or the useful. Of all.

The first who made himself last. The man saying this had the right to the first place in every room he entered. Though he was in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself by taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7). Their quarrel about rank was conducted behind the back of the only one who truly outranked them all, while he went down to serve them. And he has promised that when he returns he will dress himself for service, have his servants recline at table, and come and serve them (Luke 12:37). The first of all will wait at his own feast, and there is no greatness in heaven or on earth like the greatness of that servant.

The silent argument in church. Nobody in a church says “I am the greatest”. But the argument runs anyway, silently and constantly: who was consulted and who was not, who got thanked from the front, whose name is on it, who was asked to do the thing you were not asked to do, who is regarded as sound. It can be conducted entirely without words, and everybody in the room knows the standings.

Is it wrong to want to do great things for God? No. Jesus does not rebuke the desire to be first; he redirects it. It is right to long that your life should count and God be honoured greatly through you; what is wrong is greatness measured on the world’s scale: being seen, consulted, thanked, set above others. So ask what your ambition is for. If it is for his glory and others’ good, pursue it by serving. If it is for your name, it will show itself in resentment when someone else is chosen.

What does servant of all look like in an ordinary week? It is easy to feel humble, and impossible to be a servant in the abstract. It looks like doing the job nobody notices: stacking chairs, washing up, visiting the person who is hard work; letting someone else have the credit, and being glad; putting your family’s needs before your evening, and your colleagues’ success before your own advancement; serving people who cannot repay you. Service of that kind can be looked up in a diary.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took a child and put him in the midst of them, and taking him in his arms, he said to them, "Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me, receives not me but him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus takes a child in his arms and teaches that whoever welcomes the least important person for his sake welcomes him, and the Father who sent him. Greatness is measured by how you treat those who can do nothing for you.

A child in the midst. An acted parable: the argument was about the highest place, and he puts a child in the centre of it. We have sentimentalised the scene. Children were loved but not counted important; they had no legal standing, and in the wider Roman world unwanted babies were often exposed at birth. So the lesson is not that we should be innocent like children, for children are sinners too (Psalm 51:5). It is: here is a person who can do absolutely nothing for you.

And taking him in his arms. Mark alone records this, here and again at 10:16. Someone in that room never forgot that while he was explaining greatness to them, he was holding a child.

Whoever receives one such child in my name. To receive is to welcome a guest; “in my name” means for my sake. Jesus identifies himself with the least important people, and the way you treat the least is the way you treat him (Matthew 25:40).

Him who sent me. The chain goes all the way up: welcome a nobody in Jesus’ name, and you welcome God himself. It is also a claim: Jesus is the sent one, who fully represents the Father. And the Son whom the Father sent put his arms around a child no one counted. That is the God we worship: the high and lofty One who dwells with the lowly (Isaiah 57:15), who stoops to take up the small, and who counts a welcome given to a nobody as given to himself.

The worth of those who cannot pay us back. We no longer expose unwanted babies, a change that came largely through people who took scenes like this one seriously. But has the old measure gone? Our culture values people by what they can do, and quietly wonders what an old man with dementia or a child with a severe disability is for; the unborn, the very old and the very ill feel the question first. Jesus answers it by holding a child who could do nothing and calling him his own representative. Human worth does not rise and fall with usefulness, because it was never ours to grant; it is given by the God whose image we bear, and honoured by the Son who took our nature. And here is the reversal: before God, we are all that child. None of us has anything he needs. He welcomes us not because we are useful but because he is love, and people who know that can begin to welcome others the same way.

In everyday life. Welcome the people who can do nothing for you: the lonely, the elderly relative whose conversation goes in circles, the child in your own house at the end of a day when you have nothing left. You came to him with nothing to give and he took you in; in them you welcome him.

Does this mean every child belongs to Christ? Not in that sense. “In my name” means receiving the child for Jesus’ sake. It does not teach that children are born saved, or that they enter the covenant by birth or baptism; each child needs to be born again and come to Christ by faith, which is why we pray for our children and teach them the gospel. Our paedobaptist brothers (who baptise the infants of believers) hold that such children belong to the covenant community and should receive its sign; they too insist that each child must come to personal faith, and we differ from them in love. But Jesus’ arms around this child show how warmly he welcomes the little ones brought to him, and we believe that those who die in infancy are safe in the hands of a merciful God who saves his elect, those he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). If you have laid a little one in the grave, you may picture that child in these same arms.
verseByVerse.note: Children had little status in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: John said to him, "Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us." But Jesus said, "Do not stop him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. For the one who is not against us is for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus forbids his disciples to stop a man doing real work in his name merely because he is not one of their group. Anyone truly on Christ’s side is an ally, not a rival.

John said to him. The only time in Mark that John speaks alone, and the timing is pointed. Jesus has just said that receiving a nobody in his name is receiving him, and John reports an occasion when they stopped somebody acting in that name. Perhaps he expected approval: he is a Son of Thunder (3:17).

Someone casting out demons in your name. Someone outside the Twelve, using Jesus’ name and succeeding, when the disciples had just failed (v. 18). There may be a little jealousy here.

He was not following us. Not following you, but “us”. The man plainly was following Jesus; the objection is to his membership, not his master. Joshua made the same mistake about Eldad and Medad prophesying outside the camp, and Moses answered: “Would that all the LORD’s people were prophets” (Numbers 11:26–29).

Soon afterward to speak evil of me. Having just seen that name work, he is not about to start slandering it; whatever he lacks, he is not on the other side.

Not against us is for us. In the war between God’s kingdom and Satan (3:23–27), anyone casting out demons in Jesus’ name is on the right side. Elsewhere Jesus says the reverse: “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Matthew 12:30; Luke 11:23). The two sayings answer different questions. There the subject is Christ himself, and the men in view are Pharisees who had just called his works the devil’s: toward Jesus there is no neutral ground. Here the subject is a fellow worker plainly on Christ’s side who does not belong to the disciples’ circle: do not treat an ally as an enemy. Read together they are a pair of fences: be generous about the boundaries of the movement, and uncompromising about the claims of the King.

The power in the name. The man had no commission among the Twelve, and the demons went anyway, because the authority was never in the group. That is the plainest proof of who Jesus is: the name at which demons flee is the name God has exalted above every name, at which every knee will bow (Philippians 2:9–10). John wanted to guard the name. Jesus shows that the name guards itself, and belongs to him, not to any group.

Party spirit in one clause. There is a way of caring about the kingdom that has quietly become caring about our part of it, where the first question asked about a man’s ministry is not whether Christ is being preached but which group he belongs to. It flourishes among the entirely orthodox and entirely sincere, and leaves Christians uneasy rather than glad when good work is done by somebody outside their circle.

What it does not mean. Not that anyone who uses Jesus’ name is a true believer (Matthew 7:22–23). Nor that doctrine does not matter: the issue here is group loyalty, not truth. Paul could rejoice that Christ was preached even by rivals with bad motives (Philippians 1:15–18), and in the same years curse anyone who preached a different gospel (Galatians 1:8–9). The line is the gospel itself, not our party.

How can I tell whether someone outside my circle is truly on Christ’s side? Does he confess Jesus as the eternal Son of God come in the flesh, crucified for sinners and risen (1 John 4:2–3)? Does he preach salvation by grace through faith in him, not by works? Does he submit to Scripture as God’s final word? If so, he is a brother even if he differs from you on baptism, church order or the end times, and you should be glad when God uses him. If he denies the heart of the gospel, he is not doing a work in Christ’s name, whatever words he uses, and love for the sheep means warning against him.

In everyday life. Pray by name for another gospel church in your town, and thank God for something good he is doing through it.

parallels.desc: whoever is not with me is against me

verseByVerse.quote: For truly, I say to you, whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ will by no means lose his reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the smallest kindness shown to a follower of Christ, because he belongs to Christ, will be remembered and rewarded.

A cup of water. Jesus puts his solemn “Truly, I say to you” in front of a cup of water: not whoever preaches or heals, but a drink, the smallest kindness in a dry land, costing almost nothing and heard of by no one.

Because you belong to Christ. Literally, in the name that you are Christ’s: not because the giver was impressive or the act large, but because of whom the receiver belonged to, exactly as with the child. Kindness to a disciple for that reason is kindness to Christ.

Will by no means lose his reward. “By no means” is the strongest negative in Greek: not overlooked, not too small to register. Nothing done for Christ is lost; “God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints” (Hebrews 6:10).

The cup he was given. The Lord who promised a reward for a cup of water knew what it was to be thirsty. On the cross he would say, “I thirst”, and be handed sour wine on a sponge (John 19:28–29; Mark 15:36). And he knew of another cup, the one he would ask the Father to remove: the cup of God’s judgment, which no kindness could ease. He drank that one to the dregs, so that every cup handed to one of his people might be gathered up and honoured. The one who notices the water is the one who drank the wrath.

The list nobody sees. Most Christian work is small and unnoticed: meals cooked, lifts given, a message to somebody having a bad week, prayer for people who never learn they were prayed for. None of it will be described from a platform; all of it is on a list. He will read the list out one day, and the people named will not recognise their own lives in it: “Lord, when did we see you … thirsty and give you drink?” And he will answer, “as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:37–40).

What it does not mean. Not that we earn salvation by good works. The reward is God’s gracious recognition of what flows from love for Christ, not wages that put God in our debt (Luke 17:10). It is grace upon grace: he gives the faith, works the love, and then crowns his own gifts as if they were ours.

What is the reward? Scripture gives no price list. The heart of it is the Lord himself: his “well done”, his joy shared, a deeper capacity to know and enjoy him (Matthew 25:21; 1 Corinthians 3:14). Rewards are never a ladder of merit that makes some saints proud, but the Father’s delight in his children’s love. Every believer’s cup will be full, and every one will cast his crown before the throne.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him if a great millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To make one of Christ’s little ones stumble in faith is so grave that a terrible death would be better than the judgment it brings.

One of these little ones who believe in me. The child is still in the room, so children are included. But “who believe in me” points wider: any believer whose faith is genuine and not yet strong, the recent convert, the person hanging on by their fingernails, anyone whose grip on Christ could be loosened by what you do.

To sin. To trip up (skandalizō): to lead a believer into sin or away from faith, by false teaching, bad example, abuse, pride or contempt.

A great millstone. Literally a donkey’s millstone: not the hand-mill of a kitchen but the huge upper stone an animal walked in circles to turn, weighing hundreds of pounds. Drowning with a weight was a Roman form of execution, especially horrifying to Jews because the body would not be buried. Then hear the comparison: “it would be better for him”. Not that he should be drowned, but that judgment for such a sin will be worse than the worst death imaginable. Jesus does not speak like this about doubters or the confused. He keeps such words for the gravest sins, like the betrayal of the Son of Man (14:21), and here for damaging the faith of the small.

The tenderness behind the severity. Jesus speaks of faith in himself as the prophets spoke of trust in the LORD, and he binds the little ones to himself so closely that to wound their faith is to strike at him. He is the Servant of whom Isaiah wrote, “a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench” (Isaiah 42:3). The millstone is what his tenderness sounds like when it turns to face those who would crush what he is guarding.

Who is this word for? For anybody with influence over somebody weaker, and that is most of us: parents, whose children’s picture of God is assembled largely from what they see at home, and whose faith can be quietly ruined by a father who is one man on Sunday and another on Tuesday; anyone who teaches or leads in a church; anyone watched by a younger Christian. And you do not need to preach heresy to trip somebody up. It is done with a cynical remark about a fellow believer in front of a new convert, with running commentary on the church’s failings that a fragile person overhears, with the joke that makes something holy look small. The father in the valley shows it: disciples who let him down put that “if you can” in his mouth.

What about abuse in the church? This verse is among the most severe Jesus ever spoke, and it bears with full weight on anyone who abuses a child or a vulnerable believer, especially under cover of Christ’s name. Abuse is never to be tolerated, hushed up or managed quietly to protect a reputation, a ministry or a family. Jesus’ concern is for the little one, not for the institution. A church that loves Christ will report abuse to the civil authorities, who are God’s servants to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), will protect, believe and care for victims, and will remove offenders from any position of trust. Forgiveness for a repentant abuser is real, but it never means restoring access or silencing the harmed. If this has happened to you, it was not your fault, and Christ is on your side.

In everyday life. Ask who is watching you who is weaker than you are, and whether anything you do makes it harder for them. In the strength of his Spirit, change the thing; where you have already tripped someone, confess it to the one who forgives, and go and help them up.
verseByVerse.note: The millstone is the heavy upper stone of a mill turned by a donkey.

verseByVerse.quote: And if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deal with sin in your own life ruthlessly: whatever leads you into it, however precious, is better lost than kept on the way to hell.

From others to yourself. Having warned them about tripping up others, he turns to the nearer danger, yourself; the same verb, to trip up, runs through.

Cut it off. Not literal self-mutilation, which would not work: the trouble comes out of the heart (7:21), and a blind man can still lust. But do not soften it into nothing. This is deliberate overstatement in deadly earnest, and he chose things you cannot spare.

It is better for you to enter life crippled. “Life” means eternal life, the kingdom of God of verse 47; the alternative, three times over, is hell. Better to lose something precious now and enter life, than keep everything and lose your soul (8:36).

To go to hell. The word translated “hell” (geenna, Gehenna) was the name of a real place: the Valley of Hinnom, south of Jerusalem, where apostate Israel burned its own children to Molech (2 Chronicles 28:3; 2 Kings 23:10), and which Jeremiah called the Valley of Slaughter (Jeremiah 7:31–32). Jesus takes a valley every pilgrim knew, with a history of fire and death, and makes it his picture of final judgment.

Making it concrete. Keeping it vague takes the edge off. The hand is what you do. The foot is where you go. The eye is what you look at, and in our generation that is very often one object, in your pocket and lit up at midnight. The surgery is not moderation; it is removal. In practice that means the concrete, slightly embarrassing measure: an app deleted rather than managed, the phone that does not come upstairs, the account closed, the friendship stepped back from, the route changed, the arrangement told to another Christian so that he can ask about it. Every one of those feels disproportionate: that is the feeling of amputation, exactly what he describes.

If I keep failing at the same sin, am I going to hell? Not if you belong to Christ. These verses are not a threat hung over the believer who fights and falls; they are a warning to the person who will not fight at all, who keeps the hand because he loves it more than he fears the fire. A Christian still sins, and grieves, and confesses, and gets up (1 John 1:8–9). You may find that part of you still loves the sin while the rest of you hates it. That divided heart is what Paul describes in Romans 7:15–25, and the hating and the fighting are the Spirit’s work in you (Galatians 5:17), not proof that he is absent. What marks a true believer is not that the battle is won but that he is in it, on God’s side. Your hope is not the strength of your surgery but the Saviour who was cut off for you. Cut off what feeds the sin precisely because he has already saved you, and keep running to him.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” renders Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: And if your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than with two feet to be thrown into hell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The warning comes again for the foot, so that no part of life is left outside it. Each time the words are almost the same, and the repetition is the point: Jesus will not let his hearers hear it once and move on.

Enter life lame. Under the law a lame or blind man could not serve at the altar (Leviticus 21:18), yet Jesus pictures the lame entering life. The prophets promised that in the coming kingdom “then shall the lame man leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:6), so whatever is given up for Christ’s sake now is not lost for ever. And here the alternative is not to “go” to hell, as in verse 43, but to be “thrown” there: no one walks into judgment willingly.

verseByVerse.quote: And if your eye causes you to sin, tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than with two eyes to be thrown into hell, ‘where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the eye, the most precious and most private of the three, must go if it leads you into sin, because hell is real and its fire is never put out.

If your eye causes you to sin, tear it out. The eye comes last, the most precious of the three, and its sin is the most hidden: no one else sees where it rests. Jesus said the same in the Sermon on the Mount about the look of desire (Matthew 5:28–29).

Where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. The closing line quotes the last verse of Isaiah (66:24), which pictures the corpses of those who rebelled against God. The worm devours and the fire burns, and neither ends. These are pictures, but the reality they point to is more terrible than the pictures, not less.

The tenderest voice speaks of hell. Nobody in the Bible speaks about hell as often as Jesus does. The man who held a child while he taught will not let this subject alone, and it runs too deeply through all four Gospels to be peeled off as a later addition. He says it three times in six verses because he means his people not to go there. The Judge who warns of the unquenchable fire is the Saviour who went into the fire for us. He was cut off from the land of the living, forsaken, so that everyone who flees to him might enter life whole.

In everyday life. Name the hand, foot or eye in your life, cut it off today in a concrete way you could explain to a friend, and ask one trusted Christian to check on you next week. Your surgery will never be clean or complete; Christ’s obedience was, kept whole in your place, and it is counted as yours (Romans 5:19).

How can a loving God send anyone to hell? Because he is holy as well as loving, and a God who shrugged at evil would not be good. The marvel is not that God judges but that he came himself, in his Son, to bear that judgment for all who come to him.

Where Christians differ: the nature of hell. Some (conditionalists or annihilationists) hold that the wicked are finally destroyed and cease to exist, taking unquenchable fire to mean a fire that does its work completely, and noting that in Isaiah 66:24 the worm and fire consume dead bodies. Others (universalists) hope that all will finally be saved. This commentary’s view: the historic Christian view is that hell is conscious, eternal punishment. In Isaiah the picture is of corpses, but Jesus applies it to people thrown into hell, and for them the punishment never finishes. Jesus elsewhere sets eternal punishment alongside eternal life as equally lasting (Matthew 25:46), and Revelation says the smoke of their torment goes up for ever and ever, and they have no rest, day or night (Revelation 14:11). Jesus’ warnings are given in love, so that none would go there; they are meant to drive us to the one who bore judgment for all who come to him.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verses 44 and 46, both repeating verse 48. A reader with a King James Bible will find the refrain three times; here the numbers run 43, 45, 47, 48. The two repetitions are missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and were probably added to make the three warnings match. The ESV puts them in footnotes. Nothing has been lost: the sentence stands once, in full force, exactly where Jesus quoted it from Isaiah.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verses 44 and 46, repeating verse 48.

parallels.desc: their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched

verseByVerse.quote: For everyone will be salted with fire. Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone will meet God’s fire, either as judgment or as the refining of a life laid on his altar; so keep the saltiness of a disciple, and be at peace with one another.

For everyone will be salted with fire. One of the strangest sentences in Mark. Fire is the last word of the previous paragraph, where it meant judgment in Gehenna. Salt comes from somewhere else: “You shall season all your grain offerings with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing” (Leviticus 2:13). Salt was rubbed into every sacrifice laid on the altar, and many were burned with fire. So the saying covers two groups of people at once, and fire does opposite things to them. The unrepentant meet the fire that consumes. The disciple, who has just been told to cut off hand and foot rather than perish, meets the fire that purifies: the costly, cleansing fire of a life laid on the altar as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1).

Which fire? Everyone will meet fire; the only question is which kind. Speaking to the Twelve, Jesus means chiefly the refining fire, and Peter says the same to Christians under persecution: “do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you” (1 Peter 4:12), for tested faith is more precious than gold refined by fire (1 Peter 1:7).

Salt is good. Salt preserved and seasoned, and in the Old Testament it sealed a covenant of salt, lasting and unbreakable (Numbers 18:19). So a disciple is meant to stop the rot, give savour, and be bound to God for good.

The sacrifice salted and burned. Every salted offering pointed to one. “Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (Ephesians 5:2), and he went wholly into the fire of judgment, the same fire the unrepentant will meet. Because he was consumed in the place of his people, the fire that reaches them now is never the fire of Gehenna but a Father’s refining fire, burning off the dross and leaving gold, within a covenant of salt that Christ’s blood has made unbreakable.

But if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Pure salt cannot lose its saltiness. But much of the salt of Palestine probably came from the Dead Sea marshes, mixed with other minerals, and damp could leach out the actual salt, leaving a white powder that looked identical and did nothing. You could not restore it; you threw it out (Matthew 5:13). A disciple who has quietly lost what made him different looks the same and is in the same place on Sunday. He simply no longer preserves anything or gives savour to anything.

Have salt in yourselves. The salt is the self-denial Jesus has been describing since 8:34: taking up the cross, being servant of all, cutting off whatever leads you into sin.

And be at peace with one another. The chapter comes full circle: men who had failed in a valley, argued about greatness (v. 34) and stopped a man not of their party are told to be at peace. Salt comes first, and peace follows. Peace in a church is not produced by managing personalities; it comes when people have each dealt honestly with themselves. People who have been salted with the fire of the cross have nothing left to fight over.

Peace at his own expense. He was going to Jerusalem to make that peace at his own expense, by the blood of his cross. And on the night he was handed over, John tells us, he got up from the table, took a towel, and washed the feet of every one of them (John 13:3–5). He himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14).

Can a true Christian lose his salt and be lost? A true believer cannot finally fall away, because the God who began the work will complete it (Philippians 1:6) and no one can snatch Christ’s sheep from his hand (John 10:28–29). But Jesus’ warnings are one of the means by which he keeps us. Christians can grow cold and useless for a season, and the warning is meant to wake them; and someone who looked like salt for years may prove never to have been the real thing (1 John 2:19). So do not use this verse to torment yourself, and do not use the doctrine of perseverance to ignore it. Go back to Christ, the source of the salt.

What if peace with someone seems impossible? Do what lies with you (Romans 12:18). Own your part first, without excuses. Go to the person privately and humbly (Matthew 18:15). Forgive as you have been forgiven, which does not mean pretending wrong was not done, but releasing your claim to pay it back. If they will not be reconciled, keep your heart free of bitterness and keep praying for them. Peace does not mean tolerating abuse or ignoring serious sin; sometimes the church’s elders must be involved. But it does mean you will not be the one keeping the quarrel alive.

Uncertain wording. “Everyone will be salted with fire” is a compressed saying found only in Mark, and its exact sense is not certain. Other readings have been offered: that every believer’s work will be tested by fire (1 Corinthians 3:13), or that the wicked will be preserved, as salt preserves, in the fire of judgment. The reading given above keeps the link with the fire of verse 48 and the salt of the sacrifices, and is the more likely: everyone meets God’s fire, either as judgment or as the refining of a life given to him.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add “and every sacrifice will be salted with salt”, probably added from Leviticus 2:13 to explain the saying.
verseByVerse.note: Salt was added to every sacrifice. Salt from the Dead Sea could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

parallels.desc: with all your offerings you shall offer salt
let your speech be seasoned with salt

9.theology:
Who will not taste death? (v. 1) Mark’s own arrangement answers it: the next words are and after six days (see the note on v. 1, and the box “Where Christians differ: what did they see?” at its end).

Why could the disciples not cast it out? (v. 29) Not for lack of a technique or of authority (this is treated fully at vv. 28–29, under “Prayer as the posture of a life” and “The drift from dependence”).
9.examples:
Then: a father who had watched his son thrown to the ground since childhood came looking for Jesus, found the disciples instead, and watched them fail in front of a crowd.

Now: the if you can in his prayer was not there when he set out (see the note on vv. 20–22).

Then watch what the man does with the little faith he has: I believe; help my unbelief! (see the note on vv. 23–24). So if your faith this morning is a mess, do not wait for it to improve before you pray.

keyVerse.quote: And a cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came out of the cloud, “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.”
keyVerse.note: These are the Father’s only words from heaven in Mark after the baptism, and his only command in the Gospel. They correct Peter’s mistake of setting Jesus beside Moses and Elijah, and they answer his objection to the cross six days before: the Son who said he must suffer is the Son the Father loves, so hear him. The rest of the chapter, in the valley and on the road, shows what listening to him means.

9.reflection:
Six days after Jesus spoke of his cross, the Father said of him, “This is my beloved Son; listen to him” (v. 7). Which of Jesus’ words do you find hardest to listen to, and what would it look like to hear him there this week?

The disciples went straight from the mountain into a shouting crowd and a failure (vv. 14–18). How does God use times of nearness to him to prepare us for ordinary and difficult days, and how do we sometimes try to stay on the mountain instead?

The father prayed, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (v. 24), and Jesus did not turn him away. How does this prayer help you when your faith feels weak? Why do you think Jesus links the disciples’ failure to prayer (v. 29)?

Jesus answered an argument about greatness by taking a child in his arms (vv. 33–37). Who around you can do nothing for you in return, and how could you welcome them in his name, as he has welcomed you?

10.title: The Road, the Ransom, and the Beggar Who Followed
10.text: <sup>1</sup>And he left there and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan, and crowds gathered to him again.
