And again, as was his custom, he taught them. <sup>2</sup>And Pharisees came up and in order to test him asked, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” <sup>3</sup>He answered them, “What did Moses command you?” <sup>4</sup>They said, “Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away.” <sup>5</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment. <sup>6</sup>But from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’ <sup>7</sup>‘Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, <sup>8</sup>and the two shall become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two but one flesh. <sup>9</sup>What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” <sup>10</sup>And in the house the disciples asked him again about this matter. <sup>11</sup>And he said to them, “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, <sup>12</sup>and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.” <sup>13</sup>And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. <sup>14</sup>But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, “Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. <sup>15</sup>Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.” <sup>16</sup>And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them. <sup>17</sup>And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>18</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. <sup>19</sup>You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder, Do not commit adultery, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Do not defraud, Honor your father and mother.’” <sup>20</sup>And he said to him, “Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, “You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” <sup>22</sup>Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. <sup>23</sup>And Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, “How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!” <sup>24</sup>And the disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, “Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! <sup>25</sup>It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup>And they were exceedingly astonished, and said to him, “Then who can be saved?” <sup>27</sup>Jesus looked at them and said, “With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.” <sup>28</sup>Peter began to say to him, “See, we have left everything and followed you.” <sup>29</sup>Jesus said, “Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, <sup>30</sup>who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. <sup>31</sup>But many who are first will be last, and the last first.” <sup>32</sup>And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. And taking the twelve again, he began to tell them what was to happen to him, <sup>33</sup>saying, “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles. <sup>34</sup>And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise.” <sup>35</sup>And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said to him, “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.” <sup>36</sup>And he said to them, “What do you want me to do for you?” <sup>37</sup>And they said to him, “Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.” <sup>38</sup>Jesus said to them, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” <sup>39</sup>And they said to him, “We are able.” And Jesus said to them, “The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized, <sup>40</sup>but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared.” <sup>41</sup>And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant at James and John. <sup>42</sup>And Jesus called them to him and said to them, “You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. <sup>43</sup>But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, <sup>44</sup>and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. <sup>45</sup>For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” <sup>46</sup>And they came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. <sup>47</sup>And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out and say, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>48</sup>And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>49</sup>And Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” And they called the blind man, saying to him, “Take heart. Get up; he is calling you.” <sup>50</sup>And throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus. <sup>51</sup>And Jesus said to him, “What do you want me to do for you?” And the blind man said to him, “Rabbi, let me recover my sight.” <sup>52</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Go your way; your faith has made you well.” And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.
10.overview:
Where we are. Mark 10 is the last stretch of the road to Jerusalem that began at Caesarea Philippi (8:27–10:52; see the introduction), ending at Jericho, one climb from the city where Jesus will die.

The message. The kingdom of God cannot be earned by anything we hold, and nothing we hold may be held back from its King. It is received with empty hands, like a child, because it has been bought: the Son of Man came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (v. 45). What is impossible with man, God does, through that death.

Why it was said. Mark’s first readers lived where a husband could dispose of a wife, children counted for little, wealth looked like blessing, and rulers pressed down on those below (v. 42). Many had lost homes and families for Christ (v. 30; see the introduction), and needed to know what such losses mean.

How the chapter makes its case. The first half puts what people build their lives out of, marriage, children and money, into the hands of a man walking to Jerusalem to die. Asked about divorce, the question that cost John the Baptist his head, Jesus goes back to creation (vv. 1–12). He is indignant when children are turned away (vv. 13–16). A rich man is loved, and goes away sorrowful over the one thing he will not give (vv. 17–22); entry is impossible for anyone, but not with God (vv. 23–31). The second half is the road: the third prediction (vv. 32–34), the brothers’ request for the best seats, out of which comes the centre of the Gospel (vv. 35–45), and a blind beggar at Jericho (vv. 46–52). The chapter opens with a rich man who would not follow and closes with a beggar who did.

Where it leads. “Then who can be saved?” (v. 26) is answered not by lowering the standard but by a ransom paid in a life. The cup the brothers so lightly say they can drink is God’s wrath, which Jesus will drink alone, and the places at his right and left will go to two criminals. The King whom all nations should serve (Daniel 7:14) comes to serve, and on his way to die stops for one blind man.

For us. Ask what your one thing is. Come as a child, with nothing in your hands. Serve where you would rather be served. And when you cannot see, cry to the Son of David for mercy, and follow him on the way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–31 — Divorce, Children, and the Danger of Riches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Life in the kingdom is received, not achieved, and nothing we love may be held against God. Asked to trap himself on divorce, Jesus goes behind Moses to creation: marriage is God’s joining, not man’s to undo (vv. 1–12). He is indignant when children are turned away, because the kingdom belongs to those who receive it like a child (vv. 13–16). A sincere rich man, loved by Jesus, will not give up the one thing that owns him, and goes away sorrowful (vv. 17–22). Entry is impossible for anyone by human strength, but not with God, and no one who gives up anything for Christ will lose by it (vv. 23–31).
verseByVerse.theology:
“Why do you call me good?” (v. 18) Jesus is not denying that he is good or that he is God (this is treated fully at vv. 17–18).

Why point him to the commandments? Not because keeping them saves, but because the law is a mirror (see the note on vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man who ran, knelt, had kept the commandments since boyhood, was looked at and loved by Jesus, and went home.

Now: he is alarming precisely because there is nothing obviously wrong with him. So the question the passage asks is not whether you are a good person, but what your one thing is (see the note on vv. 21–22).

verseByVerse.quote: And he left there and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan, and crowds gathered to him again. And again, as was his custom, he taught them. And Pharisees came up and in order to test him asked, "Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the territory of the king who killed John the Baptist for condemning his divorce, the Pharisees ask Jesus about divorce, not to learn but to trap him. Their question treats a wife as something a man may dispose of, and Jesus will answer it from God’s own design.

Beyond the Jordan. Perea, east of the river, ruled like Galilee by Herod Antipas, who had divorced his wife to marry Herodias and beheaded John the Baptist for saying it was unlawful (6:17–18); Josephus says John died in Herod’s fortress of Machaerus, in this very region. Jesus has walked into the jurisdiction of the man who killed John, and the next thing he is asked about is divorce.

As was his custom. The pattern of the whole ministry: they came, and he taught (1:38).

In order to test him. The Pharisees wanted a trap, not instruction. A strict answer might offend the crowds, and Herod too, and risk John’s end; a loose one could be called undermining Moses.

Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife? All Jews agreed that divorce was permitted; the debate was over the grounds. Deuteronomy 24:1 allowed a man to divorce his wife if he found “some indecency in her”, and the argument turned on that phrase. The school of Rabbi Shammai said it meant sexual immorality only; the school of Rabbi Hillel said anything that displeased him, even spoiling a dish, and a later rabbi, Akiba, said finding a prettier woman was enough. Matthew records the question in that form: “for any cause?” (Matthew 19:3). Mark gives the bare and more radical question: is divorce lawful at all?

Nobody has mentioned the wife. The question is asked entirely from the man’s side, though a woman put away had no property, no standing and little future: they are debating a man’s freedom to dispose of a person. Jesus is about to mention her.

Testing the Bridegroom. The prophets had called the LORD Israel’s husband (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:16), the faithful partner of an unfaithful bride, who in Hosea goes after his wife and buys her back (Hosea 3:1–2), and Jesus had called himself the bridegroom (2:19). So the men asking how easily a husband may put away his wife are putting the question to the one Husband whose love has outlasted all his people’s unfaithfulness, and whose errand on this road is to win a bride at the cost of his life. He would not be trapped, flattered or frightened: he defends the defenceless, and is never afraid of kings.

In everyday life. When you find yourself asking whether something is allowed, ask why you want to know. The question of the outer boundary is usually asked by someone who has already decided what he wants.
verseByVerse.note: “Beyond the Jordan” is Perea, the land east of the river, ruled by Herod Antipas, who had imprisoned John for condemning his marriage. Rabbis debated the grounds for divorce.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, "What did Moses command you?" They said, "Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away." And Jesus said to them, "Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses permitted divorce to limit the damage hard hearts do, not because God approves of it. Jesus makes the Pharisees say so themselves.

What did Moses command you? Jesus goes to Scripture, and answers with a question that is a trap of its own, because the verb is precise: he asks what Moses commanded.

Moses allowed. They correct him: “allowed”, not “commanded”, and in doing so make his point for him. Deuteronomy 24:1–4 does not command divorce or even approve it. It regulates something already happening, and its only command is that a man may not take back a wife he has divorced who has since married another. The certificate protected the woman: it proved she had been released and was free to remarry, and without it she could live under suspicion, and in poverty, for the rest of her life. Even in his concessions God was kind. The door to divorce was already open; Moses was limiting the damage.

Your hardness of heart. A heart that has thickened until it cannot feel (compare 3:5; 8:17). Because men would divorce their wives anyway, God set limits to protect the vulnerable; a law can regulate sin without approving it. And notice the pronoun: “he wrote you this commandment”. The concession was granted to people like you, for hardness like yours, and you have turned it into an entitlement.

What God permits and what God intends. The Bible regulates polygamy, slavery, warfare and divorce in a fallen world; it does not commend them, and the regulation is a restraint on a fallen practice, not a blueprint. With slavery, the law made kidnapping a man to sell him a crime punished by death (Exodus 21:16), and Paul calls a slave his master’s brother in Christ (Philemon 16); Christians have at times twisted these texts to their shame, but Scripture’s direction runs toward freedom. To read a concession as an endorsement is exactly the mistake being made in this conversation.

Greater than Moses. Jesus goes behind Moses to the beginning, as one who knows the Lawgiver’s mind from the inside: Moses was faithful in God’s house as a servant, and Christ is faithful over it as a Son (Hebrews 3:5–6). Moses could only limit the damage hard hearts do. The Son came to do something about the hearts.
verseByVerse.note: A certificate of divorce freed a woman to remarry.

verseByVerse.quote: But from the beginning of creation, 'God made them male and female.' 'Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.' So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Marriage is God’s own work, joining a man and a woman into one flesh, so no human being has the right to tear it apart. Asked about the rules for ending a marriage, Jesus goes to what a marriage is.

But from the beginning of creation. The most important move in the passage. Before sin and before Sinai, God established marriage, and that design is the standard: Deuteronomy 24 was a concession; Genesis 1 and 2 are the pattern. “God made them male and female” (Genesis 1:27): marriage is not a human invention that societies may adapt but is built into the way people were made, the foundation of the Christian understanding of marriage as between one man and one woman.

Leave and hold fast. Genesis 2:24, the words of the writer of Genesis, which Jesus treats as God’s own. “Leave”: a new primary loyalty replaces the old, and a marriage in which one partner has never really left home will feel the fault line for decades. “Hold fast”: be glued, cleave, the word used of clinging to God himself (Deuteronomy 10:20). It is not a mood but a decision, renewed whatever the week has been like.

One flesh. A union of the whole person, of which sexual union is both the expression and the seal: one life, one home, one purse, one future, so that what wounds or gladdens one belongs to the other as well (compare Ephesians 5:28–29). “No longer two” is Jesus’ own comment, a statement of fact rather than an ideal: the union is real whatever either of them feels on a given morning. So ending a marriage is never just paperwork: you cannot separate one flesh without tearing something, and everyone who has been through it knows this in their body long before they can say it.

Let not man separate. God, not the couple or the registrar, creates the bond, in every genuine marriage, including those of people who have never given him a thought; and no husband, wife or court has the right to tear apart what God did.

The Maker in the conversation. The Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3) is standing in Perea explaining his own design. He knows what a marriage is because he made the first one, and no one has ever honoured a bride as he will honour his.

What this means on the bad days. You are not in an arrangement that lasts as long as it works; you are in something God did. So in the year that is going wrong, the question is not “Is it still working?” but “What did God join, and what am I doing to keep it?” Marriages are rarely ended by one decision, but by a thousand small permissions: the conversation not had, the resentment kept, the friendship at work that becomes the place you are understood. “Let not man separate” is addressed to the man in the mirror, and the Bridegroom who has held fast to you through all your unfaithfulness gives grace to hold fast too.

What if my marriage is very unhappy? Unhappiness is not a ground for divorce, but it is a reason to act, not to drift. Pray about it honestly, together and alone. Ask for help early: a wise pastor or older couple, and good Christian counselling. Look first at your own part, and confess it. Keep doing the ordinary acts of love when the feeling is absent, because feelings often follow faithfulness; many couples who came close to the end have later found a deeper marriage than they began with. And if the unhappiness is fear because you are being harmed, that is a different matter: you do not have to stay in danger (see “What if I am being abused?” at vv. 10–12).

What about people who never marry, or who experience same-sex attraction? Jesus’ words define marriage; they do not say that everyone must marry. He himself was single, and Paul calls singleness a gift (1 Corinthians 7:7), full and honourable, not second-class. Those who experience same-sex attraction are not beyond the love or the family of God; the call to them is the call to every believer, to deny themselves and follow Christ, and the church must be a real family to them (v. 30). But because Jesus grounds marriage in God making them male and female, the church cannot bless any other union as marriage. The reason is not dislike of anyone: Jesus defines marriage by creation, and Paul sees in that union of two different partners a picture of Christ and his church (Ephesians 5:31–32). The church has no authority to redraw what God made; what it can and must give is friendship, belonging and patient love.

Textual note. Some early manuscripts omit “and hold fast to his wife” in v. 7. The meaning is unchanged: the words stand in Genesis 2:24, which Jesus is quoting.

parallels.desc: male and female he created them

verseByVerse.quote: And in the house the disciples asked him again about this matter. And he said to them, "Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God’s bond still holds, a man who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, and the same is true of a wife. In private Jesus makes the teaching plainer, and names the discarded wife as the one who has been wronged.

In the house. A public statement, then a private question. They were startled, for his teaching was stricter than either rabbinic school: “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry” (Matthew 19:10).

Adultery against her. The certificate does not touch what God joined, so remarriage after a divorce God does not recognise is adultery. And “against her” was revolutionary. In Jewish law a man could only commit adultery against another man, by taking his wife. Jesus says a husband can commit adultery against his own wife: in a conversation that began with men debating how freely a man may dispose of a wife, he names her as the one sinned against. The raising of women’s dignity wherever Christianity went is not a modern correction to an embarrassing text; it starts here, in a house in Perea.

If she divorces her husband. Jewish law did not normally allow a wife to divorce her husband, but Roman law did, and Mark, writing probably for Roman readers, records that the teaching applies to both; Herodias had divorced her husband. There is no double standard here.

The exceptions. Mark gives the principle without exception. Matthew records one: “except for sexual immorality” (Matthew 19:9; 5:32). Paul adds another: if an unbelieving spouse leaves, the believer is not bound (1 Corinthians 7:15). These do not contradict Mark. They show that some sins so break the marriage covenant that the innocent party may lawfully end it.

Not a list of loopholes. Where Scripture allows divorce, it never requires it. Adultery and desertion give the innocent party freedom, not an obligation, and where there is genuine repentance, reconciliation is better where possible; some marriages wounded by adultery have been rebuilt, slowly and at great cost, into something stronger. But that is the wronged spouse’s free choice before God, and no one may shame them for using the freedom Christ gives.

A word to the divorced. To the reader who is divorced, perhaps remarried, and reading these hard sentences with a sinking heart: the standard has not moved, and a church that lowers it to seem gentle has only made grace unnecessary. But there is no sin named here that the blood of Christ does not cover, and no marriage so broken, by your fault, another’s, or the tangle of both, that grace cannot make something new of what remains. The gospel does not meet you in the marriage you should have had. It meets you in the life you actually have, with a Saviour who came to give his life as a ransom for many (v. 45), the divorced among them.

What if I am being abused? Abuse is never to be tolerated, excused or covered up, and nothing in Jesus’ words requires you to remain in danger. If you or your children are being hurt, threatened or controlled, your first duty is safety: get to a safe place, call the police where there is violence or threat, and tell someone you trust. Separation for protection is not sin. A husband who abuses his wife is himself breaking the covenant he vowed; headship in Scripture means self-giving love, never domination (Ephesians 5:25). Elders and churches must believe, protect and support victims, involve the civil authorities, and call the abuser to account. Whether divorce is then lawful is a further question, and persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion, which the elders help judge in each case; but you do not need to settle that question before you get safe.

What if I divorced and remarried before I became a Christian, or on wrong grounds? The sin is real and should be confessed. But a second marriage, once made, is a marriage, and the answer is not to break it, which would add another sin; Moses’ law forbade going back to the first spouse after remarriage (Deuteronomy 24:1–4). Christ forgives the repentant fully, and you are to live faithfully where you now are, honouring the vows you made (1 Corinthians 7:17–20). Your past does not disqualify you from grace or from serving God.

Where Christians differ: divorce and remarriage. Roman Catholic teaching holds that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved; remarriage while the spouse lives is never permitted, though an annulment may declare that no true marriage existed. Some Protestants hold that remarriage is never right while a spouse lives, even after divorce for adultery. Others allow divorce for many reasons, such as abuse, or simply breakdown. This commentary’s view: the Westminster Confession states the position best grounded in Scripture (Westminster 24.5–6): God’s design is lifelong marriage, and divorce is always a tragedy; but adultery, and wilful desertion that cannot be remedied, are grounds on which the innocent party may divorce and be free to remarry. Whether persistent, serious abuse amounts to such desertion is for the elders to weigh in each case; but no one is ever required to stay where they or their children are in danger, the abused should seek safety at once, and abuse is never to be tolerated or covered. Those who have divorced and remarried wrongly may repent and find full forgiveness in Christ, as with any sin.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish law did not allow a wife to divorce her husband, but Roman law did; Mark’s wording covers both.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, "Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is angry when children are kept from him, because his kingdom belongs to people like them, who have nothing to offer and simply receive.

That he might touch them. After marriage, children: Mark is showing what a household looks like under Jesus’ rule. Luke says some were babies (Luke 18:15). It was ordinary to bring a child to a respected rabbi for a blessing, and that is all these parents ask.

And the disciples rebuked them. The verb used of rebuking demons. Their reasoning was sound by any ordinary measure: somebody has to manage the Master’s diary. It is the second time in two chapters they have tried to control access to Jesus (9:38). There is something in religious people that likes to stand at the door and decide who gets in.

He was indignant. A strong word, used of Jesus only here. Days from the cross, the Son of God was angry, not at the interruption but at the gatekeeping. That is the heart of God laid open: not a busy king who tolerates the small, but a Saviour who wants them near. Nothing must stand between children and him.

To such belongs the kingdom. “To such”, not only “to these”. He is not saying that children are automatically in and adults are not. The kingdom belongs to people of this kind, who have nothing to offer and simply receive: not because children are innocent, but because they are dependent.

Who hinders children now? Rarely deliberately: by treating them as a distraction to be managed until they are old enough to matter: the church that has no room for them, the family in which faith is discussed but never with them, the parent who is too tired at bedtime and always will be, and the hypocrisy children see at home. Nobody rebukes anybody. The children simply do not get brought.

So how do Baptist parents bring their children to Christ? In every way except the sign that belongs to those who profess faith. Pray for each child and with them, from the cradle. Teach them the Scriptures and the gospel at home (Deuteronomy 6:6–7; 2 Timothy 3:15). Bring them to worship. Many churches hold a service of thanksgiving and dedication, in which parents promise to raise the child in the Lord. Speak to them of Christ as one who welcomes children, and call them to trust him themselves; when they profess faith and show its fruit, they are baptised. Our brothers who baptise their infants share every one of those aims.

What of children who die young? Scripture gives no age of accountability and no formula, and we should say no more than it says. But it gives firm ground for hope. Elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3). David expected to go to the son who died in infancy (2 Samuel 12:23). And the one who took children in his arms is the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is right (Genesis 18:25). Grieving parents may entrust their little ones to that mercy with confidence. If you are one of them, the Lord who was indignant when children were kept from him is not indifferent to your empty arms; he knows the child you lost, and has not forgotten.

Where Christians differ: children and baptism. Paedobaptists (Presbyterians, Anglicans, Lutherans, Catholics) often appeal to this passage for infant baptism: if the kingdom belongs to children, they should receive the sign of the covenant. Credobaptists (Baptists) answer that Jesus did not baptise these children; he blessed them, and the passage is about how all must receive the kingdom, not about a sacrament. This commentary’s view: the passage shows Christ’s welcome for children and the need to bring them to him, which both sides agree on. It does not mention baptism, and it cannot settle the question. The New Testament pattern links baptism to repentance and faith, so the credobaptist position is best. This is a disagreement among brothers, held charitably.
verseByVerse.note: Children had little status in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it." And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one enters the kingdom except as a small child receives everything: as a gift, with empty hands. Then Jesus shows what he does with those who come that way: he takes them in his arms.

Truly, I say to you. Put negatively, “shall not enter it”, this is a condition for everyone rather than a compliment to children: adults cannot come in as adults, with their merits.

Like a child. Not innocence: children are not morally blank, and David says he was brought forth in iniquity (Psalm 51:5). Not simplicity of mind either; this is the Lord who tells us to love God with all our mind (12:30). It is dependence. A small child in that world owned and earned nothing. He did not negotiate for his dinner; he was fed. He did not qualify for his place in the family; he was born into it. Everything came as a gift from someone bigger, and he took it without embarrassment. The kingdom must be received in exactly that way, as grace, not achievement.

Why this is so hard for competent adults. Everywhere else the self-sufficient are rewarded; here, the qualities that recommend you elsewhere disqualify you. The rich man who comes running next is the opposite of the child: he asks, “What must I do?” (v. 17). A child comes with empty hands and is welcomed; a rich man comes with full ones and cannot get in.

And he took them in his arms. Only Mark records it, here and in 9:36, and the verb, to fold in the arms, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. The people brought the children for a touch; the Lord of glory did not pat them on the head but gathered them up.

And blessed them. Fervently (the verb is a strengthened form), one child at a time, while grown men stood by wishing he would get on. They were the hands that had taken a dead girl by the hand (5:41) and lifted a convulsing boy from the ground (9:27), and within weeks they would be nailed down and unable to hold anybody at all. Yet those hands he lifted over his disciples as he was carried up into heaven (Luke 24:50–51), and from there he has never withheld his blessing from anyone brought to him with empty hands.

What does receiving like a child look like for me? Coming to God with no bargaining position. You stop presenting your record and efforts as reasons God should accept you, and trust what he has promised in Christ: he loves you because he is your Father, not because you performed well this week. And you go on receiving forgiveness, strength and guidance as gifts, rather than turning the Christian life into a new way of earning. Children who trust their father also obey him, but the obedience grows from being loved, not the other way round.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, "Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?" And Jesus said to him, "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An eager, sincere man asks what he must do to gain eternal life, and Jesus’ question about the word “good” turns him toward who is standing in front of him.

Ran up and knelt. Everything about the approach is right. He ran, when men of position did not run; he knelt, in the dirt, in public. Matthew tells us he was young (Matthew 19:20), Luke that he was a ruler (Luke 18:18). He had everything, and still lacked something.

Good Teacher. Jewish teachers were not normally called good, a word reserved for God. It is warm and sincere, and also the kind of compliment a man pays a respected figure on his way to asking a favour.

What must I do to inherit eternal life? The best question anybody asks in this Gospel, and nobody else asks it. Do not make him a villain: he is eager, humble, urgent, morally serious, and asking the right thing; if he walked into your church you would thank God for him. But note the word “do”: he thinks eternal life is something to be achieved. And an inheritance is precisely the thing nobody does anything for; you receive it because of who you are in the family. He has attached the language of gift to the language of achievement, and does not notice. The child two verses ago received. This man wants to know the price.

Why do you call me good? “No one is good except God alone.” Jesus is not denying that he is good, or that he is God; he never withdraws the word or corrects the man for using it. He holds it up to the light: goodness in the full and final sense belongs to God alone. So either the man should not have called him good, and has come running and kneeling to the wrong person; or the word is right, and he must reckon with who is in front of him. It is not a denial of his deity but a door held open to it. The man came asking what he must do; the deeper question, which he never reaches, is who this is.

Goodness that could not be flattered. Every perfection of God was there in a human face: holiness without hardness, truth without coldness, goodness that could not be flattered. He is not merely a good teacher. He is the Good, come down to seek those who are not.

What it does not mean. Not a confession by Jesus that he is a sinner: the New Testament is clear that he was without sin (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). If only God is good, it is the rich man who is not good, whatever he thinks of his record.

Compliment or confession? It is possible to call Jesus wonderful, loving, good, the greatest teacher who ever lived, and to be paying a compliment rather than making a confession. Many people today will happily call Jesus good who will not call him Lord. If he is good as only God is good, then he must be worshipped and obeyed, not merely admired.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says he was young, Luke that he was a ruler. Jesus does not deny his goodness; he asks the man to think about what he is saying.

verseByVerse.quote: You know the commandments: 'Do not murder, Do not commit adultery, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Do not defraud, Honor your father and mother.'" And he said to him, "Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus holds up God’s law as a mirror, and the man looks into it and sees nothing wrong. The question was “what must I do”, so Jesus goes to the law: not because keeping it saves anyone, but because it is the mirror the man needs.

The list. Not one of the first four commandments, about God, is mentioned. That is deliberate, and very gentle: the man’s problem is going to be a rival god, so Jesus recites only the commandments the man believes he has kept, and waits.

Do not defraud. It is the commandment on the list a wealthy landowner was most likely to break, and least likely to notice himself breaking: withholding what is owed, especially to a labourer (Leviticus 19:13). He is being probed, kindly, at the exact point of his danger, and he does not feel a thing.

All these I have kept. This time he drops the word “good”. His claim is sincere, perhaps outwardly true, and Jesus does not contest it. Paul could say the same of his life before Christ: “as to righteousness under the law, blameless” (Philippians 3:6). But it is the most self-condemning sentence in the chapter. He has not understood how deep God’s law goes, reaching the anger and lust of the heart (Matthew 5:21–28). He has treated it as a checklist and is waiting to be told the remaining item, when what he is about to be shown is that his heart belongs to something other than God.

The one who kept them all. The law that condemns us is in Christ’s hands a tool of mercy, and its whole demand was met by him, who alone could say with truth, “all these I have kept”, and kept them in our place.

Why does Jesus point him to the law if we are not saved by keeping it? Because the law shows us our sin and drives us to Christ (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24). A man who thinks he has kept it needs to see that he has not. The law is also a good guide for those already saved; what it can never do is make us right with God, because no one keeps it from the heart. Christ kept it perfectly for us, and his obedience is counted to all who trust him. Scripture’s word for this is justification: God pronounces a guilty person right with him, not because that person has become perfect, but because Christ’s perfect record is credited to him and his sins were paid for at the cross (Romans 4:5; 5:19).

Uncertain wording. “Do not defraud” is not one of the Ten Commandments, and Matthew and Luke do not include it (Matthew 19:18–19; Luke 18:20). What it stands for is uncertain: many think it sums up the tenth commandment, since defrauding is covetousness in action; others link it with stealing or false witness. The tenth is the likelier sense, put in a form that touches a rich man’s daily dealings.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus lists the commandments about one’s neighbour; “do not defraud” is not one of the Ten in so many words; it may stand for the tenth, against coveting (cf. Lev 19:13).

parallels.desc: the second table of the Ten Commandments

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, "You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Jesus loves him, he names the one thing that rules the man’s heart and calls him to give it up and follow; the man will not, and goes away grieving.

Looking at him, loved him. Only Mark records this tender half-sentence, the key to the passage. The verb means a held gaze, not a glance. And then: he loved him, the only place in this Gospel where we are told that Jesus loved a particular individual. Everything hard that follows must be read inside that: the demand is the loving cure for what was killing him.

You lack one thing. For about two seconds that sounds like a relief: only one thing. But the one thing is the centre of his life. His wealth had his heart; it was his god. He had broken the first commandment, “You shall have no other gods before me” (Exodus 20:3), and the tenth.

Sell all that you have. The surgery: cut out the idol. He had passed the list about neighbours; one sentence finds out whether he has other gods, and the answer comes at once.

Treasure in heaven. Not a payment for salvation, and not a heavenly bank balance paid out later for good behaviour. Jesus tells him to trade treasure on earth for treasure in heaven, the best terms ever offered to a human being, and your treasure is whatever your heart rests on: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). Treasure in heaven is what is kept for you with God and cannot be stolen, taxed or lost: his “Well done” (Matthew 25:21), the people you served and helped towards Christ, and above all Christ himself, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). Jesus was not asking this man to lose, but to exchange a treasure already slipping through his fingers for one that never would.

Follow me. Selling everything was the means; following Jesus was the end. Eternal life is not earned by giving away money but found in following Christ, and Jesus himself is the real prize.

He went away sorrowful. The only person in Mark whom Jesus personally calls who refuses. He wanted eternal life, but not more than he wanted his money. He is not scoffing; he knows what he is refusing, refuses it anyway, and is miserable: a sorrow that is not repentance. Mark gives the reason last, flat, without comment: “he had great possessions”. In truth it was the other way round. They had him.

Jesus let him go. He does not call after him or offer a smaller figure: love that will not lie to you. Lowering the price would have been crueller, sending him home comfortable, his idol intact, thinking himself safe. Few sights in the Gospel are sadder than a man walking down a road with everything he came with still in his hands, and without the one thing he came for.

Christ let go of all his riches. Where this man would not let go of his riches to follow Christ, Christ let go of all his riches to come after us: though he was rich, yet for our sake he became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).

In everyday life. He looks at you with the same love, and asks for your one thing only because he is better than it; the Spirit he has put in you is stronger than its grip. Loosen it this week with something concrete: a generous gift that costs you, given quietly where only your Father sees (Matthew 6:3–4); an hour given that you wanted for yourself; a plan surrendered in prayer.

Is this required of every Christian? No, and the Gospels themselves settle it. Peter kept his house in Capernaum (1:29). Zacchaeus gave away half, and was told that salvation had come to his house (Luke 19:8–9). Joseph of Arimathea was rich (Matthew 27:57), and his money bought the tomb. Jesus gives this command to no one else in the New Testament. It is not a universal rule but a scalpel, and it goes to one man’s one thing. But the principle is universal: Christ has the right to ask for anything you love more than him.

How do I know what my one thing is? Ask what you could not bear to lose, what you turn to for security when you are afraid, what you think about when your mind is free, and what you would be most angry to have taken away. Ask what you are most reluctant to bring under Christ’s word: money, a relationship, reputation, comfort, career, your plans for your children. It is usually not a wicked thing but a good thing loved too much. And the test is often money, because money is the most portable god there is. Your bank statement and your diary tell the truth about the heart.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark notes that Jesus looked at him and loved him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, "How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!" And the disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, "Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells his astonished disciples that it is hard for the rich, and then for anyone, to enter the kingdom of God: as hard as a camel going through the eye of a needle.

Amazed at his words. In the Old Testament prosperity is often a sign of God’s favour (Deuteronomy 28:1–14), and people concluded that a rich man is a blessed man. The rich could also afford alms, sacrifices and leisure to study the law. If they can hardly enter, what hope for anyone? Yet riches give a sense of not needing God (Deuteronomy 8:11–14), and full hands cannot receive the kingdom like a child.

Children, how difficult it is! The second time he leaves out the rich: verse 24 says how hard it is for anybody, and the rich man only makes visible a difficulty everyone has. And he begins, “Children”, the only time he addresses the disciples this way in Mark: he is about to say the hardest thing in the chapter, and he opens it the way a father does.

A camel through the eye of a needle. The largest animal anyone in Palestine handled, the smallest opening anyone used: deliberate, comic exaggeration, meaning impossible.

Two ways of softening it. The idea of a small gate in Jerusalem called the needle’s eye has no evidence behind it before the Middle Ages, and it turns the saying into advice that with less baggage you can just about manage, the opposite of the point. Reading rope for camel has only a few late manuscripts and would not help either. Jesus means what the disciples heard: humanly impossible (v. 27), and he does not correct them. He did not soften the impossible, because he intended to do it himself.

The man who refused the kingdoms of the world. Only one man has faced the pull of wealth at its largest and not given an inch. In the wilderness the devil offered Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and their glory for one act of worship, and he answered that God alone is to be worshipped and served (Matthew 4:8–10). The rich man could not let go of his estates. The Son turned down the world and chose the road to a cross, so that people whose hands are full of lesser things could be given the kingdom.

Am I one of the rich Jesus means here? Almost certainly. He says it to his own disciples, men who had left their boats. Anyone with a home, a change of clothes, food that is not in question this week and medical care within reach is, by every standard the world has known and most it knows now, rich. And wealth is dangerous not only for what it buys but for what it makes us feel: safe, competent, in control, without need. The question is not how much you have but whether it has you. Signs that it does: anxiety that crowds out trust, reluctance to give, envy of those with more, a life arranged around keeping what you have. The poor are not safe from it either: money can rule the man who longs for it as surely as the man who has it, for “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils” (1 Timothy 6:9–10).

Textual note. Some manuscripts add “for those who trust in riches” in v. 24 (so the King James Version). The shorter reading, followed by the ESV, makes the saying apply to everyone; either way, trusting in riches is the danger Jesus has been exposing.
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration. The idea of a gate called “the Eye of the Needle” is a much later invention.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were exceedingly astonished, and said to him, "Then who can be saved?" Jesus looked at them and said, "With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can save himself, but God can save anyone. The disciples rightly conclude that if this man cannot get in, no one can; Jesus agrees, and points them to God.

Then who can be saved? Exceedingly astonished: for once the disciples reason perfectly. If the man with every visible advantage, money, morality, eagerness, a clean record from boyhood, cannot get in, no one can: the door will not admit anyone under their own power. And it is personal for them: they have left everything, and if having wealth cannot buy entry, neither can giving it up.

Jesus looked at them. Mark’s third look in this passage (vv. 21, 23), because what is coming is the most important sentence in it.

With man it is impossible. Not difficult; impossible. No one has ever saved himself or met God halfway: not the rich man with his clean record, not Peter with his abandoned boat, not you. This is the gospel’s bad news: we are unable.

But not with God. The impossibility is real and total, and it is God’s to solve, and he has solved it. It echoes the angel’s word to Sarah, laughing at the promise of a son: “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14). Salvation is God’s work from beginning to end: he gives the new heart, grants repentance and faith, and draws us (John 6:44; Ephesians 2:8–9). If God can save a rich man, as Zacchaeus and Joseph of Arimathea prove, he can save anyone. A camel through a needle is no harder for him than a world out of nothing.

God helps those who help themselves? That popular saying is not in the Bible; it is the exact reverse of what Jesus says. God saves those who cannot help themselves, which is everybody. And how is not left in the air: the man saying it is on the road to Jerusalem, and in eighteen verses he will say why: “to give his life as a ransom for many” (v. 45). The impossibility is not overcome by a change in the requirements. It is overcome by a death.

In everyday life. If you have honestly concluded that you have no business being in the kingdom of God, you are right; Jesus said it first, and then said the words that answer it: “but not with God”. And the person you think least likely ever to be saved is not beyond those words either, so keep praying for them.

If salvation is God’s work, what do I do? Call on him. The God for whom all things are possible commands everyone to repent and believe the gospel (1:15), and promises that “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). His sovereignty is not a reason to wait passively but the reason to hope, because your salvation does not depend on a strength you do not have. If you want Christ, that wanting is already his work in you. Come to him and you will find that he has been drawing you all along.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: Peter began to say to him, "See, we have left everything and followed you." Jesus said, "Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one who gives up anything for Christ and the gospel loses by it: he gains a new family now, with persecutions, and eternal life in the age to come. But the reward is grace, not repayment, and the kingdom’s order will surprise those who count their sacrifices.

We have left everything. Peter began to say it: honest, blurted, and not quite right. He has watched the rich man go, heard that it is impossible, and what comes out is: “We did, though.” It is true (1:18, 20), and it cost them. But two verses after “With man it is impossible”, he is doing arithmetic again: the oldest temptation of religious people, to serve God in order to put him in our debt.

There is no one who has left. Jesus does not rebuke Peter but answers generously, listing everything a man in that world had. In the early church many converts were disowned by their families or lost their property (Hebrews 10:34), and in many countries they still are. As in 8:35, only Mark adds “and for the gospel”. Loss for its own sake is not praised; Jesus means what a person loses because he follows him.

A hundredfold now. Not only in heaven: now, the extravagant yield of the parable of the sower (4:8). He is not promising a hundred houses. He is promising the church: brothers, sisters and mothers in the family of God (3:34–35), homes opened, and a share in all that belongs to his people (Acts 2:44–46); Paul greets a woman in Rome as one who had been a mother to him as well (Romans 16:13). Notice that “fathers” is missing from what is received: in God’s family there is one Father (Matthew 23:9).

With persecutions. Only Mark adds this, in the middle of the blessings, as one of the things received. No recruiter was ever so honest: the hundredfold arrives with trouble in the same parcel. For Mark’s first readers, very probably believers in Rome who had lived through Nero’s persecution, the new family and the trouble had come together, just as he said.

And in the age to come eternal life. The answer to the rich man’s question (v. 17): what he would not give up everything for, they will receive. Not merely more of the same, only longer: it is the life of “the age to come”, God’s own life shared with his people, and its heart is not a place but a Person: “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). It begins the day a person comes to Christ, and the resurrection completes it. Timothy Keller often pointed out that the Bible promises not a thin, ghostly consolation for the life we lost, but the restoration of the life we always wanted, in raised bodies and a world made new. See also Eternal Life in the Theological Dictionary.

First will be last. A warning aimed at the man who said “we have left everything”. The rich man, first by every earthly measure, walked away, and the children were taken in; those who think themselves first because of their sacrifices may find themselves last. Reward is grace, not wages earned (Matthew 20:1–16).

No one has ever out-given Christ. He left his Father’s house and his glory for us, and the reward of his sacrifice is a family beyond number. Everyone treats something as their life; for the rich man it was his possessions. But Christ gave his own life as a ransom (v. 45) so that his life could become ours. So when following him costs you something, an evening, an ambition, a grudge you would rather keep, remember that Paul calls him “Christ who is your life” (Colossians 3:4), and let it go.

Can this be tested? This promise can be tested this month. The believer with no family who is never alone at Christmas. The convert cut off by his relatives who has more people praying for him than he can count. The student far from home given a key to a church family’s house. If your church is not that for somebody, this verse indicts before it comforts.

The family you would not have chosen. To modern loneliness our culture offers the chosen family: if the family you were born into failed you, gather your own people. There is wisdom in the longing, but people who chose each other can choose again. The brothers and sisters of verse 30 are not people you selected but people he selected, often unlike you in age, class, politics and taste. That is why this family can hold. It rests not on your choosing them or their choosing you, but on the Father who chose all of you in his Son. A family that never depended on your being easy to love will not let you go when you are not.

Is this a promise that God will make me wealthy if I give? No. Prosperity teaching that uses this verse to promise money for gifts turns it upside down: the hundredfold is found in the family of God, and it comes with persecutions. Jesus had nowhere to lay his head, and Paul knew hunger and need while content in Christ (Philippians 4:11–13). God does provide for his children, and generosity is never a loss in the end; but the promise is that you will never lose by following Christ, not that following him is a financial investment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–52 — The Road to Jerusalem, the Ransom, and Bartimaeus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The King walks ahead to a cross, and the greatness of his kingdom runs downward. For the third time Jesus tells the Twelve exactly what awaits him in Jerusalem (vv. 32–34). James and John ask for the best seats, the ten are furious, and Jesus turns greatness upside down: the great serve and the first are slaves of all, because the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many (vv. 35–45). At Jericho a blind beggar calls him Son of David, receives his sight and follows him on the road (vv. 46–52), the disciple the Twelve were meant to be.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 45 is the theological centre of Mark. A ransom is the price paid to set a captive free, and Jesus says his own life is that price, paid in our place. Behind it stands Isaiah 53, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isa. 53:12). To whom the price is paid, and how it answers the impossible of verse 27, is treated in the note on v. 45.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the same question, What do you want me to do for you?, is asked twice in fifteen verses: to James and John (v. 36) and to a blind beggar (v. 51).

Now: we often pray more like the brothers than the beggar (see “Praying with a blank cheque” at vv. 35–37). Bartimaeus asked for what he actually needed, from someone he had rightly named Son of David, on no ground but mercy (see the note on vv. 46–48).

verseByVerse.quote: And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. And taking the twelve again, he began to tell them what was to happen to him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus walks ahead of his amazed and frightened followers toward Jerusalem, going to his death on purpose. And he takes the Twelve aside to tell them, once more, what is waiting there.

Going up to Jerusalem. The first time Mark names the destination. The road from Jericho climbs about 3,500 feet (1,000 m) in 15 miles (25 km), but Jews said “up to Jerusalem” from any direction: the city of God was always up.

Walking ahead of them. Not carried along by events: he is setting the pace, going to his death on purpose (Luke 9:51). Isaiah had said it in the Servant’s voice: “I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame” (Isaiah 50:7). A shepherd goes before his sheep (John 10:4).

Taking the twelve again. Privately, a third time and in more detail than ever: he will not let them arrive in Jerusalem without having been told.

Amazed and afraid on the road. There are stretches of the Christian life when you are amazed and afraid. The picture gives the one thing that helps: he is in front, on the road, going first, and there is nothing coming that he has not already walked into.

Is it wrong to be afraid as a Christian? No. The disciples were afraid on this road, and Jesus himself was greatly distressed in Gethsemane (14:33). What Scripture forbids is fear that rules us and turns us back from obedience. The answer is not pretending, but looking at the one who walks ahead: “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you” (Psalm 56:3). Courage is not the absence of fear but walking on with him through it.

Uncertain wording. Mark’s sentence is compressed: “they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid”. It may describe one group, the disciples, both amazed and afraid; or two, the Twelve amazed and the pilgrims behind afraid. The Greek allows either, and two groups is perhaps the more natural reading. Either way, one man strode ahead with a set face, and those behind him sensed that something terrible lay ahead.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem stands high in the hills; one always went “up” to it.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, "See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles. And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the third time, and in the fullest detail, Jesus tells the Twelve what will happen to him in Jerusalem: betrayal, condemnation, mockery, death, and resurrection.

See, we are going up. The fullest of the three predictions (8:31; 9:31): eight steps, almost a summary of chapters 14 to 16.

Delivered over. Handed over, that word again (9:31): betrayed into the hands of the chief priests and scribes (14:10, 43), who will pass sentence in the Sanhedrin (14:64).

To the Gentiles. New and shocking: the leaders of Israel will hand their own Messiah to the pagans, since they could not carry out executions under Roman rule (John 18:31). The Jewish penalty for blasphemy was stoning; crucifixion was Rome’s. When he says “Gentiles”, he is saying “cross” without using the word. Jews and Gentiles alike would reject him; the whole world is guilty (Acts 4:27).

Mock him and spit on him. Every verb was fulfilled (14:65; 15:15–20, 24). Mocking and spitting are not necessary to an execution; the contempt is cruelty added for its own sake, and he names it in advance, walking toward it. Isaiah had foretold it: “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6).

After three days. He has never once mentioned the death without the resurrection, and the disciples have never once shown that they took it in (9:10).

The face that shone on the mountain. The face that shone on the mountain he gave to those who spat; the back that bore the cross he gave to those who struck. He hid not his face from shame, so that we would never have to hide ours from God. And on the third day he rose, exactly as he said.

Hearing only what we want. Mark has arranged the contrast: after eight stages of humiliation and death, two of his closest friends ask for the best seats, having heard only “glory”. We do the same: a sermon about the cross followed by a conversation about lunch. The disciples are us, with better excuses, for they had never seen a resurrection.

Why did Jesus have to suffer so much, and not simply die? Because he was bearing the full weight of human sin, and sin is not only guilt but shame. We treated God’s glory with contempt, and Christ received contempt in our place: the spitting, the mockery, the stripping, the curse of hanging on a tree (Galatians 3:13). He endured the cross for the joy set before him, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), and took our shame so that we might be clothed with his honour. Nothing was wasted, and nothing was accidental.
verseByVerse.note: This third prediction is the fullest, naming the Gentiles, mocking, spitting and flogging.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.quote: And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said to him, "Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you." And he said to them, "What do you want me to do for you?" And they said to him, "Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straight after hearing of his death, James and John ask Jesus for the two highest places in his glory: the crown without the cross, and above their friends.

James and John, the sons of Zebedee. Two of the inner three, the Sons of Thunder (3:17). Matthew says their mother asked on their behalf (Matthew 20:20); she may have been Mary’s sister, making them Jesus’ cousins. Both accounts are true: she asked, they stood by, and Mark puts the responsibility where the ten put it (v. 41).

Whatever we ask of you. They want him to agree before they put the question: a blank cheque, signed in advance, the way a child approaches a parent when he suspects the answer will be no.

What do you want me to do for you? He does not sign; he makes them say it out loud. He will ask Bartimaeus the same question (v. 51), and the two answers are the point of the chapter: they ask for glory, he asks for sight.

One at your right hand. The places of highest honour beside a king: the top two positions in the government of the universe, which means they have already decided the other ten are not getting them.

Something right in it. They believe him. He has just told them he is going to be spat on and killed, and they are still asking about his glory: somewhere in them is a real conviction that this man is going to reign, and they have seen that glory on the mountain. But beside that faith is a deafness to what he has said about dying, so complete it is hard to believe.

Who was at his right and left? He is walking ahead of them toward the day when there will in fact be a man on his right and a man on his left: two criminals on crosses (15:27). His glory was not a seat above others but a death beneath them, and the thrones he gives at last are given freely to sinners who once asked for them for all the wrong reasons.

Praying with a blank cheque. The same move comes in more respectable clothing: prayer that is not asking but informing, a decision already taken and brought to God for endorsement rather than judgment. “Lord, bless what I have determined to do.” The words are reverent; the transaction is a blank cheque.

Is it wrong to ask God for things for myself? No. Jesus invites us to ask (Matthew 7:7), and he does not scold James and John for asking but for not knowing what they asked. Pray freely for your needs, family, work and health. What is wrong is praying for position over others, as though God existed to serve our plans. The best prayers have the shape of the Lord’s Prayer: his name, his kingdom, his will first, and then our daily bread, forgiveness and protection. Ask boldly, and let him correct the request.
verseByVerse.note: To sit at a king’s right and left was the place of highest honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?" And they said to him, "We are able." And Jesus said to them, "The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized, but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The brothers do not know what they are asking: the road to Jesus’ glory runs through the cup of God’s wrath, which only he can drink, and the places of honour are the Father’s to give. They will suffer for him, but they cannot share what he alone bears.

You do not know what you are asking. Not “How dare you”, but a gentle word: the first mercy in the passage. God does not grant our prayers according to our understanding of them, and there is much to be thankful for in the prayers he has declined.

The cup that I drink. In the Old Testament the cup is often God’s judgment, which the wicked must drink to the dregs (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17), and in Gethsemane Jesus will pray, “Remove this cup from me” (14:36). It is filled not by an outburst of divine irritation but by the steady, holy opposition of a pure God to everything evil. This is penal substitution: penal, because it is a real penalty for real guilt; substitution, because he bears it in our place. He took the cup that was ours, foaming with the wrath we had stored up, and drank it to the bottom.

The baptism with which I am baptized. Not water: being overwhelmed, as by a flood (Psalm 42:7; Luke 12:50). Can you be drowned in what is about to drown me?

We are able. Brave and ignorant, like Peter at the last supper (14:31): genuine loyalty resting on their own strength, which will fail (14:50).

The cup that I drink you will drink. Not sarcasm but a prophecy, and it came true. James was the first apostle to be martyred, put to the sword by Herod Agrippa about AD 44 (Acts 12:2). John was on Patmos “on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus” (Revelation 1:9), by early tradition as an exile, and is said to have lived to old age. They asked for thrones, were promised suffering, and did not fall away. But their cup is not his. Only he drinks the cup of God’s wrath for sin; theirs is suffering for his sake (when Paul speaks of filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions, Colossians 1:24, he means the sufferings of Christ’s people for the church, not any lack in the atonement).

Not mine to grant. Not that Jesus lacks authority. In the work of salvation the Father appoints and the Son carries out what the Father has planned, the same willing submission as in 13:32 and 14:36.

For whom it has been prepared. By the Father, in his eternal purpose (Matthew 20:23), and not open to lobbying. No one secures a place by asking, deserving, arriving early, or knowing the right person, and there is great relief in that for anyone who has felt they were losing a race they did not want to be running.

The Son drank the right cup. He went under the waves so that we would not drown. And the Father prepared places in his kingdom for people who had asked for all the wrong things, because the Son had drunk the right cup.

Will I have to drink the cup of God’s wrath? Never, if you belong to Christ. That is the whole point of his drinking it: for those in Christ Jesus, condemnation is gone for good (Romans 8:1). He drained it, and there is nothing left in it for his people. You may be given a different cup: suffering for his name, trials, losses, the weight of following him in a fallen world. That cup is real and sometimes bitter, but it is mixed by a Father’s hand for your good, and he drinks it with you. Never confuse the two.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” is the Old Testament picture of God’s judgment poured out; “baptism” pictures being overwhelmed by suffering. James was later killed by Herod Agrippa.

parallels.desc: the waters have come up to my neck
I have a baptism to be baptized with

verseByVerse.quote: And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant at James and John. And Jesus called them to him and said to them, "You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ’s kingdom greatness is measured not by how many serve you but by how many you serve. The ten’s anger shows they share the brothers’ ambition, and Jesus gives that ambition a new road, which runs downward.

Indignant at James and John. Very likely because the two had got in first. The ten had the same ambitions, and the lesson of chapter 9 had not taken: ambition gone underground surfaces as outrage at somebody else’s ambition, which is the usual way it appears in religious company. So Jesus calls all twelve: the disease is general, and so is the treatment.

Those who are considered rulers. Rome is the example. Both verbs, lord it over and exercise authority over, mean to domineer: power pressed down on people for the ruler’s benefit, and greatness measured by how many must do what you say. And “considered” has a sting in it: they only seem to rule; the real ruler is God.

Not so among you. Literally, it is not so among you: a statement of what his people are, and so a ban on bringing the world’s way of ruling into the church. Too much of church history ignores it, wherever a man has found that a position in the things of God can be used to make other people smaller.

Your servant … slave of all. A servant (diakonos) waits at table, and can, at the end of the day, go home. A slave has no time of his own and no choice about whom he serves. The ambition is not forbidden; it is given a road, and the road runs downward. “Slave of all” removes the last escape, choosing whom to serve: all, including the ten who are furious with you, and the two who went behind your back.

The one ruler who never lorded it. Jesus is not describing an authority he lacks: he is “the ruler of kings on earth” (Revelation 1:5). He alone had the right to press power down on everyone, and he never once did. He would not cry aloud or make his voice heard in the street (Isaiah 42:2); he used his power to heal, feed, forgive, and finally to die. The kingdom’s rule for leaders is a portrait of its King, and every true leader in his church holds a borrowed towel, the one with which he washed his disciples’ feet. On how this reshapes leadership in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

What it does not mean. Not that there is no authority in the church. Elders are to lead and be obeyed (Hebrews 13:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:12). But Christian authority is exercised as service, for the good of others: shepherd the flock, not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples (1 Peter 5:1–3).

In everyday life. If you lead at work, home or church, you serve under a King who knelt to wash your feet. Name one person under your authority and, asking the Spirit to form your Master’s mind in you, do something this week that serves their good at a cost to your convenience.

What about authority at home? The same rule holds. Scripture gives husbands headship and parents authority, and both are real (Ephesians 5:22–6:4). This commentary holds that complementarian reading, because Paul ties the husband’s role to Christ’s self-giving love; other faithful Christians, egalitarians, read these passages as mutual submission without distinct roles, and they too love Christ and hate abuse. But Jesus defines all authority among his people by this verse: it is used for the good of those under it, never to dominate, control or frighten. A husband is to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25); fathers are not to provoke their children (Ephesians 6:4). A man who uses headship to demand, belittle or harm has not understood it, and abuse is never to be tolerated in the name of authority. The test of all Christian leadership is the towel and the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus came not to be served but to serve, and his greatest service was to give his own life as the price that sets many free, in their place. This sentence sums up why he came, and explains everything in chapters 11 to 16.

For even the Son of Man. He has just told them to go to the bottom, and the reason (“For”) is not a principle but a Person. In Daniel 7 one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and is given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him (Daniel 7:13–14). If anyone had the right to be served, it was he.

Came not to be served but to serve. “Came” implies he came from somewhere, with a purpose: the one figure entitled to universal service arrived and declined it; he took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7). His supreme service was his life itself, not taken from him but given (John 10:18).

As a ransom. A “ransom” (lytron) is the price paid to free a slave, a prisoner, or someone condemned to death (Exodus 21:30). We are slaves of sin and under the sentence of death (Romans 6:23): not that we sin now and then, but that, left to ourselves, we cannot stop putting ourselves in God’s place, for everyone who practises sin is a slave to sin (John 8:34). And because God is just, that rebellion stands under his sentence. Jesus pays the price of our freedom, and the currency is his own life.

For many. “For” (anti) means in place of. He does not merely die for our benefit; he dies in our stead, and the many go free because the One is handed over. “Many” sets the one who dies against the great number for whom he dies, and comes from Isaiah 53, where the Servant bears the sin of many and makes many to be accounted righteous.

The answer to the disciples’ question. They asked, “Then who can be saved?” (v. 26). This is how: not by a lowering of the requirement, but by a payment. And the sentence closes not a sermon on the atonement but a squabble about the best seats. Everything asked of you as a Christian is asked on that basis. You are not told to serve because service is noble. You are told to serve because the one who owned everything went to the bottom and stayed there, until it killed him, and bought you on the way down.

The ransomed will stand and sing. The one who owed nothing paid everything (1 Peter 1:18–19). And the many he ransomed will stand before him at last and sing that he was slain, and by his blood ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Revelation 5:9).

To whom was the ransom paid? Not to Satan, as some of the early fathers imagined, as though the devil held a rightful claim that God had to buy out. He holds no such claim; he is a thief with stolen goods (3:27), and God owes him nothing. The debt is owed to the justice of God, whose law we have broken, and God, in the person of his Son, pays it himself. There is no angry Father and reluctant Son here, but one God, Father, Son and Spirit, in perfect love, resolving in himself what could be resolved no other way.

Is it fair for an innocent man to die in place of the guilty? It would be unjust if an unwilling victim were seized and punished for someone else. But the one who dies is the Judge himself, come in the flesh, giving his life willingly (John 10:18) for people he has made his own, as a husband takes on his wife’s debts. God neither ignores sin nor punishes an unwilling party. He bears in himself the cost of his own justice, so that he is both “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). The moralist would rather pay his own way, the sceptic thinks no one should pay at all, and the cross answers both: the debt is real, and only God could pay it.

How do I know I am one of the many? Not by trying to read God’s secret decree, but by coming to Christ. The invitation is to everyone: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). If you trust Jesus as Saviour and Lord, you are one of the many, for that faith is itself the fruit of his ransom. Assurance grows as you look to his promises, as the Spirit testifies that you are God’s child (Romans 8:16), and as you see a changed life. Definite atonement is not a wall to keep you out but a guarantee that, if you are his, nothing can undo what he paid for you.

Where Christians differ: who are the many?
