Reformed theology reads the ransom as definite: Christ gave his life for his people, those the Father had given him (John 10:11, 15; 17:9), and his death actually secures their freedom, since a ransom that is paid frees the captive. Other traditions read “many” as all, a universal offer. The word alone does not settle it, since in Hebrew idiom “many” can mean the great multitude; the argument rests on what a ransom is and on Jesus laying down his life for the sheep. Many faithful Christians, Arminians among them (who hold that Christ died to make salvation possible for all and that grace can be resisted), read it otherwise and love the same Saviour. This commentary’s view: the ransom is real and effective; it does not merely make freedom possible but actually purchases it for the many. This is definite atonement. And the gospel offer still goes freely to all, since no one who comes to Christ will be turned away (John 6:37). His death is sufficient for all and is offered to all.
verseByVerse.note: A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out and say, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, "Son of David, have mercy on me!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A blind beggar who has only heard Jesus’ name sees who he is, the Son of David, and will not be silenced in crying to him for mercy.

Jericho. The last stop before the climb to the city, with Passover days away. This second healing of a blind man matches the one at Bethsaida (8:22–26); between them Jesus has taught about the cross while his disciples were blind to it.

As he was leaving Jericho. Luke says “as he drew near to Jericho” (Luke 18:35), and Matthew mentions two blind men (Matthew 20:30). There were two Jerichos, the ancient mound and the Herodian town, so he may have been leaving one and approaching the other, though it cannot be proved; and Mark names the one blind man the church knew without saying there was only one.

Bartimaeus. The only person healed in Mark who is named (“Bar” is Aramaic for son of), most likely because the church knew him: a named man is a witness others could check.

Jesus, Son of David. The crowd says “Jesus of Nazareth”; Bartimaeus has only heard a name, and answers with a far greater one. “Son of David” is a messianic title: the promised king from David’s line, whose throne God would establish for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16), the shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1), expected to give sight to the blind (Isaiah 35:5; 61:1). It is the first time in Mark anyone uses it. Everyone in this chapter who can see has misunderstood him, and the man who cannot see names him correctly at the first attempt. Jesus does not silence him: the time for keeping quiet about who he is has almost ended, and he is about to enter Jerusalem as the Son of David (11:10).

Have mercy on me! The cry of one with no claim, only need: mercy is what you ask for when the only ground of the request is the character of the one you ask (Luke 18:13). He is the only one in the chapter who gets exactly what he came for. And every cry of “Lord, have mercy”, from Jericho to this morning, has reached the ears of a King who loves to answer it.

Many rebuked him. That word “rebuked” again, as with the parents of the children (v. 13): a beggar bawling at a distinguished rabbi on a pilgrimage road was a nuisance. But he cried out all the more. Jesus is passing by and will not come this way again, and the disapproval of respectable people is a price Bartimaeus does not mind paying.

In everyday life. Pray the beggar’s prayer, “Son of David, have mercy on me”, on the way to work, before a hard conversation, when you have failed again.

What if others discourage me from coming to Christ? Do what Bartimaeus did: cry out all the more. Some are discouraged by family, some by a church that made them feel they did not fit, some by an inner voice that says they are too messy, too late. The crowd told this man to be quiet, and the crowd was wrong; Jesus stopped for the shouting. And if you are part of the crowd, be careful whom you silence.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 15 miles north-east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan. Bartimaeus means “son of Timaeus.” “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stopped and said, "Call him." And they called the blind man, saying to him, "Take heart. Get up; he is calling you." And throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stops for the one man everyone wanted silenced and calls him through the very crowd that hushed him, and the beggar throws off his cloak and comes.

And Jesus stopped. He has been walking ahead with a set face (v. 32), and the Son of God on his way to die halts the whole procession for one beggar whom everybody else was trying to silence. Nothing in his life was ever too urgent for a person.

Call him. He does not go to Bartimaeus. He tells the people who had been hushing the man to call him, and Bartimaeus must answer and come. The crowd that hindered is made to be the crowd that brings.

Take heart. “Get up; he is calling you.” Thirty seconds ago they were hushing him; the moment Jesus took an interest, so did they. A warning for any church: the person you find embarrassing, too loud or too needy may be the one Christ is calling. And these could be the words of every evangelist: take heart, get up, Jesus is calling you.

Throwing off his cloak. A beggar’s cloak was probably spread to catch coins, his bed at night and his shelter from the cold, a possession the law protected (Exodus 22:26–27): quite literally all he had. He throws it aside, blind, with no idea whether he will find it again, and springs to his feet toward a voice, not knowing what is in the way. He heard “he is calling you”, and that was enough.

How does Jesus call people today? Through the gospel, spoken by ordinary people. As he used the crowd, he uses preachers, parents, friends and colleagues to say: “Take heart. Get up; he is calling you.” When the Spirit takes that word and opens a heart, the call is effectual, and the sinner comes freely and gladly, as this man sprang up (Romans 8:30; 10:14–17). Effectual means that it does what it says: it does not merely invite but brings the dead heart to life and the sinner to Christ, as surely as Jesus’ word brought Lazarus out of the tomb (John 11:43–44). If you feel the gospel’s pull, do not wait for a voice from heaven; this is his call. And if you know him, you are part of the crowd he sends. Tell someone.
verseByVerse.note: A beggar’s cloak was spread to collect coins and was also his covering at night.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "What do you want me to do for you?" And the blind man said to him, "Rabbi, let me recover my sight." And Jesus said to him, "Go your way; your faith has made you well." And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked what he wants, the beggar asks for sight, receives it at Jesus’ word, and uses his new eyes and his freedom to follow Jesus on the road to the cross.

What do you want me to do for you? The same question he asked James and John (v. 36), and the answers could not differ more. It is obvious what a blind beggar wants, but Jesus will not do things to people over their heads, and he gives the man a dignity nobody had shown him in years.

Rabbi. Literally Rabbouni, my master, a more personal and reverent form than the ordinary Rabbi, found elsewhere in the New Testament only on the lips of Mary Magdalene when she recognises the risen Christ (John 20:16).

Let me recover my sight. Not money, which he had begged for all his life, but sight, which would end his livelihood: he asks for what will cost him his old life.

Your faith has made you well. “Made you well” (sesōken) is literally has saved you, the word Jesus spoke to the woman with the bleeding (5:34). Physical healing and spiritual salvation are both in it: the faith that received his sight received the Saviour himself. The power lay not in how much he understood, though he got the title right, nor in his persistence, though he had plenty. His faith was the empty hand that received what Jesus gave. Faith saves because of whom it takes hold of, and this man took hold of the Son of David and would not be shouted down.

Immediately. No touch, no saliva, no second stage, unlike the man at Bethsaida (8:22–25). Just the word.

Followed him on the way. The last words of the section, and the most important. Told to go his way, free to go home and start a life, he goes Christ’s way instead: the first thing he does with his eyes and his freedom is get on the road behind the man who healed him. “On the way” in this Gospel is never merely geography: it is the road to Jerusalem and the cross (v. 32). He is the last person healed in Mark before the passion, and the picture of the true disciple the Twelve should be: his eyes opened, he follows Jesus to the cross.

How the chapter ends. It began with a wealthy, moral man who went home with everything he came with, and ends with a blind beggar who threw away the one cloak he had and followed. It is what Jesus said in verse 15: the ones who get in are the ones who come with nothing and simply receive.

The first thing he saw. The first thing the healed man saw was the face of Jesus. That is the gift he gives every one of his people: to behold the glory of God in the face of Christ, and then to follow him on the way.

Does Jesus still heal the blind? He can, and he sometimes heals in answer to prayer, and we should pray for the sick with confidence in his power and submission to his will (James 5:14–15). But Mark tells this story above all as a picture of salvation: we are all born blind to God, and the greater miracle, which he performs every day, is opening hearts to see his glory (2 Corinthians 4:4–6). And for those who are not healed in this life, the promise is sure: in the resurrection the eyes of the blind will be opened for ever (Isaiah 35:5).

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

10.theology: Divorce, and what Mark leaves out. Matthew records an exception, except for sexual immorality (Matt. 5:32; 19:9), and Mark records none, while adding, for his Roman readers, the case of a wife who divorces her husband. This is a difference of purpose, not a contradiction (see “The exceptions” at vv. 10–12, and the box “Where Christians differ: divorce and remarriage” at the end of that note). Mark simply refuses to lead with the exception: Jesus begins with the joining God performs.
10.examples:
Then: a blind beggar at Jericho is called to Jesus and throws off his cloak (v. 50), quite literally all he had (see the note on vv. 49–50).

Now: set him beside the man at the start of the chapter (see “How the chapter ends” at vv. 51–52). What we hold on to when Christ calls shows what we trust. The beggar did not throw the cloak away to earn anything. He threw it away because the one calling him was worth more.

keyVerse.quote: For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.
keyVerse.note: This verse explains the whole Gospel: why the one who had every right to be served walked to Jerusalem to die. It answers the disciples’ question, “Then who can be saved?” (v. 26), with a price paid in his own life, in the place of many. And it reshapes every ambition in the chapter, because those he ransomed learn greatness from the one who went to the bottom for them.

10.reflection:
Jesus answers a question about divorce by going back to what God made marriage to be (vv. 6–9). How does starting from God’s design rather than from the limits of what is allowed change the way we think about marriage, singleness and our promises?

The rich man was sincere, moral and eager, and Jesus loved him, yet he went away sorrowful because of one thing (vv. 21–22). What might your “one thing” be, and what would it look like to hold it with open hands this week?

Jesus says that whoever does not receive the kingdom like a child will not enter it (v. 15), and that salvation is impossible with man but not with God (v. 27). Why do capable, responsible people find this so hard to accept? Where do you still try to bring something to God to earn his welcome?

James and John asked for glory, Bartimaeus asked for mercy (vv. 35–52), and Jesus said that he came to serve and to give his life as a ransom (v. 45). In your family, church or work, where is the “downward road” of serving others costly for you, and how does his ransom make it possible to take it gladly?

11.title: Leaves Without Fruit
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples <sup>2</sup>and said to them, “Go into the village in front of you, and immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. <sup>3</sup>If anyone says to you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord has need of it and will send it back here immediately.’” <sup>4</sup>And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside in the street, and they untied it. <sup>5</sup>And some of those standing there said to them, “What are you doing, untying the colt?” <sup>6</sup>And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go. <sup>7</sup>And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. <sup>8</sup>And many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches that they had cut from the fields. <sup>9</sup>And those who went before and those who followed were shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! <sup>10</sup>Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!” <sup>11</sup>And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. And when he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve. <sup>12</sup>On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. <sup>13</sup>And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. <sup>14</sup>And he said to it, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again.” And his disciples heard it. <sup>15</sup>And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. <sup>16</sup>And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple. <sup>17</sup>And he was teaching them and saying to them, “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers.” <sup>18</sup>And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. <sup>19</sup>And when evening came they went out of the city. <sup>20</sup>As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. <sup>21</sup>And Peter remembered and said to him, “Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered.” <sup>22</sup>And Jesus answered them, “Have faith in God. <sup>23</sup>Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. <sup>24</sup>Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours. <sup>25</sup>And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses.” <sup>27</sup>And they came again to Jerusalem. And as he was walking in the temple, the chief priests and the scribes and the elders came to him, <sup>28</sup>and they said to him, “By what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?” <sup>29</sup>Jesus said to them, “I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>30</sup>Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me.” <sup>31</sup>And they discussed it with one another, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ <sup>32</sup>But shall we say, ‘From man’?”—they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. <sup>33</sup>So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.”
11.overview:
Where we are. The road to Jerusalem (8:27–10:52) ends here, and Mark 11 opens the last week of Jesus’ life, to which Mark gives about a third of his book (see the introduction). The man who for ten chapters silenced those who worked out who he was now rides into the city as its King.

The message. The King has come to his house looking for fruit, and found only leaves. Jesus claims publicly to be the humble King Zechariah promised, inspects the temple, and pronounces God’s judgment on worship that is splendid on the outside and barren within. Then he shows his people where God will be met instead: by faith in God, bold prayer and forgiveness. His authority for all of it comes from no human council but from his Father.

Why it was said. Mark’s mostly Gentile readers lived around the time the temple fell, or was about to fall (see the introduction). They needed to know why God would let his own house be destroyed, whether it had ever been meant for people like them, and how anyone could draw near to God without it. This chapter answers all three.

How the chapter makes its case. The entry (vv. 1–11) shows the King: a borrowed colt, cloaks on the road, the Passover psalm shouted by a crowd that is right about who he is and wrong about what he came to do, and a silent inspection of the temple. Then Mark sets the temple between the two halves of a fig tree story, so that each explains the other. A tree in full leaf with nothing on it is cursed (vv. 12–14); the court where the nations should pray is cleared, with Isaiah’s promise and Jeremiah’s warning (vv. 15–19); and next morning the tree is dead to its roots (vv. 20–21). Out of the dead tree comes teaching on faith, prayer and forgiveness (vv. 22–25). The chapter ends with the Sanhedrin asking by what authority? and refusing the one question that would have led them home (vv. 27–33).

Where it leads. The hungry man at the fig tree is the owner’s beloved Son, come for his fruit (12:6). Within days he will hang on a tree under the curse that fruitless people deserve, and as he dies the temple curtain will be torn in two (15:38). The house of prayer for all the nations will be his own body, raised. The crowd’s Hosanna, “save, we pray”, will be answered, though almost no one who shouted it recognised the answer when it came.

For us. It is possible to be enthusiastic about Jesus and want a different Christ, and to be busy with religion that is all leaves. Let him look at your life. Bring him your barrenness, your mountains and your grudges, and do not dodge his question about who he is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — The Entry, the Fig Tree, and the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The King comes to his house looking for fruit, finds only leaves, and pronounces judgment; then he shows his disciples where God will now be met: by faith, prayer and forgiveness. He enters the city as Zechariah’s humble King and inspects the temple in silence (vv. 1–11). Next morning he curses a fig tree that is all leaf and no fruit (vv. 12–14), clears the court where the nations were meant to pray, and quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah against those who had made it a den (vv. 15–19). The withered tree confirms the sentence, and Jesus turns his disciples from a doomed building to faith in God, bold prayer and a forgiving heart (vv. 20–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
Was it fair to curse a tree out of season? The answer turns on the leaves: a tree in full leaf was claiming to have something, and it had nothing (see the note on vv. 12–14).

And look where Mark has put it. He splits the story and sets the temple in the gap: curse, temple, withered tree (on what each tells us of the other, see “The tree is the temple” at vv. 12–14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a temple full of activity, and worshippers who went home feeling delivered.

Now: does your churchgoing make you more uncomfortable about how you live the rest of the week, or less? (On that test, and the way out, see “Using the den” at vv. 17–19.)

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples and said to them, "Go into the village in front of you, and immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. If anyone says to you, 'Why are you doing this?' say, 'The Lord has need of it and will send it back here immediately.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus deliberately arranges his entry into Jerusalem as its King, sending ahead for a colt set apart for him. After ten chapters of silencing those who knew who he was, he chooses the moment, the place and the animal himself.

Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives. Two villages on the ridge east of Jerusalem; Bethany, about two miles (3 km) out, was where Jesus stayed this week (v. 11). From the Mount of Olives you look straight down onto the temple platform, and it is where Zechariah says the LORD will stand when he comes for his people: “On that day his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives” (Zechariah 14:4). He approaches from the direction the prophets had marked, and the man who has walked everywhere now sends ahead for something to ride.

You will find a colt tied. A young donkey. Matthew mentions its mother as well (Matthew 21:2), which is more detail, not a contradiction. Whether Jesus knew this supernaturally (2:8) or had arranged it beforehand, every step of this week is deliberate.

On which no one has ever sat. An animal for a sacred purpose had never been put to ordinary work (Numbers 19:2; 1 Samuel 6:7). This colt is set apart for the King.

The Lord has need of it. “The Lord” (ho kyrios) could mean simply “the master”, the one with a right to use it, but Mark’s readers would hear more: the Lord of all creation borrows a donkey.

Will send it back. Samuel warned that Israel’s kings would take what they wanted (1 Samuel 8:16–17). This King, who has every right to take, asks, and gives back. No one has ever been the poorer for lending to him: “Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed” (Proverbs 19:17).

The setting. It is Passover, when pilgrims swelled Jerusalem several times over and the governor brought extra troops, because the feasts were when riots were most feared.

He comes to us asking. The King of glory rode into his city on a borrowed colt, as he would be laid in a borrowed tomb. Blessed is the Lord who has every right to command, and comes to us asking.

Does God really need anything from me? Not in the sense of lacking it: he is not served by human hands as though he needed anything (Acts 17:25). But he chooses to use what his people give, and honours it by calling it a need. Your gifts, time and skills are not necessary to him, and they are wanted by him.
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem. An animal never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose.

parallels.desc: a heifer on which a yoke has never come

verseByVerse.quote: And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside in the street, and they untied it. And some of those standing there said to them, "What are you doing, untying the colt?" And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything happens exactly as Jesus said, and his bare word is enough to carry the disciples through.

A colt tied at a door outside in the street. They went, they found, they untied: the door, the street and the bystanders are the details of someone who was there. Nobody in a village stands by while two strangers lead off their livestock, and Mark’s report is almost comic in its restraint. The objection evaporated at the sentence Jesus had given them; perhaps the owners knew him, or had been asked in advance.

Two errands, one Lord. Mark tells a second errand in almost the same words: a man carrying a water jar and a furnished upper room, just as he said (14:13–16). The Lord who knew where the colt stood knew who would betray him and that Peter would deny him (14:30). He did not stumble into Jerusalem and get caught. He went up knowing every door and every street of the road to the cross, and walked it anyway, for us.

Going with nothing but the word. The disciples had no documents, only a sentence they had been told to say, and it held. Much Christian obedience is like that: you go with the word you were given into a situation you cannot control, and find that it holds. And the owners, whom Mark does not name, handed over their property on the strength of that sentence, and the King rode into his city on it. Like the man who lent the upper room, they are in the story because something they owned was asked for and they did not say no.

What if God asks for something and I do not know why? Obedience often comes before understanding. Test any sense of calling by Scripture and seek wise counsel, because not every impulse is his voice. But where his word is plain, to give, to forgive, to speak, to serve, do not wait to see the whole picture. You will see it later, and be glad you said yes.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. And many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches that they had cut from the fields.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By riding into the city on a colt, Jesus publicly claims to be the King Zechariah promised, a humble King who brings peace. The crowd welcomes him as a king, but not as this kind of king.

And he sat on it. With cloaks for a saddle, he rides the last two miles. Zechariah had foretold it: “Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! … Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). Mark does not quote it (Matthew 21:5 and John 12:15 do); the action speaks for itself.

An unbroken colt. Anyone who has been near an unbroken young donkey in a noisy crowd knows what usually happens. Nothing happens. It carries him. The one creature in Jerusalem that week that did exactly what he wanted was a donkey.

A donkey, not a horse. Kings rode to war on horses, but in peace on a donkey or mule, as Solomon rode David’s mule to his coronation (1 Kings 1:33–40). Zechariah goes on: God will cut off the chariot and the war horse, and the King shall speak peace to the nations (Zechariah 9:10). The choice of animal is a sermon: a king of peace, not a warrior come to overthrow Rome.

Cloaks and branches. Cloaks on the road were royal custom: when Jehu was proclaimed king, the people put their garments under him (2 Kings 9:13). A cloak in the dirt says: this is my king, and I will spend something to say so. John specifies palm branches (John 12:13), which had been waved when Simon Maccabeus took the citadel of Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 13:51). The crowd is doing something precise, and political: cloaks for a king, branches for a liberator.

He came at walking pace. The Lord of hosts could have come on the clouds with ten thousand angels. He came at walking pace, gentle with a crowd that would soon desert him, because he came not to crush his enemies but to die for them. They laid down their cloaks for him; he laid down his life for them. And when he comes again, no one will mistake what kind of King he is.

Right about who, wrong about what. The man they welcome as Israel’s liberator is riding toward an execution, and within five days a crowd in this city will be shouting for it. It is still possible to be genuinely thrilled about Jesus, to sing loudly and spend something on him, and to expect a different Christ: one who will sort out your circumstances, vindicate your side, and deliver you from whatever you want delivering from. The cloaks were sincere. And by Friday the road was empty.

How do I avoid following a Jesus of my own making? Read the whole of the Gospels, especially the parts that unsettle you, and let him define himself. The real Jesus saves from sin before he saves from circumstances, calls us to a cross before he gives a crown, and is Lord over our politics, not a mascot for them. Ask whether what you expect of him comes from his word or your wishes, and when he disappoints your plans, do not leave the road; he is doing something greater than you asked.
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey

verseByVerse.quote: And those who went before and those who followed were shouting, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd hails Jesus as the promised King of David’s line, and its cry, Hosanna, is a prayer for far more than it knows.

Hosanna! Save, we pray (Psalm 118:25): a cry for help that had become a shout of praise, like “God save the king”. Both meanings fit: the crowd praises Jesus, and unknowingly prays for exactly what he has come to do. Psalm 118 was sung at Passover, and every pilgrim knew it by heart.

He who comes. Psalm 118:26, once a greeting to pilgrims at the temple gates, but also a title for the Messiah: John the Baptist’s messengers asked, “Are you the one who is to come?” (Matthew 11:3). The same psalm speaks of the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22), which Jesus will quote against the leaders within a day or two (12:10).

The kingdom of our father David. Only Mark records this line, which says what the psalm meant to the crowd: David’s throne is about to be restored. Under Roman occupation that was a dangerous thing to shout. The kingdom is coming, but not as they imagine.

The right prayer, not recognised. “Save now” was exactly the right request, made to the right person at the right hour, and they had no idea what they were asking for. They wanted saving from Rome; he had come to save them from something worse. The salvation they were shouting for would be won by Friday afternoon, on a cross, and by then this road would be empty. He answered it, and almost nobody who prayed it recognised the answer. But every hosanna ever sung is answered in him, and blessed is he who will come again, when the whole creation shouts it and understands it at last.

Are the crowds of Palm Sunday the same people who shouted crucify him? Probably not all of them. Many on the road were Galilean pilgrims who had followed Jesus; the crowd before Pilate gathered early in the morning and was stirred up by the chief priests (15:11). But popular enthusiasm is fickle, and no one should build his faith on the mood of a crowd, including the crowd at church. All of us have the same heart that can praise him one day and reject him the next. That is why we need a Saviour, not just a hero.
verseByVerse.note: “Hosanna” means “save, we pray,” and had become a shout of praise.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. And when he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The King goes straight to the house of God and inspects it in silence, and judgment will follow.

Into the temple. Not the palace or the fortress: the Messiah goes to the house of God, as Malachi had promised: “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple… But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire” (Malachi 3:1–2). It was Herod’s temple, under construction for more than forty years (John 2:20), a wonder of the ancient world on a platform of about 35 acres (14 hectares); the word means the whole complex with its courts.

Looked around at everything. An inspection, recorded only by Mark: the traders, tables and caged birds, seen by the one person present who knew what the building was for, as God looks for fruit from his vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7). He did not say a word.

Out to Bethany. He lodged outside the city each night this week (v. 19; 14:3; Luke 21:37): Jerusalem was crowded for Passover, and dangerous for him.

Judgment, not temper. What he does next day is not a loss of temper. He saw it all the night before, slept on it, walked two miles back, and then overturned the tables: a considered act, which is what makes it judgment. He sees everything, and he is never hasty and never unjust. The inspection is itself the warning. Before God acts, God looks: he came down to see Babel (Genesis 11:5) and Sodom (Genesis 18:21), and the risen Christ walks among the lampstands saying to church after church, I know your works (Revelation 2–3).

Should I be afraid of Christ looking at my life? If you are not his, his gaze is a warning to flee to him while there is time. If you are his, it is the look of a Saviour who already knows the worst and has paid for it, and will never cast you out (John 6:37). But it is still searching, because he loves his house too much to leave it cluttered. Let it lead you to confession, not hiding. The safest place for a sinner is under the eyes of the Lord who died for him.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was about two miles east of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. And he said to it, "May no one ever eat fruit from you again." And his disciples heard it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus curses a fig tree that is all leaves and no fruit, an acted parable of God’s judgment on worship that looks alive and bears nothing. Mark sets the temple (vv. 15–19) between the curse and the withered tree (vv. 20–21), so that each explains the other, as he often sandwiches stories (3:20–35; 5:21–43).

He was hungry. The Son of God, after a two-mile walk before breakfast, wanting something to eat: truly human, as Mark keeps showing us, asleep on a cushion in a storm, hungry on a road.

A fig tree in leaf … for it was not the season for figs. The likely answer to the obvious objection lies in how a fig tree works: with its spring leaves, or before them, it produced small edible early knobs (paggim); the main crop came in June. A tree in full leaf with no early fruit was probably barren that year, and its leaves were a false advertisement. Mark’s remark is not an embarrassment but the key: Jesus was not merely cross about a missed breakfast. The curse, the only miracle of cursing in the Gospels, is an acted parable like the prophets’ symbolic actions (Jeremiah 13:1–11; 19:1–13), said aloud to be remembered (v. 21).

The fig tree in the prophets. The fig tree was a recognised picture of Israel (Hosea 9:10). “When I would gather them, declares the LORD, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree; even the leaves are withered” (Jeremiah 8:13). God came looking for fruit in his people and found none.

The tree is the temple. Israel’s worship that week was in magnificent leaf: the courts packed for Passover, the sacrifices running from dawn, the money moving. From the road it looked like the healthiest religion on earth, but it was bare of the fruit of true worship and righteousness. He came near, looked around at everything (v. 11), and found nothing but leaves. The sentence the tree received would be carried out on the building about forty years later, when not one stone was left on another (13:2).

The owner comes for his fruit. Within a day Jesus tells the rulers the same story in words: a man planted a vineyard, sent servant after servant for his share of the fruit, and last of all sent his beloved son, whom they killed (12:1–8). The hungry man at the fig tree is that Son, the Lord of the harvest come in person. He is also what Israel was meant to be, the one Israelite whose life was all fruit, loving God with all his heart and his neighbour as himself. The barren tree would wither, and the fruitful Son would be cut down for the barren, so that all who are joined to him by faith, like grafted branches, might live and bear fruit for God.

What it does not mean. Not that God has rejected the Jewish people for ever (Romans 11:1–2, 25–29). The judgment fell on the temple, destroyed in AD 70, and on the leadership that rejected their Messiah.

Leaves and fruit in my life. The tree was condemned because its leaves promised what it did not have. Leaves are what others can see: the attendance, the vocabulary, the reputation for soundness, the Bible on the table. Fruit is what is actually there: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23), and lives changed by the gospel. From a distance leaves are enough, but he comes near, and looks.

Did Jesus not know there would be no fruit? He went to the tree as a man looking for fruit, because that was the point of the sign: he had come to Israel looking for fruit, and found only leaves. In his human nature he did not display all he knew at every moment, but nothing here took him by surprise.

What if I feel fruitless? A tender conscience that grieves over little fruit is itself a sign of life; the fig tree felt nothing. Fruit is not manufactured by effort but grown by the Spirit as you abide in Christ (John 15:4–5), through his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of his people. It often grows slowly and is more visible to others than to you, so ask a mature Christian who knows you what they see. Bring your barrenness to the Lord who promised that the one who abides in him bears much fruit.
verseByVerse.note: Leaves on a fig tree normally promise early fruit. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: no figs on the fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus drives the trade out of the one court where the nations could pray, an act that both cleanses the temple and announces its judgment.

Drive out those who sold and those who bought. The trading was in the Court of the Gentiles, the only part of the temple where non-Jews could pray; beyond it, notices threatened death to any Gentile who went further. Pilgrims needed approved sacrificial animals, and the temple tax had to be paid in silver coins from Tyre, changed at a profit; the trade is thought to have enriched the high priestly family. He does not attack the sacrifices God commanded, or money-changing as such, but where it happened: the one part of God’s house open to the nations had become a livestock market and currency exchange, and a God-fearing Greek who came to pray stood among cattle pens and coin tables, in the noise.

The seats of those who sold pigeons. Pigeons were the sacrifice the poor could afford (Leviticus 5:7; 12:8), as Jesus’ own parents had offered when they presented him in this very building (Luke 2:24). Profit from the poor in God’s house was especially offensive, and those seats go over.

Carry anything through the temple. Only Mark records this. Jesus stopped the traffic through the court, and for the first time in years a Gentile could have stood there and prayed: he cleared room for the people nobody thought about.

Cleansing or judgment? Both: the temple was restored for a moment to its purpose, but like the fig tree this was an acted prophecy. Jesus was not reforming the temple but announcing its end. He himself would be the new temple, the place where God meets his people (John 2:19–21; 14:58). Within days he would be the sacrifice himself, the offering no money could buy, so that rich and poor, Jew and Gentile, could come to God without a market in between; the court he cleared for the nations for an afternoon he opened for ever when the temple curtain was torn in two at his death (15:38).

Was Jesus’ anger sinful, and may I copy it? His anger was holy: zeal for his Father’s house (John 2:17), aimed at the abuse of God’s worship and of the poor, considered overnight, without personal grudge. Ours is rarely so pure. Scripture allows anger without sin (Ephesians 4:26), but most of ours is about our own rights and comfort, and “the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:20). The passage gives no licence for violence or taking the law into our own hands, but it does call us to care about what God cares about: his worship, the outsider and the poor.

One cleansing or two? John records a cleansing at the start of Jesus’ ministry (John 2:13–22). Some think there was one, placed differently for theological reasons; but the details and words differ, and the abuse was the kind that would return, so he may well have done it twice. Nothing in the meaning hangs on it.

Uncertain wording. “Anything” translates skeuos, usually a vessel, container or piece of equipment. Mark may mean goods carried across the court as a short cut, or vessels used in the temple’s own trade; we cannot be sure. Either way, Jesus stopped the court being used as a passage for business and gave it back to prayer.
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court, the only place Gentiles could pray. Pigeons were the sacrifice the poor could afford. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax.

parallels.desc: pigeons for those who cannot afford a lamb

verseByVerse.quote: And he was teaching them and saying to them, "Is it not written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations'? But you have made it a den of robbers." And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. And when evening came they went out of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus explains his action from two prophets: God meant his house to be a place of prayer for every nation, and its keepers had made it a hiding place for people who wanted religion without repentance.

Is it not written. The tables are on the floor and the birds are loose, and Mark calls it teaching.

A house of prayer for all the nations. Isaiah 56:7 is God’s promise to the outsider, the foreigner and the eunuch once excluded from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1–8). Only Mark keeps “for all the nations”: the market stood in the one court where the nations could pray, and had pushed out precisely the people the verse was about. Mark’s Gentile readers would see themselves in it: God had always meant his house to be theirs too.

A den of robbers. Jeremiah 7:11, from his sermon at the temple gate before Babylon destroyed it. A robbers’ den is not where the robbery happens but where thieves retreat to feel safe: the people would steal and swear falsely, then stand in God’s house and say, “We are delivered!” (Jeremiah 7:9–10). The quotation carries its threat: as before, the temple will fall.

Seeking a way to destroy him. The first time the chief priests act against Jesus in Mark, as he had foretold (8:31; 10:33): the temple authorities, whose institution and income he had challenged, join the plot (14:1). With the crowd hanging on his teaching they could not arrest him openly; it will take the night, and somebody on the inside.

The eunuch and the foreigner come home. Within a few years an Ethiopian eunuch, reading Isaiah 53 on the road home from Jerusalem, was baptised into Christ (Acts 8:26–39). Jesus did not merely clear a court; he became the house. In him, crucified for all nations, God’s house of prayer stands open to every people, and the outsider Isaiah promised to make joyful is made joyful at last.

Using the den. Does your churchgoing make you more uncomfortable about how you live the rest of the week, or less? A man who holds a grudge for years, sharpens his invoices and is cold to his wife, and finds that an hour on Sunday settles his conscience without altering any of it, has not been worshipping. He has been using the den. The way out is not to stop coming but to come differently: the den is where sin is hidden, and the house of prayer is where it is confessed and forgiven (1 John 1:9). The Lord who overturned the tables welcomes every thief who comes to him empty-handed.

Is my church a house of prayer for all nations? Can a stranger, an immigrant, a person of another class or background, find a welcome and room to pray, or does he meet a closed circle, insider language and a busy programme with no space for him? Do we pray for the nations, support mission, and welcome those from other cultures as family? The temple courts were cluttered with good things in the wrong place, and ours usually are too. Clear room for the people Jesus cleared room for.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark keeps “for all the nations” from Isaiah’s words.

parallels.desc: a house of prayer for all peoples

verseByVerse.quote: As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. And Peter remembered and said to him, "Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered." And Jesus answered them, "Have faith in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The withered tree shows that the sentence on fruitless religion has fallen, and Jesus points his disciples to where God is now found: faith in God himself.

Withered away to its roots. Not wilted: dead from the roots up, from the part nobody can see, within a day. It is complete judgment: “their root is dried up; they shall bear no fruit” (Hosea 9:16; Job 18:16). Matthew, compressing, says it withered at once (Matthew 21:19); Mark, following the days as they came, gives the two mornings. The disciples walked past this tree twice, and the second time it was a dead stick.

Rabbi, look! If Peter’s preaching lies behind Mark’s Gospel (see the introduction), Peter tells this against himself: he saw a dead tree and got excited about the tree. The withering is not the point. The temple is the point, and he has walked past that twice as well.

Have faith in God. A surprising response. Jesus does not explain the tree (the temple’s end comes in 13:2); he turns to faith, because the centre of Israel’s worship is under judgment. Where will God’s people meet him now? Not in a building, but through faith in God, and prayer. They have seen a word spoken to a tree, and the tree obeyed, and they are about to be sent into a world of things far more immovable than a fig.

Faith in God, not faith in faith. Not trust in the power of your own believing, a modern superstition and a cruel one, but trust in a Person, who hears, and decides, and is good. Read the promises that follow in that light.

The curse he would carry. The disciples stand in front of a tree under a curse. Within three days the Lord who spoke that curse would himself be hanged on a tree, and Paul draws the line plainly: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us”, for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” (Galatians 3:13). The sentence on fruitless religion is real, and it falls; but the only fruitful Israelite who ever lived went under it in the place of the fruitless. That is why “Have faith in God” is good news and not a threat.

Where do I meet God now that there is no temple? In Christ, the true temple, where God dwells with men (John 2:19–21). Through him every believer may draw near to God anywhere, by the Spirit (Hebrews 10:19–22; John 4:21–24), and the gathered church is now his temple too (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:19–22), which is why meeting with God’s people on the Lord’s Day matters. You need no holy building, priest or pilgrimage; you need Christ, and faith in God through him.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus invites his people to ask God boldly for things far beyond them and to trust him to answer, because faith rests on God, not on itself.

Whoever says to this mountain. Moving a mountain was proverbial for doing the impossible (1 Corinthians 13:2; on which mountain, see “Uncertain wording” below). The point is that it is too big, and he tells them to say so out loud.

And does not doubt in his heart. To doubt here is to be divided in heart, wavering “like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind” (James 1:6–8). Its opposite is faith that rests entirely on God and believes that what he says will come to pass.

Believe that you have received it. “Have received” (elabete) is a past tense: believe it as already given. Faith counts God’s answer as certain before it is seen (Hebrews 11:1). That means not pretending you already hold the thing, but trusting that God has heard and will give what is truly good, so that you can stop pleading anxiously and leave the request with him (Philippians 4:6–7).

What it plainly does say. Do not soften it first. Most of us are not in danger of presumption; we are in danger of praying for nothing much, in case nothing happens. The God we pray to moves mountains, raises the dead and turns hearts of stone to flesh, and he invites the weakest of his children to ask him for great things.

The prayer that was not granted. The boldness of this promise rests on a garden on the same hill, where within days the one man who never doubted in his heart asked his Father to remove the cup, and the cup did not pass: “not what I will, but what you will” (14:36). The Father did not take the cup from his Son, so that he could say yes to us. The mountain of our guilt, which no faith of ours could shift, was cast into the depths of the sea when Christ drank that cup (Micah 7:19). We ask for mountains to move because the greatest one has already been moved.

What it does not mean. Not a technique for making God do our will by believing hard enough, which turns him into a force. Prayer in faith is prayer according to God’s will (1 John 5:14–15), in Jesus’ name (John 14:13–14), from a heart that seeks his kingdom (Matthew 6:10, 33).

Prayer is the opposite of magic. Our age is officially sceptical and privately full of spells, such as manifesting: picture what you want with enough conviction and the universe will deliver it, putting an out-of-control life back in your hands. C. S. Lewis observed in The Abolition of Man that the wise of old asked how to conform the soul to reality, while magic, like much of modern technology, asks how to bend reality to our wishes. Manifesting is magic in wellness clothing, with magic’s cruelty: if the thing does not come, you did not believe hard enough. Jesus’ promise looks similar and is the reverse, because its object is God. Magic wants a lever; Jesus gives you a Father. A lever can never be wiser than the one who pushes it. A Father can say no, and can also give you what you would never have thought to ask.

I prayed in faith and did not receive. Was it my fault? Very likely not, and this is written for you, because this passage most often wounds people like you; blaming your faith only adds a second grief to the first. A good Father sometimes gives what we did not ask because it is better than what we did, and sometimes withholds what we begged for, because his love sees the whole of a story we see only the middle of. His no is as wise and kind as the yes you hoped for. Keep praying, keep trusting, and bring him the grief as well.

What mountains should I pray about? The ones truly beyond you and plainly on God’s heart: the conversion of a hardened friend or child, your own besetting sin, the gospel among an unreached people, the unity of a divided church, courage in persecution, provision in real need. Pray about them specifically, persistently and expectantly, and watch for answers that often come in ways you did not foresee.

Uncertain wording. Which is “this mountain”? They were on the Mount of Olives, in sight of the temple mount. Jesus may be using the proverb of the hill under their feet, or pointing across to the temple mount, so that even the institution he had just judged could be removed by God (compare Zechariah 4:7). The words do not settle it. The likely meaning is the proverbial one, perhaps with a glance at the temple; either way the promise is the same.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “receive” instead of “have received” in verse 24; the earliest have the past tense, which most modern Bibles follow.

parallels.desc: faith like a grain of mustard seed
ask in faith, with no doubting

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forgiving others belongs to every prayer, because those who come to God as forgiven people cannot come holding a grudge.

Whenever you stand praying. Jews commonly prayed standing (1 Samuel 1:26; Luke 18:11, 13), with hands lifted. So this is not a special occasion but the daily one: every time you pray. And we stand to pray as people who have been forgiven a debt we could never repay (Matthew 18:23–27).

Anything against anyone. Having said that faith can move a mountain (v. 24), he names the second condition, the thing that will stop it, and every word widens the scope. “Anything”: not only the large injuries, but the slight, the exclusion, the remark, the thing said about you at work. “Against anyone”: no exceptions for family, for the person who has never apologised, for the one who does not know they did it, for the dead. The initiative is yours: you stand to pray, find you are holding a grudge, and put it down.

Your Father also who is in heaven. The only time Mark has this phrase, close to the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:12, 14–15). “Trespasses” are sins, pictured as false steps off the path.

The one who forgave first. Within the week he would be betrayed, deserted, mocked and nailed up, and his prayer there was for his executioners: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). Some early manuscripts lack this prayer, though many scholars judge it genuine. More than that, his death is why the Father can forgive at all. A Christian who puts down a grudge is not achieving a moral feat but passing on, by Christ’s Spirit, the forgiveness the cross won for him. In practice that means saying to God: “What this person did to me was real and it was wrong, and I will not make them pay for it, because you did not make me pay.”

What it does not mean. Not that we earn God’s forgiveness by forgiving others; God forgives freely, because a ransom was paid (10:45). But a person who has truly received God’s forgiveness will forgive others (Matthew 18:21–35; Ephesians 4:32). A man who has grasped what he has been let off does not seize a fellow servant by the throat over a few coins; if he does, the question is whether he ever understood it.

Must I forgive someone who has not repented? Letting go of the grudge before God is commanded here, repentance or not; the restored relationship waits for repentance (Luke 17:3). Someone wronged by an unrepentant person, even an abuser, need not trust where trust has not been earned or return to danger, and seeking justice is not unforgiveness.

What if I cannot feel forgiving? Jesus does not tell you to feel differently, but to let it go, in prayer, deliberately, now, and again whenever it comes back. Forgiveness is a decision before it is a feeling. Tell God honestly how much it hurts, hand the person and the wrong to him as the righteous Judge, ask him to bless them, and refuse to rehearse the injury. Feelings follow slowly; remember how much you have been forgiven, for that is the fuel. If the wound is deep, seek the help of a wise pastor or biblical counsellor. There is a name you thought of while reading this. Start there.

In everyday life. Your Father has let go of everything against you; let this go before him, then pray. You will forgive unevenly, but the Son forgave perfectly in your place, and for his sake your halting forgiveness is accepted.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add verse 26: “But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive your trespasses.” The numbers here run 25, then 27. It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts, and was probably added from Matthew 6:15, perhaps written in a margin and later taken into the text. The ESV puts it in a footnote. Nothing has been lost: the truth stands plainly in verse 25, and Jesus does teach it in Matthew, where it belongs.
verseByVerse.note: Jews commonly prayed standing. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 26: “But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive your trespasses.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus’ authority comes straight from God, and those who will not face the truth about John cannot receive the truth about him. The Sanhedrin demands to know who authorised him to act in the temple (vv. 27–28). He asks them about John’s baptism, a ministry sent from heaven without any human channel, which had pointed to him (vv. 29–30). They weigh each answer by its cost and never by its truth, plead ignorance, and are given no answer (vv. 31–33).
verseByVerse.theology: Why does Jesus refuse to answer? He never withholds truth from honest enquiry in this Gospel: he explained the parables to those who stayed and asked (4:10, 34) and told a scribe he was not far from the kingdom (12:34). What he refuses is to give an answer to men who will not deal honestly with one (see “We do not know” and “Neither will I tell you” at vv. 31–33).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the most religiously trained men in the nation weighed two answers about a prophet, and nobody asked which was true.

Now: the same temptation comes to any church or person with more to lose from the truth than from avoiding it (see “The question never asked” and “We do not know” at vv. 31–33). The one who asks the question is the one who died for those who have dodged it, and it is not too late to answer him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came again to Jerusalem. And as he was walking in the temple, the chief priests and the scribes and the elders came to him, and they said to him, "By what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rulers of Israel demand to know who authorised Jesus, and the question goes to the heart of who he is: his authority comes through no human channel, but from his Father. It opens a long day of debate in the temple (11:27–12:37).

Walking in the temple. Back in the building he has just judged, in the colonnades where teachers gathered (John 10:23), entirely at home. It is his: “My house” (v. 17).

The chief priests and the scribes and the elders. The three groups of the Sanhedrin, the supreme council, which Jesus had named in his first prediction of his death (8:31): an official delegation.

By what authority are you doing these things? Above all the clearing of the temple, but also the entry and the teaching. The temple was under the high priest; who gave this Galilean the right to interfere? It is a fair question for its guardians, but also a trap. If Jesus claimed authority from God directly, they could charge him with blasphemy; if he claimed human authority, they could dismiss him, for he had no rabbinic ordination and no official position.

Or who gave you this authority to do them? In their world authority came through channels: a man was trained, appointed and licensed, with a school or a rabbi behind him. Nobody gave it to Jesus, or rather, the Father did (1:11; 9:7). That has been the issue since Capernaum, where the crowd said he taught “as one who had authority, and not as the scribes” (1:22). Their authority was borrowed from the teachers they quoted; his is borrowed from no one. The only name he could give them is his Father’s, and if he says that plainly here, they will seize him for blasphemy before the hour he has chosen.

He needs no one’s licence. After the cross he would say, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18). The council that questioned him sat in his house by his leave, and every throne and every pulpit still answers to him.

Why should I accept his authority over my life rather than my own? Because no one lives without a master. If it is not Christ, it is our desires, others’ approval, money or the pressure of the age, and none of those has ever died for anyone. This King used his authority to clear a house of prayer for outsiders, and within the week he would use it to lay down his life as a ransom for many (10:45). Freedom is not having no Lord; it is having the right one.

Do church leaders have authority? Yes, a real but derived authority, given by Christ to serve his people through his word (Hebrews 13:17; 1 Peter 5:1–4). Elders rightly ask who sent a teacher, as these men did, and churches test those who claim to speak for God (1 John 4:1). But all church authority is under Christ and under Scripture, and must never be used, as the Sanhedrin used theirs, to shield an institution from the truth or to silence a just rebuke. When leaders and Christ conflict, Christ wins.
verseByVerse.note: The chief priests, scribes and elders together made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers with a question about John the Baptist, because John’s authority came straight from God, as his own does, and John had pointed to him.

I will ask you one question. A recognised rabbinic method and a fair bargain, not an evasion: an honest answer would answer their own question, which is why they will not give one. Only Mark records “Answer me”: Jesus is now examining them.

Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? “The baptism of John” stands for John’s whole ministry of preaching repentance and baptising. “From heaven” is a reverent Jewish way of saying from God, avoiding the divine name. Did John’s ministry come from God, or was it a merely human movement? There is no third option.

A genuine parallel. The question is not a trick. John held no office, belonged to no school, had no ordination and was not attached to the temple, though as a priest’s son he could have been (Luke 1:5). He appeared in the wilderness, preached, baptised, and was recognised by the nation as a prophet: authority directly from God, without a single human channel, precisely the kind Jesus has. You have already had one case exactly like mine; what did you conclude? If they cannot assess John, whose ministry the whole country witnessed, they are not fit to judge anyone’s claim to be sent by God.

Why this question? Because John had pointed to Jesus. He had announced one mightier than himself (1:7), and at Jesus’ baptism the Spirit descended and the Father spoke (1:10–11). If John was from God, his testimony about Jesus was true; to accept John is to accept Jesus. And there is mercy in it. Anyone who honestly settled the question of John would have been carried straight to the answer about Christ. Jesus has handed them the one question in the world that would have led them home.

In everyday life. Before you ask God for more light, obey the light you have.
verseByVerse.note: “From heaven” means from God.

verseByVerse.quote: And they discussed it with one another, saying, "If we say, 'From heaven,' he will say, 'Why then did you not believe him?' But shall we say, 'From man'?"—they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. So they answered Jesus, "We do not know." And Jesus said to them, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders weigh only what each answer would cost them, never which is true, and by refusing to judge John they lose any right to an answer about Jesus. Mark lets us listen inside their huddle.

If we say, From heaven, he will say, Why then did you not believe him? They had not believed John: Luke records that the Pharisees and lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptised by him (Luke 7:30). To concede now that he was sent by God would condemn them out of their own mouths.

They were afraid of the people. The sentence breaks off, and Mark finishes it for them. John was revered as a martyr prophet, and to deny him in the temple at Passover could provoke a riot; Luke says they feared being stoned (Luke 20:6). One road costs them their credibility, the other their safety.

We do not know. A lie, and the perfect lie, because it sounds like humility. The men whose job was to judge true and false prophets (Deuteronomy 18:20–22) declared themselves unable to judge John, and so disqualified themselves from judging Jesus.

Neither will I tell you. The bargain was one question for one; they refused, and so does he, withholding truth from those who would not receive it (Matthew 7:6). This is judgment: light is withdrawn from men who have decided against it. It is also a severe kind of mercy, because more truth given to someone determined to reject it would only deepen his guilt.

He would tell them soon enough. In the parable that follows he tells them, in a form they cannot miss: he is the beloved Son (12:1–12). Asked again at night in the high priest’s house, he will answer in full, and they will condemn him for it (14:61–64). He was waiting for the hour when the answer could not be turned into anything else, and that hour was a cross. The Truth stood in the temple, and the supreme court of Israel would not ask what was true. He walked on into the trap they were setting; on the cross he gave his answer in blood, and at the empty tomb the Father gave his.

The question never asked. The most religiously trained men in the nation, in the house of God, weigh what each answer will cost and never ask which is true. That is what happens when protecting the institution matters more than the truth, and it is the standing temptation of any church, board or person with more to lose from the truth than from avoiding it: the doctrine not preached because of who would leave, the sin not named because of whose family it is in, the question about your own life never put to God because you already know roughly what the answer would cost.

Is it wrong to say I do not know? Not when it is true. Honest uncertainty is no sin, God is patient with genuine seekers, and humility often says, “I do not yet know.” But “we do not know” can also be the cheapest position available: a way of never having to say yes or no, keeping every door open by walking through none of them. The test is whether you want the answer. If you are really seeking, keep reading, asking and praying, and God will meet you (Jeremiah 29:13). If you are avoiding, admit it.

11.theology:
A den of robbers (Jer. 7:11) is not where the robbery happens; it is the cave the robbers retreat to afterwards, where they feel safe (see the note on vv. 17–19). The charge is not mainly about commerce in church buildings. It is about using religion as a safe house.

For all the nations. Matthew and Luke quote Isaiah 56:7 without its last phrase; Mark keeps it (on why it matters, see vv. 15–16 and 17–19).
11.examples:
Then: whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours (v. 24).

Now: it calls us to pray boldly for what is far beyond us and to expect God to act, and it does not say that enough certainty compels God (both are treated at vv. 23–24). Ask for great things, and trust him enough to want his will more than your own.

And with no pause he adds: whenever you stand praying, forgive (v. 25; see “What if I cannot feel forgiving?” at vv. 25–26).

keyVerse.quote: And he was teaching them and saying to them, “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers.”
keyVerse.note: Jesus’ own words explain his action in the temple, and with it the whole chapter. God meant his house to welcome every nation to pray, and its keepers had made it a hiding place where people sinned and still felt safe. Jesus judges the den, and by his death and resurrection opens the true house of prayer to all the nations, Mark’s Gentile readers and us among them.

11.reflection:
The crowd on the road was sincerely thrilled about Jesus, yet expected a different kind of King from the one who came (vv. 7–10). What do people today, and what do you, most often want Jesus to do, and how does that compare with what he actually came to do?

The fig tree had leaves but no fruit, and the temple was busy but barren (vv. 12–17). What are the “leaves” of a Christian life or a church, and what is the fruit Jesus looks for? How can we look honestly at ourselves without either pretending or despairing?

Jesus tells his disciples to pray boldly for mountains to move, and in the same breath to forgive whenever they pray (vv. 22–25). Why do you think he puts faith and forgiveness together? Is there a mountain you have stopped praying about, or a grudge you need to put down?

The leaders asked what each answer would cost them, and never which was true (vv. 31–33). Where are we tempted to avoid a question about Jesus, or about our own lives, because we already suspect what the answer would cost?

12.title: The Beloved Son and the Widow’s Two Coins
12.text: <sup>1</sup>And he began to speak to them in parables. “A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower, and leased it to tenants and went into another country. <sup>2</sup>When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to get from them some of the fruit of the vineyard. <sup>3</sup>And they took him and beat him and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>4</sup>Again he sent to them another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. <sup>5</sup>And he sent another, and him they killed. And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed. <sup>6</sup>He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ <sup>7</sup>But those tenants said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’ <sup>8</sup>And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard. <sup>9</sup>What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. <sup>10</sup>Have you not read this Scripture: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; <sup>11</sup>this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?” <sup>12</sup>And they were seeking to arrest him but feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away. <sup>13</sup>And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk. <sup>14</sup>And they came and said to him, “Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone’s opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not?” <sup>15</sup>But, knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, “Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it.” <sup>16</sup>And they brought one. And he said to them, “Whose likeness and inscription is this?” They said to him, “Caesar’s.” <sup>17</sup>Jesus said to them, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” And they marveled at him. <sup>18</sup>And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. And they asked him a question, saying, <sup>19</sup>“Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife, but leaves no child, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. <sup>20</sup>There were seven brothers; the first took a wife, and when he died left no offspring. <sup>21</sup>And the second took her, and died, leaving no offspring. And the third likewise. <sup>22</sup>And the seven left no offspring. Last of all the woman also died. <sup>23</sup>In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife.” <sup>24</sup>Jesus said to them, “Is this not the reason you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? <sup>25</sup>For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. <sup>26</sup>And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? <sup>27</sup>He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong.” <sup>28</sup>And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well, asked him, “Which commandment is the most important of all?” <sup>29</sup>Jesus answered, “The most important is, ‘Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. <sup>30</sup>And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ <sup>31</sup>The second is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.” <sup>32</sup>And the scribe said to him, “You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him. <sup>33</sup>And to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” <sup>34</sup>And when Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions. <sup>35</sup>And as Jesus taught in the temple, he said, “How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? <sup>36</sup>David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet.”’ <sup>37</sup>David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?” And the great throng heard him gladly. <sup>38</sup>And in his teaching he said, “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and like greetings in the marketplaces <sup>39</sup>and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, <sup>40</sup>who devour widows’ houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.” <sup>41</sup>And he sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large sums. <sup>42</sup>And a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny. <sup>43</sup>And he called his disciples to him and said to them, “Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. <sup>44</sup>For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.”
12.overview:
Where we are. Jesus’ last day of public teaching in the temple, in the week of his death (see the introduction), continues the confrontation of 11:27–33 over his authority and becomes one long interrogation.

The message. Jesus is the beloved Son and David’s Lord, with every right to ask for everything. And what God asks is not a share of the harvest or a silver coin but the whole person, loving him with heart, soul, mind and strength. Leaders who keep the vineyard for themselves will lose it; a widow who gives her last two coins has given more than all.

Why it was said. The authorities came in turn to discredit him before the Passover crowds and find a charge to take to Rome. Mark’s readers lived under emperors whose coins called them sons of a god, and had seen fellow believers die; they needed to know what is Caesar’s, what is God’s, and that the dead are alive to the God of Abraham.

How the chapter makes its case. The parable of the tenants answers the question of his authority: the last messenger is the owner’s beloved son, a phrase that has twice come out of heaven in this Gospel, and the stone the builders reject becomes the cornerstone (vv. 1–12). Three questions follow: a political trap, answered with a coin (vv. 13–17); a riddle against the resurrection, answered from the burning bush (vv. 18–27); and an honest scribe, told he is not far from the kingdom of God (vv. 28–34). Then Jesus asks the one question nobody can answer: how can David’s son be David’s Lord? (vv. 35–37). After a warning against scribes who devour widows’ houses (vv. 38–40), the chapter ends with a widow who gives everything (vv. 41–44).

Where it leads. Every scene asks what is owed to God, and points to the one who will pay it. The man telling the parable is the son in it. The only man who ever loved God with all his heart, soul, mind and strength is about to do it on a cross, and the widow’s whole life dropped into the offering box is a small picture of the whole life he will give, days later, outside the city wall.

For us. Everything we have we hold as tenants, and the owner asks for fruit. Give Caesar his due and give God yourself; do not shrink God to the size of your experience, or settle for being near the kingdom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — The Tenants, Caesar’s Coin, and the Resurrection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Son who has every right to the vineyard is rejected by its keepers, and every attempt to trap him only shows who he is. Asked by what authority he acts, Jesus tells the least veiled parable he ever told: tenants who refuse the owner his fruit, beat his servants and kill his beloved son, and a rejected stone that God makes the cornerstone (vv. 1–12).
