The leaders understand it perfectly. Then come two traps. Pharisees and Herodians ask about Caesar’s tax, a trap with two jaws, and he asks whose face is on the coin (vv. 13–17). Sadducees bring a riddle to make resurrection look absurd, and he answers from the books of Moses, the Scriptures they prized most (vv. 18–27).
verseByVerse.theology:
Render to Caesar (v. 17) cuts two ways, and both must be held.

A real obligation. The coin is Caesar’s; give it to him (see the note on vv. 16–17).

A bounded obligation. Caesar may claim the coin; he may not claim the soul, which bears God’s image (on where the line falls, see vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the Sadducees, the priestly party who ran the temple, denied the resurrection (see vv. 18–23), so Jesus answers them from the burning bush (see vv. 26–27).

Now: note the diagnosis he gives first: you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Those are still the two ways to go wrong (see the note on vv. 24–25).

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to speak to them in parables. "A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower, and leased it to tenants and went into another country. When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to get from them some of the fruit of the vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God planted his people like a vineyard, entrusted them to leaders, and asks in due season for the fruit that is his.

The setting. The same scene as 11:27–33, before the chief priests, scribes and elders who had just asked by what authority he acted. He answers with one of the least veiled parables he ever told.

A man planted a vineyard. Isaiah’s Song of the Vineyard uses almost the same words: the beloved dug his vineyard, cleared it of stones, planted choice vines, built a watchtower and hewed out a wine vat (Isaiah 5:1–2). And Isaiah says what it means: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7). God “looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed”. Before a single character has acted, the delegation knows the story is about them.

Everything the owner did. Every detail is an investment: the fence against animals, the winepress cut in rock, the tower for a watchman and for storage, years and money spent before anyone else touches the land. So God chose a people, planted them in a good land, fenced them with his law and watched over them.

And leased it to tenants. Here Jesus changes Isaiah’s song. There the vineyard is at fault; here the tenants are, the leaders to whom God had entrusted his people. Tenants worked the land and paid rent with a share of the harvest; they owned nothing. So does everyone God has given anything: a church, a family, a gift, a life. None of it is ours outright, and the parable turns on what happens to a man who forgets he is a tenant.

He sent a servant. The owner went into another country, leaving the tenants time: a new planting gave no fruit to eat for years (Leviticus 19:23–25). Then he sent for his share, and the request is modest: “some of the fruit”, the agreed share, in the season it was due. He has every right, and he asks. The servants are the prophets (Jeremiah 7:25).

The teller is the Son. Isaiah sang his song for “my beloved”, the owner of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1). When Jesus retells it, the word “beloved” returns at the climax, attached to the owner’s son (v. 6). The man telling the story is the son in it: the Son who has come for the fruit, and the one Israelite who has given it, his whole life, in every season, given back to his Father. What the vineyard owed and never paid, he is about to pay with his life.

What fruit does God want from me? The fruit he wanted from Israel: justice, kindness and a humble walk with him (Micah 6:8), love for him and for your neighbour (vv. 30–31), the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23). Not a percentage of your achievements, but a life given back to the one who gave it, where he has planted you, in the season he has given you, which is now.
verseByVerse.note: The setting echoes Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, where the vineyard is Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: And they took him and beat him and sent him away empty-handed. Again he sent to them another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. And he sent another, and him they killed. And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s leaders met God’s messengers with contempt and violence, again and again, and still he kept sending. The parable summarises centuries of the prophets’ history, with the violence growing each time (2 Chronicles 36:15–16; Hebrews 11:36–38).

Empty-handed. Sending the servant back beaten and with nothing is a message as well as an assault: there will be no rent.

Struck on the head. Worse; some think Mark’s readers would hear an echo of the beheading of John the Baptist (6:27), the latest of the servants. “Treated him shamefully” means he was publicly humiliated as well as hurt.

And him they killed. With “many others” Jesus stops counting, because the pattern never changed. Jeremiah was beaten and put in the stocks by the temple’s chief officer (Jeremiah 20:2) and left in the mud of a cistern (Jeremiah 38:6). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:20–21). And within a few years Stephen will put the same charge to the same council, and it will cost him his life: “Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?” (Acts 7:52).

An owner who keeps sending. After the first beating any landlord in that room would have gone to law or come with force. This one sends another man, and another, and after a murder, more still. The astonishing thing is not human wickedness, which anyone could predict, but that after all that there is still somebody else at the gate. Every prophet who was struck or killed suffered a small share of what the last messenger would suffer in full, and the one telling the story had longed to gather Jerusalem’s children (Matthew 23:37). The patience of the owner has a face, and it is his.

Why does God put up with so much? Because he is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). His patience is not weakness but mercy giving time to turn. Yet it has an end, as the parable goes on to show (v. 9), and the time to respond is while he is still sending. Every fresh call to repent is one more servant at your gate. If you have resisted God’s word for years, his patience does not mean the matter is closed; it is the reason you are still being called.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “struck him on the head” (ekephaliōsan) occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and is very rare elsewhere, and a closely related verb in ordinary Greek means to sum up. Its link with the word for head (kephalē) makes wounded in the head the likely meaning, as almost all translations take it, but other uses cannot confirm it.

parallels.desc: they mocked the messengers of God

verseByVerse.quote: He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.' But those tenants said to one another, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.' And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Last of all God sent his own beloved Son, and the leaders, knowing who he was, would kill him to keep the vineyard for themselves.

He had still one other, a beloved son. The owner has run out of servants; the one he has left is his own son. Here the parable stops being about someone else, because that phrase has twice come out of heaven in this Gospel: at the Jordan, “You are my beloved Son” (1:11), and on the mountain, “This is my beloved Son; listen to him” (9:7). So he answers the leaders’ question about his authority (11:28): he is not one more prophet but the Son, beloved perhaps in the sense of only, as Isaac was (Genesis 22:2).

Finally. Last of all (eschaton). There is no one after the Son: “in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things” (Hebrews 1:2).

They will respect my son. A servant can be brushed aside; the heir is the owner in person. A first-century listener would feel the cost at once: this man knows what these tenants do to the people he sends, and sends his son. So the Father sent his Son to his rebellious people: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).

This is the heir. They recognise him, and that is the horror of the parable and of Good Friday: they kill him because they know who he is. (It is often suggested that land without an heir might pass to those who had occupied and worked it.) This is not ignorance but rebellion: they want the vineyard, God’s people, for themselves, without God. It is the logic of every rebellion, stated with unusual honesty, and of the serpent’s offer, “you will be like God”: sin is never finally about pleasure but about ownership. We want our lives without their Lord. And “Come, let us kill him” is what Joseph’s brothers said of the favoured son (Genesis 37:20).

Threw him out of the vineyard. Matthew and Luke say they threw him out and then killed him (Matthew 21:39; Luke 20:15), which matches Jesus’ crucifixion outside the city wall: “Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). He is describing his own murder, in the third person, to the men who will commit it.

Thrown out so we could be brought in. This is love: not that we loved God, but that “he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4:10), the sacrifice that bears God’s just wrath and so puts it away. The Heir was thrown out of the vineyard so that the tenants who killed him could be brought in as sons and share his inheritance.

In everyday life. Ask where you still say, in small ways, “the inheritance will be ours”: your time, your body, your money, your future, kept back from the Son who did not keep back his life for you. Hand one of them back to him today.

Did God not know what would happen to his Son? He knew perfectly. The parable speaks as a human landlord would, to show the tenants’ guilt and the owner’s patience, but the one telling it knows its ending. The Father sent the Son knowing he would be killed, and the Son came knowing it, by God’s plan from before the foundation of the world (Acts 2:23; 1 Peter 1:20). That is not less love but more: he sent his Son into their hands on purpose.
verseByVerse.note: “Beloved son” echoes the Father’s voice at the baptism and transfiguration.

verseByVerse.quote: What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. Have you not read this Scripture: 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will judge the tenants who killed his Son and give his vineyard to others, and the Son they rejected he will raise to the place of highest honour.

What will the owner of the vineyard do? Here Jesus answers his own question; Matthew records that the listeners answered it (Matthew 21:41), and so condemned themselves, as David did when Nathan told him the parable of the lamb (2 Samuel 12:1–7).

He will come and destroy the tenants. Fulfilled within forty years, in AD 70, when Rome destroyed Jerusalem and the temple and the priestly aristocracy and the Sanhedrin came to an end, as Jesus will soon foretell stone by stone (13:2).

And give the vineyard to others. The vineyard is not destroyed: God’s people continue, and the wicked tenants are replaced by the apostles and leaders of the church, caring for God’s people under Christ; Matthew says “a people producing its fruits” (Matthew 21:43). The “others” turn out to include Gentiles from every nation, gathered in by apostles who would soon tell this very council that the rejected stone had become the cornerstone (Acts 4:11).

The cornerstone. Psalm 118:22–23 comes from the psalm the crowds had sung at his entry two days earlier (11:9); they sang verse 26 at him, and now he reads them verse 22. The picture changes from vineyard to building, perhaps with a Hebrew play on son (ben) and stone (eben). The builders, whose job is to know which stones are usable, examined this one and threw it away; God gave it the most important place in the building (on the exact sense, see below). So the parable ends with resurrection, in a builder’s picture: the rejected stone is holding up the house.

The Lord’s doing. Rejection and raising up were both within God’s plan. The leaders meant evil and were guilty of it, yet through that very act God carried out his purpose to save (Acts 2:23). The Father raised the Son the builders rejected, set him at the head of the corner, and on him is building a living temple from every nation (1 Peter 2:4–7).

A warning to every church. No congregation owns its place outright either. A lampstand can be removed (Revelation 2:5), as churches that once preached the gospel and now deny it have learned.

Has God finished with the Jewish people? No. The parable is aimed at the tenants, the leaders standing in front of him, not at a nation, and Paul insists that “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Romans 11:2).

Uncertain wording. “Cornerstone” is literally head of the corner (Psalm 118:22). It may mean the great foundation stone at a corner, which set the line of two walls, or a capstone or keystone at the top, which completed the building. Which cannot be settled, but either way it is the most important stone in the building, and that is the point.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were seeking to arrest him but feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders understood the parable perfectly, and went away to do the very thing it exposed.

They perceived. Unlike the parables of chapter 4, which outsiders did not understand (4:11–12), this one was plain: they knew they were the tenants, who the beloved son was, and what was being said about their future.

And they were seeking to arrest him. Told they are the men who murder the heir, they go away to arrange the murder of the heir. That is what a hardened heart does with the truth: it does not soften, but takes what it has been shown and goes on with the very sin that was exposed.

But feared the people. Not conscience but fear of the crowd held them back (11:18, 32). The city is full for Passover, and a public arrest would start a riot with the governor in town. They will need to take him secretly, at night, through a traitor (14:1–2, 10–11).

Held back until his hour. Mark gives the human reason, the crowd; the deeper reason is that the Son was keeping his own appointment. He would let them act out the story he had just told only when he chose: at Passover, on the night he took bread and said, “This is my body.” The tenants thought they were deciding when the heir would die. The heir had decided, and for the sake of men like these.

So they left him. Told who he was, what they were about to do and what it would cost them, they turned and walked. Yet the truth told to their faces was still an offer: even this parable ended with the cornerstone they could still have built on. To understand the gospel and walk away because it costs too much is the most ordinary way in the world of being lost. But if a passage has found you out and you are still here, troubled and wanting to be put right, you have not done what they did. They walked away from the light; you are standing in it, and that is the Spirit’s work in you.

What should I do when a sermon or a passage exposes me? Stay under it. Admit to God plainly what it has shown you, ask him what repentance looks like here, and take the first step today, while the word is still sharp; if it involves someone you have wronged, go to them. And do not resent the preacher or friend God used. The leaders hated Jesus for telling them the truth; a softened heart thanks God for the wound that heals.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk. And they came and said to him, "Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone's opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not?" But, knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, "Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His enemies come with flattery and a trap, and Jesus sees through both before he answers.

A series of tests. Three groups now question Jesus (vv. 13–34), two with traps and one in honesty, and then he puts a question to them (vv. 35–37). Many have seen here the Passover lamb, chosen days before the feast and required to be without blemish (Exodus 12:3–6): the Messiah is examined in the temple and found without fault.

Pharisees and Herodians. An unlikely alliance, as in Galilee (3:6): the Herodians backed Herod’s family and the Roman rule that kept it in power; the Pharisees resented that rule as an insult to God’s people. Nothing unites opposites like a shared hatred of the light. Sent by the leaders of the Sanhedrin (v. 12), they come “to trap him in his talk”, a hunting word (agreusōsin) for snaring animals.

Teacher, we know that you are true. Flattery, to set him up. They praise his fearlessness and indifference to what people think, precisely what they need him to display in the next thirty seconds, and every word was true: they described him accurately in order to destroy him. Flattery is rarely a lie. It is a true thing said by somebody who wants something, and what gives it away is its timing, just before the request. Anyone with responsibility should learn to be wary when a conversation opens like this one.

Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? They ask it twice, to rule out a vague answer. This poll tax, paid by every adult directly to Rome, was imposed when Judea came under direct Roman rule in AD 6, and provoked a revolt led by Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37), who taught that paying it was treason to God, the only king. The trap had two jaws. Yes, and he would lose the crowd, who hated the tax and hoped he would liberate them; no, and the Herodians could report him to Rome as a rebel. At his trial he was accused of exactly that: “forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar” (Luke 23:2).

But, knowing their hypocrisy. He names the trap before he answers, and does not pretend the flattery was sincere. No trap held him, no flattery moved him, no fear bent him.

A denarius. The denarius was a silver coin, a day’s wage for a labourer, and the coin in which the tax was paid. Jesus apparently did not carry one; they did, even in the temple, and the scrupulous men asking whether it is right to pay Caesar are shown to be using Caesar’s money themselves.
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians supported Herod’s family and so Roman rule; the Pharisees resented Rome. The poll tax was paid directly to Rome and bitterly resented. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought one. And he said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said to him, "Caesar's." Jesus said to them, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." And they marveled at him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The coin bears Caesar’s image, so give it back to him; you bear God’s image, so give yourself to God. In one sentence Jesus gives the state its real but limited due, and claims the whole person for God.

Whose likeness and inscription is this? The whole answer is stamped on the coin. It was most likely a denarius of Tiberius, the reigning emperor, with his head in profile and, round the edge, “Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus”; on the other side, “high priest”. A small metal blasphemy, then, and doubly offensive to devout Jews: a graven image (Exodus 20:4), and a claim that a living man was the son of a god and the chief priest of Rome’s religion.

Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s. “Caesar’s,” they answer; there is only one answer, and they use his money and enjoy his roads and protection. “Render” (apodote) means give back, repay a debt: the coin bears Caesar’s image, so give it back. The state has a legitimate, God-given authority in its own sphere (Romans 13:1–7).

And to God the things that are God’s. What bears God’s image? Human beings: “God created man in his own image” (Genesis 1:27). The coin belongs to Caesar because it bears his image; you belong to God because you bear his, and no part of you does not. Your body, time, money, loves and thinking are his to direct, at work and at home as much as in church (Romans 12:1; 1 Corinthians 10:31). And Caesar’s claims are limited by God’s: his coin claimed divinity, but Caesar is owed taxes, not worship.

The fault line of the martyrs. Jesus does not say how much belongs to Caesar; that will vary with the government you live under. He fixes only the limit: when Caesar demands what belongs to God, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). That is the line the early martyrs died on. They paid every tax Rome levied and prayed for the emperor, and would not burn the pinch of incense that confessed Caesar as Lord.

And they marveled at him. The trap had failed: he had neither endorsed Roman rule unconditionally nor called for revolt.

Son of the divine, high priest. The man holding the coin is the true Son of God, days from offering himself as the great high priest who brings his own blood. And “likeness”, eikōn, is Paul’s word for Christ: “He is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). We were made in God’s image and defaced it; the Son, who is that image perfectly, came to renew it in us (Colossians 3:10). The emperor’s coin has long been melted down, but every human face still carries its Maker’s stamp. Caesar was given back his coin. God, who has every claim on us, first gave himself for us, so we are his twice over: he made us, and he bought us.

Neither a private hobby nor a party platform. Many thoughtful people want faith kept out of public life, remembering religious wars and churches that lent their pulpits to whoever was in power. Yet the square is never really empty. Richard John Neuhaus called a public life stripped of beliefs “the naked public square”, and argued that something always rushes in to fill it, since every law assumes some view of what a human being is for. Jesus will not let his followers withdraw, or take over. Caesar is real, so you pay him; God is total, so you cannot keep him to Sunday. And because you bear God’s image, no state, party or market may ever own you, the root of every limit on power we value. The King who said it did not seize Caesar’s throne. He let Caesar’s governor crucify him, and so won subjects no empire could command.

Must I pay taxes to a government I think is unjust? Yes, in ordinary circumstances. Tiberius was a pagan occupier, and Jesus still said “render”; Paul wrote Romans 13 under Nero. Paying taxes, obeying laws, praying for rulers (1 Timothy 2:1–2) and honouring them are part of rendering to Caesar, even when we disagree with how the money is spent. Christians may work lawfully to change unjust laws and should speak for justice, but disobedience is right only when the state commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, such as worship, the gospel or the protection of life. Then we obey God, openly and peaceably, and accept the cost.

Where Christians differ: church and state. This saying has been read as dividing life into separate secular and sacred spheres, as subordinating the church to the state, or as subordinating the state to the church. This commentary’s view: Jesus does not make Caesar and God equal partners. Everything belongs to God, including Caesar (Romans 13:1). The state has real but limited authority under God, and Christians should be good citizens, but their final loyalty is to God, and they may not give the state what belongs to him alone.
verseByVerse.note: The coin bore the emperor’s head, probably Tiberius, and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus.

verseByVerse.quote: And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. And they asked him a question, saying, "Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies and leaves a wife, but leaves no child, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. There were seven brothers; the first took a wife, and when he died left no offspring. And the second took her, and died, leaving no offspring. And the third likewise. And the seven left no offspring. Last of all the woman also died. In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, bring Jesus a riddle meant to make it look absurd.

Sadducees. Their only appearance in Mark. The Sadducees were the wealthy priestly party, including the high priestly families who controlled the temple Jesus had just disrupted, and cooperated with Rome. They rejected the Pharisees’ oral tradition, gave the five books of Moses the highest authority, and denied the resurrection, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8).

Moses wrote for us. They begin with Moses, the authority they prized above all: Deuteronomy 25:5–10, the law of levirate marriage (from Latin levir, brother-in-law). If a man died childless, his brother married the widow, and the first son carried on the dead man’s name and inheritance. In a world with no pensions, where a childless widow could easily be destitute, the law provided for her. It is a mercy, and the Sadducees turn it into a weapon.

There were seven brothers. Not a real case but probably a stock argument against the Pharisees, with seven chosen for maximum absurdity. Moses commanded this kind of marriage; if the dead rise, a woman will have seven husbands at once, which is absurd; so Moses cannot have believed in a resurrection.

The woman nobody noticed. In their story things are done to her, until she is disposed of at the end: “Last of all the woman also died.” Seven times widowed, childless and passed along, she is never treated as a person. Jesus, who noticed the wife in chapter 10 and will notice the widow at the end of this chapter, is answering men who use a suffering woman as a debating prop.

Whose wife will she be? A joke, meant to make Jesus look foolish, and under it the assumption he goes straight for: life after the resurrection pictured as this life continued, with the same arrangements and property law running on for ever. A great many people who have never heard of a Sadducee make the same mistake.

Asking the Resurrection about the resurrection. The clever men brought their joke to the Lord of life. Within the week the man they mocked would be laid in a tomb and walk out of it, “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). They were asking the one who is himself the resurrection and the life (John 11:25) whether there would be one. And the widow they passed from brother to brother has a better hope than any levirate law could give: not a name kept alive by a son, but life itself, kept by the Son.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection. Levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Is this not the reason you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sadducees go wrong because they know neither what Scripture teaches nor what God can do, and the risen life is not this life continued.

You are wrong. To wander, go astray (planasthe): a blunt diagnosis for the custodians of Scripture and temple.

Neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Two causes of error, then and now. They had the Scriptures largely by memory but did not see what they teach, and they could not imagine that God can raise the dead. They had shrunk God to the size of their own imagination.

Neither marry nor are given in marriage. The age to come is not this age with the same furniture. Marriage belongs to this age, and its purposes, companionship, children and the picture of Christ and the church, will by then be complete. With no more death, no one needs a son to carry on his line, and the basis of their story falls apart.

But are like angels in heaven. Not that we become angels, or lose our bodies or our identities, but that like angels we will not die (Luke 20:36) and will not marry. The Sadducees did not believe in angels either; Jesus corrects them on that too.

The quiet unbelief of realism. The second failure is common among religious people, and it sounds like realism: the settled assumption that God will not act, that this marriage will not change, this person will not be converted, nothing much will happen; an assumption formed from experience, not Scripture, and then read back into Scripture. Weariness is not the same thing. A believer worn down by long waiting who still brings the matter to God is not a Sadducee; the psalmists cried “How long, O LORD?”, and were heard (Psalm 13:1–5).

In everyday life. Name one situation you have quietly decided God will not change, and pray about it this week as one who knows the power of God.

I have buried my husband or wife: what does this mean for us? Jesus does not say love ends, or that you will not know one another. The opposite mistake to the Sadducees’ is to fear that the life to come will be less than this one, with thinner relationships and a vague eternity. Paul expected to know the Thessalonians at Christ’s coming (1 Thessalonians 2:19). Marriage ends not because it was too small but because it was a signpost to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32), and you take the signpost down when you arrive. Nothing good will be lost, not the years, not your knowledge of each other, not the love; it will be taken up into something so much larger that what you fear losing will look like the smaller version of what you have.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s words at the burning bush show that the dead will rise: he is still the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and he is not the God of the dead. Jesus rests the hope of resurrection on God’s faithfulness to his covenant.

In the book of Moses. He could have quoted Daniel 12:2 or Isaiah 26:19, but the Sadducees did not give the Prophets the authority of Moses, so he answers from the books they prized most. “Have you not read” is a pointed question for men whose profession is reading, and he asks it twice in this chapter (v. 10).

In the passage about the bush. How passages were located before chapter and verse numbers: Exodus 3, which every priest there knew by heart.

The God of Abraham. Exodus 3:6, said to Moses centuries after Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were laid in the cave of Machpelah. Mark’s Greek reads “I am”; the Hebrew has no verb at all, simply “I the God of Abraham”.

He is not God of the dead, but of the living. The argument rests not on grammar but on what a covenant is. God had bound himself to Abraham personally, “to be God to you and to your offspring after you” (Genesis 17:7). Had Abraham simply ceased to exist, God would be naming himself by a relationship with nobody, the God of a memory. If he is still their God, they are still alive to him: “for all live to him” (Luke 20:38). And his promises concerned their bodies too, the land, an inheritance: “God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city” (Hebrews 11:16). He put their names into his own title, and he will not leave his friends in the grave. Mark alone records the final sentence: “You are quite wrong.”

The voice from the bush. Jesus speaks here not as one more rabbi but as the one who would say, “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). The promise to Abraham, to be God to him and to his offspring, comes to rest on Abraham’s one true offspring, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). The patriarchs live to God because God keeps covenant, and he keeps it in his Son, who within the week would go down into death and come up again, the pledge that the God of the living keeps every one of his own.

More in your Bible than you have found. The resurrection was not invented between the Testaments. It was lying in the most familiar passage of Moses, in the name God gave himself, and the men who read it every year had never seen it. Remember that the next time you read a chapter you think you know.

Do believers who die now go to sleep until the resurrection? No, and this passage is one of the clearest answers: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were alive to God centuries before the resurrection of the body. Believers who die go at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8), conscious and at rest, as the thief on the cross was promised: “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Scripture calls death sleep because the body rests and will be woken, not because the soul is unconscious. And there is no purgatory between: the believer’s soul, made perfect in holiness, is received at once into glory, waiting for the redemption of the body at Christ’s return.
verseByVerse.note: “The passage about the bush” is how a passage was located before chapter and verse numbers existed. Jesus answers from the books of Moses, which the Sadducees accepted.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–44 — The Great Commandment, David’s Lord, and the Widow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God asks to be loved with the whole self, and the King who asks it is David’s Lord; the chapter ends by showing who gives that love and who only looks as if they do. After a day of traps, an honest scribe asks which commandment is most important, agrees warmly with the answer, and is told he is not far from the kingdom of God (vv. 28–34). Then Jesus asks the question nobody can answer: if the Christ is David’s son, why does David call him Lord? (vv. 35–37). He warns against scribes who love the best seats and devour widows’ houses (vv. 38–40), and, in his last act in the temple, points to a poor widow who puts in two of the smallest coins in circulation, everything she had (vv. 41–44).
verseByVerse.theology: David’s son and David’s Lord. Everyone agreed the Christ would be David’s son, but in Psalm 110:1 David calls him my Lord. David’s son by birth; David’s Lord from eternity (the puzzle and its answer in Romans 1:3–4 are treated fully at vv. 35–37).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: You are not far from the kingdom of God. Jesus does not say he is in. He says not far.

Now: not far is still outside, and it describes many people who have been in church all their lives (on what he lacked, and on the fear of being only near, see the note on vv. 32–34).

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well, asked him, "Which commandment is the most important of all?" Jesus answered, "The most important is, 'Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.' The second is this: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' There is no other commandment greater than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole law comes down to love: for the one true God with everything you are, and for your neighbour as yourself. Asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus begins not with what you must do but with who God is.

And one of the scribes came up. Unlike the scribes who came with the chief priests (11:27), this one has been listening, is impressed rather than hostile, and asks because he wants to know. Matthew’s account suggests it was still a test (Matthew 22:35), but Mark shows his sincerity (v. 34).

Which commandment is the most important of all? A live question. Later rabbinic tradition counted 613 commandments in the law, and teachers in Jesus’ day already debated which were heavy and which light, and whether the whole could be summarised. Rabbi Hillel, a generation earlier, had said: “What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour; that is the whole law, the rest is commentary.”

Hear, O Israel: “The Lord our God, the Lord is one.” Deuteronomy 6:4, the Shema (Hebrew for hear), recited twice daily by devout Jews and written on the doorposts of the house. Only Mark includes it. Because there is one God and no other to deserve a share of our love, he alone is to be loved with everything: he is not one part of life alongside others, but claims all of it. Christians confess the same one God, as Father, Son and Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 8:6).

And you shall love the Lord your God. Deuteronomy 6:5. Love here (agapēseis) is not mainly a feeling but a commitment of the whole person, shown in loyalty and obedience: “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15).

With all your heart. Deuteronomy has heart, soul and might; Jesus adds mind. Not four separate parts but the whole person. Heart: in Hebrew thought, the control room, what you decide and want. Soul: the life itself. Mind: your thinking, so lazy thinking about God is not humility. Strength: body, energy, money and hours, so that loving God is a question about your diary and your bank statement.

The second is this: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Leviticus 19:18. Asked for one commandment, Jesus gives two, and the second flows from the first: whoever says “I love God” and hates his brother is a liar (1 John 4:20–21). It comes from a chapter about wages, harvests, the deaf, the blind and honest scales, so this love is practical. “As yourself” assumes you already love yourself: give your neighbour the attention you give your own comfort, reputation and future. All the other commandments hang on these two (Matthew 22:40), and “love is the fulfilling of the law” (Romans 13:8–10).

Heart, soul, mind and strength, on a cross. Within three days the man who recited this would fulfil it in a single act. With all his heart he said in the garden, “not what I will, but what you will”. With all his soul he poured it out to death. With all his mind he held to Scripture to the last, praying a psalm on the cross. With all his strength he carried the beam until Simon of Cyrene was made to carry it (John 19:17; Mark 15:21). And he loved his neighbour not merely as himself but above himself, bearing the sins of the people who put him there. The greatest commandment has the shape of the cross, and that whole-hearted obedience, kept where we fail, is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19).

What it does not mean. Not that we can be saved by loving God and neighbour. No one but Jesus has ever kept these two commandments fully; nobody has kept the first for a single hour. They expose our need (Romans 3:20) and drive us to the one who kept them for us; in Christ, forgiven, we begin to keep them by the Spirit he gives (Romans 8:4; Ezekiel 36:26–27).

How can love be commanded? In Scripture love is first a direction of the whole self, not a mood. You cannot order a feeling, but you can turn toward someone, give to him, keep faith with him and seek his good, and feelings tend to follow what we give ourselves to.

Who is my neighbour? Jesus answered with the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:29–37): anyone in need whom God puts in your path, beginning with those nearest and reaching to the stranger and the enemy.

How do I love my neighbour as myself? Begin with the One who loved you first. You are not squeezing love out of an empty tank: Christ treated you as his neighbour when you were his enemy (Romans 5:10), and “we love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Then let “as yourself” guide your hands. Notice. You notice at once when you are tired, slighted or short of money; ask God to make you as quick to notice it in the person at the next desk. Speak of them as you would want to be spoken of. Defend the absent, and refuse the story that makes someone look small. Give the costly thing, often an unhurried hour for someone who cannot repay you. Seek their good, not only their comfort. Love sometimes tells the truth gently, and above all wants them to know Christ. And when you fall short, go back to the cross: that love has already been shown you in full, and his Spirit, not your resolve, grows it in you (Galatians 5:22).

Why bring God into loving people? Many people today would keep the second commandment and quietly drop the first: surely kindness is what matters, and God is an optional extra. But Jesus puts the first first, and that order protects the second. Make a person your god and you will crush them, because you need from them what no human being can give; make yourself your god and your neighbour becomes a means to your ends. Dostoevsky has an old monk in The Brothers Karamazov recall a doctor who confessed that the more he loved humanity in general, the less he could stand people in particular. Augustine saw that the problem is not that we love too much but that our loves are in the wrong order. Only a heart that has received God’s love as its deepest need can stop using people to fill it, and start serving them instead.
verseByVerse.note: “Hear, O Israel” (the Shema) was recited daily by devout Jews.

verseByVerse.quote: And the scribe said to him, "You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him. And to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one's neighbor as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices." And when Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, "You are not far from the kingdom of God." And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribe sees that loving God and neighbour matters more than all the temple’s sacrifices, and Jesus tells him he is near the kingdom, though not yet in it.

You are right, Teacher. Only Mark records this reply. The scribe agrees warmly and repeats the answer in his own words, adding “there is no other besides him” from Deuteronomy 4:35. He is not parroting; he is thinking.

More than all burnt offerings. A scribe says this in the temple courts in Passover week, with the smoke of the altar going up near by and the whole machinery of sacrifice running around him. He echoes the prophets: “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22); “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6). The temple’s sacrifices without love were empty, like the leaves of the fig tree (11:13), and he is honest enough to say so in the one place where it costs something.

Not far from the kingdom. “Wisely” (nounechōs) means thoughtfully, and the praise is genuine. But “not far” is still outside, and there is no third place between in and out: the man closest to the kingdom in this chapter is on the wrong side of a line.

No one dared to ask him any more questions. Priests, Pharisees, Herodians and Sadducees have all failed to trap him; their silence admits defeat.

What did he lack? Not information; he probably knew the law better than most of the Twelve. He needed to see that he could not keep these commandments, and to recognise and follow the King speaking to him, the beloved son of the parable, the rejected stone, David’s Lord. Understanding the law is not the same as entering the kingdom. The gap is a Person, three feet away: close enough to be spoken to in the temple, close enough to be nailed to a cross. Mark never tells us what the scribe did. The account simply stops, and the man walks out of the Gospel one step from home.

Does this mean sacrifice did not matter? No. God commanded the sacrifices, and they pointed to the one sacrifice of Christ, which does what love alone could not: it takes away sin (Hebrews 10:1–14). What the prophets and this scribe condemned was sacrifice without love. So with our worship: attendance, singing, giving and the Lord’s Supper are good gifts, but God is not pleased by them from a heart cold toward him and hard toward others.

Could I be not far but not in? Yes. A person can hold sound doctrine, love a good sermon, defend the faith and grow up in a Christian home, and be only near: describing a door is not walking through it. The test is whether you have come to Christ, turned from your sin, trusted him alone for forgiveness and given yourself to follow him. If you are not sure, do not stay in the doorway; come to him today, for he has promised not to cast out anyone who comes. And if you have come to him and still fear you are only near, take heart: your safety rests on his welcome, not on the strength of your feelings, and a heart that grieves at the thought of being outside is already being drawn by him (John 6:37, 44).

parallels.desc: to obey is better than sacrifice

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus taught in the temple, he said, "How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared, 'The Lord said to my Lord, "Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet."' David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?" And the great throng heard him gladly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Messiah is David’s son, yet David calls him Lord, so he must be far greater than a new king in David’s line.

How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? Having silenced his questioners, Jesus asks the decisive question. The scribes were right (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5), and Jesus is not attacking the doctrine: Bartimaeus had called him Son of David and been commended (10:47–52), and the crowds had hailed the kingdom of David (11:10). But is that all the Messiah is, a new king like David?

David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared. “David himself”: so the psalm is his. “In the Holy Spirit”: so it is also God’s. Two authors, one text, no tension: Scripture is God’s word through human authors (2 Peter 1:21), and that is how Jesus read his Bible.

The Lord said to my Lord. Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most often quoted in the New. In Hebrew the first Lord is the divine name, printed LORD in small capitals; the second is adoni, my master, a title of superior rank. God speaks to someone David calls his master, and seats him at his right hand, the place of supreme honour, sharing God’s throne.

Until I put your enemies under your feet. Conquered kings had the victor’s foot placed on their necks (Joshua 10:24). Surrounded by men resolved to kill him, he quotes to their faces what God will do with the enemies of his Christ.

David himself calls him Lord. In that culture the puzzle could not be solved. Honour flowed upward, from son to father and descendant to ancestor; Abraham does not call Isaac “my lord”. Yet Israel’s greatest king looks down the centuries at his own descendant and calls him Master. Mark records no answer. Nobody had one.

And the great throng heard him gladly. The ordinary people enjoy seeing the experts outmatched: the last note of his public debates in this Gospel, days before the same city shouts for his execution.

In the flow. This answers the rulers’ question earlier that same day: “By what authority are you doing these things?” (11:28). His authority is that of David’s Lord, seated at God’s right hand, as the parable said in story (v. 6) and the trial will say in plain words (14:62).

The answer Jesus leaves them to find. He is the Son of David by human birth, and the Son of God, David’s Lord, by nature: “concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power … by his resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:3–4). The one who came from David’s line existed before David did. It may be the deepest thing Jesus discloses about himself in public in this Gospel, and he does it as a riddle, because a claim like that stated flatly in the temple would have brought his arrest before the hour he had chosen. The child laid in a manger in David’s town is the Lord to whom David bowed a thousand years before. The head crowned with thorns now wears the crown at the Father’s right hand, and the Lord of David has already walked out of death’s house.

Why must the Saviour be both David’s son and David’s Lord? As David’s son, a real man, he could stand in our place, obey the law we broke and die the death we deserved. As David’s Lord, God the Son, his obedience and death have infinite worth, and death could not hold him. A merely human Messiah could be admired but not trusted with our souls; a God who never became man could not die for us. The Lord who is David’s son is the one Mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5), and he reigns now at the Father’s right hand.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110:1 is among the Old Testament verses most often quoted in the New.

verseByVerse.quote: And in his teaching he said, "Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and like greetings in the marketplaces and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beware of religious leaders who love honour and use their office to rob the defenceless: God will judge them more severely than others.

Beware of the scribes. Not every scribe; one had just been commended (v. 34). It is a public warning, to ordinary people, about what religious office does to a man who lets it.

Who like to walk around in long robes. Long linen robes marked out men of learning and rank. Note the verb: they like to walk around in them. What is condemned is not the robe but the strolling, the enjoyment of being seen in a garment that says what you are.

Greetings and the best seats. Public greetings with titles, Rabbi, master. In the synagogue, the bench at the front facing the congregation, where everyone could see them; at feasts, the seats nearest the host.

The appetite for honour. The portrait is not at first of a wicked man, but of one who has come to need the deference. A robe is a robe and a seat is a seat; what is described is an appetite, the quiet, unadmitted pleasure of being thought well of, which grows so slowly that nobody notices it arriving. It is entirely available now, without a robe: in whose name gets mentioned, who is asked to pray, who is consulted, who is thanked from the front.

Who devour widows’ houses. Now the charge turns from vanity to something far worse. Widows were the most vulnerable people in Israel, and God commanded special care for them (Exodus 22:22–24; Isaiah 1:17). Men with a religious profession were using it to strip the assets of the most defenceless people in the land (on how, see below).

And for a pretense make long prayers. Long public prayers that make them look holy while they cheat the vulnerable: the hypocrisy of honouring God with the lips while the heart is far from him (7:6; Isaiah 29:13). The long prayer is the instrument of the exploitation, persuading the widow that her money is safe with such a man. But the Lord sees through every long prayer to the heart that prays it, and he does not forget the poor.

They will receive the greater condemnation. Greater because they knew the law better than anyone (James 3:1; Luke 12:47–48), and because they used religion to cover their sins. To use the name of God as the tool of a fraud is worse than the fraud.

Robes, greetings and seats, reversed. Every honour the scribes loved, Jesus would receive in mockery within the week. They loved long robes; soldiers would dress him in purple, then strip him and gamble for his clothes (15:17, 20, 24). They loved greetings; he would be greeted with “Hail, King of the Jews!”, and spat on (15:18–19). Where they devoured widows’ houses, he, dying, provided for his mother, by then apparently a widow (John 19:26–27). The true Teacher took the lowest seat.

In everyday life. The Lord who took the lowest seat has already given you the honour that lasts, so watch your heart for the love of being seen, especially if you lead in church. Ask yourself honestly what you enjoy most about any role you hold, and whether you would serve as gladly if no one noticed.

How should a church protect the vulnerable from its own leaders? By taking this warning seriously. Leaders should be accountable to other elders, with no one beyond question. Money should be handled openly, by more than one person, with proper records. No one should be pressed to give, sign over property or trust a leader with their affairs under spiritual pressure. Widows, the elderly, the disabled and the lonely should be cared for by the whole church, not left to one person’s influence. And when a leader is found exploiting or abusing anyone, it must be dealt with openly and firmly, reported where the law requires, and never covered to protect a ministry.

Uncertain wording. Jesus does not say how the scribes devoured widows’ houses, and we do not know the practice he meant. Scribes relied on gifts, and some apparently exploited devout widows’ generosity; others may have managed widows’ estates as trustees and eaten them up. The meaning is plain all the same: men with a reputation for holiness were enriching themselves at the expense of women with no one to defend them.
verseByVerse.note: Long robes marked out men of learning and rank.

verseByVerse.quote: And he sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large sums. And a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sits and watches the giving, and the gift he singles out is a poor widow’s two smallest coins. Straight after the scribes who devour widows’ houses comes a widow, perhaps one of their victims, in Jesus’ last scene in the temple.

And he sat down opposite the treasury. The arguments are over. The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, as far as women could go. Jewish tradition describes thirteen trumpet-shaped collection chests there, and many coins made a great deal of noise.

And watched. Deliberately, for some time, on his last day in that building. Not the accounts, not the total: he watched the people, their faces and hands.

Many rich people put in large sums. Jesus does not condemn them: these were large gifts, and nothing says they were hypocrites. But everyone could hear them.

Two small copper coins. She is a poor widow (ptōchē, a beggar’s poverty). The lepton (literally thin one) was the smallest coin in circulation, about 1/128 of a denarius, a day’s wage. Mark translates it for his Roman readers: two lepta made a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin. Into a bronze trumpet, it would have made almost no sound at all.

She gave both. She could have kept one. Nobody would have known or blamed her, and half of nearly nothing is still something to a woman with no income. She had the one choice open to a person with two coins, and she gave both.

He still watches. The Lord of heaven sat in the temple court and watched a poor widow drop two coins into a box, and he cared. Nothing done for him escapes his eyes, and nothing small is small to him. There is no anonymous giving; there is only giving that other people cannot see.

Does Jesus really see what I give? Yes: the amount, what it costs, and the heart. That should humble anyone who gives for show, and comfort anyone who gives quietly and little. Giving rightly kept secret (Matthew 6:3–4) is not secret from him. He knows the gift you made when you could barely afford it, and the one you held back when you could easily have given. Give to him, not to the people who might notice.
verseByVerse.note: The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, with collection chests for offerings. Her two coins were the smallest in circulation, a tiny fraction of a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called his disciples to him and said to them, "Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God measures a gift not by its size but by its cost and the heart behind it, so the widow’s two coins were more than all the rest. They gave what they could spare; she gave all she had to live on.

And he called his disciples to him. He gathers them, as he does when something matters. Within minutes one of them will say, “Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones” (13:1); he calls them over to look at a woman with two of the smallest coins in the empire.

More than all. “Truly, I say to you” marks something not to be missed, and what follows is false by every measure the treasury could apply. They gave “out of their abundance”: real gifts, honestly given, and probably nothing in their lives changed on the way home.

All she had to live on. Literally her whole life (holon ton bion autēs): she put her life in the box, trusting God for her next meal. The kingdom’s arithmetic cuts both ways. The largest cheque is small change if it costs the giver nothing, and the gift you are embarrassed by, the small amount from a pension, the hour given by someone with almost no hours, Christ counts as larger than the great donation.

The wider meaning. She stands in contrast to the rich man who would not give up his possessions (10:22), and to the scribes who devour widows’ houses (v. 40). She has done in small what the first commandment requires (v. 30).

He was rich and became poor. She put in her whole life, and three days later he put in his. The widow gave all she had to live on into the hands of God; the Son gave all he was into the hands of sinners, for he “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45). He was rich and became poor for us (2 Corinthians 8:9). Then he walked out of the temple and never went back, because the true offering was about to be made, once for all, outside the city wall.

Should the poor give everything they have? Jesus commends her heart; he does not command the poor to give away their living. A gift is “acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have” (2 Corinthians 8:12), and a believer must provide for his own household (1 Timothy 5:8). And this comes straight after the warning against those who devour widows’ houses (v. 40): no church or ministry may press the poor to give beyond their means. A church should be giving to its widows, not taking their last coins.

If she gave everything, how much should I give? The New Testament sets no fixed percentage, but it sets a pattern: give regularly, in proportion to what God has given you (1 Corinthians 16:2), generously, cheerfully and not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:6–7), and sacrificially, so that it costs you something. Many take the Old Testament tithe as a sensible starting place and go beyond it as God prospers them. Give first to your local church, which feeds you with the word, then to the poor and the spread of the gospel. Ask not how little you can give, but what it would look like to trust God with more.

Where Christians differ: praise or lament? Some hear Jesus lamenting a temple system that took the last coins of the poor. This commentary’s view: the context of corruption is real (v. 40; 13:2), but his words are commendation: she put in more than all, and she gave to God, not to a system.

12.theology:
What is owed to God. Every scene in this chapter asks it. The tenants owe the owner his fruit. The coin is Caesar’s, but the person who bears God’s image is God’s (Genesis 1:27). The whole law is summed up as loving God with everything and your neighbour as yourself. And a widow gives God all she has.

The chapter also shows who is owed it: the beloved Son of the parable, the rejected stone made the cornerstone, and David’s Lord seated at God’s right hand. The one who has every right to ask for everything is about to give everything for those who have withheld it.
12.examples:
Then: two lepta, the thinnest coins in circulation, and she gave both (see the note on vv. 41–42).

Now: Christ measures a gift by what is left afterwards. No one buys standing with God by the size of a gift (see the note on vv. 43–44).

Is he commending her or lamenting her? Commending her (see the box “Where Christians differ: praise or lament?” at the end of the note on vv. 43–44). And she does in small what he is about to do on Friday (see vv. 43–44).

keyVerse.quote: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.
keyVerse.note: Every scene in the chapter turns on what is owed to God: the fruit the tenants withhold, the whole-hearted love of the great commandment, the widow’s two coins. Caesar may have the coin that bears his image, but the person who bears God’s image belongs wholly to God. And the one who said it was about to give himself wholly for people who had withheld themselves.

12.reflection:
The parable pictures God’s people as tenants, not owners (vv. 1–9). Which parts of your life, such as your time, money, gifts, family or role in church, are you most tempted to treat as simply yours? What would giving the owner his fruit look like there?

Jesus answers the question about Caesar’s tax by asking whose image the coin bears (vv. 16–17). If you bear God’s image, what does it mean to give all of yourself to God, and where does that set limits on what any government, employer or cause may claim from you?

The Sadducees went wrong because they knew neither the Scriptures nor the power of God (v. 24). Is there a situation you have quietly decided God will not change? What does the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who raises the dead, say to it?

The scribe was “not far from the kingdom of God” (v. 34); the widow gave “everything she had” (v. 44). What separates them? How does Christ, who gave his whole life, move a person from near to in, and from giving out of abundance to giving out of trust?

13.title: Stay Awake
13.text: <sup>1</sup>And as he came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, “Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!” <sup>2</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” <sup>3</sup>And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, <sup>4</sup>“Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?” <sup>5</sup>And Jesus began to say to them, “See that no one leads you astray. <sup>6</sup>Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and they will lead many astray. <sup>7</sup>And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet. <sup>8</sup>For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These are but the beginning of the birth pains. <sup>9</sup>But be on your guard. For they will deliver you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them. <sup>10</sup>And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. <sup>11</sup>And when they bring you to trial and deliver you over, do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say, but say whatever is given you in that hour, for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit. <sup>12</sup>And brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death. <sup>13</sup>And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. <sup>14</sup>But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. <sup>15</sup>Let the one who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter his house, to take anything out, <sup>16</sup>and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak. <sup>17</sup>And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! <sup>18</sup>Pray that it may not happen in winter. <sup>19</sup>For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be. <sup>20</sup>And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days. <sup>21</sup>And then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or ‘Look, there he is!’ do not believe it. <sup>22</sup>For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the elect. <sup>23</sup>But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand. <sup>24</sup>But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, <sup>25</sup>and the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken. <sup>26</sup>And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. <sup>27</sup>And then he will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven. <sup>28</sup>“From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. <sup>29</sup>So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that he is near, at the very gates. <sup>30</sup>Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. <sup>31</sup>Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. <sup>32</sup>“But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. <sup>33</sup>Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come. <sup>34</sup>It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake. <sup>35</sup>Therefore stay awake—for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning— <sup>36</sup>lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. <sup>37</sup>And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake.”
13.overview:
Where we are. Mark 13 stands between Jesus’ last day of teaching in the temple (chapters 11–12) and his passion (chapters 14–15). It is his longest speech in this Gospel, given privately to four disciples on the Mount of Olives, facing the temple.

The message. The most permanent-looking thing in the disciples’ world will fall within their generation, and the Son of Man will come in glory on a day no one knows. So do not be deceived or alarmed, hold on, and stay awake at the work he has given you, for heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not.

Why it was said. A disciple points at the stonework, and he had reason to: Herod’s platform covers some thirty-five acres, and the work was not finished until AD 63. Jesus says not one stone will be left on another, and seven years after the last workman went home it was gone. Mark’s first readers had seen believers betrayed and killed under Nero (see the introduction), and needed to know what was coming and what was not.

How the chapter makes its case. The discourse is most striking for what it withholds. It describes signs and says they do not mean what people will claim, the end is not yet; it promises trials, betrayal and the gospel going to all nations; and it describes the fall of Jerusalem, with a specific sign and orders to flee (vv. 5–23). After that tribulation the Son of Man comes in clouds to gather his elect (vv. 24–27), and the fig tree sets the temple’s fall inside a generation (vv. 28–31). Then, at verse 32, the discourse turns: of his own coming there is no sign and no timetable, and no one knows the day, not even the Son. What is left is a command, repeated: stay awake, which the closing parable defines as being found at your post, doing your work (vv. 33–37).

Where it leads. Mark runs the chapter straight into the passion: darkness falls first on him at noon (15:33), and the four watches in which the master may come are the four watches of his own last night, when he stays awake and his friends sleep. The one who will come in great power and glory first went out of the city to die for the people he will gather.

For us. Read the world’s troubles as birth pains, not a countdown; test every voice that claims Christ by the Christ of Scripture; hold on, knowing that he holds you; and be found doing your work when he comes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Signs, Perseverance, and the Abomination
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything that looks permanent can fall, so do not be deceived or alarmed: hold on, and when the sign comes, run. Jesus says the temple will be thrown down, and four disciples ask when (vv. 1–4). Deceivers, wars and disasters will come, but none of them means the end has come (vv. 5–8). His people will be tried and betrayed by their own families, and in the middle of the list stands the one line that is not a disaster: the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations (vv. 9–13). Then a specific sign, the abomination of desolation, and orders so urgent that a man on his roof is not to go down for his belongings (vv. 14–20). False christs will come with signs, but he has told them everything beforehand (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Two questions, two answers. Everything down to verse 30 carries signs and a timeframe, and all of it happened in AD 70; from verse 32 on there is no sign and no timetable (on the two questions, see vv. 3–4; on why Jesus was not mistaken, see vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations (v. 10), the one item in the list to be done rather than endured (see the note on vv. 9–11).

Now: Paul reached Caesar’s household because he was arrested. So a Christian reading the news is not simply watching the world fall apart. He is watching the field in which the seed is being sown.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, "Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!" And Jesus said to him, "Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temple, the most impressive and permanent-looking thing in the disciples’ world, will be utterly thrown down.

And as he came out of the temple. A solemn departure. Having watched a widow give her last two coins (12:41–44), he leaves the temple for good. In Ezekiel’s vision the glory of God left a defiled temple and went out to the mountain east of the city, the Mount of Olives, before Babylon destroyed it (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23). Now the Lord of the temple, who had come suddenly to his temple (Malachi 3:1), taught in it, cleansed it and been rejected in it, walks out and climbs that same mountain (v. 3), leaving it to its fate.

What wonderful stones! You cannot blame the man. The disciples were Galileans from the country, and Herod’s temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world. Its retaining walls were dressed limestone cut so precisely that they needed no mortar, and the largest block still visible weighs several hundred tons. The rabbis said that whoever had not seen it had never seen a beautiful building.

Do you see these great buildings? He grants the premise: yes, look at them. Jesus never pretends that human achievement is small; he measures it against eternity.

Not one stone upon another. This will surely happen: the Greek doubles its negative (ou mē). In AD 70 the Roman general Titus took Jerusalem after a terrible siege. Josephus, who was there, describes the sanctuary burning, and says the city was so levelled that visitors could hardly believe it had ever been inhabited. The fig tree had withered (11:20), and now the temple it pictured follows it.

Why does the Western Wall still stand? Because it is part of the retaining wall Herod built around the temple platform, not part of the temple itself. Jesus spoke of “these great buildings”, the sanctuary and its courts, and of them not one stone was left on another. The platform survived as a ruin; the house of God on it did not.

Heard as blasphemy. We hear this sentence as history; they heard something close to blasphemy against the house of God, the place of atonement. Jeremiah nearly died for saying less (Jeremiah 26:8–9), and a twisted version of this saying will be produced at Jesus’ trial (14:58). The house God gave as a place to meet him had become a guarantee people held over him, as if the building would keep them safe whatever they did. Jeremiah had warned against exactly that trust (Jeremiah 7:4), and every religious heart is tempted to lean on the place or the practice instead of on the Lord.

Why did the temple have to fall? Because its work was finished. It was where a holy God dwelt among a sinful people and sacrifice was offered daily so that they could draw near, and all of it pointed to Jesus, the true temple, God dwelling with us in the flesh (John 1:14; 2:19–21). Within days his body will be torn down and raised in three days, and the curtain of the temple torn from top to bottom (15:38). Once the one sacrifice for sins had been offered for all time (Hebrews 10:12), a building where lambs were slain could only deny that he had come. Its fall was judgment on a city that rejected him, and God taking away the picture once the reality had come. The glory that left that house came to rest in a crucified and risen man, and in him we have a temple no army can take: its stones are living, and its light is the Lamb.

In everyday life. That disciple was admiring the most permanent-looking thing in his world, and it had only a few decades left; what survived that generation was twelve men and a message. Everything you can point at and call impressive is on a clock: the company, the reputation, the house, the body. Build on the kingdom that cannot be shaken, already given you in Christ (Hebrews 12:27–28): his word, his people, and treasure laid up where nothing is thrown down.

Was this prediction written after the event? Some scholars date Mark after AD 70 for exactly that reason, but the argument often assumes the very thing in question: that Jesus could not know the future. Even on purely historical grounds the prediction is not strange: Jeremiah had foretold the first temple’s fall, and Josephus tells of another Jesus, son of Ananias, who cried woe on the temple for years before the war. Nor does the text read like hindsight: Mark describes no fire and no details of the siege, only warnings and a command to run, and many date the Gospel before the end came. Jesus staked everything on his word holding (v. 31), and in AD 70 it held, stone by stone.

Does this mean church buildings do not matter? They are a good gift, to be built well and cared for, but never the house of God in the sense the temple was. The church is the people, the living stones built on Christ (1 Peter 2:4–5), and the Spirit dwells in them (1 Corinthians 3:16). A congregation that loses its building has lost a roof, not God; a congregation that would rather keep its building than the gospel has already lost the thing that mattered.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great had rebuilt the temple on a vast scale, with some stones many yards long. The Romans destroyed it in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, "Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples ask when the temple will fall and what sign will warn them, and Jesus’ answer will gently separate the temple’s fall from the end of the age. How you read the chapter depends on noticing the two questions.

Opposite the temple. From this ridge across the Kidron valley you look straight down onto the temple platform. He sits, the posture of a teacher and of a judge, facing the house he has just condemned. The place carries prophecy of its own: Zechariah says that on the day of the LORD “his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives” (Zechariah 14:4). On the mountain of the prophets he spent his last free hours not defending himself but preparing four frightened men for a future he would face first.

Peter and James and John and Andrew. The first four disciples called from their nets (1:16–20): Peter, James, John and Andrew. “Privately”: the crowd that heard him gladly (12:37) is gone, and this last extended teaching before the passion is given to four men who will lead the church through everything it describes.

Tell us, when will these things be? The first question asks for a date, and not for the end of the world; Mark’s version has no such phrase. “These things” are the stones: he said the temple would be flattened, and they want to know when.

And what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished? The second asks for a warning visible in advance. The verb (synteleisthai) means brought to completion, and suggests that in their minds the fall of the temple and the end of all things belonged together, as Matthew makes explicit: “what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?” (Matthew 24:3). Jesus separates the two. The temple will fall within their generation, with signs (v. 30). The end of the age will come at a time no one knows, with no signs to announce it (v. 32).

A question refused in the form it was put. He gives signs, then says they do not mean what people will think; a timeframe for the temple, then no day or hour for his coming; and he ends with the one thing they need: “stay awake”. A man who knows the date will prepare on the last afternoon; a man who does not must live ready every day. Refusing them a date is care.

Is it wrong to be curious about the future? No. Jesus answered at length and did not rebuke the question. What goes wrong is curiosity that wants control, treating prophecy as a puzzle for the clever and the end as a date to be extracted. Almost everything he says here is an instruction: do not be led astray, do not be alarmed, be on your guard, flee, do not believe it, learn, stay awake.
