A King anointed in a leper’s house. Messiah means anointed one, and Israel’s kings were made with oil poured on the head (1 Samuel 10:1; 2 Kings 9:6). Jesus, the Christ, receives his royal anointing from a nameless woman, in the house of a man who once had to cry “unclean”, days before he is lifted up under a notice that names him King of the Jews (15:26). Nobody says the word; the oil running down his hair says it for them, and his throne is waiting at Golgotha. She broke the flask because he was about to be broken: he “loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (Ephesians 5:2). She poured out a year’s wages; he poured out his soul to death. Nothing given to him is wasted, because he gave himself without measure, and there is no flask on earth worth as much as the head she anointed.

In everyday life. Ask what in your life is sealed in an alabaster flask, kept back as too precious to spend on him, though he spent himself for you: your Sunday afternoons, a career plan, a sum of money, a child you have never really handed over, a reputation. If the word that rises when you think of giving it is “waste”, you have probably found the flask.

Was this the same woman as the sinful woman in Luke? Almost certainly not. Luke’s anointing happens in Galilee, much earlier, in the house of a Pharisee also named Simon, and the woman is known in the town as a sinner who weeps over Jesus’ feet (Luke 7:36–50). This one is in Bethany, in the last week; Simon was a common name, and anointing an honoured guest a known custom. Luke’s story teaches the love of the forgiven; this one, the love that sees what is coming and gives everything before it is too late.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “pure” (pistikēs) occurs only here and in John 12:3, and its exact sense is not known. Most take it to mean genuine or unmixed, not thinned with cheaper oil; others think it was a trade name or the name of a plant now lost. Either way, this was the real thing, and very costly.
verseByVerse.note: John names the woman as Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus. Nard was a costly perfume imported from India. Alabaster was a soft stone used for perfume flasks.

verseByVerse.quote: For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor." And they scolded her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The objection sounds generous, but it measures love by its cash value, and it comes first from a thief.

Three hundred denarii. A good objection. Three hundred denarii, about a year’s wages, would have fed many families where the only safety net was almsgiving; giving to the poor was customary at Passover, and Jesus had told a rich man to sell everything and give to the poor (10:21).

And they scolded her. The word is strong (enebrimōnto): they rebuked her harshly, with indignation. She has done the most extravagant thing of her life, in a room full of men, and they round on her. Mark records not one word from her.

Who started it. It was Judas, John tells us, who said this “not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it” (John 12:6). The others agreed because it was a reasonable thing to say. A sound principle can be cover for a bad motive, and sincere people can end up repeating it.

The poor man at the table. Within two days Judas will have his silver and this woman will have nothing left: one person in this chapter turns Jesus into money, and one turns money into worship. And the man they are arguing over is the poorest person in the room, about to be stripped of his clothes and laid in a borrowed tomb: “Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). The greatest gift ever made to the poor is reclining at the table, about to give away everything he has.

How do I balance generosity to the poor with gifts for worship? Not by choosing one. In the next verse Jesus reminds them of the command to “open wide your hand”, and the same Lord who received the perfume told the rich man to sell everything for the poor. The real contrast is not between worship and charity but between love and calculation, and a heart that has given everything to Christ will be generous to the poor, because he loves them. So give regularly to the needy and gladly to the work of the gospel, and when someone else gives extravagantly to Christ, do not appoint yourself auditor of their gift.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages. John says the complaint came from Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus said, "Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a beautiful thing to me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. But you will not always have me. She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for burial. And truly, I say to you, wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus defends the woman and calls her gift beautiful: she has done what she could, and has prepared his body for burial, and the world will remember it.

Leave her alone. He protects her first, and only then explains. “Why do you trouble her?” is tender: he has seen what the room is doing to a woman who cannot answer back.

She has done a beautiful thing to me. Beautiful (kalos) means good, fine, lovely, and it is the whole answer to “waste”. The disciples had one measure, usefulness; Jesus brings in another, beauty, for which a purely practical religion has no room. Nobody is fed by worship, nothing is produced, and God calls it lovely.

You always have the poor with you. This sentence has been misused for centuries as a shrug, but it is a quotation, and the original settles it: “there will never cease to be poor in the land. Therefore I command you, ‘You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land’” (Deuteronomy 15:11). The permanence of poverty is the reason for open-handedness, not an excuse from it. And his own clause, found only in Mark, “whenever you want, you can do good for them”, assumes they will.

But you will not always have me. Not a general rule about extravagance and charity, but a statement about a week that will not come again. The chance to do anything at all for the body of Jesus of Nazareth is closing, and this woman is the only person in Jerusalem who seems to have noticed.

She has done what she could. Only Mark has this. Not what a more capable person would have managed, but what she could: one thing, done once, with everything she had. Two small coins from a widow outweighed the treasury (12:44); a flask from a woman with nothing else outweighed the criticism of the whole room.

She has anointed my body beforehand for burial. He tells them what she has done, more than she knew. Bodies were anointed with spices and perfumes for burial, but Jesus would die as a criminal, there would be no time to do it properly, and the women who came to do it on Sunday would find the tomb empty (16:1). She is the only person who managed it, while he was still alive. She came to honour him; he tells her she has prepared his body for the grave. The one anointed for burial in Bethany is the one who rose, and the fragrance of what he did has filled the whole world.

In memory of her. A remarkable prediction two days before his death (see 13:10), and it has come true on every continent. The disciples criticised her; Jesus made her remembered. The one who made sure it was written down is the one who watched a widow put in two coins nobody heard. He receives what we bring, small and clumsy as it is, calls it beautiful, and writes it down for ever.

Is anything worth doing that is of no use? Our culture runs on usefulness, and soon measures people the same way, so that the old, the ill and the unproductive feel they must apologise for being alive; even faith gets defended as good for mental health. Augustine drew a line across all of it: some things are to be used, and one alone, God, is to be enjoyed for his own sake. We turn it round, enjoying God’s gifts and using God to get them, whether by obeying to be rewarded or by spending our lives on things that are only means. This woman did neither. She did not use Jesus for anything; she simply treasured him. And he, the one of infinite worth, let himself be poured out for people who were of no use to him at all.

Is it right to spend money on beautiful buildings, music and worship? It can be, within limits this passage sets. God commanded beauty for the tabernacle and called this woman’s act beautiful, and worship offered with care, skill and cost honours him. But her gift was love poured on Christ himself, not display. Beauty that serves pride, or is bought while the church neglects its poor, or replaces the preaching of the gospel, has lost the point. The test is the one Jesus applies: is this done to me? A plain room where Christ is adored is more beautiful to him than a cathedral where he is ignored.

What if what I can do for Christ is very small? Then this verse was written for you. Perhaps you are ill, elderly, poor, housebound, caring for small children, or simply ordinary. He does not ask what a gifted or wealthy person could do, but what you can: a prayer offered faithfully every day, a meal taken to a neighbour, a note to a missionary, a hard conversation had in love. He sees it, and calls it beautiful. No one will be asked on the last day why they did not do what someone else could.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. And when they heard it, they were glad and promised to give him money. And he sought an opportunity to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of Jesus’ own twelve goes to his enemies and offers to hand him over for money, then waits for a quiet moment to do it.

Judas Iscariot. The sandwich closes: a woman pours out a year’s wages on him, and a man goes out to sell him. Iscariot, which sets this Judas apart from the other Judas among the twelve, may mean man of Kerioth, a town in southern Judea. He went to them; they did not come to him.

Who was one of the twelve. Said here, at the table (v. 20) and at the arrest (v. 43): three times in one chapter. Appointed on the mountain (3:19), sent out with authority over unclean spirits, present at every private explanation, he had shared Jesus’ life for some three years.

They were glad. Chilling in its ordinariness: the problem they could not solve has walked through the door and offered to solve itself. An insider could tell them where to find Jesus at night, away from the crowds.

Money. Matthew gives the figure: “thirty pieces of silver” (Matthew 26:15), the compensation the Law fixed for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32), and the wage thrown to the rejected shepherd in Zechariah, with the LORD’s dry comment, “the lordly price at which I was priced by them” (Zechariah 11:12–13). Set the two halves of this passage side by side and the arithmetic is unbearable: the perfume was three hundred denarii; thirty pieces of silver was perhaps a hundred and twenty. A woman spent more on his head than the priests paid for his life.

An opportunity. A convenient time (eukairōs). Judas goes back, eats with them, and watches for a gap. He sat through the supper knowing, and, Matthew tells us, said with the rest, “Is it I?” (Matthew 26:25).

Handed over. To betray simply means to hand over (paradidōmi), and Mark uses the word like a relay: Judas hands Jesus over to the priests, the priests to Pilate (15:1), Pilate to be crucified (15:15). But the chain does not begin with Judas. Paul uses the same verb of the Father, who “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32), and of the Son, “who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). Judas handed him over for silver; the Father handed him over for sinners, and the Son handed himself over in love. The darkest word in the chapter names the brightest thing God ever did.

The price of a slave. The Son of God was sold for the price of a slave so that slaves could be bought back for God. The silver bought a potter’s field for burying strangers; his blood bought a people from every nation. No traitor’s bargain could stop the plan of grace. It only fixed the price, and he paid it.

In everyday life. Ask where your opportune time is likely to come: the meeting where silence would be easier, the deal no one would know about, the friendship where Christ is never mentioned. Decide now, in the light, what you will do then, and ask the Son who handed himself over for you to keep you. If you handle money for others, be scrupulously open about it: Judas began with the moneybag.

Why did he do it? The Gospels give reasons enough: greed, for he was a thief (John 12:6) and asked what they would give him (Matthew 26:15); and Satan, who entered into him (Luke 22:3; John 13:2, 27). Perhaps also disillusionment with a Messiah who kept talking about dying, with the “wasted” year’s wages the last straw. Mark tells us less why than how, which is more useful. Betrayal waits for a convenient moment, when nobody is watching and the cost of loyalty has suddenly become visible. Almost nobody decides to abandon Christ. A moment arrives in which it is much easier not to be associated with him, there is a way out you can explain to yourself, and it is taken. Judas found his gap in a garden after dark; Peter will find his beside a fire within hours (on what separated them afterwards, see “Peter and Judas” at vv. 71–72).

Was Judas ever a true believer? No. Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him (John 6:64), and Judas, though called and gifted, never belonged to Christ in the heart. Gifts, office and experience are not the same as faith.

Could I turn out to be a Judas, one of the twelve? Mark repeats that phrase to unsettle the comfortable, not to terrify the trembling. If you are asking with fear, that is already a good sign, for Judas never did. The question is not whether you have ever failed, since every disciple in that room failed that night, but whether you are still coming to Christ as your Saviour and treasure. If you bring your sins into the light, grieve over them and run to Christ, you are on Peter’s road, not his. Examine yourself (2 Corinthians 13:5), and then look away from yourself to the one who keeps all who come to him.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says the price was thirty pieces of silver.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb, his disciples said to him, "Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?" And he sent two of his disciples and said to them, "Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the day the Passover lambs were killed, Jesus calmly arranges the meal himself, guarding the evening he needs with his disciples.

When they sacrificed the Passover lamb. The Thursday, 14 Nisan. That afternoon in the temple the slaughter went on for hours: each household brought a lamb, the priests caught the blood in basins to be poured at the base of the altar, and the carcass was taken home to be roasted whole and eaten that night. Meanwhile the Lamb of God was arranging where he would eat. He was not hunted into the cross; he went to it by appointment.

Where will you have us go? A real problem. The Passover had to be eaten inside the walls, and the city was heaving; every room was spoken for. Preparing meant buying and sacrificing the lamb, and setting out the unleavened bread, wine, bitter herbs and sauce.

A man carrying a jar of water. No address, no name, in a city of hundreds of thousands, and it works. Carrying water in a jar was usually women’s work; men more often used skins. Either Jesus foreknew it, as with the colt (11:2), or he had arranged it secretly; Mark does not say which.

Why the secrecy? Judas is waiting for his opportunity. Had the place been announced in the morning, the arrest could have come in the middle of the meal, and the Last Supper might never have taken place. So Jesus arranges a meeting place that even his disciples cannot give away, because they do not know it. He is buying an evening, to say and give what these men must have before the arrest. He knows what Judas has done and what the priests want, and he plans around them, which is a very different thing from being caught.

The date of the Last Supper. Mark, Matthew and Luke present the Last Supper as a Passover meal. John seems to place Jesus’ death on the afternoon the Passover lambs were slaughtered (John 18:28; 19:14), which would make the supper a day earlier. The likeliest explanation is that John’s phrases refer to the whole week of the feast, with Preparation meaning the day before the Sabbath of Passover week, though the question is not fully settled. Either way, both accounts present Jesus’ death as the fulfilment of Passover.
verseByVerse.note: The lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon before the Passover meal. Carrying water was usually women’s work, so a man with a jar would stand out.

verseByVerse.quote: and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, 'The Teacher says, Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?' And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us." And the disciples set out and went to the city and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything is ready just as Jesus said: a room prepared for his last meal, by a host who asks no questions.

The Teacher says, Where is my guest room? The password works, as with the colt (11:3). Someone in Jerusalem, perhaps a disciple, knows who the Teacher is, has a room ready and asks no questions: another of this Gospel’s anonymous people who did not say no. “My guest room”: he speaks as a man with an arrangement. Guest room (katalyma) is the very word used for the inn in Bethlehem where there was no room (Luke 2:7). At his birth there was no room; at his last meal, a room is ready.

A large upper room. Large enough for thirteen men to recline, as free men did at Passover, unlike the first Passover eaten standing; furnished with couches and cushions. Many think this was the house of Mark’s mother, Mary, where the church later met (Acts 12:12), perhaps the upper room of Acts 1:13. That cannot be proved, but the church’s first address in Jerusalem was an upstairs room lent by somebody nobody bothered to name.

Just as he had told them. As with the colt (11:4–6), what Jesus predicts keeps turning out exactly right. In a few hours he will say “one of you will betray me”, “you will all fall away”, and “before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times”, and those will turn out exactly right too.

They prepared the Passover. That meant taking a lamb to the temple, waiting in the queue, holding it while its throat was cut, carrying it back, roasting it whole, and setting out the bread, herbs, sauce and wine. Two disciples spent that afternoon preparing a lamb for the man who was about to become one.

A room prepared. The Lord who had nowhere to lay his head had a room ready on the night he was betrayed, because his Father provides for his Son and his Son provides for his friends. And he has gone ahead of us to prepare another: “In my Father’s house are many rooms” (John 14:2). We will find it just as he told us.

Does Jesus still guide his people in such specific ways? As surely, but not usually in this way. These detailed instructions belonged to his unique hour and to the apostolic age, when new revelation was being given. Today he guides us through his finished word, sufficient for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16–17), through wisdom, counsel and the ordinary providence that arranges our lives without announcing it. Christians differ over whether God still gives specific guidance by prophecy or inner impressions; this commentary holds that such revelation ceased with the apostles, whose foundation was laid once (Ephesians 2:20), and those who expect it agree that nothing received that way may add to Scripture or overrule it. Do not wait for a man with a water jar before obeying what Scripture already says; but be sure that the rooms of your life are prepared before you arrive in them.
verseByVerse.note: Larger houses had an upper room reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And when it was evening, he came with the twelve. And as they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, "Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me." They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, "Is it I?" He said to them, "It is one of the twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me. For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the meal of friendship Jesus announces that one of the twelve, sharing his bread, will betray him; it fulfils Scripture, and the betrayer is still fully to blame.

When it was evening. The Passover was eaten at night (Exodus 12:8), and evening is the first of the four night watches he named on the Mount of Olives: evening, midnight, when the rooster crows, and morning (13:35). This night will pass through them all.

One who is eating with me. The words do not narrow the field, since all twelve are eating with him; they are there for their weight. Sharing a meal created a bond of loyalty, and to eat a man’s bread and then harm him was the deepest treachery there was. The phrase is a quotation: “even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9), a psalm Jesus quotes in John’s account of this evening (John 13:18).

Is it I? Nobody looks at Judas. Eleven men have lived with him for some three years and trusted him with the money bag, and not one turns his head: Judas was not obviously a Judas. The Greek expects the answer no, “surely not I?”: not a confession but a fearful hope. Still, every one of them looked first at himself. That instinct is the healthiest thing in the chapter, and the opposite of Peter’s boast ten verses later. To suspect yourself is not morbid but sane: “let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12).

Dipping bread into the dish. They dipped bread and bitter herbs into a common bowl of sauce. He does not name him. Matthew and John record a further exchange that identified him to those close enough to hear; Mark leaves a description that fits everyone at the table. Judas is given every chance, to the last minute, to stop. He could have got up.

As it is written. “Goes” means goes to his death, as foretold in Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22. The cross is not the failure of the plan; it is the plan.

Woe to that man. Yet God’s plan does not excuse Judas by an inch. Woe is a cry of lament and of judgment together, and the betrayer is fully answerable.

Better if he had not been born. Few sentences Jesus spoke are more terrible, and it should not be softened: something is worse than never having lived. That implies conscious, everlasting loss, not annihilation (simply ceasing to exist), and shows that Judas was not saved in the end (John 17:12). And it is said in his hearing, while he could still have moved: a last warning to a man’s face, which makes it mercy as well as judgment.

He goes for those who ask. No treachery takes Jesus by surprise. He knew the betrayer’s name and the others’ weakness, and he still goes to the cross for people who say, “Is it I?”, and mean it.

Is it fair that Judas was lost if his betrayal was written beforehand? Yes. God foretold what Judas would do; he did not make Judas want it. Judas acted from his own greed and unbelief, after some three years of seeing Christ’s goodness and hearing his warnings. Nobody will be condemned for what God planned, but for what they themselves chose and loved. How God rules over a sinner’s free choice is a mystery (see the note on vv. 1–2), but it is not injustice. And Jesus spoke of it not with satisfaction, but with woe.

Should I live in fear that I might betray him? Live in humility, not in terror. The disciples’ question keeps you from trusting your own strength, but the answer is not found by staring inward. It is found at the table, where Christ gives himself to sinners who know they are weak. The twelve all failed that night, and all but one were restored, because their hope was in him. Ask “Is it I?”, and then take the bread.
verseByVerse.note: Dipping bread in a shared dish was a mark of close fellowship.

parallels.desc: my close friend, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, "Take; this is my body." And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it. And he said to them, "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gives the Passover bread and cup a new meaning: his body given and his blood poured out to make a new covenant, in the place of many. Before anyone lays a hand on him, he explains his death, so that the arrest, the trial and the cross read as the ransom of 10:45, paid on purpose.

The Passover meal. As later Jewish sources describe it, the head of the household explained each element, retelling the exodus: the lamb (God passed over our houses), the unleavened bread (we left in haste), the bitter herbs (the bitterness of slavery). Four cups of wine were drunk at fixed points, and every man there knew the script by heart. Jesus takes the bread and the cup at their appointed moments and says something else, about himself.

He took bread. He took, he blessed (thanked God over it), he broke, he gave: the four verbs of the hillside feedings (6:41; 8:6). What he did for the hungry crowds he now does for the twelve, and this time the bread is himself.

Take; this is my body. Not the bread of affliction from Egypt, but his own body, about to be given in death for them. And “take”: whatever else the Supper is, it is Christ given to be received, not looked at, admired or discussed, but taken.

He took a cup. “Given thanks” (eucharistēsas) gives us Eucharist, an old name for the Lord’s Supper. Probably the third cup, the cup of blessing (1 Corinthians 10:16), drunk after the meal (Luke 22:20). “They all drank of it”: Luke places Judas still at the table (Luke 22:21), though John may mean he had already gone out (John 13:30). Either way, to take the bread and the cup is not the same as to have the Christ they point to.

This is my blood of the covenant. These are Moses’ words at Sinai, when he threw the blood of the sacrifices over the people: “Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you” (Exodus 24:8). A covenant is a binding bond God makes with his people, ratified by sacrifice and blood. And it is new, as Luke and Paul record (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25), which takes us to Jeremiah: a covenant in which God writes his law on hearts and remembers sins no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Hebrews 8–9). At Sinai the blood was thrown over the people from outside, and the law stood outside them, on stone. Here the blood is handed round in a cup to be drunk, and in the new covenant God changes the person inside, so that you begin to want what he commands and to love the one who gave it (Ezekiel 36:26–27).

Poured out for many. The blood of sacrifice was poured out at the altar (Leviticus 4:7): a death given deliberately, for people. “For many” is Isaiah 53 again, where the Servant “poured out his soul to death” and “bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12), and his own word that the Son of Man came to “give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45). His blood is shed in the place of many, for the forgiveness of sins (Matthew 26:28). This is the heart of the gospel, Christ’s substitutionary, atoning death: in our place he died the death our sins deserved, and so dealt with sin and brought sinners back to God, at one with him again (Romans 5:10–11).

The host of the feast and its food. On the night he was betrayed, with Gethsemane an hour away, he took into his hands the sign of his own broken body and thanked God for it. He handed men who would run within the hour a covenant sealed in his blood, with their forgiveness written into its terms. The Lamb of the Passover became the host of the feast and its food, and he still comes by his Spirit to his people at his table, and gives them himself, until he comes.

What all Christians agree on. Do not let the argument cost you the thing itself. Nearly every tradition agrees that this meal is commanded, central, more than a memory exercise, and that Christ is truly given to faith in it. Jesus’ first point is not how he is present, but that he gave it and said, “Take”.

In everyday life. Before the next Lord’s Supper, prepare during the week: confess the sins you know, put right anything between you and another believer, and ask the Spirit to feed you. At the table, do not only remember; receive. Hold the bread and say in your heart: “this is for me.”

What does it mean to feed on Christ by faith? More than thinking about him, and less than chewing his flesh: as you eat the bread trusting his promise, the Holy Spirit unites you to the risen Christ, so that you truly receive him and his benefits.

Who should come to the Lord’s Supper? Those who belong to Christ and have publicly confessed him. In the New Testament the Supper is for the church, those who have repented, believed and been baptised (Acts 2:41–42). Each is to examine himself and so eat (1 Corinthians 11:28), not to prove himself worthy, but to come as a sinner trusting Christ, at peace with his brothers. This commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that baptism is for believers and comes before the table, because in the New Testament those baptised are those who have heard, repented and believed; paedobaptist brothers who baptise their children also generally require a credible profession of faith before admitting them to the Supper. Those who do not yet trust Christ should not take it, but should take him, and then come.

What if I feel unworthy to take it? Then you understand what the table is for: it was given to men who would all run away within hours. Nobody comes because he is worthy; the Supper is medicine for the sick, not a reward for the healthy. Paul’s warning about eating “in an unworthy manner” (1 Corinthians 11:27) is about coming carelessly, despising the body of Christ or one’s brothers, not about coming while feeling weak. If you are holding on to a known sin with no intention of leaving it, or refusing to be reconciled to someone, deal with that first. Otherwise, come. The bread is for the hungry.

Where Christians differ: for whom was it poured out? Many Christians read “for many” as a Hebrew way of saying “all”, the multitude set against the one (see Romans 5:15–19), and so as a death for every person; they are brothers who love the same cross. This commentary’s view: the Reformed reading. Christ’s blood was poured out for his people and actually secured their forgiveness, because “the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11, 15) and a ransom actually paid sets its captives free. “For many” is not a limitation grudgingly admitted but a promise gladly made: a multitude whose sins were not made able to be dealt with that Friday, but dealt with; if you are trusting him tonight, you are one of the many he had in mind as he held that cup. Both readings agree that his death is sufficient for all, offered to all, and that no one who comes is turned away.

Where Christians differ: the Lord’s Supper. Four main views. Roman Catholic teaching holds transubstantiation: the substance of the bread and wine becomes Christ’s body and blood while their appearance remains, and the Mass is a sacrifice. Lutherans hold that Christ’s body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine. Zwingli taught that the Supper is chiefly a memorial, reading “this is my body” as “this represents my body”. Calvin and the Reformed confessions teach that Christ is truly and spiritually present, and believers by faith, through the Holy Spirit, truly feed on him, though his body is in heaven. This commentary’s view: Calvin’s view is the best reading. When Jesus said “this is my body”, his body was sitting at the table, and the disciples would not have thought they were eating his flesh; he speaks as he did in “I am the door”. But the Supper is more than a reminder. It is a real communion with Christ by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 10:16), in which believers are nourished by him. And it is not a repeated sacrifice; Christ was offered once for all (Hebrews 9:25–28; 10:10–14).

Textual note. The earliest manuscripts of Mark read “my blood of the covenant”, without “new”, so most modern Bibles omit it here; later manuscripts add it, as in the King James Version (“new testament”), in line with Luke and Paul. The new covenant is meant either way.
verseByVerse.note: At the Passover meal the head of the household explained the bread and cups; Jesus gives them a new meaning. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert “new” before “covenant.”

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God." And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the last night of his life Jesus looks past the cross to a feast in God’s kingdom, then sings and walks out to meet his death.

The fruit of the vine. The last thing he says at the table is not about his death but about a party. “I will not drink again”: this is the last meal on this side of the cross, and he is truly giving something up. Some think he did not drink the fourth Passover cup, the cup of completion, and would finish it only in the kingdom.

Until that day. He looks past the nails and the grave, and speaks without an “if” of a future meal at which he will be present. The prophets had promised it: “On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine … He will swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:6–8; see Matthew 8:11). Revelation names it: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). Every time the church takes this cup it looks back to a death and forward to a dinner, and he said he would be there.

When they had sung a hymn. By the custom later recorded in the Mishnah, the meal ended with the second half of the Hallel, the psalms of praise, Psalms 115 to 118. If so, Jesus sang on his way to Gethsemane, “The snares of death encompassed me … Then I called on the name of the LORD” (Psalm 116:3–4), and “I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD” (Psalm 116:13), an hour after lifting the cup of the covenant. And very probably the final words he sang before he walked out into the dark: “Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever” (Psalm 118:29). In a voice that would be praying in agony within the hour, he sang that God is good and his love does not stop.

They went out to the Mount of Olives. Across the Kidron valley to Gethsemane. Luke says this was his custom (Luke 22:39), so Judas knew where to find him. He did not change his habits to avoid arrest.

How can I sing when my heart is breaking? By singing what he sang. The psalms hold grief and praise together, as he did on the way to Gethsemane, and give you words when you have none. You need not feel cheerful to sing that God is good and his love endures; you need only believe it, and sometimes singing it is how you come to believe it again. Paul and Silas sang in prison with their backs bleeding (Acts 16:25). Your song may be quiet and full of tears; it is still a song he has sung before you.

Will there really be eating and drinking in the kingdom? Scripture speaks of it plainly, and we should not thin it into mere symbol. The risen Jesus ate fish before his disciples (Luke 24:42–43), and the new creation will be a world, not a cloud: fellowship, joy, abundance, and the King at the head of the table. What we will eat we do not know. That we will sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and with Christ himself, we do.
verseByVerse.note: The hymn was probably from the Hallel psalms (Pss 113–118), sung at Passover.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Son accepts the cup of God’s wrath in prayer, and goes alone to be taken, while every friend fails him. On the walk out he tells them that they will all fall away, and in the same breath tells them where he will meet them afterwards; Peter insists he will not, and the rest say the same (vv. 27–31). In Gethsemane he falls to the ground, asks his Father to take the cup away, and submits, while three times he finds his friends asleep (vv. 32–42). Then Judas arrives with an armed crowd and a kiss, a sword is drawn, and everybody runs, even a young man who escapes leaving his linen cloth behind (vv. 43–52).
verseByVerse.theology:
What is the cup? Everything in Gethsemane depends on it, and it is not the general dread of dying but the wrath of God (see the note on vv. 35–36).

And he drank it. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). There is nothing left in that cup for anyone who is in him, and that is why a Christian can face death more calmly than Christ faced it in the garden.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: You will all fall away (v. 27), and then, before Peter has said a word, but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (v. 28): the restoration announced before the failure (see the note on vv. 27–28).

Now: the angel at the empty tomb repeats it with one addition: go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee (16:7).

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "You will all fall away, for it is written, 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.' But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells his friends that they will all desert him, as Scripture foretold, and in the same breath promises to meet them after he rises.

You will all fall away. Not some: all, said on the road with them in the dark. The verb (skandalisthēsesthe) means to be tripped up, the word used of the seed on rocky ground that falls away when the heat comes (4:17), and of the offence Nazareth took at him (6:3).

I will strike the shepherd. He quotes Zechariah 13:7, and the striking thing is who strikes. In Zechariah God says: “Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, against the man who stands next to me … Strike the shepherd”. Jesus gives it as God’s own act: “I will strike the shepherd.” The hand behind tomorrow is not finally Judas’s, Caiaphas’s or Pilate’s, but the settled purpose of the Father: “it was the will of the LORD to crush him” (Isaiah 53:10).

After I am raised up. The force of the sentence is in where it stands: before the failure. Peter has not yet boasted; nobody has run. Having told eleven men that every one of them will abandon him within hours, he tells them where he will meet them afterwards, with no condition attached: not “if you repent”, or “if you prove yourselves”.

Go before you. A shepherd walks ahead of the flock so they can follow (John 10:4). The scattered sheep will be gathered, in Galilee of all places: not Jerusalem, where it all went wrong, but home, where they were called off their boats. An angel in an empty tomb will repeat the promise (16:7).

Struck so that we would be spared. The Father strikes the Son, in judgment for the sins of his people. This is penal substitution in the words of the prophet: the penalty is the punishment God’s law demands for sin; the substitution is that someone else bears it, so that God’s justice is satisfied and his people go free (Isaiah 53:5). And the one struck is “the man who stands next to” God: no ordinary man. He was struck so that we would be spared, scattered so that we would be gathered, forsaken so that we would be found.

In everyday life. Christ knows your failures before you commit them, and has already planned your restoration. If you wonder whether there is any road back, notice the order: the meeting place was fixed while they were still swearing they would never need it. Go to him today, where he said he would be: in his word, in prayer, among his people.

If the Father struck the Son, was God angry with Jesus? The Father never stopped loving his Son; Jesus was never more pleasing to him than when he obeyed to the death (John 10:17). But on the cross the Son stood in the place of sinners and bore the wrath their sins deserved. God was not angry with Jesus for anything Jesus had done; he poured out on him the judgment due to us, and Jesus willingly drank it: “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). It is not a Father punishing an unwilling victim, but the Father and the Son together, in one love, saving the guilty.

parallels.desc: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered
he is going before you to Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, "Even though they all fall away, I will not." And Jesus said to him, "Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." But he said emphatically, "If I must die with you, I will not deny you." And they all said the same.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter insists that he alone will never deny Jesus, and Jesus tells him exactly how he will. The love behind the boast is real; the confidence, resting on Peter’s own heart, is not.

Even though they all. It is just like Peter: meant well, and wrong. In four words he accepts the prophecy for the other ten and makes himself the exception, in front of them, a low estimate of his brothers said aloud in their hearing. The man who thinks he alone will stand has already begun to fall, because he has stopped needing anybody.

Before the rooster crows twice. Jesus does not rebuke him; he gives him the details: this very night, twice, three times. Matthew, Luke and John say “before the rooster crows”; only Mark says “twice”, with a first crowing Peter ignored and a second that broke him (v. 72). One account is simply more detailed, and the exactness fits the early tradition that this Gospel carries Peter’s preaching: this is the sentence that broke him, as he remembered it.

Emphatically. Over and over, and he means it. Peter was not lying; he loved him. In a few hours he will draw a sword against an armed crowd (v. 47; John 18:10), more than the other ten manage. He was not a coward. But courage in a fight is different from courage alone in a courtyard, and he did not know himself.

They all said the same. Mark will not let Peter carry it alone. Every one of them said it, and every one of them ran (v. 50).

Die with you, or die for you. Peter offers to die with Jesus, and the offer is upside down: Peter cannot die with him; Jesus must die for Peter. The one faithful to death in this chapter is not the disciple but the Master. He does not say, “then you were never mine”, or withdraw the promise of Galilee. He tells Peter exactly what he will do, takes him into the garden anyway, dies for him on the Friday, and has him named by an angel on the Sunday. And grace turns it round once more: restored and filled with the Spirit, Peter did at last glorify God by his death (John 21:18–19). He kept his promise in the end, because Christ had first kept his.

The danger of untested confidence. The danger is the quiet assumption that you would hold, that you would speak up, that you would not do what those people did. The boast was hollow; the love behind it was not, and Christ knew the difference.

Is it wrong to promise loyalty to Christ? No. Christians rightly make promises: at baptism, in membership, in marriage, in hymns that say “I will follow thee”. What went wrong with Peter was not the promise but its ground: confidence in his own heart, contradicting his Lord, comparing himself favourably with his brothers. Promise, then, leaning on Christ: “by your grace, I will.” Pray that he will keep you, and when Scripture warns you, do not argue with it as Peter did; let it send you to your knees.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts lack “twice” here and the first crowing at verse 68, probably because copyists brought Mark into line with the other Gospels; most modern Bibles keep them.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark mentions the rooster crowing twice.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went to a place called Gethsemane. And he said to his disciples, "Sit here while I pray." And he took with him Peter and James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. And he said to them, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Gethsemane the Son of God is overwhelmed with horror at what lies before him, and asks his three closest friends to stay awake near him.

Gethsemane. The name means “oil press”: an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives. Here Jesus will be pressed. “Sit here while I pray”, he tells eight of them; as at the beginning of his ministry (1:35) and at every turning point (6:46), he prays.

Peter and James and John. The three who saw Jairus’s daughter raised (5:37) and saw him transfigured (9:2) now see him at his lowest. James and John had said they could drink his cup (10:39); Peter had said he would die with him (v. 31). Now they will see what that cup is.

Greatly distressed and troubled. Two of the strongest words available. Greatly distressed (ekthambeisthai): overwhelmed with horror, shuddering. Troubled (adēmonein): anguish with no bottom to it. And he “began”: this is not a sorrow carried all week. It falls on him in that garden.

My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. The Son of God, in the worst hour of his life, tells three friends how bad it is. The phrase echoes the psalms, “Why are you cast down, O my soul?” (Psalm 42:5, 11; 43:5), using the word of the Greek Old Testament there. “Even to death”: a sorrow heavy enough to kill a man. Luke the physician records what it did to his body: “his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground” (Luke 22:44). Those verses (Luke 22:43–44) are missing from some early manuscripts, and Luke says “like great drops of blood”, not that he bled.

Remain here and watch. Stay awake: the word from the parable (grēgoreite, 13:35, 37). He is not asking them to fix anything. He wants their company, and their prayer.

Why such anguish? Many martyrs have faced death calmly, even joyfully. Jesus was not less brave: he faced what no martyr has faced: the cup of God’s wrath against sin (v. 36), separation from the Father (15:34), being made sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21). The holy Son, who had known only the Father’s love from eternity, was about to bear his wrath in the place of sinners. That wrath has nothing of human spite in it; it is perfect holiness set against every evil, and the purer the one who sees it coming, the more terrible it looks. Jesus, who alone was without sin, saw it more clearly than anyone ever has. This is the measure of what our sin deserved, and of his love.

Weaker than any of us. The olive press closed on the Son of God, and he let it. He went down into the anguish our sin deserved, all of it, and came out the other side still saying “Father”. Our high priest can sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), because on that night he was weaker than any of us, and loved us through it.

How can I keep watch with someone who is suffering? Stay. Usually you can neither explain the suffering nor end it, and you are not asked to. Be present, be quiet more than you speak, pray with them, and keep coming back; do not hurry them to feel better or quote verses to close the conversation. Jesus asked for exactly this, and his friends could not give it. You can give it to his people, and so to him (Matthew 25:40).

How can the Son of God be so distressed? Because he is truly man as well as God. His human soul shrank from the cup of God’s wrath, as any holy man would, and he said so (on how his human will and the Father’s stand together, see “What it does not mean” at vv. 35–36).

Is it sinful for a Christian to be overwhelmed with sorrow? No. Jesus was sinless, and he was overwhelmed. Grief, dread and anguish are not in themselves failures of faith but what a true human heart feels in a fallen world. What matters is where you take them: Jesus took his to his friends and to his Father. Do not pretend to a calm you do not have, or let anyone tell you that a Christian should never be cast down. Tell God the truth about your state, and tell a friend.
verseByVerse.note: Gethsemane (the name means “oil press”) was an olive grove on the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley.

parallels.desc: why are you cast down, O my soul?

verseByVerse.quote: And going a little farther, he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. And he said, "Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks his Father, honestly, to take away the cup of God’s wrath if there is any other way, and then gives his own will up to the Father’s. Here the obedience that saves us is won, and every Christian prayer finds its pattern.

He fell on the ground. Not knelt: fell, though Jews normally prayed standing (11:25). The man who slept through a storm and faced down a legion is face down among the olive roots.

That the hour might pass. The hour is the appointed time of his suffering and death (v. 41; John 12:27). And “if it were possible”: he is not demanding but asking whether there is another way, and the asking is real.

Abba, Father. Mark keeps the Aramaic, the actual sound of Jesus praying. Abba is the ordinary family word for a father at home: not “Daddy”, since grown men used it all their lives, but unmistakably intimate. Jewish prayer very rarely, if ever, addressed God that way. Jesus did, because he was the Son, and in the deepest agony of his life that is the word he reaches for.

All things are possible for you. Before he asks, he says what he believes about God (10:27): first that God is able, then the request. That is the reverse of how most of us pray in a crisis.

Remove this cup from me. The cup is not simply death. It is a fixed Old Testament image for the wrath of God (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15): not the nails, but the undiluted anger of God against every sin of everyone he came to save, to be drunk to the dregs. It is a true request from a true human will, shrinking from the horror: if there is any other way to save sinners, let it be found.

Yet not what I will, but what you will. He does not withdraw the request; he asks honestly, and then submits, and both are prayer. The asking is not unbelief and the submitting is not resignation. In Eden a man was told the Father’s will and said, in effect, “my will”, and the world broke. In this garden a man who could have had anything said “not what I will, but what you will”, and it was mended. This is the obedience that undid Adam’s disobedience (Romans 5:19), counted to every disciple whose own obedience still falters. He drained the wrath of God to the last drop, and handed us instead the cup of blessing.

The name he handed over. Abba did not stay his alone. Twice the New Testament says that the Spirit puts this very word into the mouths of ordinary Christians: “you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). The name he used in Gethsemane is the name he gave away. We pray as sons and daughters because of the Son, and because on this night he was willing to be treated as though he were not.

What it does not mean. Not that there was conflict or sin in Jesus, or that his will was against the Father’s. His human will shrank from suffering, as it should, and he willingly submitted it. The early church taught from this passage that Christ has two wills, divine and human, in perfect harmony: he is one person, truly God and truly man, and a true man has real desires and a real recoil from horror. As man he wanted the cup to pass; as the obedient Son he wanted his Father’s will more, and chose it (Hebrews 5:8).

A pattern for every prayer. Honest about our desires, and submitted to God’s will (Matthew 6:10). Take the hardest thing you are praying about this week and pray it in two halves, aloud if you can: first the plain request, with nothing held back, then the handing over. And when the answer is no, remember that the cup did not pass from him, and he drank it, and that is why there is nothing left in it for you.

Was there really no other way? Gethsemane is the answer: the Son asked the Father, who can do all things, whether the cup could pass, and the answer was no. If sinners could have been saved by teaching, by example, or by God simply overlooking sin, the Father would not have handed his beloved Son that cup. Sin is so serious, and God so just, that nothing but the death of a perfect substitute could pay for it (Hebrews 9:22; Romans 3:25–26). If there had been another road to God, the Father would have opened it in that garden.

If the plan was already fixed, why did Jesus ask at all? Because prayer is not informing God or bending his mind, but a child speaking honestly to his Father. Jesus knew he must suffer (8:31), and still told his Father what his human heart desired, then laid it down. God’s plan does not make prayer pointless; it makes it safe, for we pour out our real wishes to a Father who will never give us anything less wise than his will. And God has appointed prayer as one of the means by which he carries out his purposes (James 5:16).

Is it a lack of faith to pray if it is your will? Not as Jesus meant it; he prayed it at his moment of greatest need, and he did not lack faith. Where God has plainly promised something, such as forgiveness to those who confess, pray with confidence. Where he has not told you his will, such as whether a sick friend will recover, ask boldly, and then entrust it to him. That is not a hedge against disappointment, but the trust of a child who knows the Father is wiser than he is.
verseByVerse.note: “Abba” is Aramaic for “father,” the word a child used at home. The “cup” pictures God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, "Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus finds his friends asleep and gently warns them that only watchful prayer will carry them through the test about to come, because good intentions cannot hold up weak human nature.

Found them sleeping. Two days before, on this hillside, he told them of a master who might “come suddenly and find you asleep” (13:36). He came. They were asleep.

Simon, are you asleep? The only time in Mark that Jesus is recorded calling him by name, and he uses the old one: not Peter, the rock, but Simon, the fisherman. Gently said, it must have cut deep. The man who said that night “Even though they all fall away, I will not” cannot stay awake.

Could you not watch one hour? Not the night; an hour, the smallest possible request, from a man dying of grief a stone’s throw away (Luke 22:41), and it was too much. The reproach is more sad than angry, and it is fair to remember that it was late, they had eaten a festal meal with its wine, and Luke kindly records that they were “sleeping for sorrow” (Luke 22:45). They were not indifferent but shattered. That explains the failure without removing it, and Jesus explains it too.

Watch and pray. Temptation (peirasmon) is a test that could make them fall, coming within the hour, and their only defence is watchful prayer. They slept through the preparation, and failed the test. The battle is lost or won before the moment of temptation arrives: the man who falls in the moment fell in the hours before it, when nothing seemed to be happening and there was no obvious reason to be on his knees. Peter’s denial in the courtyard was decided here, while he slept.

The spirit indeed is willing. Having named their failure, he explains it, with a sympathy that is almost unbearable. “Spirit” is the inner person with its good intentions; “flesh” is human nature in its frailty, not wickedness but weakness. Their intentions were real, “but the flesh is weak”. They are not hypocrites, but men (see Romans 7:18–25).

He stayed awake for us. The one diagnosing their weakness has just been on the ground under a weight none of them can imagine. He has been more tired, more frightened and more alone than we have ever been, and he stayed awake for us.

In everyday life. Think of the hour when you are most likely to fall, late at night, after a bad meeting, alone with a screen, and pray before it arrives. Name the temptation to God in the morning. And if you have failed again, hear him call you by your old name, gently, and then say “the spirit indeed is willing”. He has not given up on you.

Why does prayer help against temptation? Because temptation is a lie that looks true in the moment, and prayer puts you in the presence of the truth before the moment comes. In prayer you confess your weakness and stop trusting your own strength; you ask for help, which God has promised (1 Corinthians 10:13); you set your mind on Christ, so that other loves look smaller; and you remember you are not alone. Willpower is the spirit being willing; prayer is how weak flesh is held up.

verseByVerse.quote: And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus prays the same prayer again, and again finds his friends asleep, with nothing to say for themselves.

The same words. He prayed the same words again, and Matthew says a third time (Matthew 26:44). Matthew records the second prayer, and its wording has moved on: “My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done” (Matthew 26:42). He now speaks of drinking the cup: the submission deepens.

Not vain repetition. Jesus warned against heaping up empty phrases to wear God down (Matthew 6:7). This is the same cry from the same heart, because the need has not changed. Paul did the same about his thorn: “Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this” (2 Corinthians 12:8). And when there are no words left, the Spirit himself intercedes with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). If all you can do tonight is say the same desperate sentence over and over, you are not praying badly. You are praying in Gethsemane.

They did not know what to answer. Very possibly Peter’s own memory: eyes heavy, failed twice, nothing to say. At the transfiguration Peter had blurted out a suggestion about tents, “for he did not know what to say” (9:6). The same three men, on the mountain of glory and in the garden of agony, both times with nothing to say. A community inventing a founding story would hardly write down that its leaders slept through the crisis. The only one in that grove who did not fail was the one on his face, praying.

While we sleep he watches. Three times he prayed in the dark, three times his friends failed him, and he never once failed them. The prayer did not end among the olive trees: the one who knelt there lives for ever at the Father’s right hand, pleading for all who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). While we sleep he watches; when we do not know what to answer, he answers for us. The Son who prayed “your will be done” in Gethsemane now asks for what the Father has already willed: that not one of his people will be lost.

What if God says no to my prayer? Then you are in good company. The Father said no to his beloved Son in this garden, not because he loved him less, but because that no was the way to the greatest yes in history. God’s no to a believer is never indifference, but the refusal of a Father who sees what you cannot, and who works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28). Keep praying, as Jesus did, until your will is shaped to his, and trust him with what you do not understand.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came the third time and said to them, "Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The time of prayer is over: the hour has come, the betrayer is here, and Jesus rises to go and meet him.

The third time. Three times he prayed, three times he came back, three times they were asleep, and within hours Peter will deny him three times. Mark’s numbers are not accidental. Whatever the exact force of his words (see the box below), the tone has changed: he is no longer asking them for anything.

The hour has come. The hour he prayed might pass (v. 35) has not passed. It has arrived, and he announces it.

Into the hands of sinners. He has said it before (8:31; 9:31; 10:33); now it is happening. And “sinners”: the leaders, who thought themselves righteous and the Gentiles sinners, are the sinners into whose hands he is given.

Rise, let us be going. For half a second it sounds like an escape; it is the opposite. Torches are probably already coming up from the Kidron valley (John 18:3), and he walks towards them, laying down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). And notice “my betrayer”, not “the betrayer”: he does not disown him even now.

Settled in prayer. He went into the grove appalled and shaking; he comes out settled, and every sentence from here to the cross has the same steadiness. He rose from his knees and went, his face set like flint (Isaiah 50:7), towards the cup he had accepted for us.

In everyday life. If you are dreading something, the appointment, the confession, the conversation, the operation, take it to God until you can say “Rise, let us be going”, and then go and meet it. You will not go alone.

How did Jesus go from anguish to such calm? Through prayer and submission. He did not talk himself into courage or stop feeling the weight; he laid the matter before the Father three times, until his human will rested in the Father’s. The cup was no smaller, but he had accepted it. That is the peace Paul describes: “by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God … will guard your hearts” (Philippians 4:6–7). Not the peace of having your way, but of having given it up to someone you trust.

Uncertain wording. “Are you still sleeping and taking your rest?” can be read either as a question or as a weary statement, “sleep on now and take your rest”; the Greek allows both, and the sense is much the same. “It is enough” translates a single word (apechei) whose meaning here is genuinely uncertain: “that is enough”, “it is settled”, or even “paid in full”, as it was used on receipts. Most take it as “enough” (of sleeping, or of waiting): the moment has come.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, "The one I will kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard." And when he came, he went up to him at once and said, "Rabbi!" And he kissed him. And they laid hands on him and seized him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas arrives with an armed crowd and marks Jesus out for them with the sign of love, a kiss, and they seize him.

Judas came. “One of the twelve”: the third time in the chapter.

Swords and clubs. An armed party sent by the Sanhedrin, probably the temple police with servants; John adds a detachment of Roman soldiers and their commander, with lanterns and torches (John 18:3, 12). All this for one unarmed teacher and eleven tired men.

A sign. At night, among a dozen Galileans dressed alike, they could not reliably pick him out: nothing distinguished the Son of God from the fishermen beside him. “Under guard”: perhaps Judas remembers that Jesus had passed through hostile crowds before (Luke 4:30), and is taking no chances.

Rabbi! And he kissed him. The kiss was the ordinary greeting of a disciple to his teacher: respect, affection, belonging. Mark’s verb (katephilēsen) may mean he kissed him warmly. The sign chosen to mark him for execution was the sign of love, and it was not done by halves. The Bible knows this wickedness: Joab took Amasa by the beard to kiss him, and killed him (2 Samuel 20:9–10). “Rabbi”, not “Lord”, is the last word Judas speaks in this Gospel. Matthew records the answer, “Friend, do what you came to do” (Matthew 26:50); Luke another, “Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48). He did not turn his face away.

They laid hands on him. Here the Gospel turns: from now until the resurrection, everything is done to him. The one no legion of demons, storm, fever or death could bind lets a temple guard put its hands on him in the dark and take him away.

Handed over by a kiss. The Lord of glory offered his cheek to the traitor, and then held out his hands to be bound. He did not need to be identified; he was going to give himself up. He was handed over by a kiss so that we could be welcomed with one, like the son who came home and was embraced by his father before he could finish his confession (Luke 15:20).

In everyday life. Ask whether any outward sign of devotion in your life, the songs, the words, the church, has become a kiss without a heart.

How can someone so close to Jesus betray him? Because closeness of position is not the same as love. Judas had the same sermons, miracles and meals as Peter, but not a heart that treasured Christ, and years of nearness without love hardened him: the danger of familiarity with holy things. The cure is not to stay away from Christ, but to keep asking whether you love him, and to be honest when you find something else on the throne. If your love feels cold, come nearer to him, not to despair: he receives the weak and warms them.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. And Jesus said to them, "Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled." And they all left him and fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One disciple lashes out with a sword, Jesus exposes the cowardice of a night arrest and submits to the Scriptures, and every one of his friends runs away.

One of those who stood by. Mark does not name him. John, writing much later, says it was Peter, and the servant Malchus (John 18:10); perhaps Mark, writing while Peter was alive or, as tradition holds, recently martyred, protected him. Be fair to Peter: eleven men are about to run, and he draws a weapon against an armed party. He was keeping his promise (v. 31), and whatever else he got wrong tonight, he got it wrong bravely.

The wrong kind of loyalty. He also got it entirely wrong. Taking only an ear suggests a wild swing in the dark, at a servant, and Jesus’ kingdom does not advance by the sword (John 18:36). Luke the physician records the last healing before the cross: “he touched his ear and healed him” (Luke 22:51). The last thing Jesus did with his hands free was to repair what his own disciple had done to a man who came to arrest him.

As against a robber. Robber (lēstēs) is not a pickpocket but a bandit, an armed insurrectionist: Josephus’ word for the rebels against Rome, John’s word for Barabbas (John 18:40), and Mark’s for the two men crucified beside him (15:27). You have turned out in force, at night, armed, as though I were a terrorist.

Day after day. He has stood in their own temple, in public, all week, and they did not arrest him because of the crowd (12:12; 14:2). The swords, torches and midnight raid are not a security precaution but a confession: men who take a prisoner in the dark know their case would not stand in daylight.

Let the Scriptures be fulfilled. With that he stops arguing and submits, perhaps thinking of Isaiah 53:12, he “was numbered with the transgressors”, and of the struck shepherd of Zechariah 13:7 (v. 27).

They all left him. Mark does not soften it by a syllable. “All”: the eleven who had said they would die with him, the three who could not stay awake, Peter with his sword. “Left” is the verb Mark used when they left their nets and followed him (1:18). They left everything to follow him; now they leave him. From here he is alone.

Alone, so that we never will be. The Shepherd is struck, and the sheep are scattered (v. 27). He stood alone in the torchlight so that the sheep could run, and then went to gather them again. There is no loneliness like his that night, and because of it, no believer will ever be truly alone.

How should I defend Christ when he is attacked? With truth, love and courage, never with the world’s weapons. Peter’s sword has modern versions: are online abuse, mockery of opponents, manipulation, and political power used to coerce faith. After Pentecost the apostles spoke boldly, suffered patiently, and blessed those who cursed them (Acts 4:29; 1 Peter 3:15–16). Christ does not need protecting. He needs witnesses.

Does this forbid Christians to use force? Matthew records Jesus’ rebuke, “all who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matthew 26:52), and John his reason, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Jesus forbids the sword to defend his kingdom or to stop the cross. He does not abolish the state’s sword (Romans 13:4), nor the defence of life (Exodus 22:2). Christians may protect themselves and others; they may never advance Christ’s cause by force.
verseByVerse.note: John names the swordsman as Peter and the servant as Malchus; Luke adds that Jesus healed the ear.

verseByVerse.quote: And a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even a young man who tries to follow is caught, and runs off naked rather than be taken with Jesus: the desertion is complete. Only Mark records it, and it may be his own signature.

A young man followed him. Many have suggested he was Mark himself, which would explain why he appears at all: an eyewitness painting himself into the corner of the picture. If the supper was eaten in the house of Mark’s mother (Acts 12:12), a young man of that household might well have heard where they had gone, thrown a sheet round himself and followed. It cannot be proved. Linen was expensive, suggesting a family of some means.

He ran away naked. “They all left him and fled” (v. 50), and now the desertion has a face: one person caught in the torchlight who would rather lose everything he was wearing than be taken with Jesus. Amos spoke of the day of judgment: “he who is stout of heart among the mighty shall flee away naked in that day” (Amos 2:16).

Two pieces of linen, two young men. The disciples had left everything to follow Jesus (10:28); this young man leaves everything to escape him. Next day Joseph of Arimathea wraps Jesus’ body in a linen shroud (15:46), and Mark uses the same word, sindōn, for both. The young man leaves his linen to save himself; within a day his Lord lies wrapped in linen, the one who saved others and would not save himself (15:31). And the word for young man, neaniskos, occurs only once more in Mark: “they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe” (16:5). So Mark frames the passion with two young men: one fleeing from Christ stripped and ashamed, one seated in an empty tomb, clothed in white, announcing that he has risen. That is the gospel in two pictures, and if the young man is Mark, the man who wrote it put himself in the first.

Why would Mark tell such an embarrassing story about himself? We cannot be sure it was Mark, but if it was, the reason is the one for which Peter told of his denial: the gospel is not about how faithful we were, but about how faithful Christ is. A writer who shows himself running away naked points away from himself, to the one who did not run. And it tells every reader who has fled from Christ in shame that the story does not end there. Mark, who once deserted Paul as well (Acts 15:37–38), later became useful to him for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11), and wrote this Gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records the young man. Many have guessed he was Mark himself, but the text does not say.

parallels.desc: he who is stout of heart shall flee away naked in that day

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 53–72 — The Trial and the Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Inside, Jesus confesses who he is and is condemned; outside, Peter denies who he is and saves himself. The council meets at night to find evidence for a verdict already reached, and finds none that holds (vv. 53–59). Jesus says nothing until the high priest asks the direct question, and then answers plainly for the first time in this Gospel: “I am”. He is condemned for it, and they spit on him (vv. 60–65). In the courtyard below, a servant girl looks at Peter across the fire, and three challenges bring three denials, the last with oaths and a curse; then the rooster crows, he remembers, and he breaks down (vv. 66–72; on how Mark sets the two scenes side by side, see vv. 53–54).
verseByVerse.theology:
A court with its verdict already made (v. 55): it had the penalty and went looking for grounds (see the note on vv. 55–56).

I am is the fullest confession in the Gospel, and with Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13 the man in the dock tells the court that he will be their judge (see the note on vv. 60–62).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the blindfolded prisoner is struck and told, Prophesy! (v. 65). He had prophesied that very night: betrayal, desertion, and Peter’s three denials.

Now: every word Jesus spoke about his friends’ failure came true, and so did every word about his rising and their restoration. His word can be trusted at the worst moment as well as the best.

verseByVerse.quote: And they led Jesus to the high priest. And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together. And Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. And he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is taken to the high priest’s house for a trial by night, and Peter, who has followed at a distance, sits down at the guards’ fire.

To the high priest. Caiaphas, high priest from AD 18 to 36 (Matthew 26:57). John records a first hearing before Annas, his father-in-law and the power behind the office (John 18:13). Caiaphas had already said it was better that one man should die for the people (John 11:50).

They came together. The Sanhedrin, the council of seventy-one, or a quorum of it, met in the middle of the night, irregular by any standard, to finish before the crowds could react.

The structure. Another Mark sandwich: Peter in the courtyard (v. 54), Jesus before the council (vv. 55–65), Peter in the courtyard (vv. 66–72). Inside, Jesus confesses who he is and is condemned; outside, Peter denies who he is and saves himself.

At a distance. Among the saddest descriptions of discipleship in the New Testament. Yet do not despise Peter too quickly: the others have fled, and he followed. But at a distance: near enough to keep your conscience quiet, far enough to keep your safety. Nobody stays there long. He followed right into the courtyard, the open yard at the centre of a wealthy house; John says another disciple, known to the high priest, got him through the gate (John 18:15–16).

Warming himself at the fire. Sitting with the guards, not standing at the edge: he has sat down among the men who arrested his Lord an hour ago. He has not denied anything yet; he has simply taken a place at the enemy’s fire because the spring night was cold and he wanted to see what would happen, and the next thing that happens is that the firelight falls on his face (v. 67).

The High Priest before the high priest. When Caiaphas said one man should die for the people, John adds, he unknowingly prophesied (John 11:51–52). Tonight the high priest of the old covenant sits in judgment on the great high priest of the new (Hebrews 4:14). Caiaphas’s office was to offer the blood of animals, year after year (Hebrews 9:25); the prisoner before him is about to offer himself, holy, innocent, unstained (Hebrews 7:26–27), once for all. The man in the robes is condemning the only priest who could take his own sins away. And while his friend warmed his hands below, Jesus stood upstairs in the cold of their hatred and did not flinch.

Is it wrong to keep quiet about Christ among people who have no time for him? Not always; you need not preach at every lunch table. But there is a version of Peter’s fire in every Christian’s life: the place where you can be near Christ and comfortable at once, sitting with people who mock him and saying nothing, because it is warm and leaving would cost something. The question is not whether you speak every time, but whether you have settled in. If your company regularly requires you to hide that you belong to Jesus, it is time either to speak or to move away from the fire.
verseByVerse.note: John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death, but they found none. For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council has already decided on death and searches for evidence to justify it, but even with false witnesses it cannot make a case.

Seeking testimony against Jesus. Mark convicts the court in one line: the verdict, death, is fixed, and they are hunting for evidence to fit it.

But they found none. The supreme court of Israel, with every motive and the whole night, could not assemble a credible case from three years of public ministry watched by hostile professionals. That does not by itself prove he was sinless, but it is striking testimony: a hostile prosecution had every reason to produce something, and could not.

Their testimony did not agree. The witnesses were lying, and the lies did not match.
