They broke the ninth commandment to convict the Son of God (Exodus 20:16), as the psalmist foretold: “false witnesses have risen against me” (Psalm 27:12; 35:11). The Law required at least two agreeing witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and a false witness in a capital case was to suffer the death he had sought to inflict (Deuteronomy 19:18–19). None of these is charged with anything.

The irregularities. The later Mishnah required capital cases to be heard by day, in the temple’s own hall, and a condemnation to wait overnight, though how much of that was in force in AD 30 is uncertain. This trial is held at night, in a private house, at Passover, with sentence passed within the hour. But Mark does not lean on any of that.

The spotless Lamb. He was innocent, a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:19): every word true, every deed holy, every thought pure. That is exactly why he could stand in the place of the guilty.

In everyday life. If you are falsely accused, remember that Jesus was, and commit your cause to God, who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Do not pay back slander with slander; the Spirit of the Lamb who was silent before his accusers lives in you. Tell the truth plainly, accept help, and leave the outcome with him.

Why did God let an innocent man be convicted? Because only an innocent man could save the guilty; had Jesus been condemned for sins of his own, his death would have paid for nothing but those. That his enemies could find nothing is what makes his death a substitution: “the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). God did not approve of the injustice, and the men who committed it were guilty. But he wove it into the greatest act of justice in history, in which sin was truly punished and sinners truly pardoned.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin. The law required two agreeing witnesses.

parallels.desc: false witnesses have risen against me

verseByVerse.quote: And some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying, "We heard him say, 'I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.'" Yet even about this their testimony did not agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most damaging charge, that Jesus threatened to destroy the temple, twists something he really said, and even it collapses.

I will destroy this temple. A lie built out of something true, which is how the most effective lies are made. John records what he did say, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”, and the explanation the witnesses have conveniently lost: “he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:19–21). He had predicted the temple’s destruction (13:2), but not that he would do it.

Count the alterations. He said “Destroy this temple”, a challenge to them; they report “I will destroy this temple”, turning a saying about his own death into a plot against the national sanctuary. Jeremiah nearly lost his life for prophesying against the temple (Jeremiah 26:8–11), and Stephen will lose his on the same accusation (Acts 6:13–14). Nothing is invented; everything is turned. That is still the commonest way Christ and his people are misrepresented: quoting part and leaving out what explains it.

Not made with hands. “Made with hands” was used of idols and man-made temples (Acts 7:48). The witnesses may have been twisting Jesus’ teaching that a new temple was coming, not a building but a people built around himself (1 Corinthians 3:16).

Even about this. Even the best lie in the room could not survive two men telling it, and the charge failed on the Law’s own safeguard (Deuteronomy 19:15). The whole trial turns here: unable to find a crime, they asked him who he was, and he told them, and that was enough. The charge that kills him comes out of his own mouth.

The irony. The false testimony was, in a deeper sense, true. By putting Jesus to death they would destroy the temple of his body; in three days he would rise; and his resurrection would bring into being the true temple, not made with hands, the church, “in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:21). The lie told at his trial became the truth of Easter.

In everyday life. Before you repeat a report about someone this week, especially a Christian leader or a person you dislike, ask whether you have the whole of what was said, or only a sentence with the key removed.

How should I respond when my words, or my faith, are twisted? Calmly, with the truth. Clarify what you actually said, once, without bitterness, and do not twist their words in return. Do not be surprised: if they twisted the words of Jesus, they will twist yours. When Christianity itself is caricatured or quoted out of context, restore the missing context gently, as John restores it for us. The truth usually needs only to be stated fully to defend itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, "Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?" But he remained silent and made no answer. Again the high priest asked him, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?" And Jesus said, "I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus will not defend himself against lies, but asked whether he is the Christ, the Son of God, he answers plainly, “I am”, and tells his judges that they will see him enthroned beside God and coming as their Judge.

Have you no answer to make? The case has collapsed, and Caiaphas stands up and moves into the middle of the room to rescue it. His first move is to get the prisoner talking.

He remained silent. Mark says it twice over, because the silence is the point. Pointing out that the witnesses disagree, or explaining what he said about the temple, would have taken thirty seconds. Instead: “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). Every instinct in a wronged man is to explain. He will not say a word in his own defence, because a defence would have worked, and he had not come to be acquitted.

Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? The direct question, the question the whole Gospel has been asking since 1:1. “The Blessed” is a reverent substitute for the divine name; Caiaphas will not say “God” aloud. Matthew adds that he put him under oath (Matthew 26:63).

I am. All through this Gospel Jesus has told people to keep quiet about who he is, because the title would have been misunderstood. Now he is bound, and when it can only cost him his life, he says it plainly. The words are egō eimi, the words he spoke on the water in the dark (6:50), and they may echo the name God gave Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:14).

Seated at the right hand of Power. He joins two Old Testament texts. “Seated at the right hand of Power” is Psalm 110:1, the psalm he had put to these very men as an unanswerable riddle two days before (12:36); “Power” is another reverent way of saying God. “Coming with the clouds of heaven” is Daniel 7:13, the one like a son of man given dominion and glory and a kingdom, whom all peoples serve. A bound prisoner tells the court about to sentence him that he will be on the throne and come as their judge. The dock and the bench are about to change places, and that is why the high priest tore his robes.

The truth about the universe. A prisoner with bound hands spoke two words, and they were the truth about the universe. Caiaphas sat on the bench that night; one day he will stand before the man he judged. Until that day the same throne is a throne of grace, and the Judge on it pleads for all who come to him.

Why was he silent before, and then answer? Because the questions were different. The first invited him to defend himself against lies, and he would not: his was the silence of the Lamb, who had come to be condemned. The second asked, under oath, who he was, and silence then would have denied the truth. That is a pattern for his people. We need not always defend our own reputations, and often should not; but when we are asked whether we belong to Christ and who he is, we must answer, whatever it costs.

When would they see this? Some take it as Christ’s vindication in his resurrection, ascension and the judgment on Jerusalem, since in Daniel the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days to receive his kingdom. Others take it as the final coming, when “every eye will see him, even those who pierced him” (Revelation 1:7). The more likely reading holds both: from his resurrection Jesus is enthroned at God’s right hand, and his judges saw the signs of it; all will see him coming with the clouds at his return, when they stand before their Judge.
verseByVerse.note: “The Blessed” is a reverent way of saying “God.” Jesus’ “I am” is his plainest claim in Mark.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest tore his garments and said, "What further witnesses do we need? You have heard his blasphemy. What is your decision?" And they all condemned him as deserving death. And some began to spit on him and to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him, "Prophesy!" And the guards received him with blows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council condemns Jesus to death for blasphemy on his own confession, then spits on him, blindfolds him and beats him.

Tore his garments. The formal gesture on hearing blasphemy. The Law forbade the high priest to tear his clothes: “The priest who is chief among his brothers … shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes” (Leviticus 21:10). This probably referred to mourning, and later practice allowed the gesture at blasphemy. The deeper irony is that in a room full of experts on the law, the only person wholly keeping it was the one they were about to kill for breaking it.

What further witnesses do we need? Relief: the problem of the witnesses is solved, in the one honest sentence any of his judges speaks all night. Blasphemy was punishable by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). Strictly it meant using the divine name irreverently, and claiming to be the Messiah was not in itself blasphemy; others had done it. But claiming to sit at God’s right hand and come on the clouds, sharing God’s throne and his role as judge, was claiming to be equal with God. If it was false, it was blasphemy. If it was true, they were condemning God.

Only two options. There were never more than two in that room, and there are never more than two now. Either the man in the dock is God’s Son, or he said the most blasphemous thing a human being has ever said. Caiaphas at least sees what is at stake, and the trial leaves no room to call Jesus merely a fine moral teacher.

They all condemned him. Unanimous among those who voted. Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council, had not consented (Luke 23:51); perhaps he was absent.

Spit on him. The deepest contempt in that culture (Deuteronomy 25:9), as Isaiah said the Servant would receive: “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6).

Prophesy! A cruel game: they blindfold him, hit him and demand that he name who did it (Luke 22:64); then the guards take him over with blows. “Prophesy!” is the most ironic word in the chapter, for his prophecy of Peter’s denials was at that moment coming true below them, in the courtyard.

Blindfolded, he saw everything. The face that angels cannot look upon was covered with a rag and slapped by servants, so that God would never turn his face from us. The blindfold was on his eyes, and still he saw everything: the servants, the council, the friend at the fire below.

In everyday life. Let the picture of his spat-on face cure you of self-pity the next time you are mocked for his sake, and refuse to join, even with a laugh, in the mockery of Christ that passes for wit in your office, your family or your feed.

Did Jesus really claim this, or did the church put it in his mouth later? The trial is the best answer: nobody crucifies a man for telling people to love their neighbours. Jesus was condemned by his own nation’s court for blasphemy and handed to Rome on a charge of claiming to be king (15:2, 26), and those charges make sense only if he said something like this. Within about twenty-five years of his death Paul, a strict Jew who confessed that God is one, was writing of “one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6). The claim is not a later decoration. It is why he died.

Who was responsible for the death of Jesus? Scripture answers: the leaders who condemned him, the governor who sentenced him, the soldiers who crucified him and the crowd who called for it, Jew and Gentile together (Acts 4:27). Behind them stood the purpose of God, who delivered him up for us all (Romans 8:32). And in the deepest sense every sinner, for it was for our sins that he died (Isaiah 53:5). That rules out for ever the wicked charge that the Jews as a people are uniquely guilty, which has caused so much suffering. It also rules out every comfortable view of the cross in which someone else did it: “it was my sin that held him there.”
verseByVerse.note: Tearing one’s garments was a sign of horror or grief.

parallels.desc: I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting

verseByVerse.quote: And as Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the servant girls of the high priest came, and seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said, "You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus." But he denied it, saying, "I neither know nor understand what you mean." And he went out into the gateway and the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Challenged by a servant girl, Peter denies knowing Jesus with a vague evasion, and the rooster crows for the first time.

Below in the courtyard. Mark gives us the architecture: upstairs, Christ confessing who he is and being struck for it; downstairs, in the same house, Peter at the fire, about to be asked the same question. One says “I am”, and it costs him his life. The other says, in effect, “I am not”, and it costs him everything else.

One of the servant girls. Not a soldier, nor one of the temple police who had seen him draw a sword, but a servant girl, among the lowest in the household (John calls her the girl at the door, John 18:17), with no power over him whatever.

She looked at him. She stared across the fire, with the light on his face. It is because he sat down at that fire that she can see him at all; in the shadows at the edge of the yard, nobody asks you anything.

You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus. Not “you are a disciple”, but “you were with him”: association, that is all, and being with him was the very purpose for which Peter was chosen (3:14). “The Nazarene” is faintly contemptuous.

He denied it. Not a flat lie so much as a fog, the answer of a man buying time. We imagine Peter’s denial as dramatic and unlike us, but it begins as an evasion at a fire: not “I renounce Christ”, just a vague sentence said to somebody unimportant, to make a moment go away.

The rooster crowed. He moves out to the entrance passage, further from the light, and the rooster crows, the first of the two Jesus foretold (v. 30). There is mercy in it: the first crow was a warning, and there was still time. Even while Jesus was being struck, he was still caring for the friend who was letting him down. Peter heard it, and it meant nothing to him.

In everyday life. Listen for the roosters in your life: the conscience that stings, the verse that comes to mind, the friend’s question. They are mercies, sent while there is still time.

Why do the small denials matter so much? Because the large ones begin there, and because they are the ones we commit most. Very few of us will be asked under threat of death whether we follow Jesus. Many will be asked lightly, at work or at a party, whether we are religious or what we think of something Christ forbids, and will be tempted to answer with fog. The remedy is to decide in advance what you will say, simply and kindly, so that when the servant girl asks, you are not deciding in the firelight. Underneath the fog there is usually an idol, the approval of the people at the fire. “The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (Proverbs 29:25), and the cure for craving their approval is to remember that in Christ you already have his.

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit “and the rooster crowed” here, but it fits Jesus’ “twice” (v. 30) and the second crowing in verse 72.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders, "This man is one of them." But again he denied it. And after a little while the bystanders again said to Peter, "Certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The questions spread to the bystanders and harden into an accusation, and Peter keeps on denying, though his Galilean accent gives him away.

This man is one of them. The pressure widens from private to public, and the wording hardens: not “you were with him” but “he is one of them”, a group, a party.

Again he denied it. Mark does not even record the words, and the tense means he kept on denying. The first denial makes the second cheap: having said “I neither know nor understand”, he must defend that as well as himself, and the only way is to say it again with more force. A man who tells one lie has taken out a loan; every later lie is interest.

You are a Galilean. Now they have evidence: his accent. Galilean Aramaic was noticeably different from Jerusalem speech; later rabbinic stories joke about Galileans swallowing their consonants. Matthew makes it explicit: “your accent betrays you” (Matthew 26:73). He can deny knowing Jesus; he cannot deny the sound of his own mouth.

Peter’s accent was more faithful than Peter was. And upstairs another Galilean, from a village Jerusalem despised, was on trial, and did not hide where he came from or whose Son he was. The Galilean in the dock owned his Father; the Galilean at the fire disowned his friend. Yet Peter carried deeper marks than an accent, put there by Jesus himself: he had been with Jesus, and had come to resemble the company he kept. That is what following Christ does to a person, and it is a mercy even when it is inconvenient. His Spirit writes his likeness into ordinary lives until it cannot be hidden.

In everyday life. If you have told one small lie this week to avoid being identified with him, go back and correct it now, before the interest grows.

What should give a Christian away? Not a special vocabulary or a religious manner, but the marks of having been with Jesus (Acts 4:13): gracious speech, without cruelty, gossip or filth (Colossians 4:6); honesty and generosity with money; kindness to people with no power to help you; grief with hope in loss; quiet refusals without a show. None of these makes you a Christian, but if you are one, they will grow, and people will notice before anything is said: “Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father” (Matthew 5:16).
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent.

verseByVerse.quote: But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, "I do not know this man of whom you speak." And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, "Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." And he broke down and wept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter swears with an oath and a curse that he does not know Jesus; then the rooster crows a second time, he remembers his Lord’s words, and he breaks down in tears.

To invoke a curse. Not bad language but something formal and terrible: the oath formula of that world, “may God do so to me and more also if I am lying”. Peter calls God to witness, and calls down God’s curse on his own head, to guarantee a lie about God’s Son.

This man. He will not say the name, and puts as much distance into the sentence as the grammar allows. He knew him better than almost anyone alive, and had said at Caesarea Philippi, “You are the Christ.” At that very moment, upstairs, this man was confessing that he is the Son of God.

A second time. Exactly as Jesus had said. God used the most ordinary sound in the world, and timed it to the second.

Peter remembered. Remembering is where he begins to turn back. Luke adds the detail that finishes him: “the Lord turned and looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61). If the prisoner was being moved across the courtyard at that moment, their eyes met as the bird called.

He broke down and wept. His lowest point is the beginning of his way back. However Mark’s unusual phrase is best translated (see the box below), the tense means he went on weeping: bitter tears of repentance (Luke 22:62).

Peter and Judas. Two men failed Jesus that night, both of the twelve, both warned to their faces. Judas betrayed him and despaired, and died by his own hand (Matthew 27:3–5). Peter denied him and wept, and was restored (16:7; John 21:15–19). The difference was not in the size of the sin; denying him three times with oaths is not obviously better than selling him for silver. It was in what each did with the wreckage. Judas felt remorse, and it drove him away from Christ; Peter felt grief, and it drove him back. That is the difference between remorse and repentance, which is not only feeling bad about a sin but turning from it back to God, trusting his mercy. “Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). And on the third morning an angel in an empty tomb will say: “go, tell his disciples and Peter” (16:7). The one who denied him is the one singled out by name to be told.

He bore the curse Peter called down. The Lord who turned and looked at Peter was at that moment being condemned for Peter. He bore the curse Peter called down on himself, so that Peter would never have to bear it. The tears in that courtyard are the beginning of the man who preached at Pentecost, so that everyone who has warmed their hands at the wrong fire would know there is a way back. That is our Saviour: he looks at us at our worst, with eyes that break our hearts and then heal them.

Why record this? The early church did not hide its greatest leader’s failure: Peter, whose preaching Mark probably records, told this story against himself, again and again, as a testimony to the grace that restored him. No Christian is too great to fall, and no fallen Christian is beyond restoration. That was a pressing word for Mark’s first readers, very probably the church at Rome, where under Nero some believers had broken under pressure and named others (see the note on 13:12–13): a disciple who had denied his Lord was not thereby finished, and the way back was open.

In everyday life. If you have denied Christ, in word or deed, do not despair like Judas. Weep like Peter, and come back: tell him exactly what you did, without excuse, and let him restore you among his people. And if someone you know has fallen, be the angel at the tomb for them: go and tell them, by name, that he is waiting.

But did Jesus not say he would deny those who deny him? He did: “whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father” (Matthew 10:33; compare 2 Timothy 2:12). Those words describe a final, settled denial, by someone who will not come back. Peter’s was a terrible fall, but not a final one. Jesus had prayed that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), and it did not. A believer can fall badly; Christ keeps him from falling away for good. If you have denied him and your heart is breaking over it, that grief is the proof that you are not the person those verses describe.

I keep failing in the same way. Is there still a way back? Yes, as many times as you come. Peter did not fall only once; years later he drew back from Gentile believers out of fear and had to be rebuked to his face (Galatians 2:11–14). Restoration is not a single event but the pattern of the Christian life: fall, grieve, return, be received. Do not let the size or repetition of your failure persuade you that Christ is tired of you. He told Peter to forgive seventy-seven times (older versions say seventy times seven); he will not do less himself. Come back today, confess it plainly, and get up.

Uncertain wording. “To invoke a curse” has no object in the Greek: most take it that Peter called a curse down on himself if he was lying, but some think he cursed Jesus. And “he broke down and wept” translates an unusual phrase (epibalōn eklaien) whose first word is obscure here: it may mean “he thought about it and wept”, “he threw himself down and wept”, or simply “he began to weep”. The broad sense is clear: a man undone by what he had done.

14.theology:
Gethsemane reverses Eden. In a garden a man said, in effect, “my will”, and the world broke; in a garden a man said not what I will, but what you will, and it was mended (on this and on the cup he accepted there, see the note on vv. 35–36).

Abba (v. 36), the family word a child used at home, did not stay his (see “The name he handed over” in the note on vv. 35–36).
14.examples:
Then: the chapter ends with two men who failed him, Judas and Peter, and what each did with the wreckage (see “Peter and Judas” in the note on vv. 71–72).

Now: if you have failed him badly, notice where Peter’s fall began: at a distance, and then at the enemy’s fire (see the note on vv. 53–54).

keyVerse.quote: Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter turns on this prayer. The Son asks honestly whether the cup of God’s wrath can pass, and when it cannot, he chooses his Father’s will, the obedience that undoes Adam’s “my will” and saves people who sleep, run and deny him. Because he drank that cup, there is nothing left in it for anyone who trusts him, and his own “Abba” is now on their lips.

14.reflection:
The room called the woman’s gift waste, and Jesus called it beautiful (vv. 4–6). What is the “alabaster flask” in your life, the thing you are most reluctant to give him? What does “she has done what she could” (v. 8) say to someone who feels they have little to offer?

At the table each disciple asked, “Is it I?” (v. 19), yet an hour later Peter boasted, “Even though they all fall away, I will not” (v. 29). Why is self-confidence so dangerous for a Christian, and how does the Lord’s Supper, given to men who would all run away, answer both fear and pride?

In Gethsemane Jesus asked plainly for the cup to pass, and then prayed, “Yet not what I will, but what you will” (v. 36). How does his prayer shape the way you pray about hard things? Where do you find it hardest to pray the second half?

Peter and Judas both failed Jesus that night. What made the difference between them (vv. 10–11, 72)? What would it look like for you, or for your group, to be “the angel at the tomb” for someone who has fallen?

15.title: Truly This Man Was the Son of God
15.text: <sup>1</sup>And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate. <sup>2</sup>And Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” And he answered him, “You have said so.” <sup>3</sup>And the chief priests accused him of many things. <sup>4</sup>And Pilate again asked him, “Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you.” <sup>5</sup>But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed. <sup>6</sup>Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. <sup>7</sup>And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. <sup>8</sup>And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. <sup>9</sup>And he answered them, saying, “Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?” <sup>10</sup>For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up. <sup>11</sup>But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release for them Barabbas instead. <sup>12</sup>And Pilate again said to them, “Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?” <sup>13</sup>And they cried out again, “Crucify him.” <sup>14</sup>And Pilate said to them, “Why? What evil has he done?” But they shouted all the more, “Crucify him.” <sup>15</sup>So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified. <sup>16</sup>And the soldiers led him away inside the palace (that is, the governor’s headquarters), and they called together the whole battalion. <sup>17</sup>And they clothed him in a purple cloak, and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on him. <sup>18</sup>And they began to salute him, “Hail, King of the Jews!” <sup>19</sup>And they were striking his head with a reed and spitting on him and kneeling down in homage to him. <sup>20</sup>And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him. <sup>21</sup>And they compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. <sup>22</sup>And they brought him to the place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull). <sup>23</sup>And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it. <sup>24</sup>And they crucified him and divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take. <sup>25</sup>And it was the third hour when they crucified him. <sup>26</sup>And the inscription of the charge against him read, “The King of the Jews.” <sup>27</sup>And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left. <sup>29</sup>And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, “Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, <sup>30</sup>save yourself, and come down from the cross!” <sup>31</sup>So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another, saying, “He saved others; he cannot save himself. <sup>32</sup>Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe.” Those who were crucified with him also reviled him. <sup>33</sup>And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. <sup>34</sup>And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” <sup>35</sup>And some of the bystanders hearing it said, “Behold, he is calling Elijah.” <sup>36</sup>And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying, “Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down.” <sup>37</sup>And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last. <sup>38</sup>And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. <sup>39</sup>And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” <sup>40</sup>There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. <sup>41</sup>When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem. <sup>42</sup>And when evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, <sup>43</sup>Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. <sup>44</sup>Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died. And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. <sup>45</sup>And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph. <sup>46</sup>And Joseph bought a linen shroud, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. <sup>47</sup>Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.
15.overview:
Where we are. This is the day the whole Gospel has been heading towards since Jesus first foretold his suffering (8:31). From dawn to sunset on the Friday he is handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, crucified and buried, exactly as he said (10:33–34).

The message. The King everyone mocks dies in the place of the guilty, and by his death God opens the way to himself. Mark tells it almost without adjectives: fifteen hours from the garden to the grave. Every hand in it acts from envy, fear, cruelty or indifference, yet nothing is out of control. The mockers speak the truth without meaning to: he is the King; he saved others and will not save himself. And as he dies, a Roman officer confesses: “Truly this man was the Son of God!”

Why it was said. Mark’s first readers knew Roman governors, Roman soldiers and Roman crosses, and some would face them for Christ’s sake (see the introduction). They needed to know that a crucified Messiah was not an embarrassment but the heart of the gospel, and that their Lord had walked this road first.

How the chapter makes its case. Before Pilate (vv. 1–15) Jesus is almost silent, and Barabbas, guilty of the very rebellion Jesus is falsely charged with, goes free while the innocent man is condemned. The soldiers’ mock coronation (vv. 16–20) and the placard at Golgotha (v. 26) get every detail right, and the mockers all say the same thing: come down and save yourself (vv. 29–32). The darkness at noon and the cry of Psalm 22 (vv. 33–37) show what he bore, God’s judgment on sin; the torn curtain and the centurion’s confession (vv. 38–39) show what his death achieved. The women and Joseph (vv. 40–47) witness his death and burial.

Where it leads. Mark’s long-kept secret is out: the Son of God is seen most clearly not in his miracles but in his death, as the Servant who gives his life as a ransom for many (10:45). He was forsaken so that his people never will be, and the way to God, barred since Eden, is torn open from God’s side.

For us. Everyone in this chapter does something with Jesus. Pilate’s question is still ours: “What shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?” Do not ask him to come down from the cross. Look at him there, and trust him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — Before Pilate and the Mocking
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The innocent King is condemned and a guilty rebel goes free, while everyone who handles Jesus passes him on to someone else. At first light the council hands him to Rome, and before Pilate he gives one guarded answer and then silence (vv. 1–5). Pilate sees that the charge comes from envy and tries to release him through a festival custom, but the chief priests work the crowd, the crowd asks for Barabbas, and Pilate, after asking what evil he has done and getting no answer, hands him over anyway (vv. 6–15). Then the soldiers dress him in purple, crown him with thorns and salute him as king, telling the truth without knowing it (vv. 16–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Barabbas is the atonement acted out in a Jerusalem courtyard. A rebel guilty in fact of the crime Jesus is falsely charged with walks free, and the innocent one dies on the cross prepared for the guilty (see the note on v. 15).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: what evil has he done? (v. 14) is the right question, asked by the one man with the authority to act on it, who then signed the order anyway, wishing to satisfy the crowd.

Now: that is the commonest failure of people in authority: the doctrine not defended because of who would leave, the wrong not named because of whose son it was, the decision made by counting who is for it rather than weighing what is right. Pilate did not decide that Jesus was guilty. He decided that being right was more expensive than being popular. That is a different sin, and one far easier for any of us to commit.

verseByVerse.quote: And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate. And Pilate asked him, "Are you the King of the Jews?" And he answered him, "You have said so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At first light the council hands Jesus over to Rome, and when the governor asks whether he is a king, Jesus gives a guarded yes. He is the King, but not the kind Pilate fears.

As soon as it was morning. Within nine hours Jesus will be dead. He had told his disciples to stay awake, for the master might come in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow or in the morning (13:35). This night has had all four: evening at the supper, midnight in the garden, cockcrow in the courtyard where Peter wept (14:72), and now morning. The disciples have slept or run through every one.

A consultation. They meet again at first light, probably because a capital verdict reached at night was irregular (by the rules later written down in the Mishnah): a daylight formality, held by men who had fixed the sentence before they looked for evidence (14:55). They also agreed how to present the case. Blasphemy would mean nothing to a Roman governor, so they made it political: Jesus claims to be a king, a rival to Caesar (Luke 23:2).

They bound Jesus. Isaac was bound on the altar (Genesis 22:9); the true sacrifice is bound now. “Delivered over” is Mark’s word for Judas’s betrayal (14:10) and for what the Son of Man must undergo (9:31; 10:33), and it will be used of Pilate (v. 15). Everyone in this chapter hands him on to somebody else. Nobody wants to be the last pair of hands.

Why Pilate at all? Because under Roman rule the council could pass a religious sentence but could not carry out a death sentence (John 18:31). Pontius Pilate governed Judea from AD 26 to 36, coming up from Caesarea at festivals with extra troops. Ancient writers call him harsh and contemptuous of the Jews (compare Luke 13:1).

Are you the King of the Jews? Pilate’s first words, before any evidence is heard: he had been told in advance. “King of the Jews” is a Gentile phrase; Jews said “King of Israel” (v. 32). The title runs through the chapter. Judea had a history of messianic risings, and Rome tolerated no king without Caesar’s permission, so Pilate is not asking about theology but whether this man is a threat.

You have said so. Jesus is not dodging the question but refusing the meaning Pilate gives the word “king”, loaded with everything Rome feared: insurrection, a rival throne, tax revolt. He will not deny the kingship, because he is the King; he will not affirm it in Pilate’s terms, because in those terms it means something he has never claimed. John gives the fuller exchange: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36–37). It is his last recorded answer to a question in this Gospel. From here, almost nothing, until a cry at three in the afternoon.

In everyday life. Most of us have a king we consult on Sundays and a small kingdom of our own that runs the rest of the week: the money, the evenings, the way we speak at home. He does not storm that kingdom. He waits to be asked in, and he rules it far more kindly than we do.

Should Christians seek political power for Christ’s kingdom? Christians may vote, campaign for justice and hold office, as Joseph and Daniel did (Romans 13:1–4). But Christ’s kingdom does not come by legislation or force. It comes by the word and the Spirit, through the new birth (John 3:3–5). A church that confuses the two either tries to make people Christian by law or makes the gospel a political badge, and both betray the King who answered Pilate as he did. Seek the good of your city; do not mistake any party or nation for the kingdom of God.

Uncertain wording. Jesus’ reply is two words in Greek, sy legeis, literally “you say”. Some take it as a plain yes; others as non-committal: that is your word for it. Since he has just answered the high priest “I am” (14:62), and goes to the cross as King of the Jews without protest, it is best read as a real but qualified yes: true, though not in the sense you mean.
verseByVerse.note: Under Roman rule the council could not carry out a death sentence. Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

verseByVerse.quote: And the chief priests accused him of many things. And Pilate again asked him, "Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you." But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Charged with many things, Jesus will not say a word in his own defence, and the governor is amazed.

Many things. Luke lists them: misleading the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar, and claiming to be Christ, a king (Luke 23:2). Every one is false or twisted; he had told them to pay the tax (12:17). The chief priests’ strategy is volume: if no single charge will hold, pile them up.

Have you no answer to make? Roman law let the accused defend himself, and a man who did not was normally convicted. Pilate, it seems, is trying to help: a governor who wanted a conviction would let the accusations stand, but Pilate prompts the prisoner to speak, because he can see the case is thin. Matthew adds that his wife told him to have nothing to do with this righteous man (Matthew 27:19). He is looking for a way out.

No further answer. Jesus will not take it, just as he was silent before the high priest (14:61). A single sentence would have collapsed the case: I told them to pay the tax; ask them. He says nothing (Isaiah 53:7).

Pilate was amazed. He had seen every kind of defendant, the pleaders, the bribers, the weepers, and every one of them fought. He had rarely seen a man decline to save himself. “Kings shall shut their mouths because of him” (Isaiah 52:15).

His defence has never been refused. The Word through whom the worlds were made stood silent before liars, not from weakness but in submission to his Father’s will, and his silence was the price of our acquittal. He kept his mouth shut so that ours could be opened. Because he was silent then, he speaks for us now as our advocate with the Father, and his defence of his people has never once been refused.

Why would an innocent man refuse to defend himself? Because he had not come to be acquitted. He was not on trial to clear his name but to bear our sentence, and his silence was the most deliberate act in the room. That is also why it is not a rule for every Christian in every courtroom. Paul defended himself and appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:10–11). Jesus’ silence belonged to his unique work as the Lamb.

parallels.desc: like a sheep that before its shearers is silent

verseByVerse.quote: Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. And he answered them, saying, "Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?" For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate, seeing that the charge is driven by envy, tries to free Jesus through a festival custom, and the choice is set between him and Barabbas.

The Passover release. A goodwill custom at the feast of liberation (Passover). It is attested nowhere outside the Gospels, but governors did grant such amnesties, and a local custom would hardly leave much record. And the Lord of the feast of liberation was not released, so that every prisoner of sin could be.

Barabbas. Not a common criminal but a political prisoner, a rebel who had committed murder in the insurrection, perhaps one of the armed nationalists later called Zealots. He is guilty of exactly what Jesus is falsely accused of, sedition against Rome, and he is exactly the kind of king many wanted. His name, Bar-abbas, is Aramaic for “son of the father”, and some manuscripts of Matthew give his first name as Jesus (Matthew 27:16–17). So the crowd chooses between two sons of the father: a murderer, and the Son of the Father who prayed “Abba” a few hours before (14:36).

The crowd came up. They initiate it, and they have somebody in mind. It is not necessarily the crowd from Sunday: early on a Friday, those present are whoever men with influence could assemble at short notice (v. 11).

Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews? A shrewd move: Pilate offers the amnesty with his preferred outcome first, and the title needles the priests: this is your king? He will have it nailed to the cross and refuse to change it (John 19:22).

Out of envy. Mark tells us what Pilate had worked out, and it settles his guilt. Not public order, not theological outrage: they wanted Jesus dead because the crowds hung on his teaching (11:18; 12:37), because his real authority showed how hollow theirs was, and because he had overturned their tables. Pilate knows the charge is malicious and the man innocent. Envy, one of the sins Jesus said comes from the heart (7:22), sent him to the cross.

How do I recognise envy in myself? Envy is sorrow at another’s good and quiet pleasure at his harm, and it usually calls itself concern, or justice, or high standards. Watch for the signs: you find it hard to rejoice when a colleague, sibling or fellow Christian is praised; you feel a small lift when someone you resent stumbles; you mention another’s gifts with a qualification attached. Do not pretend. Confess it to God, thank him specifically for the other person’s gifts, pray for their good, and remember that in Christ you already have more than you could ever envy (1 Corinthians 3:21–23).

Uncertain wording. Mark says “the insurrection”, as if his readers would know which one, but no other record tells us of it. It was probably one of the outbreaks of violence in Jerusalem during Pilate’s years; beyond that we cannot say.
verseByVerse.note: Barabbas means “son of the father.” The “insurrection” was one of many uprisings against Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release for them Barabbas instead. And Pilate again said to them, "Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?" And they cried out again, "Crucify him." And Pilate said to them, "Why? What evil has he done?" But they shouted all the more, "Crucify him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worked by the chief priests, the crowd asks for Barabbas and shouts for Jesus to be crucified, and to Pilate’s question, “What evil has he done?”, nobody has an answer.

Stirred up the crowd. The key to the next hour: the crowd is being worked. They did not arrive with a view about Barabbas; somebody gave them one (Matthew 27:20). There was no new fact about Jesus; people with authority told them what to think. A crowd makes louder whatever it is given, and whoever reaches it first decides what that is (Exodus 23:2).

Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews? “Again”: Mark is keeping count, and this is Pilate’s second attempt. He has put to a crowd, out loud, the question every person who hears of Jesus must answer, as though it were theirs to answer for him. His tragedy is that he asked it in the one way that guaranteed the wrong answer: he asked the room instead of deciding himself.

Crucify him. Two words, no charge, no reasoning: a demand for the most shameful death Rome knew, reserved for slaves, rebels and the worst criminals. And the Law said a man hanged on a tree was cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23). They wanted not only his death but his disgrace. The crowd that shouted “Hosanna” (11:9), or one like it, now shouts for this.

Why? What evil has he done? The third attempt, and the only honest question of the morning; Luke records that Pilate three times found no guilt in him (Luke 23:4, 14, 22). The answer is nothing, and Mark records no reply, because there was none. Nobody could name a crime, and that silence shows the trial for what it was. The only reply is all the more: when a case cannot be made, volume does the work, and it worked.

The curse he came to bear. The Lord who could have silenced the crowd with a word let their cry stand, because the curse they demanded for him was the curse he had come to bear for them (Galatians 3:13). The judge’s own words testify that he died not for his own sins but as “the righteous for the unrighteous” (1 Peter 3:18).

How do I stand firm when a crowd has been worked up? Notice when you agree with something mainly because everyone around you does, or because it was said loudly and often. Ask the question the crowd ignored: why? what is the evidence? Online, where crowds form in minutes, slow down before you share, sign or join. Test what you hear by Scripture rather than by its popularity, and be willing to be the one person in the room who says, quietly, that you do not think it is true. The crowd that shouted “crucify him” was sure it was right.

Is there a neutral answer to Pilate’s question? No. Pilate tried to find one by handing the question to others, and it did not save him. Everyone who hears of Jesus bows to him, rejects him or postpones him, and postponing is a decision too: “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Matthew 12:30). That is not a threat but the plain logic of who he is. If he is the King, the only right answer is to receive him.

verseByVerse.quote: So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To keep the crowd quiet, Pilate frees the guilty rebel, has Jesus scourged, and hands him over to be crucified. A judge who knows the truth chooses his own safety.

Wishing to satisfy the crowd. Mark gives the motive in one phrase, and it is not a legal judgment. Pilate gives way because his position could not survive a riot at Passover or a complaint to the emperor: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19:12). His record with Rome was already poor (Philo records a rebuke from Tiberius himself), and he was recalled a few years later anyway. He weighed an innocent life against his career, chose the career, and lost it in any case.

Washing his hands. Matthew records that he washed his hands to declare himself innocent (Matthew 27:24). But a judge who condemns a man he knows is innocent is not innocent, and his name is fixed in the creed, “suffered under Pontius Pilate”, as a witness that this happened in real history and that the governor was guilty.

He released Barabbas. Before nine that morning a convicted murderer walked into the street a free man and did not know why. He is the first person in history who could say, literally, that Jesus died instead of him. He had not repented, or asked, or understood; somebody else’s name was called instead of his. It is a picture of substitution: one man dying in another’s place.

Having scourged Jesus. The normal preliminary to crucifixion: the prisoner stripped, tied to a post and beaten with leather thongs weighted with bone or metal, with no fixed number of strokes. It tore the flesh, sometimes to the bone, and men died under it; this is why Simon must carry the beam (v. 21). “He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).

He delivered him to be crucified. The final handing over. And behind every human hand in the chain stands the Father, who gave up his Son for us all (Romans 8:32).

In everyday life. Where are you most tempted this week to do what you know is wrong because the pressure is rising: to sign off something dishonest, to stay silent while someone innocent is blamed? Decide now, before the noise, what you will do; the one who stood under that noise for you will stand with you in yours.

Was Pilate really guilty if he did not want to do it? Yes. Not wanting to do evil is not the same as refusing to do it. Pilate had the authority, the knowledge and the duty to release an innocent man, and he chose his own safety; Scripture names him among those who gathered against God’s holy servant Jesus (Acts 4:27). His reluctance makes him more instructive, not less guilty: most evil is done not by monsters but by people who know better and give way. Every heart has its own version of Pilate’s master: the good opinion of people we feel we cannot live without. Only a heart already accepted by God in Christ can afford to disappoint the crowd (Galatians 1:10).

Did Jesus die for Barabbas? We do not know whether Barabbas ever believed; Scripture does not say. His release is a picture, not a guarantee about him, and the picture is exact: a guilty man goes free because an innocent man takes his place, and he contributes nothing to it. That is what happens to every sinner who trusts Christ. It becomes your story not by being near the cross, as Barabbas was, but by faith, as you stop pleading your own case and rest on the one who took your place.
verseByVerse.note: Roman scourging used a whip weighted with bone or metal; it could itself kill.

parallels.desc: with his wounds we are healed

verseByVerse.quote: And the soldiers led him away inside the palace (that is, the governor's headquarters), and they called together the whole battalion. And they clothed him in a purple cloak, and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on him. And they began to salute him, "Hail, King of the Jews!" And they were striking his head with a reed and spitting on him and kneeling down in homage to him. And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers stage a mock coronation, robing, crowning and saluting Jesus as a king, and without knowing it they honour the true King.

The governor’s headquarters. The praetorium, the governor’s residence in Jerusalem: either Herod’s palace on the west side of the city or the Antonia fortress beside the temple.

The whole battalion. A cohort, nominally six hundred men, though probably only those on hand: auxiliaries recruited from the Gentile cities of the region, on riot duty at a festival they did not understand. A Jew handed to them as a king is entertainment.

A purple cloak. Purple, an expensive dye, was the colour of royalty. What they had to hand was probably a faded red soldier’s cloak (Matthew 27:28 says scarlet), passed off as a king’s robe.

A crown of thorns. A parody of the emperor’s laurel wreath, perhaps of long palm thorns sticking out like the rays of a crown on coins. And thorns arrive in Genesis 3 as part of the curse on the ground (Genesis 3:17–18). The first visible mark of a world under judgment is pressed onto the head of the man who came to lift it.

Hail, King of the Jews! A parody of the imperial greeting, “Ave, Caesar”, with the name changed: a bleeding provincial given an emperor’s honours. The reed was his mock sceptre (Matthew 27:29), and they beat him on the head with it, driving the thorns in. “Kneeling down in homage” is the language of worship (5:6; Matthew 2:11): they bow the knee to the Son of God as a joke.

Every element is true. He is the King of the Jews; Pilate will nail the words over his head within the hour. At the name of Jesus every knee will bow (Philippians 2:10–11), one day including every knee in that room. The soldiers staged a coronation as a joke and got every detail right. They were the only people in Jerusalem that morning conducting the correct ceremony. They simply thought it was funny.

They led him out. The robe comes off, because it belongs to somebody and will be wanted back, and soon they will gamble for the clothes he is standing in. Out of the city, for “Jesus also suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12).

Why did God allow his Son to be so humiliated? Because shame is part of what sin deserves, and he came to bear all of it. Adam and Eve’s first experience of sin was shame, and they hid (Genesis 3:7–10). He was stripped, mocked and spat on so that sinners covered in shame could be clothed and honoured before God; he endured the cross, despising the shame, for the joy set before him (Hebrews 12:2). If you carry shame, for what you have done or what was done to you, he has carried it too, and he can lift your head.
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. The ESV notes that a battalion (cohort) was a tenth of a Roman legion. Purple was the colour of royalty.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the cross Jesus refuses to save himself, bears the judgment of God in the dark, and by his death opens the way to God, even for a Gentile soldier. A passer-by is made to carry the beam, and at Golgotha Jesus refuses the drugged wine; Mark records the crucifixion itself in a few words (vv. 21–27). Passers-by, chief priests and robbers all take their turn, and the taunt is always the same: come down and save yourself (vv. 29–32). At noon the light goes out; at three he cries the first line of Psalm 22 and dies with a loud cry (vv. 33–37). The temple curtain tears from top to bottom, a Roman officer confesses him, and the women who have been there all along are named (vv. 38–41).
verseByVerse.theology: The cry of dereliction, the cry of one forsaken (v. 34), must be kept from two errors. The first would soften it, as though Jesus were merely reciting a psalm and was not truly forsaken. The second would break God in two, as though the Father ceased to love the Son. Both are answered at vv. 33–34, where his my God, my God and its comfort for the believer who feels forsaken are treated fully.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: He saved others; he cannot save himself (v. 31): the chief priests state the gospel accurately without believing a word of it (see the note on vv. 31–32).

Now: their demand, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe (v. 32), is still the common one: “show me and I will trust you” (see vv. 31–32). But the gospel still asks us to trust him there, on the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: And they compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. And they brought him to the place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Too weakened to carry the beam himself, Jesus is led to Golgotha while a passer-by, Simon of Cyrene, is forced to carry his cross.

They compelled a passerby. The condemned man normally carried his own crossbeam (patibulum), perhaps 75–100 pounds (35–45 kg), to the place of execution, where the upright stood waiting. John says Jesus set out carrying it (John 19:17); the likeliest reason it was taken from him is that he no longer could. After the night, the scourging and the mockery he is physically finished, and the soldiers needed him alive at Golgotha. “Compelled” is the word for a soldier’s right to make a civilian carry a load, the word behind “if anyone forces you to go one mile” (Matthew 5:41). Simon does not volunteer.

Coming in from the country. Into the city, as Jesus was being led out. Cyrene, in modern Libya, had a large Jewish community (Acts 2:10; 11:20), and Simon was probably a pilgrim who had come a very long way to keep the Passover. A soldier picks him out of the crowd, and the day is not his any more.

The father of Alexander and Rufus. Only Mark has this, and the likeliest reason he names them is that his readers knew them, probably as fellow Christians. Paul’s letter to the church at Rome, where this Gospel was probably written, greets “Rufus, chosen in the Lord; also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well” (Romans 16:13). It cannot be proved, but it strongly suggests that the man pressed into carrying the cross had a family in the church.

Golgotha. Aramaic for “skull”; Calvary comes from the Latin calvaria. It lay outside the wall but beside a road, because passers-by were meant to see (v. 29). The Church of the Holy Sepulchre has a strong claim to be the site.

The wood and the Lamb. Simon bears the beam a few hundred yards; Jesus will bear on it the sins of his people, a weight nobody could carry for him. Long before, Isaac carried the wood up Moriah and asked where the lamb was (Genesis 22:6–8). Now the wood goes up another hill, and the Lamb God provided walks in front of it, too spent to lift it, not too weak to finish what it was for.

What that morning did. A pilgrim is dragged out of a crowd and made to carry a condemned man’s cross, and it turns out to be the best thing that ever happened to his family. Luke says he carried it behind Jesus (Luke 23:26), the very picture of a disciple (8:34). Nobody pressed into carrying something for Christ is the poorer for it in the end, though it rarely feels like that at the time.

What does it mean to take up my cross today? Accepting whatever it costs to follow Jesus, rather than choosing the convenient parts. For Simon it was a beam he did not ask for. For you it may be loss of approval at work, a temptation refused every day, a costly forgiveness, or a call to serve somewhere unglamorous. It is not every hardship of life, such as illness or traffic, but the hardships that come because you belong to him. And Simon carried it behind Jesus: you never carry your cross ahead of him or alone, and he has carried the heavier one first.

Uncertain wording. Mark explains that Golgotha means “Place of a Skull”, but not why it was so called. It may have been a rocky outcrop shaped like a skull, or simply the name of an execution ground; we do not know.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community. Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.” Rufus may be the man Paul greets in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it. And they crucified him and divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus refuses the drugged wine so as to bear his suffering with a clear mind, and he is crucified while the soldiers gamble for his clothes, as Psalm 22 had said.

Wine mixed with myrrh. A rough anaesthetic. Jewish tradition records that the women of Jerusalem provided it as a mercy to the condemned, on the strength of Proverbs 31:6: “Give strong drink to the one who is perishing.” He did not take it, and it was a decision. He had said he would not drink wine again until he drank it new in the kingdom (14:25), and the cup given him in Gethsemane was to be drunk to the bottom (14:36). The mockery, the darkness and the cry he goes through fully conscious. He would not be half-present at his own crucifixion, or dull what he had come to bear.

They crucified him. Three words in Greek, and that is all. None of the Gospels describes the process; the nails are mentioned only after the resurrection (John 20:25). The victim was nailed or tied to the beam, hoisted onto the upright, and left, sometimes for days, until he died of exhaustion and suffocation; Cicero called it the cruellest of penalties. The Gospels do not try to move you by the horror but to show you its meaning: a reader overwhelmed by the physical agony can miss the darkness at noon and the cry at three, which are the heart of what he bore.

Divided his garments. The clothing of the executed belonged to the soldiers, and the Romans normally crucified men naked; the shame was total and public. The four soldiers (John 19:23) gambled a few feet away. The terrible thing is the ordinariness: the Son of God is dying above their heads, and the men closest to him are playing for a coat, because it is a working day.

Psalm 22. Mark does not point out the quotation; anyone who knew the Psalms would have recognised it with a shiver: “they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots” (Psalm 22:18). It is the first echo of the psalm of the righteous sufferer, laid in quietly until the man on the cross says its first line aloud. Behind it lies Eden, where God clothed Adam and Eve after the first sin (Genesis 3:21).

The Lord who clothes the lilies. The Lord who clothes the lilies of the field hung without a thread, while four soldiers diced for all he owned. He was stripped to clothe us in his righteousness. They won a tunic. He won a people, and dressed them in garments of salvation that no one can gamble away (Isaiah 61:10).

In everyday life. Notice what you reach for to dull the edge of a hard day: the screen, the drink, the noise, the shopping. Not all of it is wrong, but some of it keeps you from facing God with what is actually happening. Choose one evening this week to sit with the hard thing in prayer, clear-headed, instead of numbing it.

Is it wrong for a Christian to take painkillers or sedation, since Jesus refused? No. His refusal belonged to his unique work: he had a cup to drink that no one else could drink, and he had to drink it with full awareness as our substitute. You are not bearing God’s wrath, and you are not asked to suffer more than you must. Scripture approves of medicine and relief: Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and Luke was a physician. Receive pain relief with thanks as a gift of God’s kindness, not a failure of faith. What we learn here is not to refuse medicine but to marvel at what he chose to endure for us.
verseByVerse.note: Wine mixed with myrrh was a drugged drink to dull pain; Jesus refused it. The clothes of the condemned went to the execution squad.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: And it was the third hour when they crucified him. And the inscription of the charge against him read, "The King of the Jews." And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At nine in the morning Jesus is crucified between two rebels under a placard reading “The King of the Jews”, and the charge meant as a sneer is the plain truth.

The third hour. About 9 a.m., counting from sunrise as Mark does throughout: the sixth hour is noon (v. 33), the ninth three in the afternoon (v. 34). Arrested around midnight, before Pilate at first light, crucified at nine, dark at noon, dead by three.

The inscription of the charge. A placard stating the crime was fixed to the cross as mockery and warning: this is what happens to rebel kings. But this charge was the plain truth. John adds that it was written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek, and that when the chief priests asked Pilate to change it, he refused: “What I have written I have written” (John 19:19–22). The one decisive thing Pilate did all day was to leave a true sentence standing.

Two robbers. The word Jesus used at his arrest (14:48), probably meaning rebels like Barabbas, perhaps his companions; Jesus may well hang on the cross meant for Barabbas. “One on his right and one on his left”: James and John had asked for those places in his glory and were told they did not know what they were asking (10:37–40). The cross was his glory, and the places at his right and left went to two condemned men.

He reigns from the cross. The cross was not the interruption of his kingship but the way he exercised it. A king fights for his people and defeats their enemies, and on the cross Jesus defeated sin, death and the devil, disarming the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15). He gave his life for his subjects rather than taking theirs. The placard was truer than Pilate knew: the Lord we worship is a crucified King, whose crown was won at Golgotha before it was shown on Easter morning.

In everyday life. When you wish for a place of honour, at work, in the church, in the family, remember who had the places at his right and left, and ask whether you want the places beside him on his terms.

What of John’s “sixth hour”? John says it was about the sixth hour when Pilate handed him over (John 19:14), which on Mark’s reckoning would be noon. Some hold that John counts from midnight, though it is not certain anyone counted that way; others note that without clocks both writers work in rough three-hour blocks, and John says only “about”. Believers who hold Scripture true can leave this open. Mark’s account is consistent to the hour, and all four Gospels agree on the day, the place, the manner and the outcome.

Does a verse in the footnotes make the Bible unreliable? No. It shows how carefully the text has been preserved and studied. We have thousands of New Testament manuscripts, far more than for any other ancient book, and by comparing them scholars can see where a copyist added something, here probably a note from the margin. Modern Bibles tell you openly, the words themselves are true Scripture from Isaiah and Luke, and no doctrine depends on this verse.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verse 28: And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, He was numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12, quoted in Luke 22:37). It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added from Luke. The KJV and NKJV print it; the ESV puts it in a footnote. It is true, though not original to Mark. That is why the numbers in your Bible run 27, then 29.
verseByVerse.note: The third hour was about 9 a.m. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 28: “And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘He was numbered with the transgressors.’”

verseByVerse.quote: And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, "Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself, and come down from the cross!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Passers-by jeer at Jesus with the charge about the temple and dare him to save himself and come down.

Derided him, wagging their heads. The first of three groups to mock: the public on the road. “Derided” is literally “blasphemed”: he was condemned for blasphemy, and the real blasphemers are those who mock the Son of God. The wagging heads are Psalm 22 again: “all who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads” (Psalm 22:7).

You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days. They throw back the false witness from last night (14:58), which even the court could not get two men to agree on. Of all the things they might have mocked, they chose the one about to come true: the temple of his body was being destroyed, and in three days he would raise it.

Come down from the cross! Recognise the voice. In the wilderness Satan offered him the kingdoms of the world without a cross (Matthew 4:8–9). At Caesarea Philippi Peter rebuked him and was told “Get behind me, Satan!” (8:32–33). In Gethsemane he prayed that, if possible, the cup might pass, and then yielded to his Father’s will (14:36). Now, from the foot of the cross, the same offer in another voice: be the Christ without the cross. Why he did not come down is treated at vv. 31–32.

Could he have stepped down if he had chosen to? Yes (Matthew 26:53). He was held there not by the nails or the soldiers but by his own will and his love for his Father and his people. Nobody would take his life from him; he would lay it down himself, and take it up again (John 10:18). If he had been unable to come down, his staying would not have been obedience. Every minute of those six hours was chosen, and every taunt was an invitation he declined, for us.

In everyday life. The crown without the cross is still every Christian’s temptation, and it always sounds reasonable. Listen this week for the voice that says: come down; you have suffered enough; nobody will know; protect yourself first. Recognise it, and answer it in the strength his Spirit gives, the strength of the one who stayed on the cross for you (8:35).

verseByVerse.quote: So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another, saying, "He saved others; he cannot save himself. Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe." Those who were crucified with him also reviled him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests mock Jesus in words that state the gospel exactly: he saved others, and he will not save himself. Even the men dying beside him join in.

Mocked him to one another. The second group, and the worst: the religious leaders of Israel, sharing the joke among themselves with the satisfaction of people whose problem has been solved. Those who use religion to earn their place with God can hate grace more fiercely than open unbelievers do, because grace says that place can never be earned.

He saved others; he cannot save himself. They state the gospel more accurately than anyone else in Mark, and do not believe a syllable of it. “He saved others”: a concession from enemies, and all the stronger as evidence for that; they never disputed the miracles (3:22). “He cannot save himself”: true too, not because the power was gone, but because saving himself and saving others could not both be done. If he comes down, he is safe and we are lost; if he stays, we are saved and he is not. Love bound him to the cross more firmly than nails. The priests thought they had found a contradiction. They had found the heart of the atonement, the Saviour not sparing himself so that God can spare us (Romans 8:32).

That we may see and believe. “The Christ, the King of Israel” is the Jewish form of the title on the placard (v. 26), mocking his claim before the council (14:61–62) and offering belief on their own terms (8:11–12). It is a lie, and they had already proved it. They had seen a withered hand restored and gone out to plan a murder (3:5–6), and within days they will pay soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matthew 28:11–15). He would do something greater than come down from the cross: he would come up from the grave, and still they would not believe (Luke 16:31).

Also reviled him. The third group. Two men in the same agony join in; even shared suffering wins him no sympathy. Mark, showing Jesus’ total abandonment, records only the reviling. But Luke tells us that one of them, before the afternoon was out, said “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom”, and was told “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:39–43).

Love enough to stay. Had he come down, the crowd would have seen a wonder and gone home exactly as they came: impressed, and unforgiven. He stayed, and within three hours a Roman officer who had asked for no sign was confessing him. The priests meant their words as the final insult, and God has made them the song of his people for ever: he saved others. He saved a reviling robber before the afternoon was out, and Peter after his denials and Paul after his persecutions, every one because he would not save himself. The two halves of their sneer are the two halves of his glory: power enough to save anyone, and love enough to stay.

The strong who will not save themselves. “Save yourself” is the creed of the mockers, and much of the wisdom of our age: protect your peace, put yourself first, never let anyone take advantage of you. Friedrich Nietzsche saw the cross clearly enough to despise it, calling Christianity a slave morality, a religion of the weak. Nobody would have invented a God who dies like this; but Nietzsche mistook what he was looking at. The man on the cross was not too weak to come down; he was strong enough to stay. The self-assertive save themselves by power and the self-righteous by goodness, and both are still saving themselves. The one man who could have saved himself refused, and so the cross is the only place where the weak are saved by the strong without being crushed by him.

In everyday life. Is there someone you have written off: a family member hostile to Christ, a colleague who mocks, perhaps your own heart on a bad day? Both robbers reviled him, and one was in paradise by evening. Pray for that person again today.

Why does God not give unbelievers the sign they ask for? Because the problem is not a lack of evidence but a refusal to submit. These men had seen miracle after miracle and had already decided. God has given the greatest sign of all, the resurrection (Matthew 12:39–40; Romans 1:4), and he gives his Spirit to open blind eyes through the preaching of Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 1:22–24). So when a friend says he would believe if God showed himself, do not despair of him, and do not try to manufacture wonders. Point him to the cross and the empty tomb, and pray for the Spirit to do what signs cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?" which means, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At noon darkness, the Bible’s sign of God’s judgment, covers the land, and out of it Jesus cries that God has forsaken him, because he is bearing the judgment our sins deserve.

Darkness over the whole land. Noon until three, the brightest hours of a spring day, and the light goes out. It is not an eclipse: Passover falls at full moon, when a solar eclipse is impossible, and none lasts three hours. The ninth hour was the hour of prayer at the evening sacrifice (Acts 3:1).

Darkness in Scripture. “‘On that day,’ declares the Lord GOD, ‘I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight. I will turn your feasts into mourning … I will make it like the mourning for an only son’” (Amos 8:9–10). Darkness at noon, at a feast, mourning for an only son: Amos said it eight hundred years before. And at the first Passover a darkness to be felt came before the night the firstborn died (Exodus 10:21–23); it comes before the Firstborn dies again. In the Bible darkness at midday is never scenery. It is the sign of God’s judgment, the day of the LORD, and here that judgment falls on Jesus. The mockers demanded to see (v. 32); God’s answer is darkness, and Mark records no voice in it. Whatever passed between the Father and the Son in those hours happened where nobody could watch.

Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani? Out of the dark comes the loudest sound of the day. For a crucified man every word cost an agonising push upwards to breathe; this is not a whisper but a shout. Mark keeps the Aramaic Jesus spoke, as with Talitha cumi, Ephphatha and Abba (5:41; 7:34; 14:36): the actual sound of his voice, and the only words from the cross that Mark records.

My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? There are no darker words in Scripture. It is Psalm 22:1, the psalm that has been surfacing all chapter, now spoken aloud by the one it was written about. Jesus, who always called God Father, Abba (14:36), now says “my God”, the only time in the Gospels he addresses his Father as anything but Father (Matthew 27:46 records the same cry). He is not losing faith; he still says “my God”, twice, claiming as his own the One he can no longer feel. But he experiences what no one else ever has: being forsaken by God. Why?
