Because he was bearing our sin. God made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21); he became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The holy God turns away from sin, and Jesus, bearing it, experienced the abandonment sinners deserve, the essence of hell: separation from the favour of God. He endured it in the place of his people, so that they would never be forsaken. This is penal substitution: Jesus bore the penalty our sins deserved, in our place, so that it is not left for us to bear (Isaiah 53:5–6).

Psalm 22. Quoting a psalm’s first line brought the whole psalm to mind. It moves from abandonment (vv. 1–21), through mockery (vv. 7–8), pierced hands and feet (v. 16, where the standard Hebrew text reads “like a lion” and the ancient Greek translation reads “pierced”) and the dividing of garments (v. 18), to victory and praise: “all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD” (vv. 22–31). Its last words are “he has done it.” Jesus’ cry is real abandonment, but it is the cry of one who knows the end of the psalm.

A darkness that gave no answer. From before the foundation of the world the Son had known nothing but the Father’s delight, and at three in the afternoon he cried “my God” into a darkness that gave no answer. That silence was the silence our sins deserved, and he took the whole of it. The Father hid his face from the Son; and because he hid it there, he will never hide it from us, and has made the word Abba safe in the mouth of every sinner who trusts him.

What it does not mean. Not that the Trinity was broken, or that the Father stopped loving the Son. The Father was never more pleased with him than in this act of obedience (John 10:17; Ephesians 5:2). The Son, in his human nature, bore the Father’s wrath against sin and lost all sense of his favour, yet remained the beloved Son, and God, through every moment of the dark. What he lost was the comfort of his Father’s presence, not his Father’s love or his own deity. The mystery is beyond us; the fact is clear: he was forsaken so that we would be accepted. Timothy Keller often pointed out that the deeper a relationship, the more it hurts to lose it: an acquaintance’s coldness stings, but a spouse’s abandonment can crush you. The Son had known the Father’s delight from all eternity, so the loss of its comfort was an agony beyond our measuring.

In everyday life. Read Psalm 22 slowly this week, all thirty-one verses, and notice how much of this chapter is in it, and how it ends. Then, when you next sin, do not tell yourself it is small. Look at the darkness at noon, hear the cry, and know what it cost, and that it is paid.

What if I feel forsaken by God? Then pray as he did: “my God”, to the God you cannot feel. Real God-forsakenness, with its full weight, has already been entered by the Son, so that it would never fall on you. A believer may feel abandoned, as the psalmists often did, but is never actually forsaken; “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5) was bought with this cry. Keep praying, even if all you can say is “why”. Keep going to his people and his word. The darkness is not proof that he has let go; the cross is proof that he never will.

Is it fair to punish the innocent for the guilty? It would be unjust if God seized an unwilling third party and punished him for someone else’s crime. That is not the cross. The one who bears the sin is God the Son, the Judge himself, who came willingly (John 10:18) and stands as head of the people he dies for, as Adam stood for the human race (Romans 5:18–19). In his own Son God bore the cost of his own justice, so that he is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). At the cross justice and love do not compete; they meet.

Did Jesus descend into hell? The Apostles’ Creed says he “descended into hell”, and Christians have understood the phrase in different ways. Scripture does not teach that he went to a place of torment after death; he told the dying thief, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), and committed his spirit to the Father (Luke 23:46). Calvin and the Heidelberg Catechism (Q. 44) take the phrase to mean the hellish agony he suffered in soul on the cross, above all in this cry. Others understand it as his remaining under the power of death until the third day (Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 50). Either way, the hell he entered was the forsakenness of these hours, and he entered it so that we never will.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m. Jesus cries out in Aramaic the opening words of Psalm 22.

parallels.desc: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
I will make the sun go down at noon

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the bystanders hearing it said, "Behold, he is calling Elijah." And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bystanders take his cry for a call to Elijah, and someone gives him sour wine to keep him alive a little longer, to see whether Elijah will come. To the end he is misunderstood and watched as a spectacle.

He is calling Elijah. They mishear, or deliberately misunderstand: Eloi sounds like Eliyahu, and popular belief seems to have held that Elijah came to help the righteous in trouble. The cry of the Son bearing our sin is taken for a superstitious call for help, as all through this Gospel the crowd hears the words and misses the meaning (8:28).

Sour wine. Cheap vinegary wine, the drink of soldiers and labourers, kept at the site for the squad. Not the drugged wine of verse 23, which he refused, but a mouthful for a man dying of thirst, and somebody ran. John records that Jesus said “I thirst” and received it (John 19:28–30). It is also Psalm 69:21: “for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.”

Let us see whether Elijah will come. The reason turns the kindness into something else: keep him going a little longer and see whether anything happens. The whole crowd has become an audience waiting for an ending.

The irony. Elijah had already come. Jesus had said so: “Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased” (9:13), meaning John the Baptist, beheaded for telling a king the truth, and nobody rescued him either. There was never going to be a rescue, because rescue was never the plan: he had come to die.

Was the man with the sponge being kind or cruel? Perhaps both, as people often are. He ran, which suggests pity; the words that follow sound like curiosity and mockery, and in Mark they may come from him or from those around him. We need not decide. Even this small act fulfilled Scripture, and Jesus, who refused the anaesthetic, accepted the drink. He thirsted truly, as a man, so that he could give living water to all who thirst (John 7:37). No kindness done to him, however mixed, went unnoticed.
verseByVerse.note: Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank.

parallels.desc: for my thirst they gave me sour wine

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus dies with a loud cry, not drained of life but laying it down, his work finished.

A loud cry. This is not how crucified men die, and the centurion in the next verse knows it. Death came when a man had no strength left to push himself up for another breath; near the end even speech was a struggle. He shouted. John tells us what: “It is finished” (John 19:30), tetelestai, it is complete, the debt settled. Luke gives the words that came with it, from Psalm 31:5: the Son committing his spirit into his Father’s hands (Luke 23:46). That is not a man dying of exhaustion. It is a man finishing something.

He breathed his last. A real death, of a real man: the Son of God died. He had come to give his life as a ransom (10:45), and nobody took it. Crucified men often took days to die, and Pilate was surprised he had died so soon (v. 44). His suffering before the cross had been terrible, but his early death also shows that he laid down his life when the work was done.

Like a conqueror ending a battle. His death is not the moment the Romans finally overcame him but the last act of his freedom, at three o’clock in Passover week, a few hundred yards from the temple where the lambs had been killed. He did not die as Rome’s victims died, the last strength drained out of him; he died with a shout, like a conqueror ending a battle, and the record of debt that stood against us was cancelled (Colossians 2:14). Nothing he finished that afternoon has ever needed finishing again. And in that same instant, in that temple, a curtain tore.

What does his finished work mean for me? That there is nothing left to pay. Everything needed to forgive your sins and bring you to God was completed on the cross: the law fully obeyed, the penalty fully borne, God’s holy anger against sin fully met, not ignored or softened, so that none of it remains for those who are in Christ (Romans 8:1). You cannot add to it by good works, sacraments, suffering or religious effort, and you do not need to. The gospel calls you not to achieve but to receive. When your conscience accuses you, do not answer it with your record; answer it with his receipt.

In everyday life. Stop trying to finish what Christ finished: a forgiven person is not on probation. Your obedience will stay patchy to the end; his was finished and is counted as yours (2 Corinthians 5:21), so your faltering work is accepted for his sake. And if you fear death, for yourself or someone you love, his last words, “Father, into your hands”, can be yours too.

Where did Jesus go when he died? His body lay in the tomb; his human soul went to the Father: “into your hands I commit my spirit”, and “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43, 46). He did not cease to exist, sleep unconsciously or pass through a place of purging. So it is for every believer who dies: absent from the body, at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), consciously with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), awaiting the resurrection of the body. The death of Jesus has turned the death of his people into a homecoming.

verseByVerse.quote: And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the instant Jesus dies, God himself tears the temple curtain from top to bottom: the way into his presence is open, through the death of his Son.

The curtain of the temple. Probably the inner curtain before the Most Holy Place, God’s throne room (see the note on the wording below), which Jewish tradition says was about 60 feet (18 m) high and as thick as a man’s hand. It was a locked door made of cloth. Behind it no one went, except the high priest, once a year, on the Day of Atonement, and never without blood (Leviticus 16:2; Hebrews 9:7). For well over a thousand years it said one thing: sin has separated a holy God from unholy people, and you cannot come in on your own terms. It was a mercy as well as a barrier, for God’s holiness is a burning majesty that sin cannot survive. So the tearing does not mean that God became less holy that afternoon. It means a sacrifice had been offered that makes sinners fit to come in.

Was torn in two. Not three days later at the resurrection, but the instant he died. The verb is the one Mark used when the heavens were torn open at Jesus’ baptism (1:10), and he uses it only these two times: heaven ripped open at the start, the veil at the finish, and between them the whole ministry.

From top to bottom. Men would have started at the bottom, where hands reach. This one opened from the top: Mark’s way of telling you whose hands did it. The way into God’s presence was not forced open from our side but torn open from his. The most exclusive room in the world was opened to everybody at three o’clock on a Friday afternoon, and the man who opened it did it by dying. The God who once said “keep out” now says “come in”, and the hand that tore the veil is the hand of a Father running to meet his children.

Its meaning. Two things together. First, access: we may enter the holy places with confidence by his blood, by the new and living way he opened through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). His body was torn so the veil could be. Second, judgment: the temple and its sacrifices are finished, as Jesus foretold (13:2). The place where God meets sinners is now Christ himself.

In everyday life. When you pray tonight, an ordinary person with an ordinary week’s failures behind you, there is no queue, no annual appointment, no priest to send in on your behalf: the blood has been shed and the door is off its hinges. Pray boldly, about large things and small, and do not hang back as if the curtain were still there.

Do we still need priests to come to God? No. Every believer has direct access to the Father through Christ, our one great high priest (Hebrews 4:14–16; 1 Timothy 2:5). Pastors and elders teach, shepherd and pray for the church, and we should honour them, but they are not mediators and offer no sacrifice. The whole church is a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9), offering spiritual sacrifices of praise and service. You need no one’s permission to pray, confess or draw near.

Does the torn curtain mean anyone can come to God any way they like? No; that would turn its meaning upside down. The curtain was torn at the moment of Christ’s death because his death is the way through it. The access is open to all, but through his flesh, by his blood, and in no other way: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). The door is wide open, and it has one name on it.

Uncertain wording. The temple had two great curtains: one at the entrance of the Holy Place, and an inner one before the Most Holy Place. Mark says only “the curtain of the temple”, and the word is used of both. Most take it to be the inner curtain, the one that barred the way to God’s presence, as Hebrews suggests (Hebrews 10:19–20); if it was the outer one, many more people would have seen it torn. The meaning is the same either way: the barrier is down, and God has removed it.
verseByVerse.note: The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple; only the high priest entered, once a year.

parallels.desc: a new and living way through the curtain

verseByVerse.quote: And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, "Truly this man was the Son of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watching how Jesus dies, the Roman officer in charge of the execution confesses him the Son of God.

The centurion, who stood facing him. A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers, and this one was in charge of the execution: a professional, a Gentile and a pagan, who had very likely supervised many crucifixions. He stood in front of the cross, close enough to see a man’s face, for six hours.

In this way. What convinced him was not a miracle but the way this man died: the refused wine, the silence under mockery, the absence of cursing, the prayer in the dark, and a shout from a man who should not have had breath for a whisper. He had watched men die before and had never seen anything like it.

Truly this man was the Son of God! The climax of Mark’s Gospel, the sentence the whole book has been travelling towards. It opened with “the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1). (A few early manuscripts lack “the Son of God” there, but most, including some of the oldest, have it.) Since then the title has been spoken by the Father (1:11; 9:7) and shrieked by demons (3:11; 5:7), but no human being in fifteen chapters has said it. Peter got as far as “You are the Christ” and then argued about the cross. The first person in this Gospel to call Jesus of Nazareth the Son of God is not a disciple, not a Jew, but a Roman execution officer, at the cross.

The secret revealed. All through Mark, Jesus silenced those who would announce him. Now the secret is out. He can be proclaimed as Son of God, because the cross shows what that means: not a conqueror who takes life, but one who gives his life as a ransom for many. You learn who Jesus is by watching him die. Not by the healings; the crowds saw those and stayed baffled. Not by the teaching; the scribes heard it and planned a murder. At the cross, where he looks least like the Son of God, a human being finally sees it. He reveals his glory most clearly where it is most hidden, in weakness, shame and death.

The wall has been leapt. The confession comes from a foreigner, an occupier, a man outside God’s covenant people and without the Scriptures, at the very hour the chief priests stand jeering. The emperor’s coins called him divi filius, son of a god; a Roman soldier gives the title to a crucified Jew instead. The nations are coming in, and the first of them stands in front of a cross with blood on his boots.

Did the centurion become a Christian? Scripture does not tell us, and we should not pretend to know. Luke records that he praised God and said, “Certainly this man was innocent!” (Luke 23:47). The question for the reader is not whether the centurion was saved, but whether we will make his confession our own, with all that it means.

Uncertain wording. The Greek has no “the” before “Son of God”, so some translate “a son of God”: a Roman might have meant only a divine man or a hero, and “was”, past tense, speaks of a dead man. The centurion may have understood less than he said. But a title placed before the verb, as here, often lacks the article in Greek, so “the Son of God” is a fair translation, and Mark records the words as the confession his whole book has been building towards (1:1). Whatever the centurion understood, Mark wants us to hear the full confession.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the men have fled, women who had followed and served Jesus since Galilee stay and watch him die, and Mark names them as witnesses.

Women looking on from a distance. Mark has said little about them for fifteen chapters; now, when everyone else has gone, he tells you they were there. “From a distance” is the phrase used of Peter (14:54), but Peter kept his distance for safety; theirs was probably as near as the soldiers allowed, and at one point some stood by the cross itself (John 19:25). There was nothing they could do, and they stayed to the end.

Mary Magdalene, Mary and Salome. Named witnesses, whom anyone in the early church could find and question. Mary Magdalene, from Magdala on the Sea of Galilee, had seven demons cast out of her (Luke 8:2), and she will be the first to see him alive (John 20:11–18; also 16:9, in the longer ending of Mark, which the earliest manuscripts lack). She was not the sinful woman of Luke 7, as later Western tradition assumed without evidence. Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses is identified by her sons, presumably because the church knew them; she was perhaps the wife of Clopas (John 19:25). Salome was probably the mother of James and John (Matthew 27:56); if so, the woman who once asked for the best two seats in the kingdom for her sons (Matthew 20:20–21) is watching what those seats cost, with two rebels occupying them.

They followed him and ministered to him. “Followed” is this Gospel’s word for discipleship (1:18), used of women without comment in a world where a rabbi did not normally have female disciples. “Ministered” is the word of the angels in the wilderness (1:13) and of his mission: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (10:45). They provided for him out of their means (Luke 8:3), and nobody wrote down what it cost them.

Many other women. Mark has arranged the contrast. The twelve are not in this chapter: one sold him, one denied him with oaths, and the rest, who swore they would die with him (14:31), are probably hiding in the city. The women watched him die, watched where he was buried, and will be at the tomb at dawn on Sunday with spices they will not need. The witnesses who link the cross, the burial and the empty tomb are women, in a culture where a woman’s testimony carried little weight in court: a writer making the story up would hardly have built it this way.

The Servant served. They gave him bread and money; he gives them his life. They can do nothing at the cross but look, and looking is what the cross asks of sinners: “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth!” (Isaiah 45:22; John 3:14–15).

In everyday life. Thank God for the faithful women in your church, and tell one of them this week, specifically, what her quiet service has meant. Service no one notices is noticed by Christ.

What does this teach about women in the church? That women are full and honoured disciples of Jesus, faithful when men failed, and chosen by God as the first witnesses of the resurrection; the church that forgets this has forgotten its own foundation. Scripture also assigns the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the church to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), a pattern this commentary holds, with Jesus himself, who chose twelve men as apostles. Paul grounds it in creation (1 Timothy 2:13), not in the customs of his day. Many faithful Christians read these passages differently and welcome women as pastors, and they are to be respected as brothers and sisters in Christ. The pattern is a difference of calling, not of worth, and never a licence to belittle women. Some of the most faithful service in every church is done by women whose names only Christ records.
verseByVerse.note: Salome may be the mother of James and John, named in Matthew as “the mother of the sons of Zebedee.”

parallels.desc: the women who provided for him

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus truly died and was truly buried, in a known tomb and before witnesses, and it took courage to bury him. Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council that condemned him, asks Pilate for the body on the day when association with Jesus could only cost him (vv. 42–43). Pilate, surprised that he is already dead, has the centurion confirm it (vv. 44–45). A linen shroud, a grave cut in rock, a stone rolled across the entrance, and two women watching where he is laid: the place is marked for Sunday morning (vv. 46–47).
verseByVerse.theology: The burial is evidence, not a postscript. In six verses Mark establishes four facts: he was really dead (vv. 44–45); he was buried in a known tomb; it was closed with a stone; and the place was witnessed (vv. 46–47). There is no room in this account for a faint mistaken for death, a visit to the wrong tomb or a grave nobody could find.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John tells us Joseph had been a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews (John 19:38), and he came out on the Friday afternoon (on the timing, see “Took courage” in the note on vv. 42–43).

Now: if you have been quiet about Christ for a long time and are waiting for an easier moment, it does not come, and it is not supposed to. The cross that made Joseph brave is the same cross you look to, and the Spirit who made frightened disciples bold is given to you.

verseByVerse.quote: And when evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the Sabbath approaches, Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council who was waiting for God’s kingdom, takes courage and asks Pilate for the body of Jesus.

The day of Preparation. Late afternoon; the Sabbath would begin at sunset, and no burial could be done on it. The Law also required that an executed man’s body not remain all night on the tree, for “a hanged man is cursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), the verse Paul applies to this event (Galatians 3:13). Romans often left corpses hanging or threw them into a common pit, and no one has come to claim this one.

Joseph of Arimathea. Arimathea was a town in Judea, probably about 20 miles (30 km) north-west of Jerusalem. Joseph appears in all four Gospels, and only at the burial. Matthew says he was rich, a disciple of Jesus (Matthew 27:57); John says “secretly for fear of the Jews” (John 19:38).

A respected member of the council. The Sanhedrin, the body that condemned Jesus at midnight. Luke tells us he was “a good and righteous man, who had not consented to their decision and action” (Luke 23:50–51). He has a position, colleagues, a reputation and a rock-cut tomb, an expensive thing to own.

Looking for the kingdom of God. A believer’s description, like Simeon and Anna watching for God to act (Luke 2:25, 38). The word (prosdechomai) is warmer than our “waiting”: to watch for someone you expect, ready to welcome him. But look where Joseph’s waiting ended. The kingdom he had prayed for came, its King was a dead man on a cross, and Joseph’s first open act of allegiance was to take that body down. God’s reign did not arrive by overthrowing Rome. It arrived by the King bearing the curse for his people.

Took courage. To ask for the body of a man executed for treason was to identify yourself with him before both Pilate and the council, and Jesus’ family was not there to ask. The timing is what is remarkable. Joseph does not come out on Sunday, when the tomb is empty, or on the day of the entry, when it would have cost nothing. He declares himself on the Friday afternoon, when Jesus is a dead criminal, the twelve have vanished, and association means ruin. Fear of his colleagues had kept him silent; now the disciples had fled, and Joseph came out of hiding. Jesus had openly borne shame for Joseph, and that broke Joseph’s fear of bearing shame for Jesus.

Waiting now. Everyone is looking for some kingdom, a settled career or the day life is finally under control, and whatever you are watching for will run your life. The kingdom has come in Christ and is not yet complete, so believers live “waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13), the same verb Mark uses of Joseph. In practice that means praying “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10) and then doing one thing this week that only makes sense if it is coming, such as owning Christ where it will cost you. See also Kingdom of God in the Theological Dictionary.

Is a secret believer a real Christian? He may be, for a time, as Joseph and Nicodemus were. Faith can be real and still timid, and Jesus does not break a bruised reed. But faith is not meant to stay hidden: “whoever is ashamed of me and of my words … of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed” (8:38), and “with the mouth one confesses and is saved” (Romans 10:10). The normal way to confess him is baptism and joining his church. If you have believed quietly for a long time, Joseph’s story is not permission to stay hidden but a summons to come out, and a promise that the cross will give you courage.

How can Friday afternoon to Sunday morning be three days? Jews counted any part of a day as a day, so “after three days” and “on the third day” name the same span (compare Esther 4:16 with 5:1). Even “three days and three nights” (Matthew 12:40) is a way of saying three days, not a count of seventy-two hours. Mark is plain that Jesus died on the day before the Sabbath, not on a Wednesday or Thursday as some have argued. When John calls this Friday “the day of Preparation of the Passover” (John 19:14), that most likely means the Friday of Passover week, the preparation for that week’s Sabbath, exactly as Mark explains the term here (see 14:12).
verseByVerse.note: The day of Preparation was Friday, the day before the Sabbath. Arimathea was a town of Judea. Bodies of the crucified were often left unburied.

parallels.desc: not left on the tree overnight

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died. And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before he releases the body, Pilate has a Roman officer confirm that Jesus is really dead. Mark records it because everything depends on it.

Pilate was surprised. A professional’s surprise. Crucifixion was designed to be slow, and victims could last a day or more; soldiers sometimes broke the legs to hasten it, as they did to the two men beside him (John 19:32). Six hours was fast enough to be worth checking.

Summoning the centurion. Pilate does not take Joseph’s word for it. He sends for the officer commanding the detail, very probably the man who has just confessed Jesus as the Son of God.

He learned from the centurion. The body is not released until a professional soldier has confirmed the death to the governor’s face. That closes the door on the claim, made since the eighteenth century, that he only fainted and revived in the tomb (the swoon theory); John adds that a soldier pierced his side, and blood and water came out (John 19:34). Any such theory must get past a Roman officer’s report, and then explain how a man scourged and crucified rolled away the stone from inside and convinced terrified men that he was the risen Lord of life.

He granted the corpse to Joseph. Elsewhere the body is called a body. Here Mark uses ptōma, a corpse, the blunt word he used once before, of John the Baptist (6:29). He is being exact: what Joseph carried down was a dead man, with a Roman officer’s word on it and a governor’s release.

The Author of life became a corpse. He did not look into death from the doorway; he went all the way in, the cold, still, certified way every one of us will go. And because death had him completely, his rising is complete: not a recovery but a conquest, death beaten on its own ground.

Why does it matter so much that Jesus really died? Because a Saviour who did not die could not pay the penalty of death, and a resurrection without a death is no resurrection at all. “The wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23), and he received those wages in full in our place. And death, the enemy every one of us will face, needs a Lord who has been there and come back. Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3–4): every link matters. If he only fainted, your grave is as final as it looks. Because he truly died and truly rose, it is not.
verseByVerse.note: Crucified men often lingered for days; a death within hours surprised Pilate.

parallels.desc: the soldiers find him already dead

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph bought a linen shroud, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph wraps the body in linen and lays it in a rock tomb closed with a stone, and two women watch where he is laid. The Lord lies in a known grave, with witnesses ready for Sunday.

A linen shroud. Fine linen, bought quickly before the shops closed for the Sabbath. The word is sindōn: a chapter ago a young man fled the garden leaving his linen cloth behind (14:51–52). One man abandoned his linen to get away from Christ; another bought linen to wrap him in.

Taking him down. Somebody had to draw the nails, take the weight of the body and wrap it, and it was a member of the Sanhedrin, on the eve of the Sabbath, making himself unclean for a week by handling a corpse (Numbers 19:11). John adds that Nicodemus, another member of the council, brought about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (John 19:39). Two members of the council that condemned him are the only men in Jerusalem attending to his body. It was done in haste; the women would come to complete the anointing (16:1).

A tomb cut out of the rock. Wealthy families had chambers carved into the limestone hillsides around Jerusalem (see tombs). This was Joseph’s own new tomb (Matthew 27:60), where no one had yet been laid, in a garden near the place of crucifixion (John 19:41–42), so there could be no confusion about which body was there. Joseph gives away his own grave. Executed among criminals, buried in a rich man’s tomb: both halves of Isaiah 53:9 happened on the same afternoon.

He rolled a stone. Heavy work, which is why the women will worry about it on Sunday (16:3–4); Matthew adds a seal and a guard (Matthew 27:62–66). It is the last thing anybody does for Jesus of Nazareth: a stone across a door, and then everyone goes home because the sun is going down.

Saw where he was laid. Two women stay in the fading light and note which tomb it is, so on Sunday morning they would not go to the wrong one. Mark makes the same women witnesses of the death (v. 40), the burial (v. 47) and the empty tomb (16:1): “crucified, dead and buried”, as the creed has it.

The silence of Friday night. The King of the Jews is dead, the body in a borrowed grave, the disciples hiding, the women walking home in the dark. Everyone who loved him believed that night that it was finished. They were right, but not as they thought: his saving work was finished, not his life. He had told them three times that he would rise after three days, and not one of them acted as if they remembered.

He made the grave a bed. He who rested on the seventh day when the world was made rested that Sabbath in the rock, the work of redemption finished. He went down into the place of our deepest fear and made it a bed: since that night, a believer’s grave is only a room where the body rests until its Lord calls it. The stone across his door was already waiting for the morning.

Why does the burial matter? It confirms the death and makes the resurrection unmistakable: a known body in a known tomb, sealed and watched, and found empty. It also means that Jesus has gone where all his people go, and sanctified the grave by lying in it. The bodies of believers, being still united to Christ, rest in their graves till the resurrection (Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 37). At the grave of a believer you stand where the Lord himself lay, and it is not the end of the story any more than this tomb was.

How should I live on the Fridays of life? As people who know that Sunday is coming, even when we cannot feel it. The women did the next faithful thing: they watched, went home, kept the Sabbath and prepared spices. They did not understand, but they did not leave. When God seems silent and his cause looks buried, keep to the ordinary means of faithfulness, worship, prayer and service, and wait. The darkest Friday in history was followed by the brightest morning, and the God who did that has not changed.
verseByVerse.note: Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone, often disc-shaped, rolled into a groove.

15.theology: The curtain (v. 38) may be the most important sentence in the book. For centuries it said that sinners could not come into God’s presence on their own terms. It was torn at the instant he died, and torn from the top (on what that means, and on the heavens torn at the baptism, see the note on v. 38).
15.examples:
Then: what convinced the centurion was not a wonder but how Jesus died (see the note on v. 39).

Now: that is still where people learn who Jesus is. If you want a friend to see him, do not first reach for wonders or arguments; take them to the cross, and let them watch him die.

keyVerse.quote: And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”
keyVerse.note: This is the confession Mark’s whole Gospel has been travelling towards since its first line (1:1), and the first time a human being makes it. It comes not at a miracle but at the cross, from a Gentile who had watched how Jesus died. Mark wants every reader to learn who Jesus is in the same place.

15.reflection:
Pilate knew Jesus was innocent (vv. 10, 14) yet handed him over, “wishing to satisfy the crowd” (v. 15). Where are you most tempted to do what you know is wrong because other people’s pressure is rising, and how does it help to know that Christ stood under that pressure for you?

Barabbas walked free because Jesus was condemned in his place, and he contributed nothing to it. How does his release picture what Christ has done for you? What difference does it make that you contribute nothing either?

Passers-by, priests and robbers all said the same thing: “save yourself, and come down from the cross” (vv. 30–32). Why did Jesus stay on the cross? Where do you hear the same voice inviting you to follow him without a cross?

The cry of verse 34, the torn curtain (v. 38) and the centurion’s confession (v. 39) come within a few verses of each other. What do they teach about what Jesus’ death achieved, and how should that shape the way you pray and the way you speak of him to others?

16.title: He Has Risen; He Is Not Here
16.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him. <sup>2</sup>And very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb. <sup>3</sup>And they were saying to one another, “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” <sup>4</sup>And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large. <sup>5</sup>And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed. <sup>6</sup>And he said to them, “Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. <sup>7</sup>But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.” <sup>8</sup>And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. <sup>9</sup>Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. <sup>10</sup>She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. <sup>11</sup>But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it. <sup>12</sup>After these things he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country. <sup>13</sup>And they went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. <sup>14</sup>Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen. <sup>15</sup>And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. <sup>16</sup>Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned. <sup>17</sup>And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; <sup>18</sup>they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover.” <sup>19</sup>So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. <sup>20</sup>And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.
16.overview:
Where we are. This is the last page of Mark, the morning after the Sabbath on which Jesus lay in the tomb. Since the hinge of the book at 8:31 everything has pointed here: the Son of Man must be killed, “and after three days rise again.”

The message. The crucified Jesus is risen, exactly as he said, and he is calling his scattered, failed followers back to himself, Peter by name. The resurrection is not a feeling or an idea but an event at a place that can be pointed to: “He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him.” And because he lives, the gospel Mark called a “beginning” (1:1) runs on, carried by people who at first could not even speak of it.

Why it was said. Mark’s first readers knew fear and failure: under Nero believers were betrayed, some died, and some no doubt denied the faith (see the introduction). A Gospel that ends with frightened witnesses and a message sent to the man who denied Jesus speaks straight to them.

How the chapter makes its case. Three women set out to finish a burial, worried only about a stone too heavy to move (vv. 1–4): nobody wanted a resurrection so badly that they imagined one. Inside, a young man in white announces it, invites them to inspect the empty place, and sends word to the disciples “and Peter” (vv. 5–7). The women flee and say nothing, for they are afraid (v. 8), and there the oldest manuscripts end. Verses 9–20, printed in brackets, were very probably added early by another hand (see the notes on v. 8 and vv. 9–11). They gather appearances told elsewhere, each met with unbelief until Jesus confronts it (vv. 9–14), the commission to the whole creation with its signs (vv. 15–18), and the ascension, as the disciples go out and preach everywhere, the reversal of verse 8 (vv. 19–20).

Where it leads. The one who rose is still “Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified”: the cross is not undone but vindicated, his sacrifice accepted by the Father (Romans 4:25). The shepherd who was struck goes ahead of his scattered flock to Galilee, as he promised before any of them fell (14:27–28). And the prisoner who told Caiaphas he would be seen “seated at the right hand of Power” (14:62) sits there now, working with those he sends.

For us. Mark leaves every reader at the empty tomb with the question the women faced: will fear keep you silent? And if you have failed him, put your own name where Peter’s stands. He has risen, and he is asking for you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The crucified Jesus is risen, just as he said, and he is calling his failed disciples back. Three women go to finish a burial, worried only about a stone too heavy for them, and find it already rolled back (vv. 1–4). Inside, a young man in white announces the resurrection, invites them to see the empty place, and sends word to the disciples, adding Peter by name (vv. 5–7). They run and say nothing, for they are afraid (v. 8). That is where the oldest manuscripts of this Gospel stop, and the question it raises is dealt with plainly in the notes.
verseByVerse.theology: Why is 16:9–20 in brackets, and can I trust my Bible? Before verse 9 the ESV notes in square brackets that some of the earliest manuscripts do not include these verses, and Mark very probably did not write them. The evidence is set out in the textual note at v. 8 and in the note on vv. 9–11, which also answers whether this should unsettle your confidence in the Bible.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: tell his disciples and Peter (v. 7): the first message from the other side of the grave names the man who had denied him (see the note on v. 7).

Now: if you have failed badly enough to wonder whether there is a road back, the answer is in those two words (see “Have I failed too badly to be called back?” in the note on v. 7).

verseByVerse.quote: When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him. And very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women who watched Jesus die and saw where he was laid go back to finish his burial, expecting to find a body. Nobody in the story is hoping for a resurrection; love is simply doing the last thing it can.

When the Sabbath was past. Jesus died at about three on Friday and was buried in haste before sunset (15:42–47). Then came the Sabbath, the longest day of his friends’ lives, and Mark says nothing about it at all. It ended at sunset on Saturday, when the shops could open again.

Bought spices. The same women stood at the cross (15:40), and two of them, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary (see the Marys of the Gospels), watched the burial (15:47): named witnesses who saw him die, saw where he was laid, and now go back to the same tomb.

To anoint him. Fragrant oils for the body, an act of love and honour, to finish a burial done racing the sunset. So not one of them expected a resurrection, though he had told them three times (8:31; 9:31; 10:34). They did not want one so badly that they imagined it: the story begins with his friends buying ointment for a dead man.

The first day of the week. Very early, and yet with the sun up: most likely they set out in the dark (John 20:1) and arrived as the sun rose. Within a generation Christians were meeting on that day (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2), which John very probably calls the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10). The Sabbath commemorated God’s rest after the first creation; the Lord’s Day celebrates the beginning of the new. The Sabbath had rested over a sealed tomb; the first day broke over an empty one.

Anointed already. Their spices will never touch him: a woman at Bethany had anointed him for burial days before (14:3–8). They are carrying gifts for a funeral to the one person in history who will never need one again.

In everyday life. Every Lord’s Day is the risen Lord’s gift: plan your week around it rather than squeezing it into the gaps. Prepare on Saturday night as these women prepared their spices: go to bed in good time, pray for the preaching, decide whom you will welcome. And when you wake on Sunday, say first: “he is risen.”

Why did no one remember that he had said he would rise? Grief and unbelief are deafening, and what he said did not fit what they expected of a Messiah. Each time he foretold his death and resurrection, the disciples argued, misunderstood or were afraid to ask (8:32; 9:32): they heard the death and could not hear the rising. Many of us forget God’s promises the moment trouble comes. That is why Scripture keeps saying “remember”, and why the angel will soon say, “just as he told you.”

Where Christians differ: is Sunday the Christian Sabbath? Many, following the Westminster and 1689 London Baptist Confessions, hold that the Sabbath command still stands and has moved to the first day; others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10). This commentary’s view: the second fits the New Testament best: the Lord’s Day is his gift, gladly set apart for worship and rest, and no one may bind another believer’s conscience over it (Romans 14:5), though gathering with God’s people each week is not optional.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown on Saturday; the first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were saying to one another, "Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?" And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women worry all the way about a stone they cannot move, and find that God has already moved it.

Who will roll away the stone for us? The tense is continuous: they kept saying it, all the way there. They had watched Joseph roll it across (15:46); it was too heavy for three women, and Matthew says it was sealed and guarded as well (Matthew 27:66). Yet they set out anyway, to do what love required without knowing how. A more calculating person stays at home until the problem is solved.

Looking up. Perhaps the tomb was up a slope, or they had walked with their heads down in grief. “Had been rolled back” names nobody: it was God’s doing. Matthew says an angel rolled it away and sat on it (Matthew 28:2).

It was very large. Mark puts the size last, as someone tells a story afterwards: “and it had been moved, and it was enormous.” His verb, “rolled”, suggests the rarer kind of stone found at the tombs of the wealthy (see Burial Customs and Tombs): a disc set in a channel, perhaps a ton or more, far easier to roll into place than out again. The stone was very large, and it was nothing to him.

Moved so the world could look in. The stone was not moved to let Jesus out; he would come through locked doors that evening (John 20:19). It was moved so the witnesses could look in. And here is the plainest comfort in the chapter: they spent the walk on a difficulty already settled. God had gone ahead of them in the dark, while they were still certain nothing had changed.

Does God always remove the obstacles I worry about? Not always as we hope. Sometimes the stone stays, and he gives strength to live beside it. But the empty tomb tells you that the greatest obstacle, death itself, is already rolled away, and nothing you face is beyond his power or outside his care. Very often the thing you rehearse at four in the morning is dealt with before you reach it; when it is not, he walks with you through it. Either way, it is right to set out in faithful love without having the solution.

verseByVerse.quote: And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Inside the tomb the women find a messenger from heaven sitting calmly where the body should be.

Entering the tomb. A rock-cut tomb of this kind had a low doorway and an outer chamber, with a shelf cut into the rock for the body. They stoop through and stand up inside a room built for the dead.

A young man in a white robe. An angel in human form, as angels often appear (Genesis 18:2; Daniel 9:21); Matthew says so plainly (Matthew 28:2–5). White is the colour of heaven and glory, like Jesus’ clothes on the mountain (9:3).

Sitting on the right side. The posture of one whose work is finished, on the side of honour, where Jesus himself now sits (v. 19). The messenger sits because the Son has finished: “after making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (Hebrews 1:3).

They were alarmed. Utterly astonished, overwhelmed with awe, the strong word used of Jesus in Gethsemane (14:33). They came for a corpse and found a living stranger.

The two young men. The phrase “a young man” (neaniskos) occurs exactly twice in Mark. The first left his linen cloth in the garden and ran away naked (14:51–52), perhaps Mark himself, putting his own worst moment into his book. One fled from Christ stripped and ashamed in the dark; the other sits in the place of death, clothed in white, with the news that Christ is risen. Whether or not Mark intended every echo, the picture is the gospel: that is the change Christ’s death and resurrection make in people.

Heaven sat down in the grave. The angel had nothing to guard and nothing to fight, only news to give, because death had nothing left to hold. The room built for an ending has become the doorway of the world’s beginning.

Why do the Gospels differ about the angels? Matthew has one angel, Luke two men in dazzling clothes (Luke 24:4), John two angels; the women and the times vary too. None says there was only one: if there were two, there was certainly one, and a writer may mention only the one who spoke. The women evidently came in more than one group. Such differences mark independent witnesses, not a story agreed in advance, and the core is the same in all four: the women came first, the tomb was empty, and the message was that he had risen. Careful believers propose different orders of events, and not every detail can be fitted together with certainty; but the differences lie at the edges of the story, not at its centre.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crucified Jesus has been raised bodily from the dead, and the empty place where he lay is there to be seen.

Do not be alarmed. He takes up the very word of the last verse and deals with their terror before he gives the news, as heaven habitually does: Zechariah, Mary, the shepherds and John on Patmos all heard “do not be afraid” (Luke 1:13, 30; 2:10; Revelation 1:17).

Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. The personal name, the village that made people take offence (6:3), and a Greek form (estaurōmenon) for a past event with lasting effect: the one who has been crucified and remains the crucified one. He will show Thomas the wounds (John 20:27). Christianity has never offered a Jesus who got past the cross, but one who went through it and is known by it for ever: “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6). The resurrection does not erase the cross; it declares that the cross achieved what he died for.

He has risen. Literally “he has been raised” (ēgerthē): God raised him (Acts 2:24; Romans 10:9). It is the Father’s public verdict on the Son, the answer to the cry from the dark: the court of heaven has overturned the court of Caiaphas (12:10). It proves that he is who he claimed to be (Romans 1:4), that death is defeated (1 Corinthians 15:54–57), and that his sacrifice was accepted, for he was raised for our justification (Romans 4:25), our acquittal in God’s court for Christ’s sake. Had God refused the sacrifice, he would still be lying dead.

He is not here. A bodily resurrection: not that his spirit lived on, or his disciples felt his presence, or his cause continues, but a claim about a physical place on a spring morning, a room the women had watched him carried into (15:47).

See the place where they laid him. The angel does what legends rarely bother to do: he invites inspection. Come and look at the shelf. John records the grave clothes still lying in place (John 20:5–7). The location was known and the authorities had soldiers: had the body still been there, they had only to produce it to end the whole movement. Instead, Matthew reports, they did not dispute the empty tomb but claimed the disciples had stolen the body (Matthew 28:11–15).

Evidence for the resurrection. Besides the empty tomb: appearances to many witnesses, including over five hundred at once, most still alive when Paul wrote (1 Corinthians 15:5–8); frightened, scattered disciples turned into bold witnesses ready to die; sceptics like James and Paul converted; and Jewish believers, raised to keep the seventh day, gathering for worship on the first. Sceptics explain each in turn, but no one explanation accounts for them all. And without the resurrection, Paul says, our faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:17).

In everyday life. When you are tempted to despair, go back in your mind to the empty shelf: your greatest enemy is already beaten. And if someone asks why you believe, do not begin with your feelings. Begin where the angel began: with Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified, and a tomb that was empty.

Could the appearances have been grief visions? Grief can give a mourner a vivid sense of someone’s presence, but it does not empty a tomb, nor come to five hundred people at once, to a sceptical brother, or to an enemy like Saul. And first-century Jews who had seen a vision would have said they had seen his spirit or his angel (Acts 12:15), not that he had been raised bodily, which none of them expected before the end of the world. The women were not imagining a presence. They were shown an empty place.

Will my risen body be like his? Yes. Christ will “transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body” (Philippians 3:21). It will be truly your body, recognisably you, as Jesus was recognisably himself, scars and all; he ate, he could be touched, he was not a ghost (Luke 24:39–43). But it will be changed: raised imperishable, in glory and in power (1 Corinthians 15:42–44), with no more sickness, ageing, disability or death. The empty tomb is God’s pledge that he does not throw away what he made. He redeems it.

verseByVerse.quote: But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Lord sends for the disciples who deserted him, and names the one who denied him, so that Peter cannot think himself left out.

Go, tell his disciples. The first commission of the new age goes to three women in a graveyard, in a culture where a woman’s testimony carried little weight: nobody inventing the story to persuade would have done that. And the men who deserted him are still “his disciples”.

And Peter. Two extra words, found only in Mark, that have comforted failing Christians ever since. Peter was one of the disciples; the word covered him. There was no need to add anything, unless heaven knew that one man in Jerusalem was certain it no longer included him. He had denied Jesus three times, with oaths and a curse on his own head, and had broken down and wept (14:71–72), and had probably spent Saturday with nothing to think about but that. And the first message from the other side of the grave has his name on the end of it. Before Peter could find his way back, Christ had sent a message to find him. Mark probably heard it from Peter himself. The risen Lord appeared to Peter personally (Luke 24:34; 1 Corinthians 15:5) and restored him publicly (John 21:15–19).

He is going before you to Galilee. Not new information but a quotation: before anybody had failed, Jesus had said, “after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee” (14:27–28). The restoration was promised before the denial, the meeting place fixed while they were still swearing they would never fall away. “Go before” is a shepherd’s picture: the struck shepherd is out in front of the scattered flock again. And Galilee, not Jerusalem where it all went wrong, but home, the boats, the place they were called in chapter 1. He takes them back to the beginning to start again.

Just as he told you. Gentle and slightly pointed: every part of this weekend had been announced in advance, and none of them had held on to it. He keeps his word even when nobody believed it.

Have I failed too badly to be called back? If Peter was not beyond it, you are not. His failure was public, repeated, sworn and at the worst possible moment, and the first message of the risen Christ named him. Christ does not restore only those whose failures were small; he restores those who come back. Your feelings may say you have used up his patience; his word says, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). Put your own name after the words “and Peter”, and go to meet him where he has promised to be: in his word, in prayer, among his people.

In everyday life. Somewhere in your church is a believer who failed badly and now stays away out of shame, sure the general welcome cannot mean them. Be the messenger: send them a message this week that says, in your own words, “he is asking for you.”

But did he not appear in Jerusalem first? Yes, that Sunday and the week after (Luke 24; John 20). The meeting in Galilee followed (Matthew 28:16; John 21), and then they returned to Jerusalem to wait for the Spirit, which is where Luke’s command to stay in the city belongs (Luke 24:49). Mark points to Galilee because it was the promised meeting and the place of their calling, not because nothing happened before it.
verseByVerse.note: Peter is named: the one who had denied him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women run from the tomb shaking with awe and, for the moment, tell no one, because they are afraid. The oldest manuscripts of Mark stop here.

Trembling and astonishment. Not unbelief but overwhelming awe: trembling (tromos), and ekstasis, being beside oneself. Awe has followed his power through this Gospel from the first storm to the last morning (4:41; 5:42).

They said nothing to anyone. Matthew and Luke say they went and told the disciples (Matthew 28:8; Luke 24:9), so this was most likely a stunned silence on the road, not lasting disobedience. There is a superb irony in it: all through this Gospel, people commanded to be silent could not keep quiet (1:45; 7:36). Here, commanded to speak, the women say nothing at all.

For they were afraid. In Greek the sentence ends with the small word gar, “for”: “they were afraid, for”. It is a little like ending a book with the word “because”.

What an ending at verse 8 does. The last human beings in the book fail, for a time, to pass the message on. His people’s obedience is never complete; his was, and the empty tomb is God’s verdict that it counts for them (Romans 4:25). And the women are sent to Galilee, where chapter 1 began, so the end of the book sends the reader back to its beginning. Nothing is lost: the resurrection is stated as fact in verse 6, and the appearances are recorded by Matthew, Luke, John and Paul, whose list of witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8) was written within about twenty-five years. Mark ends with frightened women running from an empty grave, not with any doubt that it was empty.

God did not wait for brave messengers. He used frightened women, then deserting men, then a persecutor, then us. The power of the resurrection does not depend on the courage of those who carry it; it is the power of God, who still sends the news out of the mouths of the weak to the ends of the earth.

In everyday life. The women were silent at first, and the risen Lord did not give up on them; the power is his Spirit’s, not yours. Ask what keeps you quiet: fear of ridicule, or of not having answers. Then tell one person this week, simply, that you believe Jesus rose from the dead, and why.

Why were they afraid, if the news was good? Because it was too great to take in at once: the holy fear of creatures who have seen God act, not the fear of punishment. Matthew says they ran “with fear and great joy” (Matthew 28:8). A faith that has never trembled at the resurrection may not have understood it; but such fear is meant to give way to witness, as theirs did.

Textual note: the ending of Mark. The two oldest complete manuscripts of the New Testament (Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both fourth century) end Mark’s Gospel here, at verse 8. Early church writers, Eusebius and Jerome, said that most of the Greek manuscripts they knew ended here. Other manuscripts have a short ending of a sentence or two; most later manuscripts, followed by the KJV and NKJV, have the longer ending (vv. 9–20), which differs from Mark’s style and vocabulary and appears to be a summary drawn from the other Gospels and Acts. The ESV prints verses 9–20 in brackets.

Where Christians differ: did Mark end here? Some think Mark meant to end at verse 8. Others think the original ending was lost, perhaps from the end of a scroll or the last leaf of a codex, or that Mark could not finish; early tradition places him in Rome under Nero, around the time the early church remembered as Peter’s death there. This commentary’s view: the evidence is strong that verses 9–20 were not written by Mark but were added early, probably in the second century. Whether Mark meant to end at verse 8 is less certain. If he did, it is a powerful ending, leaving the reader with a question: the women were silent for fear; will you be? Mark’s Gospel began with “the beginning of the gospel” (1:1). It ends where the church’s preaching begins.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some of the earliest manuscripts end the Gospel here, and brackets verses 9–20.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The risen Lord overcomes his disciples’ unbelief himself, sends them out, and works with them from his throne. Before verse 9 the ESV notes that some of the earliest manuscripts do not include these verses; they were very probably added early by another hand, and the notes answer the question plainly. Three appearances, to Mary Magdalene, to two disciples walking into the country and to the eleven at table, are each met with disbelief until Jesus rebukes it in person (vv. 9–14). He commissions them to preach to the whole creation, with a promise of signs, including the sentence about serpents and poison that a few churches have built a deadly practice on (vv. 15–18). Then he sits down at the right hand of God, as he told the high priest he would (14:62), and the disciples do what the women of verse 8 could not (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved (v. 16) can sound, read at speed, as though baptism were half of what saves; why it is not is treated at vv. 15–16. That is why a dying thief with no water within reach could be told, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: they will pick up serpents with their hands (v. 18). On the strength of that sentence a handful of churches have handled snakes and drunk poison in their services to prove their faith, and people have died.

Now: these are among the most doubtful words in Mark, and even at face value they describe what may happen to Christ’s servants, not what they are to seek out (see the note on vv. 17–18).

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Jesus showed himself first to Mary Magdalene, a woman he had rescued from seven demons, and the grieving disciples would not believe her.

About verses 9–20. These verses are not in the earliest manuscripts and were very probably not written by Mark. They were added early and long read in the church, so our Bibles print them, in brackets. They largely summarise appearances recorded elsewhere; where they agree with the rest of Scripture they are true and useful, but no doctrine should rest on them alone. The evidence is set out below.

He appeared first to Mary Magdalene. As John 20:11–18 records. The first person on earth to see the risen Christ was not Peter, not his mother, not a priest, but a woman whose past was so wrecked that seven demons had to be cast out of her (Luke 8:2). Grace does not choose the impressive; it chooses the rescued, and nobody would invent such a first witness to impress the ancient world.

They would not believe it. On Easter Sunday the disciples are mourning and weeping, not waiting hopefully; they thought it was over. This is the first of three refusals in four verses: “these words seemed to them an idle tale” (Luke 24:11). They refused the news, and he did not refuse them.

In the flow. Verses 9–14 move in three steps, Mary, the two on the road, the eleven, and each time the news is refused until the Lord himself confronts the unbelief; then verses 15–20 send those same doubters out with the gospel. The writer is answering the fear of verse 8: the silence was not the end.

The facts, laid out plainly. The two oldest complete manuscripts, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, end Mark at verse 8, and so do some of the oldest versions in other languages. Eusebius, in the early fourth century, says the accurate copies known to him ended there; Jerome says the same a century later. Some manuscripts have a much shorter ending instead, and a few have both, which is what copyists do when they know of two and cannot decide. The Greek does not read like Mark: more than a dozen words appear nowhere else in the book. Most tellingly, verse 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as though for the first time, although she was named in verse 1. That is not how a writer refers to someone he has been following all morning. It is how a different writer begins.

The other view. Some Christians defend the longer ending as Mark’s own: it is in the great majority of manuscripts, Irenaeus quotes verse 19 around AD 180, and it seems unlikely Mark meant to end with “for they were afraid”. Their concern to lose none of God’s word is honourable. But the oldest manuscripts and the early writers who knew the evidence point the other way.

Should this unsettle my confidence in the Bible? No, for three reasons. First, nothing has been smuggled in: the appearance to Mary is in John 20, the two on the road in Luke 24, the commission in Matthew 28 and Acts 1, the ascension in Luke 24, Acts 1 and Hebrews 1:3. No doctrine of the faith stands or falls here. Second, this is what a reliable text looks like. We have thousands of New Testament manuscripts, vastly more and earlier than for any other ancient document, so we can see exactly where copyists differed, and our Bibles show it openly in the footnotes. A faith that could not survive its own manuscripts would hide them. Third, the empty tomb, the announcement of the resurrection and the promise of the appearances are all in verses 1–8, in every manuscript there is.

Why would God allow words not written by Mark into most Bibles? God has preserved his word not by making copyists infallible, but by giving his church so many copies that errors can be seen and corrected. For centuries most readers had no easy means of telling this early addition apart; now that the earlier manuscripts are known, translations mark it honestly. That is not a failure of God’s care but an example of it: he has kept the text so fully that we can see even the additions. The canon of Scripture is closed, and its message has reached us intact.
verseByVerse.note: These verses are not found in some of the earliest manuscripts; the ESV prints them in brackets. They largely summarise appearances recorded in the other Gospels.

parallels.desc: Mary Magdalene meets the risen Lord
from whom seven demons had gone out

verseByVerse.quote: After these things he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country. And they went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two more reports of the risen Jesus are refused, until he appears to the eleven themselves and rebukes their unbelief.

In another form. Luke 24 in one sentence: the road to Emmaus, where two disciples walked with him for hours and knew him at last when he broke the bread (Luke 24:13–35). Luke puts it differently: “their eyes were kept from recognizing him” (Luke 24:16). His risen body was the same, but changed and glorified (1 Corinthians 15:42–44), and Mary too took him for the gardener (John 20:15).

They did not believe them. The second refusal, and harder to fit with Luke, where the two are greeted with “The Lord has risen indeed” (Luke 24:34). Most likely faith and doubt were mixed in that room, as they still “disbelieved for joy” minutes later (Luke 24:41), and this summary stresses the doubt. It is a real difficulty, and not every question about it can be settled.

Reclining at table. The Twelve minus Judas (Luke 24:36–43; John 20:19–29), at a meal, which is where the risen Christ keeps turning up: at Emmaus, in the upper room asking for fish, on a beach in Galilee cooking breakfast.

Hardness of heart. The phrase used of the men who watched a withered hand restored and planned a murder (3:5), and of the disciples who had carried the baskets and understood nothing (6:52; 8:17). He rebuked his friends because he loved them, and then trusted them with the world.

Not easily convinced, and sent anyway. The apostles are often accused of wanting a resurrection so badly that they talked themselves into it. Every account says the opposite: they dismissed the women and the two from the road, had to be confronted in person, and even then some doubted (Matthew 28:17). And he sends them anyway: men who had run away in a garden, denied him in a courtyard and refused two reports are handed the gospel for the whole creation. He does not wait for better material. There was none, and there never has been.

In everyday life. Jesus calls blessed those who believe without seeing (John 20:29). This week, read 1 Corinthians 15:1–20 and watch Paul pile up the witnesses. Then ask whether your own unbelief, in some area of your life, is a question that wants answers or a hardness that does not want to change, and bring either one to him.

Is it a sin to doubt as the eleven did? Doubt as a struggle is not the same as unbelief as a refusal. Scripture is full of believers who wrestled: Thomas, John the Baptist in prison (Matthew 11:2–3), the father who cried, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (9:24); and Jesus met them with patience and evidence. What he rebukes here is not a mere intellectual difficulty but the hardness that will not believe credible testimony because it does not want to. So bring your doubts to him honestly, as that father did; do not nurse them as a badge of sophistication, or hide them in shame. He is able to strengthen weak faith. The eleven were rebuked not for having questions but for refusing two sets of witnesses, and once they had seen him, they became his witnesses (Acts 1:8).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Lord sends his disciples to announce the gospel to everyone, and makes faith in him the line between salvation and condemnation. Baptism is the believer’s first obedience, but it is unbelief, not the lack of water, that condemns.

Go into all the world. The commission, as also in Matthew 28:18–20, Luke 24:47 and Acts 1:8, and every phrase widens it. “Go”: the Old Testament pattern was largely that the nations would come to Zion (Isaiah 2:2–3); now the people of God are sent out. “Into all the world”: said to eleven men from one small province, with no money, organisation or standing. “Proclaim”: the herald’s word (kēryssō), to announce publicly what a king has decreed. A herald does not improve the message; he carries it: the King crucified as a rebel now sends a royal decree of pardon. “To the whole creation”: all people everywhere, and more, for the rescue is the beginning of the repair of everything (Romans 8:21–22; Ephesians 1:10). The gospel that must first be proclaimed to all nations (13:10) is now the church’s task.

Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved. Faith and baptism belong together in the New Testament: those who believed were baptised (Acts 2:41; 8:12; 16:31–33), and nobody in Acts comes to faith and then quietly declines the water. A believer who refuses baptism is refusing his Lord’s plain command.

Whoever does not believe. It does not say “whoever is not baptised”. If baptism were part of what saves, its absence would be part of what condemns, and the sentence carefully does not say so. We are saved by grace through faith, not by any work, not even a good and commanded one (Ephesians 2:8–9).

What it means to believe. Many hear “believe” as agreeing to facts, or as a feeling of confidence to be worked up, and wonder whether they have believed enough. In Scripture believing is relying on someone: putting your whole weight on Christ and what he has done. That is why faith saves and baptism does not; faith brings nothing of its own to God, it simply receives. All of us already lean on something, our record or our sincerity, and neither can hold the weight of a soul. Timothy Keller pictured it as a man falling from a cliff who grabs a branch: a strong grip on a weak branch fails, and a weak grip on a strong branch holds, because what saves is not the strength of your faith but the one it rests on, the risen Christ who says, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). So when your conscience accuses you, answer it not with how hard you have tried but with whom you are trusting. See also Faith in the Theological Dictionary.

What it does not mean. Not that baptism itself saves, or that a believer who dies unbaptised is lost; nor is this verse, from the longer ending, a foundation for any doctrine of baptism on its own. Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read Acts 2:38 and 22:16 as teaching that God gives forgiveness through baptism; but there, as here, baptism is joined to repentance and faith as their outward sign; forgiveness is given to faith (Acts 10:43).

In everyday life. The commission is yours too. Write down three people who need to hear the gospel, pray for them by name every day this week, and look for one opportunity to speak, leaning on the Spirit he promised his witnesses (Acts 1:8). And do not despise baptism, nor lean your weight on it: a confidence resting on something done to you with water rests on the sign, not on Christ, to whom it points.

Why should not believing be enough to condemn someone? Because unbelief is not an innocent lack of information but the refusal of God’s own remedy. Everyone already stands guilty for sins against the light he has (Romans 1:20; 3:23); to turn away the rescue is to stay where one already was: “whoever does not believe is condemned already” (John 3:18). God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11), which is why the warning comes wrapped in a command to go and tell everyone.

I was baptised as an infant: should I be baptised now? On the view this commentary holds (below), yes: ask to be baptised as a believer, without contempt for your parents’ love or for the many godly Christians who regard infant baptism as true baptism.

Where Christians differ: the order of believing and baptism. Paedobaptists (those who baptise infants) baptise the children of believers before faith, seeing baptism as the sign of God’s covenant promise to believers and their children, as circumcision was (Genesis 17:7; Acts 2:39). Credobaptists (believer-baptists) baptise on a credible profession of faith. This commentary’s view: this verse, like the New Testament pattern generally, places believing before baptism, which fits the credobaptist position: every baptism the New Testament describes in detail follows a profession of faith (the household baptisms are read differently by each side), and baptism pictures a union with Christ received by faith (Romans 6:3–4; Colossians 2:12). Because this verse belongs to the longer ending, the case rests on that wider pattern, not on this verse alone. It is held charitably toward brothers who differ.

verseByVerse.quote: And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Signs would accompany the message and confirm it, as Acts shows they did; they are the Lord’s doing, not feats for his servants to stage.

These signs will accompany. The signs are not the point; they follow the message and confirm it (v. 20).
