Most are found in Acts: casting out demons (Acts 16:18), tongues (Acts 2:4; 10:46), surviving a snake bite (Acts 28:3–6), healing by laying on of hands (Acts 28:8). Drinking poison unharmed is not in the New Testament. Signs confirmed the apostles’ message in the founding of the church (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12), and every one pointed away from the apostles to the risen Lord whose name they carried.

In my name. The authority is borrowed, never possessed, as the disciples forgot when they failed to cast out a demon at the foot of the mountain (9:18, 28–29). In Acts 2, at least, the new tongues were real languages, understood by people from many nations.

Serpents and poison. This sentence has done real harm. On the strength of it a handful of churches, mostly in the Appalachian mountains of the United States and rejected by almost all Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, have handled venomous snakes and drunk poison in their services to demonstrate their faith. Some have died, pastors among them, some refusing medical treatment on principle. Two things must be said. First, these are among the words whose place in Mark is most doubtful of all, and to build a dangerous practice on a text the oldest copies do not contain is unwise twice over. Second, even taken at face value, the verse describes what may happen to Christ’s servants, not what they are to go looking for. Paul, shipwrecked on Malta, was gathering firewood to warm shipwrecked strangers when a viper fastened on his hand, and he shook it into the fire unharmed (Acts 28:3–6). He did not seek it and was proving nothing; it happened while he was serving others.

The sting of death already drawn. The Lord who crushed the serpent’s head let a viper fall harmless from his servant’s hand, because the sting of death had already been drawn. The signs have done their work and the foundation is laid, but the greater wonder goes on in every new birth, as dead sinners are raised by the same power that emptied the tomb.

What it does not mean. Not a command to handle snakes or drink poison. Inviting danger to prove one believes is what Satan urged in the wilderness, quoting a promise of protection (Psalm 91:11–12), and Jesus answered, “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (Luke 4:12). Engineering a crisis to see whether he will come through, or refusing the doctor to prove one has faith, is not trust. Faith trusts God; it does not dare him.

Does God still heal today? Yes, as he wills, in answer to the prayers of his people (James 5:14–15) and through doctors and medicine, though he has not promised that every sickness will be healed in this life; every believer’s final healing is certain at the resurrection.

What about Christians I know who say they speak in tongues or prophesy? Receive them as brothers and sisters in Christ, not as suspects; many love Christ deeply, and you can hold that the apostolic sign gifts have ceased and still learn from their prayerfulness and expectancy. Where you differ, test everything by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:21), and be clear that no experience adds to the closed canon of God’s word. Speak gently, with your Bible open, and do not let it break fellowship over what is not the gospel.

Where Christians differ: do the signs continue? Pentecostal and charismatic Christians (often called continuationists) hold that the miraculous gifts, tongues and healing continue in the church today as normal, pointing to Peter’s word that the Spirit is poured out in the last days (Acts 2:17–18) and to Paul’s teaching on the gifts (1 Corinthians 12–14). Cessationists hold that the sign gifts were given to confirm the apostles and their message while the New Testament was being written, and ceased with the apostolic age. This commentary’s view: the cessationist position fits Scripture best. The signs authenticated the apostles as the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 2:3–4). God still answers prayer and still heals according to his will (James 5:14–15), but not through the apostolic sign gifts. It is held charitably toward those who differ; the question is how God works today, not whether he is at work.

verseByVerse.quote: So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is taken up and enthroned at God’s right hand, and from there he works with his disciples as they preach everywhere.

Taken up into heaven. The ascension in one sentence, forty days after the resurrection (Luke 24:50–51; Acts 1:9–11), and the last thing this book says about Jesus. “Was taken up”: the Father receives him, as Elijah was taken up (2 Kings 2:11).

At the right hand of God. Psalm 110:1, the verse Jesus quoted in the temple (12:36) and before the high priest (14:62). Bound, with the case against him in ruins, he had said, “you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power”, and they condemned him for it. Here, in one flat sentence, it has come true, within weeks of his execution for saying it.

He sat down because it was done. Priests in the temple never sat down; there were no chairs in the holy place, because the work of sacrifice was never finished. Hebrews makes the point: “every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:11–12).

They went out and preached everywhere. The book of Acts in a sentence, and the exact reversal of verse 8. It was not a change of temperament: the risen Christ stood in the room, and he poured out his Spirit. Early tradition says most of them died for it and none recanted.

The Lord worked with them. He has just sat down in heaven, and in the same sentence he is working alongside them on earth, by his Spirit: “behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). That is how things stand for the whole age of the church. The mission was never the disciples carrying on alone after Jesus left; it was, and is, his work, done through people who had recently proved entirely unreliable.

The end of Mark. Whether one reads to verse 8 or verse 20, Mark’s Gospel ends at a beginning. Its first line was “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1): sixteen chapters, from the baptism to the empty grave, are the beginning. It was carried along the roads of an empire, and it has reached you.

The beginning that has no end. The man who was greatly distressed in a garden, who cried out in the darkness, who lay as a corpse behind a stone, is seated at the right hand of God, and will never again need to offer himself. The prisoner who stood before Caiaphas is the King before whom Caiaphas will stand. The gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, has a beginning, and no end.

What does this mean for my witness? You never speak for Christ alone. When you share the gospel, pray for someone, explain your hope or serve your neighbour in his name, the Lord works with you. Results are his responsibility; faithfulness is yours. You need not be eloquent, brave by nature or theologically trained; the disciples were none of those. You need to go, tell, and trust that the King at the Father’s right hand is confirming his own word.

Where is Jesus now, and what is he doing? He is in heaven, bodily, at the right hand of the Father, the same Jesus with the same scars, now glorified. He is reigning over all things for the good of his church (Ephesians 1:20–23), until all his enemies are under his feet. He is praying for his people, and his intercession never fails (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25): he pleads his finished sacrifice before the Father, so that their acceptance never hangs on the strength of their own prayers (1 John 2:1). He is building his church by his word and Spirit. And he will come again, visibly, to judge the living and the dead and make all things new. He is not absent. He is enthroned, he is busy, and he is with you.

16.theology:
Does Mark end at verse 8? The last word is gar, “for”, and we do not know whether Mark meant to stop there (the possibilities are weighed in the box “Where Christians differ: did Mark end here?” at the end of the note on v. 8, and what such an ending does is shown in the same note).

Whatever is decided about verses 9–20, nothing in the question touches verses 1–8, which are in every manuscript there is.
16.examples:
Then: and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid (v. 8), though they had been commanded to speak (on the irony, see the note on v. 8).

Now: the last verse of the chapter is the reversal: the same frightened company went out and preached everywhere (on what changed them, see vv. 12–14 and 19–20). His Spirit still makes frightened people into witnesses.

keyVerse.quote: Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him.
keyVerse.note: This is the announcement the whole Gospel has been moving towards since Jesus first foretold his death and rising (8:31). The one who is risen is still “Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified”, so the cross is vindicated, not left behind, and the empty place is offered for inspection. Everything else in the chapter, the message to Peter, the commission and the throne, flows from this sentence.

16.reflection:
The women set out to anoint a body, worrying all the way about a stone they could not move (vv. 1–4). Why does it matter that nobody expected the resurrection? Where are you rehearsing a problem that God may already have dealt with?

The angel says, “He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him” (v. 6). If a friend asked why you believe Jesus rose from the dead, what would you say, and where would you begin?

Only Mark records the words “and Peter” (v. 7). Why do you think the risen Lord named him? Who do you know who needs to hear that the welcome includes them, and how could you tell them?

The oldest manuscripts stop at the women’s frightened silence (v. 8); the longer ending closes with the disciples preaching everywhere as the Lord worked with them (v. 20). What keeps you quiet about Jesus, and what difference does it make that the risen Lord works with those who speak?
